– Israel's downing of an unmanned drone over the weekend may have been a one-off, but it's still raising tensions. An Israeli lawmaker tweeted that the drone was an "Iranian drone launched by Hezbollah," and an Iranian military official said today that the incident showed that Israel's Iron Dome missile defense system "does not work and lacks the necessary capacity," Reuters reports. The Israeli military, which released a 10-second video of the drone's downing, says the drone had been in Israeli airspace near the Hamas-ruled Gaza Strip. Meanwhile, the Israeli army says it has struck "Hamas terror activity sites and terrorist squads responsible for the rocket fire," but gave no details, reports the AP. In related news, Palestinian officials in Gaza say an Israeli airstrike killed a militant and wounded two others today, in what Hamas says was a response to the rocket fire.

– A stolen Picasso painting worth millions of dollars was shipped to the US in a package that described it as a $37 "art craft"—but it will soon be on its way back to France, the AP reports. Federal prosecutors in Brooklyn filed papers Thursday to forfeit the century-old cubist painting, which was reported missing from a Pompidou storeroom in 2001. "A lost treasure has been found," US Attorney Loretta Lynch said in a statement. The 1911 cubist painting "La Coiffeuse," which translates to "The Hairdresser," was bequeathed to France's National Museum and was placed in storage at the Center Georges Pompidou, where staffers discovered it was missing when they received a loan request for it. It was shipped by Federal Express from Belgium in December and seized at the Port of Newark. Officials said the shipper was identified only as "Robert" and the destination was a climate-controlled storage facility in Queens. Court papers did not indicate whether the sender or intended recipient have been identified. US and French authorities have not announced any arrests in the case.

– A Dallas police officer has died from his injuries after being shot while responding to a call at a Home Depot store Tuesday afternoon, the Dallas Morning News reports. According to CBS DFW, Officer Rogelio Santander was shot in the back of the head and fellow officer Crystal Almeida was shot in the face. A store employee and a security guard also were shot in the incident, which took place in the store's loss-prevention office. The suspect fled the scene in a white truck, which was spotted on surveillance video. A police chase ensued, and the suspect was apprehended late Tuesday. He has been charged with two counts of aggravated assault against a public servant and is being held in the Dallas County Jail.

– The US Coast Guard says it's looking for a man who has cost the service about $500,000 after responding to nearly 30 of his fake distress calls, the AP reports. In a press release published Friday, the Coast Guard says the 28 calls have originated from around the area of Annapolis, Maryland. Each call involved the same male voice and used an emergency radio channel. He's been making the calls since July 2014. The two most recent calls were made on the night of July 21 and the early morning of July 22. The Coast Guard also says hoax calls distract rescuers from real emergencies, putting both the public and the responding crews at risk. "A hoax call is a deadly and serious offense," says Lt. Cmdr. Sara Wallace. "Calls like these not only put our crews at risk, but they put the lives of the public at risk." The Coast Guard provided an audio file of the caller, in which the caller repeats "mayday"—a word used to indicate distress at sea. Making false distress calls is a felony, punishable by a maximum of six years in prison, a $10,000 civil fine, $250,000 criminal fine, and a reimbursement to the Coast Guard for their efforts, the Coast Guard said.

– An erupting volcano has created a new island in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Tonga. The volcano has been erupting for a month in the ocean about 40 miles northwest of the capital, Nuku'alofa. Last week it disrupted international air travel to the Pacific archipelago for several days. New Zealand volcanologist Nico Fournier said he traveled by boat to within about a mile of the new island on Saturday to take a closer look. He said it's made mainly of loose scoria and its dimensions are about 1.1 miles by 0.9 miles, and that it rises about 109 yards above the sea. "It's quite an exciting site, you get to see the birth of an island," he tells the AP. "Visually it was quite spectacular, but there was no big sound coming with it, no boom. It was a bit eerie." He said that once the volcano stops erupting, it will likely take the ocean no more than a few months to erode the island entirely. – The number of American kids who rely on food stamps has spiked since the start of the Great Recession, according to a US Census Bureau survey released today. The number of kids who received assistance in 2014 was 16 million, or one in five of all kids, up from 9 million, or one in eight, before the recession, reports Reuters. "The rate of children living with married parents who receive food stamps has doubled since 2007," the Census Bureau says. The number of people using food stamps has almost doubled since the start of the recession, to nearly 48 million in 2013, but only dipped a little last year, to about 46 million people, reports the Washington Post. Republicans have tried to cut the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program, or food stamps, as part of a plan to balance the budget, but President Obama signed a final bill last year that cut the program by $8.7 billion over 10 years. The survey also found that more children are being raised in single-parent homes, with 27% of kids under 18 living in such homes last year, up from 9% in 1960. The median age for people first getting married in 2014 was 29 for men and 27 for women, up from 24 and 21 in 1947.

– "This is what I'm talking about!" That's how 28-year-old Rebecca King of St. Augustine, Fla., begins a video she posted to Facebook this week that has since gone viral. King, who is deaf, was ordering a drink at a Starbucks drive-thru on Tuesday when a woman's voice rang out from the intercom, per Action News Jax. "Hi, welcome to Starbucks," she says. "What can we get started for you today?" King doesn't respond, but a woman who appears on a monitor soon does. "Starbucks! This is what I'm talking about!" King writes in her post. "Share it away! We can change the world!" The video shows a barista using sign language to communicate with King, and the two quickly complete an order. "I think more people need to know about what we're doing because it moves customer service to a whole new level," the barista, Katie Wyble, tells Action News Jax. "I hope it helps make more people aware of what they can to do serve others in their communities." King, meanwhile, says she hopes the video will inspire other businesses to get on board with this new technology.

– Starting Thursday, Americans will no longer be able to swipe their credit cards at checkouts to make purchases. Instead, they'll be able to tap their cards into payment terminals to make purchases instead, the Wall Street Journal reports. The change is part of a major shift in how credit and debit cards are handled in the US, with the goal of cutting down on credit card fraud, which has more than doubled in the US over the past 15 years. According to the Tech Times, credit cards with security chips—short for Europay, MasterCard, and Visa—are more secure than magnetic strip-based cards because they contain a microprocessor that's unique for each transaction. "They can't create a counterfeit card, which is two-thirds of the fraud we see in the system," says a Visa exec. But while the new cards are more secure than magnetic strip-based cards, they'll take longer to process than their magnetic-strip counterparts and could lead to long checkout lines during high-traffic periods like Black Friday, Tech Times reports. Banks and retailers will be responsible for fraudulent transactions if their payment terminals don't have the proper equipment to process chip-enabled cards. MasterCard and Visa have set the Oct. 1 deadline for the change.

But when they heard male Maasai voices, they started gathering together, started smelling, and moved more cautiously. And when they heard young Kamba men, they started gathering together, started smelling, and moved more cautiously, too. "The ability to distinguish between Maasai and Kamba men delivering the same phrase in their own language suggests that elephants can discriminate between different languages," says a co-author of the study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. – Someone in Romania thought he'd made a few bucks by selling an old typewriter at a flea market—but he was wrong. The "typewriter" turned out to be a German Wehrmacht Enigma I cipher machine used by the Nazi military during World War II, and it sold for $51,500 at auction Tuesday, Reuters reports. The collector who bought it for just 100 euros ($114) "is a cryptography professor and ... he knew very well what he was buying," the collectible consignment manager at Artmark auction house tells Reuters. The Enigma machine was used to encrypt and decode messages sent by the various branches of the Nazi military, but the British mathematician Alan Turing and his team at Britain's wartime codebreaking center, Bletchley Park, cracked the codes, shortening the war by at least two years. Romania was an ally of Nazi Germany until 1944, when it switched sides to the allies. Historians say it may host many other cryptographic machines not yet discovered. Last month, Christie's New York Books set a world auction record of $547,500 with its sale of a "four-rotor Enigma machine, 1944."

– For the first time, scientists have successfully harvested stem cells from cloned human embryos, a breakthrough that could lead to new treatments for diseases like Parkinson's and diabetes, the AP reports. Scientists have tried to get stem cells from cloned embryos for about a decade, but they've failed generally because the embryos stopped developing before producing the cells. In 2004, a South Korean scientist claimed to have gotten stem cells from cloned human embryos, but that turned out to be a fraud. In today's edition of Cell, researchers in Oregon report harvesting stem cells from six embryos created from donated eggs. Two embryos had been given DNA from skin cells of a child with a genetic disorder, and the others had DNA from fetal skin cells. Dr. George Daley, a stem cell expert at Children's Hospital Boston who didn't participate in the work, called the new results "one landmark step in a very long journey" toward creating DNA-matched transplant tissue. Now, Daley says, scientists must compare the embryo-cloning approach with another technology that reprograms blood or skin cells directly into substitutes for embryonic stem cells. This reprogramming approach is technically simpler and doesn't involve embryos or require the donation of human eggs, and it was widely acclaimed when it was reported in 2007.

Such programs—which typically involve renting a bike from an automated station by paying a daily fee, or using a keychain token for annual members—have been spreading rapidly in recent years and can now be found in at least 40 US cities. Major cities have established large bikesharing systems, including Boston, Chicago, Denver, Minneapolis-Saint Paul, New York City, Salt Lake City, the San Francisco Bay Area, Seattle, Washington DC, and others. These systems began operating as early as 2010, and no fatalities have occurred within the US as of this writing. However, three have happened in North America—two in Canada and one in Mexico. Bikesharing has some qualities that appear inherently unsafe for bicyclists. Most prominently, helmet usage is documented to be quite low in most regions. "She's feeling great and looking forward to starting work this week on her two upcoming films." Click for more, including Zeta-Jones' thoughts on husband Michael Douglas' cancer.

– Three surfers are dead after getting caught in a rip current off a beach in Cornwall, England. Two men and a woman in their 40s were among seven people who got into trouble at Mawgan Porth beach, near the town of Newquay, around 1pm Sunday, the BBC reports. Four children who were with the group were rescued but the three adults were airlifted to a hospital in Truro, where they were pronounced dead. "It's a very sad day for us," says the manager of a local pub, who describes the children as "teenagers" who stayed with him after the incident. The beach is "not really very good for surfing and bodyboarding," the owner of a nearby surfing school tells ITV News. "The waves were bigger, they were quite big. It wasn't the safest of days to be in the sea but it wasn't particularly dangerous. There were lots of safe places to be and they were just in the wrong place at the wrong time." (A 23-year-old man drowned at the same beach on Saturday.)

– A building on Vanderbilt University's campus in Nashville will no longer be known as Confederate Memorial Hall after more than a decade of pressure from students, faculty, and administrators, the Tennessean reports. Chancellor Nicholas S. Zeppos announced Monday that the university will pay back an 83-year-old donation from the United Daughters of the Confederacy that helped build the building. "It's a symbol that is, for many people, deeply offensive and painful," Zeppos tells the newspaper. "And to walk past it or to have to live in that space is really something that I just don't think is acceptable." Vanderbilt tried to rename the building in 2002 but was thwarted by a lawsuit from the Tennessee Division of the United Daughters of the Confederacy, which claimed the original $50,000 donation was meant to honor Confederate soldiers who died in the Civil War. The state's 6th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in 2005 that Vanderbilt could remove "Confederate" from the building's inscription only after it had returned the donation at its current value. The university raised $1.2 million for the change, which will be approved by the state Board of Regents. The Daughters of the Confederacy, which filed the lawsuit, calls the move "a real slam on the history of our country."

Dash Snow, who died in 2009, started tagging high-profile locations in the 1990s, including the Brooklyn Bridge and the High Line in New York City, as part of a graffiti crew known as IRAK, reports Fashion Law. The artist's former girlfriend, Jade Berreau, is suing McDonald's for "copyright infringement, trademark infringement, unfair competition, falsification of 'copyright management information' under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, and negligence," claiming the "SACE" tag—one of Snow's signature designs—is "so prominently placed" in McDonald's that it's "the only element singled out and spotlighted in media coverage surrounding McDonald's display campaign." Berreau, who is also the administrator of Snow's estate, first asked McDonald's to remove the graffiti in June, but the chain refused, per ArtNet News. The lawsuit, filed Oct. 3 in Los Angeles, claims McDonald's is "clearly attempting to trade on Mr. Snow's name and reputation." Boehner told his lieutenants that he was already thinking about a pared-down Plan B as details of his talks with Obama leaked. One by one, top Republicans backed Plan B—and against the broader deal—because it didn't make enough changes to entitlements or tax rates. Obama told Boehner he wasn't willing to play games with the debt ceiling. "I put $800 billion [in tax revenue] on the table," Boehner told the president. "What do I get for that?" "You get nothing," the president said. "I get that for free." Obama repeatedly lost patience with Boehner as negotiations faltered. In an Oval Office meeting last week, he told Mr. Boehner that if the sides didn't reach agreement, he would use his inaugural address and his State of the Union speech to tell the country the Republicans were at fault. The negotiations offer little evidence November's election brought the president and House Republicans closer together. If anything, the talks poisoned an already distrustful relationship. – The Baltimore Ravens are mourning cornerback Tray Walker, who died Friday after a crash in Miami. Police say the 23-year-old was riding a motor bike Thursday night when he collided with a Ford Escape, WBAL reports. Walker wasn't wearing a helmet at the time. Police don't suspect alcohol or drugs were involved in the crash, and don't believe Walker was racing. Walker was wearing dark clothing, and the bike he was riding didn't have lights. "We have two sons not too much older than Tray, and we can't imagine how much his family is suffering," says Ravens owner Steve Bisciotti. "This is so sad. The right words are hard to find at a time like this. As much as we can comfort Tray's mom and the rest of his family, we will." Head coach John Harbaugh says Walker had a good and kind heart. "He loved his teammates, the practice, and the preparation, and that showed every day. He was coachable, did his most to improve, and worked to become the best," he says. "I'll never forget that smile."

– The man who ran onto the field at Yankee Stadium Monday night with a picture of Alex Rodriguez with an X on his face and a gun pointed at his head has been identified as 33-year-old Grim LeRogue, the New York Post reports. LeRogue, who legally changed his name from Joe Rogan, was carrying five pictures, including one of A-Rod with the message, “You have to go bud, you’ve ruined too many of our white queens.” He also had a picture of Cameron Diaz with the message, “We will be together soon.” LeRogue, who was tackled by security just a few feet from the stands, told police he wanted publicity for his 700-page novel about a ninja or something, his mother says. “He drank in his day when he was younger, he’s not like this saintly kid, but he’s 33 years old now, so give me a break,” she says.

– Chris Christie is tired of hearing about the Buffett Rule. "He should just write a check and shut up," the New Jersey governor told Piers Morgan last night. "If he wants to give the government more money, he’s got the ability to write a check—go ahead and write it," Christie continued. "I’m so tired of talking about Warren Buffett," he added. "What are you going to bring up next, his secretary? I mean, this is the old song." When Morgan pressed Christie on the billionaire, the governor said he "doesn't live in New Jersey," Politico reports. "Of course, during difficult economic times you’re most concerned about the people who have the potential to suffer the most." Christie said he was "not going to get into this class warfare business," and that everyone "deserves to have the government responsive to their concerns."

– San Francisco police are investigating an apparent arson at the home where Mrs. Doubtfire was filmed after someone tried to set fire to the garage and front door last night, CBS San Francisco reports. No suspects have been identified, and police say the incident doesn't appear to be a hate crime, NBC News reports. The Pacific Heights home became a memorial to Robin Williams after his death last year, and plastic surgeon Douglas Ousterhout, who owns the home, told police that he is having problems with a former client, but is not sure who is responsible for the fire, CBS reports.

– The Carpenters are suing Universal Music Group and A&M Records for at least $2 million, claiming they've ripped them off in the digital age. Richard Carpenter says the record labels "improperly classified" revenue from digital downloads as sales of records instead of licensing revenue, and that they applied an incorrect base price to the sales of CDs, reports the Hollywood Reporter. Karen Carpenter died in 1983. "I regret that I have been unable to amicably resolve this serious royalty dispute with Universal and A&M," Carpenter said in a statement. "The Carpenters recordings are among the best sellers in the history of popular music and after 48 years continue to contribute a substantial amount to UMG/A&M’s annual bottom line." He says the courts have agreed with him and that it's time to pay up, reports Billboard.

– Dominique Strauss-Kahn was arraigned in New York City today on charges of attempted rape, criminal sexual act, and unlawful imprisonment, reports Reuters. The IMF chief, who was removed from a plane minutes before it was to take off for Paris, will be held in a Rikers Island jail cell for at least 24 hours. Strauss-Kahn's wife, French TV personality Anne Sinclair, released a statement saying she "does not believe for a single second the accusations leveled against my husband," reports the New York Times. "I ask that you respect the presumption of innocence and allow the legal process to take its course," she said. Strauss-Kahn is a possible candidate for France's presidency next year and had been a frontrunner in early polls.

– Delegates from around the world were en route to Australia for the International AIDS Conference when the Malaysia Airlines flight was shot down over Ukraine today. "A number of colleagues and friends en route to attend the 20th International AIDS Conference taking place in Melbourne, Australia, were on board the Malaysia Airlines MH17 flight that has crashed over Ukraine," says a statement from the International AIDS Society. "At this incredibly sad and sensitive time the IAS stands with our international family and sends condolences to the loved ones of those who have been lost to this tragedy." Among the dead are several World Health Organization staffers, reports the Sydney Morning Herald. Dutch HIV researcher Joep Lange was president of the IAS for 10 years and was known for his work on the disease. "He was a kind man and a true humanitarian," wrote US medical professor Seema Yasmin on Twitter. "How do we measure how much a person has done for humanity? People like Joep change the course of epidemics." A WHO media adviser is also believed to be among the dead, reports the BBC. The AIDS conference, which began Sunday, is the world's largest and is held every two years.

– A Washington, DC, coffee shop is in the news this week for refusing to serve a customer who wanted an espresso-over-ice drink. The owner of the now-closed Murky Coffee explained the policy in a letter to the editor in the Washington Post. "We have our reasons, and we're happy to share them," he wrote. "Who knew a cup of coffee could create such a tempest in a teapot?" Murky is not the first coffee shop to have a hard time serving a customer who wants an espresso-over-ice drink. In 2008, then-D.C. resident Jeff Simmermon documented his experience at a different Murky location in a blog post that went viral. "You're goddamned right you can't stop me," he told the barista. "I happen to have a personal policy that prohibits me from indulging stupid bullshit like this—and another personal policy of doing what I want with the products I pay for." The barista eventually poured the espresso onto the ice.

– A worldwide email worm hit NASA, Comcast, AIG, Disney, Proctor & Gamble, the Florida Department of Transportation, and Wells Fargo yesterday, slowing work and forcing some employees to go without email altogether. The subject line of the email, "Here you have," was the second most-searched term on Google yesterday, ABC News reports. Security firm McAfee identified the worm as a Trojan and said the origin is unknown. The fact that it managed to spread widely through various multinational businesses doesn't say a lot for the security savvy of the workers, writes Adam Clark Estes on Gizmodo. "People! DO NOT click links in email messages from unknown people. DO NOT even click links in email messages from your friend, since the real source of the message might be a virus. DO keep your computer protected with an antivirus or a security suite. That way if you click the wrong link in a fit of weakness you'll still be protected from whatever new threat replaces 'here you have,'" he writes.

– A Maryland high school was locked down last night after two students were shot outside the gym during a basketball game, reports the Frederick News-Post. The victims, both teenagers, are expected to survive. "Earlier this evening, two students were wounded in an incident at Frederick High," tweeted Frederick County Public Schools. "They are receiving care." The school system later tweeted that "all other staff and students at Frederick High are safe and accounted for." The shooter or shooters are believed to have fled the scene on foot. School officials locked down Frederick High and nearby West Frederick Middle while police searched the building and questioned witnesses. The victims attend a Frederick County school, but not Frederick High, says a school spokesman. "I guess that's why there was a heightened panic," he says. "It was a very peaceful, very quiet game."

– It's official: Gilmore Girls is coming back to Netflix. The streaming service confirmed Friday that a "final season" of the show, which ran for seven seasons from 2000 to 2007, will be followed by four 90-minute films, per the Hollywood Reporter. The original cast—including Lauren Graham, Alexis Bledel, Kelly Bishop, Scott Patterson, Sean Gunn, and Keiko Agena—will return, along with creator Amy Sherman-Palladino and her husband, Daniel Palladino, who will write and direct all of the episodes, reports the Los Angeles Times. No word yet on the title or premiere date.

– US and Mexican authorities have uncovered two more drug-smuggling "super tunnels" between San Diego and Tijuana, reports USA Today. The latest passages, which cost millions of dollars to build, are the sixth and seventh found between Tijuana and San Diego since 2010. A 73-year-old woman was arrested this week in connection with the first tunnel, and faces federal charges of conspiring with others to maintain a drug-involved premises. The second tunnel was uncovered by Mexican investigators following leads from their US counterparts. "While technology certainly plays a part in our ongoing efforts, ultimately these investigations often owe more to the powers of observation and old fashioned detective work—and that was exactly what happened here," says an ICE agent in San Diego.

– The leaders of the world's biggest economies agreed today on a plan to halve their annual budget deficits within three years, reports the Wall Street Journal. The deficit targets were agreed upon at the G20 summit in Toronto, but they were couched in caveats to make sure they didn't hurt growth, reports the Washington Post. "Every country will chart its own unique course, but make no mistake—we're moving in the same direction," said President Obama at the end of the two-day meeting. He also called for continued spending to support growth. "But we must recognize that our fiscal health tomorrow will rest in no small measure on our ability to create jobs and growth today," he said.

– With the death of Thailand's beloved King Bhumibol Adulyadej, the country has declared a year of mourning—and black is the color of mourning. Most people in Bangkok have been wearing black since the king's death on Thursday and shoppers have been flocking to markets to get new clothes, Reuters reports. The country's commerce minister says demand for black clothing has soared since the king's death and officials have been sent out to scour markets for price gougers. "Regarding black shirts which have become more expensive, the commerce ministry has sent teams to inspect white and black clothing vendors to make sure the shirts are not being sold at prices that are too expensive," a spokesman for the prime minister's office said on Saturday. Black is the color of mourning in Thailand but white, a color that symbolizes purity, is also sometimes worn. White is also worn by ethnic Chinese people at funerals. Most people in Bangkok have been wearing black since the king died and shoppers have been flooding to markets to get new clothes. "If you compare, the price is higher than before, but this isn't about prices," says a nurse buying black shirts for herself and her family. "We're going to wear them for a year."

– Authorities say an argument over a break room light led to a deadly stabbing involving three workers at Philadelphia International Airport, the AP reports. The stabbing occurred around 11:30am Thursday near Gate E6 in what city police say was a "secure area." They say the three men work for a company that cleans planes for Frontier Airlines, but their names weren't released. Police say one worker turned off a break room light, angering another worker. The third worker soon pulled out a knife, cutting one of the men across the abdomen. The 28-year-old stabbing victim was pronounced dead at a hospital. Authorities say the two other workers ran off but were soon confronted by police. It wasn't clear what charges they may face. Frontier Airlines referred all questions to the cleaning company.

Some 70% of the Afghan army's armored vehicles are out of commission, and 20% of its Humvees have been blown up, the Washington Post reports. "How can we fight a war like this?" asked the battalion commander, who like many Afghans uses one name. The US has been handing over the repair of Afghan equipment to the Afghans for years, but with the Afghan supply chain still undeveloped and the Defense Ministry still hobbled by corruption, the Afghans aren't getting the gear and parts they need. "We don't have enough trained professionals to take care of this equipment," said a Kandahar battalion commander, who said his unit lost 15% of its Humvees in the past four months. Some Afghan battalions have waited three years to get their Humvees replaced, because of bureaucratic inefficiency. It's much easier to replace the army's Ford Rangers, but because those trucks aren't armored, they are not as desirable, especially in violent eastern Afghanistan. – An Alabama man accused of drowning his wife during their Australian honeymoon in 2003 has been acquitted of capital murder. Jefferson County Circuit Judge Tommy Nail said there was no evidence that a reasonable person could consider to be proof beyond a reasonable doubt that Gabe Watson committed an Alabama crime by intentionally killing Tina Thomas Watson for monetary gain on Oct. 22, 2003. "The evidence is sorely lacking that it was an intentional act," Nail said. "The only way to convict him of intentional murder is to speculate. Nobody knows exactly what happened in the water. I'm sure we'll never know." Watson, 34, had faced life in prison without parole if convicted. He already served 18 months in an Australian prison after pleading guilty there to a manslaughter charge involving negligence. Nail agreed with defense arguments that prosecutors failed to show Watson intentionally killed his wife to collect on a life insurance policy, the AP reports. Prosecutors claimed he drowned her for insurance money, but the only eyewitness testified he thought Watson was trying to save his wife's life. The Thomas family found out from Watson's father more than a day after the death, he said. The dismissal by Nail came this afternoon after the prosecutors had rested their case against Watson.

– If you're in the market for a romantic email, Indiana University researchers have some advice: Don't leave a voicemail. "The bottom line is that email is much better when you want to convey some information that you want someone to think about," says one of the authors of the study, published in the journal Computers in Human Behavior. The researchers asked 72 college-age people to send romantic emails and voicemails. They found that people who sent romantic emails used stronger and more thoughtful language than those who left voicemails. "When writing romantic emails, senders consciously or subconsciously added more positive content to their messages, perhaps to compensate for the medium’s inability to convey vocal tone," the researchers write. The researchers also found that the content of romantic emails was more likely to be edited when written by the sender. – A pair of researchers say they've found the oldest fortified settlement ever found in the US, and it's not just any old settlement. Fort Caroline, built by the French in 1564, is older than the Lost Colony of Virginia, Jamestown, and the Pilgrims of 1620, Florida State University historian Fletcher Crowe says. "This is the oldest fortified settlement in the present United States," he adds. "It's older than St. Augustine, considered to be the oldest continuously inhabited city in America. It's older than the Lost Colony of Virginia by 21 years; older than the 1607 fort of Jamestown by 45 years; and predates the landing of the Pilgrims in Massachusetts in 1620 by 56 years." The Fort Caroline National Memorial was originally thought to be located near downtown Jacksonville, on the south bank of the St. Johns River, but Crowe and his co-author say it's actually on an island at the mouth of the Altamaha River two miles southeast of the city of Darien, Ga., reports the Florida Times-Union. – Jonathan Pollard will be released on parole Nov. 21, his lawyer announced Tuesday. – If you're headed to one of the 10 most polluted beaches in the US, you may want to steer clear. The National Resources Defense Council has released its annual report on water quality at the country's beaches, and it finds that 10% of them don't meet EPA water safety standards, meaning they're likely teeming with bacteria, reports LiveScience. The worst offenders: New England, on the Gulf Coast and along the Great Lakes. New York, New Jersey, and California fare the worst, with a failure rate of 10% or higher. stormwater runoff is the main culprit, and the group notes that hundreds of billions of gallons of untreated sewage end up in our oceans each year, causing some 3.5 million Americans to fall ill. In California, the report found that 9% of water quality samples collected at the state's beaches last year failed to meet EPA safety standards—and that's on par with the country's overall failure rate. The good news: There are a number of world-class beaches in the state, and the NRDC suggests you check them out here.

– A record 41% of US births in 2008 were to unmarried women, up from 28% in 1990, according to a Pew Research Center study released today. The study also found that the average age at which women have their first child is now 25—a year older than in 1990—and the share of women with at least some college education before giving birth has jumped from 41% in 1990 to 71% in 2008. "The rise in women's education levels has changed the profile of the typical mother of a newborn baby," the report says. The study also found that half of mothers surveyed said parenthood "just happened," the Los Angeles Times reports.

The memo exempts the International Space Station, which is operated by Russia, as well as meetings with other partners, such as Canada, Europe, and Japan, the Monitor notes. – A masked man wielding a sword or a knife stabbed four people, two of them fatally, at a school in Trollhattan, Sweden, on Thursday, authorities say. The 21-year-old suspect was shot and killed by police at the scene, CNN reports. A male teacher, 20, and a student, 17, were killed in the attack at the Kronan primary and middle school, which has around 400 students between the ages of 11 and 15, the Local reports. A male student, 11, and a 15-year-old student were seriously injured. "This is a dark day for Sweden," Prime Minister Stefan Lofven said. "My thoughts go out to the victims and their families, pupils, and staff, and the entire community that has been affected. There are no words to describe what they are going through right now." Police say the suspect entered the school with "several knife-like objects" and attacked the victims after knocking on classrooms' doors, the AP reports. Authorities say they don't believe anyone else was involved in the attack. Police searched the suspect's home and found "interesting" things, a police spokesman says, without elaborating.

– Itzcoatl Ocampo, a 25-year-old ex-Marine charged with murdering six people in Orange County, died in jail last week after apparently ingesting Ajax in his cell, his lawyer tells the AP. Ocampo, who was awaiting trial for the murders of four homeless men, a woman, and her son, was found shaking and vomiting and pronounced dead at a hospital. The death raises serious questions about how well Orange County jail deputies were supervising Ocampo, who had mental health issues, attorney Michael Molfetta says. "With that being said, this was a guy who should have garnered the highest level of scrutiny ... and it wasn't done." The district attorney's office is investigating and an autopsy will be performed in the coming days. Ocampo was placed on suicide watch in March after banging his head on a metal toilet, and told his attorney he was trying to stop voices.

– Google's new parent company, Alphabet, officially took effect Tuesday, but it's already causing some confusion. The New York Times reports that BMW is "looking into whether Google's Alphabet has infringed on its trademark." The German automaker owns a fleet services company with the same name and the domain Alphabet.com. A spokesperson for BMW tells the Times the company isn't planning on selling its domain and that Alphabet was a large part of its business. The New York Daily News notes that more than 100 companies have trademark registrations for the "alphabet" in some capacity, including Ohio-based Alphabet, Inc., which was founded in 1965 and makes electrical components for the auto industry. The confusion has caused Alphabet.com to be down, likely due to the increased traffic it is undoubtedly receiving, Mashable reports. (In other Google news, Sergey Brin has a new job title.)

– The Food and Drug Administration is out with a warning about dark chocolate—and it's not good news. The FDA tested 100 different dark chocolate bars and found that two out of three contained milk, CBS Pittsburgh reports. That's even though the FDA allows dairy as an ingredient in dark chocolate. "Even one small bite of a product containing milk can cause a dangerous reaction in some individuals," an FDA researcher says in a statement. The FDA found milk in 33% of bars that had no mention of the ingredient anywhere on the label, Yahoo Health reports. It also found milk in 15% of bars that claimed to be "dairy-free." The FDA says dairy labeling on chocolate bars is inefficient and dangerous. "I would say no dark chocolate unless you had an absolute declaration on the bar that you were absolutely certain from the manufacturer that it was made in a milk-free facility and that it was completely clear of that," an allergist tells KDKA. The FDA says it is working on stricter labeling and manufacturing legislation, including a proposed "Preventive Controls for Human Food" rule that would go into effect in the fall. (The FDA found milk in half of all milk-based foods.)

– The White House initially said President Trump played a few holes of golf with professional golfer Rory McIlroy at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida on Sunday, but it has since changed its tune. "As stated yesterday the President played golf. He intended to play a few holes and decided to play longer," White House spokesperson Sarah Sanders said Monday, per Politico. The White House initially said Trump, who recently golfed with Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, had only intended to play a few holes.

"This would be a blatant misuse of military funds and tied up in court for years. Secretary Mattis ought not bother and instead use the money to help our troops."

– Israel and Hamas have agreed to a 72-hour ceasefire beginning at 8am local time tomorrow, John Kerry and UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon announced today. "We urge all parties to act with restraint until this humanitarian ceasefire begins, and to fully abide by their commitments during the ceasefire," Kerry and Ban said in a joint statement. "This ceasefire is critical to giving innocent civilians a much-needed reprieve from violence." The announcement came as Israel's security cabinet ordered the military to continue fighting in the Gaza Strip, Haaretz reports. The death toll in the Israeli operation now stands at 1,360, according to Palestinian health officials, and more than 6,500 Palestinians have been wounded, the New York Times reports. Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas has declared Gaza a "humanitarian disaster area" and accused Israel of committing war crimes, the Times reports. In Cairo, meanwhile, Egypt's foreign minister says the country is working to broker a longer-term ceasefire between the two sides, Reuters reports.

The 250-pound female bear was euthanized to protect park visitors and staff, a park spokesman tells the Los Angeles Times. The investigation into the mauling remains open, and officials might never know definitively whether the same bear killed John Wallace of Michigan in August. – The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has postponed a teaching session on the public health response to a nuclear blast, the Washington Post reports. The session was scheduled to be broadcast Tuesday as part of the CDC's monthly Public Health Grand Rounds. According to the New York Times, the CDC's announcement for the session featured a photo of a mushroom cloud from a nuclear blast. The postponement was announced Friday, the same day the CDC said it was changing the topic of the session to influenza and taking down the photo of the mushroom cloud. The CDC says the session will be rescheduled for a future Grand Rounds.

"I think not having the estate tax recognizes the people that are investing, as opposed to those that are just spending every darn penny they have, whether it's on booze or women or movies," the Republican senator tells the Des Moines Register. "It's harder than ever for families to pass down the family-run farm or business from one generation to the next. The death tax creates financial hardship for family businesses to survive and thrive." The estate tax is applied to assets above $5.5 million for individuals and $11 million for couples. The House and Senate bills double that exemption to $11 million and $22 million, and the House version abolishes the tax completely in 2024. But a review of federal tax data and nonpartisan research on the subject shows that family farmers and small business owners represent a tiny share of estate tax payers, and that the taxes they owe rarely force them to sell land or quit farming. The agent, from Sotheby's, told China's CCTV that the woman told him her daughter was going to Columbia, NYU, or Harvard and needed to be in the center of the city, reports Time. He showed her apartments all over the city before she picked one at One57, a still-unfinished, 90-story luxury building on 57th Street. – The race to succeed David Cameron as prime minister is down to two: Theresa May and Andrea Leadsom. The latter was declared the winner of the second round of voting in the race to replace Cameron as leader of the Conservative Party on Wednesday, the AP reports. May received 199 votes, while Leadsom got 84 and Michael Gove 46. The final vote will be held Sept. 9. May had been leading the charge to keep the UK in the European Union, while Leadsom argued for a clean break from the bloc. The two women will now face off in the final round of voting in the race to succeed Cameron, who announced his resignation after the UK voted to leave the EU last month. May will be the first woman to lead the country since Margaret Thatcher. Leadsom, an energy minister, would be the first female leader of the opposition.

– "This is a tricky drug-resistant bacteria, and it isn't easily found," CDC Director Thomas Frieden tells the Washington Post. "What we're seeing is an assault by the microbes on the last bastion of antibiotics." According to the CDC, carbapenem-resistant enterobacteriaceae, or CRE, bacteria have been found in at least 43 people in 19 states between June 2010 and August 2015. All cases were confirmed by the CDC. CRE bacteria are resistant to most antibiotics, and in some cases they can kill up to 50% of patients who get infected, the Post reports. The CDC calls CRE one of the country's most urgent public health threats. According to the New York Times, CRE bacteria are found in hospitals all over the US, and they're especially dangerous to those with weakened immune systems. They're also resistant to the antibiotic colistin, which is commonly used to treat infections. Scientists have been calling CRE a "phantom menace." According to the Times, this type of CRE bacteria isn't as antibiotic-resistant as other types of CRE because it's less likely to be passed from person to person. – Eminem fans may soon be able to get a slice of the rapper's fortune. Bloomberg reports brothers Jeff and Mark Bass have agreed to sell up to 25% of their stake in a new company called Royalty Flow, which plans to go public. If the company hits its minimum funding target of $11 million to $50 million, it will be listed on the NASDAQ stock exchange. “If you’re a fan and wanna bet on that artist, you’ve got some skin in the game,” Joel Martin, a business partner of the Bass brothers, tells Bloomberg. “It takes the average investor and puts them in a position they wouldn’t be in before.” Royalty Flow plans to raise the money via a Regulation A+ crowdfunding effort, according to Billboard. If it hits the minimum funding target, it will buy up to 25% of the income stream from Eminem's music, and fans and investors will be able to share in that income. “Eminem is not involved in any deals for the sale of recording royalties and has no connection to this company,” a rep for Eminem tells Variety. “The decision to offer the royalty stream for sale or otherwise was made independently by a third party who retains royalties for an early portion of his catalog and Eminem was not consulted.”

– Fidel Castro's oldest son has killed himself less than a year after his father's death. Fidel Castro Diaz-Balart, 68, was found dead in his home in Havana on Thursday morning and state media said he had been suffering from depression for months, the BBC reports. He had been hospitalized and treated as an outpatient in recent months. Castro Diaz-Balart, a nuclear physicist, was nicknamed "Fidelito" or "Little Fidel" after his father, who trained as a physicist in the Soviet Union. He headed Cuba's nuclear program from 1980 to 1992 before it was suspended after the Soviet Union's collapse, the BBC reports.

Trump is said to have told Lavrov that the FBI chief had leaked classified information to the press and put the president's ability to negotiate with Russia at risk. "James Comey better hope that there are no 'tapes' of our conversations before he starts leaking to the press," the president was quoted as saying. The adviser is someone close to the president, and investigators are expected to intensify their efforts in the weeks ahead.

– The town of Barron, Wis., is reeling after the deaths of James Closs, 56, and Denise Closs, 46, who were found shot to death in their home early Monday. Their 13-year-old daughter, Jayme, hasn't been seen since the night of Oct. 15, and police are still searching for her. On Thursday, more than 100 volunteers fanned out across the town looking for any evidence related to Jayme's disappearance, reports the Wausau Daily Herald. But as of Friday morning, the Barron County Sheriff's Office said in a Facebook post that no evidence related to Jayme's disappearance had been found. Meanwhile, a school resource officer and a therapy dog from the police department in Wausau were sent to Barron schools Thursday to help students deal with the tragedy, reports USA Today. "There isn't anyone in this community that this hasn't touched," says Kristen Devitt, director of the state's Office of School Safety. "We have certainly experienced that need for help."

– Women who eat a lot of potatoes before they get pregnant are more likely to develop a condition called gestational diabetes during pregnancy, according to a new study. Researchers found that women who ate more than five servings of boiled, mashed, baked, or chips a week were 50% more likely to develop the condition, which can lead to high blood sugar levels during pregnancy, the BBC reports. The study followed 21,693 women during their pregnancies and found that those who ate two to four servings of boiled, mashed, baked, or chips a week were 27% more likely to develop gestational diabetes. Women who ate more than five servings a week were 50% more likely to develop the condition, according to the study, published in the British Medical Journal. The study did not prove cause-and-effect, but "the evidence tells us that we need to eat more starchy foods, such as potatoes, bread, pasta, and rice, as well as fruit and vegetables to increase fibre consumption and protect bowel health," says a public health expert in England. "Our advice remains the same: base meals around a variety of starchy foods, including potatoes with the skin on, and choose wholegrain varieties where possible." – The Harvard professor who first announced the discovery of a so-called "Gospel of Jesus' Wife" in September 2012 has been silent since, but a Live Science investigation suggests she may have been wrong. The Coptic-language papyrus contains a translation of the line, "Jesus said to them, 'My wife ...'" and also refers to Mary Magdalene. Christian Askeland, a Coptic specialist, analyzed a second papyrus that was said to have been purchased by the same anonymous owner in Germany in 2002, and he concludes that it's also a fake, reports Live Science. The first papyrus, he writes in the Harvard Theological Review, has writing on one side and is copied from a papyrus published in 1924. The lines on the second papyrus have the same style and ink, which suggests it's a fake, as does the fact that it breaks (the same line breaks on the Gospel of Jesus's wife). The anonymous owner of the second papyrus, however, says he bought it from Hans-Ulrich Laukamp in Potsdam, what is now East Germany, in 2002. Laukamp, who died in 1963, didn't own this papyrus, didn't have an interest in antiquities, and couldn't have traveled across the Berlin Wall to buy it

– More than 50 "potential terrorist events" have been foiled thanks to the NSA's phone and Internet surveillance programs, National Security Agency Director Keith Alexander told a House intelligence hearing today. Of those, 90% were disrupted by the NSA's PRISM program, and the rest by other means, he said, according to Politico. Four of those incidents were detailed at the hearing, including plots to bomb the New York subway system and the New York Stock Exchange by linking known suspects in Pakistan and Yemen to contacts in the US, CNN reports. Deputy Attorney General James Cole also said the Patriot Act provision allowing the surveillance has been twice reauthorized. "This is not a program that’s off the books, that’s been hidden away," Cole said. "All of us in the national security [community] are constantly trying to balance protecting public safety with protecting people’s civil liberties," he added. Alexander and other NSA officials were testifying as part of an investigation into the agency's surveillance programs, which have been criticized by lawmakers from both parties. "Has this helped America’s enemies?" asked Rep. Michele Bachmann. "I believe it has and I believe it will hurt us and our allies."

The group's "Sarah Doesn't Speak for Me" website features a video of women in bear costumes mocking the "Mama Grizzlies" slogan, the Washington Post reports. EMILY's List President Stephanie Schriock called the Mama Grizzlies "backwards-looking" and said the group was trying to "get out the vote hub" for its 32 endorsed female candidates. "Clearly, in this 'Year of the Pro-Life Woman,' which Sarah Palin helped make possible, women have found their political voices," the president of the pro-life Susan B. Anthony List said. "Pro-life 'Mama Grizzlies' represent the majority of women across the country."

Bush were in attendance Saturday at the dedication of the National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington, DC, and the moment that's getting the most attention isn't exactly a photo of the two of them hugging. Instead, it's a selfie taken by former White House photographer David Hume Kennerly that's going viral, reports Mediaite. "I love this picture," writes Guy Cecil on Twitter. The Washington Post notes that the two have been "increasingly chummy" over the past eight years, and that Bush asked Obama for some help taking a selfie during the ceremony.

Most of the women are still pregnant and the effects of the virus on their babies aren't yet known, USA Today reports. "Here's the upshot: This is something that is solvable. This is not something we need to panic about. But this is something we have to take seriously," President Obama said Friday after meeting with his top public safety advisers. "Congress needs to get me a bill. They should not be going off on recess before this is done." The CDC released the new numbers as Congress debates how much emergency funding to approve for Zika response before going on recess after Memorial Day. The Senate has approved $1.1 billion; the House has approved $622 million. The White House has threatened to veto the House bill if it's sent to the president's desk. "We didn't just choose $1.9 billion from the top of our heads. This was based on a public health assessment of all the work that needs to be done," Obama said. – UPS is looking to make up for the lousy holiday season it had last year by tacking on a surcharge for residential deliveries. The company says the new prices will be applied over several years as contracts with major customers are renegotiated, Reuters reports. UPS spent $500 million last year to improve its network and prevent a repeat of the mistakes it made in 2013, when a late rush of online packages left 1.3 million undelivered on Christmas Eve, reports Ars Technica. "These pricing strategies will be designed to ensure we are properly compensated for the value we provide," UPS CEO David Abney said on a conference call yesterday. UPS says the new prices won't be "immediately applied everywhere," but will be rolled out as the company renegotiates its shipping contracts with its largest customers, Reuters reports. The company says residential deliveries cost three times as much as deliveries to businesses, and the new prices won't apply to Amazon Prime subscribers or to businesses that only receive a single package per day, according to Ars Technica. The company says the new prices won't be the only way to make up for the huge increase in shipping costs last year.

– A Detroit teen who tried to rob a bank Monday almost made it all the way out before realizing he was a sitting duck, MLive.com reports. Police say the 16-year-old walked into Chase Bank on the city's west side and handed the teller a note that said he had a bomb and demanded money. The teller complied, gave him some money, and as he attempted to leave, the teller hit the button for the doors that automatically lock and the suspect was trapped inside, the Detroit Free Press reports. "The teller engaged what is called a 'man-trap,' basically a security system that locks would-be intruders between the two sets of doors leading outside where they remain caged until police can arrive and take them safely into custody, which Detroit police soon did," the Free Press notes. "Often the glass is also bulletproof." The teen was detained by police and transported to a juvenile facility. It's unclear if he'll face charges as a juvenile or as an adult.

– Feel younger than your chronological age? You're more likely to live longer, according to a new study published in JAMA Internal Medicine. "Self-perceived age reflects appraisals of health, physical limitations, and well-being in later life," write the authors of the study from University College London. "Older people typically feel younger than their chronological age, and it is thought that those who feel younger than their actual age have reduced mortality." To study this, the researchers analyzed data from more than 6,000 participants who answered the question, "How old do you feel you are?" The average self-perceived age was 56.8 years, but 25.6% of participants felt close to their actual age; 4.8% felt more than a year older; and 69.6% felt 3 or more years younger. The mortality rate for those who felt younger than their actual age was 14.3%, and for those who felt older than their actual age than their actual age, it was 24.6%. "Although baseline health, physical disability, and health behavior accounted for some of the association, after adjusting for all covariates, there remained a 41% greater mortality hazard in people who felt older than their actual age compared with those who felt younger than their actual age," write the authors.

– President Obama's letter to Iran's Hasan Rouhani was read aloud at a top-level meeting of the country's leadership yesterday, and the response was generally positive, a political commentator who was present at the meeting tells the New York Times. – The first of two warnings was heard in the cockpit of a UPS cargo jet that crashed in Alabama earlier this week, reports the AP. The Airbus A300 was descending at an unusually high rate of descent 16 seconds before impact, says the National Transportation Safety Board, but investigators haven't determined the cause of the crash. "We haven't ruled anything in, haven't ruled anything out," says a board member. Investigators will analyze the plane's weight to determine whether it should have attempted a landing on the shorter of two runways at Birmingham Shuttlesworth International Airport, reports the Wall Street Journal. With a large hill and trees at one end, the runway lacks the electronics for a full instrument landing. That forces pilots to make key judgments about altitude while aiming a descending aircraft at a runway that's 5,000 feet shorter than the airport's main runway, which was closed for maintenance work at the time of the crash. Some pilots simply avoid landing on the runway when possible, says veteran commercial pilot Ross Aimer. "When I heard they were using Runway 18 it caught my attention because of that hill," says Aimer. "It's sad, but it didn't surprise me."

– An international search and rescue team arrived in Haiti today along with tons of food and medicine, as the world began arriving to help the devastated nation. An Air China plane carrying the Chinese team, medics and tons of food and medicine landed at Port-au-Prince airport before dawn, along with three French planes with aid and a mobile hospital, the AP reports. A British relief team arrived in neighboring Dominican Republic. The US and other nations said they were sending food, water, medical supplies to assist the Western Hemisphere's poorest nation, where the international Red Cross estimated 3 million people—a third of the population—may need emergency relief. In the streets of the capital, survivors set up camps amid piles of salvaged goods, including food being scavenged from the rubble. "This is much worse than a hurricane," said Jimitre Coquillon, a doctor's assistant working at a makeshift triage center set up in a hotel parking lot. "There's no water. There's nothing. Thirsty people are going to die."

But the court said abortion clinics failed to prove that the restrictions would unduly burden a "large fraction" of women. The ruling, made by a three-judge panel, is the 5th Circuit's latest decision in a lawsuit challenging some of the toughest abortion restrictions in the country. The New Orleans-based court—considered one of the most conservative in the nation—allowed Texas to enforce the restrictions when abortion providers first sued in 2013, but the US Supreme Court put the law on hold last year and ordered the 5th Circuit to reconsider. – The Federal Reserve's latest report on the "economic well-being" of US households finds that one in five people who are near retirement age have zero money saved for it. That includes 19% of people between the ages of 55 and 64, or those closest to retirement age, as well as 19% of people between the ages of 55 and 64, or those closest to retirement age, Bloomberg reports. The report also found that 41% of people aged 45 and over now plan to retire at a later date than they had before the recession, and only 5% of people who gave at least some thought to retirement now plan to retire sooner than they had prior to 2008. "This is a scarier notion than improper planning—it is not having a plan at all," writes Megan McArdle at Bloomberg. The report found that 54% of people with incomes under $25,000 reported having no retirement savings or pension. This compares with only 10% of those earning $100,000 or more. The Fed surveyed more than 4,100 people online last year between mid-September and early October. The study offered a stark reminder that as more Americans are made responsible for their own retirement, most are not saving nearly enough. Overall, 31% of people said they have zero money saved for retirement and do not have a pension.

– The trial of a former University of Illinois graduate student accused of kidnapping a Chinese scholar, torturing her to death, and dumping her body is likely to be delayed. On Friday, federal prosecutors announced they will seek the death penalty against 28-year-old Brendt Christensen, the AP reports. Christensen was admitted to the university's highly competitive physics graduate program in 2011, but Yingying Zhang, a 26-year-old visiting scholar from China, has been missing since June 9 of last year. She was last seen getting into Christensen's car on the campus in Urbana-Champaign. Prosecutors say Christensen lured Zhang into his car by saying he needed a ride because she was late to an appointment. They say he then killed her, tortured her, and burned her body. Christensen initially told the FBI he was home all day playing video games on the day Zhang disappeared, the Chicago Tribune reports. He was charged with kidnapping and faces the death penalty if convicted. Christensen's trial had been tentatively set for Feb. 27 in federal court in Urbana-Champaign. (The last person to be sentenced to death in a federal courtroom in Illinois was nearly a decade ago.)

– A tourist from China was fined $1,000 for walking off a boardwalk at Yellowstone National Park and collecting thermal water, apparently for medicinal purposes, park officials said Wednesday. A witness reported seeing the man break through the fragile, rock crust surrounding the Mammoth Hot Springs area. The witness took photos of the man that were turned over to park rangers, officials said. The incident came only a week after an Oregon man died after falling into one of Yellowstone's hot springs, the AP reports. The Chinese tourist told rangers he did not read the safety information given to him when he entered the park. Reid said in an emailed response to questions about the case the "stiff fine" was levied in large part because of "the irreplaceable nature of the thermal feature." The 2.2 million-acre park has seen a string of incidents over the past month where tourists got into trouble. Some got too close to wildlife and several others walked off boardwalks near hot springs. Park officials were unable to recover his body.

Found across Asia, the nuts are harvested from the Areca palm and are chewed for their warming glow and stimulating properties. – A UK mother of two died last month from sepsis, a potentially life-threatening complication of an infection, after scratching her hand while gardening, her family says. Lucinda Smith, 43, went to her doctor earlier this year after experiencing pain in her shoulder, the Telegraph reports. The doctor diagnosed a trapped nerve and prescribed anti-depressants and a physiotherapist to ease her pain. But within three days, Smith's fingers and arm became red and swollen, and she also was vomitting. She saw a second doctor who thought she might have a blood clot and sent her to Basildon Hospital, where a blood test revealed she had sepsis. Sepsis is a potentially life-threatening complication of an infection, according to Mayo Clinic experts. It happens when chemicals released into the bloodstream to fight the infection trigger inflammatory responses throughout the body. Septic shock occurs when the person’s blood pressure drops dramatically, which may lead to death. Smith, a lawyer from Billericay, Essex, immediately received intravenous antibiotics and was moved to a critical care unit, but she suffered organ failure and died. The man was driving with a woman to Windidda Station, a cattle ranch in the remote Wiluna region of Western Australia state, when their car broke down on Sunday, police said in a statement. After no car passed on the lonely road over Sunday night, the man set out on foot across semi-desert country early Monday with what police described as a "small container of water." When no traffic had passed by Tuesday morning, the woman also decided to walk to Windidda Station. She was rescued by passersby on Wednesday afternoon and taken to her destination, where she raised the alarm. Station residents launched a search and found the man dead late Wednesday 1 mile from Windidda. Police urged people driving across the remote Outback during the current summer months to carry plenty of water and to stay with vehicles that break down. Wiluna, a village of several hundred residents which is the biggest population center in the region, had a forecast maximum temperature of 39 degrees Celsius on Thursday.

– Scientists from the US and Denmark are seeking to map out the plumbing system hidden inside the earth's crust that's responsible for the famous Old Faithful geyser and other hydrothermal features at Yellowstone National Park, the AP reports. Throughout November, the research team will conduct flights over the park using a giant, hoop-shaped electromagnetic system suspended from a helicopter. The device acts like an X-ray to determine where and how hot water flows beneath the surface. The team also hopes to gain insights into the infrequent but sometimes massive hydrothermal explosions that occur in the park. One such explosion, or possibly multiple explosions, that occurred roughly 13,800 years ago left a crater that measures 1-1/2 miles across beneath at the bottom of Yellowstone Lake. – A new rule that goes into effect Jan. 1 is designed to make sure financial advisers are acting in the best interests of their clients. The Wall Street Journal explains the difference between "registered investment advisers" and "broker-dealers." Registered advisers are paid directly by their clients, and typically charge based on the size of the fund they manage; broker-dealers, on the other hand, are often paid commissions and often receive "revenue-sharing" payments from the banks and mutual funds that generate the investments the brokers sell. Under the new rules, registered advisers will be required to act in the best interests of their clients, while broker-dealers will be required to disclose conflicts of interest. It's all part of the Department of Labor's effort to reduce risk in middle-class savers' retirement savings after the 2008 financial crisis. Under the new rules, savers will have the right to sue or initiate arbitration against advisers who don't meet ethical standards or who fail to disclose conflicts. The effect, say both experts and many industry advocates, will be to drive many advisers to change their business models, while pushing others entirely out of the business. According to a press release, emoji "have come to embody a core aspect of living in a digital world that is visually driven, emotionally expressive, and obsessively immediate." Oxford University Press, which publishes the Oxford English Dictionary and Oxford Dictionaries Online, partnered with keyboard-app company SwiftKey to determine which emoji was used the most in 2015. The "Face With Tears of Joy" emoji, also known as LOL Emoji or Laughing Emoji, took 20% of all emoji use in the US and the UK. Other words that made Oxford's short list this year included Brexit, Dark Web, lumbersexual, and refugee. "It's not surprising that a pictographic script like emoji has stepped in to fill those gaps—it's flexible, immediate, and infuses tone beautifully," Oxford Dictionaries' president says. "They can serve as insightful windows through which to view our cultural preoccupations, so it seemed appropriate to reflect this emoji obsession."

– The New York Mets' owners have agreed to pay $83 million to settle a lawsuit brought by the trustee handling Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme, the team's owners and the trustee announced in a New York courtroom today. The settlement ends a long-running battle over who should get the money, the New York Times reports. The men had been accused of being among those who benefited from Madoff's scheme. But the lawsuit was dropped from bankruptcy court, and a federal judge took over the case, and the trustee, Irving Picard, ended up settling for much less than he could have. “I certainly consider this a capitulation by the trustee,” says a former federal prosecutor. “It seems quite one-sided.” The settlement also ends a separate lawsuit brought by the trustee against the Madoff family. The family accused the Mets' owners of being among its biggest beneficiaries.

– When Matthew Hickey retired as a police officer in Marietta, Ohio, last month, he thought he could keep his K-9 partner, Ajax. The German shepherd is valued between $3,500 and $4,000, Hickey tells CNN, but Ohio law says police dogs must be treated as city property and sold at auction if their handler leaves the force. "Ajax is a family member; he's one of my children," says Hickey, who has raised more than $70,000 in an online campaign to keep Ajax. On Thursday, the city council will consider options for Hickey, including offering him an auxiliary officer position on the force, CNN reports. The position will allow Hickey to keep Ajax for another five or six years.

– Chris Brown's lawyer went to the NYPD yesterday to present evidence that Drake and Meek Mill were the aggressors in Brown's bar fight, but sources tell TMZ Brown is not currently a suspect—he's just "a witness and a victim." Drake, meanwhile, has been "cooperating" with police, but it's not clear if he's spoken to them yet. Sources also tell the gossip site that the bad guy in Brown's camp may have been someone in Drake's camp who was "inciting Drake and his people all night." (In other Chris Brown news, he's still not doing so well with his latest album.)

– They're fluffy, they're cute, and they're causing a lot of trouble in a small town on Washington's Whidbey Island. The Record reports that Langley is home to hundreds of wild rabbits, which are digging holes in the earth, damaging buildings, and posing a health risk to people and pets. "They are cute, but they have an impact on our community," the facilities director for the South Whidbey School District tells KING-TV. The bunnies are believed to be the result of escaped European hares from the Island County Fairgrounds decades ago. Some people feed them and there are plenty of buildings under which to burrow. "Everybody is saying we've never seen it like this before," the facilities director says. The school district is considering spending $60,000 to fence off a middle school football field that was recently paid for by the district. A community meeting is scheduled for Oct. 7 to discuss how to handle the problem. The mayor of Langley says he doesn't think the city will hire a trapper or euthanize the rabbits. "I don't think we're going to get into the business of trapping and euthanizing rabbits," he tells the Record. "I don't think that would go over well in Langley

– Google's third-quarter earnings blew past analysts' estimates, jumping 26% to $2.73 billion, or $9.72 per share, the company announced today. That's up from $2.17 billion, or $8.29 per share, in the same period last year, the Seattle Post-Intelligencer reports. "We had a great quarter," said Larry Page, Google's CEO. "Google+ is now open to everyone and we just passed the 40 million-user mark." The stock rose 6% in trading after the market closed. "The real interesting thing here is the expenses weren't as high as the Street was anticipating," said UBS analyst Brian Pitz. "This is the fourth quarter in a row the company has accelerated their revenue on top line." Revenue rose 33% to $9.72 billion—just shy of having a quarterly turnover of $10 billion. Google reported an effective tax rate of 18.8% in the second quarter, less than half the average combined US and state statutory rate of 39.2%, Bloomberg reported a year ago. The company has cut its worldwide tax bill by about $1 billion a year using a pair of strategies called the "Double Irish" and "Dutch Sandwich," which move profits through units in Ireland, the Netherlands, and Bermuda

– The International Space Station may need to have a spacewalk to deal with a serious problem with its cooling system, NASA says. The problem, which affects one of the station's two cooling loops, isn't considered a life-threatening emergency, but normal operations have been cut back and the six-person crew has been asked to prioritize what systems are important, NBC News reports. "The crew was never in any danger," says a NASA spokesman. "They're fine for the near future." Officials are still trying to figure out what caused the pump to shut down, but they suspect a malfunctioning valve is to blame. It's not the first time the station has had a problem with its cooling system, notes Space.com: In 2011, astronauts had to venture out on a spacewalk to fix a leaky pump.

– Shermain Miles has been arrested 396 times since 1978, and on Monday, the 52-year-old Chicago woman was released from prison after serving almost one year for assaulting a city council member, the Chicago Sun-Times reports. Miles, who has been in and out of prisons and jails over the years for offenses ranging from disorderly conduct and theft to attacking a city council member, says she is determined to turn her life around. "If they can find it in their hearts to forgive me ... I'm really not that bad a person," she tells the Sun-Times. "It was the alcohol I was drinking that turned me into a monster. I'm just not going to go back around there. I can love [my friends] from a distance. Anybody that's drugging, I can't be around." The chair of the Illinois Prisoner Review Board says he is optimistic that Miles will make it out of prison this time. "Hopefully, she's seen the light and is tired of being incarcerated," he says. "She's indicated she's willing to change her behavior."

– In a wide-ranging interview with the New York Times, Mahmoud Ahmadinejad said Iran would be willing to stop its nuclear enrichment in exchange for the cheaper option of buying enriched uranium for “cancer treatment medication.” “If they were willing to sell us the 20 percent enriched uranium, we would have preferred to buy it,” he said. “It would have been far less expensive. It’s as though you wish to purchase a vehicle for yourself. No one is willing to sell it to you, then you must set up your own production line to produce your own vehicle.” The interview comes on the heels of Ahmadinejad’s much-derided interview with the Washington Post in which he said Iran would be willing to stop its enrichment in exchange for the cheaper uranium. – A car bomb exploded near government buildings in the Turkish capital of Ankara today, killing at least three people and wounding 15, Reuters reports. "The explosion took place in a parked car, and was followed by explosions of other cars because they had guerrillas," said the country's interior minister. No one immediately claimed responsibility for the attack, which comes at a time when Kurdish rebels have been stepping up their attacks on Turkish targets. "I saw vehicles on fire and an injured man said people lost their limbs," said one witness.

The couple, identified only as John and Jane Doe, say they chose a white family because "it's been my experience in these cases that most of the birthparents identify problems with family, alcoholism, and other dysfunction, and they don't want kids placed in that kind of environment," their lawyer tells the Star Tribune. The couple's lawyer says this is the first lawsuit he's aware of challenging the notification requirements, imposed in 1997, which are an exception for Indian children. Federal law bans discrimination in adoptions on the basis of race, but makes an exception for Indian children. If either the couple or the adoption agency chose not to tell the tribe, they would open themselves to fraud charges and risk having the adoption voided if the truth were discovered, the lawyer says. He notes that if the couple chose to have an abortion, they would not have to tell the tribe. The baby was born in April in Minneapolis and is currently living with the potential adoptive couple. "With current techniques, it's not feasible," an ecologist tells National Geographic. "Our government just grabbed that paper, and the surrounding evidence and public goodwill, and announced this policy." The country's native fauna has nearly halved in the 750 years since humans first arrived, and at least 51 species of bird have disappeared in the past few decades, per the Guardian. Most of the losses come from agriculture, but government officials also worry about the hit to the country's reputation as a destination for natural beauty. "Last year, tourism overtook agriculture as our biggest revenue earner," says Maggie Barry, the minister of conservation. "Our environment is what attracts people here." To that end, the government has announced a $6 billion project to eradicate the pests by 2050. It plans to start with new baits, species-specific poisons, and genetic tweaks to interfere with animal fertility, among other things.
