– With the threat of a terrorist attack looming over the Sochi Winter Olympics, the US government has taken the unusual step of hiring a private security firm to help get American athletes out of Russia, the New York Times reports. The firm, Global Rescue, has been hired by the US Ski and Snowboard Association and the US Olympic Committee to help athletes get to safety in the event of a terror attack. The company has six planes that it could use to get athletes to safety in or around Sochi, the CEO of Global Rescue tells NBC News. The US Olympic Committee says it is "working with the US Department of State, the local organizers, and the relevant law enforcement agencies in an effort to ensure that our delegation and other Americans traveling to Sochi are safe," but it hasn't said what would happen in the event of an evacuation. The US military has plans to use two warships in the Black Sea to evacuate American athletes if a terrorist attack occurs, but security experts say that's unlikely. "As far as being able to do things without Russian cooperation, it's basically a nonstarter," a former Russia expert in the Clinton White House tells NBC. "This is their territory, their country."

– "There's no battle at all," Brian Dalton says. "Maybe more of a balance of the sexes." The assistant professor at the University of British Columbia set out to find out whether women are physically superior to men when it comes to endurance. His "pretty definitive" conclusion: "Women can outlast men by a wide margin." In the study published in Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism, Dalton recruited eight men and nine women at a similar level of fitness and had them flex their feet against a set of sensors as quickly as they could 200 times. "We chose to measure foot movements because it makes use of calf muscles on the back of the leg, which are essential for practical, everyday tasks like standing and walking," Dalton says in a press release. "What we found is that males were faster and more powerful at first but became more fatigued much faster than females." Dalton says his results are consistent with previous research that shows males complete ultra-trail running events faster but females are considerably less tired by the end. "If ever an ultra-ultra-marathon is developed, women may well dominate in that arena," he says. – If developers have their way, Miami will soon have the largest mall in the US and the most expensive to ever be built. County commissioners have approved a plan to build the American Dream Miami, a 6.2-million-square-foot retail and entertainment complex with a water park, indoor pool, indoor ice rink, artificial ski slope, dozens of restaurants, and up to 1,200 stores, Business Insider reports. The $4 billion project, which will be located off the Florida Turnpike, will be twice the size of the current largest mall, the King of Prussia Mall in Pennsylvania. Developers Triple Five Group, which is also behind the Mall of America in Minneapolis, expect 30 million people to visit the property each year. That's about 10 million fewer visitors than the Mall of America, which generates nearly $2 billion annually for Minnesota, according to the developers. But not everyone is thrilled with the idea. A number of existing malls in Miami argue the city doesn't need another mall (especially of this scale), and environmentalists are concerned about potential water and energy use and impact on the city's stormwater system. During a meeting of the Miami-Dade County Commission on May 17, Miami resident Megan Sorbo called the project "an environmental abomination," according to the Miami Herald. Triple

– Jim Carrey says Cathriona White, the woman who killed herself in 2015, tried to extort him by falsely accusing him of giving her herpes, TMZ reports. White's estranged husband, Mark Burton, and her mother, Brigid Sweetman, are suing Carrey, claiming he supplied the drugs that killed her. According to the New York Post, Carrey will finally be forced to answer questions about White's death in a sworn deposition next week. "We are very much looking forward to Mr. Carrey finally being placed under oath next week and forced to answer the questions he has been dodging for years, such as why he provided illegal drugs to Ms. White, why he gave Ms. White multiple STDs and then lied about it, and why he has engaged in a public charade of innocence crafted by his handlers," says Michael Avenatti, the lawyer for Burton and Sweetman. Carrey's lawyer, Ray Boucher, has denied the actor's involvement in White's death, saying he had "nothing to do" with it.

– An Australian man is facing a charge of endangering life, health, or safety after police say he took his small plane—without wings or a steering wheel—to a local pub so he could get a drink, ABC News Australia reports. According to police, the 37-year-old man bought the Beechcraft plane from a man on the other side of town and took it to the Purple Pub in the town of Newman on Friday. Police say he was taking the plane home when he decided to stop at the pub. "The danger obviously taxiing a prop plane down Newman Drive, bearing in mind that kids have just come out of school," a local tells ABC. "It's a busy Friday afternoon. I know it's Newman, but we do get a fair bit of traffic." The plane was towed away from the pub and the man has been charged with an act likely to endanger the life, health, or safety of a person.

– If you've ever wondered what it's like to be tracked while visiting Disney parks, well, you're in luck: The Walt Disney Co. has been granted a patent for a "system and method using foot recognition to create a customized guest experience," the Orlando Sentinel reports. The system would involve a robot at the park's entrance that would place sensors "angled towards the ground" and take photos of at least one foot, according to the patent. The sensors would be "out of a person's line of sight, to 'unobtrusively capture' information," the patent states. Disney would then use the data to determine which rides and paths are most popular, how many people walk on those paths, and how much time they spend on those rides and other attractions, the Guardian reports. Disney says the technology would be less invasive than other forms of identification, such as facial recognition or retinal scans. "Less invasive manners, such as comparing a user's clothing or the like, can produce inaccurate results as many guests may have similar clothing or may change clothing, such putting on or taking off an outer layer or sweater, which can make detection unreliable," the patent states. – A 14-year-old boy is in custody after his 13-year-old sister was found dead in their home in Rocklin, Calif., on Tuesday, the Sacramento Bee reports. According to CBS Sacramento, police were called to the home around 11am Tuesday and found Ashley Wood dead in her bedroom. The mother found her daughter's body. Police say the boy fled the home and was found about a mile away in a field after a search. He was arrested and is being held in a juvenile detention facility. Police say they don't know if the boy and his sister were related. The victim was found with blunt-force trauma to the head. "It's a difficult situation. It's something you don't think you'll ever talk to your child about," a neighbor says.

– Reader's Digest has filed for bankruptcy for the second time in four years, as the 91-year-old publisher tries to shed half a billion dollars in debt. The company's biggest unsecured creditors include the Federal Trade Commission with an $8 million claim, Bloomberg reports. It plans to emerge from the Chapter 11 process with around $100 million in debt, and says it will continue to publish its magazines, including the flagship Reader's Digest, as it restructures. The company, which went public in 1990, was bought in 2007 by a private-equity group for $1.6 billion. "The brand will carry on, and that name has value," says the chief executive of a turnaround management firm.

– "HAPPY THANKSGIVING, your Country is starting to do really well," President Trump tweeted early Thanksgiving morning. "Jobs coming back, highest Stock Market EVER, Military getting really strong, we will build the WALL, V.A. taking care of our Vets, great Supreme Court Justice, RECORD CUT IN REGS, lowest unemployment in 17 years....!" USA Today has the full text of the president's message, which he delivered via video from Mar-a-Lago.

– Police have seized 254 guns and arrested 19 people in the biggest gun bust in New York City's history. Authorities say a pair of South Carolina perps smuggled guns into the city on cheap buses, then sold them on the black market, the AP reports. An undercover police officer posing as a gun broker bought some of the weapons in dozens of transactions. "There is no doubt that the seizure of these guns—the largest bust in the city’s history—has saved lives," said Mayor Bloomberg. "For that reason, every New Yorker, in every part of our city, owes a debt of thanks to all those involved in this investigation." The investigation began last year, when police learned that guns were being sold in a Brooklyn neighborhood, the New York Daily News reports. Police found aspiring rapper Mathew Best in the same building, and he helped Walter Walker, also of Sanford, NC, transfer the guns to Brooklyn. Walker "made trips to New York City practically every week and sometimes multiple times a week just to sell guns," said Police Commissioner Ray Kelly. The guns sold for at least three times their original price.

– NSA leaker Edward Snowden has asked for asylum in 21 countries, including China, France, Ireland, and Venezuela, according to WikiLeaks—but eight of those countries say his request is invalid, and Russia says he has now withdrawn his request to stay in Russia, the BBC reports. Venezuela says it hasn't received Snowden's asylum request, but Venezuela's President Nicolas Maduro is on a visit to Moscow and says Snowden "deserved the world's protection" for doing "something very important for humanity." Maduro says Snowden "abandoned his intention [of staying] and his request to be able to stay in Russia" after learning of Vladimir Putin's warning that he should stop "harming our American partners." Meanwhile, India says it has turned down Snowden's request for asylum, saying it has "concluded that we see no reason to accede to that request," the BBC reports.

According to the Baltimore Sun, Tawon Boyd called 911 himself because he was feeling "confused and paranoid" and needed an ambulance. The police report states Boyd was "under the influence of a narcotic and/or suffering [REDACTED] and needed to be taken to the hospital for emergency evaluation." But Boyd's lawyer, Latoya Francis-Williams, says Boyd called 911 himself because he was feeling "disoriented" and needed help. Francis-Williams says Boyd was "literally attacked" by police, who used their body weight to keep him on the ground. The report states Boyd was "kind of foaming at the mouth or spitting and his body goes limp." Boyd was taken to the hospital, where he was pronounced dead. The police report states Boyd was "combative" and "confused and paranoid" when officers arrived at his home. Boyd asked officers to enter the home, and the report states he was "confused and paranoid" and asked a neighbor to call the police. – President Obama marked the 75th anniversary of the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor on Tuesday with a plea to never turn inward and to "resist the urge to demonize those who are different," the Washington Post reports. On Wednesday, President-elect Donald Trump took to Twitter to complain about the "many inflammatory President O statements and roadblocks." "Doing my best to disregard the many inflammatory President O statements and roadblocks," he tweeted. "Thought it was going to be a smooth transition - NOT!" Trump went on to slam the Obama administration for not vetoing a UN resolution condemning Israeli settlements in the West Bank and East Jerusalem. "We cannot continue to let Israel be treated with such total disdain and disrespect," he tweeted. "They used to have a great friend in the U.S., but ... not anymore." In another tweet, he said the "beginning of the end" was the "horrible" Iran nuclear deal and the UN resolution. "Stay strong Israel, January 20th is fast approaching!" The White House declined to comment on Trump's tweets. Earlier Wednesday, Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida that he had a "very nice conversation" with Obama.

– President Obama today ramped up sanctions against Russia in the wake of Crimea's vote to secede from Ukraine, reports USA Today. He announced that he was freezing the US assets of seven Russian officials for their support of Crimea's referendum to join Russia. "We are imposing sanctions on specific individuals for undermining the sovereignty, territorial integrity, and government of Ukraine," said Obama. "We are making it clear that there are consequences for their actions." He added that the US is "prepared to take additional steps to impose further political and economic costs" if Russia doesn't back down. The White House also announced sanctions against four Ukrainians involved in the separatist effort in Crimea. Those include Crimea-based separatist leaders Sergey Aksyonov and Vladimir Konstantinov; former Ukrainian presidential chief of staff Viktor Medvedchuk; and former President of Ukraine Viktor Yanukovych. Obama said the US stands "ready to take additional steps to impose further political and economic costs" if Russia doesn't back down.

In fact, modern engines don't even need to be warmed up at all, according to Chris Lague, a service writer at Partner Tire & Service in Colchester, Vt. "Most cars are engineered now so they'll actually warm up faster if you drive them than if you just let it sit there," Lague tells USA Today. But if you're in Vermont, where a law was passed in 2014 that prohibits idling for more than five minutes out of any 60-minute period, you're out of luck. "It so happens cars fit their law," Lague says. "You don't have to sit there for 10 minutes. Even though there are less emissions now than ever, you're still emitting something. The state rightfully wants to protect the environment." But not everyone is convinced. "I'm old school," Bill Brisson tells the Burlington Free Press. "You don't want to start the car and start going down the road immediately. Let the crankshaft pull the oil to the top of the heads and warm up." Beer and wine will still be allowed in rooms of students 21 and older, but mixed drinks and shots of hard alcohol will be banned, the San Jose Mercury News reports. "Our intention is not a total prohibition of a substance, but rather a targeted approach that limits high-risk behavior," says the director of the university's Office of Alcohol Policy and Education. The move comes after several incidents on campus, including the rape of an unconscious woman by former student Brock Turner, who was sentenced to just six months in jail, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. "Our focus is on the high risk of the rapid consumption of hard alcohol," Castro says. "We want to make sure that our students are aware that this behavior is unacceptable and that it will not be tolerated." Under the new policy, alcohol will only be allowed at parties hosted by student organizations and residences where graduate students live.

– The taste of beer doesn't just make you want to drink it—it may actually trigger the pleasure chemical dopamine in the brain, a new study suggests. Indiana University researchers gave 49 male volunteers a tiny taste of beer (half an ounce, or 15 milliliters) over 15 minutes; at other times, they were given a sports drink or water, LiveScience reports. When the men tasted the beer, their brains showed a boost in the chemical linked to pleasure. "We believe this is the first experiment in humans to show that the taste of an alcoholic drink alone, without any intoxicating effect from the alcohol, can elicit this dopamine activity in the brain's reward centers," says the study's senior author. The men also reported higher beer cravings after tasting the beer than water or the sports drink. The findings suggest that even the taste of beer (without the intoxicating effects of alcohol) can trigger that flow of striatal dopamine in the brain. The findings suggest that the jacking-up of dopamine levels in response to alcohol-related triggers could be a hereditary risk factor for alcoholism. – A Montana water and sewer district is suing the National Park Service over arsenic in wastewater coming from Yellowstone National Park, Courthouse News reports. According to the Billings Gazette, the Gardiner Water and Sewer Treatment District first noticed high levels of arsenic in sewage coming from the town of Mammoth, which is just inside the park, in February 2015. The district's engineer said the arsenic was coming from manholes or holes in underground pipes and wasn't coming from the park, but it needed to be addressed since 95% of the arsenic to the treatment system was coming from Yellowstone wastewater. The district says it tried to work with the Park Service for years to resolve the issue, but it couldn't get a response in time for the district to take on an estimated $2 million sludge treatment pond replacement as part of its routine maintenance. “Given that the district has been directed by the Montana Department of Environmental Quality to dispose of the sludge and replace the liners in its treatment ponds and cannot await the Park Service’s responses any longer, it has been compelled to file suit,” the district said in its lawsuit. The district claims Yellowstone National Park is creating a "danger to public safety" by not addressing the arsenic. It also says the park breached an oral contract to help pay for the sludge

– Three inmates, including two accused of capital murder, escaped from a rural Alabama jail early this morning after one of them started screaming, saying another was very sick, the local sheriff tells CNN. The inmates jumped the jailer, stole his keys and cell phone, then fled on foot. The sheriff says they were either picked up or had a vehicle waiting for them. The FBI and US Marshals are assisting in the search. "I've got three bad inmates, two capital murders, and one armed robber, who are on foot," the sheriff tells the Choctaw Sun-Advocate. "They took off from the jail." Two of the escapees, Demarcus Woodward, 23, and Germayel Culbert, 32, are accused of killing two people at a private club, while the third, Justin Terrell Gordon, 23, is accused of robbing a convenience store. The three were locked down in a single cell around 2am, after one started screaming, saying another of them was very sick, the sheriff says. The jailer was treated and released at a local hospital.

– Robert Zemeckis' Flight tells the true story of Capt. Whip Whitaker, who crash-landed a plane after high levels of alcohol and cocaine were found in his system. Denzel Washington stars as Whitaker, and critics are mostly impressed: "Flight soars when it crashes and crashes when it soars," writes Roger Ebert in the Chicago Sun-Times. But it "goes into its own tailspin" when the focus shifts from an intriguing aeronautical drama to a bland psychodrama, as boozy Whip refuses to admit he's an alcoholic—albeit a remarkably functioning alcoholic, which raises another problem. "Flight reminds us of what Washington can do when a role hits him with a challenge that would floor a lesser actor," writes Ty Burr in the Boston Globe. "He's a ball of fire, and his detailed, depth-charged, bruisingly true performance will be talked about for years." Betsy Sharkey agrees in the Los Angeles Times. " Zemeckis gives good plane crash. He did it well in the early frames of Castaway, and the one here is even better," she writes. " Alas, this isn’t a direct Flight."

Following Kohlhepp's arrest, he confessed to a 2003 quadruple slaying at a motorcycle shop in the small town of Chesnee, said Spartanburg County Sheriff Chuck Wright. – Stephen Colbert sat down with two members of Pussy Riot last night on the Colbert Report, and the results were, as Mediaite puts it, "so sharp, funny, and at times poignant, that the presence of the translator only served to hang the viewer on every word." Nadya Tolokonnikova and Masha Alyokhina talked about their two-year stint in prison, Vladimir Putin, and Russia's anti-gay laws, among other things. Click for the full video.

– Four years after Japan's worst nuclear disaster since Chernobyl, the job of decommissioning the Fukushima Dai-ichi plant is officially under way. The New York Times reports workers with Tokyo Electric Power Co. began removing protective covers from one of the reactors on Tuesday. The covers were installed in October 2011 to stop radioactive materials from escaping; they're expected to be removed by the end of next year, and the spent fuel rods will be extracted in 2020. According to Reuters, Tepco hopes to start extracting the fuel rods in 2020. Meanwhile, tens of thousands of evacuees remain in temporary housing, and electricity bills in Japan have risen 25% since the disaster. The government has approved an increase in compensation payments to $57.18 billion, Reuters reports.

– The legal team prosecuting Dominique Strauss-Kahn on sexual assault charges has gone on the offensive, enlisting a prominent French lawyer to help them track down Strauss-Kahn's past victims. Thibault de Montbrial, 42, is not considered "one of the star criminal lawyers in France," a legal correspondent for Le Monde tells France 24. But he is "very respected and has worked on some of the big French political and financial cases," she says. Montbrial has represented victims of the Karachi bombings and Tunisia's former president, and has also worked on high-profile cases in France, including the Clearstream trial, in which he defended a former EADS head accused of spying. He is not known for working on rape or sexual assault cases, the correspondent adds. The maid's lawyers have urged other women to come forward if they have been attacked by Strauss-Kahn, and Montbrial tells Reuters that he was hired to "see if we can contact other victims."

– Iran's president-elect, Hasan Rouhani, has made it clear that he's willing to pursue a more moderate course than Mahmoud Ahmadinejad did, and he's calling on the government and the country's powerful clergy to come together for the good of the people. "There shouldn't be any rift or division between the government or the clergy, especially at a time when people have pinned their hopes on seeing some sort of change in society," he said today, according to Reuters. Rouhani has also called for greater Internet access and a loosening of the "security atmosphere" in the country. He has also criticized the state broadcaster for ignoring issues inside the country. "When IRIB airs the birth of a panda in China but nothing about unpaid workers protesting, it is obvious that the people and youth will ignore it," he tweeted, referring to the state's monopoly over terrestrial television.

– The European Space Agency's plummeting satellite has burned up in the atmosphere and at least 25% of it is believed to have survived, reports Reuters. The 1-ton Goce satellite was launched in 2009 to map Earth's gravity. It ran out of fuel a month ago. "Goce survived for a few minutes longer than we expected—but since re-entry are difficult to predict, this is not very surprising," says a spokesman for the Esa's Space Debris Office. It's the first uncontrolled re-entry for the space agency in more than 25 years, notes the BBC. "No damage to property has been reported from any debris," says a status report on the website of the European Space Agency.

– When Seth Dixon dropped his engagement ring into Kansas City's Loose Park Pond earlier this month, it fell through the murky water and into the pond below. The couple, who have been dating for four years, decided to pop the question on a bridge over the pond, but when Dixon tried to pop the question on the bridge's railing, he dropped the ring into the water as he jumped in to pop the question, KSHB reports. That's when Michael Long decided to get up there and help. "I had a metal detector. I just thought it would just be nice to get up there, help a random couple out and find the ring before someone else found it," Long tells KSHB. On Saturday, Long spent two days and three hours searching the pond, finding 25 nails, a toy car, and the ring. He gave it to a friend of the couple on Tuesday. Dixon and Ruth Salas, who were on Jimmy Kimmel Tuesday night to talk about the rescue, posted about it on Facebook Wednesday before flying back to Kansas City from California. They also got a new ring, and Kimmel gave them another.

Thanks to a website called Field Expedition Mongolia, more than 7,000 people around the world have been helping scientist Albert Lin search for the Mongolian emperor's tomb. Volunteers are instructed to look for objects on satellite images of the region, from "roads" to "rivers" to "ancient structures." They are also told to tag places as "other" if they see something strange. “What a computer can’t do is look for ‘weird things,’ but when you ask a human brain, you don’t have to tell it what ‘weird’ is; we know,” Lin tells the Washington Post. Last summer, Lin and his colleagues were in Mongolia inspecting the places tagged by the online volunteers. “We’d literally jump on horses or get in a helicopter and go check it out,” says Lin. “Every tag was weighted on how many other people tagged the same thing.” Some volunteers led Lin to unexpected finds, like a herd of sheep on a satellite photo that looked like an ancient structure. “These are hard to find on horseback, but from space and in the images, you can

– "We're going to get hit with a storm like we haven't seen before in the Houston area," a National Hurricane Center forecaster tells the Houston Chronicle. Hurricane Harvey is expected to make landfall Friday night as a Category 3 storm, the strongest to hit the US in more than a decade, the AP reports. The latest: The storm is expected to dump 20 to 30 inches of rain on the Houston area, with up to 50 inches in some places, until it moves out over the Gulf of Mexico, the Chronicle reports. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has declared a state of disaster in 30 counties, NBC News reports. The National Hurricane Center says the eye of the storm is expected to make landfall Friday night between Port Aransas and Corpus Christi, CNN reports. The storm is expected to be the strongest to hit the continental US so far this year, the AP reports. President Trump has called Abbott to discuss the storm, KVUE reports. Trump told the governor that the federal government will help Texas prepare and get through the storm.

Authorities believe the burns may have been caused by lighter fluid or gasoline. A GoFundMe page has been set up to raise funds for Fergus' medical bills.

– Hidekichi Miyazaki may be 105, but he's still running fast. The Japanese centenarian set a 100-meter world record yesterday in Kyoto, clocking 42.22 seconds, USA Today reports. Miyazaki, who was born in 1910, recently celebrated his 105th birthday. "I shed tears of disappointment because I was not in good condition," he says. "I am not satisfied with today's time. But I am satisfied that I could cross the finish line." Miyazaki—dubbed the "Golden Bolt" by the Guinness Book of World Records—says he wants to race Usain Bolt. "I would still love to compete against him," he tells AFP. "Two or three years ago Bolt came to Japan and said he wanted to meet me. There was a call about it but I was out and he left without meeting me. I felt deeply sorry." Miyazaki, who trains for races by taking a catnap in his early 90s, says he'll "have to train harder" but "I'll say this: I'm proud of my health. Training was going splendidly, so I had set myself a target of 35 seconds. I can still go faster."

– "This video is not from Miami International Airport." So tweeted Miami International Airport on Sunday after White House social media director Dan Scavino tweeted a video he said was from the airport as Hurricane Irma raged nearby, the Washington Post reports. "This video is not from Miami International Airport," the airport tweeted. Scavino deleted the tweet and replied to the airport. CNN notes that it's not clear why Scavino thought the video he tweeted was from the airport, or how he was verifying the information he was sharing with President Trump and Mike Pence.

The Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party has sent a letter to police demanding that the man be arrested, the Guardian reports. "CIA station chief is not a diplomatic post, therefore he does not enjoy any diplomatic immunity and is within the bounds of domestic laws of Pakistan," the letter says. The party says it hopes the man will reveal the names of the pilots of the drone, the AP reports. The strike was one of the first to take place outside the country's tribal areas, where most drone attacks have taken place. Khan has been a vocal critic of drone strikes, and his party has blocked supplies to NATO troops in Afghanistan, the Guardian notes.

– Despite President Trump's plans to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act, a majority of Americans still support the health care law, according to a new poll from Politico and Morning Consult. The poll found that 45% of registered voters approve of ObamaCare, compared to 45% who oppose it. "As the threat of the Affordable Care Act's repeal has moved from notional to concrete, our weekly polling has shown an uptick in the law's popularity, and fewer voters support repealing the law," Morning Consult's co-founder and chief research officer tells Politico. The poll found that voters were split on whether to completely repeal the ACA or partially repeal it. Some 24% said they wanted to completely repeal the law, 27% wanted to partially repeal it, and 26% said they wanted to see the law "kept as is." Voters were split on nine other provisions of the ACA, with 57% saying they wanted to keep the individual mandate requiring most Americans to have health coverage and 57% saying they wanted to keep the Medicaid provision allowing people under age 26 to be covered by their parents' health plans, CNN reports. – A 17-year-old high school student in New York City killed herself after being caught cheating on a German exam, the New York Daily News reports. Omotayo Adeoye was sitting in the back of a German class at City College High School for Math, Science, and Engineering when her teacher noticed she was using her phone. The teacher took the phone away and confronted Adeoye, who "said she was sorry," a classmate tells CBS New York. Adeoye then left the class and went to Fort Washington Park along the Hudson River. She left her phone and wallet on a rock and walked into the water, where she sank beneath the surface. A fisherman says he tried to stop her. "I said, 'Come here, come here, don’t go to the water,'" he tells the New York Post. "She was just crying, crying all the time." Police haven't recovered a body, but they're looking for a female who went into the water on Thursday. Adeoye, who was planning to become a medical doctor, left behind a suicide note that read, "I just want to go away forever on the bottom of the river," the Daily News reports.

The agency defines domestic terrorism as "Americans attacking Americans based on U.S.-based extremist ideologies." It's currently hunting down seven people charged with such crimes. Five are women.

– The World Cup may be over, but that doesn't mean residents of Samara, Russia, are letting go of their bathing suits. The city's water company on Wednesday asked residents to shower in pairs in an effort to cut down on water use, the Guardian reports. "Thousands of the city's visitors, who also consume water, are contributing to the increase," Samarskiye Kommunalniye Systemy said in a press release. Samara is one of 12 host cities for this year's tournament.

The third volume of the Joseph Smith papers, which includes the printer's manuscript of the Book of Mormon, was unveiled at a news conference in Salt Lake City yesterday. The photos show different angles of a stone that is dark brown with lighter brown swirls. The photos also show a weathered leather pouch where the stone was stored that is believed to be made by one of Joseph Smith's wives, Emma Smith. The church has always possessed the stone, which was transported across the country during Mormon pioneers' trek from Illinois to Utah in the mid-1800s. But it decided to publish the photos to allow people who prefer visuals to words to better understand the religion's roots, said Richard Turley, assistant church historian. The stone will remain in the vault. "The picture brings a kind of tangibility to something that has been previously been talked about just in words," Turley said. – Two SUNY Brockport students have been charged with animal cruelty after a photo of a dog doing a keg stand at an off-campus party went viral, the Democrat and Chronicle reports. The photo was tweeted Sunday by @SUNYPartyStory, which is affiliated with the State University of New York system. "Keg stands n Bits!" read the caption. The photo of the black lab, Mya, being held by its hind legs with the keg's nozzle in its mouth quickly went viral, Time Warner Cable News reports, prompting an investigation into animal abuse. Shane Oliver, 20, and Robert Yates, 19, were both charged with torturing and injuring animals. Police say Mya's owner was not home when the photo was taken, and the dog is in good condition. "Don't get me wrong," one SUNY Brockport student tweeted. "I love the nightlife in Brockport, but making a dog do a keg stand is ridiculous."

– Dr. Conrad Murray was found guilty today of involuntary manslaughter in the death of Michael Jackson, and immediately was taken to jail, reports the Los Angeles Times. Murray's attorney had argued that the cardiologist should remain free until his sentencing, but the judge disagreed. “This is not a crime involving a mistake of judgment,” he said. “This is a crime where the end result was the death of a human being. That factor demonstrates rather dramatically that the public should be protected.” Murray faces up to four years in prison and a minimum sentence of probation. TMZ reports that he'll be assigned a single cell, with an "escort" to keep an eye on him, and won't be allowed to mingle with the general jail population.

– Pole vaulting is one of the most dangerous events in college track and field, with more than two dozen injuries reported to the National Center for Catastrophic Sports Injury Research between 1982 and 1998, according to a study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association. The injuries—which included catastrophic head injuries and a thoracic spine fracture that resulted in paraplegia—occur when an athlete lands with his or her head on the hard ground surrounding the vault box, misses the landing pad by a few feet, or lands with their body on the landing pad and their head stuck in the box, NBC News reports. The study found that 53% of injuries occurred when an athlete landed with their body on the landing pad and their head on the ground surrounding the vault box. The researchers, who reviewed data on 135 vaulters from 15 universities, found that 41% of injuries occurred during the vaulting portion of the season, with the most common injury being to the low back. The researchers, who found that the odds of injury were 2.7 times greater in vaulters with multiple prior injuries, recommend that the minimum landing pad size be increased to 20 feet, and that the rule requiring soft surfaces next to the landing pad be enforced. – Israel has begun evacuating Jewish settlers from five illegal outposts in the West Bank, but it's not clear whether the government's novel plan to save the homes will work. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wants to save the homes by slicing them into smaller pieces and shipping them to a site on the West Bank, where they will be reassembled, the AP reports. Construction experts say it would take a week for each apartment to be dismantled and reassembled, and the cost could be as high as $125,000 for each apartment. "Sawing is not the problem. The problem is how to put them together again," says one. "It's absurd." Netanyahu says he came up with the plan to save the homes after Israel's Supreme Court ordered the outposts to be demolished. "By the first of July, the plan is to have the buildings vacated and sealed," a government official said this week. "The prime minister said he wanted these buildings relocated, not destroyed." But Palestinians say the plan goes against international law and will only make things worse. "This is a black day for us," said one Ulpana resident. "This is a moral and legal injustice."

– A 1-year-old from Georgia has been named Gerber's 2018 "spokesbaby" after an exhaustive search that saw more than 140,000 entries, People reports. Lucas Warren is the first child with Down syndrome to win the title since the contest began in 2010. "He's very outgoing and never meets a stranger," mom Cortney Warren tells Today. "He loves to play, loves to laugh, and loves to make other people laugh." Lucas and his parents will receive a $50,000 cash prize and will have their photo documented on Gerber's social media platforms. "We're hoping this will impact everyone—that it will shed a little bit of light on the special needs community and help more individuals with special needs be accepted and not limited," dad Jason Warren says. "They have the potential to change the world, just like everybody else."

"You have this bloke presented to you as the local nutter, yet he was tremendously compos mentis," Scott tells the Daily Mail. "He spoke brilliantly. He was very clever. He nearly had the US ambassador crying into his tea, impressed with wonderment." Scott, 67, was born in Zambia to a British mother and Scottish father, and he has known Mugabe for decades. He called Mugabe "very sensible" when he addressed a recent trade summit in Malawi. "What has happened is very cruel and nasty and doesn’t reflect well on anybody. But it is worth trying to understand what is happening, rather than saying it’s the lunatic act of one man. It’s not."

"We found ancient DNA evidence of wheat that was not seen in Britain for another 2,000 years," says lead researcher Robin Allaby of the University of Warwick. "However, it was already being grown in southern Europe. This is incredibly exciting because it means Bouldnor's inhabitants were not as isolated as previously thought. – A Harvard graduate and his Venezuela-born husband are fighting to keep him in the US. Henry Velandia, a salsa dancer and teacher, came to the US in 2002 and married Josh Vandiver in August. But because of the Defense of Marriage Act, Velandia is in danger of being deported to his home country, Fox News reports. “It’s frustrating to find my passion and the love of my life, yet still run the risk of deportation,” he says. Vandiver, a PhD student at Princeton, met Velandia online and moved to the US four years ago. “I never imagined that I would face this kind of discrimination from my own country and potentially have to flee it to be with the one I love,” Vandiver says. The couple is appealing to members of Congress to stop deportation hearings against foreign-born spouses of US citizens. “Part of our fight is to bring awareness to people and make them see what’s really going on in this issue that nobody is talking about,” Velandia says.

– The Darrell Issa-Eric Holder showdown over Fast and Furious just got a lot more heated. In a letter to President Obama today, the House Oversight Committee chair accused the president of either withholding information or having his aides conspire with the Justice Department to hide information from Congress, Politico reports. "Either you or your most senior advisors were involved in managing Operation Fast & Furious and the fallout from it ... or, you are asserting a presidential power that you know to be unjustified solely for the purpose of further obstructing a congressional investigation," he wrote. The letter comes as the House prepares to vote this week on whether to hold Holder in contempt of Congress for refusing to turn over documents related to the botched program. The White House has said it wasn't involved in the program, and a spokesman for Obama said Issa's "analysis has as much merit as his absurd contention that Operation Fast and Furious was created in order to promote gun control."

"Anyone have a connect for coke," one member of the Pi Kappa Alpha chapter wrote. "Not me, a friend wants, lol." Another offered to sell Adderall for non-brothers: "30mg of addy 10 starting tomorrow. 15 for non brothers." The screenshots were sent to media outlets by an anonymous FIU administrator. The university says it is investigating possible violations of its code of student conduct. The fraternity says it "had no previous knowledge of this Facebook group" and was informed of its existence Tuesday. The Facebook posts "are definitely not the exception," an expert on hazing tells the Herald. "They are the rule."

– A man is brain dead and five others are seriously ill after taking part in a French drug trial, the BBC reports. According to the Guardian, the men, aged 28 to 49, were in good health until taking the drug on Jan. 7. One started feeling ill on Sunday and the other five after that. The drug in question was part of a clinical trial for Portuguese pharmaceutical firm Bial. According to the BBC, the trial was conducted by a French company called Biotrial, which has a reputation for conducting such trials. Biotrial says it followed "international regulations and Biotrial's procedures were followed at every stage." The drug in question was administered to 90 people in the trial. The BBC reports there is no known antidote to the drug. One of the men is brain dead, three are suffering from "handicap that could be irreversible," and another has neurological problems. All of the patients in the trial are currently in the hospital in Rennes, France. The drug in question is not a cannabis-based painkiller, according to the BBC. – A 23-week-old baby in China has survived a "spontaneous abortion"—a procedure in which the mother's cervix is completely blocked, the Telegraph reports. The baby was delivered by C-section last week in Chongqing, and she's now in stable condition in an incubator. According to the Daily Mail, doctors had warned the parents the baby would be born severely premature and would have no chance of survival. But the baby girl, who is now eight days old, managed to survive the abortion. "The fact the baby survived a 'spontaneous abortion' was very rare," says the hospital's chief of Paediatrics. "It is almost impossible for a baby to live through something like this." The baby was born at just 23 weeks, weighing just 660 grams, and medical staff say she hasn't fully developed yet and has had some complications from the medication and nutrients she's been given. Local media has dubbed her "chopstick girl," a reference to the fact that she's the same height as a chopstick. (A 2-year-old in the US also survived a C-section.)

– If you're having a hard time understanding what someone is saying, just say "huh." Dutch, Icelandic, Mandarin Chinese, the West African Siwu, and the Australian aboriginal Murrinh-Patha all have the same version of the word "Huh," according to a study published Friday in PLOS One. The word, which is defined as "a simple syllable with a low-front central vowel, glottal onset consonant, if any, and questioning," appears to be "universal" in all 10 languages studied by Dutch, Icelandic, Mandarin Chinese, the West African Siwu, and the Australian aboriginal Murrinh-Patha, according to a press release. "Without words like this, we would be unable to signal when we have problems with hearing or understanding what was said, and our conversations would be constantly derailed by communicative mishaps," the release states. The study was part of a larger investigation into language and social interaction, according to the European Research Council. The researchers traveled to cities and remote villages on five continents to listen to native speakers of 10 languages. Their nearly 200 recordings of casual conversations revealed that there are versions of "Huh?" in every language they studied—and they sound remarkably similar. – E-book subscription service Oyster will be shutting down over the next few months, its founders announced in a blog post today, though they didn't go into much detail. "Looking forward, we feel this is best seized by taking on new opportunities to fully realize our vision for ebooks," they wrote. "We believe more than ever that the phone will be the primary reading device globally over the next decade," they wrote. "Looking forward, we feel this is best seized by taking on new opportunities to fully realize our vision for ebooks." The company, which launched in 2012 and offered a subscription service for e-books for $9.95 a month, didn't do well enough to compete with Amazon's $10-a-month Kindle Unlimited service, CNET reports. Google confirmed that it has hired "a portion of the Oyster team" to work at Google Play Books. Sources tell Re/code that CEO Eric Stromberg and co-founders Andrew Brown and Willem Van Lancker are among the Oyster team members joining Google. The sources say Google will end up paying investors, who put a reported $17 million into the company, for the right to hire some of its staff. – West Virginia's water may be safe to drink again, but the investigation into a chemical spill that tainted the Elk River is far from over. Federal investigators are expected to arrive at the site of the leak today, the New York Times reports. The US Chemical Safety Board says it has asked the state three years ago to create a program to prevent accidents in the Kanawha Valley, and the state hasn't produced it. "We need to look at our entire system and give some serious thought to making some serious reform and valuing our natural resources over industry interests," says the executive director of the West Virginia Rivers Coalition. Meanwhile, some 300,000 people in Charleston and surrounding areas remain without running water for a fifth day, the Wall Street Journal reports. "The numbers look good, and like last night, they are very encouraging," said Gov. Earl Ray Tomblin yesterday. "I believe we're at a point where we can say we're seeing light at the end of the tunnel." But he warned that it could take weeks to get the water back to normal.

Strauss-Kahn, who is still facing a civil suit from Nafissatou Diallo, said the encounter with the maid "did not involve violence, constraint or aggression" and that she "lied" in accusing him of attacking her, the BBC reports. – The mysterious disappearances of ships in the western North Atlantic may be caused by huge bubbles of methane gas rising from the ocean floor, Australian researchers say. The bubbles could swamp a ship if they turned to foam and sank it quickly, the researchers say. The phenomenon is known as a "gas bubble theory," but no one has ever seen such an eruption, Reuters notes. The Australian researchers discovered the huge methane deposits in the North Sea while investigating mysterious craters in Siberia. "Sonar surveys of the ocean floor in the North Sea have revealed large quantities of methane hydrates and eruption sites," the researchers write in the American Journal of Physics. "A recent survey revealed the presence of a sunken vessel within the center of one particularly large eruption site, now known as the Witches Hole." Click here for more.

One of the men pulled a gun and started shooting when a second man tried to stop them. Police say the mall was locked down after the shooting, but it has since reopened. Authorities say the mall will remain closed Monday while police investigate.

The system wirelessly links vehicles to traffic-management computers in certain US cities. Drivers see the countdown in the instrument cluster. Once four seconds are left before the traffic light turns green, the counter stops so drivers will look up. If the system thinks a driver won't make it through a green light, it will also start counting down as if the light were red. The system is available on the 2017 Q7 SUV and A4 sedan built after June 1. Drivers must opt for the Connect Prime service, which costs $199 for six months. In an industry first, German carmaker Audi is equipping its latest models with a feature that will allow cars to show when a red light is about to turn green. The feature, which allows the cars to receive traffic light information in areas that have centralized control, will roll out city by city. The carmaker expects five to seven cities to be up and running by the end of this year, though Audi won't say which ones are expected to be first. The list includes Syrian government forces and their allied "shabiha" militias for the first time, the BBC reports. The UN special representative for children and armed conflict said that while new crises erupted in 2011, "with a heavy toll on children such as in Syria, and also in Libya, violations against girls and boys have come to an end in other parts of the world." Meanwhile, the US has expressed fears that the Syrian government "may be organizing another massacre" in the town of Haffa, where UN military observers have been denied access. "The UN made a particular appeal to be able to get into Haffa because it had heard concerning reports about regime plans," a State Department spokeswoman said. "At the same time, if you follow Syrian media, they were claiming that the opposition would cause a massacre."

– The Class of 2012 graduated college with an average debt of $29,400, according to an annual report from the Institute for College Access and Success. That's up from $26,600 in 2011, USA Today reports. "Rising tuition and high tuition are certainly a contributor to increasing student debt, but it's far from the full picture," says the institute's research director. "Family incomes and families' own ability to contribute to college costs has just been stagnant." Parents' income and savings are covering just 27% of college costs, down from 37% in 2010. And many grads are struggling to find work that will pay enough to pay off their loans. For-profit colleges are especially prone to student debt, the report found, with 68% of graduates having debt, compared to just 68% and $23,450 for private colleges. The highest debt load was in Delaware, with an average debt of $30,000. Private colleges in Massachusetts and Oregon had the lowest debt loads, around $49,000 and $49,000 respectively.

– The United States is retaliating against Russia by forcing closure of its consulate in San Francisco and scaling back its diplomatic presence in Washington and New York, the AP reports. The State Department says move is in response to the Kremlin forcing a cut in US diplomatic staff in Moscow. Spokesman Heather Nauert says the move brings the US and Russia into "parity," with each having three consulates in the other country. Moscow forced the cut in American diplomatic staff earlier this year in retaliation for US sanctions. Washington had to reduce its diplomatic staff by 755 people. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson had said the US would respond by September. The Russian offices must close by Saturday. The order affects Russia's "chancery annex" in Washington and a "consular annex" in New York.

– President Trump met for more than two hours with Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the G20 summit in Hamburg, Germany, on Friday, and the Guardian reports that the two leaders are expected to emerge from the meeting with little more than a vague agreement to set up a working group on non-interference in future elections. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson said Trump was "rightly focused on how do we move forward" on the issue, while Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Trump had told Putin he accepted the Russian leader's denials of involvement in the hacking of the 2016 US election. The two leaders were joined in the meeting by their respective foreign ministers and two translators, meaning there was no chance of leaks, and the room was personalized, meaning no one in Trump's team was present who was more skeptical about Russia, such as national security adviser HR McMaster and senior Russia adviser Fiona Hill. Trump tweeted about the meeting Friday afternoon, writing, "I look forward to all meetings today with world leaders, including my meeting with Vladimir Putin. Much to discuss. I will represent our country well and fight for its interests!" Reuters reports that the Kremlin says the two had a "brief" handshake, and that the leaders will meet again later Friday in the afternoon.

His spokesman says he feels "very, very pained" when he hears about it and compares Mugabe's eyes to that of Nelson Mandela, who was reportedly sensitive to bright lights, the BBC reports. "In the case of Mandela, if you remember, you were not allowed to even use flashes whenever he was in the room," George Charamba says. "That is what happens at 93, and Mandela, I do not think lived as long as the president did. Let us disabuse ourselves." – It's that time of year again: time to welcome 2017 and make up for lost time due to Earth's slowing rotation, Phys.org reports. According to the International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service, the extra second will be used to align astronomical time with Coordinated Universal Time, which is "extremely stable and has been determined by atomic clocks since 1967," per the Paris Observatory. For those living in Coordinated Universal Time countries (including the UK, Ireland, and West African nations), the extra second will make the year's final minute 61 seconds long. For others, the timing will be determined by the time zone they live in, relative to UTC. "This extra second, or leap second, makes it possible to align astronomical time, which is irregular and determined by Earth's rotation, with UTC which is extremely stable and has been determined by atomic clocks since 1967," the Paris Observatory said in a statement.

The card, which could be used at airports, hospitals, and other places where it's likely to be used, would be "biometric," meaning it would be unique to the US and would not be issued to anyone who isn't a citizen. – Morley Safer, the iconic 60 Minutes correspondent who won rave reviews for his 1965 report on US troops burning huts in Vietnam, has died at age 84. He had been in declining health since announcing his retirement last week, the AP reports. "Morley was one of the most important journalists in any medium, ever," said CBS Chairman and CEO Leslie Moonves. "He broke ground in war reporting and made a name that will forever be synonymous with 60 Minutes. He was also a gentleman, a scholar, a great raconteur—all of those things and much more to generations of colleagues, his legion of friends, and his family, to whom all of us at CBS offer our sincerest condolences over the loss of one of CBS' and journalism's greatest treasures." Safer was "a fixture, one of our pillars, and an inspiration in many ways," Moonves said. "No correspondent had more extraordinary range, from war reporting to coverage of every aspect of modern culture."

– The USDA has approved a new genetically modified potato, but one of the company's oldest business partners—McDonald's—has not. The fast-food giant says it doesn't use genetically modified potatoes, the Idaho Statesman reports. "McDonald's USA does not source GMO potatoes, nor do we have current plans to change our sourcing practices," the company said in a statement. The USDA this month gave Idaho-based JR Simplot permission to begin commercial planting of its new spud, called the "Innate" potato. The company altered the potato's DNA so it produces less acrylamide, which is suspected to be a human carcinogen. Potatoes naturally produce the chemical when they're cooked at high temperatures. The potato is also engineered to resist bruising. Simplot is a major supplier of french fries, hash browns, and other potato products for restaurant chains like McDonald's. This isn't the first time the fast-food industry has resisted GMO potatoes. More than a decade ago, Monsanto brought its bug-resistant "New Leaf" line of genetically modified potato to market. Buyers, led by the fast-food industry, rejected the Monsanto spud, and it was pulled from production due to lack of business. Simplot

– A sinkhole that started out the size of a small swimming pool and continued to grow in Florida swallowed a boat, destroyed two homes, and prompted officials to evacuate residents from 10 other homes on Friday. Dramatic video showed the home, north of Tampa in Pasco County, collapsing into the hole on Friday morning. The hole quickly grew to 200 feet wide—about two-thirds the length of a football field—and 50 feet deep. Pasco County Fire Chief Shawn Whited told reporters that no one was at the home when crews arrived just after 7:30am. Someone had called about a "depression" under a boat parked in the backyard of a home in Lake Padgett Estates in Land O'Lakes. Within minutes, he said, "the hole opened up," and the boat fell in. Firefighters were able to get two dogs out of the home and retrieve some belongings before the first home started collapsing into the quickly-expanding hole. By early afternoon, the home next door also had been destroyed by the sinkhole. No injuries have been reported. County property records show there was a sinkhole previously at the property where the first house was swallowed up, and that it had been "stabilized," in 2012. The home last sold in 2015, according to records. Sinkholes are stabilized by boring holes

– A 31-year-old Texas man helping to repair homes damaged by Hurricane Harvey has become the third person to die from a flesh-eating infection related to the storm, the Houston Chronicle reports. Josue Zurita went to the hospital Oct. 10 with an infected arm and was diagnosed with necrotizing fasciitis, according to the Galveston County Health District. The infection can spread quickly and kill the soft tissue of an infected wound within hours. "I have seen these things spread over hours," Galveston County health authority Dr. Philip Keiser tells CNN. "Even in one case, as I was examining a patient, I could see the red spread in the minutes I was examining him, and that's the real danger to it." Zurita, who moved to the US from Mexico to help his family, "remained to help with the rebuilding after hurricane Harvey," according to an obituary on the Carnes Brothers Funeral Home's website. The other two victims, Nancy Reed, 77, and JR Atkins, a former first responder, survived the bacterial infection.

– Baby boomers, it turns out, aren't the only ones who've been in the job for a while. A Pew Research Center analysis of government data finds that millennials—the generation born between 1981 and 1998—are just as likely to stick with their employers as Gen Xers were in 2000, when they were the same age. Specifically, 63.4% of employed Millennials reported having worked for their current employer at least 13 months in January 2016, compared to 59.9% of Gen Xers that same year. And 22% of today's Millennials had been with their employer for at least five years as of 2016, similar to the 21% of Gen Xers that same year. One possible reason for the longer-lasting employment is that college-educated Millennials are more likely to have completed a bachelor's degree, which is associated with longer tenure, per Pew. The analysis also finds that 75% of college-educated 25- to 35-year-olds reported having worked for their employer at least 13 months in 2016, compared to 70% of Gen Xers that same year. (Interestingly, the percentage of Gen Xers with at least a bachelor's degree has fallen over the last 15 years.)

– The Treasury Department's inspector general is out with his report on the IRS targeting scandal, and while it doesn't single out anyone for lying to Congress, it does criticize the IRS for using "inappropriate criteria" to identify groups applying for tax-exempt status based on their names or policy positions, the Washington Post reports. The report doesn't accuse the IRS of partisanship, but it does say that the criteria gave the appearance that the IRS was "not impartial in conducting its mission," Politico reports. Tea Party groups were singled out for extra scrutiny because they had names like "Tea Party," "patriots," and "9/12" in their names, and only about 15% of the applications had those names. The report also says the IRS destroyed donor lists that were sent in for potential political cases that the IRS determined it should not have requested. The report doesn't accuse the IRS of lying to Congress, but it does say that Acting IRS Commissioner Steven Miller and former Commissioner Doug Shulman didn't tell Congress about the extra scrutiny after May 2012, the New York Times reports. Miller wrote letters to the House Ways and Means Committee and Senate Republicans months after he was briefed, but never disclosed that the IRS was giving an extra critical eye to conservative groups.

– A new study published in the CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report finds that the number of young women seeking treatment for self-inflicted injuries has spiked over the past few years. Specifically, the study found that the rate of self-inflicted injuries among females aged 10 to 14 rose 18.8% between 2009 and 2015, from 109.8 per 1,000 females in 2009 to 317.7 per 1,000 females in 2015. That's a 7.2% increase over the course of the study, which began in 2001 and tracked 43 138 self-inflicted injury visits to US hospitals between 2001 and 2015. Poisoning was the most common method of self-inflicted injury for females, with rates remaining stable until 2007 and increasing 5.3% annually thereafter. Female rates for blunt object injuries also rose from 5.2% to 8.9% over the course of the study. The study's lead author, Melissa Mercado, tells the New York Times that the increase in the rate of self-inflicted injuries among young women could be due to more people seeking treatment for depression or anxiety, as well as increased access to health care. She adds that the increase in the rate of self-inflicted injuries among young females could also be due to the increased availability of knives and other sharp objects at their disposal, as well as increased bullying

– China's slowing economy isn't slowing down Starbucks. The coffee giant plans to open more than one new store a day in the country for the next five years, CEO Howard Schultz tells CNN. But five years ago, "most of our business, believe it or not, was expats and tourists in China," Schultz says. "Today, it's mostly Chinese." Schultz says he expects China to eventually overtake the US as the company's largest market, though he hasn't said exactly when. McDonald's, meanwhile, is looking for a partner to take over its China business. "They have other challenges," Schultz says. "I can't speak for them."

– Women who drink alcohol before their first pregnancy are more likely to get breast cancer later in life, according to a new study. Researchers found that women who had at least one alcoholic drink a day in the years before their first pregnancy were 11% more likely to get breast cancer later, HealthDay reports. The link held regardless of whether a woman had had alcohol after the first pregnancy. The study looked at data from more than 91,000 women who had no cancer history when they started drinking. The study also looked at whether the women contracted benign breast disease, and found that the more they drank, the more likely they were to get it. "The risk increased by 11% for every 10 grams a day of intake, about six drinks per week," says the study author. "One drink was defined as one bottle or can of beer, a 4-ounce glass of wine or a shot of liquor."

The airport was shut down for nearly five hours, stranding incoming planeloads of passengers on the tarmac until buses could arrive to pick them up, reports the AP. At least one plane was already preparing to depart at the time of the evacuation, but no flights were allowed to take off following the evacuation. "As someone that's describing the species you get to pick what the specific name is," Stephanie Bush tells Science Friday. Bush discovered the octopus last year while working on an exhibit at the aquarium, and specimens have been collected since 1990, reports the San Jose Mercury News. Opisthoteuthis adorabilis is the same genus as Pearl, the pink flapjack octopus found in Pixar's Finding Nemo, and the two species have been collected as far back as 1990. The octopus in question is about 7 inches long and inhabits up to 1,476 feet deep in the ocean, and its webbed tentacles give it the appearance of an umbrella when it spreads them. – "Donald Trump says he wants to make America great again. Well, he could start by actually making things in America again," Hillary Clinton said in her acceptance speech at the Democratic National Convention on Thursday. "In the end, it comes down to what Donald Trump doesn't get: that America is great because America is good," she said. "So enough with the bigotry and bombast. – An Atlanta-area man reported kidnapped last week turned up safe Sunday night, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports. According to WSB-TV, 19-year-old Aftab Aslam left his parents' home in Johns Creek around 10am on April 27. That's when his parents received a text from someone claiming to be his kidnapper. Aslam's parents reported him missing, and police found the phone used to send that text. It was purchased by Aslam, the Journal-Constitution reports. According to WSB-TV, Aslam told police he left home for "personal reasons." Aslam is still missing, and police are trying to verify his account.

– The "object of interest" found in the search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 has turned out to be nothing more than trash, jellyfish, and fishing gear, officials say. The piece of metal, which had rivets on one side, washed ashore in Australia, around 1,000 miles from where the plane is believed to have crashed, CNN reports. " Detailed pictures of the object were enough to convince investigators that it wasn't a lead in the search for the missing plane," says the Australian agency in charge of the search. "The search will continue and we will not rest until we are able to solve this mystery." The search area has now been expanded to include the last 370 miles of the plane's flight path, a specialist tells CNN. "We may well rethink the search, but we will not rest until we have done everything we can to solve this mystery," says Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott.

– The hobbits may have been diminutive, but they lived far earlier than thought, according to new research out of Canada's Lakehead University. Homo floresiensis was discovered in Liang Bua cave on the island of Flores in 2003 and was originally thought to have lived 12,000 years ago, National Geographic reports. But new research out of Lakehead suggests they lived much earlier—between 100,000 and 60,000 years ago. "Every finding just makes it more mysterious," says a paleoanthropologist not involved with the study. "Nobody could ever have imagined a hominid that looked like the one from Flores. It's the kind of thing only nature could come up with." H. floresiensis stood three-and-a-half feet tall and weighed 75 pounds, and its stone tools date back as far as 190,000 years. The new research suggests that hobbits didn't live long after modern humans arrived on the island 50,000 years ago. Researchers used chemical clues in the soil around the fossils to figure out how old the bones and tools were, but the layers of sediment weren't evenly deposited and so varied widely in age even at similar depths. The new age estimates are based on five different dating methods, including uranium decay rate and luminescence

– For the first time since 1969, no Roman numerals will be used in the logo for the 50th Super Bowl, which will be held in the San Francisco Bay Area in 2016. Instead, the NFL has released a logo that uses the Arabic numeral 50, rather than the Roman numeral L, which has been used since Super Bowl V in 1971. Representatives from the host committee had been lobbying the league to allow them to ditch the "L," Deadspin reports. "We think what we have makes a very powerful statement for the NFL brand," the league's VP of brand and creative says. "When we developed the Super Bowl XL logo, that was the first time we looked at the letter 'L,'" she says. "Up until that point, we had only worked with X's, V's, and I's. And, at that moment, that's when we started to wonder what will happen when we get to 50?" The NFL will also go back to using roman numerals for Super Bowl LI in Houston in 2017.

– "We believe Mr. Joyce was greedy, plain and simple." That's how FBI Special Agent in Charge Hank Shaw describes former Massachusetts state Sen. Brian Joyce, who was arrested Friday and faces more than 100 charges, including racketeering, wire fraud, extortion, and money laundering, CBS Boston reports. According to an indictment, the 55-year-old used his position as a state senator to accept "a stream of concealed bribes and kickbacks" in exchange for official actions. He's accused of pressuring state and municipal officials to take action on government matters, including a bill that benefited a coffee shop franchisee, WBUR reports. The FBI raided Joyce's law office in 2016, days after he announced he wouldn't seek re-election. He has pleaded not guilty to the charges, which include racketeering, extortion, wire fraud, conspiracy to defraud the IRS, and money laundering. "He had a duty to serve (his constituents) honestly, and he violated that duty by accepting bribes and kickbacks in exchange for his official action," US Attorney William Weinreb says. Joyce, who was first elected to the state Senate in 1998, was taken into custody at his home in Westport.

Ben says he sped up to 85mph in a 55mph zone as he passed a police officer who had started following him. "The baby is coming now," he tells NBC13. "I did tell him not to stop," Rachel says. – Bangladesh authorities say they've arrested the main suspect in the murder of American blogger Avijit Roy, who was hacked to death on a Dhaka street last week. Roy's parents say suspect Farabi Shafiur Rahman had called for Roy's death in numerous Facebook posts, including one last year in which he wrote, "It's a holy duty of Bangalee Muslims to kill Avijit," CNN reports. He also allegedly posted photos of the crime scene. A spokesman for Bangladesh's anti-terrorism unit says Rahman confessed to the killing after being arrested at a bus stop in the country's capital, reports Reuters. Roy's wife and another blogger were also injured in the attack, and she lost a finger.

The directive, issued in October last year but never published, says the US can offer "unique and unconventional capabilities to advance US national objectives around the world with little or no warning to the adversary or target and with potential effects ranging from subtle to severely damaging." The document states that the government will "identify potential targets of national importance where OCEO can offer a favorable balance of effectiveness and risk as compared with other instruments of national power." A senior administration official tells the Guardian that the goal of the document was "to put in place tools and a framework to enable government to make decisions" on cyber actions. The move comes as President Obama prepares to confront Chinese President Xi Jinping over alleged cyberattacks on the US. "We hack everyone everywhere," an intelligence source tells the Guardian. "We like to make a distinction between us and the others. But we are in almost every country in the world."

– Nestle wants to trademark the shape of its four-finger KitKat chocolate bar in the UK, but it's going to be a tough sell. The European Court of Justice ruled yesterday that trademarking a shape is only possible if the shape itself is distinctive enough for consumers to identify it, reports the BBC. Nestle says the four fingers have become "almost completely associated" with KitKats over the 80 years since the chocolate bar was first sold in Britain. Rival Cadbury, however, says the shape is not distinctive enough and has been fighting Nestle's application for a trademark for more than 10 years, reports Bloomberg. The case will now return to the UK High Court for a final decision.

– President Obama called the threat of nuclear terrorism "one of the greatest threats to global security" during his fourth and final nuclear security summit in Washington, DC, on Friday. "If these madmen ever got their hands on a nuclear bomb or nuclear material, they would certainly use it to kill as many innocent people as possible," he said, per Reuters. "It would change our world." Obama said no group has been able to get their hands on bomb materials, but he cited the recent attacks in Paris and Brussels as further evidence of the threat, reports the New York Times. "There is no doubt that if these madmen ever got their hands on a nuclear bomb or nuclear material, they would certainly use it to kill as many innocent people as possible," he said. "It would change our world." More than 50 world leaders were in attendance at the summit, which focused on securing vulnerable nuclear facilities. In his opening speech, Obama said the world must do more to prevent terrorists from getting their hands on materials needed to make a nuclear bomb, reports the Washington Post. He called for increased cooperation between the US and other countries, reports the AP.

– Police in India have arrested three men for allegedly gang-raping a 22-year-old Japanese academic near a Buddhist pilgrimage center, reports the Times of India. The woman says she was lured to the site by a man pretending to be a tour guide. He and four others allegedly held her captive for 12 days and raped her near Bodh Gaya, reports the New York Times. The woman escaped when she contacted a group of Japanese tourists in the city of Varanasi, and police say they have arrested two brothers from Kolkata in connection with the case. They're also looking for two more suspects, reports the BBC. The woman says she was forced to remove money from her bank account during her captivity.

– She's known as "the terror" of drug traffickers in Colombia, but Sombra the drug-sniffing dog is now the target of her own killers. Sombra, a 6-year-old German shepherd, has sniffed out at least 9 tons of cocaine in her career with the Colombian National Police, reports the Washington Post. She's also been called "the terror" of drug traffickers by the Colombian press, and her busts have led to more than 200 arrests, per the BBC. Sombra has now been moved to an airport outside the Urabeos drug gang's heartland in Bogot, and she'll be accompanied by extra police officers. The Urabeos, also known as the Gulf Clan, is considered Colombia's most powerful criminal organization. It's not unusual for the gang to offer money to get rid of those standing in their way, and in 2012, police found leaflets signed by the gang offering $500 to anyone who killed a police officer. Sombra has been with the counter-narcotics police since she was a puppy.

We do this because we need to and have rights." The 9-year-old was one of many speakers at a citizens' forum hosted by the city council in the wake of last week's police shooting of Keith Scott, the Charlotte Observer reports. Zianna's mother, Precious Oliphant, tells NBC News that she brought her daughter and her brother to the meeting because "I shouldn't have to enlighten my kids on discrimination and racism." "I was kind of emotional, because, like, the things that I said is like powerful to me," Zianna tells NBC. "So that's why I started crying." Zianna, who says she wants to be a doctor, was one of many speakers at the forum who called for the resignation of Charlotte's mayor and police chief. "We need our fathers and mothers to be by our side," Zianna told the council.

– Aung San Suu Kyi is making her first visit to Europe since 1988—and she's not doing it without a little drama. The Myanmar opposition leader stopped speaking at a press conference in Bern today after falling ill and vomiting, reports Reuters. "I'm so sorry," she said. "She is tired and has gone to her hotel to rest." The 66-year-old Nobel Peace Prize winner, who was given a standing ovation after a speech in Geneva today, will visit Norway, Britain, Ireland, and France during her 17-day trip. She hasn't been to Europe since 1988, when she was under house arrest.

David Benes told her he was trying to "exorcise her and get the devil out of her" against her will, the woman told police. She called 911 after the alleged exorcism again on Tuesday, and Benes was found passed out on a couch with bruises and scratches on her arms. He told police his girlfriend started the fight "because she is crazy," according to the arrest report. He was charged with domestic battery on a person 65 or older, tampering with a witness, and false imprisonment. He's been convicted of battery twice in Pasco County and once of violating a domestic violence injunction.

The law also defines gestational age as beginning on the first day of a woman's last period—typically about the same time a doctor would perform ultrasounds. Eight other states ban abortions after 20 weeks, but Arizona is the only one with a law that actually pushes the ban back to 18 weeks into the pregnancy. According to state records, women in Arizona terminate about 100 pregnancies a year after 20 weeks, but it's unclear how many of those are because of a problem with the pregnancy. The new law requires doctors to offer information about perinatal hospice services to women considering abortion at any stage of their pregnancy because of a fatal fetal abnormality. It also requires the state to maintain a website list of organizations that provide services. The two organizations that offer such help, MISS Foundation and Embrace, provide counseling and comfort, help develop birth plans, attend births, organize meals, create mementos, make funeral arrangements, and prepare families for every outcome.
