– Bitcoin's value may be on the rise, but a new study out of Germany warns that the cryptocurrency could be at risk of being tainted by child pornography. Researchers at RWTH Aachen University found 1,600 files stored in the blockchain, the open-source system that underpins bitcoin, containing links to child pornography, the Guardian reports. Of those, at least eight contained images of child abuse, including two that contained 274 links to dark web services. "Our analysis shows that certain content, eg, illegal pornography, can render the mere possession of a blockchain illegal," the researchers write. "Although court rulings do not yet exist, legislative texts from countries such as Germany, the UK, or the USA suggest that illegal content such as [child abuse imagery] can make the blockchain illegal to possess for all users." "This especially endangers the multi-billion dollar markets powering cryptocurrencies such as bitcoin," the Central Bank of Argentina's governor told CNBC after a closed-door meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors in Buenos Aires on Tuesday. Bitcoin rose above $9,000 for the first time in a week after the study was published, though it's still down about 25% from its all-time high of nearly $20,000 hit in December, reports

– A Minnesota woman who is wanted in connection with her husband's death is now charged with killing a Florida woman who resembled her and stealing the woman's identity as she eluded authorities, officials said Friday. Lois Riess, 56, of Blooming Prairie, Minn., has been charged in the shooting death of Pamela Hutchinson, 59, of Bradenton, Fla. Authorities were called to an area of Fort Myers Beach on Monday and found Hutchinson dead, with gunshot wounds. "Ms. Hutchinson's purse was found to be in disarray and all cash, credit cards, and identification appeared to be removed," Lee County Undersheriff Carmine Marceno said, per the AP. "Further investigation revealed that Ms. Hutchinson was targeted by the suspect due to the similarities in their appearance." Riess is believed to be driving Hutchinson's car, a white Acura TL with Florida license plate Y37TAA. The car has been seen in Louisiana and Corpus Christi, Texas, since Hutchinson died. – For years, doctors have been telling young women that having their appendix or tonsils removed would reduce their chances of getting pregnant. But a new study suggests that's not the case. Researchers at the University of Dundee in the UK studied the medical records of more than 530,000 women and found that those who had either an appendix or tonsils removed were more likely to get pregnant than the rest of the population, they report in the journal Fertility and Sterility. For every 100 pregnancies in women who'd had no procedures, there were 134 in women who'd had their appendix removed and 149 in women who'd had their tonsils removed. Rates of pregnancy were 54% and 53% for women without an appendix and 53% for women who'd had both, reports CNN. "For many years medical students were taught that appendectomy had a negative effect on fertility, and young women often feared that having their appendix removed threatened their chances of later becoming pregnant," says lead researcher Sami Shimi. "We have found that women who have had an appendectomy or tonsillectomy, or even more particularly both, are more likely to become pregnant, and sooner than the rest of the general population," he adds. "This scientifically challenges the myth of the effect of appendectomy on fertility."

– The Boy Scouts of America will propose lifting its ban on gay scouts but continuing to bar gay adults from leading the troops, it announced today. The Scouts said it would submit the proposal to its National Council next month, but the Mormon church, the Scouts' biggest sponsor, says it will "fully review the language and study the implications of this new proposal," Reuters reports. If the proposal is approved, "no youth may be denied membership in the Boy Scouts of America on the basis of sexual orientation or preference alone," a spokesman says. But gay rights groups say the change is not enough. "By refusing to consider an end to its ban on gay and lesbian parents, the Boy Scouts have missed an opportunity to exercise leadership and usher the organization back to relevancy," says a spokesperson for GLAAD, which promotes lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender rights. The Scouts' survey of more than 1,400 members found that 60% were in favor of allowing both youth and adult leaders to participate, the New York Times reports.

– It's that time of year again: the time of year when sports fans start filling out fantasy football rosters for the upcoming season. And if you're one of them, you may be tempted to quit your job to play, reports the Wall Street Journal. It quotes one man who quit his job as an investment analyst to play fantasy sports full-time, and NPR has the story. Drew Dinkmeyer makes $500 a day playing, and that's not counting the time he spends researching, drafting, and trading for his rosters. "What you're doing is you're trying to find a company that is trading for less than it's really worth," he explains. "So if there's a company out there that's priced at $50 on a given day, and you think that company is really worth $60 or $70, you want to own that company and invest in that company, and that's the same thing daily fantasy players are doing."

The bird-like creature, which lived 161 million years ago in what is now China, had fuzzy feathers and pennaceous feathers, which look like writing quills, on its head, neck, and chest, Reuters reports. It also had crests above its eyes that looked like bony eyebrows. "It is extremely similar to some early birds such as Archaeopteryx," a Chinese paleontologist says. "Its forelimbs were configured like wings. The nearly complete skeleton was discovered in Hebei Province in China in 2016, and the discovery "suggests a more colorful Jurassic World than we previously imagined," says evolutionary biologist Chad Eliason of the Field Museum in Chicago, one of the researchers in the study published in the journal Nature Communications. – When a 25-year-old German man was buried in an avalanche during a 2008 ski trip, he suffered a ruptured spleen and hip fracture and got too little oxygen for 15 minutes, researchers report in the journal JAMA Neurology. That left him with a condition known as hypoxia, which reduced the amount of oxygen in his body and caused a type of seizure known as spontaneous tonic clonic seizures. These seizures began in his left arm and continued when he tried to solve a Sudoku puzzle, LiveScience reports. Researchers eventually figured out why: The man had a "very intense three-dimensional imagination" that was activated when he solved a Sudoku puzzle and allowed him to sort and put the numbers in sequence. "When he stopped this 3D imagination, the seizures stopped immediately," says Dr. Berend Feddersen, the lead author of the case report. The man has been seizure-free for more than five years now, thanks to anti-epileptic medication, and he's been able to continue Sudoku without incident since last year. (A woman suffered seizures while playing Sudoku.)

– A new drug that mimics the sun's ability to tan skin has the potential to prevent skin cancer and slow the appearance of aging, according to researchers at Massachusetts General Hospital. The drug, which mimics the natural production of skin pigment melanin, produced dark skin in tests on skin samples and mice without the use of sun beds or lotions, the BBC reports. "Under the microscope it's the real melanin, it really is activating the production of pigment in a UV-independent fashion," says a researcher. The team hopes to combine their drug with sun cream to give maximum protection from UV rays, and to prevent skin cancer. "Our real goal is a novel strategy for protecting skin from UV radiation and cancer," the researcher says. "Dark pigment is associated with a lower risk of all forms of skin cancer—that would be really huge."

– The Midwest and Northeast are hunkering down for some seriously cold temperatures this weekend, with a massive winter storm dumping up to 20 inches of snow on parts of New England and sub-zero wind chills expected in much of the rest of the country. "It's going to be brutal," a Weather Channel meteorologist tells NBC. "People that are vulnerable are really going to be hurting." Hundreds of flights have been canceled across the country, and New York City has closed John F. Kennedy Airport until 8:30 this morning. Schools are closed across the Northeast, and some 2,000 flights have been canceled. In the Midwest, the wind chill could reach 40 below zero tomorrow, and 40 below zero on Monday. "Even Atlanta's northern suburbs could be in single digits by Monday night," says another Weather Channel meteorologist. "True hypothermia cases turn up more often in more southern regions because people are not prepared and don't know what to do."

– Employees at a moving freight company in Redford, Mich., heard moaning from a bathroom stall yesterday morning and discovered blood on the floor and the wall. They asked a 25-year-old woman if she was OK, and she said she was lightheaded but didn't mention that she'd just given birth, USA Today reports. Police and paramedics were called, and the woman was taken to a hospital, where the baby was pronounced dead. The woman, who works for a temp agency, had told people at Ceva Logistics that she wasn't pregnant, the company's logistics director tells Fox 2 Detroit. She is now recovering at the hospital. Police say the baby was found in a bag under her desk, and it's not clear if the baby was born alive or if the death was a homicide. "All I can say is it is under investigation," the logistics director says. "We were asked not to say anything, until the investigation is over." The company, which handles moving freight for companies including the Big Three, informed its 150-plus employees and offered grief counseling. But at this point, the logistics director says the company isn't ready to comment. "All I can say is it is under investigation," he says.

So reads a statement from the Great Hearts Monte Vista Charter School in San Antonio, Texas, after an assignment for an eighth-grade American History class was posted to social media Wednesday. The assignment asked students to identify the "positive" and "negative" aspects of slavery, per the San Antonio Express-News. "The assignment itself weighing the pros and cons of slave life and slave perspective quite honestly is just gross," Robert Livar tells KSAT. "There are no pros to one human being owning another." Livar's wife posted a photo of the assignment on Facebook, and it quickly went viral. "Our review of the situation found this incident to be limited to one teacher at just one campus," the school said in a statement. Castro asked the school to send him a copy of the assignment, which was given at the school's Monte Vista North campus. Great Hearts says the teacher involved has been placed on leave while the incident is investigated.

The chain, which has been known as Dunkin' since 1971, will now be known as Dunkin' Donuts starting in January, reports the AP. The Massachusetts-based company, which has more than 12,500 stores worldwide, says the name change is part of a plan to become a "beverage-led" company that focuses on coffee, tea, and other beverages, not just doughnuts. Dunkin' Donuts will continue to have its familiar rounded font and orange-and-pink color scheme, reports NBC News, which notes that the name change will eventually be adopted by international stores. (In other Dunkin' news, the chain is changing its name again.)

– Larry Ellison's Oracle Team USA pulled off what the AP calls "one of the greatest comebacks in sports history" today to win the America's Cup, beating Emirates Team New Zealand in a winner-take-all race in San Francisco Bay. Oracle had trailed 8-1 in the best-of-17 series before pulling off what the Guardian calls "one of the most impressive comebacks in sailing history." The Australian skipper and his crew twice rallied from seven-point deficits to win 9-8. How big a win this? In sailing terms, it was the equivalent of the 2004 ALCS over the New York Yankees, the only 3-0 comeback in major league baseball. Ellison, who skipped an Oracle conference to be with his crew, is the software billionaire who created the America's Cup as a high-tech version of the schooners that have held the cup since 1841. The 72-foot catamarans used in today's races are much faster than the slower boats of the past. "It was Ellison's vision that helped bring these catamarans to the competition," the Guardian writes.

– A Florida jury has awarded $80 million to the daughter of a longtime smoker who died of lung cancer in 1996. James Cayce Horner was 10% responsible for his death, while RJ Reynolds was 90% at fault, according to the Smoking Gun. The jury found that RJ Reynolds sold Horner cigarettes that were "defective" and "unreasonably dangerous." The verdict reverses a recent streak for the tobacco industry, which had won defense verdicts in eight straight Engle progeny cases, the most recent on Friday. "People need to be reminded, again and again, of the true cost—in precious human life—that RJ Reynolds has imposed and continues to impose on our society," plaintiffs' counsel said in a statement. The case is one of more than 7,000 smoking lawsuits pending in Florida.

– A lawsuit accusing President Trump of violating the Constitution's emoluments clauses has moved forward. The Washington Post reports a federal judge ruled Monday that Maryland and the District of Columbia have legal standing to sue the president. The lawsuit filed last year claims that Trump is profiting off the Trump International Hotel in Washington, DC, violating the Constitution's ban on accepting improper payments from foreign governments. According to the New York Times, Judge Peter Messitte found that Maryland and the District have standing to sue because they could suffer "economic harm" from the hotel's business with foreign governments. The lawsuit claims that Trump is profiting off the hotel in a way that violates the Constitution's Emoluments Clause, which bans accepting gifts from foreign governments. The lawsuit claims that the hotel is doing a lot of business with foreign governments, including Kuwait and Bahrain, and that it has an "unlawful effect on competition" from other hotels. Messitte's ruling narrows the lawsuit's scope to the Washington hotel, but it could still allow Maryland and the District to seek documents from the Trump Organization to find out how much money the hotel has taken in from foreign governments. The Justice Department did not immediately say whether it would appeal.

– Prozac has been linked to a decrease in libido, but a new study out of the University of York suggests that the antidepressant also has an effect on birds' mating habits. Reporting in the journal Ecology Letters, researchers say that starlings that had been exposed to relatively low doses of Prozac became less attractive to male starlings, which sang less often and treated the birds more aggressively. "We found no effect of female treatment on female courtship behavior," they write. "Our findings suggest that exposure to an antidepressant reduced female attractiveness, adding to growing evidence that environmental concentrations of pharmaceuticals can alter important traits related to individual fitness and population dynamics." The study involved starlings that had been fed worms laced with low doses of Prozac at sewage treatment plants, where the birds like to eat worms, flies, and maggots, reports the Washington Post. When paired with female starlings that had been eating the worms, male starlings sang half as often and for half as long as they did with females that hadn't been exposed to the drug. "They could be aggressive, and they could be passive," says one of the study's authors, Kathryn Arnold. "The equivalent of reduced libido, in a wild animal, is how they behave during courtship." – Sperm whales can weigh up to 45 tons and have the largest brain of any mammal on the planet, but a new study in the journal Molecular Ecology suggests they've all descended from a single female. Scientists analyzed mitochondrial DNA from 1,633 whales and found low genetic diversity. But that was no surprise: Past research has shown that many of what scientists call "megafauna" (really big animals) aren't that genetically diverse. In 2002, for example, researchers found that killer whales lack diversity in their genes despite their large population size—likely due to some past event that once dramatically reduced their population. So the study's lead author, Alana Alexander, expected to find low diversity, reports Hakai Magazine. But she found even lower diversity than she imagined. More data didn't help uncover more diversity—instead, it confirmed ties to a single female whale who, at some point in the last 80,000 years, became the "mother" of all sperm whales who followed. Though it would make sense to have a single mother in a single area—an ancestor who, say, really loved the Pacific Ocean—this mom's genes have been found in sperm whales all over the world. Sperm whales are matrilineal, meaning most females stick together

The water was found to be tainted with perfluorinated compounds during a routine inspection on Oct. 12. "There was no risk to the drinking water," says a spokesman for Colorado Springs Utilities. The chemical in the water is a perfluorinated compound that the EPA says can cause ailments including liver and kidney damage and may trigger cancer. The Air Force has banned the use of firefighting foam containing the compound at all of its bases around the world. The boys, aged 11 to 16, and their 25-year-old coach have been staying with Thai navy special forces divers in the cave complex, where they've been trapped since June 23, the AP reports. The group was found on a rock shelf 2.5 miles from the mouth of the cave, which is regularly flooded during the rainy season. In a video posted by the Thai navy special forces, the boys are seen sitting on a ledge above water, responding to the divers who found them and saying they were very hungry. The divers tell them they have to wait, but say people will come back for them. One boy replies: "Oh. See you tomorrow." – The FDA warned in 2005 that taking antidepressants while pregnant could increase a baby's risk of a heart defect, but a new study suggests that's not true—at least in the first three months of pregnancy. Researchers looked at nearly a million women who had given birth between 2000 and 2007, and found no link between taking selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) like Paxil and sertraline and one type of birth defect, HealthDay News reports. "The most critical period in the development of an embryo or in the growth of a particular organ is during the time of most rapid cell division," says the lead author of the study, published in the New England Journal of Medicine. "So, it is in the first three months of pregnancy that the risk for developing major malformations is highest." The FDA's 2005 warning was based on two previous studies that found SSRIs could increase the risk of heart defects. The new study, however, found no link between taking antidepressants while pregnant and one type of birth defect. The study also found no link between taking SSRIs while pregnant and other birth defects, such as Down syndrome, Psych Central reports.

Manning, who had two neck surgeries this year, didn't throw in yesterday's game against the Jacksonville Jaguars, his last of the season. – Seven high school students and one teacher were killed in an avalanche Monday at a ski resort in Japan, the BBC reports. According to the Guardian, the students and teachers from seven high schools were taking part in a climbing lesson at the Nasu Onsen ski resort when the avalanche struck around 8:30am local time. The Tochigi Prefectural Police says 40 students and eight teachers were on their way to walk in the accumulated snow when the avalanche occurred. The group was supposed to ascend the mountain on Monday but was canceled due to heavy snow. The Tochigi education board says 51 students from mountaineering clubs and 11 teachers from seven high schools were taking part in the climbing lesson event that began Saturday. A police official says the bodies of the dead students and teachers have been found with no vital signs. The Tochigi police are looking into whether the deaths were caused by professional negligence.

– A team of scientists in the Netherlands has created a sperm-like robot that it hopes will someday be used for in vitro fertilization, the BBC reports. "We have built a biologically inspired micro-robot that looks like a sperm cell but is completely fabricated in the lab," says robotics engineer Sarthak Misra. The device is made up of a metal-coated head and a flexible body about six times longer than a human. It can wiggle along at up to 0.5 body lengths per second, compared to a human sperm's several times that. The researchers used a magnetic field no stronger than a fridge magnet to steer the device toward a set point. "The magnetic head is used to orient it in a certain direction and then, just by flapping its tail, it starts to move forward," Misra says. "The flapping happens because we change the current in the coils." The researchers say the device could be used to position materials in nanomanufacturing, or for medical purposes. "It opens up a lot of applications, from targeted drug delivery to in vitro fertilization—where you want to reach precise locations," Misra says. The team is working on making the device smaller and faster.

The placenta is the tissue that attaches to the umbilical cord in the womb, and it's surrounded by amniotic fluid, which is made from cow's placenta. It's unclear how much of the fluid is actually in the placenta, but it is said to speed healing. Liverpool's Glen Johnson and Fabio Aurelio both flew into Belgrade to get treatment from the so-called horse placenta healer last night, the Independent reports. Liverpool manager Rafael Benitez has put his trust in her, and is said to be paying as much as $3,650 for three days of treatment, which uses fluids derived from horse placentas.

– Oklahoma's Frank Lucas won the Republican primary for his congressional seat this week, but his opponent isn't taking it lightly. Tim Murray, who received 5.2% of the vote, is contesting the results on the grounds that Lucas is dead and has been replaced by a body double, CNN reports. "It does come as kind of a shock to read that you're not you," says Lucas, who has been in Congress for 20 years. "A lot of stupid things happen in Oklahoma politics, but this may be the stupidest I've ever heard. Welcome to Oklahoma," says a University of Oklahoma politics professor. Murray's campaign website claims that Lucas was hanged in Ukraine in 2011 and that he has been "displayed by a look alike," KFOR reports. "Many things have been said about me, said to me during course of my campaigns," Lucas says. "This is the first time I've ever been accused of being a body double or a robot." The deadline for challenging a candidate's qualifications is today.

He "doesn't care if the anti-tobacco groups or the liberal nanny-staters whine about it," Kornacki writes.

– Electronic Arts is taking heat for including gay characters in its games, but the video game giant is standing firm: "We believe that whether or not a gamer or All Out member supports EA, they can agree that the decision to distribute the games with gay relationships in the face of opposition," says an EA statement. Anti-gay boycott groups have been pressuring EA over the inclusion of gay characters, but AllOut.org—which has more than a million signatures on a petition supporting EA's decision—was hit with spambots and spammers yesterday, Forbes reports. "We are not arguing that Electronic Arts is a perfect company, but we know that today, on this issue, they are taking an important stand that should be celebrated and supported," says an AllOut community manager.

– Sarah Catherine Long was found dead in her North Carolina home in July, with a gunshot wound to the head, and the death was ruled a suicide. But now, nearly four months later, authorities are looking into her death as a possible murder, CBS News reports. Long was having an affair with a married man, William Becker, and just days after Long's body was found, he produced documents showing that she had left him everything in her will—a $1 million fortune, People reports. Becker told police that Long had recently been diagnosed with cervical cancer, but Long's doctor later disputed that, saying she only had abnormal cells on her cervix, which could cure a minor outpatient procedure. Police searched Long's computer, router, and Yahoo Mail in November in an attempt to recreate the last days of Long's life, and they've identified a person of interest, but no arrests have been made. Investigators are also looking into Becker's wife's claim that he gave Long a "funny" smoothie in May, and that he flushed it down the toilet after she asked if it had medicine in it, according to documents obtained by the Charlotte Observer.

– President Obama's concession that he's willing to admit he's a Muslim has been met with a yawn from the president's Republican critics, and a laugh from his Saudi media critics. "Obama doesn't mind coming out as a Muslim if that will satisfy the Republicans," said one headline in a Saudi newspaper. "Obama: 'I'm ready to announce that I am a Muslim,'" said another on a news website controlled by the Saudi interior ministry, reports AFP. Both newspapers repeated a joke by US humorist Andy Borowitz, who wrote that "in agreeing that he is a Muslim, Mr. Obama is sending a clear signal that he is trying to find consensus." Obama's willingness to back down on his claim that he's a Christian does not seem to have satisfied his Republican opposition, as GOP leader John Boehner today insisted that the president must also agree that he was born in Kenya.

– If you've updated to iOS 8, you may have noticed a new feature called "Wave" that allows your iPhone to be charged in the microwave—but it's a hoax, 9to5mac.com reports. The hoax has been making the rounds on Reddit and Twitter since iOS 8 was released last week, and Reddit users are pointing to a 4chan thread as the source, according to 9to5mac.com. It's not the first time this has happened: YouTube videos have long touted the fake feature, and 4chan has attempted similar hoaxes in the past.

– The World Health Organization has declared Cuba the world's first country to stop the transmission of HIV from mothers to their babies, Reuters reports. "This is a major victory in our long fight against HIV and sexually transmitted infections, and an important step towards having an AIDS-free generation," WHO Director-General Margaret Chan said in a statement. According to NBC News, Cuba's success shows that "universal access and universal health coverage are feasible and indeed are the key to success, even against challenges as daunting as HIV." The Pan American Health Organization and WHO sent an international delegation to Cuba in March to determine the country met the criteria for the designation. In 2013, only two children in Cuba were born with HIV and five with syphilis. "Cuba's success demonstrates that universal access and universal health coverage are feasible and indeed are the key to success, even against challenges as daunting as HIV," PAHO Director Carissa Etienne said in the statement. WHO estimates that 1.4 million women with HIV become pregnant every year. Without treatment, there's as much as a 45% chance that they'll infect their newborns. In the US, 162 children were infected at birth in 2010. "It shows that ending the AIDS epidemic is possible," WHO's Sidibé says.

At least seven people were injured in the disaster, reports the AP, which notes that the hillside that collapsed is the same one that partially collapsed in 2006. "I have a sense we are going to have some hard news here," said Gov. Jay Inslee.

– A Christian university in San Diego has launched a crowdfunding campaign to help survivors of human trafficking get a college education, the San Diego Union-Tribune reports. Point Loma Nazarene University's "Beauty for Ashes" campaign has raised more than $32,000 so far, and it plans to provide $40,000 in tuition, room, and board for at least one student who has been accepted as a student at the institution. "We believe one of the most critical components to the long-term rehabilitation of a survivor is a college education," the university says on its crowdfunding page. "An education in the loving, academically challenging and carefully mentored environment of a Christian university can take someone from Victim to Survivor to Thriver." The university's Center for Justice and Reconciliation has been working to combat sex and labor trafficking for years, the Union-Tribune notes. The campaign was started by a group of students, faculty, and alumni who were moved by the stories of survivors they'd heard. "It's hard to imagine what it's like to be a victim of human trafficking," one of the students tells the Union-Tribune. "It's hard to imagine that you can't go to college."

– President Obama made it clear last night that the US will not be dragged into another ground war in Iraq, but that didn't stop him from launching airstrikes against Sunni militants. The first strikes took place early this morning near the northern city of Irbil, where American personnel are stationed, reports CNN. A Pentagon spokesman says four F/A 18 fighters dropped two 500-pound laser-guided bombs on an ISIS convoy, and a drone hit an ISIS mortar position. A second round of strikes took place about an hour later, dropping eight laser-guided bombs on ISIS convoys, he says. "As commander in chief, I will not allow the United States to be dragged into fighting another war in Iraq," said Obama in his address last night. The strikes were in response to a speech by the leader of the Islamic State, aka ISIS, or ISIL, in which he threatened to march on Baghdad and called for the US to join the fight. "The United States will not be dragged into another ground war in Iraq," he said. Obama also promised that there would be no American "boots on the ground" in Iraq.

– We've all heard of microplastics, the tiny pieces of plastic that have been found in everything from our tap water to table salt. Now researchers at the Medical University of Vienna say they've found them in our own poop, reports Live Science. "The results were astonishing," says lead author Philipp Schwabl. " plastics ultimately reach the human gut." In the small pilot study, researchers collected stool samples from eight people from Finland, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, Poland, Russia, the United Kingdom, and Austria. They found that all of the samples contained microplastics. The most common were polypropylene and polyethylene terephthalate, two types of plastic used in plastic bottles and other packaging. On average, they found 20 microplastic particles per 10 grams of stool. "Now that we have first evidence for microplastics inside humans, we need further research to understand what this means for human health," says Schwabl, who presented his findings at a European gastroenterology meeting. The researchers say the microplastics could enter the bloodstream and lymphatic system and reach the liver, where they could damage the intestines and affect how well the body absorbs nutrients. The findings are the first to quantify the particles in human stool, and the researchers say more studies

– The world's longest and highest glass-bottomed bridge is set to open in China next month, and its operators want to make sure it's safe—so they invited BBC reporter Dan Simmons to smash it with a sledgehammer. Simmons stood on top of one of the panels that make up the Zhangjiajie Grand Canyon Bridge, the world's longest and highest glass-bottomed bridge, and slammed the sledgehammer on it several times. At his first swing, the top layer of the panel showed visible cracks, but after several more hits, the glass panel remained intact, ABC News reports. The bridge, located in Hunan province, can hold 800 people at once, and plans are in the works for it to be used as a fashion runway and as a bungee jumping point. Officials in Honduras said shaking was registered across much of the nation and there were some reports of cracks in homes in Colon and Atlantida provinces along the northern coast and Olancho in eastern Honduras. Tsunami centers issued advisories and warnings for Puerto Rico, the Cayman Islands, Cuba, Jamaica and other Caribbean islands as well as on the coasts of Mexico and Central America, cautioning that sea levels could rise from a foot to 3 feet above normal, but no tsunami materialized. The US Geological Survey measured the quake at a preliminary magnitude of 7.6. The tremor struck in the sea about 125 miles north-northeast of Barra Patuca, Honduras, and 188 miles southwest of George Town, Cayman Islands. – Hundreds of bottle-nosed dolphins have been dying between New York and North Carolina in what's likely the biggest die-off of its kind on the East Coast since the '80s, reports the Christian Science Monitor. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration thinks it's a measles-like virus called morbillivirus, which causes lesions on the animals' skin, as well as in their brains and lymph nodes. "I don't know of anything that screams morbillivirus when you look at the inside of the animal," a Smithsonian scientist tells the Washington Post. "Some of the animals seem to be emaciated and debilitated, and others seem to be rather robust and healthy." NOAA has tested 33 beached dolphins for the virus, and 32 have either confirmed or suspected cases. Based on a similar outbreak 26 years ago, NOAA expects dolphins will continue dying until spring 2014. "At this point, there isn't anything we can do to stop the virus," says a NOAA official. "We don't have a vaccine that is developed that could be easily deployed in a wild population of bottle-nosed dolphins."

The sub would be able to explore Titan's lakes and rivers of liquid methane and ethane, as well as its weather, shoreline, tides, and even possible life forms, according to a NASA press release. The team expects the sub to splash down on Titan in about 2047, according to Phys.org.

– Archaeologists have uncovered what they believe was an escape tunnel from the infamous Sobibor Nazi death camp in Poland, LiveScience reports. "We were excavating near where the sonderkommando barrack was and we came across two rows of buried barbed wire," one of the Polish researchers tells the Telegraph. "Digging down we found the traces of the tunnel. It was about as wide as a human, and we are 99% certain that it was an escape tunnel." The sonderkommando were tasked with herding victims to the gas chambers and disposing of their bodies, and their function at Sobibor would have spared them the death on arrival that awaited so many of the camp's victims, and given them the time to the tunnel. There were no escape attempts from Sobibor until 600 prisoners broke out during a 1943 uprising, and experts say the tunnel was probably discovered and everybody who might have been connected with it executed. The excavation was apparently filled in. Only 50 escapees are believed to have survived the war. Sobibor killed an estimated 250,000 people, most of them Jews.

Med Express apologized immediately and offered to reimburse her for the postage due, but Nicholls posted the review anyway. She didn't back down, and she lawyered up, obtaining pro bono counsel with help from Paul Levy at Public Citizen. "This is an important win for consumers," Levy said in a statement about the ruling. "It shows that consumers have recourse when companies such as Med Express try to bully and silence consumers from telling other potential customers about their bad experiences." Radey had a history of such lawsuits, and the judge in this case found that his testimony "varied from the first hearing" and that some of Nicholls' statements were "undeniably true," but that he had no "objective reason whatsoever to question their veracity."

– The so-called "dead zone" in the Gulf of Mexico has shrunk a bit this year, but it remains far too big for the creatures that live at the bottom of the water, scientists say. This year's low-oxygen zone is 5,052 square miles, down about 800 square miles from last year's record-setting size of 8,100 square miles, the New Orleans Times-Picayune reports. The zone, caused by too much nitrogen and phosphorus in the Mississippi and Atchafalaya rivers, is killing off phytoplankton and other organisms that live at the bottom of the water and can cause hypoxia, which kills fish, shrimp, and other creatures that live there, the scientists say. The scientists, who conducted their annual survey this year, say the area would have been even bigger if not for heavy rains in the Upper Midwest in June and a record high nitrate concentration in the Mississippi River in July, the Times-Picayune reports. "If the heavy rains in the Upper Midwest in June and the record high nitrate concentration in the Mississippi River at Baton Rouge on July 18 had coincided with a later survey, chances are that the area would have been larger," the lead researcher says. – The Los Angeles Times won the Pulitzer Prize for public service today for its series on the scandal-plagued city of Bell, Calif. "The Bell coverage was a classic exercise in gang tackling gang violence," said Times Editor Russ Stanton after the awards were announced. The documents show that the first phase of Speargun was completed in 2012 or early 2013, and the second phase was scheduled to begin in mid-2013. – The unemployment rate fell from 7.2% to 6.7% in December, but the number of jobs added was nowhere near what analysts were expecting. The 74,000 jobs added were the fewest added in three years, the AP reports, and the unemployment rate is the lowest since October 2008. Economists had expected a gain of 190,000 jobs, according to the Wall Street Journal, but the jobs report showed that the economy added an average of 182,000 jobs per month in 2013. For the year, the economy added an average of 182,000 jobs per month, roughly in line with 2012's average of 183,000. December's hiring is far below the average gain of 214,000 jobs a month in the preceding four months. But monthly gains averaged 182,000 last year, nearly matching the previous two years. Some economists had predicted before the report that colder weather could be to blame. Construction firms cut 16,000 jobs, the biggest drop in 20 months.

– One of two Wisconsin girls accused in the "Slender Man" stabbing of a classmate has been found competent to stand trial, reports the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel. Morgan Geyser, 12, and Anissa Weier, 13, are charged as adults in the May attack, which occurred after a sleepover to celebrate the birthday of Weier's friend, Payton Leutner. Both have been held in a juvenile detention facility, and their cases are expected to be moved to juvenile court. Geyser had been found competent to stand trial in August, but today her lawyer dropped that objection and agreed that she is now competent to proceed, reports the Journal Sentinel. At today's hearing, three mental health experts testified that Weier was bright, articulate, and cooperative, but lacked the "strategic decision-making ability" to make good decisions, reports the AP. They agreed she seemed to understand the charges she faces, at least at the very broadest level, but disagreed that she was competent to stand trial based on her age and immaturity.

– The average age of a member of Congress is 57, and the combined age of the two senators representing Hawaii is 172. But Illinois Rep. Aaron Schock, a party-line Republican with a middle-class, Rust Belt background, is the first US rep born in the 1980s and the grandson of many. He's committed to helping his generation embrace health and fitness as a personal responsibility—and he's doing it not just with words, but actions. "The biggest misconception people have about me is that when they see how young I am, they think, 'Oh, this guy must have always wanted to be in politics, his parents must have been politically connected,'" he tells Men's Health. "I'm a finance major and always intended to go into business. We would read the newspaper at home, but that was about as politically involved as my family got. I'd never even been to the state capital until I joined the school board." Schock is launching an initiative—the Fit for Summer, Fit for Life challenge—to help Americans take control of their health. "One of my favorite quotes is from Ben Franklin, who said, 'A good example is the best sermon,'" Schock says.

– Three Marines accused of hazing a fellow Marine who later killed himself in Afghanistan will be tried in a court-martial, the Marine Corps announced today. Sgt. Benjamin Johns, Jacob Jacoby, and Carlos Orozco III are charged with wrongfully humiliating and demeaning 21-year-old Lance Cpl. Harry Lew, who shot himself in a foxhole in April, the San Jose Mercury News reports. At an Article 32 hearing last month, witnesses testified that the Marines had physically abused Lew, making him do pushups, do side planks, and pour sand in his face. Commanders at the time said Lew may have been suffering from depression or some other medical condition, and that his sleeping may have been a symptom, the Los Angeles Times reports. Lew's aunt, Rep. Judy Chu of California, has held congressional hearings on military suicides since his death. The three Marines have yet to face disciplinary action, and it's unclear what punishment they would face if convicted by a military panel. In the only other similar case in recent years, two Army soldiers received several months in confinement and a third was fined for hazing an Ohio soldier who committed suicide.

"You can't drain the swamp and leave all the people in it," White House Office of Management and Budget Director Mick Mulvaney tells reporters. – Police in Pennsylvania are investigating the death of a 61-year-old man on the set of a movie about Fred Rogers. James Emswiller, a sound mixer working on the film You Are My Friend, fell two stories off a balcony in Mount Lebanon on Thursday evening, reports USA Today. Police say he may have suffered a medical event before the fall. Tom Hanks, who is playing the late children's television host, was on the set at the time and left after the incident, reports the Pittsburgh Tribune-Review. "This is a devastating tragedy and the studio is investigating the matter," Sony's TriStar Pictures division said in a statement. "Our thoughts and prayers are with Jim's loved ones, friends, and colleagues." Emswiller was pronounced dead at a nearby medical center. The movie is about journalist Tom Junod, who wrote a 1998 profile of Rogers.

– A 1-year-old boy in China was eating chow mein with his parents when he tripped and fell, sending a chopstick flying up his nose. His parents removed the chopstick and took him to the hospital, but doctors didn't notice the punctured brain or pieces of the chopstick still stuck in his head, Central European News reports. "When we got home after our first visit to the hospital, my husband broke all the chopsticks in half and threw them away as we were worried something like this could happen again," the boy's mom says. "But we had no idea there was still one inside of his head." When the boy started vomiting and showing signs of drowsiness, his parents brought him back to the hospital for a second time, and doctors noticed the piece of chopstick in his brain. "We were beside ourselves with worry," his mom says. "After removing the remaining six centimeters his condition improved immediately, but he does have a brain infection so will be staying in the hospital for further treatment," a doctor says. "Luckily it did not affect him much." Central European News has a photo of the chopstick lodged in the boy's brain. (Click to read about another case of a chopstick piercing a toddler's brain.)

– A volunteer for Ben Carson's presidential campaign died Tuesday after being hospitalized with injuries suffered in a car accident in western Iowa that hurt three other campaign workers, the AP reports. The volunteer, 25-year-old Braden Joplin, died late Tuesday afternoon. Campaign spokesman Jason Osborne said the crash occurred when a van carrying three Carson volunteers and a paid staffer flipped onto its side on an icy road and was hit by another vehicle. The others in the van were treated at a hospital in Atlantic, Iowa. Carson posted a picture of himself and Joplin on Twitter Tuesday night, writing: "Rest In Peace Braden Joplin. Our thoughts and prayers are with his family." Carson was in South Carolina at the time of the Tuesday morning accident and suspended his campaign events. The campaign projected that he would return to campaigning Thursday in Iowa, where the critical Republican caucuses are scheduled Feb. 1. Other candidates, including Republican Sens. Ted Cruz and Marco Rubio and Democratic former Secertary of State Hillary Clinton, and Donald Trump's campaign manager sent their prayers and wishes Tuesday: "I'm so sorry to hear about this terrible tragedy. My heart goes out to Braden's family and colleagues."

– It's not every day that a woman tweets about her breast cancer diagnosis, but that's exactly what Emily Gould did in a piece for New York. The 26-year-old, who'd never had a mammogram, decided to do so as a way to make her friend's news all about her, and to make fun of herself. "Maybe by doing so, I thought while I was driving, other women like me who'd never done this would also feel like it was less weird, less scary, more normal and worth doing without hesitation," she writes. "I'd crack some 140-character jokes. I'd make fun of myself and others. ... How can anything go bad when the doctor's name is Funk, and there are so many funny things to tweet?" Gould's Twitter feed is her way of letting people in on her experience, and she's already received more than 10,000 likes and 4,000 retweets. But she's not the only one tweeting about her diagnosis: Dr. Kristi Funk, the doctor who gave her the news, tweeted about it, too, along with a photo of her bandaged breast, reports the Washington Post. The unnamed British couple spent 10 days on a beach in Martinique before both developed rashes on their backsides, Live Science reports. They went to the ship's medical staff, who prescribed antibiotics, anti-fungal medications, and a steroid cream to try to ease the rash, but it didn't work. Both went to the hospital, where doctors diagnosed them with "cutaneous larva migrans," a skin condition caused by a hookworm infection. The couple was given anti-parasitic medication, and by the time they got back home, the woman was having shortness of breath, a dry cough, and chest pain, and her husband was having a dry cough and chest pain. The case report says the couple's condition was so severe that the 52-year-old woman had to have a heart transplant. – The top US general in Europe told lawmakers Thursday that Russia may be supplying the Taliban, Reuters reports. "I've seen the influence of Russia of late, increased influence in terms of association and perhaps even supply to the Taliban," Army Gen. Curtis Scaparrotti said during a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing. Scaparrotti didn't say what type of equipment the Taliban might have received or when, but the New York Times notes that any material support would be a "significant escalation" of Russia's involvement with the Taliban. "These claims are absolutely false," Zamir Kabulov, head of the Russian foreign ministry's department responsible for Afghanistan, tells the AFP. "These fabrications are designed, as we have repeatedly underlined, to justify the failure of the US military and politicians in the Afghan campaign. There is no other explanation." Russia considers the Taliban a terrorist group, and Kabulov in 2015 said Russia was exchanging information with the Taliban on fighting ISIS.

– The Federal Communications Commission is set to vote Dec. 14 on whether to gut net neutrality, meaning internet service providers like Comcast, Verizon, and AT&T would be free to mess up the internet as we know it. Here's what you need to know about the proposal, which the FCC says would make the system "more robust and competitive": The New York Times takes a look at the "far-reaching implications" of the proposal, which, if approved, would make it easier for ISPs to experiment with "fast lanes" and "slow lanes" and to prioritize or block traffic to their own services or content. It would also make it easier for states to enact their own net neutrality laws, which the FCC says "could pose an obstacle to or place an undue burden" on consumers. Ars Technica takes a look at the ramifications of the proposal and explains why it's a "huge leap" to think that the FCC is "attempting to significantly loosen the regulatory leash around ISPs so that they can go off and try new practices, even if they may put consumers at risk." – McDonald's customers in the UK and Ireland will soon be getting paper straws instead of plastic ones. The chain says the move, which will begin in September, is in response to customer feedback and will be complete by 2019, CNN reports. The company says plastic straws will still be available "for those that require it," but they will be kept behind the counter. McDonald's—which says it uses 1.8 million plastic straws a day in the UK and Ireland—says the paper straws will be offered on request. McDonald's UK and Ireland CEO Paul Pomroy says the change will be a "significant contribution" to reducing plastic waste. Environment Secretary Michael Gove praised the move as "a fine example to other large businesses." McDonald's is the latest company to make the move away from plastic, but it won't be the last to do so. Pizza Express and Wagamama have already stopped using plastic straws, and a group of more than 40 companies, including Coca-Cola, Nestle, and Procter & Gamble, pledged to reduce the amount of plastic they use and throw away in the UK.

– Detained Chinese artist Ai Weiwei has been allowed to meet with his family for the first time since his arrest more than 40 days ago. The artist met his wife at an unknown location on Sunday and told her he is well, his sister told the BBC. The family were then warned by police not to discuss the visit with the media as they were told it could "be bad for Mr. Ai's case." Ai's wife Lu Qing was taken by Chinese police to meet her husband on Sunday afternoon. The artist's sister told the BBC Lu Qing was summoned to a police station and taken to another location where she was allowed a brief meeting with her husband. She reported that Ai told her those holding him were taking good care of him, he was healthy and she should not worry. However the meeting was very brief, she said, and there were many other people present, some of them taking notes, so she was afraid to talk much more with her husband. The family were then warned by police not to discuss the visit with the media as they were told it could "be bad for Mr. Ai's case." Ai is a vocal critic of the government, complaining about a lack of basic freedoms and often incorporating these political themes into his work.

– A Texas woman is in jail after police say she passed out at a red light, then ran over her husband when he got out of the car to try to rouse her. Dallas police say Mary Jane Lane, 50, was driving with her husband when she stopped at a red light. Randall Lane got out of the SUV, opened the driver's side door, and tried to unbuckle his wife's seat belt, according to the Dallas Morning News. Mary Lane "came" and pressed the accelerator, police say. He was dragged until he fell from the SUV, suffering injuries to his head and both legs. Lane fled the scene, in violation of a law that requires a motorist to stop and render aid, police say. She was arrested for intoxication assault, although the charge was later reduced to driving while intoxicated. The condition of her husband is not known.

– The CIA has just released a trove of once-classified UFO documents—and it's using them to make a joke. "To help navigate the vast amount of data contained in our FOIA UFO collection, we've decided to highlight a few documents both skeptics and believers will find interesting," the agency says in a blog post. Included are documents the CIA declassified in 1978 that date back to the 1940s and 1950s, including 1952 reports of "flying saucers" over Spain and North Africa, "two fiery disks" over a uranium mine in the Congo, and minutes of a CIA branch chief's meeting on UFOs, LiveScience reports. "We also pulled five documents we think his skeptical partner, Agent Dana Scully, could use to prove there is a scientific explanation for UFO sightings," the blog post says. "The truth is out there," the CIA adds.

– The government shutdown has forced the National Institutes of Health to close its doors to new patients. The "most painful consequence" of the shutdown is "for the clinical center, the largest research hospital in the world," says NIH Director Francis Collins. Many of the hospital's patients have cancer, a rare genetic disease, or a serious infection that hasn't been relieved elsewhere. Meanwhile, workers will show up to feed and care for animals in NIH labs, but basic research conducted by NIH scientists there will stop. "The vast majority of CDC's activities will be shut down completely," according to an agency spokesperson. "Only about 4,000 of the CDC's 13,000 staff members will continue to work." The FDA "will not be conducting multi-state outbreak investigations," but will keep the emergency operation center working "at a reduced capacity," that can be geared up quickly if a serious outbreak of illness is discovered. The National Institutes of Health's Clinical Center is home to 1,437 studies—of which 255 are looking at cancer treatments for adults and children. Four had been scheduled to begin this week, but won't if the shutdown continues. The US Geological Survey is home to 8,600 employees, 43 of whom are deemed essential and working during the shutdown. – Finland's state-owned postal service is hoping to boost its sagging business by offering a lawn-mowing service this summer, the BBC reports. Customers will have to provide their own lawnmower and pay $73 a month for 30 minutes or 60 minutes of lawn-mowing time on Tuesdays. "We have genuinely tried to find services that would make people's lives easier," says a manager at Posti. "Using power-driven machinery and equipment requires a certain expertise," says the head of a real estate employers group. "It is hard to believe that just anyone can start to cut lawns." The service will be available nationwide between May and August, according to Yle.

– The Carolina Panthers have deactivated star defensive end Greg Hardy for today's game against the Detroit Lions, reports ESPN. Hardy was found guilty in July of assaulting and threatening ex-girlfriend Nicole Holder, but the Panthers decided not to punish him while he appealed. He was expected to start today. "I know y'all are wondering [about Greg Hardy]," Panthers coach Ron Rivera said after the team's 24-7 victory yesterday. "I made the decision this morning. It was my decision because it was in the best interest of the Carolina Panthers." Rivera wouldn't say why, but ESPN notes that the team has come under heavy fire for not punishing Hardy sooner after the Ray Rice controversy.

– The parents of a 2-year-old Missouri boy who died after being left alone in a room with a space heater on for 38 hours have been charged. Police in St. Charles say Kathleen Peacock, 22, and Lucas Barnes, 25, were cooking meth at the time of their son Braydon's death and ignored the boy's cries, the St. Louis Post-Dispatch reports. Peacock, who is pregnant, and Barnes, who is 25 years old, have been charged with child abuse and neglect and manufacturing meth. Police say the couple was on a drug binge when they left Braydon in his room with the heater on on Friday night and didn't check on him for more than 38 hours, CNN reports. An autopsy found that the boy died of hyperthermia after the heater never turned off, KTVI reports. Police say the parents told them they had been manufacturing meth in the home the week before the boy's death. Neighbors say they are devastated by the death of the toddler, who they say appeared malnourished recently. "I just know that baby is in a better place. He was innocent. He was the most innocent most pure human being that could have happened," a neighbor tells KTVI. "So you know he's an angel in heaven

– As the international epidemic of Zika virus disease has unfolded and led to devastating birth defects for at least 1,300 children in eight countries, an agonizing question has persisted: What is the chance that an infected pregnant woman will have a baby with these defects? Researchers don't yet have a complete answer, but they are slowly homing in on one, reports the AP. The largest study to ever look at the question says the risk of one especially severe type of birth defect is "substantial"—in the range of 1% to 14%. It also reinforces the understanding that women infected in the early stages of pregnancy face the greatest risk. The range is so unusually wide because researchers are relying on imprecise and incomplete information as they to try to quickly estimate the level of risk in advance of what they say is likely transmission of Zika by mosquitoes in the US later this year. The study focused on what was seen in just one place, a state in northeast Brazil. And it looks only at microcephaly, a condition in which a baby's skull is much smaller than expected because the brain hasn't developed properly. But health officials say Zika can cause other birth defects, too. "These numbers are probably only the tip of the iceberg," says UCLA professor of obstetrics who has been

– A high school in Alabama refused to give a Native American student her diploma after she wore an eagle feather to graduation—because she had to pay a $1,000 fine for wearing it, AL.com reports. "I feel like this wasn't fair," 17-year-old Chelsey Ramer says. "It really did hurt my feelings. I have watched others wear it and I looked forward to it my whole four years there. Now when it was my turn, [they said] I couldn't." Ramer says she and three other American Indian seniors asked the private Escambia Academy for permission to wear the feathers and were told "no" and that if they did, they would be removed from the field. She says she was given a contract that said she would not be given her diploma or transcripts until she paid the fine. Ramer says she was told by the school's headmaster that she had been fired. "I asked why she got fired and the people told me they didn't know," she says. "I didn't say anything, but Coach Walker said some people from Indian country were calling him and asking for a statement, but he didn't know what to tell them." – President Obama's jobs bill is dead, and he's throwing his former Senate colleagues under the bus as he scrambles to win another term, writes Joseph Curl in the Washington Times. Obama's strategy is clear: blame Congress for the mess America's in. But in so doing, he has caught up his fellow Democrats who, pressed to the wall, are fully prepared to bail on him and save their own skins. They want no part of the amateurish strategy to try to blame Congress, half-controlled by Democrats. In fact, even some of the most rabidly liberal Democrats are planning to abandon the president because they see he’s only interested in saving his job, not theirs. More, Mr. Obama is throwing his former Senate colleagues under the bus as he scrambles to win another term. So, this jobs bill is dead. And no matter how many times Mr. Obama repeats the lie that his 'is the kind of proposal that's been supported by both Democrats and Republicans,' it will be House Republicans who write a bill that can actually pass the Senate." The driver was taken into custody after the crash around noon in the coastal city of Huludao in Liaoning province, said the spokesman for Jianchang county in the city's suburbs, who declined to give his name as is standard with Chinese bureaucrats. He described the crash as "a major traffic accident" and that the cause was under investigation. Security camera footage showed a line of children crossing the street in front of their school when a car approaches, which then changes lanes and swerves into the crowd of children. It wasn't clear if the crash was a deliberate attack or whether the driver was swerving to avoid obstacles in front of him. Last month, a knife-wielding man drove a vehicle into a crowd of pedestrians in the eastern city of Ningbo, killing two people and wounding 16. And in September, 11 people were killed and 44 hospitalized after a man drove an SUV deliberately into people at a plaza in the central province of Hunan, before jumping out and attacking victims with a dagger and shovel. – Farmers, lumberjacks, and fishermen have the highest suicide rate in the US, while librarians and educators have the lowest, according to a large study that found enormous differences across occupations. The study didn't explore the reasons behind the differences, but researchers found the highest suicide rates in manual laborers who work in isolation and face unsteady employment, the AP reports. High rates were also seen in carpenters, miners, electricians, and people who work in construction. Mechanics were close behind. Dentists, doctors, and other health care professionals had an 80% lower suicide rate than the farmers, fishermen, and lumberjacks. Thursday's report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is perhaps the largest US study to compare suicide rates among occupations. But it is not comprehensive. It only covers 17 states, looking at about 12,300 of the more than 40,000 suicide deaths reported in the entire nation in 2012. Because of the limited data, they could only calculate suicide rates for broad occupation categories, but not for specific jobs. The categories, which sometimes seem to group professions that have little to do with each other, like athletes and artists, are based on federal classifications used for collecting jobs-related data. So it's not clear what the suicide rate is just for farmers. Or for mathematicians

Cruise is at his best, and Annabelle Wallis is "terrific" as a "faux-archeologist/genuine anti-evil secret agent." The movie is "amazingly relentless in its naked borrowing from other, better horror and sci-fi movies that I was able to keep occupied making a checklist of the movies referenced," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Times. "It's a monster movie, not a horror movie," she writes, and it's "well-made, well-paced, and well-acted." Cruise and Wallis are "mesmerizing" together, but the movie as a whole is "a bit of a letdown." "The Mummy is an over-the-top, over-the-top, over-the-top spectacle," writes Joe Morgenstern at

– Starting May 23, new lawyers in California will have to swear to do their best to be civil with their clients, other attorneys, and judges. The state's Supreme Court approved a pledge to be "dignity, courtesy, and integrity" in a unanimous decision yesterday, the Los Angeles Times reports. The move is the first change to an oath taken by all 250,000 lawyers in the state, but the pledge is being pushed through by a lawyers' association nationwide. The former president of California's State Bar says he pushed for the change after 45 years of practice to remind lawyers that there's more to being a lawyer than winning cases and billing clients. "Many have forgotten these very principles to which we, as professionals, should always adhere," says a former president of the American Board of Trial Advocates, which pushed for the change. Some have expressed concern that the pledge will lead to discipline for uncivil behavior, but a court spokesman says it's not a basis for discipline. "It's a reminder of positive professional behavior, rather than a stick," he says.

– Former All in the Family star Sally Struthers was arrested early yesterday for drunk driving in Maine, reports TMZ. The 65-year-old was charged with criminal operating under the influence and released on $160 bail. Struthers has been in the state performing in the musical 9 to 5 at the Ogunquit Playhouse. "Sally is working and she is fine and she loves The Ogunquit Playhouse and her yearly time in Ogunquit. We deny these charges," her publicist tells the AP.

– Bernie Sanders may be a long way from winning the Democratic nomination, but he's got big money—and it's coming from people like Donna Mae Litowitz. The Miami Beach retiree tells the New York Times that she donated $10,000 to the Vermont senator's campaign last year, and his campaign returned most of it because it was more than he was allowed to take under federal election law. "I like what Sanders stands for, and he says what needs to be said," she says. "And I don't like Hillary Clinton." According to the Times' analysis of campaign finance reports, Sanders has raised more money from small donations of $200 or less than any candidate, Democrat or Republican, and 75% of his money has come from small donations routed through ActBlue, an online site that facilitates contributions to Democrats. The average donation to Sanders' campaign is $31.30. "I like what Sanders stands for, and he says what needs to be said," Litowitz says. "And I don't like Hillary Clinton." Sanders' campaign manager says it's "absolutely possible to win without the super PACs." Super PACs supporting Hillary Clinton have raised more than $20 million, while two super PACs backing Jeb Bush raised more than $108.5 million.

– Three years after the Mumbai terror attacks that left 165 people dead, Indian police have arrested a man they say was the "handler" of the 10 gunmen who stormed the city, the BBC reports. Police say Sayed Zabiuddin alias Abu Jindal, who was arrested in New Delhi on June 21, is also believed to have trained the attackers in the Hindi language. The sole surviving gunman, Mohammad Ajmal Amir Qasab, was convicted of murder and waging war on India in 2010 and given a death sentence. The 30-year-old Jindal arrived in India from a Gulf country and was wanted on an Interpol Red Corner notice for crimes involving the use of weapons, explosives, and terrorism.

It's the third year in a row the US has had the top spot, with Walmart second with $3.5 trillion and Amazon third with $3.5 trillion. – Joan Lee, the wife of Marvel Comics icon Stan Lee, died Thursday at age 95, Variety reports. "I can confirm the sad news that Joan Lee passed away this morning quietly and surrounded by her family," a spokesperson for Lee and his family said in a statement. "The family ask that you please give them time to grieve and respect their privacy during this difficult time." Joan Lee, a former British hat model, met Lee, 95, when he was supposed to take her on a blind date in 1947. Together, they had two children: Joan Celia (J.C.) and Jan, who died three days after her birth in 1953. Lee authored a novel, The Pleasure Palace, in 1987 about a man's mission to create the world's most luxurious ocean liner while simultaneously balancing three romances. The couple met when Lee was supposed to take a friend on a blind date. After a six-week stay in Reno, Nevada, a judge granted her divorce and they married in a room next door. They moved to New York, where Stan Lee worked for Timely/Atlas Comics, now known as Marvel Comics. Stan cited Joan as inspiration for the burgeoning Fantastic Four project he co-created with Jack Kirby in 1961. Joan did voice work

– Amanda Knox says she won't go back to Italy if she's found guilty again in the murder of Meredith Kercher. In an interview with La Repubblica published today, Knox said she would be a "fugitive" if convicted. "In that case, I will be defined a 'fugitive,' but I will continue to fight for my innocence," she said. "I will not willingly submit myself to injustice." Knox's comments were condemned by the Kercher family's lawyer, who told an Italian news agency, "Amanda must act like a defendant ... she should stop making these statements." Knox released a statement to Today clarifying her comments. "I will not willingly submit myself to injustice," she said. "I still want to talk with them, tell them directly that I had nothing to do with Meredith's death, that I cared about her and that we were friends. But I know that they see me as their daughter's murderer [and] are convinced that it was me who killed her, and so it is still not the moment to speak with them. But that day will come." A verdict is expected later this month.

– Ted Haggard, the former president of the National Association of Evangelicals and the subject of a 2006 sex and drug scandal, is getting his own reality show. Haggard and his wife, Gayle, will appear on ABC's Celebrity Wife Swap, in which they'll swap partners (without sex) with actor Gary Busey and his partner and baby mama, Steffanie Sampson, reports the Colorado Springs Gazette. The show is scheduled to shoot today in Colorado Springs. "On the surface, it might seem like an unlikely pairing, but there are several surprising parallels between Busey and Haggard," observes the Gazette. "Busey is a born-again Christian and active minister with Promise Keepers, and Haggard has returned to the ministry as pastor of St. James, a new nondenominational Christian church in Colorado Springs."

– The famous chestnut tree that comforted Anne Frank as she hid from the Nazis in an Amsterdam attic has collapsed, reports Reuters. The 150-year-old tree broke off across a fence, missing the Anne Frank House, which has been turned into a museum and was full of tourists. "It broke off like a match. It broke off completely about one meter off the ground," a spokesman for the house said. The tree was one of the few signs of nature visible to the Jewish teenager from the concealed attic she hid in for over two years during World War II. "Our chestnut tree is in full blossom. It is covered with leaves and is even more beautiful than last year," she wrote in May 1944, not long before she was betrayed to the Nazis. The tree had developed fungus and was set to be felled in 2007 due to concerns for the safety of the 1 million people who visit Anne Frank’s house each year. But officials and conservationists later agreed to secure it with a steel frame to prolong its life and saplings from the tree were planted last year in an Amsterdam park and other cities around the world. – Gilad Schalit is finally home, having been freed by Hamas after five years in captivity. The Israeli soldier, who was exchanged for 1,000 Palestinian prisoners, arrived in Israel today and was greeted by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other top officials, the AP reports. After a medical examination, Israeli officials said Schalit showed signs of malnutrition. The 25-year-old appeared to struggle to speak at times, and his breathing was noticeably labored as he awkwardly answered questions in an interview with Egyptian TV. Israeli officials reacted angrily to the interview, saying it was inappropriate to force Schalit to answer questions in such difficult circumstances. But the circumstances of his release, along with the awkward TV interview, raised questions about the conditions the 25-year-old had endured. Schalit's father said his son will need time to recover from psychological and physical wounds. He said his son is still suffering from shrapnel wounds he suffered during his 2006 abduction by Hamas militants. He said his son is struggling with all the attention after spending the last few years in "isolation." "Naturally he can't be exposed to so many people because he was in isolation so many days and years and couldn't interact with people in his language, and all he could do was communicate with his abductor

– Starting today, New Yorkers will no longer be able to use the city's iconic subway token to get onto the subway. The fare hike that took effect in the wake of the Sandy Hook shooting will make the blue and yellow MetroCards the only means of transportation for riders, the New York Times reports. The tokens, which were introduced in 1953, are expected to save the transit authority $6 million a year. "It says 'NYC' on it, so that's certainly a big part of its appeal, but it's also popular because it's a very democratic symbol," says a historian. The subway token has been a fixture in the city's history since it was first issued. It's "so deeply embedded in New York's identity and so many different kinds of people use it, the token by symbolizing the subway comes to symbolize the city," says the historian. But don't look for it to be replaced: "The MetroCard," she says, "doesn't have the visual presence of the token." Click for more.

– Gunmen stormed the five-star Corinthia Hotel in Libya's capital this morning, setting off a battle with security forces that has so far killed at least two attackers and forced dozens of guests to flee, the AP reports. The attack began with an explosion in the hotel's parking lot, and the New York Times notes that it's not clear whether it was a bomb, a rocket-propelled grenade, or some kind of missile. The hotel is one of Tripoli's most luxurious and is also home to the offices of several foreign embassies. The attack comes amid chaos in the country, which has been split between an Islamist-dominated government and an Islamist-dominated parliament and government since the overthrow and killing of Moammar Gadhafi last year. The Islamic State has claimed responsibility for the attack, saying it was retaliation for the capture and killing of a Libyan al-Qaeda operative in the US last year.

– The five teens killed in a fiery car crash in Newport Beach, Calif., on Monday were headed to the beach for a fun Memorial Day. Robin Cabrera, 17; Aurora Cabrera, 16; Cecilia Zamora, 17; and Nozad Al Hamawendi, 17, all students at two high schools in the Irvine Unified School District; and Abdulrahman Alyahyan, 17, the driver, were in the car. "It was a horrific accident," a police spokeswoman tells the AP. Speed is believed to be a factor in the crash, which split the car in two and set it on fire. The traditional way to avoid passing defective mitochondrial DNA to their offspring is to fertilize both the mother's egg and a donor's egg with the father's sperm. However, the couple wanted to keep the mother's egg instead of discarding the donor's egg, so scientists used a new technique called spindle nuclear transfer, which involves removing the nucleus from the mother's egg and inserting it into a donor's egg. The resulting egg was then fertilized with the father's sperm. The technique, which was used in Mexico, is expected to be presented at the American Society for Reproductive Medicine's Scientific Congress in Salt Lake City in October. – A new study finds that the men of the Internet are the ones who are most likely to be sexist. Researchers watched 163 plays of the video game Halo 3 and discovered that no matter their skill level or how well the game was played, men tended to be nice to women, the Washington Post reports. But when it came to making nasty comments, the men were the ones who were "literally losers," the paper says. "Sexist dudes are literally losers." The study, published in Plos One, is the first to look at the behavior of male gamers in an online environment, the Guardian reports. "Sexist behavior is prevalent in almost all workplaces and rampant in online environments," the researchers write. "Although there is much research dedicated to understanding sexist behavior, we have almost no insight into what triggers this behavior and the individuals that initiate it." The researchers hypothesize that the behavior is caused by the disruption of a male hierarchy caused by the rise of female gamers. "The increase in hostility towards a woman by lower-status males may be an attempt to disregard a female’s performance and suppress her disturbance on the hierarchy to retain their social rank," the researchers say. The researchers say their findings should be applied to other online spaces, like Twitter and 4chan.

If Congress can't get a bigger package done by the March 1 sequester deadline, "then I believe that they should at least pass a smaller package of spending cuts and tax reforms that would delay the economically damaging effects of the sequester for a few more months," said the president. Bush, but Bush lost the Electoral College.

– Three astronauts are back on Earth after spending a record-breaking 288 days in space on the International Space Station, the AP reports. The Soyuz spacecraft carrying NASA astronaut Peggy Whitson, Russian cosmonaut Fyodor Yurchikhin, and NASA astronaut Jack Fischer landed in Kazakhstan late Saturday. According to Space.com, Whitson set a new record for the most cumulative time in space by an American, with 665 days spent on the ISS. Fischer and Yurchikhin arrived at the ISS in April with an empty seat. Whitson, the oldest woman in space, joined the crew in November to finish out the last leg of the station's three-month mission. She will be the first American to spend more than 200 days in space.

The new sanctions include a ban on ballistic missile and nuclear tests, the expulsion of Kim Jong Un's regime's diplomats in the country, and a ban on the sale or transfer of small arms and light weapons to North Korea. According to CNN, the new sanctions are the strongest ever imposed on North Korea. North Korea's foreign ministry called the new sanctions "heinous provocation aimed at depriving the DPRK (Democratic People's Republic of Korea) of its legitimate right for self-defense." It said the sanctions were "fabricated by the US employing all sorts of despicable and vicious means and methods." Meanwhile, President Trump said the new sanctions are "just another very small step, not a big deal." He added that the new sanctions pale in comparison to "what ultimately will have to happen" to North Korea.

Trump tweeted: "I am pleased to inform you that I have just named General/Secretary John F Kelly as White House Chief of Staff. He is a Great American... and a Great Leader. "It will probably take me two-and-a-half or three hours," he says. "I had music in my head. I was just walking, not worried about nothing, I was just moving my feet." Lewis says his job "got more important" to him when his daughter was born. "I didn't have a job when she was born," he tells KATV. "I wanted to be with my daughter, to be able to support her. I wanted to be a father." So he started walking before midnight, sometimes getting rides, but most of the time walking. He never missed a shift and was never late to work. When his co-workers heard about his walk, Kenneth Bryant, a veteran UPS driver, started collecting donations from other workers. "Man, that's got to be a dedicated young man to walk to work," he says. They raised $1,900 and bought him a Saturn. "That's actually the third car because a couple of them fell through," Bryant says.
