Fresno police say they pulled Noble over after receiving reports of a man with a rifle in his pickup truck, but they later learned he had no weapons on him or in his truck, the Guardian reports. New York and New England are bracing for a storm that's expected to dump a foot or more of snow on parts of the region today, with more on the way, the AP reports. "This one doesn't come along every day. This is going to be a dangerous winter storm," says a National Weather Service meteorologist. – President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump have paid their respects to former President George HW Bush at the US Capitol, where the body of the nation's 41st president is lying in state at the Capitol Rotunda. The Trumps stood in front of the casket Monday evening with their eyes closed for a few moments. After Trump saluted the casket, the pair walked out. Trump skipped an earlier service at the Capitol, where Bush was eulogized by Vice President Mike Pence, among others. Trump plans to attend Bush's state funeral Wednesday at Washington National Cathedral, the AP reports. Trump has a fractured relationship with the Bush family, whom he has repeatedly criticized. But he has praised Bush since his passing as "just a high-quality man who truly loved his family" and a "terrific guy" who will be missed. In his remarks Monday, Pence praised Bush as a "sound counselor and loyal adviser to an outsider who came to Washington, DC, to shake things up, cut taxes, rebuild the military, and together they did just that." – A New Jersey high school quarterback died Friday night after being injured during a football game, the AP reports. Evan Murray of Warren Hills Regional High School was hurt in the third quarter of a game against Summit. He was taken off the field on a stretcher and pronounced dead at a hospital. NJ.com reports officials were still trying to figure out what happened. "We lost a fine kid," says Warren Hills coach Larry Dubiel. Murray was a three-sport athlete at the high school, playing football, baseball, and basketball. He was also the starting quarterback for three years. "He's one of the greatest kids in this whole community. It's unbelievable. I still don't believe it," classmate Anthony Veneziano tells the Jersey Journal. "Everyone honored him, and they should because he deserves it," he adds. "They should continue to honor him forever." Murray's death is the latest tragedy to hit the Warren Hills community, which was already struggling after the death of a 17-year-old student in an auto accident in July and the death of a 2012 graduate who contracted bacterial meningitis while studying abroad in Paris over the summer.

– Mahmoud Ahmadinejad kicked off the Non-Aligned Movement summit in Tehran today by promising that Iran would continue its nuclear program in peaceful fashion. "Our motto is nuclear energy for all and nuclear weapons for none," he told the assembled heads of state, according to Reuters. The Iranian president is hoping the two-day summit will prove that sanctions against his country have failed. The summit is also being attended by Egypt's Mohamed Mursi, the first Egyptian leader to visit Iran since the country's 1979 Islamic Revolution, but the Syrian delegation walked out after Mursi called for the nations to support the Syrian opposition, the AP reports. The summit is expected to declare deep concern about the violence in Syria and support for a UN-Arab League envoy trying to broker a resolution.

So don't expect any grand revelations but based on the way Shargel has behaved already, I would not be surprised to hear some theatrics from the defense.”

– The mayor of one of Italy's most polluted cities has issued a temporary ban on wood-burning pizza stoves in an effort to combat the city's worsening air pollution, the BBC reports. According to the Local, San Vitaliano residents spent 114 days in 2015 breathing air that exceeded safe levels. "We are still unsure of the cause of the pollution, but the situation has got worse during the winter and we need to take maximum precautions to ensure the problem doesn't deteriorate," the mayor of the town north of Naples wrote in an order banning the use of wood-burning stoves in bakeries and pizzerias. "The only exceptions are for those which have filter systems in place that will guarantee the elimination of 80% of all polluting Pm10 particulates." According to the Local, San Vitaliano is one of the most polluted cities in Italy, while nearby Naples is seen as one of the most polluted cities in the world. The temporary ban will be in place until March 31 next year. According to the BBC, pizzeria owners and residents protested the ban outside town hall on Sunday. – South Korea's main opposition party ended its nine-day filibuster of the country's National Assembly on Wednesday evening, the BBC reports. According to Yonhap News, Lee Jong-kul, floor leader of the Minjoo Party of Korea, was the last speaker of the filibuster, speaking for 12 hours, 31 minutes—breaking the record set by a fellow MP on Sunday. The Minjoo Party of Korea is opposed to an anti-terrorism bill that would give the country's intelligence service the authority to collect information on private communications, travel, and financial transactions of potential terrorists. The MPK claims the bill would give the intelligence service too much power and could even be used to monitor civilians and opposition lawmakers. The filibuster began on Feb. 23. According to the AP, 39 opposition lawmakers spoke for 192 hours and 25 minutes over the course of the filibuster to block a vote on the anti-terrorism bill. The longest filibuster in the world was a 57-hour filibuster by a Canadian party in 2011, the BBC reports. According to Yonhap, the filibuster was the first in Korea since 1969. Thousands of people attended the National Assembly to watch the opposition lawmakers speak. "Everyone participated with enthusiasm," Lee said. – Joe Wilson says he'll be a "gentleman" during tonight's State of the Union address—but he's not exactly keeping a low profile. He'll be live-streaming the speech on Facebook, he tells Talking Points Memo. "I'm going to be a gentleman and listen to the president's speech," he says. "I'm not going to do anything to hurt the president. I'm going to be a gentleman and listen to his speech." Wilson's not the only one hoping for a quiet night. "Any time a president comes to Capitol Hill it is an historic occasion," Eric Cantor told Talking Points Memo. "I hope the president has listened and learned that his agenda is not supported by the American people."

– Kathy Griffin has a new target in her sights: Michele Bachmann. In an appearance on Conan last night, the comedian recounted a run-in she had with the congresswoman when she was researching an article on her website about the repeal of Don't Ask, Don't Tell. "Congresswoman Bachmann, were you born a bigot or did you, like, grow into it?" she asked on tape. Bachmann's response: "That's a good question. I'm gonna have to get back to ya." In other Bachmann news, Politico reports that her campaign staff has been involved in at least five "unusually hostile encounters with the traveling media"—pushing, shoving, and threatening reporters. The most aggressive aide is a former Secret Service agent who often makes physical contact with reporters. A spokeswoman says he is "extremely professional." "He's guarded presidents and vice presidents and knows exactly what needs to be done," she says. "When he gives a warning to whoever it may be, the person needs to heed the warning."

– The captain of the Costa Concordia is on trial for the deaths of 32 passengers and crew members, and today Francesco Schettino got to see the ship he's accused of abandoning for the first time. The AP reports that Schettino was taken to the wreck on a small boat, two days after arriving on the island of Giglio, where the cruise ship capsized in January 2012. He's being allowed on the ship "as a defendant, not a consultant," says the judge. Schettino, who is accused of manslaughter, abandoning ship, and causing a shipwreck, says he wept when he saw the wreck from a ferry taking him to Giglio, the BBC reports. "They want to show that I am weak, just like two years ago. It's not true. I want to show I'm a gentleman, not a coward," he said, per Italian media. "There is a frenzy that is making me nervous. You have to respect civility." The ship, which was righted in September last year, is still stuck off the coast of Giglio.

– A region of the human brain that monitors alternative choices appears to be unique to humans and could help us make better decisions in the future, according to a new study. Researchers from Oxford University scanned the brains of 25 healthy people before and after the study, then compared that data to MRI scans of the brains of monkeys, the Guardian reports. They found that a region of the human ventrolateral frontal cortex, called the lateral frontal pole, was only found in humans. "We have established an area in human frontal cortex which does not seem to have an equivalent in the monkey at all," the lead researcher says. "This area has been identified with strategic planning and decision making as well as 'multi-tasking,'" he adds. The researchers believe the area is responsible for our ability to be flexible and to be able to plan for the future. "There are a few brain areas that monitor how good our choices are, and that is a very sensible thing to have," the lead researcher tells the Guardian. "But this region monitors how good the choices are that we didn't take. It tells us how green the grass is on the other side of the fence." – A California high school photography teacher is dead after students found her hanging from the ceiling of her locked classroom yesterday morning. Jillian Jacobson, 31, was found by several students at El Dorado High School in Placentia, the Los Angeles Times reports. Another teacher unlocked the door and found Jacobson hanging from the ceiling. "If you take into account how everyone reacted by crying and being upset, you'll see how everyone was completely surprised that it was her," a student tells the Orange County Register. "She gave no signs of being depressed or sad." Police say she may have died before paramedics arrived, but she was declared dead at the scene and may have died before paramedics arrived, KTLA reports. No suicide note was found. The entire student body was released after about an hour, and grief counselors were on hand to help students deal with the tragedy, the Register reports. "I'm so sad today. Mrs. J was amazing to our family after Logan passed and one of his fav teachers RIP," tweeted the mother of 16-year-old Logan Wells, who was struck and killed by an SUV while skateboarding on campus last year.

– Today is the 20th anniversary of Take Our Daughters to Work Day, and Jennifer Allyn at the Christian Science Monitor thinks it's time for parents to take their daughters to the C-suite. "That disparity is costing our companies talent, hurting the country's competitiveness, and undermining our ideals of fairness and social equality," she writes. "Simply showing our daughters what an office looks like is no longer enough. We need to take our daughters into the C-suite now so they can lead in the future." The Take Our Daughters to Work Day has "definitively accomplished" its mission of demystifying the workplace for girls, but it's time to expand to the C-suite. "Girls no longer need help picturing themselves in a job; what they do need is encouragement to become leaders," she writes. "It's time to take them to the C-suite, where the corporate chiefs work." – President Obama left the G20 summit in St. Petersburg today with little progress on his plan to launch a military strike against Syria, reports the Washington Post. He met face-to-face with Vladimir Putin and emerged with a statement from 10 nations calling for the Assad regime to be held accountable for the alleged chemical weapons attack, but it did not explicitly support military action. Obama's big hope was to use the summit to convince Congress to support a strike, but it looks like he'll have to settle for a statement from the likes of Britain, France, Germany, and Italy, reports the New York Times. "This is not something that I think a lot of folks around the world, you know, find an appetizing set of choices," said Obama. "But the question is, do these norms mean something? And if we're not acting, what does that say?" At a news conference, Putin said he and Obama "remained unconvinced by each other's opinion," but that there was a "dialogue" and they "understand arguments, but we don't agree with them." He added that Russia will continue to supply weapons to Assad in his battle against the rebel opposition, reports the LA Times.

– President Trump and Sarah Palin won't be invited to John McCain's funeral, multiple sources tell People. "Two names you won't see inside the invite list: Trump and Palin," says a Capitol Hill source. Carla Eudy, a fundraiser who has been friends with the McCain family for decades, confirmed that "toughs were not extended" to the two political figures. A source says several longtime McCain staffers were also removed from the invite list in recent days. "My guess is, it came from Cindy," says the source. "She is very protective of John's memory and legacy. She's also a grieving widow. I think she wants to get through this best she can." Another source says Cindy McCain is expected to be appointed to replace her husband in the Senate. Trump, meanwhile, is expected to visit Washington, DC, on Saturday to discuss filling McCain's seat in the Senate. "I will always cherish my friend John's friendship," Palin said in a statement Saturday. "John never took the easy path in life—and through sacrifice and suffering he inspired others when he failed the 10-year re-election campaign in 2008."

– It's been three years since Taylor Swift last released a major record, but she's finally ready to drop one. On Wednesday, Swift announced on Instagram that her sixth album, Reputation, will be released Nov. 10 and that the first single will be released Thursday night. Reputation will be Swift's first major record in three years, Rolling Stone reports. Swift also released a three-part video series in which she makes a snake.

– Gambian President Yahya Jammeh has announced that all of the country's death row inmates will be executed by the middle of next month, reports the AFP. The West African nation hasn't executed anyone in 27 years, notes CNN, but Jammeh didn't give a precise number. He did, however, vow to "take whatever legal action is necessary to expunge these deadly and heinous acts from the country." Amnesty International is not happy. "President Jammeh's comments are deeply troubling and will undoubtedly cause severe anguish to those on death row and their families," says the group's Africa director. "Any attempt to carry out this threat would be both deeply shocking and a major setback for human rights in Gambia." Gambia has the death penalty for crimes including murder, treason, and drug trafficking.

– Two years after being arrested and sentenced to eight years in prison on espionage charges, Shane Bauer and Joshua Fattal have been freed by Iran. The two 29-year-old hikers were released on bail of $1 million each in Oman, where they were reunited with family members after flying out of Tehran, the New York Times reports. "We're so happy we are free," Fattal told reporters at Muscat International Airport in Oman. "Two years in prison is too long. We hope this will lead to freedom for political prisoners in America and Iran." Bauer's fiancee, Sarah Shourd, was on hand to greet him as he ran down the stairs from the plane upon his release. "Today can only be described as the best day of our lives," the family said in a statement, according to the AP. "We have waited for nearly 26 months for this moment. We now all want nothing more than to wrap Shane and Josh in our arms, catch up on two lost years, and make a new beginning, for them and for all of us." The release came a day before Mahmoud Ahmadinejad was scheduled to address the UN General Assembly in New York, and it seemed timed at least in part as a goodwill gesture ahead of the speech.

– Critics are swooning over the documentary Babies, which follows four babies from around the world over their first year of life. Here's what they're saying: "This extraordinary film and its adorable stars without a goofy smile will be hard to watch," writes Eric D. Snider of the Washington Post. "But it will be hard to watch this extraordinary film and its adorable stars without a goofy smile." Director Thomas Balmes "has a light touch capturing the captivating moments of early life," writes Roger Ebert of the Chicago Sun-Times. "It's not a traditional documentary; there's no narration, subtitles or scientific information imparted. There's far more gurgling and cooing than dialogue." "There's nothing Hollywood or Gerber about Babies. But it will be hard to watch this extraordinary film and its adorable stars without a goofy smile," writes Ty Burr of the Boston Globe. "And while that's pleasant to watch now and then, it gets tiresome when it lasts 80 minutes." "There is almost literally no difference between watching Babies and just watching a baby," writes James Berardinelli of ReelViews. "Babies is life with the dull bits intact."

– Two Georgia police officers were fired Thursday, a day after authorities say one punched a man who had his hands up and the other kicked the man in the head once he was handcuffed on the ground, the AP reports. The Gwinnett County Police Department said Thursday afternoon that Master Police Officer Robert McDonald violated department policy and the law. Video showed McDonald assaulting the handcuffed man, identified as Demetrius Bryan Hollins, while assisting a supervisor who had called for backup during a traffic stop about 4pm Wednesday, police said. Several hours later, police said that supervisor, Sgt. Michael Bongiovanni, had also been fired after a second video surfaced of him punching Hollins in the face as Hollins put his hands in the air. "We acknowledge that the actions of these two officers have implications that will be felt for some time," a police department statement says. "However, we also believe that our decisive action in terminating both officers speaks volumes about what is expected of each officer that wears a Gwinnett County Police badge." The department also has opened criminal investigations into the behavior of the two officers. The results will be turned over to the county district attorney, who will decide whether to prosecute the two officers. – YouTube is about to make its biggest acquisition ever: Sources tell the Wall Street Journal that Google has reached a preliminary deal to buy Twitch, a company that streams video games, for more than $1 billion. The deal is expected to be announced soon. Twitch has 45 million monthly users and claims more than 1 million members who upload videos each month. The Journal's sources say that YouTube—which was bought by Google for $1.65 billion in 2006—is preparing to challenge the deal with the help of the Justice Department, which could take a hard look at whether it raises anticompetitive issues in the online-video market. Twitch also plays in the separate "e-sports" market covering live professional gaming competitions.

– When a woman in Thailand was 14, she was bitten by a Malayan pit viper, a venomous snake native to Southeast Asia. Ten years later, she developed a calcified membrane, or eggshell, in her leg so large it broke through her skin and was surgically removed, Live Science reports. According to a study published in the British Medical Journal, the 66-year-old woman's case is one of only a few reported in the world. Calcific myonecrosis is a rare condition in which a calcified cavity grows in an area of the body that has been injured by a venomous snake. In this case, the woman's leg was completely healed by a month after doctors removed the mass. While the woman's case is rare, it's not unheard of: A study published in the same medical journal in 2015 reported on the case of a man who developed a calcified mass in his leg after he was bitten by a poisonous snake when he was 20. According to Live Science, the woman's case is one of only a few reported in the world. – On Thursday, Pope Francis is expected to deliver his first major teaching letter on the environment—and scientists say it could have a bigger impact than international talks on climate change this year. "I'm not a religious person at all," a NASA climatologist tells USA Today, but "the pope's encyclical is probably going to have a bigger impact than the Paris negotiations." Francis has said that climate change is largely settled on by science, and the encyclical will focus on the plight of the poor and the environment in general, the New York Times reports. "The encyclical is going to go out to over 1 billion Catholics—that's a way of getting a message across to a segment of society that the scientific community could never do," says Jeff Kiehl of the National Center for Atmospheric Research. "I mean it's just unbelievable." The pontiff is expected to cite Jesus Christ's call to care for the poor and the environment as a "moral imperative," the Guardian reports. The pope has already faced criticism from right-wing religious figures, including Rick Santorum, who says the church "has gotten it wrong a few times on science," and a Catholic cardinal who called global warming a "existential threat" to the church's teachings

– Madonna’s new film, WE, opened at the Toronto International Film Festival yesterday, and the reviews have been brutal—but the Material Girl isn’t fazed by them. “I had the same kind of pressure when I began my music career,” she told reporters, Reuters reports. “I was nervous, and I didn't know what to expect, and people didn't know what to expect.” She continued: “I can tell when people are reviewing my film and when they're reviewing me personally. So when they stick to the film, then I do care.” The Globe and Mail reported that before the premiere, Madonna had volunteers turn their backs on her as she made her way to speak with the media. But Madonna’s camp denies that, according to PopEater. “Neither Madonna nor her security ever gave instructions for the volunteers to turn away from Madonna,” it says. “In fact she was so impressed with the volunteers that she publicly thanked them from the stage for their hard work before the premiere of her film last night which earned a standing ovation. We are still trying to figure out who and why anyone would ask the volunteers to turn away from Madonna. She has never and would never ask anyone to do that ever.”

– President Obama's former nanny, Evie, was born a man but believes she is really a woman. She says soldiers shaved her long, black hair to the scalp and smashed out glowing cigarettes onto her hands and arms. The turning point came when she found a transgender friend's bloated body floating in a backed-up sewage canal two decades ago. She grabbed all her girlie clothes in her arms and stuffed them into two big boxes. Half-used lipstick, powder, eye makeup—she gave them all away. "I knew in my heart I was a woman, but I didn't want to die like that," says Evie, now 66, her lips trembling slightly. "So I decided to just accept it. ... I've been living like this, a man, ever since." Indonesia's attitude toward transgenders is complex. Nobody knows how many of them live in the sprawling archipelagic nation of 240 million, but activists estimate 7 million. Because Indonesia is home to more Muslims than any other country in the world, the pervasiveness of men who live as women and vice versa often catches by surprise. They hold the occasional pageant, work as singers or at salons, and include well-known celebrity talk show host Dorce Gamal

– Bill Clinton and Helen Keller aren't going to be in Texas third-graders' history lessons any time soon. The State Board of Education voted Friday to remove the two historical figures from lessons on "citizenship" and "the characteristics of good citizenship," the Houston Chronicle reports. The board also approved changes to other lessons, including one about the Battle of San Jacinto, which will now be known as Constitution Day. "If Helen Keller was an important historical figure when I was in school (and she was), then she still is today," tweeted Democratic Rep. The 4.1-magnitude quake hit around 11:30pm and was followed by a 3.2-magnitude aftershock, according to the US Geological Survey, which says the quakes were centered near the town of Black Canyon City, about 20 miles north of Phoenix, the Arizona Republic reports. The Academy "would hope that every studio knows that this is a bad idea," says an Academy spokesperson. "The Red Carpet is not about stunting." Click for more on Baron Cohen's plan.

– Chimpanzees, bonobos, and orangutans are the closest relatives of humans, and like us, they can tell when a person is wrong in their beliefs. Great apes were also willing to help a person who was mistaken about the location of an object, according to the study in the journal PLOS ONE. "This study shows for the first time that great apes can use an understanding of false beliefs to help others appropriately," says a researcher. Researchers used a test developed for human babies to determine if they could understand when a person held a false belief—a mark of advanced social cognition. A person would place an object on one of two boxes, while a great ape looked on. For some of the tests, the original person would step away, while another person took the object out of the box and put it into another box. When the original person came back, they tried to open the first box, where they believed the object to be, not realizing it had been moved. This was known as the "false-belief" portion of the study. For other parts, the person stayed in the room and could see when the object was moved. In the false belief portion, the apes chose the correct box significantly more often than chance.

Paramedics, however, waited 150 yards away because police had not declared the terminal safe to enter. It's not clear when Hernandez died, but the president of the union that represents TSA workers says "we may be talking about Officer Hernandez as a survivor." – The Italian-born author and conservationist Kuki Gallmann was shot at her Kenyan ranch and airlifted for treatment after herders invaded in search of pasture to save their animals from drought, officials said Sunday. Gallmann, known for her bestselling book I Dreamed of Africa, which became a movie by the same name starring Kim Basinger, was patrolling the ranch in Laikipia when she was shot in the stomach, local police chief Ezekiel Chepkowny said. The 73-year-old Gallmann had been with rangers from the Kenya Wildlife Service, assessing damage done to her property Saturday by arsonists who burned down buildings at one of Laikipia Nature Conservancy's tourism lodges, said Laikipia Farmers Association chairman Martin Evans. After the attack, the rangers transported her to a location where she could be airlifted to the capital, Nairobi, he said. British Army medics attended to her before she was airlifted to the capital, Nairobi, he said. On Sunday night, Evans said Gallmann was in stable condition after surgery but had serious injuries. He cited a family member. Richard Constant, the association's deputy chairman, said suspicion falls on herders from the Pokot community who have invaded Gallmann's ranch several times.

More than 125 people were injured in the fighting outside the presidential palace, reports the Los Angeles Times, which describes the scene as "a charged air of a flourescent-lit battlefield with competing banners, bandaged men, and dinner trays used as shields to block barrages of rocks. The reaction has been swift, with the Republican National Committee using its Tumblr account to show photos of Obama in "world-changing events you didn't know Obama played a part in," ABC News reports. – If you're a psychopath, your brain may be different than yours, according to a new study published in Lancet Psychiatry. Researchers used fMRI imaging to scan the brains of 50 men, 12 of whom had been convicted of murder, rape, attempted murder, or grievous bodily harm; 20 of whom had antisocial personality disorder but not psychopathy; and 18 non-offenders. While the men were being scanned, they were asked to play a matching game, and while their brains were being scanned, they were also asked to change their behavior based on feedback they were getting from the game. The psychopathic men had a much harder time with changing their behavior, and they took significantly longer to adapt when the game changed its rules. The abnormalities in their brains were seen in areas of the brain where emotions like guilt, embarrassment, and moral reasoning are processed. Some of those abnormalities were linked to a lack of empathy, Time reports. "Offenders with psychopathy may only consider the possible positive consequences and fail to take account of the likely negative consequences," says a study co-author. "Consequently, their behavior often leads to punishment rather than reward as they had expected." The findings could lead to programs to help children who are at risk of psychopathy

– Hiroo Onoda, one of the last Japanese soldiers to hold out in the Philippines during World War II, has died in Tokyo at the age of 91. He was declared dead in 1959 but was found alive in 1974 by a student who had been searching for him, the New York Times reports. He refused to surrender and spent the next 29 years living off coconuts and bananas in bamboo huts built to withstand the heat. He was given a military pension and signed a ghost-written memoir. "I am sorry I have disturbed you for so long a time," he told his brother. "To this soldier, duty took precedence over personal sentiments. There is much more in life than just material affluence and selfish pursuits. There is the spiritual aspect, something we may have forgotten."

– Police in Maine say a woman's body has been found in the woods less than a mile from the home of a missing elementary school teacher. Kristin Westra, 47, was last seen at her home in North Yarmouth on Sunday night, reports the Portland Press Herald. Her husband, Jay Westra, says she had been experiencing anxiety and "sleepless nights" before she disappeared. Jay Westra says he woke up Monday to find his wife gone, without her car or cellphone. Police say the body has yet to be positively identified. "My heart was crushed today," Jay Westra wrote on Facebook. "Please keep us in your thoughts and prayers." – A new Wisconsin law that bans doctors from performing abortions if they don't have admitting privileges to hospitals within 30 minutes of their practice has been put on hold by a federal judge. US District Judge William Conley granted a temporary restraining order after the Planned Parenthood of Wisconsin filed a lawsuit alleging the requirement is unconstitutional and treats doctors who perform abortions differently from doctors who perform other types of medical procedures, CNN reports. "There is a troubling lack of justification for the hospital admitting privileges requirement," he wrote in his 19-page ruling. He added that the US Supreme Court precedent places the burden upon states to show such laws are "reasonably directed to the preservation of maternal health." To that end, "the record to date strongly supports a finding that no medical purpose is served by this requirement," he said. The law had been expected to cut the number of abortion clinics in the state from four to two and cause one of them to close, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reports. The restraining order will stay in place pending a fuller hearing on July 17.

– Archaeologists in London say they've found the final resting place of some of the city's Black Death victims. DNA from the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis was found in the teeth of at least four of 25 skeletons unearthed in a shaft near Charterhouse Square last year, the BBC reports. Researchers believe the skeletons were killed by the plague between 1348 and 50. "This discovery is a hugely important step forward in documenting and understanding Europe's most devastating pandemic," says the project's lead archaeologist. "Further excavations will follow to see if—as we expect—we are coming across a much bigger mass burial trench." The skeletons were found alongside pottery dating to the mid-14th century, and researchers say they show that Londoners of the time were extremely susceptible to the plague. "The combination of a poor diet and generally a struggle to live life ... means they were very susceptible to the plague at that time and that's possibly known to answer questions like why the plague still killing people 600 years ago," says the archaeologist. The BBC notes that the discovery solves a 660-year-old mystery: Records say thousands of Londoners died and their corpses were dumped in a mass grave outside the city, but its exact location was a mystery.

– An outbreak of Ebola has killed at least 16 people in Uganda, and health officials fear the disease could spread to the country's capital city of Kampala, CNN reports. "We do expect the number of suspected cases to increase," says a district health officer. "It's important to break transmission and reduce the number of contacts that suspected cases have." So far, 30 suspected cases have been diagnosed at the hospital in Kibaale where the outbreak began, including five inmates at the prison, CNN reports. There's no treatment for Ebola, which is spread through close contact with bodily fluids such as saliva, vomit, feces, sweat, semen, and blood. "Right now there is no treatment for Ebola, so the most effective measure we can take is to contain the spread of the disease," says a Doctors Without Borders emergency coordinator. Ugandan health officials say they've isolated 232 people suspected of having contact with the victims of the current outbreak, Reuters reports. The country saw an outbreak of Ebola in 2000 that killed 425 people.

– An aide to Rep. Louise Slaughter says the 88-year-old Democratic congresswoman from upstate New York has died. Slaughter was serving her 16th term in Congress and was the top Democrat on the House Rules Committee. She was the first woman to chair that committee when she led it from 2007 through 2010. Liam Fitzsimmons is her chief of staff. In a statement, he says Slaughter died early Friday at George Washington University Hospital after injuring herself in a fall in her area home, the AP reports. Fitzsimmons said on Wednesday that she'd sustained a concussion but no broken bones. Slaughter, the oldest member of Congress, is currently 88. She was elected to the House of Representatives in 1986, taking office in January 1987. She represents the 25th Congressional District, which comprises most of Monroe County. "The congresswoman is tough as nails and she will bring that same spirit to this recovery," said Fitzsimmons. "We appreciate the outpouring of support and the community's patience during her recuperation." Slaughter was repeatedly re-elected, sometimes narrowly, and was the longest-serving member of Congress from New York. She was the first woman to chair the House Rules Committee. "Louise was a trailblazer," House Democratic Leader Nancy Pelosi said in a statement

– China resumed rare earths exports this morning, just hours before Hillary Clinton raised the issue with Japan’s foreign minister during a visit to Hawaii. China produces 95% of the world’s supply of the minerals, used in high-tech products like wind turbines and electric cars, and Clinton said the country’s recent suspension of exports was a “wake-up call” that the US and Japan would have to find other sources of rare earths. The New York Times reported yesterday that China had not lifted the embargo, but later said it was still seeking clarification. China’s commerce ministry officials have insisted that they had not issued any regulations halting shipments. They have suggested at various times—implausibly, in the view of industry executives—that the halt resulted from a spontaneous and simultaneous decision by the country’s 32 authorized rare earth exporters not to make shipments, whether because of a deterioration in Sino-Japanese relations or a greater thoroughness on the part of customs inspectors. Under this year’s quota, just a few thousand metric tons of rare earths remain to be exported. Meanwhile, annual demand outside China for raw rare earths approaches 50,000 tons, according to industry estimates.

It was filmed using state-of-the-art camera technology, including remote cameras that capture intimate moments between a mother Pallas' cat and her kittens, and low-light cameras that reveal a rare puma preying on Magellanic penguins. A fire department spokesman says the spike is more than double the number of overdoses the city saw at this time last year. Manning and Kenneth Norman asked participants to recall or forget a series of words, then asked them to look at what happened next. The brain that tries to forget keeps looking at the mental context, while the brain that tries to remember keeps looking at the context. A provision in a massive spending bill introduced this week would limit the Pentagon's authority to use drones or transfer them from the CIA to the military. The move is designed to prevent the Pentagon from taking over the drone program, according to the Post's sources, who say it's an "unusually direct intervention by lawmakers into the way covert operations are run." Sen. Dianne Feinstein, chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, has expressed concern about the possibility of the CIA ceding control of drone strikes to the military. Obama announced his plan to shift the drone program from the CIA to the Pentagon last year, saying it would allow the CIA to focus on gathering intelligence instead of launching strikes against suspected terrorists. The provision in the spending bill would restrict the Pentagon from using any funds to transfer drones or to carry out strikes from the CIA. It's not clear how the measure would affect the CIA's drone program.

Pennsylvania's State Employees' Retirement System has notified the former Penn State coach that it will revoke the payments, which began after he retired in 1999, and inform his wife, Dottie, that she is no longer entitled to a survivor's benefit, the AP reports. Sandusky's lawyer says he will fight any attempt to revoke the pension. – The TSA could save hundreds of millions of dollars a year by waiving the $85 fee for TSA PreCheck, according to a new study by University of Illinois researchers. The study looked at several scenarios for how many people would have to enroll at different airports for the fee waiver to be cost-efficient, and found that the average travel frequency would have to be six round-trips, or 12 screenings a year, the Los Angeles Times reports. "We only look at the direct cost savings in labor and equipment. We don't even talk about the savings in time of the passengers who would no longer have to wait hours in line," the study's lead author says. "That could add tens or hundreds of millions of dollars a year, which would be a bonus to the economy. More people could decide to fly, because of the time and cost savings." The study found that waiving the fee for 25 million travelers would cost the TSA $425 million a year, but the savings would total $459 million a year, thanks to lower staff expenses and equipment costs. The TSA could not be reached for comment, but the lead author says the agency asked for a copy of the study yesterday.

– It's well established that using a device to check email, surf the Internet, or make phone calls before bed does not help one get a good night's sleep. Now researchers at Harvard are reporting in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences that reading on an iPad for four hours prior to sleep actually took longer to fall asleep and made people less alert the next morning. They also found that subjects who read on the iPad for four hours reported feeling less sleepy at night and less alert the next morning. The researchers aren't saying that reading on an iPad causes people to go to sleep less, but they do think that the light from the device—not the cognitive stimulation it provides—is responsible for the known sleep effects of screens. The study doesn't prove that reading on an iPad causes people to go to sleep less, but it's a step in the right direction, reports New Scientist. "The idea of stimulus control made sense to a lot of people," writes Christopher Ingraham. "But to what degree is the light from a device, not the cognitive stimulation it provides, responsible for the known sleep effects of screens? And is that light worse than, say, the light from a light bulb?"

– A new study out of the University of Lyon suggests that a good night's sleep not only keeps us alert, but also improves our ability to re-learn certain words. Reporting in the journal Psychological Science, researchers say that French-speaking adults who'd had 12 hours of sleep were able to recall an average of 10 word pairs twice as quickly and three times as effectively as those who'd had no sleep. They were also able to re-learn the words twice as quickly and three times as effectively as participants in a control group who'd had no sleep for the same amount of time. The study builds on previous research showing that sleep improves the ability to remember certain words, as well as the ability to recall auditory tones, maze locations, and more. "Our results suggest that sleep may play a critical role in the re-acquiring of forgotten information," the researchers write. "This is important because, unlike in the waking world, we cannot possibly remember all of the information that we encounter, so it is often necessary to go back and learn that information again." – Two North Carolina police officers who investigated a noise complaint decided to let it slide—and then they slid down the street along with neighbors who were enjoying a makeshift water slide, the AP reports. The Asheville officers got national media attention, including a nod from Good Morning America, after their trips down the slippery slide were captured on video and shared by the department. Police spokeswoman Christina Hallingse said the officers were responding to a noise complaint Sunday morning when they arrived at the holiday block party. Hallingse said the noise of children playing turned out to be at an acceptable level, so the officers issued no citations. They also determined the slide laid out along the street allowed cars to pass, so they joined in the fun. Resident Katlen Joyce Smith said one of the local dads decided to build a slip-and-slide for the neighborhood kids to enjoy during the annual block party. "When the police came, they quickly realized that wasn't the case and asked if they could take a turn," Smith said.

– The creator and operator of a now-defunct "revenge porn" website was paying a hacker to steal nude photos from innocent people's email accounts, the FBI says. The FBI arrested 27-year-old Hunter Moore and 25-year-old Charles Evens yesterday on conspiracy and computer intrusion charges, NBC News reports. Moore's now-defunct isanyoneup.com invited ex-boyfriends and ex-girlfriends to send in explicit photos of their former partners, but to keep up with new images, he allegedly instructed Evens to hack email accounts to steal private photos for $200 a week via Paypal. Moore wrote Evens an email in December seeking nude photos of "6 guys and 6 girls," and even sent him more images, according to the indictment. Moore and Evens were charged with 15 counts, including computer crimes and identity theft. "The moral of the story is that his revenge porn site wasn't a good enough business model, and that he had to engage in illegal activity to populate the site with pictures," says a US attorney.

Moncef Hamdoun, an official with the Charles Nicolle hospital where many victims were taken, said seven of the dead remain unidentified. Spain's foreign minister said in Valencia that two Spanish tourists were found safe after hiding out in the museum all night after yesterday's attack, the BBC reports. – If you're trying to figure out what the most popular four-digit password is, odds are it's "1234," writes Will Oremus at Slate. If you're trying to figure out what the least popular four-digit password is, it's "0000." Researchers at Data Genetics crunched the numbers from 3.4 million stolen passwords and found that the three most popular combinations—"1234," "1111," and "0000"—account for close to 20% of all four-digit passwords. And every four-digit combination that starts with "19" ranks above the 80th percentile in popularity, with those in the late—er, upper—1900s coming in the highest. The least popular combination, "8068, appears to be less than 0.001 percent of the time. (Although, as Data Genetics acknowledges, you probably shouldn't go out and choose "8068" now that this is public information.) Rounding out the bottom five are "8093," "9629," "6835," and "7637."

The bikes of Elizabeth Collins, 8, and her cousin, Lyric Cook-Morrissey, 10, were found abandoned near a lake in Evansdale, the Des Moines Register reports. The girls were reported missing by their grandmother after they failed to return home from a bike ride. "We're bracing for the worst, but hoping for the best," Lyric's mother, Misty Cook-Morrissey, told CNN. "They're very outgoing. They're very sweet, talkative, they're fun. They smile a lot. They're pretty persistent in the things that they want. They're great, they're really great. You know what I mean?" Authorities have searched about 40% of the lake and are "grasping for straws" to find information on the girls' whereabouts, a sheriff's deputy says. "It's as though they disappeared into thin air in broad daylight," says their aunt.

– Baltimore's Department of Public Works is calling it a "fatberg," a congealed lump of fat, wet wipes, and other items that don't break down in the city's sewer systems. It was discovered earlier this month in a 24-inch-wide sewer main between Baltimore Penn Station and the 1700 block of Charles Street, CBS Baltimore reports. According to the Baltimore Sun, 85% of the pipe was clogged with the congealed fat, along with wet wipes and other items that don't break down in sewer systems. The fatberg has been responsible for two major sewer overflows in the past two weeks. On Sept. 21, nearly 1.2 million gallons of sewage overflowed into a falls. On Sept. 22, nearly 300,000 gallons of sewage overflowed into a stormwater system. A similar fatberg believed to weigh more than 140 tons was recently found in London's sewer system and is expected to take weeks to destroy, CBS Baltimore reports. Baltimore's fatberg has been mostly scraped off and sent to the landfill. The city has a fats, oils, and grease (FOG) prevention program targeting restaurants and other food service establishments. Von Trapp died at her home in Vermont on Tuesday, according to her brother Johannes von Trapp. "She was a lovely woman who was one of the few truly good people," he tells the AP. "There wasn't a mean or miserable bone in her body. I think everyone who knew her would agree with that." Maria von Trapp was the last surviving member of the seven original Trapp Family Singers made famous in The Sound of Music. Georg von Trapp and his first wife, Agathe Whitehead von Trapp. Their seven children were the basis for the singing family in the musical and film. – President Obama’s approval rating has jumped nine points in the wake of the killing of Osama bin Laden, according to the latest Washington Post/Pew poll. Overall, 56% of those polled approve of the way Obama is handling his job. That’s the highest rating in either poll since 2009. The president’s approval rating also rose on handling the threat of terrorism, where he scored a career high of 69%, and on dealing with the economy, where he scored a career high of 60%. But when it comes to handling the economy, the president’s numbers are essentially unchanged. In a Newsweek/Daily Beast poll of 1,200 adults, conducted in the two days immediately before the bin Laden announcement and the two days immediately after, only 30% think the country is on the right track, and only 27% think the economy is on the right track. When asked who did better prosecuting the war on terror, 48% said Obama, compared to 45% who said Bush.

– Casey Kasem's near-death situation took another turn for the worse today when a judge revoked an order that doctors give the 82-year-old life-preserving fluids and artificial nutrition. Kasem's wife, Jean, stormed out of the courtroom after the ruling, the New York Daily News reports. "You have blood on your hands," she said. "You just imposed a death sentence." Jean had argued that her husband had expressed his wish to live using eye and eyebrow movements, and that daughter Kerri, who has been designated her father's temporary conservator, had stopped giving him medication and "decided to stop all medication and kill him." Kerri's lawyer countered that Jean has been "trying for nine days to keep him alive. There’s nothing we want more than for our dad to be here with us." The judge also upheld Kerri's authority to make health care decisions for her father.

– Scientists at UC Berkeley have taken a big step toward being able to read our minds. They studied the brain patterns of study subjects as they watched YouTube videos and then produced a video of their own based on the findings, reports PC Magazine. "This is a major leap toward reconstructing internal imagery," says a study co-author. "We are opening a window into the movies in our minds." The team used MRI scans to measure blood flow in the visual cortex of subjects' brains, and then fed that data into a computer to create a "movie reconstruction algorithm." The computer then watched 18 million seconds of random YouTube videos to figure out what neural patterns matched what was happening in the video. The resulting video is like a "surrealist painting," says co-author Jack Gallant. "The brain isn't just one big blob of tissue. It actually consists of dozens, even hundreds, of modules, each of which does a different thing," he adds. "We hope to look at more visual modules, and try to build models for every single part of visual system." The next step is to use the technology to watch people's dreams or memories, or even fantasies.

– A 21-year-old University of Virginia student was detained at Pyongyang airport on Jan. 2 while on a five-day "New Year's Party Tour" in North Korea, the tour company says. Otto Frederick Warmbier "was caught committing a hostile act against the state" and was "tolerated and manipulated by the US government," North Korea's official KCNA news agency says, per Reuters. The tour company, Young Pioneer Tours, says it is working with Warmbier's family, the US State Department, and the Swedish Embassy in Pyongyang "to secure his release." A high-school friend and former classmate tells Reuters that Warmbier is "a wonderful, warm person who should never have to go through anything like this. ... The idea that any of this happened is crazy." According to the tour company's website, Warmbier was on the tour to watch New Year's fireworks and take a helicopter ride in the heart of Pyongyang. It's not the first time North Korea has detained an American tourist. Last year, Canadian pastor Kenneth Bae was released after six months. In 2014, three Americans—including a South Korean national—were released by Pyongyang.

– President Trump isn't happy with the Federal Reserve, and he tells the Wall Street Journal that Fed chief Jerome Powell is. "It almost looks like he's happy raising interest rates," Trump says. "Every time we do something great, he raises the interest rates." Trump says he "maybe" regretted nominating Powell to lead the Fed because "every time we do something great, he raises the interest rates." He says the biggest risk to the economy is not a trade war or a trade dispute with Saudi Arabia, but the fact that the Fed is raising interest rates too quickly. "I'm just saying this: I'm very unhappy with the Fed because Obama had zero interest rates," Trump says. "How the hell do you compete with that?" The Fed has raised interest rates three times this year, with a fourth increase likely in December, and Powell has warned that the US economy is in danger of overheating. Earlier this month, Trump said the Fed was "going loco" and "out of control." Presidents have long refrained from commenting on the Fed, a policy established to protect the central bank's independence and its credibility, notes CNN.

– Taylor Swift fans are in for a treat: The singer's website, Instagram, Twitter, Tumblr, YouTube, and even her own Facebook page are all black today, suggesting she's about to release a new album, CNN reports. The move comes on the three-year anniversary of the release of Swift's "Shake It Off," and the hashtag "#TS6IsComing" is now trending on social media. Swift hasn't released any new music since 2015's Speak Now, though she did release the music video for "Bad Blood" earlier this year.

– Sen. Ted Cruz woke up Tuesday to find his name trending on Twitter after someone with access to his account "liked" a porn video tweeted by Pornhub. Cruz, who didn't name the staffer responsible, says it was an "honest mistake" made by a "number of people" on his staff, CNN reports. "It was not me, and it's not going to happen again," he says. Cruz—who was solicitor general of Texas from 2003 to 2008 and defended a state ban on sex toys during a legal battle—says the senator's account was quickly deleted and the staffer responsible will be punished. Cruz—who was trending worldwide after his office removed the offensive tweet—says he could have used the attention of the porn "during the Indiana primary" when he was running for president, NBC DFW reports.

The woman, identified only as Xiang Liujuan, was shopping with her husband at a mall in Hubei province on Sunday when the escalator collapsed, the South China Morning Post reports. Video shows Xiang pushing her son forward as the escalator rolls away. A panel in the floor gives way, and Xiang is seen falling through the gap, AFP reports. It took rescuers more than four hours to pull her body from the escalator, which had sucked her whole body into the treads. It's not clear how many people were on the escalator at the time, but the Morning Post reports that the husband was walking behind Xiang and his son. It's not clear why the escalator didn't stop after Xiang fell through the gap. Video shows employees standing at the top of the escalator as Xiang and her son approach. It's unclear who was at the top of the escalator at the time, but it's thought to have been mall staff. Photos of the scene on China's Twitter-like Weibo platform show police guarding the accident scene, the Telegraph reports. – Apple is trying to get people to upgrade to the iPhone 5 with a new trade-in program that will pay people to turn in their old iPhones, sources tell Bloomberg. The program, which will only be available at Apple stores, is aimed at people who already own an iPhone and want to upgrade but don't want to spend the $199 or more AT&T is paying to buy an iPhone 4S. "This will help them sell more phones, because it will lower the consumer’s out-of-pocket expense," says one analyst. But there's another side to the trade-in program that's not yet clear: It will only be available in the US, where Apple's share of the smartphone market is lower, and will only be sold to people in emerging markets, where demand for cheap phones is higher, sources say.

But on Sunday, he shared some words of wisdom from their 7-year-old daughter, Alice. "When your mom dies you're the best memory of her," Alice tweeted. "Everything you do is a memory of her." "She wrote lines that stung & hummed. 13 years in her presence was happily humbling. #RIPMichelleMcNamara," Oswalt tweeted. He also shared a link to 826LA, an arts organization that helps students strengthen their writing skills, People reports. Victor Barrio was fatally gored Saturday during a bullfight in the town of Teruel in Spain's Aragon region, NBC News reports. Barrio was first gored in the thigh by the 1,166-pound bull's left horn and his body was flipped over. He was gored a second time in the chest and the blow penetrated a lung and his aorta as the matador was on the ground. Medics were at his side almost immediately, but attempts to save his life were unsuccessful, the AP reports. The goring was broadcast live on television and news of his death stirred widespread reaction ranging from the bullfighting community to well-known politicians. "My condolences to the family and colleagues of Victor Barrio, the deceased bullfighter this evening in Teruel. Rest in Peace," Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy tweeted. Prominent bullfighter Enrique Ponce said he was "deeply saddened by the death of my colleague in the ring. Let God embrace him in all his glory. Great matador." – Two Republican lawmakers who opposed the latest version of the GOP health care bill emerged from a last-minute meeting with President Trump on Wednesday saying they would vote for the measure, Politico reports. Rep. Fred Upton of Michigan and Rep. Billy Long of Missouri had opposed the American Health Care Act because they said it didn't go far enough in protecting people with pre-existing conditions. They met with Trump at the White House on Wednesday and said an amendment to add $8 billion to cover people with pre-existing conditions would return them to the "yes" column. The amendment is expected to be added to the AHCA on Thursday. The GOP has 22 "no" votes in the House, and Paul Ryan says a vote could come as soon as Thursday.

– Things are not looking good for the Kaesong Industrial Complex: South Korea says it's pulling all its workers from the jointly run factory park in North Korea after the North rejected Seoul's call for talks today, the AP reports. "We've made the inevitable decision to bring back all the remaining personnel in Kaesong for the protection of our people as their difficulties continue to grow," said the South's minister for inter-Korean relations. About 175 South Koreans remain at the park, which is the last symbol of inter-Korean cooperation. North Korea barred South Korean managers and cargo from entering the North early this month, then recalled the 53,000 North Koreans who worked at the assembly lines. More than 800 South Korean managers were stationed in Kaesong before the ban. "If they are truly worried about the lives of South Korean personnel in the (complex), they may withdraw all of them to the south side where there are stockpiles of food and raw materials and sound medical conditions," the statement from an unidentified spokesman for the North's National Defense Commission said today. "If the South's puppet group looks away from reality and pursues the worsening of the situation, we will be compelled to first take final and decisive grave measures."

– Two Ukrainian-Russians have been arrested and charged with stealing more than $150,000 in bee equipment after a sting in California's Fresno County, the Great Falls Tribune reports. The organized crime ring is believed to be responsible for a rash of bee thefts in the region, including one in January in which 488 hives from a nearby property were stolen. "It's kind of new to us, too," Fresno County Detective Anders Solis tells the Tribune. "This has been going on for about three years." The Fresno County Ag Task Force started investigating the thefts in January after a Missouri beekeeper reported one of his hives missing. A few weeks later, one of the American hired hands on one of the Ukrainian-Russian bee farms noticed one of the hives matched the description of the hives reported by a friend in Missouri. Law enforcement officials found three locations on the properties linked to the suspects: a bee nursery space, a cow pasture, and a freeway-facing property where the hives had been hidden in a drainage. The two suspects were arrested and charged with possession of stolen property, which carries a maximum penalty of five years in prison. The US Attorney's Office in Fresno says it will be investigating the case to see if there's a federal law on the books

The Bostonian Society, which manages the historic Old State House, had expected the box to contain letters, newspaper clippings, and other items from 1901, the year it was placed in the statue on the Old State House. But the book, which the AP describes as being roughly the size of a modern shoebox, was found in its fragile condition. It had no visible markings, and nothing was taken out of the box because of the items' fragile condition. So, the contents of the book remain a mystery, for now. The inside of the box and its contents—there was no mold or water damage—thrilled society President Brian LeMay. LeMay said he was "absolutely delighted" with the conditions inside the box. The time capsule was sealed inside the lion's head since 1901 and then forgotten—until recently. Rumors of its existence were confirmed last month when the statue was taken down from the Old State House for refurbishing. "There was an officer providing exterior security to the president on that day on the phone with the supervisor," says the anonymous source. "The supervisor said to that particular officer, 'You're down there right? So, you can take a couple of shots, you might have to kill yourself, but you can take a couple of shots.'" Another officer in the background allegedly said, "Yeah, somebody should plant a bomb underneath the stage while they're on there and blow it up." The source adds that Michelle Obama was also the target of inappropriate remarks. "Nobody wants to see her anyway—unless she gets undressed or get naked," the source says. The Secret Service investigated and found no wrongdoing, but the police department fired the officer on Tuesday for violating department policy by doing an interview with the station. The officer wants his job back. A Virginia employment attorney says the officer should have been protected under the First Amendment because he was "speaking about a matter of public concern as a citizen."

– Hawaii Gov. Neil Abercrombie has named his pick to replace the late Daniel Inouye, and it's a safe bet that Brian Schatz will be sworn in this week, reports the Honolulu Star-Advertiser. The 40-year-old is currently the state's lieutenant governor, and will serve until an election is held in 2014. Schatz is a former state representative and former chairman of Hawaii's Democratic Party, notes the AP. Harry Reid had urged Abercrombie to name a successor before the end of the year. Inouye had asked Abercrombie to name Rep. Colleen Hanabusa, who represents Honolulu's 1st Congressional District, as his "last wish" before he died last week at 88 of respiratory complications. "While we are very disappointed that it was not honored, it was the governor's decision to make," said Inouye's chief of staff. "We wish Brian Schatz the best of luck."

– Following the Boston Marathon bombing, a majority of Americans called installing surveillance cameras in public places a good idea, according to a New York Times/CBS News poll. Some 78% said such cameras were a good idea, while just 26% thought the government had gone too far in restricting civil liberties in the fight against terrorism. The poll also found that 56% said information about how to make explosives should not be available to aspiring terrorists online, even if some would view that as censorship. Thirty-one percent said it should be permitted in the interest of free expression. The poll also found that most people are willing to accept tougher measures to prevent attacks. "People, I think, understand that we’ve got to do everything we can to prevent these kinds of attacks from taking place," President Obama said at a news conference yesterday. "But we’re not going to stop living our lives because warped, twisted individuals try to intimidate us."

– A shipwreck off the coast of Oman has yielded what researchers say is the world's "earliest known" marine astrolabe, an instrument used by sailors to measure the altitude of the sun and the position of the stars. The 7-inch bronze disc was one of more than 2,800 artifacts recovered from the wreck of the Esmeralda, which sank in 1503, according to a press release. When Blue Water Recoveries pulled it from the depths in 2014, David Mearns, the group's expedition leader, said he and his team suspected the 7-inch bronze disc could be an astrolabe. "It was like nothing else we had seen and I immediately knew it was something very important because you could see it had these two emblems on it," he tells the BBC. "One I recognized immediately as a Portuguese coat of arms ... and another which we later discovered was the personal emblem of Don Manuel I, the King of Portugal at the time." Mearns and his team usedpioneering analysis and 3D imaging to reveal hidden "etches around the edge of the object, each separated by five degrees." – Trayvon Martin's parents made their first public appearance since George Zimmerman's acquittal today, appearing on CNN's State of the Union, the Washington Post reports. Martin's mother, Sybrina Fulton, and father, Tracy Martin, said they were "disappointed" in the verdict and called for calm. "Trayvon did not deserve to be killed," said Fulton. "We are disappointed in the verdict, but we are also disappointed in the acquittal of George Zimmerman." Trayvon's brother, Jahvaris Fulton, said he was "disappointed in the justice system" and called for the Justice Department to take a civil rights case against Zimmerman, the AP reports. Rep. Steve King told Fox News today that President Obama had politicized the case, Politico reports. "The president engaged in this and turned it into a political issue that should have been handled exclusively with law and order," King said. "The evidence didn't support prosecution, and the Justice Department engaged in this." The president has not commented on the case yet.

Greenman found that many of the 78 sentences in Dylan's lecture seem to have been cribbed from the SparkNotes site, and that many of the key phrases in these passages do not appear in the novel Moby-Dick at all. – Ted Cruz was on the Senate floor today railing against President Obama's nominee for attorney general, but he skipped the final confirmation vote—the only senator to do so. Cruz's spokesperson wouldn't say why, but Politico reports that Cruz's "opposition to the nomination has been clear," and that he voted to filibuster Loretta Lynch's nomination earlier in the day. Cruz's campaign later explained that he had to fly home to Texas for a fundraiser, and that "once invoked, her confirmation was guaranteed." The Senate voted 56-43 to confirm Lynch, but Cruz was the only senator to skip the vote.

– Residents of Flint, Mich., are once again under a boil-water advisory after a water main break was discovered Tuesday, the Detroit Free Press reports. According to MLive.com, the city's utilities administrator says the main break was "completely isolated" Tuesday night. "Crews are still assessing the damage and starting on the actual repair of the affected water main," he says. Residents are being told to boil their water for one minute, then cool it before drinking it. "Bacteria are generally not harmful and are common throughout our environment," the city says, per the Free Press. "A decision on whether to suspend the boil-water notice will be made once the results are in," officials say. Flint's water is contaminated with lead after the city switched to the Flint River for its drinking water in 2014, CNN reports. The city has been under a boil-water advisory since last month.

The New York-based software developer was upset after a photo he posted to the photo-sharing app was labeled as "gorillas," the BBC reports. "This is 100% not OK," Yonatan Zunger, Google's chief architect of social, tweeted. "Lots of work being done, and lots still to be done," he added. "We're very much on it." Google says it is "taking immediate action to prevent this type of result from appearing" and is "looking at how we can prevent these types of mistakes from happening in the future." Alcine says the photo service also mislabeled a photo of him and a friend. "I do have a few questions, like what kind of images and people were used in their initial priming that led to results like these," he tells the BBC. "Only time will tell if that'll happen and help correct the image Silicon Valley companies have with intersectional diversity—the act of unifying multiple fronts of disadvantaged people so that their voices are heard and not muted." This isn't the first time Google Photos has mislabeled one species as another, CNET notes

– The Shroud of Turin has long been the subject of a scientific mystery: How was it made, and how did it show up on the body of Jesus of Nazareth? It's been dated to between 1260 and 1390, but there's no way it could have been made by a body lying flat on it, according to a new study in the Journal of Forensic Sciences. Two researchers used a forensic technique called bloodstain pattern analysis to determine that the stains on the linen cloth are inconsistent with each other—some by a person standing upright, and some by a person lying on their back, LiveScience reports. "Even supposing possible different episodes of bleeding (e.g., movements of the body, postmortem bleeding), these are not only non-documented, but also, as for the lumbar stains, they appear to be unrealistic," the researchers write. The researchers used a live subject and a mannequin to analyze the blood flow on wounds on the left hand, forearms, the "lance wound" in the torso, and blood stains around the figure's waist. – Workers replacing water mains under Manhattan's Washington Square Park made a grisly discovery this week: two centuries-old burial vaults containing the remains of more than a dozen people, the New York Daily News reports. According to NBC New York, one of the vaults was clearly disturbed, with the skeletons and skulls of between nine and 12 people pushed into a corner. The other contained more than a dozen stacked wooden coffins. "You bury people to memorialize them and these people were forgotten," says the project's principal investigator, Alyssa Loorya. Officials believe the burial vaults were part of a Presbyterian church cemetery. They were found just 3 12 feet beneath the street with utility cables running on top of them. The city policy is to leave burial grounds undisturbed, so project engineers are planning a new route for the water main. "We knew we could be encountering remains or other items in this area," says an associate commissioner with the city's Department of Design and Construction. "We'll do some exploring to discover what other lanes we might have." The 9-year, $9 million project is adjacent to Washington Square Park, which was used as a Potter's Field for yellow fever victims in the early 1800s.

– In a heist reminiscent of the movie Ocean's Eleven, 100 thieves in Japan pulled off an impressive $12.7 million heist in just three hours. Police say the criminals used forged credit cards containing account details illegally obtained from a bank in South Africa to make 14,000 coordinated withdrawals from 1,400 convenience store ATMs, the Guardian reports. Police believe the suspects, who made a single withdrawal of $913 at each ATM, may have bought themselves time in Japan by using cards that were issued in a different country from the one in which the fraud took place, the Independent reports. Authorities have asked South African authorities to investigate how the credit card information was obtained. Police are examining CCTV footage to identify the suspects, who are believed to have left the country. No arrests have been made, but local media reports suggest that the suspects—believed to be part of an international crime syndicate—may no longer be in Japan. (This gang made $19.5 million using fake credit cards in a similar heist last year.)

The Porsche clan, which controls more than half of VW's voting shares, lost $2 billion as a result of the scandal, which has already cost the company more than $18 billion and caused the resignation of CEO Martin Winterkorn. But the family, which has controlled VW since the 1930s, hasn't spoken out publicly about the scandal because it's kept its traditions of consensus and discretion in check. "I am of the rock-solid conviction that Volkswagen can weather the situation and emerge even stronger," says 72-year-old Wolfgang Porsche, the oldest member of the clan and chairman of Porsche SE, VW's holding company. His grandfather, Hans Peter Porsche, is 86, and his son, Peter Daniell Porsche, is 38. "They're not a bunch of technicians," says Wolfgang Porsche of VW's next generation. Peter Daniell Porsche is seeking a bigger role at VW, while his father, Hans Peter Porsche, is the owner of PDP Holding GmbH, VW's holding company.

Concern about the threatened species intensified last year when an American dentist killed a lion named Cecil in a hunt in Zimbabwe that officials said was illegal. The circumstances of the stray lions also fueled questions about whether to dart a potentially dangerous predator with a tranquilizer and return it to a fenced area, or kill it before it can attack people. Such decisions depend on factors including the training of wildlife experts, their resources, and whether the area where a lion is roaming is densely populated. In some cases, local residents have killed lions before officials arrived on the scene. Wildlife officials in Kenya shot the escaped lion several times after it injured a man in the Kajiado district, near Nairobi, the capital. – Peru's police chief has suspended an investigator who claimed to have caught a gang of serial killers who were harvesting human fat and selling it on the black market, the BBC reports. The investigator turned a legend about serial killers known as "Pishtacos" into a hoax, turning the legend into reality and scaring away tourists. "This has been a ruse of bad taste," said the president of the region where the alleged killers lived and worked. "We wouldn’t throw out hundreds of liters of human fat if it were worth $15,000 a liter," said a member of Peru's board of medicine. Police say the gang killed up to 60 people and sold their fat for thousands of dollars a liter to Italian cosmetics makers. The police chief says he is embarrassed by the bungled investigation, Reuters reports.

– Ukraine's acting president has called an emergency meeting of security chiefs in Kiev after pro-Russia protesters seized three government buildings in the east of the country. The protesters in Donetsk, Luhansk, and Kharkiv hoisted Russian flags and demanded a referendum on joining Russia, reports the BBC. The move came after Vladimir Putin "ordered and paid for the latest wave of separatist disorder in the east of the country," said Interior Minister Arsen Avakov, according to Reuters. "The situation will come back under control without bloodshed. That is the order to law enforcement officers, it's true. But the truth is that no one will peacefully tolerate the lawlessness of provocateurs." The interim government in Kiev has accused Putin of orchestrating the "separatist disorder," reports the New York Times. "Putin and Yanukovich ordered and paid for the latest wave of separatist disorder in the east of the country," Avakov said. "The people who have gathered are not many, but they are very aggressive." – A new virus has been discovered in the human blood supply, but researchers say they're not in a hurry to panic. The virus, which can be transmitted through blood transfusions, looks a little like the hepatitis C virus and the harmless human pegivirus, but there's no evidence it causes disease, and half of those infected have cleared it, LiveScience reports. "So far there is no need to be concerned," the lead researcher says. "We really don't know if there is ongoing transmission of this virus. It may be good for you." Another infectious disease expert, however, tells NBC News, "We don't know if it is going to be a significant cause of human hepatitis. It is the first transfusion-associated virus that's been described in a long time." The virus was found in two of 46 people who received blood transfusions between 1974 and 1980. All of them had hemophilia, and all received blood products to treat the disease. "This is not SARS. This is not MERS. This is not HIV."

– Yahoo's new CEO, Marissa Mayer, will get a cool $100 million in compensation over the next five years, reports the Wall Street Journal. That includes a salary of $1 million, equity grants of $12 million, stock options of $6 million, and a "make-whole payment" of $14 million for the stock she left behind at Google. The retention award is $30 million over five years, notes Kara Swisher at re/code. Mayer's salary is typical, she adds, but she could get a bonus of up to 400% of it if she hits performance targets. Yahoo's board "raised concerns about her and paying so much to retain her," writes Swisher. "But since such company ups and downs happen all the time, others argued that Mayer was just the kind of disruptive agent of change that Yahoo needs, especially because she could inspire its engineers and also attract much needed talent." The compensation was pushed through, sources say, by Dan Loeb, Yahoo's largest shareholder, who owns about 6% of the company.
