– Iouri Podladtchikov of Switzerland won gold in the inaugural slopestyle snowboarding competition at the Sochi Olympics tonight, giving the host nation its first medal in the event. Japan's Ayumu Hirano won the silver and Taku Hiraoka the bronze, while Shaun White placed fourth. It's the first time the US has failed to medal in the event since it was added to the Olympics in 1998. "For me to be remembered in the sport, I don't think tonight makes or breaks my career," White said, per the New York Times. "I've been snowboarding for so long, and I love it so much, that I'm happy to take this for what it is and move on and continue to ride." The Swiss won gold and the bronze, while Hirano and Hiraoka took the silver and bronze, respectively. The only other American in the final was Christian Haller, who placed sixth.

– The US Navy has joined the search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, with the USS Ocean Shield using its " towed pinger locator" to look for debris in the southern Indian Ocean, Reuters reports. The high-tech device is designed to detect pings from a plane's black box, and the head of the search says it's being used for the first time as the battery life of the device expires, the BBC reports. "The two ships will search a single 240km track converging on each other," says the search chief. "There is some hope we will find the aircraft in the area we are searching." The US Navy ship and an Australian naval vessel will be following a 150-mile path in an attempt to detect the pings. The head of the search says it's "getting pretty close to the time when it might expire," but there is still a "great possibility of finding something on the surface" of the ocean. "There's lots of things in aircraft that float."

– If you're in the market for a little extra cash on your grocery bill, Consumer Reports has some good news: Store-brand products are better than name-brand products when it comes to taste. The magazine compared store- and name-brand prices on 30 everyday items at five supermarket chains and found that, on average, shoppers saved 30% on store-brand products, but saved as much as 52% on some items. "The study reaffirms that store brands are worth a try," says an editor. "For a family that spends $100 a week on groceries, the savings could add up to more than $1,500 a year." Consumer Reports also found that store-brand products had the same nutritional value as their name-brand counterparts, though some differences were more noticeable than others: Mott's applesauce has more sugar than Publix, Ore-Ida fries have more sodium than Jewel, and Kellogg's Froot Loops have 3 grams of fiber versus 1 gram in Stop & Shop Fruit Swirls.

Jorge Barahona, 53, has been charged with aggravated child abuse in the death of his daughter, Nubia, but his adopted son, Victor, is fighting for his life in a Miami hospital. Barahona has confessed to putting Nubia's body in the back of his truck on Monday, but said he had second thoughts about lighting himself on fire because Victor's head was resting on his lap. The children have been removed from the Barahona home and are now in foster care. A 6-year-old girl who stayed at the grandparents' home said she saw the children locked in a bathroom, a shower curtain taped to the walls, or standing in garbage bins, notes the Sun Sentinel. Barahona has told police he was so "distraught" over his daughter's death that he tried to kill himself as he sat in his truck on the side of the highway.

– One of the Great Lakes' biggest side-wheel steamers has been found off the coast of Michigan—153 years after it sank during the Civil War. The Keystone State was bound for Milwaukee when it ran a special run on Nov. 8, 1861, carrying what was labeled "iron implements," or farm machinery, the Detroit Free Press reports. Since then, rumors have swirled that the ship was carrying military supplies to the war, and on Monday, shipwreck hunter David Trotter announced the discovery of the ship in Lake Huron, about 50 miles north of Michigan's thumb in less than 200 feet of water. "She wasn't where she was supposed to be," Trotter says. "I probably thought I'd never find her." Trotter's team used side-scan sonar to find the wreck in July, and has since made dozens of dives to document the site and attempt to answer questions about the ship's mysterious cargo, which some believe was intentionally mislabeled on the manifest. "Even if it's only a quarter of a mile-per-hour difference, well, a quarter of a mile-per-hour in 10 hours starts adding up. You get to be 2 to 3 miles apart, and then you start getting 15 to 20 miles apart. Then you're 30," says Mitch Roffer, founder of Roffer's Ocean Fishing Forecasting Service. "Then if one of those possible trajectories goes into the core of the Gulf Stream, now you're moving twice as fast. They could be anywhere from 60 to 180 miles away from where they started, just as a function of where they were in the Gulf Stream. That's a huge difference, between 60 and 180 miles. So you're talking about a 120-mile variance in your estimate of where they might be." – If you're looking to live longer, it might be time to up your intake of nuts and peanuts. A study published in the British Medical Journal suggests that nut consumption is linked to a lower risk of death. Researchers looked at more than 100,000 Dutch men and women aged 55 to 69 and found that those who ate five or more grams of nuts per day had a 9% lower risk of death than those who ate zero or less. Those who ate 10 or more grams of nuts per day had a 7% lower risk of death, while those who ate five or more grams of peanut butter had a 4% lower risk of death, reports the New York Times. "Our findings suggest that nut consumption is associated with reduced overall and cause-specific mortality," the researchers write. The researchers did not find a link between nut butter and death, but they did find a link between nut consumption and a lower risk of cancer, diabetes, and respiratory disease, reports the Los Angeles Times. "Our findings suggest that nut consumption is associated with reduced overall and cause-specific mortality, but not with cardiovascular disease," the researchers write. – Police in Cocoa, Fla., say they'll file charges against five teens who laughed as a man drowned in a pond earlier this month. Jamel Dunn drowned July 7 after entering the pond on his own, and police initially said the teens wouldn't be charged because there was no law requiring them to report a death. But on Friday, Cocoa Police Chief Michael Cantaloupe said charges would be filed under a state law that requires people to report deaths, the Orlando Sentinel reports. "It is the duty of any person in the district where a death occurs, who becomes aware of the death of any person occurring ... must report such death and circumstances to the district medical examiner," the law states. "As far as we know, the statute has never been used in this way," Cantaloupe said, adding it's possible Dunn would still be alive today if one of the teens had called for help. The teens, who are between 14 and 16, are being investigated by the State Attorney's Office, which has yet to decide whether to file charges. In video of the drowning, one of the teens can be heard saying, "Ain't nobody going to help you, you shouldn't have got in there." Dunn's body

The 20-year-old would have started her sophomore year at the school Monday, and the vigil was organized by students from the University of Iowa Student Government and the UI Dance Marathon, reports the Des Moines Register. Jake Tibbetts, Mollie's brother, asked that people meet new people. "You can always attribute that friendship you just made to my sister, and that would mean the world to her," he said. "Knowing that a thousand people just made a friend tonight in her name." Students spoke about Mollie's courage to go from a high school class of 37 to a university class of thousands, as well as her passion for mental health, reports USA Today. "Even if she was just passing on the way to class, she would smile, and you would feel some sort of comfort," said a friend. "That was kind of the embodiment of Mollie." Jake Tibbetts said his family has been receiving so much kindness since Mollie's death. – Russian officials say three people have been killed and four injured in a shootout at a courthouse in a Moscow suburb, the AP reports. Russia's Investigative Committee, the country's chief investigative body, said in a statement on Tuesday the incident took place when five handcuffed defendants tried to escape as they were escorted by two guards at the Moscow Regional Court. The body said one of the defendants tried to strangle one of the guards, and the defendants managed to escape and seized the guards' weapons. A shootout with the court's guards ensued, and three of the defendants were killed. Two guards were injured. Authorities said the incident took place before a hearing in a case of a gang of nine people who are suspected of killing more than a dozen motorists. Russia media dubbed the accused "the Grand Theft Auto gang" after the violent video game. The men on trial are accused of terrorizing Moscow motorists for months in 2014. Prosecutors said the gang members were placing spikes on roads, forcing the motorists out of their vehicles and shooting them dead. The nine men, all from Central Asia, are charged with 17 murders and two attempted murders. Reuters reports that the defendants are accused of being members of a group, dubbed in Russian media the Grand Theft Auto Gang after the computer game

– A powerful 7.3-magnitude earthquake has hit off the coast of Japan's Okinawa island, according to the US Geological Survey. A tsunami warning has been issued, but there have been no reports of major damage, Reuters reports. "We felt the quake pretty good this morning," says an Okinawa resident. "I just walked down to the coastline and the kids are walking to school as they always do. No sirens, or any destruction from where we are." US Pacific Command commanders in Japan and Hawaii are trying to get casualty reports and damage reports from US military stations on Okinawa, but have heard nothing in the immediate aftermath, a spokesman tells CNN.

– A week after the repeal of Don't Ask, Don't Tell was signed into law, a new social network is up and running for gay military members. Out Military is sort of a Facebook for gay and lesbian service members, with 53 members as of this writing, Reuters reports. "I think a social networking site specifically for that niche of gay and lesbian service members is a natural fit," says the site's web designer. He encourages members to join, but warns against coming out before Don't Ask, Don't Tell takes effect.

Emanuel Lopes, 20, will either be arraigned in his hospital bed or in court for the deaths of Weymouth officer Michael Chesna, a six-year veteran of the force, and 77-year-old Vera Adams, who was shot after the suspect spotted her through a sliding glass door. Weymouth Police Chief Richard Grimes described Chesna as a 42-year-old Iraq and Afghanistan war veteran who leaves behind a wife and two young children, ages 4 and 9. Monday was the sixth anniversary of the day he was hired to join the Weymouth force. Grimes said he had spoken to Chesna's mother and she told him that her son joined the military "to open the doors to get in this job." The department set up a fund for Chesna's family on Monday, after receiving reports of possible scam phone calls collecting money for the family. Lopes was out of jail on pre-trial probation on a drug charge, according to WBZ. Weymouth Police said he was selling cocaine to a minor and resisted arrest when he was charged in 2017. "I'm usually not surprised and I was surprised by this," says microbiologist John Golobic, who tested the beards. "Those are the types of things you'd find in (fecal matter)." Golobic says he was "shocked" by the results. "There would be a degree of uncleanliness that would be somewhat disturbing," he says. "If the city were to find similar samples in the water system, Golobic says it would need to be shut down for disinfecting. "I'm usually not surprised and I was surprised by this," Golobic says. Riverdale principal Tom Nolan says he is suspending Riverdale coach Cory Barrett for the first two games of the 2015-16 school year. "It's a total embarrassment," Nolan says. – Lindsey Graham's deal with the White House on Guantanamo Bay has set off a flurry of criticism from both sides of the aisle. Here's what they're saying: The GOP purity police are out to destroy Graham, writes Ezra Klein in the Washington Post. "His Republican colleagues in Congress, wetting their pants out of fear of the Tea Party movement, show no sign of joining him," he writes. "But Graham's latest offer should still be taken seriously by Obama's White House, which needs a way to recover from its self-inflicted wounds over Gitmo." Graham's compromise will help the administration recover from its "self-inflicted wounds over Gitmo," writes Michael Grunwald in Time. "It will take some courage for Obama to defy his liberal base—but nothing like the courage Graham will need to take on the Republican purity enforcers." Grunwald calls Graham's proposal a "victory for common sense" and a "turning point" in the war on terror. "If Graham's plan is enacted, it will reduce the likelihood of another attack on the United States," he writes. "It will also send a message to terrorists that the United States is serious about defending itself."

– If you're prone to erotomania, a new study suggests that sleeping on your stomach may help. Researchers asked about 670 people to self-report their nighttime sex dreams, and those who slept on their stomachs with their arms raised were more likely to have such dreams as "being tied up," "being unable to move," and "being locked up," Medical Daily reports. The most common dream theme was "erotomania," also known as De Clérambault's Syndrome—the belief that you have a wealthy, often famous, secret admirer. "I believe that the brain during sleep is not at all totally detached from the external world, and stimuli, including those stemming from the environment, are probably incorporated into dream content more often than people observe or are aware of," the lead researcher said when the study was first released. "The unconscious brains of the dreamers try to make sense, and even make use of, the external stimuli." The study, published in the journal Dreaming, also found that people who slept on their stomachs were more likely to have lower back pain after sleeping on their stomachs, according to a press release. (Another recent study found that half of Americans have sex while they're asleep.)

– A Russian researcher stationed in Antarctica is accused of stabbing his colleague in the chest at the remote station they had been living and working at for six months, the BBC reports. According to Interfax, Sergey Savitsky attacked "B" at the Bellingshausen station on King George Island on Oct. 9 and tried to kill him. Interfax reports Savitsky "surrendered on his own and without resistance" to the station manager and has been placed under house arrest until Dec. 8. A source tells Interfax that Savitsky may have stabbed his colleague because he was sick of being close to him. The source says the two men had been living and working together for months at the station, which was built in 1968 by the Soviet Union and is named after a 19th-century Russian Antarctic explorer, the Guardian reports. The unnamed victim is currently in a Chilean hospital. The attack took place in the cafeteria of the station, which sits 650 feet from Chile's primary Antarctic outpost, the Frei facility. The source tells Interfax that Savitsky surrendered to the station manager without resistance and "did not object to house arrest."

– It's the first day of 2016, and it's been a brutal one for stocks. The Dow fell more than 400 points in the first minutes of trading, reports the Wall Street Journal, and the S&P 500 and Nasdaq were down more than 2% each as of this writing. The numbers: Dow: Down 371, or 1.9%, to 16,441 Nasdaq: Down 104, or 2.1%, to 4,903 S&P 500: Down 31, or 1.5%, to 2,012 "It is not surprising to see such a selloff considering negative headlines from China and tensions between Iran and Saudi Arabia. What is surprising is that it is happening on the first day of the year," says Ryan Larson, head of equity trading at RBC Global Asset Management. "While trading desks are busier than they normally would be on Mondays, this is not a panic selling, it's orderly. We are likely to see this kind of volatility a lot in 2016," he adds.

– Piers Morgan says Alex Jones was the "best advertisement for gun control" when he went on a rant against him on CNN last night. "That kind of vitriol, hatred, and zealotry is really quite scary," Morgan tells Politico. "I didn't feel threatened by him, but I'm concerned that someone like him has that level of influence." Morgan says he knew what he was going to be getting into when he invited Jones on to discuss gun control. "I know about his background and his reputation, so I know he's kind of shock jock," he says. "He said last night that his show now airs in 140 networks, he has a huge online presence—every day his message gets sent out to millions of Americans. Through vitriol and rhetoric he is able to spur heavy gun sales and ammunition sales. He works off of fear." Jones, who started a petition to deport Morgan, "is clearly a smart guy under the craziness," Morgan says. "Look, you could tell from the way he ranted that he's not a stupid man. But that makes him more dangerous. There will be lots of people who follow him avidly who are not so intelligent, who believe everything he says."

The book, which will be a guide to being the perfect party hostess, has been in the works for a while, and Middleton is determined to wait until after the Queen's Diamond Jubilee next summer to cash in on her royal connections. "She wanted to publish it next year, but it will be timed to come out after the Jubilee," says one book industry insider. But not everyone is thrilled: "Not many people are fans of Pippa's alleged contract," writes Mary Elizabeth Williams on Salon. Kate's coattails probably look like a lot of fun to ride, but she shouldn't hop on just because it's easy."

The 15-car Union Pacific train was returning to Denver on Saturday evening from a daylong trip to Cheyenne Frontier Days in Wyoming when the woman was hit at a crossing in Henderson at about 7:45pm. The victim was among several people taking photos of the train as it traveled back to Denver. Her name has not been released. Her name has not been released. No other injuries were reported. The passengers were bused back to Denver. The 21-car train, being pulled by Locomotive 844, was returning Saturday evening from a daylong trip to Cheyenne Frontier Days. The train, called the ' Denver Post Special,' because the trip was sponsored by the Post, was southbound, and had just arrived at the 124th Avenue crossing near Henderson, at 7:45pm, when the accident happened. UP Steam tweeted about the incident shortly afterward. UP Police will be on scene for several hours assisting local authorities with the investigation.

– President Trump says he didn't know about his son's meeting with a Russian lawyer last year until "a couple of days ago." In an interview with Reuters, the president said he didn't fault Donald Trump Jr. for holding the meeting with Natalia Veselnitskaya. "I think many people would have held that meeting," Trump said. "It was a 20-minute meeting, I guess, from what I'm hearing. Many people, and many political pros, said everybody would do that." Trump said he didn't believe Vladimir Putin's denial that Russia interfered in the election. Trump said he had a "very good" meeting with Putin on the sidelines of the G7 summit last week and that Putin told him he wasn't involved in meddling. The New York Times, meanwhile, reports that the Justice Department is looking into conversations overheard by US intelligence agencies in the spring of 2015 that captured Russian government officials discussing associates of Trump. In some of the conversations, the Russians talked about meetings held outside the US involving Russian government officials and Trump business associates or advisers, according to the Times. White House officials say Trump Jr.'s meeting with Veselnitskaya was not related to Trump Jr.'s decision to meet with the Russian lawyer

– Chris Brown was arrested Friday for violating his probation for assaulting Rihanna, and now he's back in jail for another month, TMZ reports. Sources say the singer was kicked out of a Malibu rehab facility for violating three "internal rules," including one rule that only applies to him—that he stay at least two feet away from other women. Brown allegedly violated that rule by touching a woman's elbows and hands, leaving the facility on an unauthorized outing, and initially refusing to take a random drug test when he returned. Sources say he also acted out during a rehab group session by making harsh comments. The judge in Brown's probation violation case, Superior Court James R. Brandlin, revoked Brown's probation in December, but turned down a prosecutor's request in February to jail the singer again because of the DC assault case. Brandlin said at the time that Brown appeared to be making progress in rehab, and a probation officer seconded that emotion during a court hearing on February 28. Brown was supposed to finish rehab in August, but with 750 hours of community labor left to complete, it's likely his probation will be extended once again.

– Stephen King has a novel coming out next month, and he's giving fans a sneak peek. Author RL Stine will be live-tweeting his new book, The Graveyard Book, from 6pm to 9pm on Oct. 28, reports the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. The book will be the sequel to The Graveyard Book, which was released last year. "This is the first time I've ever done a live tweet," says Stine, who has more than 74,000 followers on Twitter. "I'm hoping it's a safe bet that it's not going to be the last book in the series." The new book will be set in the same universe as the earlier books in the series, The Graveyard Book and The Graveyard Book 2, reports People.

– A 2-year-old Kansas boy is in good condition after doctors removed an octopus from his throat, KWCH reports. According to the Wichita Eagle, the boy's 21-year-old mother returned home Tuesday night to find her 36-year-old boyfriend performing CPR on her son. The boy wasn't breathing and was transferred to the hospital in critical condition. Doctors removed a small octopus—about 2 inches in diameter—from the boy's throat. Police say the octopus was likely meant to be used as sushi. The boy's mother's boyfriend was arrested on suspicion of child abuse. Police say he was unable to explain how the boy ended up with the octopus in his throat. He has since bonded out of jail. The boy's condition is "a very delicate situation," a police spokesperson says.

– A Chilean mother says a hospital is restricting her right to see her newborn daughter because she acknowledged smoking marijuana days before she gave birth, the AP reports. Sindy Melany Ortiz says she smoked pot to alleviate pain in one of her arms. She says she's only allowed to see her daughter two hours a day and isn't allowed to breastfeed her. Hospital officials in the southern city of Talcahuano say they were just following protocol when they alerted a local court that tests found traces of substances that could put the baby at risk. The court ordered the baby to remain at the Las Higueras hospital until it takes a decision during a hearing on Thursday. "They have violated my rights as a mother," says Ortiz. "I use this drug only for the pain in my arms, it was recommended by a medical professional to me, and I am absolutely not a drug consumer." Currently, Chileans are allowed to consume marijuana in private, but it is illegal to sell or grow the drug. In July Chile's Congress approved by a wide margin a bill that seeks to decriminalize personal use and cultivation of marijuana. The law, if passed, currently allows the possession of up to 10g of cannabis and the growing of up to six plants.

– If you're trying to lose weight but quickly gain it back, you may want to think twice about yo-yo dieting. A study presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions found that women who lost and regained weight after starting out with a normal weight were 3.5 times more likely to die from sudden cardiac arrest than women who kept their weight stable, Live Science reports. The study was based on more than 155,000 women over the age of 50 who completed the American Heart Association's Women's Health study. Researchers found that women who lost and regained weight after beginning the study were 3.5 times more likely to die from sudden cardiac arrest than women who kept their weight stable, according to a press release. The study also found that women who experienced the "weight cycling"—weight loss, steady gain, maintained weight loss, and weight cycling—were three times more likely to die from coronary heart disease, the most common type of heart disease in the US, than women who didn't experience the yo-yo effect. "More research is needed before any recommendations can be made for clinical care regarding the risks of weight cycling, since these results apply only to postmenopausal women and not to younger-aged women or men," the study's lead author

"No, I’m not participating," Romney told Fox News. "We have two debates in December I have agreed to participate in. The rest of the month is going to be spent campaigning, doing the political work you have to do to get the support of people in Iowa and New Hampshire, South Carolina, Florida, so we’ll be hitting the trail." Romney said he spoke to Trump earlier today and "indicated that we just can’t make this debate and we foe cuts on the other two we’ve got and some campaigning." Trump "understands my perspective and wished me well," Romney said. "It wasn’t more colorful than that?"

– After declaring "war" on ISIS in the wake of the Paris attacks, Anonymous is now leaking the personal information of suspected extremists, the Independent reports. According to Business Insider, Anonymous has been busy shutting down social media accounts and websites linked to ISIS since January, when the satirical French magazine Charlie Hebdo was attacked. The hacking collective claims to have taken down nearly 800 Twitter accounts and 50 email addresses associated with ISIS. However, Anonymous has wrongly identified people, including alleged extremists from ISIS and Al Qaeda, in the past. So, it's important to not begin a witch hunt for these people based on this information alone. Anonymous operates almost exclusively online and does most of its "activist" work through hacking and distributed denial-of-service attacks, which basically overload servers with tons of bogus requests. Anonymous activists have wrongly identified alleged extremists in the past.

– Bill Clinton has made more than $75 million from paid speeches since leaving the White House, according to a CNN analysis of federal financial disclosure reports released yesterday by Hillary Clinton. The former president made $10.7 million for 52 paid speeches last year, his most ever, and almost half of that came from 18 speeches in 13 other countries. He has delivered a total of 417 paid speeches, and has earned an average of $181,000 per event. Almost two-thirds of his speech earnings have come from 215 overseas events in 48 countries. The former president's most popular destination outside of the US has been Canada, where he has participated in 54 paid events for a total of $9.1 million, followed by the United Kingdom, where he earned $3.2 million for 16 events, and Australia and Mexico, where he delivered 13 speeches apiece for $2.3 million and $2.8 million, respectively. Within the US, Clinton has delivered 54 paid events in New York, 35 in California, 22 in Florida, and 15 in Las Vegas.

– A 10-year-old boy is recovering from minor injuries today after he was bitten by a shark in Daytona Beach Shores, Fla., the second child to be attacked in the state in a week. The boy, who was bitten on the calf, was treated at the scene by a lifeguard and didn't need to go to the hospital, reports NBC News. It's the fourth shark attack in Volusia County this year, which was named the "shark bite capital of the world" earlier this year by the International Shark Attack File at the University of Florida, reports the Orlando Sentinel. In North Carolina, meanwhile, a 12-year-old girl lost her arm below the elbow and a 16-year-old boy lost a leg this week. The attacks have prompted calls for a ban on shark fishing, the AP reports.

– Minka Kelly and Derek Jeter have broken up after three years together. “The split was amicable,” a source tells Just Jared, but “they remain friends. They still really care for each other.” Kelly, 31, is currently shooting the Charlie’s Angels reboot in Miami, while Jeter, 37, is playing for the New York Yankees. Click for more on their split.

– After a decade on the run, a New Hampshire woman accused of kidnapping her 8-year-old daughter and fleeing the state with her daughter has turned herself in, CNN reports. Genevieve Kelley and her husband, Scott Kelley, were featured on CNN's The Hunt with John Walsh in August. The pair allegedly fled New Hampshire in November 2004 with Kelley's daughter, Mary Nunes, after the child's father, Mark Nunes, had full custody rights because of allegations of mistreatment. The pair are now wanted on federal warrants for unlawful flight to avoid prosecution. "I am happy that (she) is in custody and will face justice for these charges, but we will all be the happiest, when we know Mary Nunes is safe," said US Marshal David Cargill Jr., who credited the media and investigators for providing the "push needed to get Genevieve Kelley to surrender." Kelley is in the custody of the Coos County Sheriff's Office and has made an initial court appearance. The whereabouts of Mary, now 18, remain unknown.

– A Houston-area high school senior was found dead in a hotel room Saturday morning, the day after her prom. Jacqueline Gomez, 17, had spent the night with her date at the Hyatt Hotel, where the prom was held the night before. The next morning, her date called 911 and told dispatchers Gomez wasn't breathing, police say. Rescue crews found her body, the Houston Chronicle reports. "The boyfriend, at this point, is being completely honest with us and we have no reason to believe that he at all contributed to this death," says a homicide detective. "But in my line of work, you have to be absolutely sure." Police are investigating whether alcohol or prescription painkillers played a role. Gomez's friends say she was excited for prom, showing them her dress and asking advice on getting ready. But something went wrong. "I told her right before left—I told her, 'Come here,'" says one. "She whispered in me, 'Come here,' and I told her, 'Come here,'" says another.

– A letter laced with ricin was intercepted at the US Senate's off-site mail facility in Washington, DC, and has been sent to the office of Mississippi Sen. Roger Wicker, CNN reports. The letter had a Memphis, Tenn., postmark and no return address, according to a message sent to congressional staffers by the Senate Sergeant-at-Arms. The mail facility has been closed for testing, and Sen. Claire McCaskill says a suspect has been identified, but no one is in custody, Politico reports. The Senate went into recess shortly after 6pm, and Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano and FBI Director Robert Mueller began briefing senators.

"For many, this was just teenage love, for some, the love of their lives," Erna Solberg said Wednesday, per the BBC. "Today, in the name of the government, I want to offer my apologies." The so-called "German Girls" were targeted for reprisals after Norway's liberation in 1945, most of whom have since died. The "Lebensborn" maternity centers set up by the Nazis in Norway allowed German soldiers to have children with Norwegian women, and Heinrich Himmler, the head of the Nazi SS, encouraged Norwegian women to have children with German soldiers, reports the Independent. "We cannot say women who had personal relations with German soldiers were helping the German war effort," says historian Guri Hjeltnes. "Their only crime was breaking the unwritten rules." Solberg's apology came on the 70th anniversary of the UN's Universal Declaration of Human Rights. In 2000, Norway formally apologized to about 12,000 children born to Norwegian women and German soldiers who were targeted for reprisals. The agent was conscious and alert when he went into surgery at Kings County Hospital, the sources say. The agent was on duty performing surveillance for a drug investigation in Canarsie when the suspect, in a BMW, drove the wrong way down a one-way street and opened fire into the agent's vehicle, the sources say. The agent may have tried to intervene with the driver before the gunshots began, the sources say. The agent pulled his car around to pursue the BMW, then got out when he stopped at a corner and fired more than 10 times at the BMW. The suspect ditched the BMW at an auto body shop and got a friend to drive him to the hospital, the sources say. The suspect was in custody and in surgery for a gunshot wound to the hand, the sources say. The agent was rushed to Kings County Hospital with injuries that aren't believed to be life-threatening. NYPD Chief of Department Terence Monahan tweeted that there "are no outstanding suspects at this time." – The death toll from Sunday's devastating earthquake in Napa Valley has risen to three, with scores of people still hospitalized and hundreds of homes deemed uninhabitable, reports the Los Angeles Times. But the scope of the damage is becoming clear: The 6.0 quake was the biggest to hit the Bay Area in a quarter-century, and it was the strongest to hit the San Francisco Bay Area since the Loma Prieta quake in 1989, the AP reports. More than 100 aftershocks have hit in the last 24 hours, and authorities warn that more temblors are on the way. "The scale of this earthquake is beyond anything that we have ever experienced," says the mayor of Napa. "It's going to take a while to get a handle on what's happened, but we're going to get through this." In the meantime, thousands of volunteers have joined in the cleanup effort. "When you meet people who are helping each other, there's no difference between religions or between colors," says an engineer from the Czech Republic who was in San Francisco vacation when the quake hit. "I love the energy about it."

– US employers notched another solid month of hiring in March by adding 215,000 jobs, driven by large gains in the construction, retail, and health care industries, reports the AP. Despite the jump, the Labor Department said Friday that the unemployment rate ticked up to 5% from 4.9%. But that increase includes some good news: more Americans came off the sidelines to look for work, though not all found jobs. The figures suggest that employers remain confident enough in their business prospects to add staff, even as overall growth has slowed since last winter. Many analysts estimate that the economy grew at a 1% annual rate or below in the first quarter. Continuing job gains indicate that employers may see the slowdown as temporary. Steady hiring is also contributing to higher pay, which rose a modest 2.3% from a year earlier to $25.43. That figure has increased since the early years of the recovery, but is below a peak of 2.6% reached in December. Paychecks typically grow at a 3.5% pace in a strong economy. Construction firms added 37,000 jobs, likely aided by warmer weather. – Pepsi on Wednesday pulled an ad after it was widely mocked and criticized for appearing to trivialize protests for social justice causes. "Pepsi was trying to a global message of unity, peace, and understanding," the company said. "Clearly we missed the mark, and we apologize." It said it was "removing the content and halting any further rollout." The ad shows Kendall Jenner, member of the "Keeping Up With the Kardashians" reality TV family, stepping away from modeling shoot to join a crowd of smiling, young protesters. The protesters cheer after Jenner hands a can of Pepsi to a police officer, who takes a sip. PepsiCo Inc. previously said the ad was created by its in-house team and that it would "be seen globally across TV and digital" platforms. It initially described the spot as featuring "multiple lives, stories, and emotional connections that show passion, joy, unbound and uninhibited." The Purchase, NY, company had stood by the ad assailed on social media, the AP reports. By Wednesday, it was apologizing to Jenner for putting her "in this position." Critics say the image of Jenner handing the officer Pepsi evoked a photo of Black Lives Matter protester Ieshia Evans approaching an officer at a demonstration in Baton Rouge

– Gretchen Carlson has settled her sexual harassment lawsuit against former Fox News boss Roger Ailes for $20 million, Vanity Fair reports. "21st Century Fox is pleased to announce that it has settled Gretchen Carlson's lawsuit," 21st Century Fox said in a statement. "During her tenure at Fox News, Gretchen exhibited the highest standards of journalism and professionalism. She developed a loyal audience and was a daily source of information for many Americans. We sincerely regret and apologize for the fact that Gretchen was not treated with the respect and dignity that she and all of our colleagues deserve." Carlson was one of several women to accuse Ailes of sexual harassment before he resigned from Fox in July amid a sexual harassment investigation. Ailes has denied the allegations. Carlson's lawyer, Nancy Erika Smith, tells Politico that the settlement is about more than money. "Opportunists wasted not one second to exploit tragedy for political gain," LaPierre, executive vice president of the nation's most prominent gun-rights lobbying organization, said at the Conservative Political Action Conference, per NBC News. In a wide-ranging speech stocked with red meat for conservatives and attacks on Democrats, LaPierre called for increased school security, repeatedly ripped the "rogue" leadership of the FBI, and blasted the left for promoting a "socialist agenda." Name-checking a long list of prospective Democratic 2020 presidential candidates and lawmakers like Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, a leading advocate for gun control measures, LaPierre condemned those he said were "eager to smear" the NRA. "For them, it's not a safety issue," he said of protecting students. "It's a political issue." Schumer quickly fired back on Twitter. – Police have found the bodies of a former Dutch international volleyball player and her partner, who went missing in Spain two weeks ago. Ingrid Visser, 35, and Lodewijk Severein, 57, checked into a hotel in the city of Murcia on May 13, but failed to show up for a doctor's appointment the next day or for an appointment in a hospital where they were supposed to undergo fertility treatment, reports the BBC. The bodies "are extremely tall, which is a good indication it is the missing couple," a police spokesman told Dutch media. Police have arrested at least one person and are searching a house in the town of Molina de Segura, some 12 miles from Murcia. The bodies were found in a shallow grave in a lemon grove, according to local media reports. Three people have been arrested in connection with the case, including the former director of a Spanish volleyball club. Police have not disclosed details of the investigation.

– Rupert Murdoch met today with the family of murdered girl Milly Dowler, whose phone was hacked by the now-defunct News of the World, and offered "a full and sincere apology," said a lawyer for the family. Murdoch appeared humbled and had offered "a heartfelt and what seemed to be a very sincere apology, telling them that the events that transpired at the tabloid were not in keeping with the standards set out when his own father entered the media industry," said the lawyer. Murdoch also released a copy of an apology that will be printed this weekend in British newspapers, saying News International is "deeply sorry for the hurt" caused by phone-hacking victims. It adds that, "we regret not acting faster to sort things out." Murdoch emerged from the meeting at a London hotel to hecklers of "shame on you" from hecklers. He said that "as founder of the company I was appalled to find out what had happened and I apologized." Murdoch's tone was dramatically different from an interview published Thursday in the Wall Street Journal, in which he said the company had made only "minor mistakes" and had handled the crisis "extremely well in every way possible." Murdoch added that he was "getting annoyed" at all the negative headlines.

– Bob Casale and Mark Mothersbaugh of '70s rock band Devo have been married for more than 30 years and have two children, but they're still very much on the road. In an interview with US Weekly, Casale says he and Mothersbaugh, who are in their 60s and 70s, still tour together and have a "really great time." "We go out on the road and have a lot of fun," he says. "We still have a lot of things that we're interested in and we still have a lot of things that we want to do. But we're not in the business of making music anymore. We're in the business of making clothes. We're in the business of making clothes for people. We're not in the business of making music for money. We're in the business of making clothes for people to wear to work."

– Police in Walnut Creek, Calif., say a 21-year-old man who killed his former girlfriend and then himself last month used parts he ordered online to build the gun he used, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. "Basically, anyone can buy parts," Lt. Lanny Edwards says. "These places sell the metal. They sell a trigger assembly. They sell handles and stocks. Essentially, you can buy 80% of a gun. That's what he did." Edwards says police have found no evidence that the retailers that sold the parts illegally sold the parts to Scott Bertics. Bertics and 19-year-old Clare Orton had dated for a while but hadn't seen each other since 2013, the San Jose Mercury News reports. Police say Bertics shot Orton in the doorway of her family's home on July 21 with one of two unregistered "ghost guns" he built himself. The guns had no serial numbers. Bertics was a one-time Stanford University student who worked on a project called "Controlling Robot Dynamics with Spiking Neurons" and wrote a paper titled, "Controlling Articulated Robots in Task-Space with Spiking Silicon Neurons." – When the St. Roch set sail from Vancouver, BC, in 1700 to explore the Northwest Passage, it was the first ship to do so via the passage and the Panama Canal. It's still one of the most popular attractions in the Canadian city, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police say it's worth a visit even if you're not a fan of whale tooth carvings. The museum, which features the sailing vessel as its centerpiece, does tours once in a while, but you'll have to shell out $11 for an adult—or free if you walk across the street, the CBC reports. There are also interactive exhibits, a model ship, and a remote-controlled submersible that you can control with buttons on the side of the display. "The ship inside is very cool to climb around and explore," one visitor writes on TripAdvisor. "It's crazy to me that an Inuit family lived on deck to help the sailors while on an expedition. There was also a changing art gallery part of the building as well as a walk-through area with more artifacts and bits of history."

– A New York City toddler is in critical condition after falling from a fifth-story window—but her parents say her pink winter coat may have saved her life. "It just may have broken her fall, because she is so little, just a baby," the girl's father tells the New York Daily News. The father was giving the girl's twin brother a bath when the 14-month-old fell, and neither he nor the mother noticed the accident for at least seven minutes, the New York Post reports. A neighbor says she ran outside and saw the baby "twisted up with blood coming from her head." A first responder says he found the baby "laying lifelessly" on a bloody pavement, but no one came to help her until two minutes later, when the father stuck his head out the window and screamed, "Oh my God! Oh my God!" The girl was rushed to the hospital with head trauma and is expected to survive.

– Starting in September, non-flyers at Pittsburgh International Airport will be able to enter gates, shops, restaurants, and artwork at the airport year-round, the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette reports. According to NBC Washington, this is the first time in the US that non-flyers will be allowed to access areas beyond security checkpoints. The change will require them to check in at a special desk, have their name checked against a no-fly list, and show a valid photo. The Association of Professional Flight Attendants is not happy about the change. “Allowing the non-flying public to go through security at the Pittsburgh International Airport for the sole purpose of shopping is a terrible precedent and an ill-conceived decision,” Bob Ross, the union's national president, says in a news release. Ross says he's "stunned" by the timing of the change. “Days prior to the anniversary of 9/11 is when we should be reminding the public of the need to remain vigilant, not sending the message that the airport is no different than their local mall.” The TSA supports the change, but says no additional staff have been hired for the program yet.

– Newark Mayor Cory Booker has cruised to an easy victory in the Democratic primary for New Jersey's open Senate seat, reports the New York Times. Booker will now face Republican Steve Lonegan in the special election to replace the late Frank Lautenberg on Oct. 16. The seat has long been seen as one of New Jersey's safest, and Booker is seen as a rising star in the state's Democratic party, notes the Star-Ledger. He has already been mentioned as a possible presidential candidate. Lonegan, a former mayor of Bogota, won the Republican primary earlier this month.

– Billionaire fashion designer Peter Nygard says he's taken "perhaps more stem cell treatment than anybody else in the world" and it's working for him, the BBC reports. "I am taking perhaps more stem cell treatment than anybody else in the world," the 70-year-old tells the Bahamas Tribune. "I have been doing it for four years now, so I am sort of a testimonial that this stem cell really works." Nygard says he's in favor of opening a stem cell clinic in the Bahamas, and he's looking at sites in Freeport, including the shuttered Port Lucaya Resort. Why swim against the current at Lyford Cay, when you can swim with the current in Freeport." Nygard says he's been taking stem cell treatment for years, but it wasn't until recently that he realized it could reverse his aging process, the BBC notes. – Louisville's Kevin Ware underwent surgery last night to repair a gruesome broken leg, and the school says he's expected to make a full recovery, reports USA Today. Ware broke the bone in his right tibia during a game against Duke in the Midwest Regional of the NCAA basketball tournament, and his teammates immediately wept. "The bone's 6 inches out of his leg, and all he's yelling is, Win the game, win the game,'" says coach Rick Pitino. CBS stopped showing replays of the injury, notes AP. "I've never seen anything like that," says teammate Chane Behanan. "I don't remember the last time I cried." Ware had the bone reset, and a rod was inserted into his leg.

The new testing will involve new, more sophisticated DNA kits required by the FBI's Combined DNA Index System, the database that includes genetic profiles from more than 15.1 million known offenders and arrestees and more than 738,000 unsolved cases. "We should be doing all reasonable testing that we can do, and we will be," says Boulder County District Attorney Stan Garnett. The new testing will be conducted with new, more sensitive "kits" required of crime labs by the FBI's Combined DNA Index System, the database that includes genetic profiles from at least two people in addition to the 6-year-old. The 9NEWS/Camera investigation found that DNA evidence in the case doesn't support the controversial decision by former District Attorney Mary Lacy to clear the girl's family members from all suspicion in her death. The two news organizations obtained exclusive access to the test results, laboratory notes, reports, and correspondence relating to testing conducted in 2008, at Lacy's request, by a forensic laboratory in Virginia then-known as Bode Technology. – Israel launched another round of airstrikes on the Gaza Strip overnight, after Palestinian militants fired more than 200 rockets into the country, injuring four people. China has called on Israel to stop the raids, Reuters reports. "We call upon the Israeli side to stop air raids against Gaza," a foreign ministry spokesman said. "We hope parties concerned can stop firing immediately in order to avoid casualties of innocent civilians." The Palestinian death toll now stands at 21, including 10 civilians killed in yesterday's strikes, according to Palestinian officials. Israel says it launched the raids in response to the rocket attacks. Hillary Clinton will meet with top diplomats from the US, Russia, and the UN in New York today to discuss the latest in a series of tit-for-tat attacks, the Telegraph reports.

– The death toll has risen to six in yesterday's horrific building collapse in Philadelphia, reports the Philadelphia Inquirer. The city's medical examiner's office has confirmed the victims' identities: Kimberly Finnegan, 35; Borbor Davis, 68; Juanita Harmin, 68; Mary Simpson, 66; Anne Bryan, 24; and Roseline Conteh, 41. The 13 people pulled alive from the rubble are Susan Randall, Betty Brown, Shirley Ball, Linda Bell, Jennifer Reynolds, Nadine White, Margarita Agosta, Richard Stasiorowski, Rosemary Kreutzberg, Rodney Geddis, Felicia Hill, Daniel Johnson, and Myra Plekan. The Inquirer has more details on the victims here.

– The mystery of Huguette Clark, the 104-year-old copper heiress who died in May, may be solved. A New York court has suspended the attorney and accountant who were named as her executors after the public administrator accused them of a massive tax fraud, reports the Los Angeles Times. The public administrator says Wallace Bock and Irving Kamsler failed to file federal gift tax returns for Clark between 1997 and 2003 that would have netted them about $4 million in IRS penalties. They also allegedly lied to the IRS and allowed Clark to give more than $56 million to individuals, including herself and Clark's nurse, Hadassah Peri, the New York Daily News reports. The public administrator has asked the court to remove Bock and Kamsler as executors, a position that would normally pay each about 2% of Clark's $400 million estate, or $8 million each. A lawyer for Bock and Kamsler says they acted "in Clark's best interest and at her express wishes." No criminal charges have been filed.

– The Sandy Hook Elementary students who survived the Dec. 14 massacre in Newtown returned to school today, but they'll stay at a nearby middle school until it's no longer considered a crime scene, reports NBC News. "Most of the kids were excited," said a police lieutenant. "They were anxious to get into the hallways and meet up with the other kids, and you could see the teachers had the same response." The new school in Monroe, Conn., was transformed into a place where the students and teachers could feel at ease. Parents were allowed to stay in the building, and therapy dogs were on hand. Security was very low-key, but "we don’t want them to think this is a police state," said the police lieutenant. "We want them to know that this is a school and a school first, and that’s a place that they are to come to learn, enjoy their friends, and grow up. We want to move on and let the kids move on, too."

– Bodybuilding star Rich Piana was given two doses of Narcan and placed in a medically induced coma after collapsing at his Florida home on Monday, according to a police report seen by TMZ. Paramedics found white powder on a table, along with a credit card and straw, and Piana's girlfriend, Chanel, told them the 46-year-old former Mr. California bodybuilding champ had 20 bottles of steroids in his home. She said he had been juicing for more than 20 years and had battled opiate addiction in the past, but she believed he was clean at the time of the medical emergency. Piana was rushed to a hospital, where he was placed in a medically induced coma. He is still alive and fighting, Chanel said, but has asked for prayers.

– The number of half-marathon runners in the US has exploded over the last quarter-century, with this year's 1.96 million finishers making it the fastest growing standard distance among road races, reports Runner's World. In 1990, there were an estimated 303,000. That total had more than doubled by 2004. This year's record total of 1.96 million means that, in just less than a quarter-century, there's been more than a six-fold increase in finishers. Much of the growth has been driven by increased female participation. In 2013, women made up a record 61% of US half-marathon finishers, compared to 53% in 2006. The percentage of men finishing half marathons has fallen each of the last several years, but the absolute number continues to increase. There were more than 760,000 male finishers of US halfs in 2013, which was more than all finishers in 2006. The half-marathon isn't just a US phenomenon. Although 14 of the 20 largest half marathons in the world in 2013 were US races, the three biggest were overseas. The 45,126 finishers in Goteborg, Sweden, was the most in history for an annual half marathon. Since 2000, the number of half-marathon finishers in this country has quadrupled (482,000 to 1,960,000)

– Portland police are re-opening the sexual assault case against Al Gore because they found "procedural" mistakes in how they handled the case last year, reports the Oregonian. The woman accused Gore of groping and kissing her during a late-night massage at the Hotel Lucia in 2006, but police never contacted him or consulted with the district attorney's office. "It is our responsibility to both parties involved to conduct a thorough, fair, and timely investigation," said the police chief in a statement. Click here for more.

– Syria's civil war has prompted the first withdrawal of seeds from a "doomsday" vault built in an Arctic mountainside to safeguard global food supplies, officials said on Monday. The seeds, including samples of wheat, barley, and grasses suited to dry regions, have been requested by researchers elsewhere in the Middle East to replace seeds in a gene bank near the Syrian city of Aleppo that has been damaged by the war. "Protecting the world's biodiversity in this manner is precisely the purpose of the Svalbard Global Seed Vault," said Brian Lavie, the project's director. The vault, which opened in 2008, is "a fail-safe seed storage facility, built to stand the test of time—and the challenge of natural or man-made disasters," per its website. It holds backups of seeds from seed banks around the world, with the goal of preserving a legacy of crop diversity in the face of changing climate, natural disasters, and human conflicts. On Friday, news spread that water from melting permafrost had gushed into the tunnel and frozen, making the floor slick with ice but not impacting the seeds. It would seem the fail-safe had failed. – The Marburg virus has made its way to Uganda, where at least four people have died from the disease, the BBC reports. The latest victim is a 16-year-old girl, according to a press release from the country's health ministry. The girl's father says the virus is present in the family's home village of Makerere and that the family has been in contact with doctors who have been able to identify the cause of the girl's death. "The virus is present in the family and they have been in contact with the doctors who have been able to identify the cause of the death," the release quotes the father as saying. According to the CDC, the virus causes hemorrhagic fever, which can be fatal, and is spread through contact with infected bodily fluids, such as urine, saliva, blood, or semen. Symptoms include fever, chills, severe headache, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and jaundice, the BBC reports. The virus has made its way to Uganda before, most recently in 2008 when a woman who had recently traveled to the country fell ill and died. She had tested positive for the Marburg virus, according to the CDC, which says there have been no other reported cases of the disease in Uganda.

– A 42-year-old police officer in Punjab, India, went to the doctor complaining of stomach pain and losing weight, and when he was asked why he had been eating knives for the past two months, he said, "I felt like eating them," per the Times of India. The reason? "Some sort of psychological problem, because of which he had swallowed 40 knives of different sizes in last two months," says Dr Jatinder Malhotra of the Corporate Hospital in Amritsar. A CT scan revealed "some solid mass in his stomach, shaped like cancer," and an endoscopy revealed "a few metallic knives inside the stomach," says Malhotra. A five-member surgery team spent five hours over the weekend removing the knives, reports the Indian Express. "This was very unnerving. Have never witnessed something like this in my career as a doctor," says Dr Jitendra Malhotra. "In my 20 years of practice, this is the most dreadful surgery I have ever seen or done," says Jatinder. The patient, identified as Jarnail Singh, is now recovering.

– Abdelkader Merah, the brother of Mohamed Merah, the man who killed seven people in three attacks in Toulouse, has been charged with murder and involvement in terrorism. Abdelkader Merah, 29, denies the charges and says he was there when his brother stole a scooter used in the attacks, the BBC reports. Abdelkader Merah says he is "not at all proud" of his brother's actions. "Otherwise, he just hopes he does not become the scapegoat for his brother's acts because this is in some ways what is happening," says his lawyer. The Paris prosecutor's office says Abdelkader Merah has "grave and matching pointers that suggest his participation as accomplice in crimes relating to a terrorist enterprise is plausible."

The US had been 0-23-1 against El Tri in 75 years of games at Mexico, including 0-19-1 in the thin air at altitude in Mexico City—where they had been outscored 81-14. "I think it's huge. It's huge for I think all American fans, it's huge for the team, and it's historic," US coach Jurgen Klinsmann said. "We were very well aware that we've never won here at the Azteca Stadium. This is an amazing experience for the all the players. We told them before the game: This moment is for you, go and grab it. We are all aware that it was a lot, a lot of work." The US went ahead on a move created by a trio of second-half substitutes. Brek Shea cut inside Severo Meza on the left flank and crossed to Terrence Boyd at the top of the 6-yard box. – Sex offenders in California will no longer be banned from living within 2,000 feet of a school or park after the state's Supreme Court ruled that the law was unconstitutional in San Diego County, reports the San Francisco Chronicle. The decision means that high-risk offenders convicted of sexually abusing children will still be banned from living within a half-mile of any K-12 school, but other sex offenders will be allowed to live near parks and schools on a case-by-case basis. The move is expected to leave the restrictions in place for offenders who sexually abused children, while relaxing the rules for some others.

– China is beefing up defenses along its 880-mile border with North Korea in case of war, the Wall Street Journal reports. A review of official military and government websites and interviews with experts show that Beijing has initiated a number of changes in recent months, including the formation of a "newly formed border defense brigade" and the placing of surveillance drones, patrol cars, and high-tech cameras in areas close to the border. According to CNN, the changes also include realigning forces in surrounding regions to prepare for a possible US military strike. The North Korean-Chinese border has seen conflict during World War II and the Korean War, but one of China's chief concerns is not military forces crossing the border, but refugees. "A mass movement of North Korean civilians across the border into China is a major concern, particularly given the dense population centers not far from the border, and the economic importance of Northeast China," according to a recent report by the US-based Jamestown Foundation. Analysts say a conflict on the Korean Peninsula would likely result in hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of civilians heading north into China, a "huge worry for Beijing."

– Women still lag far behind their male counterparts when it comes to donating to political campaigns, according to a new report from She Should Run and the Center for Responsive Politics. Women made up just 26% of the total given to candidates, PACs, and party committees in 2010, down from 31% in 2008 and 27% in 2006. “Women are far more motivated to want to see changes in their neighborhood and city on a social level than men are, but they have not yet made that connection [with politics],” Sam Bennett, president and CEO of She Should Run, tells the Daily Caller. “In fact, women, far more than men, see the hard, sausage-making dimension of politics as something they are not willing to be engaged in. They find it distasteful.” The group says that if women voters across parties give as little as $5 to one female candidate, it would be enough to run a female candidate in every House race with a budget of over $1 million each.

The number of climbers—most of them amateurs—on the mountain is on the rise, and the weather is becoming more unpredictable. There's no cap on the number of climbing permits issued, and it's up to individual climbers to decide whether they go or stay put. Plus, Nepal doesn't regulate who gets a permit, and the weather can change at any time. "Despite the best efforts of the established players to improve communication and cooperation," writes Heil, "despite a full-time independent medical clinic now operating at base camp ... the mountain’s two biggest problems—the sheer number of climbers and the deteriorating conditions—have expanded beyond anyone’s control." The number of climbers on the south side of the mountain, where the weather is more stable, is also on the rise. – When President Obama unveiled his new slogan, "Winning the Future," he ripped off Newt Gingrich. The former House speaker registered a new political group with the IRS called American Solutions for Winning the Future in October of 2006, reports the Atlantic. Since then, the group has operated as Gingrich's main political arm. "We think it's great," says a spokesman. "We intend to have a head on debate of whose policies will actually win the future and whose policies will lose the future." The White House uses the slogan frequently, and is likely to keep using it as the 2012 campaign heats up, notes Chris Good of Gawker.

– Bill Cosby's sexual assault trial begins Monday in suburban Philadelphia, and while the 79-year-old star has been accused by more than 50 women of sexual assault, only two of them will be allowed to testify at the trial, CNN reports. "There is a big contrast," says James Cohen, a criminal law professor at Fordham. "What Cosby is hoping for is that the jury forgets about the other 48." Cosby faces three counts of aggravated indecent assault for allegedly drugging and assaulting Andrea Constand, a Temple University employee, in 2004. Constand first went to the police in 2005, but the district attorney at the time declined to press charges. Cosby settled a civil suit with Constand in 2006, and dozens of other women came forward with similar accusations before the statute of limitations ran out. Cosby was arrested in 2015, and the deposition he gave in Constand's civil suit was unsealed in December. He has said he doesn't plan to testify in the trial. Constand says Cosby drugged and assaulted her in 2004, and the trial will focus on the testimony of just one other accuser.

– A New York family just scored a hefty payday at a garage sale—for a bowl that's been in their mantle for years. Sotheby's sold the 1,000-year-old bowl for $2.2 million yesterday, more than four times the pre-sale estimate, the New York Daily News reports. The bowl, which dates back to the 10th or 11th century, was purchased by London art dealer Giuseppe Eskenazi. It's one of only two Ding bowls in the world, Sotheby's notes, and the only one of its size known to exist. The bowl had been in the British Museum for more than 60 years. Eskenazi, a Turkish-born dealer, says he plans to display the bowl in his London gallery, the Telegraph reports.

– A fugitive murder suspect in Japan has been arrested more than 45 years after he allegedly killed a police officer with a Molotov Cocktail petrol bomb during a protest. Masaaki Osaka, 67, was arrested in May after police raided a communist hideout in Hiroshima, the BBC reports. He was initially arrested for an unrelated offense of obstructing a police officer, but police say they were able to identify him through DNA. Osaka is accused of killing the 21-year-old officer during a protest by the Japan Revolutionary Communist League in Tokyo's Shibuya Ward in 1971. The JRCL was protesting against the recognition by Japan of the US military presence in the country. Osaka is alleged to have assaulted the officer with a steel pipe before setting him alight. Police say they were able to confirm Osaka's identity through DNA tests because fingerprints were not available at the time of the crime. Police say Osaka was able to remain on the run for so long because he was a former high-ranking member of the JRCL and was assisted by sympathetic party associates. The man allegedly to be Osaka's accomplice in the 1971 attack was charged in 1972, but his case was suspended because of mental illness. The country has no statute of limitations for murder after the law was revised in 2010.

The magazine's editor-in-chief, 89-year-old Hugh Hefner, agreed last month to stop publishing pictures of naked women, the New York Times reports. – George W. Bush has called off a visit to Switzerland, where he was to give the keynote address at a Jewish charity gala, over fears that he would face legal action for torture. Human rights groups had planned to file a 2,500-page complaint against Bush in Geneva on Monday, and a right-wing member of the Swiss parliament had called for his arrest last week, Reuters reports. "President Bush has admitted he ordered waterboarding, which everyone considers to be a form of torture under international law," said a lawyer for Human Rights Watch. "Under the Convention against Torture, authorities would have been obliged to open an investigation and either prosecute or extradite George Bush." Swiss officials say Bush would still be protected by diplomatic immunity as a former head of state, but the former president's visit was called off on security grounds.

In Lebanon, the smallest of the host nations and the most politically fragile, Syrian refugees are expected soon to make up a quarter of the population. "Finding several gunshot sea otters at the same general location during such a short time frame is very unusual," says Ashley Spratt of the US Fish and Wildlife Service. Sea otters are protected by state and federal law, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. University Hospital Zurich says Marchionne was treated by "cutting-edge medicine" but "unfortunately passed away" because of the "serious deterioration" in his condition, CNBC reports. The plant's director of production, Michel Dheilly, and human resources chief, Bernard Glaser, have not been allowed to leave the plant, the BBC reports. The plant has become an emblem of France's labor issues, and the seizure Monday morning resurrected the once-common practice of boss-napping. "It's a reaction of despair," a labor lawyer who has worked on similar issues says. "They have no room to maneuver in the closing of the factory." The Amiens plant has an especially contentious past. Boss-nappings typically have lasted from a few hours to a couple of days. Police raided Salling's home in Sunland, Calif., early Tuesday and allegedly found hundreds of images of children younger than 15 years old on one of his personal devices, reports Crime Watch Daily. – A new analysis of 26 peer-reviewed studies and one unpublished data set on indoor dust samples from 14 states finds that the dust we breathe is full of toxic chemicals that have been linked to cancer, liver damage, and other health problems. Researchers found that the 10 most common chemicals were found in more than 90% of samples, which suggests they're present in most people's homes and communities, they report in Environmental Science & Technology. The most abundant chemical in the analysis was di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP), a phthalate that is used in flexible plastics as well as in cosmetics and personal care products. In mice and rats, ingesting high doses of DEHP interferes with the development of the male reproductive system and is linked to liver cancer. When the investigators ranked the chemicals according to how much preschool-aged children were likely to ingest, the flame retardant tris(2-chloroethyl) phosphate (TCEP) came out on top. TCEP has been linked to cancer and brain damage in mice, but like many of these household chemicals, it's also present in everyday products, including building materials, electrical cords, and perfume. – Nelson Mandela's grandson is demanding an apology from President Obama after a former CIA agent revealed that the agency had a hand in the anti-apartheid icon's 1962 arrest, the Telegraph reports. "We call on freedom-loving people of the world to come out in condemnation of this betrayal of our nation, the peoples of Southern Africa and all who suffered as a consequence of the USA's support for the brutal apartheid state," Mandla Mandela says. In a taped confession, former CIA agent Donald Rickard says he told South African police to arrest Mandela because he was a "toy of the communists" and "the world's most dangerous communist outside of the Soviet Union," the Daily Mail reports. Rickard, who died in March at the age of 88, was a diplomat with the US State Department during the height of apartheid and served as the US vice consul in Durban, South Africa, and consular officer in Washington, DC, the Daily Mail notes. Mandela's political associate says the CIA's role in the arrest was a "shameful act of betrayal" that "hindered the struggle against apartheid."

– Struggling Finnish phone maker Nokia plans to cut as many as 10,000 jobs—about 20% of its workforce—as part of a major cost-cutting drive. The company's stock slid 18% to a 16-year low today, reports Bloomberg, which notes that Nokia's market value is now below $10 billion. The job cuts, which will include some 3,700 positions in Finland, Germany, and Canada, are part of CEO Stephen Elop's strategy to slash costs and turn the company around. Nokia has been losing market share to Apple and Samsung in the smartphone market, and today said its second-quarter operating margin will be worse than expected. "They are trying to survive," said an analyst in London. "They can't continue like this."

Romney's lead held at 3 points yesterday, the same as Wednesday's, but Obama held a 1-point lead among registered voters, 48-47. – Turkey and Japan today joined the US, Britain, Canada, Australia, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and Bulgaria in expelling Syrian diplomats in protest of the Houla massacre. Turkey ordered the Syrian embassy in Ankara to leave within 72 hours and Syria's consulate in Istanbul to remain open only for consular duties, the AP reports. "It is out of the question to remain silent and without any reaction in the face of this action, which amounts to a crime against humanity," Turkey's foreign ministry said in a statement. "This grave crime against humanity by those who have attempted a massacre of civilians cannot go unpunished." Meanwhile, Syrian forces shelled rebel-held areas in the same province where the Houla killings occurred, although no casualties were immediately reported, activists said. Survivors blamed pro-regime gunmen for at least some of the carnage in Houla as the killings reverberated inside Syria and beyond, further isolating President Bashar Assad and embarrassing his few remaining allies. The UN's top human rights body planned to hold a special session Friday to address the massacre. Damascus had said it would conclude its own investigation into the Houla deaths by today but it was not clear if the findings would be made public.

So the Duffners sued the city, and on Tuesday, a federal judge sided with the couple, ruling that St. Peters can fine them up to $200,000 if they don't comply with the ordinance—even if they don't plant turf grass. On Monday, Clean Harbors crews began power-washing sidewalks and street areas with a bleach and chlorine solution, the San Diego Union-Tribune reports. The cleanings will continue in other downtown areas on Wednesday and Friday and repeat every other week. A hepatitis A outbreak has left 15 homeless people dead and hospitalized nearly 300 others over the past 10 months. A lack of adequate access to restrooms, showers, and hand-washing stations is believed to have contributed to the spread. Besides starting the washing program Monday, the city announced it was extending the hours of 14 restrooms in Balboa Park, which will be open 24 hours a day starting Tuesday. "By disinfecting our sidewalks and making additional public restrooms available 24/7, we're following the direction of County health officials to address the unsanitary conditions that have helped fuel this outbreak," said Craig Gustafson, senior director of communications for Mayor Kevin Faulconer. "We're taking swift action to eradicate this virus from our streets and keep our most vulnerable residents safe." Alan Miller McCarty, who was on suicide watch at the Volusia County Branch Jail when he watched his trial from behind a mirror-like glass in an adjacent room, shouted in court that his rights had been taken away and that his children had been taken away from him unfairly. The 36-year-old also yelled that he had invited the judge to perform oral sex on him. The judge declined to do so, and the jury took about 30 minutes to find McCarty guilty of extortion, corruption by threat against a public official, and threats to kill Circuit Judge Stasia Warren, who had ruled against McCarty in a custody case involving his ex-wife and their two children. – Google's plan to create the world's largest digital library and bookstore has been derailed by a federal judge's rejection of a $125 million settlement that would have allowed the company to make every single book available online. The judge said the settlement went too far, giving Google a "de facto monopoly" and the right to profit from books without the permission of copyright owners, the New York Times reports. The settlement would have given authors and publishers new ways to earn money from digital copies of their works. The decision is also a setback for the Authors Guild and the Association of American Publishers, which sued Google in 2005 over its book-scanning project. After two years of painstaking negotiations, the authors, publishers and Google signed a sweeping settlement that would have brought millions of printed works into the digital age. The deal turned Google, the authors and the publishers into allies instead of opponents. Together, they mounted a defense of the agreement against an increasingly vocal chorus of opponents that included Google rivals like Amazon and Microsoft, as well as academics, copyright experts, the Justice Department and foreign governments. – A radical British Muslim has been sentenced to life in prison for trying to kill a former government minister. Roshonara Choudhry, who stabbed Stephen Timms twice in May, told police she did so to punish him for voting for the Iraq war, the Telegraph reports. Choudhry said she had been radicalized online by a website called Revolutionmuslim.com, which praised her as a "mujaahidah," or holy warrior. The site published a list of all the MPs who voted for the war together with an instruction to Muslims to try to kill them, saying: “We ask for her action to inspire Muslims to raise the knife of Jihaad against those who voted for countless rapes, murders, pillages, and torture of Muslim civilians as a direct consequence of their vote.” The site also published details of Timms' surgery times and venues, and a link to a store where you can buy a kitchen knife similar to the one Choudhry used, the Independent reports.

– It's called ITER, for "the way," and it's the most expensive scientific instrument in the world. But it also has the potential to save the planet, reports the New Yorker in a lengthy look at the project. ITER, or the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor, is being built in the French Alps. It's 100 feet tall, weighs 23 thousand tons, and will eventually power a synthetic sun that's 10 times hotter than the sun's core. ITER will use a vacuum chamber to create a super-hot cloud of hydrogen that will rotate faster than the speed of sound, twisting like a strand of DNA as it circulates. The cloud will be scorched by electric current (a surge so forceful that it will make lightning seem like a tiny arc of static electricity), and bombarded by concentrated waves of radiation. Beams of uncharged particles—the energy in them so great it could vaporize a car in seconds—will pour into the chamber, adding tremendous heat. In this way, the circulating hydrogen will become ionized, and achieve temperatures exceeding two hundred million degrees Celsius—more than 10 times as hot as the sun at its blazing core. Then Brown's wife, Peggy, noticed Watson's license plate had a Purple Heart logo and sent him emails about a picture of a hawk. Then, on Oct. 27, she noticed a baseball cap in Watson's car reading "9th Infantry," the same infantry Brown had served in. "To tell you the truth, I was flabbergasted," Brown, 68, tells the Detroit Free Press. "We’ve been neighbors for 18 years and didn’t realize, here we were."
