– Attorneys for the family of a 19-year-old Chicago woman found dead in a walk-in freezer at a Chicago-area hotel say they will conduct their own investigation and seek a second autopsy. Lawyers for Kenneka Jenkins' family say video released by police Friday shows the teen "staggering alone through a deserted hotel kitchen and disappearing around a corner," the Chicago Tribune reports. Jenkins was found dead in the walk-in freezer at the Crowne Plaza hotel in Rosemont on Sept. 9 after she failed to return from a party. Rosemont officials say surveillance video shows no one entered the freezer until 1am on Sept. 10, when a police officer found Jenkins' body. Jenkins' family says they will conduct their own investigation and seek a second autopsy. "Now there has to be an answer to how that happened," attorney Sam Adam Jr. says. "Better yet, there has to be an answer to why that happened." The attorneys say the hotel "never checked. They never searched, they never did anything while a young, 19-year-old disoriented girl was sitting in their freezer." Jenkins' family says she had a light tolerance for alcohol and wasn't the type to disappear.

– The US is sending 80 troops to Chad in an attempt to speed up the search for more than 200 Nigerian schoolgirls kidnapped by Boko Haram militants, the White House announced today. The troops, mostly Air Force personnel, "will support the operation of intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance aircraft for missions over northern Nigeria and the surrounding area," the White House said in a statement. They will remain in Chad "until its support resolving the kidnapping is no longer required," the Washington Post reports. The Pentagon has already sent eight experts to Nigeria to help search for the girls and two dozen US law enforcement and intelligence personnel to advise the Nigerian government on the recovery effort, the Post reports. A Pentagon spokesman said having the new force in Chad will allow the US to spend more time flying over the search area, the Post reports. "I don't think anybody's underestimating the level of difficulty in both finding them and then being able to launch some kind of recovery mission," he said yesterday. – Morgan Stanley has been hit with a $5 million fine from Massachusetts regulators over its role in Facebook's IPO. A senior banker wrote a script for Facebook's then-treasurer to update research analysts on the company's revenue outlook before the IPO, breaking a 2003 pledge not to influence analysts, the Boston Globe reports. The treasurer and the senior investment banker had rehearsed the calls beforehand, and the banker had emailed another executive the night before to say the treasurer "was a champ." The order found Morgan Stanley in violation of securities law against dishonest and unethical practices, without specifying what those practices were. The bank "paid a little bit of lunch money as a fine, they’re not getting disqualified, and they agreed once again to abide by a consent order they agreed to nine years ago," a business professor tells Reuters. "Coming from Massachusetts, where they could’ve gotten hit a lot harder, if anything, this is not encouraging to attorneys general." Click for more on the Facebook case.

– A Pennsylvania town has banned trick-or-treating for Halloween as the manhunt for accused cop killer Eric Frein drags on. Barrett Township in Monroe County has also postponed its annual Halloween parade and 5K Scarecrow Race, which had been scheduled for Oct. 19, ABC News reports. "This parade is probably one of the biggest events that the town has every year," says the township's chairman. "Everyone looks forward to the parade. Myself and my family personally have been away and cut our vacation short to get home in time for the parade. Thousands of people line the streets." The parade would have been the town's 50th anniversary. Frein, who is believed to be hiding out in the Pocono Mountains, has been the subject of a massive manhunt since he allegedly killed one state trooper and wounded another in an ambush shooting earlier this month. "I'm the father of a 9-year-old," the chairman says. "We do things a little differently now. I'm not so comfortable with him going outside and playing anymore." Officials say the manhunt has already cost about $40,000 to businesses.

Fermanova bought the scopes online for her husband, who wanted them for a friend who is a hunter, the lawyer says. She returned to the US this month and was arrested when she tried to fly to Moscow. She faces up to 10 years in prison on charges of "knowingly and intentionally" attempting to export "defense articles on the United States Munitions list."

She tried sending 10 messages over the next hour and a half, all of which were rejected because of poor cellphone coverage. The Warden Service says the search for Largay would have taken seven days if it hadn't been for "several false leads, false identifications, and locating and finding hikers who had valuable information and continued to hike the trail." – European leaders are hailing Greece’s vote yesterday on new austerity measures as a “giant step in terms of conception,” but analysts warn that it’s only a “baby step” and the country will still be in dire straits long after the new measures are in place. “Greece is basically being bribed not to default,” a former IMF chief economist tells the New York Times. “But as long as Greece doesn’t grow briskly for a sustained period, it’s in hot water.” The austerity measures, which will save Greece from bankruptcy, were approved by a vote of 155 to 138, with all but one Socialist lawmaker voting in favor. They will save Greece from bankruptcy and allow it to receive a second, $122 billion bailout from Europe and the International Monetary Fund. “It’s a vital step back—from the very grave scenario of default,” European Commission President José Manuel Barroso and European Council President Herman Van Rompuy said in a joint statement. “It would also allow for work to proceed rapidly on a second package of financial assistance, enabling the country to move forward and restoring hope to the Greek people.”

– If you want to live a long and healthy life, it's best to follow five healthy habits. That's according to a new study published Monday in Circulation: Cardiovascular Quality and Outcomes, which looked at the lifestyles of more than 34,000 Americans over 34 years. Researchers found that those who followed the "low-risk" habits of not smoking, maintaining a healthy body mass index, drinking no more than 30 minutes of alcohol per day, exercising regularly, and eating a healthy diet were associated with an extra 14 years of life expectancy, CNN reports. Those who followed the habits were also significantly less likely to die from cancer, heart disease, and other causes. "We can do so much better for having a long healthy life by pretty simple minimal changes in our behavior, and only 8% of adults in our country are adhering to these," says a co-author of the study. About 610,000 Americans are expected to die of heart disease this year, according to the American Cancer Society, and about 609,640 Americans are expected to die of cancer. The study found that those who followed the "low-risk" habits were also significantly less likely to die from all causes, as well as cancer, than those who didn't follow any of the factors

But "it's not a question of either condoms or PrEP. It's about both important tools." – If Elon Musk has his way, people and cars could zip between Washington, DC, and New York City in just 29 minutes. The Tesla and SpaceX founder has announced plans to build a Hyperloop between the two cities, and the Washington Post reports that an "early, and vague, building permit" has been issued for preparatory work at a DC lot next to a McDonald's. A spokesperson for Musk's Boring Company says "a New York Avenue location, if constructed, could become a station" in a broad network of stops across the Hyperloop network, which would also include stations in Baltimore and Southern California. Musk says the New York Avenue lot is just the beginning of the project, which would involve passenger pods that could carry up to 16 people each, as well as electric sleds that could carry cars to and from various stations. The Washington Post notes that tunnel experts say the project is technically feasible, if slow and expensive, and tunnel advocates worry it will undercut mass transit systems. But others say Musk has a vision. "Just the idea of going to New York to have lunch and come back, it'll be awesome," says a housekeeping director at a Hyatt Place hotel a few doors down from the New York Avenue lot.

– A dozen children were injured, one critically, when a swing ride broke down at a Connecticut festival yesterday, sending them careening into each other, the AP reports. The Norwalk Oyster Festival's Zumur ride came to a sudden halt, "causing riders to collide with each other," according to a police statement. Twelve children and one adult were taken to the hospital. An 8-year-old boy remains hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries. "It was a big boom, a big crash, three or four times over," a witness tells News 12. "They slammed into the base of (the ride), and then you heard a whole bunch of screaming." The ride was one of several at the festival, and the president of Stewart Amusement, which owns and operates it, says it was a mechanical failure. "It never happened before. We hope it never happens again," he tells CNN. The company says its rides are inspected by local, state, and federal inspectors weekly.

But this season, hitters will be granted a walk if they get a signal from the opposing team's dugout that they're ready to take advantage. "The change will make it easier for players to get on base with no outs, and it will also help in terms of pace of play," MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred says. But not everyone is happy about the change. "I'm kind of disappointed to see the intentional walk disappear if only because I loved to see it botched every now and then," MLB.com quotes one Twitter user as saying. "That's fun, too!" – The man suspected of sending at least a dozen mail bombs to prominent Democrats has been identified as 56-year-old Cesar Sayoc of Florida, reports the AP. Law enforcement officials tell CNN that they got a break when a fingerprint on a package sent to Rep. Maxine Waters helped them identify Sayoc. The officials say Sayoc has a criminal record dating back to the early 1990s, including a 2002 arrest for threatening a power company, reports the Miami Herald. His social media accounts show him as a fervent supporter of President Trump, though he also posted criticism of CNN and other media outlets. Attorney General Jeff Sessions says it's too early to say whether Sayoc had a political motive. "Other than what you might normally expect, he may have been partisan but that will be determined by the facts as the case goes forward," Sessions said. Sayoc was arrested Friday morning at an AutoZone in Plantation, Fla. He has been charged with five federal crimes: illegal mailing of explosives, threats against former presidents and others, and assaulting current and former federal officers, reports CNN. (Conspiracy theorists have been claiming that some of the packages were fake, but Sayoc's fingerprints helped authorities identify him.)

– The roar of the Tyrannosaurus rex might have sounded more like a bird than a dinosaur, according to a study published Monday in Evolution. The Washington Post reports that the researchers found that dinosaurs likely had vocal cords instead of bones, which would make it easier to reconstruct the sounds. Instead, the researchers believe dinosaurs likely had air sacs and closed-mouth vocalizations, similar to the low murmurs and chirps of birds today. “A cool thing about this is that closed-mouth behavior evolved many times,” Tobias Riede, a physiology expert at Midwestern University, says in a press release. “That suggests it can emerge fairly easily and be incorporated into mating displays.” The study looked at 16 animal lineages, including crocodiles and birds, and found that closed-mouth vocalizations were most common in large-bodied birds, like doves and ostriches. “Looking at the distribution of closed-mouth vocalization in birds that are alive today could tell us how dinosaurs vocalized,” study author and University of Texas biologist Chad Eliason says in the press release. – The discovery of a 150-million-year-old fossil in Siberia has "completely changed our vision of dinosaurs," the lead researcher tells the BBC. – Drinking alcohol on the beach is illegal in San Diego. But drinking alcohol on a raft or other vessel just a few feet from shore is not. "This is the best day ever, that's all I have to say," a 26-year-old man told the Wall Street Journal at one such party last weekend. Now, the city council is expected to vote Monday on expanding the alcohol ban to include "bathers"—people who don't own a boat but use kayaks, canoes, or other forms of paddling to get around the law. Floatopias have been organized anonymously on Facebook, and police say they have cost the city tens of thousands of dollars in extra police and lifeguards costs. "If you slip off and the first deep breath you take is seawater, chances are you're not coming back up," says a police captain. "That's what we're concerned about."

– Sir Roger Bannister, the first person to run a mile in under four minutes, has died at the age of 88, the BBC reports. – The world's oldest wine cellar was found 8,000 years ago in the former Soviet republic of Georgia, National Geographic reports. Now, archaeologists say they've determined that the people who lived at Gadachrili Gora were the world's first wine-makers. "They were pressing it in cooler environments, fermenting it, and then pouring it into smaller jugs and transporting it to the villages when it was ready to drink," archaeologist Stephen Batiuk tells National Geographic. The findings, published this week in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, suggest that humans were making wine much earlier than thought. Researchers found wine-making equipment, jars, and containers in Gadachrili Gora, as well as evidence that people there were making wine long before the world's oldest wine cellar was discovered in France more than a century ago. "This shows just how inventive the human species is," archaeologist Patrick McGovern tells National Geographic. "They're working out horticultural methods, how you transplant it, how you produce it. It shows just how inventive the human species is." – Florida's busiest airport is becoming the first in the nation to require a face scan of passengers on all arriving and departing international flights, including US citizens, according to officials there. The expected announcement Thursday at Orlando International Airport alarms some privacy advocates who say there are no formal rules in place for handling data gleaned from the scans, nor formal guidelines on what should happen if a passenger is wrongly prevented from boarding. Airports in Atlanta, Boston, Chicago, Houston, Las Vegas, Miami, New York, and Washington already use face scans for some departing international flights, but they don't involve all international travelers at the airports like the program's expansion in Orlando would. The image from the face scan is compared to a Department of Homeland Security biometric database that has images of people who should be on the flight, in order to verify the traveler's identity. US citizens at these airports can opt out, but the agency "doesn't seem to be doing an adequate job letting Americans know they can opt out," Harrison Rudolph, an associate at the Center on Privacy & Technology at the Georgetown University Law Center, tells the AP. Rudolph says he has concerns about the face scans' accuracy, since some research shows they are less accurate with racial minorities, women, and children

– As the search for the missing Malaysia Airlines jet enters a seventh day, investigators are looking into the possibility that pilot Zaharie Ahmad Shah, 59, committed suicide. If that's the case, it would be the first time that a pilot has killed himself while in the cockpit of a plane, the Wall Street Journal reports. The last recorded conversation between Shah and the co-pilot before the plane went down was on Feb. 8, when the pilot asked, "Are you all right?" and the co-pilot replied, "Yes, I'm all right." The last recorded conversation between the two pilots before the crash of Flight 370 is on a flight simulator in Shah's home, and investigators are examining it, the Journal reports. But while pilot suicide is a possibility, the AP reports that it remains "almost taboo," with investigators reluctant to conclude that a pilot purposely crashed a plane in order to commit suicide even when the evidence appears compelling. A 2014 FAA study found that only eight of 2,758 fatal aviation accidents in the US were caused by pilot suicide, a rate of 0.3%. Seven of the cases involved the death of only the pilot; in the eighth case, a passenger also died.

– Saudi Arabia's deputy crown prince says the country has "developed a case of oil addiction" and the oil-rich kingdom will be able to survive without it by 2020. Mohammed bin Salman, who is in charge of the country's economy, announced major reforms Monday aimed at weaning the country off of its dependence on oil, the AP reports. The reforms include privatizing state oil company Saudi Aramco, raising the capital of the country's public investment fund by $2 trillion, and allowing women to have a bigger role in the economy, Reuters reports. "We will not allow our country ever to be at the mercy of commodity price volatility or external markets," the 31-year-old prince said at his first news conference with international journalists. "We have developed a case of oil addiction in Saudi Arabia," bin Salman told al-Arabiya TV. "I think by 2020, if oil stops we can survive." In December, the Saudi government cut subsidies and raised fuel prices by 50%. "Being dependent of just one source of income makes an economy incredible vulnerable to price shocks and makes forward planning very difficult," an analyst from Saxo Bank tells the Khaleej Times.

– The quest to find the smallest thing in the universe is getting a big boost from the discovery of a "quantum" black hole in the southern sky, reports the BBC. The black hole in question is about the size of a grain of sand and appears to be pulling gas away from a companion star. If that's true, that would make it the smallest thing in the universe, but scientists are still trying to figure out whether it's the smallest matter in existence. "My guess is that [black hole singularities] are quite a lot smaller and away too small for any instrument to measure, but I don't believe they're of infinite density," a Cambridge physicist tells LiveScience. "Most likely they are maybe a million million times or even more than that smaller than the we've seen so far." The black hole in question is about the size of the "Planck length," which is about the size of a grain of space-time and is the theoretical limit of the universe's smallest measureable length. The Large Hadron Collider at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) in Switzerland just announced that it has found evidence of a black hole in the southern sky.

– Drugs used to treat Parkinson's disease are linked to an increased risk of pathological gambling, hypersexuality, and compulsive shopping, according to a new study. Researchers looked at 1,580 reports of abnormal behavior among Parkinson's patients who took drugs that mimic the function of the neurotransmitter dopamine. They found that 710 of the cases occurred among patients taking drugs called dopamine receptor agonists, compared to 870 among patients taking all other drugs combined. The proportion of abnormal behavior among patients taking these drugs was 277.6 times higher than among those taking other drugs, LiveScience reports. "In our view, these medications should be used less frequently and with great caution, paying close attention to possible untoward effects on behavior and impulse control," wrote two doctors in an editorial for JAMA Internal Medicine. "During an office visit, a patient is unlikely to spontaneously mention, 'By the way, doctor, I lost $250,000 in casinos last year, and I purchase $500 of lottery tickets every week' or 'I spend all of my 401(k)s in a single day.'" The study author says doctors need to be "on the lookout for this kind of behavior" and warn patients and their caregivers about the possible side effects of the drugs.

– A historian searching through old boxes belonging to wealthy families in Hans Christian Andersen's home town of Odense, Denmark, stumbled upon a 700-word manuscript at the bottom of one. It's believed to be one of the author's earliest stories, seven years before his official debut in 1830. "I often get calls about stuff thought to have been off Andersen's hand. Most of the time, it is not. This time I was thrilled," a senior curator at the Hans Christian Andersen Museum tells the AP. The story, titled "Tallow Candle," is dedicated to a vicar's widow named Bunkeflod who had lived across from Andersen's home, notes the BBC. She was his close friend. "I have no doubt that it is Christian Andersen who wrote it," the curator says. "The text is not at the level of the more mature fairy tales that we know from Andersen's later writing. I have no doubts."

– If you're in a position of power—say, negotiating with a boss—your voice may change in a fundamental way, according to new research out of San Diego State University. "Our findings suggest that whether it's parents attempting to assert authority over unruly children, haggling between a car salesman and customer, or negotiations between heads of states, the sound of the voices involved may profoundly determine the outcome of those interactions," says lead researcher Sei Jin Ko in a press release. To test this, the researchers recorded 161 college students reading aloud and assigned them to one of two ranks: high, with a strong offer, valuable inside information, or low, without power. Low-rank students were told to imagine they had a weak offer, no inside information, or low workplace status, or they were asked to recall an experience in which they lacked power. – A new study suggests that doctors may be able to spot skin cancer early by counting the number of moles on a person's arm. Reporting in the journal JAMA Internal Medicine, researchers say that the number of moles on a person's right arm was the best indicator of their overall risk of skin cancer. Specifically, females with more than seven moles on the arm were nine times more likely to have more than 50 on the whole body, and those with more than 11 were more likely to have more than 100. "The findings could have a significant impact for primary care, allowing GPs to more accurately estimate the total number of moles in a patient extremely quickly via an easily accessible body part," says lead author Simone Ribero of King's College London. "This would mean more patients at risk of melanoma can be identified and monitored." The researchers used data from 3594 female Caucasian twins between January 1995 and December 2003 as part of the TwinsUK study protocol. Twins underwent a skin examination including recording skin type, hair and eye color, and freckles as well as mole count on 17 body sites performed by trained nurses. The decision was yet another indication of the influence of President Trump's nominee to the Supreme Court, Neil Gorsuch, who joined the court in April. – JPMorgan's massive trading loss may not be the bank's only problem. Reuters takes a look at the complex strategy that led to the loss, and how it could affect other companies. JPMorgan's problem is tied to a group of indexes that track the performance of corporate bonds. One of the indexes, the Markit CDX NA IG Series 9, is essentially a portfolio of credit default swaps—basically contracts that protect against default by a borrower. JPMorgan used that index, and others, to bet that credit markets would strengthen. Because that position is widely known on Wall Street, many traders are betting the opposite way in the hope of profiting as the bank's losses increase. The index has been moving against JPMorgan in recent days. Oppenheimer & Co used the average of the index in 2011—141—to estimate on a straight line basis a theoretical additional loss for the bank of $5.9 billion. Oppenheimer analysts, however, cautioned that such a large loss was unlikely. For starters, they said, JPMorgan likely offset the trading position before announcing the loss. Their analysis also reflects a trade in a vacuum without any counter-bets. Additionally, credit quality has been improving so "the underlying market has moved in JPM's favor," they said.

– For the first time in a quarter century, there were fewer new cases of diabetes in the US last year than there were in 2008, according to new data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. There were 1.4 million new cases in 2014, down from 1.7 million in 2008, the New York Times reports. "This is the first time I think we can really comfortably say we've seen a decrease in incidence in the rate of new cases," Edward Gregg, chief of epidemiology and statistics in the division of diabetes translation at the CDC, tells CBS News. "For a while we were calling it a plateau." The number of adults between 18 and 79 with newly diagnosed diabetes cases more than tripled between 2008 and 2014, jumping from 493,000 to more than 1.4 million new cases a year. About 21.9 million Americans have type 2 diabetes, and the number of people with prediabetes is estimated to be more than a third of those who develop the condition. But there's still a lot to be done, Gregg says. "Our incidence rate is 60% higher than it was back in the early nineties. – Three members of a single family were found dead Sunday in the wreckage of Genoa's bridge collapse, bringing the death toll to 43, Reuters reports. According to the BBC, the bodies of the family members were found in a car crushed by concrete slabs on the A10 motorway bridge, the last of the bridge's victims found alive. Nine people remain in the hospital, four in critical condition. The cause of the bridge's collapse is still unclear, and investigators are still working to determine what went wrong. Autostrade per l'Italia, the toll-road operator that operated the bridge, has pledged half a billion euros to help victims' families. The Italian government has also allocated 32 million euros to help those displaced by the bridge collapse.

– The world's internet has been slowed down by what security experts are calling the biggest cyber-attack of its kind, reports the BBC. The so-called "denial-of-service" attack, which Spamhaus says it's been under for "well over a week," was launched in retaliation for a spat with a Dutch hosting firm. The non-profit Spamhaus maintains a database of servers it believes are being used for malicious purposes, and recently blocked Cyberbunker's servers over the latter's stance on child pornography and terrorism-related material. A Cyberbunker spokesman tells the BBC that Spamhaus is abusing its position, and should not be allowed to decide "what goes and does not go on the internet." Five national cyber-police forces are investigating the attack, which Spamhaus says is peaking at 300 Gbps (gigabits per second). "If you aimed this at Downing Street, they would be down instantly," says Spamhaus' CEO. "They would be completely off the internet." The group says it has "built the biggest DNS server around" and has "hundreds of thousands of servers in more than 100 countries."

– Fort San Marcos was built in 1577 on what is now Parris Island, SC, to protect Spanish sailors from Native Americans. It went up in six days, with large pieces of wood already made off-site to protect against Native Americans. The general location of the fort had been noted in documents archived in Spain. There was a drawing of the fort and a written description but nothing detailing the location. Traditional digging methods had failed to find the fort. "We can't go to a map and say 'oh, this is where Pedro Menendez lived or this is where that fort was or this is where anything was,'" archaeologist Chester DePratter says. "So we have to figure it out." The location was nailed down using radar and magnetometers. The machines have been in play for archaeologists for years, but the computer programs interpreting the data have vastly improved in recent years, says University of Georgia archaeologist Victor Thompson. "Anytime humans occupy an area for an extended period of time, they alter the physical characteristics of the subsurface," Thompson says. "If floors become compacted, we can see that. – The White House made a big announcement today about the Affordable Care Act: It will delay the requirement for employers to provide health insurance to their workers until 2015, reports the Washington Post. It's a "stunning announcement," says the Wall Street Journal, which calls the move "the biggest revision so far to the federal health-care overhaul." The move is a big victory for businesses that had lobbied against the requirement, and is sure to be a big talking point in next year's midterm elections, notes the Hill. The delay will not affect the individual mandate, which requires most Americans to buy insurance or pay a penalty.

"Then, in 2014, the proportion of interracial marriages jumped again." Ortega and Hergovich say that when people meet in this way, they are usually "complete strangers" who don't have any existing social links. But if people add random links between people from different ethnic groups, the level of interracial marriage changes dramatically. "Our model predicts nearly complete racial integration upon the emergence of online dating, even if the number of partners that individuals meet from newly formed ties is small," say Ortega and Hergovich. – The Leonid meteor shower will be at its peak Tuesday night, and Space.com has a primer on what to expect and how to see it. The Leonids peak around Nov. 17, when the Earth passes through debris left behind by the comet Tempel-Tuttle. This year, the Earth will be passing through debris left behind by the comet, and there's no chance we'll hit the comet itself. The Leonids peak mid-cycle, and this year, NASA predicts we'll see one meteor about every four minutes. But in this year's favor, the moon will be a crescent, which means a darker sky that makes streaks of light easier to spot. Strike against: the current cloud-cover forecast predicts overcast skies for a good fraction of the US that night. (Meteors will peak Wednesday and Thursday.)

– Dominion Diamond Mines has just announced the biggest diamond ever found in North America. The 552-carat yellow gem was found in October at the Diavik mine in the Northwest Territories, reports Bloomberg. It's almost three times the size of the next largest stone ever found in Canada, and would be among the 30 largest stones ever unearthed in the world. Dominion CEO Shane Durgin calls it "a beautiful gem-quality diamond," but says it's somewhat of a "miracle" that the stone survived the mining process. "It's very unusual for a diamond of this size in this part of the world," he says. "So it's a very unique discovery." The company, which owns 40% of Diavik, plans to have the stone cut and polished by an unnamed gem expert soon. The previous record for the largest diamond found in North America was set in 2015 by the Diavik Foxfire, an 187.7-carat diamond.

– Kim Jong Un has been named a four-star general, making him the highest-ranking member of North Korea’s military since Kim Jong Il himself was a four-star general. If that happens, it will be a strong sign that North Korea intends to continue its cult of personality around the family for another generation, the BBC notes.

The RQ-180, which is scheduled to be in production by 2015, will be able to fly in countries where the US doesn't have permission to do so. It will also be able to carry out electronic attack missions, officials say. Northrop Grumman, which beat out Boeing and Lockheed Martin for the classified contract, is known to be working on other spy drones, including the next generation of the Global Hawk and the X-47B unmanned combat air system. The RQ-180 is expected to replace the Air Force's RQ-4B Global Hawk, which is scheduled to be retired in 2014.

– Two years ago, a massive solar storm almost hit Earth, knocking out power and GPS, among other things, the Los Angeles Times reports. Now, a new NASA study says the storm was actually two storms that merged to create the most powerful solar storm ever recorded. "I have come away from our recent studies more convinced than ever that Earth and its inhabitants were incredibly fortunate that the 2012 eruption happened when it did," says Daniel Baker, lead author of the study in Space Weather. "If the eruption had occurred only one week earlier, Earth would have been in the line of fire." The 2012 storm was a direct result of two solar flares, or coronal mass ejections, that erupted from the sun on July 23, 2012, NASA reports. The flare was so powerful it knocked out satellites, GPS systems, and electrical grids. The National Academy of Sciences estimates that such a storm could cause more than $2 trillion in economic damage. "If it had hit, we would still be picking up the pieces," Baker says in a NASA statement.

– When Chris and Dana White of Pensacola, Fla., boarded Carnival's Fantasy for a three-day Caribbean cruise last October, they had no idea what to expect. "I said, 'Is that what I think it is?'" Chris tells Inside Edition. "And [Dana] looked at it and she became concerned. And we were just really flabbergasted that there's a camera in the room and it's plugged up and it's working." The Whites called Carnival security, and an employee inspected the device and took it apart. "I was thinking, 'I can't believe this is actually happening to us,'" Chris says. Carnival initially said the camera wasn't a camera at all. "It was wired up. It was working. It was warm to the touch," Dana says. "I just immediately felt like we had been invaded; our privacy had been invaded." The Whites called Carnival after the cruise, and a full investigation was carried out. Carnival acknowledged in a statement to USA Today that the "video transmitter" was found, but it was "not connected to an electrical source and not capable of recording." The Whites say they'll never book with Carnival again. The FBI was called in

– A West Virginia Department of Transportation worker faces charges of driving a state snow plow while drunk, the AP reports. The McDowell County Sheriff's Department says Thomas Keith Henderson of Elkhorn was arrested late Wednesday during a traffic stop on Burke Mountain near Keystone. A criminal complaint says Deputy R.L. Jones stopped the snow plow because the driver's side headlight was out. The deputy smelled alcohol and saw that Jones' eyes were bloodshot and glassy. The sheriff's department says Henderson's blood alcohol level was 0.09. That's more than twice the 0.04 legal limit for commercial driver's license holders. DOT spokeswoman Carrie Bly confirmed Henderson is employed by the department. She says the DOT can't comment because it's an ongoing legal matter. A telephone listing for Henderson in the Elkhorn area couldn't be found.

The video, "A Fire in My Belly, A Work in Progress," was produced by David Wojnarowicz, who died in 1992 after suffering from AIDS. It began screening Saturday at the New Museum, which is devoted exclusively to contemporary art. The complete video is over 30 minutes long and includes graphic sexual content—including masturbation and full frontal nudity—and has renewed opposition from religious groups offended by the depiction of Jesus covered by insects. "I think that in the artistic community, directors, curators are tremendously insensitive to Christians, they respond by claiming victim status and I find it appalling," says Catholic League President Bill Donohue. "You can't make fun of the Holocaust, you can't make fun of black slavery ... and you can't even depict anything about Mohammed." The video was recently removed from a Smithsonian exhibit after Donohue led protests against it and petitioned Congress to cut the institution's funding after it presented the video. – The second most wanted Nazi war criminal on the Simon Wiesenthal Center's most wanted list has died in Canada at the age of 93. Vladimir Katriuk, a native of Ukraine who lived in Ormstown, Que., for decades, died of a stroke last week, his lawyer tells the Canadian Press. Katriuk, who lied about his service in a Ukrainian battalion during World War II to gain Canadian citizenship, is accused of taking part in a 1943 massacre in Khatyn, Belarus, in which Jews were killed. "Those who have been involved in war crimes will find no haven in Canada—they will be located and they will face the consequences," a spokeswoman for Justice Minister Peter MacKay tells the CBC. Katriuk's lawyer says his client had been ill for a long time. "He would get calls in the middle of the night from nasty people," he says. "He was ailing, he had heart problems ... and he would call me and I would basically do a hand-holding exercise, you know, tell him, 'Not to worry, nothing in it, we've been through all this, been there, done that, so please, please relax.'"

– Twenty-two states and the District of Columbia have come together to fight a challenge to Montana's law banning corporate campaign spending. The states, led by New York, want the Supreme Court to keep the law in place, arguing that it's different from the federal ban the court struck down in Citizens United, the AP reports. Montana's law applies to a "wide range of state and local offices, including judgeships and law enforcement positions such as sheriff and county prosecutor," New York's attorney general writes in a legal brief. "By contrast, Montana's law applies to a wide range of state and local offices, including judgeships and law enforcement positions such as sheriff and county prosecutor." But legal observers don't expect the Supreme Court to reverse its Citizens United decision. "It is highly unlikely that the Court would reverse its decision in Citizens United," one law professor says. "At best, the court would listen to arguments and might agree a clarification is needed to allow the Montana law to stand. But even that is a long shot."

– Michele Bachmann has decided she doesn't want her Swiss citizenship. After news broke that she and her family had applied for the papers, the Minnesota congresswoman issued a statement saying she had taken the action "because I want to make it perfectly clear: I was born in America and I am a proud American citizen. I am, and always have been, 100% committed to our United States Constitution and the United States of America. As the daughter of an Air Force veteran, stepdaughter of an Army veteran and sister of a Navy veteran, I am proud of my allegiance to the greatest nation the world has ever known." Bachmann's husband, Marcus, is of Swiss descent, so she had been eligible for dual citizenship since they married in 1978, but "recently some of their children wanted to exercise their eligibility for dual citizenship so they went through the process as a family," her spokeswoman said. The LA Times notes that Bachmann's statement said that "under Swiss law, Bachmann automatically received dual citizenship when she married her husband, a dual American and Swiss citizen, in 1978." But Mark Zdechlik at the Star Tribune thinks that contradicts her earlier statement. "She was probably just confused and meant to become a citizen of Sweden. Or Swaziland. It might have given her

– A 22-year-old Brooklyn man has been arrested for the third time in as many months for riding the outside of a New York City subway train. Isaiah Thompson was arrested at his home in Brooklyn on Tuesday on charges of reckless endangerment and disorderly conduct, the New York Daily News reports. He was caught riding the C train Friday morning, surfing through a tunnel while other commuters watched, the Washington Post reports. "It was just sort of like spur-of-the-moment, take a camera out not knowing what was happening, but realizing as I'm taking this video that this guy is clearly hanging on," subway rider Matthew Beary tells Pix 11. Beary says he took the video "because I thought it was awesome and also scary as hell." Thompson was arrested in March and November of last year for riding the outside of a train, and transit chief Andy Byford tells Gothamist that subway surfing is "incredibly dangerous, disruptive, and foolish—it can cause major delays and easily result in death." "This young man is lucky he ended up in police custody and not in a hospital or worse," Byford says. – It's that time of year again: time for the CDC to release its annual list of the country's most sedentary people. This year's list includes those who were totally sedentary—meaning they didn't do any of the 104 physical activities listed—or those who were at least moderately sedentary—meaning they didn't do any of the physical activities at all in the last year, the Wall Street Journal reports. The percentage of Americans who were totally sedentary last year rose to 28%, the highest level since 2007, according to the survey of 26,000 people. The percentage of people who were moderately sedentary rose to 31%, while the percentage of people who were totally sedentary rose to 78%. The list is based on responses from people between the ages of 18 and 64, the Journal notes.

– A stampede among pilgrims near the holy city of Mecca today killed at least 717 people and left hundreds more injured in the deadliest disaster to strike the annual Hajj pilgrimage in 25 years, the BBC reports. According to the AP, the stampede occurred as pilgrims were walking toward a structure known as the Jamarat Bridge, where they had to throw stones at three pillars representing the devil. "Dead bodies stretch as far as my eyes can see," says the BBC's Abuja editor, who was in Mina. "People were climbing over one another just to breathe." Saudi Arabia's health minister says the disaster happened because many pilgrims moved "without respecting the timetables" set by authorities, the BBC reports. Ayatollah Ali Khamenei blamed the Saudi government, saying it "must accept the huge responsibility for this catastrophe," adding that "mismanagement and improper actions" were to blame. Saudi Arabia's King Salman has ordered an investigation into the stampede.

– Tiger Woods has a secret love child, according to a British journalist who says he knows the mother of the child. “There is a lot more to come out,” Neal Boulton tells Channel 4’s Tiger Woods: The Rise and Fall. “Tiger will eventually admit to fathering a child.” The golfer is one of about 15 women linked to him in secret affairs, Radar reports. Porn star and escort Devon James claims to have had a two-and-a-half-year affair with Woods, paying him and another woman $2,000 each for a “two-girl party.” James gave birth to her son in early 2001, before Woods and Elin Nordegren were married. “She says Tiger is the father of her child,” a source says. “And she’s insistent about it.”

– "The lives of people in poor countries will improve faster in the next 15 years than at any other time in history," Bill Gates writes in his annual letter to the world's richest people, released today. The Microsoft co-founder and his wife, Melinda, are hoping the world's richest will join them in their "Big Bet for the Future." The letter lays out goals for the next decade and a half, including getting rid of polio, reducing child deaths by half, and making Africa capable of feeding itself. Gates tells Wired that he worries that the UN's current set of Millennium Development Goals—which aim to reduce extreme poverty by 50% and cut the maternal mortality rate by three-quarters in the next 15 years—could become too broad. "If you have malnutrition, you can't do education very well," he says. "I do think the MDGs were so powerful because they were so succinct. But the MDGs were so powerful because they were so succinct. Do you worry that if these goals become too broad, it will be harder to keep people focused? That absolutely is a concern that I have."

"I'm not running for president, so, period. End of story," Ryan told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt on Tuesday, per the Hill. "I'm here in Israel. I'm not going to be president of the United States. I'm not going to be president of the United States while I'm here," he added, per the Washington Post. "I've said that before. I'm not going to be president of the United States while I'm here. I'm not going to be president of the United States while I'm in Israel." – At least 13 people, including children, died after a boat carrying tourists capsized and sank on a lake during a thunderstorm in a country music mecca in southwest Missouri, authorities said Friday. Missouri State Highway Patrol Sgt. Jason Pace said four people remain missing Friday after the Ride the Ducks boat sank on Table Rock Lake in Branson Thursday evening. He said 14 people survived, and that seven of them were injured. Patrol divers found two more bodies early Friday, raising the death toll from 11 to 13, Pace said. A spokeswoman for the Cox Medical Center Branson said four adults and three children arrived at the hospital shortly after the incident. Two adults are in critical condition and the others were treated for minor injuries, Brandei Clifton said. Stone County Sheriff Doug Rader said Thursday that stormy weather likely made the boat capsize. Another duck boat on the lake made it safely back to shore. Steve Lindenberg, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Springfield, Missouri, said the agency issued a severe thunderstorm warning for the Branson area Thursday evening. Lindenberg said winds reached speeds of more than 60mph. "It's a warning telling people to take shelter," he said. – Two New Jersey men are facing a litany of charges after police say they took a taxi to a house, asked the driver to wait outside, then returned with a TV set and a few liquor bottles, the Asbury Park Press reports. According to NJ.com, Timothy Foote, 38, and Kenneth Burke, 46, called for a taxi to a home in Deal on Friday night. Police say the men told the driver to wait outside before returning with the TV and the bottles. The driver took the men to an apartment in Asbury Park, where they allegedly didn't pay the fare. Police say they were alerted by Asbury Park police at 10:31pm, and the house was found to have been burglarized. Burke and Foote were charged with burglary, conspiracy to commit burglary, criminal trespass, and theft. They're being held on $20,000 bail each.

– A tractor-trailer carrying seafood went over the side of the Chesapeake Bay Bridge- Tunnel in Virginia on Thursday afternoon, sending the vehicle into the water below, WAVY reports. The driver was pulled from the water by a Navy helicopter, but he was pronounced dead at the hospital. The cause of death has been ruled accidental drowning and hypothermia. A relative of the driver identifies him as 47-year-old Joseph Chen of North Carolina, and he had been hauling seafood for Evans Transports. A Virginia Beach Police Department rep says the accident occurred around 12:30pm on the southbound side of the bridge, which connects Virginia Beach and Norfolk. The bridge was closed on both sides at the time, the Virginian-Pilot reports, and WAVY has video of the scene.

– Uber drivers across Europe went on strike today, snarling traffic in cities from London to Madrid and Berlin. In London, thousands of black cabs and private hire cars descended on tourist hubs Trafalgar Square and Parliament Square, blocking some of the city's busiest streets, Bloomberg reports. Scooter and motorbike riders studying for the cab-driver exam joined in, honking their horns as the police tried to regulate traffic. London taxi drivers have said that the app's fare calculator amounts to a meter, which aren't allowed in hired cars that aren't registered taxis. Last month, TFL asked the High Court to rule on whether the fare system was legal. "We have to have a license to own a cab, we have to have a driver's license, a cab driver's license," said a 58-year-old black-cab driver, who took part in the protest. "For some reason they seem to be outside the law." In Madrid, drivers blocked the Charles de Gaulle and Orly airports this morning and prevented private-car services from picking up passengers, says an official. Cabbies also slowed down traffic the A1 highway that circles Paris, local TV reported. The vast majority of France's 55,000 professional taxis and Paris' 15,000

– Darwin's finches are some of the best examples of speciation—the process by which new species arise. Now, some of the birds are on the verge of extinction thanks to a parasitic fly brought to the Galpagos by humans in the 1960s, National Geographic reports. "This is like a really bad horror flick," senior author Dale Clayton tells National Geographic. "The babies can't withstand even one night with these parasites." The medium-ground finches, also known as the mangrove finch, are vulnerable to Philornis downsi, a nest fly that lays its eggs in bird nests and feeds on the eggs laid by adult finches and their babies. The eggs hatch into maggots, which feed on both brooding adult finches and their babies. The adult birds are unaffected, but P. downsi kills huge numbers of baby birds among Darwin's finches and other land birds. The flies can be found on every island in the Galpagos. Clayton's team used five years of field data to predict the species' long-term viability and found that, in two out of three scenarios, medium ground finches could be gone within the next century. – A video of a newborn calf getting warmed up with a blow dryer has gone viral on Facebook—but not in a good way. After Yankee Farmer's Market posted the video of Diego, a Scottish Highland calf born in a snowstorm, last week, it received more than 138,000 shares and 12 million views, the Concord Monitor reports. But not everyone is charmed by the baby animal's appearance. "Why are you posting videos of cute baby animals when you're going to kill them and sell them as food?? There's something really twisted about that," wrote one woman from the UK. Others have offered to adopt Diego to save him from slaughter. "I'm not sure how you get that much negativity out of a picture of a baby cow," wrote one man. But Brian Farmer, who runs the farm in New Hampshire with his wife, says he's been "humbled" by the support he's received from his customers and the community at large. "A large amount of our customer base are basically in the sense that they don't agree with what the food industry does with animals," he says. – An 86-year-old New Jersey woman was found dead in her bathroom on Feb. 15 after she tripped and strangled herself with a necklace attached to her walker, the Star-Ledger reports. According to NJ.com, Roseann DiFrancesco was wearing a necklace with a lanyard that was attached to her walker, but it's not clear whether the necklace or the lanyard itself was the cause of the death. DiFrancesco had last spoken to her on Feb. 12. A visiting nurse couldn't summon her to the bathroom after she tripped and strangled herself, according to the report from the Cumberland County Coroner's Office. It's unclear how long she had been dead. DiFrancesco was a retired employee of the federal government who had been a clerk for the Pennsylvania Department of Labor and Industry for 25 years, according to her obituary. She was also a member of a Catholic church and a parishioner at a local church.

– The small town of Kuky, Turkey, is home to a unique "bird language" that has been around for centuries—and a new study sheds light on how it works in the brain. German-born biopsychologist Onur Gntrkn, a native of Turkey, set out to learn what locals called ku__ dili, or "bird language," by having people listen to pairs of syllables played simultaneously through headphones in both spoken and whistled Turkish. When Gntrkn gave the volunteers spoken Turkish, they usually understood the syllables played through the right speaker. When he switched to whistled Turkish, however, participants understood both syllables in roughly equal measure, suggesting that the left hemisphere was processing the sound. "They tell us that the organization of our brain, in terms of its asymmetrical structure, is not as fixed as we assume," Gntrkn tells the New Yorker. "The way information is given to us appears to change the architecture of our brain in a radical way." – Dominique Strauss-Kahn is on suicide watch at New York City's Rikers Island, NBC New York reports. Guards check him every 15 to 30 minutes, and he's wearing shoes without laces. A source says he's been on the watch because of his "mood and the delicate nature of the case." Strauss-Kahn, who has been charged with attempted rape, is also on a medical device to ensure he doesn't stop breathing during the night, the AP reports. His cell is empty, but there's a toilet and sink. He's also allowed to leave his cell for an hour a day, and a corrections union spokesman says he's being monitored because of a mental health assessment.

– The idea was simple: Scientists would try to replicate the results of 100 psychology studies recently published in major journals. But in a study published today in Science, they report that only 39 of the studies were able to be replicated. That's a "significant failure," according to the study's co-author, but researchers say it's not a failure of science at all. "I don't see this story as negative or pessimistic," University of Virginia researcher Brian Nosek tells NPR. "The results present an opportunity." The scientists behind the Reproducibility Project: Psychology even worked with the original researchers who published the studies to make sure they were on the same page. The results, however, suggest that there's a problem with the reproduction process, Nosek says. "Despite its central importance, there is little known about the reproducibility of research in general," he says. "And there has been a growing concern that reproducibility may be lower than expected or desired." The 39 studies that were able to be replicated had smaller effects than the original studies, usually around 50%, though Nosek says there's a possibility that the original studies were wrong and the researchers didn't detect a real difference. – The president of the University of Cincinnati says he twice tried to kill himself. Santa Ono made the admission over the weekend at a fundraiser, where he told about 200 people that when he was 14, he locked himself in his bedroom and tried to overdose on cold medication and beer, the Cincinnati Enquirer reports. He tried the same thing in his late 20s. Ono, 53, says he recovered from both depression and the suicide attempts. "There's light at the end of the tunnel," he tells the Enquirer. "If you have the proper counseling and support, it's really possible for you to move past that and move back into functioning life." Ono, who became UC's president last year, says he wants to erase the stigma surrounding mental illness. A university official says Ono was moved to speak out after the 2014 suicide of 21-year-old student Brogan Dulle. "It's amazing that he was willing to share that to help other people," Dulle's mother tells the Enquirer. "It's not easy for people to talk about things like that." The week after Dulle's death, Ono helped arrange for five free counseling sessions for UC students, the official says.

– The race for Virginia's 94th District House seat was so close after Election Day that Democrats thought they'd flipped a GOP seat in the state's House of Delegates for the first time in 17 years. But a recount uncovered enough additional ballots to give Democrat Shelly Simonds a one-vote victory, and on Wednesday, a three-judge panel declined to certify the result, the Washington Post reports. "The court declares there is no winner in this election," Newport News Circuit Court Judge Bryant L. Sugg said after the panel deliberated for more than two hours. He said that the ballot in question contained a mark for Simonds as well as a mark for Republican Del. David Yancey but that the voter had made another mark to strike out Sim­onds's name. Officials presiding over the five-hour recount on Tuesday had discarded that ballot en route to a historic reversal of the original election outcome. Yancey had emerged from Election Day with a 10-vote lead in the 94th District, but the recount uncovered enough additional ballots for Simonds to give her a one-vote victory. That seemed to set up the House for a rare 50-50 split between Republicans and Democrats, ending 17 years of GOP dominance and making headlines

– Some 80 people were hospitalized last night after a concert by electronic dance music star Avicii at Boston's TD Garden, reports WHDH-TV. Most had trouble with alcohol, drugs, or dehydration, officials tell the Boston Globe. "There was a lot of drinking and some drugs. It was really hot in there," a concertgoer tells the Boston Herald. Three men were arrested near the venue, each facing drug charges. Avicii, real name Tim Bergling, was performing as part of his True Tour, notes CNN.

– Burger King is trying out something new with its Whopper, but it's not exactly what you'd call a Whopper. Instead, the chain is testing a Whopperito, a burger wrapped in a tortilla, Grub Grade reports. According to Munchies, a sign was spotted at a few Pennsylvania Burger King locations advertising the new menu item, but it's not clear if it's the work of rogue franchisees or Burger King itself. Reaction on social media has been mixed. "The Whopperito looks like a terrible idea," one person tweeted. "Now imagine all those ingredients wrapped in a flour tortilla and you've got yourself a Whopperrito." Another called it a "whopper minus bun plus tortilla." Burger King hasn't announced when the new menu item will be available in other states.

Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Hua Chunying said the request had been passed to Trump's transition team and to the current administration of Barack Obama, the AP reports. "We urge the US side once again not to allow the Taiwan administration to send the so-called delegation to attend the inauguration and to avoid any forms of official exchange with Taiwan," Hua said at a daily briefing. China firmly opposes "anyone from the Taiwan administration engaged in activities that interfere or undermine the China-US relationship in the US under any pretext," she said. delegation leader and former Premier Yu Shyi-kun departed for Washington on Monday together with politicians from both Taiwan's ruling Democratic Progressive Party and the opposition Nationalists. Along with attending the inauguration, the delegates plan to hold talks with politicians, academics, and overseas Chinese community representatives. Trump angered Beijing and upset decades of diplomatic precedent by talking by phone with Taiwanese President Tsai Ing-wen shortly after winning November's presidential election. – Palau is famous for its pristine beaches, world-class scuba diving, and forest-covered volcanic islands, but the Pacific island nation's president wants to make it a little more expensive to visit. Tommy Remengesau is proposing a new law that would allow only five-star hotels to open on its islands, the BBC reports. He's offering tax breaks for high-end investors who design their own infrastructure, such as roads and water treatment systems, for the resorts. Palau relies heavily on tourism, but in recent years locals have complained about an influx of visitors causing overcrowding at popular sites, damaging coral reefs, and disturbing wildlife. The biggest increase has been among Chinese tour groups, and in 2015 the government announced it was halving the number of charter flights arriving from China. Remengesau says the proposed law focuses on "quality rather than quantity," and he makes clear that Palau wants to attract big spenders. But he says it's also about developing the islands in a way that respects the natural environment and those who call the country home. – The Supreme Court is upholding the broad reach of a federal law that bans people convicted of domestic violence from owning guns. The justices on Monday rejected arguments that the law covers only intentional acts of abuse and not those committed in the heat of an argument, the AP reports. The case involved two Maine men who said their guilty pleas for hitting their partners should not disqualify them from gun ownership. The dispute drew interest from advocates for victims of domestic abuse who say the law applies to reckless behavior as well as intentional misconduct. Gun rights groups argued that the men should not lose their constitutional right to bear arms because of misdemeanor abuse convictions. A federal appeals court ruled against the men. The court, in a 6-2 ruling, was unpersuaded by arguments from two Maine men who said their past convictions weren't the type that should subject them to a federal ban on firearm possession, the Wall Street Journal reports.

– Nigeria's military says it has arrested a businessman who "participated actively" in the kidnapping of more than 200 schoolgirls, as well as in the killing of a traditional leader in May, the BBC reports. Babuji Ya'ari was arrested as part of a raid on an intelligence cell linked to Boko Haram, the military says. The military says Ya'ari was also involved in "several deadly attacks" in Maidugiri, the capital of Borno state, since 2011. Ya'ari was also a member of a vigilante group fighting Boko Haram, the military says. The US has sent experts to help locate the missing girls, but negotiations appear stalled, the AP reports. Boko Haram says the girls will not be freed until all imprisoned militants are released. The militants have killed more than 2,000 people this year.

– Russia's track-and-field team has been banned from the Rio Olympics in the wake of a doping scandal, USA Today reports. The International Association of Athletics Federations, the sport's governing body, made the decision Friday in a unanimous vote. “Politics was not playing a part in that room today,” says Sebastian Coe, the head of the IAAF. “It was unambiguous.” The decision comes after a World Anti-Doping Agency report found Russia was running a state-sponsored doping program in the sport. The Russian government oversaw the doping program, according to the New York Times. “The head coach of the Russian athletic team and many of the athletes on that team appear unwilling to acknowledge the nature and extent of the doping problem in Russian athletics, and certain athletes and coaches appear willing to ignore the doping rules,” says Rune Andersen, the chair of the IAAF task force monitoring the Russian team's anti-doping systems. “A strong and effective anti-doping infrastructure capable of detecting and deterring doping has still not been created.” Russia's track-and-field team won 18 medals—eight of them gold—at the last Rio Olympics. Now, no Russian track-and-field athletes will compete under the Russian flag.

– The UK's election is over, and David Cameron will keep his job as prime minister. Cameron's Conservative Party won the most seats in Parliament, but fell short of a majority, reports the AP. The Labour Party led by Ed Miliband came in second, with around two-thirds of the vote, while the Scottish National Party (SNP) won the most seats—putting it in third place—and is expected to play a key role in forming a new government, reports the New York Times. – A new study on smoking prevalence around the world finds that China has gained more smokers than any other country over the past three decades. The country gained almost 100 million smokers between 1980 and 2012, leaving it with 281 million smokers, or one-third of the world's population, researchers at the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation tell the New York Times. That puts China in second place behind the US, which has a population of 4.4 billion but has a smoking prevalence of just 19.6%. The study, which looked at data from surveys, WHO data, and other sources, also found that the average number of cigarettes consumed per smoker per day in China has risen from 18 to 22 over the same period, while prevalence has plateaued, the Times reports. "The study shows that the tobacco epidemic is going to be a whole lot worse before it gets better, particularly in lower income countries," says a World Lung Foundation adviser. "If they do nothing at all, there are going to be massive costs for China in terms of premature deaths, health care costs, environmental costs, economic costs, family costs—there are all manners of costs." – Scientists at the National Institute of Standards and Technology say they've created the world's most precise atomic clock—and if they're right, you should be able to tell it apart from the current gold standard. The ytterbium optical lattice clock measures a second in 1018, and doesn't change by more than one part in that span, meaning it's in about the 18th decimal place, reports CNN. "This is like measuring time over a hundred years to a precision of several nanoseconds," says a co-author of the study, published in Science. The clock uses lasers to excite the electrons of ytterbium atoms, unlike in the cesium clock, which uses a microwave light source. The new clock's oscillations are about one quadrillion per second, compared to billions of oscillations per second in the cesium clock, says the co-author. "You divide time into finer and finer intervals," he says. "The first instrument would make more precise measurements." The clock could be used for navigation and communications, as well as for studying Einstein's theory of general relativity, but it won't fit on your wrist or wall, and cost anywhere from $500,000 to half a million dollars.

The person, dressed in dark clothing, can be seen on surveillance video near the home Thursday morning. Police also released video footage that appears to show a man in a hoodie moving quickly behind a building. Police believe the other three victims in the fire—Savvas Savopoulos, 46; his wife, Amy, 47; and housekeeper Veralicia Figueroa, 57—were the couple's 10-year-old son, Philip, and Figueroa was the family's housekeeper. – The mass extinction that wiped out 70% of land vertebrates and 90% of marine species on Earth 252 million years ago may have been even worse than the one that wiped out the dinosaurs 65 million years ago, according to a new study. MIT researchers say a microbe called Methanosarcina—a single-celled organism distinct from other types of bacteria—could be to blame for the disaster, which occurred during the end of the Permian period, Reuters reports. "I would say that the end-Permian extinction is the closest animal life has ever come to being totally wiped out, and it may have come pretty close," says one of the researchers. "Many, if not most, of the surviving groups of organisms barely hung on, with only a few species making it through, many probably by chance." According to the study, Methanosarcina became a major producer of methane through the consumption of accumulated organic carbon in ocean sediments. This caused huge amounts of methane to be released into the atmosphere, which in turn heated up the oceans and changed the chemistry of the oceans. US District Judge Ann Donnelly said the restraining order will keep the government from detaining legal permanent residents, green card holders, and refugees from the countries until the case is heard in court. She also put a hold on the part of the US government that would allow it to suspend the refugee program for 120 days. A lawyer for the ACLU, which filed the suit on behalf of two Iraqi men being held at New York's JFK Airport, tells Reuters that the rulings add to questions about the constitutionality of the order. – A British Airways flight from Geneva landed safely at London's Heathrow Airport Sunday after being hit by what is believed to have been a drone, authorities say. The Airbus A320 was approaching the airport around 12:50pm when the pilot reported that an object had hit the front of the plane, the BBC reports. The plane was carrying 132 passengers and five crew, and authorities say the incident highlights "the very real dangers of reckless, negligent, and some times malicious use of drones." Police say no arrests have been made and they are asking anyone who finds drone parts in the area to come forward. British Airline Pilots Association spokesman Steve Landells says it had been "only a matter of time before we had a drone strike" and the group is calling for better enforcement of existing rules against flying drones near airports, the Guardian reports. Landells says drones "just have no place to be" near airports and the group has been "seeing incidents up to 8,000 feet, where drones just have no place to be, so we've got to do something." Under current rules, drones are banned from flying above 400 feet, and drone operators face up to five years in prison if they are found to be using them near an airport.

– Police found 18 mutilated, headless bodies in two vans near a lake popular with tourists in western Mexico, reports the Los Angeles Times. Police received a call alerting them to the presence of the vehicles on a dirt road near Lake Chapala, which is popular with tourists and American retirees. The area has been the scene of bloody turf battles between the Jalisco New Generation gang, allied with the Sinaloa cartel, and the Zetas drug cartel. Police believe the victims were killed by the Zetas, who are battling the Jalisco New Generation gang for control of the drug trade.

– The first domesticated dogs came from central Asia, according to the biggest-ever study of canine DNA. The study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, analyzed 185,800 genetic markers in 5,392 dogs from 38 countries, including 549 "village dogs" from 38 countries who lived alongside humans in Nepal and Mongolia 15,000 years ago. Central Asia has the highest genetic diversity of any region in the world, and the region is home to Afghanistan, Egypt, India, and Vietnam, the study found. "It mirrors what we see in humans and how they spread out of East Africa," the study's lead author, Adam Boyko of Cornell University, tells New Scientist. "Everybody wants a golden retriever," he adds. The study suggests that the first domesticated dogs came from central Asia, not Europe, where archaeological evidence suggests that dogs were first domesticated around 16,500 years ago, the lead author says. The study also found that the first domesticated dogs came from a group of indigenous dogs called village dogs, which have lived alongside humans for thousands of years. – A pizza joint in Port-au-Prince is feeding more than a thousand hungry Haitians a day, thanks in large part to the generosity of its neighbors. The owners of Muncheez, which was too expensive for most Haitians to afford, decided to cook up food instead of losing it when their ingredients spoil, NPR reports. They're now serving rice and beans, chicken, spaghetti, and anything else the owners can get their hands on. "So instead of losing the food, we said let's cook the food and give it away to people that need it," says co-owner Gilbert Bailly. "And then two days after, we were running out of diesel, running out of gas, running out of food. We had people that has businesses and started to bring food to us. And we are doing that since." Muncheez is just one of a number of makeshift soup kitchens springing up around Port-au-Prince, NPR notes.

– When Facebook employees move into a new office in Mountain View, Calif., this fall, they won't be able to get free food. That's because the city of Mountain View barred the company from subsidizing employee meals more than 50%, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. The move was made after local restaurants complained that free meals at Google, the city's largest employer, had damaged their business. "We wanted to make sure businesses that were there were successful," says a city councilman. Now, San Francisco is considering a similar ban on on-site workplace cafeterias, the Guardian reports. The move would affect new developments in the city, but would not be retroactive. "This is not a prohibition on catering or providing free food," says a restaurant trade group official. "The whole point is you get more foot traffic, restaurant and retail patrons and overall vitality in the streets. But if people are bussed in, go to work and never leave the building, the effect isn't felt." A labor union official says the move could mean the loss of well-paid jobs in nearby restaurants. "We're not convinced an outright ban makes a lot of sense," he says.

– An instructor's "poor English" is to blame for a Dutch teen's bungee jump death in Spain in 2015, the New York Times reports. According to the Telegraph, 17-year-old Vera Mol jumped from a 130-foot-high bridge in Cantabria while wearing a harness that hadn't yet been secured to the bridge. Mol plunged to her death. A Spanish appeals court this month upheld a ruling that the instructor for Aqua21 Aventura, the company that organized the bungee jump, could face criminal charges, including accidental homicide, should prosecutors decide to proceed with the case. The judge in the case says the instructor should have used the correct phrase "No jump, it's important, no jump" when speaking in English. "The use of the poor English 'no jump' could perfectly well be understood as an explicit order to jump by the victim," the Times quotes the judge as saying. The judge also says the instructor should have checked Vera's ID and made sure she was over the age of 18 before starting the jump. bungee jumping from road bridges is banned in Spain.

In an interview with CNBC, Steinhafel says that on Dec. 15, "our number one priority was ... making our environment safe and secure. By six o'clock at night, our environment was safe and secure. We eliminated the malware in the access point, we were very confident that coming into Monday guests could come to Target and shop with confidence and no risk." He defended the four-day delay, saying, "Day 2 was really about initiating the investigation work and the forensic work ... that has been ongoing. Day 3 was about preparation. We wanted to make sure our stores and our call centers could be as prepared as possible, and Day 4 was about notification." The interview comes as Target launched a PR campaign with full-page newspaper advertisements today, Reuters reports.

– Tensions at Jerusalem's Western Wall are heating up once again, this time between ultra-Orthodox Jews and liberal women worshippers. The latter group, known as Women of the Wall, has been seeking to allow them to wear prayer shawls at the sacred site, which is reserved for men. The Orthodox, who control the site, say the shawls violate their traditions. Yesterday, thousands of ultra-Orthodox protesters arrived and tried to drive the women away, Reuters reports. They threw chairs, water, and stones at the women, then stoned their buses. Two police officers were injured. The clashes came after a court ruled in the Women of the Wall's favor last month, allowing them to hold monthly prayers at the site. This time, police avoided any confrontation with the group by forming a cordon to keep them away. "I'm seeing signs of progress," one woman worshipper said. "However, the rabbis stressed there is no need to act provocatively or violently." Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has asked for a compromise to allow the Women of the Wall to hold prayers without exacerbating tensions with the ultra-Orthodox, Reuters notes.

– Albert Einstein's theory of special relativity may be kaput. Scientists at CERN, the world's largest particle physics lab, say they've clocked particles traveling faster than the speed of light—and if it's true, it would be the biggest physics discovery in 50 years, reports ScienceNOW. The discovery would wreck Einstein's theory of special relativity, which demands that nothing can travel faster than light. In fact, the result would be so revolutionary that it's sure to be met with skepticism all over the world. “I suspect that the bulk of the scientific community will not take this as a definitive result unless it can be reproduced by at least one and preferably several experiments,” says a physicist at Indiana University. CERN's press release refers to the findings as "one of the most significant scientific achievements in the last 50 years." The AP notes that the uncertainty in the measurement is 10 nanoseconds, but that's still a big number to get right.

In February, a member of Four Paws International, a charity that works with animals, found Simba the lion and Lula the bear in their cages, covered in dirt and excrement. The Confederate HL Hunley went down with the USS Housatonic off the coast of South Carolina on Feb. 17, 1864, but researchers have yet to find evidence of how the eight men aboard died, CNN reports. The sub was raised from the ocean in 2000, but the bodies of the crew—who hadn't left their stations for nearly 150 years—weren't found, and there was no damage to the hull that could be definitively traced back to the day of the sinking. To solve the mystery, researcher Rachel Lance set off explosions near a miniature replica of the Hunley, called the CSS Tiny. She found an eight-acre pond on a family-run farm in North Carolina. The farm's owner, 65-year-old Bert Pitt, tells CNN he was "a little concerned" when Lance told him she'd be using the pond. "I think people would like to know what did happen to the crew," he says. – It's official: Barbara Walters is retiring from TV journalism next summer, she announced today on The View. "Let me just say I have been on television continuously for over 50 years," Walters said. "But in the summer of '14 I plan to retire from appearing on television at all. ... I'm perfectly healthy. This is my decision. This is what I want to do." The 83-year-old will continue as a co-host of The View through the 2014 season, but will step down after the end of that season, according to the Hollywood Reporter. She'll continue to be a co-executive producer of the show, and will be involved in selecting new co-hosts to replace Joy Behar and Elisabeth Hasselbeck. Rumors of Walters' retirement first surfaced in late March, after she fell and bumped her head at the British Ambassador's residence days before the presidential inauguration; doctors later diagnosed her with chicken pox. – A woman is dead after a smoke-filled DC Metro train stopped today in a tunnel near the L'Enfant Plaza station, leaving dozens of people trapped inside, the Washington Post reports. "There was a woman who was in distress on that train, and I'm sorry to say she's passed away," Metro General Manager Richard Sarles said. The woman's cause of death and identity remain unknown.
