The changes have been in the works for a while, and Post style editor David Postman explains in a Post op-ed that they're the result of "confusion over the difference between an abbreviation and a short form." Mic is an abbreviation, never intended to be pronounced as a word. "Mic is an aberration," he writes. "Words like that aren't pronounced like that. A bicycle is a bike, not a bic. Bic, as in the pens, rhymes with Mick. So do hic and Nic and pic and Ric and sic and tic and Vic. That's how short forms work: They're intended to be pronounced, and so they're spelled phonetically. – A Southwest Airlines jet en route from Chicago to New Jersey had to make an emergency landing in Cleveland Wednesday morning after one of its windows cracked, reports the AP. There were no reports of injuries on Flight 957, which landed safely at Cleveland Hopkins International Airport at 11:20am. A Southwest spokeswoman says Flight 957 never lost cabin pressure and that the pilots didn't declare an emergency before landing Wednesday morning. There were no other mechanical problems with the plane that has been taken out of service. The emergency landing comes two weeks after a Southwest Airlines plane made an emergency landing in Philadelphia after an engine exploded and a blown out window in a deadly accident. Airline consultant Robert Mann says windows are periodically polished to remove the formation of tiny cracks in the acrylic windows from exposure to chemicals and the sun's rays. He says the pilots were right to make a quick landing. Anthony Roman, a commercial pilot and flight instructor based in New York, says problems with windows should be detected during regular inspections and maintenance.

He was treated at the veterinary college for wounds and sores on his paws, as well as cold laser therapy on his hind paws and hindquarters

– A 36-year-old Pennsylvania man has been charged with hacking into more than 100 Google and Apple accounts belonging to more than 100 celebrities, stealing nude photos and videos, NBC News reports. According to the AP, Ryan Collins of Lancaster has agreed to plead guilty to one count of gaining unauthorized access to a protected computer to obtain information. Prosecutors say Collins sent fake emails claiming to be from Apple or Google and got victims to hand over their usernames and passwords. He then used that information to get into their email accounts, swiping nude photos in some instances, and sometimes downloading full backups from Apple's iCloud. Police began investigating an apparent iCloud hack that resulted in leaked nude photos of Jennifer Lawrence and other celebrities, mostly women, in September of 2014. Collins was charged in Los Angeles with violating the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and has agreed to plead guilty to one count of unauthorized access to a protected computer to obtain information, prosecutors say. The charge carries a maximum of five years in prison, but prosecutors will recommend a sentence of 18 months. – Parents are risking their babies' health with the increasingly popular practice of swaddled babies, a surgeon warns. The technique, which involves binding a baby's arms and legs with blankets, is used to calm babies and prevent crying, the Telegraph reports. But Prof. Nicholas Clarke warns that swaddling is damaging developing hips and could lead to hip dysplasia. "In order to allow for healthy hip development, legs should be able to bend up and out at the hips," he writes in the Archives of Disease in Childhood. "The babies' legs should not be tightly wrapped in extension and pressed together." The Royal College of Midwives warns that swaddling poses "significant problems" for the baby, including overheating and increased risk of cot death. "Similar effects may be seen in all devices or maneuvers that place the legs in a purely straight position for prolonged periods in this critical age of early infancy," says another surgeon.

– Gabrielle Giffords is in critical condition after being shot in the head at close range, but doctors are optimistic about her recovery. "I am very optimistic about her recovery," said a doctor at the University Medical Center in Tucson, while acknowledging that the bullet went through her brain. In 2007, Michelle Tsai explained how one might survive a gunshot to the head for Slate. A gunshot to the head isn't always fatal; when the gun is aimed upward from the chin, the recoil can angle the muzzle toward the face. In this case, the bullet travels through the mouth and nose instead of back into the head, where the brain lies. The victim of such a wound would suffer serious injuries to the face; he might also suffocate if the bullet hit part of his nose, or if bits of flesh block the breathing pathway. But the pain isn't necessarily excruciating; survivors say it's like being punched or kicked in the face. A victim might even remain alert enough to use his hands, or, in the case of the sheriff's deputy, to reposition his gun and try again. A Starbucks customer watched as Ramineh Behbehanian, 50, removed the bottles from her Starbucks bag and placed them in the open-air fridge, police say. Employees called 911, and police tracked Behbehanian down at her home, the AP reports. Tests on the bottles revealed they had traces of OJ, a household solvent that can cause death. It's not clear why Behbehanian allegedly tried to sneak the booze into the store, but she worked for Janssen, a pharmaceutical subsidiary of Johnson & Johnson, according to her LinkedIn page.

– A colony of hundreds of thousands of wood ants has survived for years in an abandoned Soviet nuclear bunker in Poland—and they're not going anywhere, Science reports. The bunker, located near the border with Germany, was built during the Cold War to store nuclear weapons. The ants built their nest over a metal pipe, and hundreds of thousands of them fall down the pipe every year to build a new mound. The pipe rusted away, leaving the ants with no way to climb out. But they're not done: The mound keeps growing, and researchers believe it could be home to a million ants, according to Science. "The conditions in the bunker are so harsh, constantly cold, and mostly barren, that the ants seem to live in a state of near-starvation," the researchers write in the Journal of Hymenoptera. "They produce no queens, no males seem to live in a state of near-starvation, and no evidence that any of them had ever returned to the mother colony above." Researchers discovered the colony in 2013 after finding bats living inside the bunker. In a statement Sunday night, Munoz apologized "for the overbook situation" and said employees had no choice but to call authorities when the doctor refused to get off the plane. So say researchers out of Baylor, Florida State, and Louisiana State universities in a study published in the Archives of Sexual Behavior. They asked 1,656 married adults ages 57-85 about their sex lives and found that people in their first marriages were more likely to have more sex than those in their second marriages. Those in their third marriages were more likely to have more sex than those in their fourth. But when it comes to actual physical pleasure and emotional satisfaction, the order of marriage didn't seem to have an effect. "Growing old as a couple, with the experience and knowledge that come with that, may play a part," says Samuel Stroope, a former Baylor researcher now at Louisiana State. The fire didn't cause any damage to the gallery itself, but it destroyed a piece of art by the performance trio SuttonBeresCuller. The piece, "There Goes the Neighborhood," is a painting of a house that looks like a stack of Post-Intelligencer ads, complete with a giant red "I" and a giant blue "Tumbleweed." It's been sitting in the gallery's courtyard for months, unnoticed, until it was set on fire. The trio says it wasn't a performance, but an arsonist. "It is both a fascination and a disappointment, maybe inevitably. Little of the art on display has the bilious, committed power of an actual spite house (and much of it seems peculiarly impersonally motivated) or the ability to compete with an odd and unexpected intervention: nature's own fury," writes Will Owen in a new chapbook. Protesters gathered in Cairo's Tahrir Square, where they were met by thousands of police, who fired tear gas and rubber bullets as they tried to stop them from reaching the presidential palace. Police also used tear gas on protesters who tried to remove metal barriers outside the state television building. In Suez, security forces opened fire on protesters after they threw petrol bombs and firecrackers at them, according to witnesses. One member of the security forces was killed and at least four others were injured, Reuters reports. In Port Said, protesters attacked a state-owned building and set it on fire. – An Air Force pilot was killed when his plane crashed during a training mission near Nellis Air Force Base in Nevada on Tuesday, the Air Force says. Lt. Col. Eric Schultz was flying the aircraft when it went down on the Nevada Test and Training Range about 100 miles northwest of Nellis, the Las Vegas Review-Journal reports. It's not clear whether Schultz was killed in the crash or at the crash site. On Wednesday, two fighter jets crashed at the Nevada Test and Training Range during a routine training mission, but both pilots ejected safely. They were released with survivable injuries. It's not clear why the planes flew the day after the fatal crash.

Police say 55-year-old Stephen Pasceri, who was found dead in an examination room with an apparently self-inflicted gunshot wound, "had some issue" with his mother's medical treatment at the hospital and targeted Davidson because "there was a particular reason he targeted this doctor," Boston Police Commissioner William Evans says. Police say Pasceri walked into the hospital Tuesday morning and asked to speak with Davidson, who had treated Pasceri's mother, MyFox Boston reports. Police say Pasceri fired two shots at Davidson, who was rushed to the emergency room and underwent surgery. Police found a gun near Pasceri's body that they believe he used in the shooting. "Dr. Davidson was a wonderful and inspiring cardiac surgeon who devoted his career to saving lives and improving the quality of life of every patient he cared for," the hospital's president says in a statement. "It is truly devastating that his own life was taken in this horrible manner." Police haven't speculated about a motive.

– A new study out of Switzerland suggests that terminally ill cancer patients who took LSD as part of talk therapy may be able to deal with their fears of death in a more effective way than chemo. The small study, published in the Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease, involved 30 patients who went on supervised "trips" over two months in which they experienced a "mystical experience" with "pure distress at all the memories I had successfully forgotten for decades," one participant tells the New York Times. A year later, those who took 200 micrograms of LSD per session saw a 20% improvement in their anxiety levels, compared to those who took a lower dose. The researchers aren't ready to declare LSD effective, but the fact that the study took place at all bodes well for future research. "We want to break these substances out of the mold of the counterculture and bring them back to the lab as part of a psychedelic renaissance," says the executive director of the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies, which has funded many of these studies.

The two-sided cards have 15 bullet points, some of which tell the reader to keep his or her emotions in check with police, such as "Don't bad mouth police" and "Answer all questions pertaining to your identity," reports Cleveland.com. Other advice on the card includes "Stay in the driver's seat with both hands in sight on the steering wheel" and " obey the law just like we do." The idea for the cards came from a meeting of an anti-violence youth group called Akron PeaceMakers, which raised $1,500 to print 50,000 of the cards, reports NPR. The group's president says the cards will be looked back on by students when they're done with police encounters. "When they get put in the situation, they're going to look back at that card and be like, 'Wow. You know, that helped when I actually read that,'" she says.

Brooks tells CNN that Capitol Police contacted him after the shooting and told him his name and office number were on the list. Hodgkinson, who was pro-Bernie Sanders and anti-Republican, maintained a social media presence that was pro-Bernie Sanders and anti-Republican, according to the FBI, which is investigating his motive.

– Pregnant women's lungs are already considered to be some of the most polluted in the world, and now scientists say they've found evidence of air pollution entering pregnant women's placentas and possibly reaching their fetuses, the Guardian reports. "It is a worrying problem—there is a massive association between air pollution a mother breathes in and the effect it has on the fetus," says researcher Lisa Miyashita. "It is always good if possible to take less polluted routes if you are pregnant—or indeed if you are not pregnant. I avoid busy roads when I walk to the station." Miyashita and her team at Queen Mary University of London found 72 black sooty particles in the placentas of five pregnant women in London, England, who all gave birth to healthy babies. "We do not know whether the particles we found could also move across into the fetus, but our evidence suggests this is indeed possible," researcher Norrice Liu says in a press release. "We also know that the particles do not need to get into the baby's body to have an adverse effect, because if they have an effect on the placenta, this will have a direct impact on the fetus." The research was presented Sunday at the European Respiratory Society's international congress in Paris

Daniel Ellsberg, who worked on the report and later provided it to the Times as part of an effort to stop the war, says he's stumped. "Of course, I don’t know what they are," he tells the paper. "I couldn’t begin to guess where those words came from." Gelb guesses they might have come from sections on peace negotiations, which were left out of the first versions of the report that were leaked. Click for more on the mystery.

– The new official presidential portrait of George W. Bush was unveiled at a White House ceremony yesterday, but the story behind one of the paintings is a little more complicated than you might think. As Slate explains, Bush loved to regale visitors with what he thought was the story behind "A Charge to Keep," a painting of Methodism circuit riders that he kept by his desk and named his 1999 autobiography "A Charge to Keep." But as Slate points out, that story "is not the title, message, or meaning of the painting." In fact, it's a "very similar-looking but different Koerner composition, also depicting a man working his way up a hill on a horse." A University of Illinois professor points out that an illustration in the Saturday Evening Post that ran with the horse thief story "The Slipper Tongue" is actually a very similar-looking but different Koerner composition, also depicting a man working his way up a hill on a horse. Both professor Cara Finnegan and Slate's Jacob Weisberg point out that the painting is not about Methodist missionaries, but about a son's fight to keep his land, inherited from his father, from "rapacious timber barons."

– Tiger Woods shot a 77 in the first round of the PGA Championship today, his worst score in a major as a professional, ESPN reports. "I'm not down, I'm just very angry right now," Woods said. "I thought I could play by feel, see the shot, hit the shot. I'm not at that point yet." The 77 is his highest score in a major as a professional, and his worst in any tournament since he shot 79 at the Australian Open in 1996. "Got off to a great start today, was having mechanical thoughts through those holes ... and I thought, 'I can let it go,' and play by instinct and feel," Woods said. He had the dolls recite familiar verses, like "Hickory Dickory Dock," but " Edison himself thought they were unpleasant," says Jerry Fabris, who curates sound recordings at the Thomas Edison National Historical Park. While the parents of 22-year-old Otto Warmbier and President Trump have accused the North Korean government of torturing him, Dr. Lakshmi Sammarco said evidence has led to no "scientific facts" to solve Warmbier's mysterious death, the AP reports. "We don't know what happened to him, and this is the bottom line," she said. A coroner's report dated Sept. 11 shows the cause of death for the University of Virginia student as complications from brain-damaging oxygen deprivation through "an unknown insult more than a year prior to death." The medical term for his condition was called "chronic adamagingic/ischemic encephalopathy." The manner of death was listed as "undetermined." While Warmbier's family declined an autopsy, Sammarco said her office used extensive medical scanning and imaging for a "virtual autopsy" and that nothing more would have been gained by doing an autopsy so long after his brain damage occurred. The museum commissioned a 2013 report from the Smithsonian National Museum of American History and Chicago History Museum that found insufficient documentation to say whether Lincoln had ever owned the hat. – Richard Grenell, Mitt Romney's newly hired foreign policy adviser and openly gay spokesman, has resigned, CNN reports. "While I welcomed the challenge to confront President Obama’s foreign policy failures and weak leadership on the world stage, my ability to speak clearly and forcefully on the issues has been greatly diminished by the hyper-partisan discussion of personal issues that sometimes comes from a presidential campaign," Grenell said in a statement. "I want to thank Governor Romney for his belief in me and my abilities and his clear message to me that being openly gay was a non-issue for him and his team." Grenell's resignation comes after a two-week controversy over his appointment, during which the Romney campaign did not put Grenell out to comment on national security matters and did not use him on a press foreign policy conference call. Grenell's sexual orientation was also the subject of controversy on his Twitter account, where Grenell had insulted Rachel Maddow, Hillary Clinton, and Newt Gingrich. The Romney campaign said it was "disappointed that Ric decided to resign from the campaign for his own personal reasons. We wanted him to stay because he had superior qualifications for the position he was hired to fill."

– The giraffe is on the brink of extinction, according to the latest update to the International Union for the Conservation of Nature's (IUCN) Red List of threatened species. In 1985, there were 155,000 giraffes living in Africa. In 2015, there were 97,000, reports the BBC. "While there have been great concern about elephants and rhinos, giraffes have gone under the radar," says Dr. Julian Fennessy, who co-chairs the giraffe specialist group at IUCN. "Unfortunately, their numbers have been plummeting, and this is something that we were a little shocked about, that they have declined by so much in so little time." Fennessy says giraffes are "war fodder" in war-torn countries like Somalia, Ethiopia, and Kenya, where giraffes are hunted as "war fodder" and "extremely curious" that can feed a lot of people. The population of giraffes in southern Africa is increasing "two to three times over the last three decades," says Fennessy, but populations in East Africa "have plummeted some by up to 95% of the population in the last three decades alone." "I'm so tired of erroneous sh*tstorms," she writes. "# MeToo is about survivors and their experiences, that cannot be taken away. I'm proud of us. Onwards." The actress, who has been among the first to speak out against sexual misconduct in Hollywood, says it has been "one of the hardest years of my life," the Guardian reports. – Researchers say they've found a way to boost the libido of men who suffer from low sex drives: exposure to bright light. Reporting in the journal Frontiers in Psychiatry, researchers from the University of Siena in Italy say that men who were exposed to a light box of at least 10 times the intensity of a normal household light for half an hour in the morning saw their sexual satisfaction scores triple, while those who received a less intense light box saw their scores stay the same. "The use of the light box really mimics what nature does," says lead researcher Andrea Fagiolini, per the BBC. "In the northern hemisphere, the body's testosterone production naturally declines from November through April and then rises steadily through the spring and summer with a peak in October," he says. "You see the effect of this in reproductive rates, with the month of June showing the highest rate of conception." He adds that testosterone levels increased in men who had been exposed to the bright light, which he thinks inhibited the pineal gland in the center of the brain, which allows more testosterone to be produced. The researchers say that while more research is needed before the light-box treatment can be recommended as a treatment for men suffering from low sex drives, they believe it could be used

– A missing statue of the Virgin Mary stolen from a Vermont nativity scene more than two years ago has been found unharmed and returned to its owner, the AP reports. The statue was stolen from Lyndonville in January 2016 and it was recently discovered in an apartment house storage area by Lyndonville Police Chief Jack Harris acting on a tip. It was returned to the Lyndon Ecumenical Council. The Caledonian Record reports Municipal Administrator Justin Smith recognized the missing statue in photos of the building's interior taken by the town health officer during an inspection. Police say mostly college students live in the building and it will be impossible to determine how it got there. A statue of the baby Jesus that was stolen at the same time remains missing.

– When Lauren Bacall died last week at the age of 89, she left behind an estate worth an estimated $26.6 million—and one thing in particular she wanted to make sure of was her beloved Papillon Sophie. The New York Daily News reports that the actress specified in her 2013 will that her son, actor Sam Robards, would care for the dog and set aside $10,000 for its care. "I was always a dog yearner," Bacall once told Glenn Close, according to Yahoo. "I didn't have a dog growing up in the city with a working mother. As an only child, I yearned for someone to talk to. When I was 16, we got a champagne-colored Cocker Spaniel and named him Droopy. From the first moment, [Droopy] was very possessive of me. All my dogs have been possessive of me." The rest of Bacall's estate, which includes her Upper West Side apartment, is to be split between her three children, Stephen Bogart, Leslie Bogart, and Robards. She also left $250,000 to each of her six grandsons, as well as $15,000 to two of her employees, according to papers filed Friday in Manhattan Surrogate's Court.

– bars and restaurants aren't the "ugly stepchildren of the modern urban economy"—they're "its greatest strength," and cities need to recognize that when they allow them, they should think about the overall benefits to the region, not the particular complaints of nearby neighbors. That's the message from Matthew Yglesias at Slate, who writes about a recent battle in Washington, DC, over whether to allow new liquor licenses to be issued on Logan Circle and U Street. NIMBYs (not in favor of bars and restaurants) were outnumbered at a listening session by a group called In My Backyard—D.C., which argued for growth-friendly policies. "The good news for cities is that Amazon has been crushing the big-box sector, and e-commerce levels the shopping playing field between traditional urban neighborhoods and suburban ones," Yglesias writes. "And those smallish and idiosyncratic structures are ideal spaces for bars and restaurants—much better than personality-free malls." In short, bars and restaurants "should be a key economic development priority for cities." Click for his full column.

– "Act now to preserve your life." That's the message from the National Weather Service regarding mandatory evacuations in North Carolina's McDowell County due to a landslide at the Lake Tahoma Dam, NBC News reports. The evacuations were ordered at 1am Wednesday after an engineer determined the landslide had compromised the dam's integrity. "This is causing significant and life-threatening flooding countywide," the National Weather Service tweeted. The National Weather Service added flooding "has reached levels not seen since the September 2004 floods associated with Hurricanes Frances and Ivan." The North Carolina Department of Transportation says two of its workers were swept away in a mudslide Tuesday while trying to clear debris from a previous mudslide, but they were able to stand on a truck that had fallen into the Catawba River until they were rescued, WCNC reports. North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper declared a state of emergency for McDowell County on Wednesday. The North Carolina Department of Transportation says I-40 is now closed from Asheville to the Virginia border due to high water.

– John Boehner's response to President Obama's request to address a joint session of Congress on Sept. 8—and the subsequent White House response to Boehner's response—is shaping up to be a nasty one. The Hill reports that Boehner wrote to the president yesterday, noting that the House isn't scheduled to reconvene until 6:30pm that night. "With the significant amount of time—typically more than three hours—that is required to allow for a security sweep of the House Chamber before receiving a president, it is my recommendation that your address be held on the following evening, when we can ensure there will be no parliamentary or logistical impediments that might detract from your remarks," Boehner wrote. The White House, which was apparently surprised by Boehner's move, said last night that the president had agreed to the later date. The RNC, however, called it a " thinly-veiled political ploy" and accused the White House of ignoring "decades, if not centuries" of protocol on such events.

– The NYPD has taken a 54-year-old Manhattan man into custody in connection with a string of fake bombs left around Staten Island. The suspect is believed to be the jealous ex-lover of a 32-year-old woman who recently married her new boyfriend, the New York Daily News reports. Three devices were left around the borough beginning on Sept. 2, one of them containing propane cylinders taped to a bottle of gasoline and the other two containing nails and screws. The devices had threatening notes in Spanish attached, and police fear they could have exploded if they had been rigged properly. The suspect was taken in for questioning at his job in Manhattan. No charges have been filed yet.

– The parents of a Connecticut teenager who killed himself on the first day of his sophomore year in 2013 are suing the town and the school district, accusing them of failing to protect him from years of bullying, NBC Connecticut reports. Bart Palosz's parents, Anna Izabela Palosz and Franciszek Palosz, are seeking $15,000 in damages. They say their son was "subjected to a years-long history of unremitting bullying" at both his middle school and high school, and that school administrators, teachers, and counselors knew about the bullying but "failed to comply" with the district's anti-bullying policy, which requires them to provide emotional support, intervene in and investigate bullying cases, contact the parents of bullying victims, and discipline bullies. According to the complaint, Palosz was kicked and hit on the back of the neck, had his pencil stolen and thrown at him, and had his smartphone smashed, NBC Connecticut reports. He also stopped turning in his homework and his grades plummeted, the complaint alleges. The lawsuit states that school officials knew he was "very socially akward" and "annoyed" but "didn't tell anyone, needs to be connected, wants to be liked." The lawsuit states that the town's

– Thomas Piketty's book Capital in the 21st Century has been called "the most important economics book of the year" and "maybe of the decade"—but the French economist has turned down France's Legion of Honor, the country's highest award. Piketty says he refused the honor because he doesn't think it's the government's job to decide who is honorable, the BBC reports. "They would do better to concentrate on reviving (economic) growth in France and Europe," he says. Piketty, who was once close to the Socialist Party but has since distanced himself from the policies of President Francois Hollande, is the latest in a long line of French thinkers to turn down the award, the Wall Street Journal notes. Last year, cartoonist Jacques Tardi turned down the award, which is given to those "who have made an enormous contribution to French culture and society."

– Glen James, a homeless man in Boston, turned in a backpack last weekend that contained $42,000 in cash and traveler's checks—and police tracked down the owner. Now, Ethan Whittington, a 27-year-old marketing manager in Virginia, is so moved by James' honesty that he started a crowdfunding website to raise money for James to buy a house, the BBC reports. "The fact that he's in the situation he is, being homeless, it blew my mind that he would do this," Whittington says. "It's brought me a lot of hope. This isn't only about rewarding a great guy. I think it's a statement to everyone in America." James, a former Boston courthouse employee, says he would not have kept "even a penny" of the money he had found in the backpack—even if he were desperate. Police honored him with a special citation Monday.

– Google is now accepting applications to try on Google Glass. Previously, only software developers who signed up for the glasses at Google's developer's conference were allowed to try them, the Los Angeles Times reports. Now anyone can get a pair, provided they can come up with 50 words or fewer about what they'd like to do with them. "We’re looking for bold, creative individuals who want to join us and be a part of shaping the future of Glass," the company posted on Google Plus. Those who win will get a pair of the glasses, along with the chance to buy them along with developers when they become available, for $1,500 plus tax. To apply, applicants must post a photo or video on Google Plus or Twitter of 50 words or fewer with the hashtag #ifihadglass.

"I think death would probably be merciful," Ross Cassidy tells Sky News. Cassidy, 61, met Skripal, 66, and his family when they lived next door to him in Salisbury in 2010. "We became great pals and I introduced Sergei to a lot of things, including English beer and he introduced me to vodka," he says. "I can't say I approve of treachery, but that was none of my business." Skripal and his daughter Yulia, 33, are in critical condition after being exposed to the Russian nerve agent novichok. Cassidy—who has been interviewed by police investigating the attack—says he doesn't think he will ever see the Skripals again. "I started thinking, 'Hang on a minute, Sergei and Yulia are in hospital and are probably going to die, and I actually felt guilty that I hadn't thought more about that,'" he says. – "If that person hadn't made that call, we'd be having a much different conversation right now," says Indiana State Police Supt. Doug Carter of the 911 call made Thursday by a mother that may have saved lives. The call came from Mary York, the mother of 14-year-old Brandon Clegg, who police say brought a gun to Dennis Intermediate School in Richmond and exchanged fire with officers before killing himself, the Indianapolis Star reports. York called 911 at 8:11am after her son had taken another family member hostage and forced them to drive to the school. Police say they were able to lock down the school and that because of the call, "the school was able to follow procedure to help protect students." Dozens of people turned out for a candlelight vigil Sunday to support York, reports WTHR. "She's a human. She's a mother. She lost her child," said vigil organizer Shawn Wright. "We wanted to bring her to let her know that she is supported too because at the end of the day she did a lot. She saved a lot of lives." The school remains closed Monday. Clegg was not a student at the school, but lived in the area, reports WTHR. His cousin says he was bullied and

– The annual Values Voter Summit is in the books, with Herman Cain emerging victorious in the presidential straw poll with 37% of the votes, reports the Washington Post. Rick Perry came in second with 15%, and Mitt Romney finished third with 4.4%. Michele Bachmann and Rick Santorum tied for fourth with 7.9%, and Newt Gingrich and Jon Huntsman finished fifth and sixth with 0.7% and 0.1%, respectively. The summit is seen as a test of Cain's viability among religious conservatives, and the results were no surprise. “The rule about straw polls: They only matter if someone’s trying to win,” writes David Weigel. “In 2010, Rep. Mike Pence made an effort to take the straw poll, and he won it. And then he decided not to run for president.”

– Oliver Stone is making a movie about Edward Snowden. The director will write and direct The Snowden Files: The Inside Story of the World's Most Wanted Man, a film based on Luke Harding's book, reports the Guardian. "This is one of the greatest stories of our time," Stone said in a statement. "A real challenge." Stone has started to write the screenplay and is fast-tracking the film as a European co-production to start filming before the end of the year. "To me, Snowden is a hero because he revealed secrets that we should all know, that the United States has repeatedly violated the Fourth Amendment," Stone said in a press conference at the Karlovy Vary Film Festival in the Czech Republic. Sony Pictures last month purchased the big-screen rights to Glenn Greenwald's No Place to Hide: Edward Snowden, the NSA, and the US Surveillance State. The film is being produced by James Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. Stone has advocated for the former NSA contract systems analyst, who is living in Russia on a temporary grant of asylum after leaking massive amounts of NSA documents to the media. "This is one of the greatest stories of our time," Stone said in a statement. "A real challenge."

– Remember when Charlie Sheen said the collapse of the World Trade Center looked like a "controlled demolition"? Well, 9/11 conspiracy theorists aren't too happy about it. "Charlie should be asking hard questions about what happened on 9/11 and the resulting wars ... not bragging about smoking crack and sleeping with hookers," a member of the 9/11 Truth Movement tells the New York Post. If Sheen doesn't address the issue soon, the theorists say they'll protest in front of his upcoming shows.

– Puerto Rico on Friday reported its first death from a paralysis condition that developed from a Zika infection as the US territory fights an epidemic of the mosquito-borne virus, the AP reports. The victim was a man between 35 and 45 years old from the San Juan metro area who died from Guillain-Barre, according to state epidemiologist Brenda Rivera. The condition can cause temporary paralysis and in rare instances, death. Rivera noted that it's unusual for the victim to be so young. "What does this tell us? That all of us are susceptible," Rivera said. The US territory has a total of 13,186 confirmed Zika cases, with 34 cases of Guillain-Barre. The number of Zika cases is believed to be much higher because eight of 10 people have no symptoms and many do not go to the doctor. Those infected include 1,106 pregnant women, which is a concern because Zika has been linked to severe birth defects. "We are not going to see the effects of Zika today," Rivera said. "We are going to see them in the next couple of months, in the next several years." – If you work in Washington state, you're in luck: The state's minimum wage is going up 15 cents an hour starting today, making it the highest in the nation. Nine other states are also raising their minimum wage today, and NPR reports that nearly a million workers will benefit. Idaho is the only state that won't be raising its minimum wage, but it's still the lowest in the nation at $7.25 an hour. "It's not much, but it's something," says a 16-year-old high school student who works at a cafe in Olympia. "Every bit helps." Rhode Island, meanwhile, is the first state in five years to raise its minimum wage, to $7.75.

– The Harry Potter creator has a message for the world: No more orphanages. In an op-ed for the Guardian, Daniel Radcliffe calls for an end to "the unjustifiable incarceration of 8 million children around this world." He says he first came across such institutions as a 6-year-old boy locked in a cage in a newspaper 20 years ago. "The sad truth remains that my instinctive reaction to that picture could stand as a metaphor for the attitude that has enabled the unjustifiable incarceration of 8 million children around this world to take place with little outrage or comment," he writes. "The idea of any child being taken from their family and locked away, all too often in atrocious conditions, is particularly poignant at this time of year," he writes. "For children in institutions, life too often resembles the darkest of Grimms' fairytales." Radcliffe is the founder of Lumos, a charity that aims to close such institutions. He says most of the children in such institutions aren't orphans, but are separated from their families because of poverty, disability, or discrimination. – Online dating is a billion-dollar industry, and some 20 million Americans use it each year, the New York Times reports. But it's also rife with criminals, identity thieves, sexual predators, and even felons. So now some companies are offering to run background checks on potential dates—for a small fee. MyMatchChecker.com, for instance, offers a basic search for $9.95, which can be used with any of the nation's 1,500 dating sites. The founder of MyMatchChecker, a retired New York State Police captain and former police chief, says they want to "provide some degree of safety." But most online dating companies question whether such checks can be effective. They contend that because state and county databases are incomplete, the checks give daters a false sense of security. Even advocates of criminal screenings concede that they are imperfect. "You’re talking pennies per check," says the president of True.com, one of the first major dating sites to offer background checks.

– Aretha Franklin wanted Halle Berry to play her in a biopic, but Berry said she couldn't sing and wouldn't do the role, E! reports. Instead, Jennifer Hudson played the Queen of Soul in the film, which is in the early stages of production. A man in a barbershop in Suffolk, Va., was shot Thursday morning after an argument about the casting choice, WTKR reports. According to the Virginian-Pilot, 44-year-old Michael Jermell Hatton was treated at a local hospital for his injuries and released, then taken to the Western Tidewater Regional Jail, where he's being held without bond. The shooting victim, 47-year-old Tony Jonathan Lundy, is in critical condition.

– A 77-year-old Texas woman died from a flesh-eating bacteria after she fell into floodwaters during Hurricane Harvey, the Houston Chronicle reports. According to KTRK, Nancy Reed fell into the floodwaters at her son's home in Kingwood, broke her arm, and was treated at a hospital before dying there on Sept. 15. The Harris County Institute of Forensic Sciences determined Reed died from necrotizing fasciitis, which spreads quickly through muscle tissue and can cause organ failure. Reed is the county's 36th death to be officially linked to Hurricane Harvey and its aftermath, which contributed to more than 75 deaths statewide. Reed was the second known case of the bacteria related to the floodwaters. Rescuer JR Atkins survived after he was infected by an insect bite while helping flood victims in Missouri City. "It's tragic," says Missouri City's director of emergency medical services. "This is one of the things we'd been worrying about once the flooding began, that something like this might occur. My heart goes out to the family." The infection is not considered a reportable disease in Texas, meaning doctors or laboratories who diagnose it aren't required to alert health authorities. – Ukraine is mobilizing its troops, a government official tells CNN, after Vladimir Putin asked Russia's parliament for permission to use military force in the country. The move comes after Russia's parliament approved Putin's request to use military force in Ukraine, the New York Times reports. Ukraine's ambassador to the UN says Russia now has 15,000 troops in Crimea, and their number is "increasing every hour," according to CNN. In a phone call with Putin yesterday, President Obama warned that Russia's "continued violation of Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity would negatively impact Russia's standing in the international community," according to a statement released by the White House. Meanwhile, pro-Russian forces continue to patrol key infrastructure sites in Crimea.

– A 13-year-old California boy says he was just trying to have a good time at school—but his classmates at Ethan Chase Middle School in Menifee weren't having it. After school on Thursday, Austin Lacey was ordered to take off his Elsa costume, which he had been wearing as part of the school's Disney-themed spirit day, reports KTLA. "I wore it for fun because I'm just one of those people, I like to go all out," Austin tells KTLA. But the school said it was causing a disruption and asked him to pose for selfies with other students. "It wasn't a disruption," one student tells the Riverside Press-Enterprise. "Everybody was taking pictures with him. Nobody had a problem with it." Superintendent Julie Vitale issued a statement saying that "at no time was there an indication that the student was expressing any particular message. The Principal's action was based upon the need to stop a general disruption to the school environment." She says Austin won't be disciplined, and the incident "was based upon the need to stop a general disruption." – A 40-foot-deep sinkhole opened up beneath the National Corvette Museum in Bowling Green, Kentucky, yesterday, swallowing eight prized sports cars. Now the museum has posted videos of the hole opening up, the cars being sucked down, and what it looks like inside the pit, reports the Bowling Green Daily News. It's not clear when the cars will be removed from the hole, and engineers need to make sure it's safe to work inside the pit before repairs can be made to that wing of the museum.

As part of a plan to reduce waste and save energy, the city of Paris began selling thousands of tons of cobblestones earlier this year, and Sainte-Lage's company, Mon Pavé Parisien, now offers three styles: a classic hand-painted in the colors of France's flag, one gilded in 22.5 carats of gold, and the May 68 series, whose bottom half is sheathed in sand and features the inscription "sous les pavés," a popular phrase used during the protests of the May 1968 revolution. "Each one is a real piece of the city you can take home, a real piece of history," Sainte-Lage tells Bloomberg. She has already personalized one for Paris' mayor, with the number 75, and another for a Chinese bride and groom, painting their names side by side on the rock's surface. – The 25-year-old woman accused of driving her car into a crowd of people at an Oklahoma State University homecoming parade Saturday, killing four and injuring dozens more, has been charged with four counts of second-degree murder, CNN reports. If convicted, Adacia Chambers could face life in prison. Chambers was arrested on suspicion of DUI after the crash, but her lawyer says she was not drunk and suffers from mental illness, KFOR reports. He says she was out with her grandmother and aunt the night of the parade and had no alcohol or drugs in her system. "I was not satisfied that I was communicating with a competent person," he says. "Miss Chambers suffers from mental illness, as to what type has yet to be determined." He says he will ask for a psychiatric evaluation and a competency hearing.

He's referring, of course, to Rush Limbaugh calling a Georgetown law student a "slut" on his radio show, and of course, Robert De Niro joking that Michelle Obama might not be ready for a "white first lady." "When did we get it in our heads that we have the right to never hear anything we don’t like?" asks Maher. "We’ve been shocked and appalled by the unbelievable insensitivity of Nike shoes, the Fighting Sioux, Hank Williams Jr., Cee Lo Green, Ashton Kutcher, Tracy Morgan, Don Imus, Kirk Cameron, Gilbert Gottfried, the Super Bowl halftime show, and the ESPN guys who used the wrong cliché for Jeremy Lin after everyone else used all the others." – A $25 million settlement for students of Trump University who say they were defrauded by the now-defunct school has been approved by a federal appeals court. The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco finalized the settlement after it was first approved by a judge last March, NBC News reports. The court rejected a challenge from Sherri Simpson, a Florida bankruptcy lawyer who said she paid $19,000 for classes and a mentorship program at the now-defunct school, Politico reports. Simpson argued that she should be allowed to opt out of the class-action suits and pursue a separate suit against Trump, but the appeals court panel disagreed. "Reading the notice as a whole and in context, we conclude that it promised only one opportunity to opt out," Judge Jacqueline Nguyen wrote in a 21-page opinion. "The correct inquiry here is what an average class member would have understood the notice to guarantee ... and the actions of the class members in this case bolster our conclusion that a reasonable reading of the notice precludes Simpson's interpretation." The court said that plaintiffs are expected to receive 80% to 90% of what they paid for Trump University programs. New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman praised the settlement, saying it "opened the door for student victims to finally obtain the restitution they deserve."

– Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder's chief of staff has apologized for the state's lead-tainted water crisis in Flint, saying he was "truly sorry" for what happened. Dan Wyant, Snyder's chief of staff, said in a statement Saturday that he is "sorry and deeply sorry" for the situation in the city, where the water supply has been contaminated with lead for nearly two years, the Detroit Free Press reports. "I am also deeply sorry for the negative press this has caused the city of Flint," Wyant said in the statement. "I apologize to the residents of Flint for the mistakes that have been made and I ask that the people of Flint know that I am deeply sorry for what has happened." Snyder, who declared a state of emergency last week, has been criticized by both sides of the political aisle for his handling of the crisis. Democratic presidential candidate Bernie Sanders called for Snyder's resignation Saturday, the AP reports. "There are no excuses," he said. "The governor long ago knew about the lead in Flint's water. He did nothing. As a result, hundreds of children were poisoned. Thousands may have been exposed to potential brain damage from lead. Gov. Snyder should resign." (Snyder

– If you've ever wanted to know what it was like to fight in World War II, you're in luck: The Pentagon has released a detailed timeline of the conflict based on data from the Wikidata project, the Telegraph reports. The timeline, which can be viewed here, shows how long it took the US to defeat Nazi Germany in the war's second Boer War, as well as how long it took Allied forces to do the same in the Battle of Thermopylae. It also shows how long it took the Japanese to defeat the Nazis in the Battle of Okinawa in WWII, and how long it took the Japanese to defeat the Nazis in the Battle of Passchendaele in World War I.

– It's one of the best times of year to look up at the sky. Jupiter is currently rising in the east as the sun is setting below the western horizon, and astronomers call it an opposition of Jupiter. It's the middle of the best time of year to see a planet because it's when the planet is up all night and generally closest for the year, reports Universe Today. Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system and is the very bright planet it is. It shines more brightly than any star in the evening sky. Only Venus, the brightest planet in our solar system, outshines Jupiter. The next Jupiter opposition, in 2019, is scheduled for June 10.

– More than a quarter-million people have signed a petition calling for Donald Trump to be banned from entering the UK, CNN reports. "The UK has banned entry to many individuals for hate speech," the petition reads. "This same principle should apply to Donald J. Trump. We cannot see how the United Kingdom can condone his entry to the country when many people have been barred for less." The petition was created by Suzanne Kelly, a Scottish woman who has campaigned against Trump's political and business activities. "If the United Kingdom is to continue applying the 'unacceptable behavior' criteria to those who wish to enter its borders, it must be fairly applied to the rich as well as poor, and the weak as well as powerful," the petition states. Kelly's petition was created on the British government's official petitions website in response to Trump's call for a ban on Muslims entering the US. According to the Independent, the petition is being reviewed by Parliament's petitions committee. If the petition gets more than 100,000 signatures, it will be considered for debate in Parliament. – The head of the Senate Criminal Justice Committee in Texas has written to the head of the state's Department of Criminal Justice to express his outrage over the "privilege" given to convicted murderer Lawrence Russell Brewer, the Houston Chronicle reports. Brewer, who was executed this week for the racially motivated murder of a black man in Texas in 2002, asked for a variety of last-minute meals, including two chicken fried steaks, a triple-meat bacon cheeseburger, fried okra, a pound of barbecue, three fajitas, a meat lover's pizza, a pint of ice cream, and a slab of peanut butter fudge with crushed peanuts. Prison officials say Brewer didn't eat any of it. "It is extremely inappropriate to give a person sentenced to death such a privilege," Sen. John Whitmire wrote in a letter yesterday to Brad Livingston, the executive director of the Texas Department of Criminal Justice. "I urge you to immediately cease this practice." The head of the Texas Board of Pardons and Paroles, meanwhile, says the board has no plans to change its policy, which allows inmates on death row in Texas to choose their meals, the AP reports. (Last week, the nation's most active executioner was put to death.)

– A group of 3,000 file-sharers in Sweden has won the right to be called the Church of Kopimism. The church believes that sharing and communication are sacred, and that it's wrong to monitor and eavesdrop on people, Wired reports. The group has been trying to gain official recognition since 2010, and had its request denied several times before being approved as an official religion by the Swedish authorities. "Our main ritual is the act of copying and connecting with each other by sharing information," says founder Isak Gerson. "Just being recognized by the state of Sweden will help strengthen our identity." The new religious status doesn't make file-sharing legal in Sweden, but Gerson hopes it will be considered in future legislation. "I hope in the name of Kopimi that this will change," he tells TorrentFreak.

– Eric Swenson, a skateboarding icon and co-founder of San Francisco-based Thrasher magazine, killed himself in front of a police station Monday morning. The 64-year-old shot himself in front of the Mission Police Station with a high-caliber handgun, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. "The offering documents did not correctly describe the mortgage loans," Judge Denise Cote wrote in her ruling. "The magnitude of falsity, conservatively measured, is enormous." She ordered the Federal Housing Finance Agency, which filed the case, to propose how much the banks should pay. "Nomura is confident that it was consistently candid, transparent, and professional in all of its dealings with Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac," a spokesman for the bank said in a statement. "Nomura will appeal."

Kimberly Pappas was charged with first-degree murder in April after the baby boy was found dead in a plastic bag at her desk at CEVA Logistics in Redford on March 31. Pappas told first responders she had a miscarriage, but an autopsy found the baby died of asphyxiation and the death was a homicide. The judge ruled Monday the case is "very difficult," the AP reports. Pappas' sister says Pappas texted her about an hour before work to ask if she was pregnant. She says Pappas asked her to bring a change of clothes to the bathroom where she gave birth, and her sister handed it to her underneath the door. Pappas allegedly cut the umbilical cord with cuticle scissors before hiding the baby, a detective told a reporter at the Free Press. Pappas told officials she had a miscarriage, but an autopsy revealed the baby's death to be a homicide and found that the child lived 20 to 30 minutes before dying of suffocation. She was found mentally competent to stand trial in July.

– A great white shark has been caught on camera for the first time off the coast of North Carolina, the Charlotte Observer reports. According to the Atlantic, the 9-foot, 1,400-pound shark was tagged by researchers with the OCEARCH organization in August. It was caught by a camera mounted on the back of a research vessel called the St. Mary's Dolphin. The video shows the shark surfacing just off the coast of Wilmington, NC. It was filmed by the St. Mary's Dolphin's crew using a high-definition camera. "It's the first time we've ever seen a great white with a camera mounted on board," a St. Mary's Dolphin spokesperson tells the Observer. "It's also the first time we've ever seen a great white with a camera mounted on board off the coast of North Carolina." Researchers hope to use the footage to learn more about sharks and their habitat. They're currently searching for a great white in the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of Florida.

Archaeologists from the University of Reading made the discovery while excavating Wilsford henge in the Vale of Pewsey. The body was found in a foetal position and wearing an amber necklace. "Scientific analysis will provide information on the gender of the child, diet, pathologies, and date of burial," says Reading University archaeologist Dr. Jim Leary. "It may also shed light on where this young individual had lived." Marden Henge was once one of the biggest and most impressive henges in Britain, the Guardian reports. "Avebury had the huge ditches, Stonehenge upped the ante with the massive trilothons, Marden had this enormous enclosure," says Leary. "It could well be that this was really where it was at in the Neolithic." Archaeologists have already found pieces of flint tools from 4,300 years ago dropped on the floor of a house as old as Stonehenge. The study looked at 162 countries and found that more than one in 10 newborns die from complications related to premature births—including pneumonia, diarrhea, measles, HIV, and tetanus—every day. In the US, 8,100 children under the age of 5 died from complications related to premature births last year. The US ranks 141st out of 162 countries on the list. – Ikea is recalling 27 million chests and dressers because they can tip over and crush children, the Consumer Product Safety Commission announced Wednesday. Two children died after Ikea's Malm chests fell on them in 2014, USA Today reports. Ikea says it knows of three additional deaths since 1989 from tip-overs involving other models of Ikea chests and dressers. While Ikea's new repair program is considered a recall, consumers aren't supposed to return the furniture. Instead, they should order or pick up a new free wall anchoring kit for the affected chests and dressers. Consumers should move unanchored chests and dressers into storage or other areas where they cannot be accessed by children until the chests and dressers are properly anchored. Ikea says it is "committed to helping raise the awareness of this serious home safety issue and to provide consumers with the tools and knowledge they need to prevent these accidents." The recall affects about 7 million Malm chests and 20 million other Ikea chests and dressers sold between 2002 and 2015. To receive a free wall-anchoring kit, consumers can visit www.IKEA-USA.com/safe Malmstogether or call toll-free at 888-966-4532.

One would have the NSA running the program, while the other two options would have the NSA retaining the data and letting phone companies do the same. – The world's most common malaria-spreading mosquito has evolved resistance to insecticides thanks in large part to mating between itself and its cousin, according to a study published Wednesday in PLOS Pathogens. The two species of malaria-spreading mosquitoes, Anopheles coluzzii and Anopheles gambiae, mated for a few years in Mali in the late 1990s and early 2000s. But during that time, the A. coluzzii mated with the A. gambiae on chromosome 2—a move that was "convinced by the start of a major insecticide-treated bed net campaign in Mali," according to the study. "This suggests that insecticide exposure altered the fitness landscape, favoring the survival of A. coluzzii/A. gambiae hybrids, and provided selection pressure that swept the 2L divergence island through A. coluzzii populations in Mali," researchers say. The hybridization was "a rare example of adaptive introgression in an animal species and elucidates the dynamics of how insecticide resistance evolved in A. coluzzii," the study's lead author says in a press release. Researchers believe it's the first time insecticide resistance has been successfully acquired in a mosquito species, according to the CDC. (

– In 2009, NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope spotted a ring so large it appeared to be a dot in the middle of Saturn's entire ring system. The ring, which can't be seen in visible light, is 10 to 20 times larger than the second-biggest ring, and scientists have been trying to figure out why, Phys.org reports. "I was giving talks saying Saturn has a giant invisible ring, which makes you sound just perfectly crazy," says lead author Douglas Hamilton of the University of Maryland, College Park. "It is 10 to 20 times larger than the second-biggest ring, so this thing is absolutely gargantuan." The new study, published in the journal Nature, shows the ring is more than twice as thick as previously thought—and the researchers believe most of the particles within it are smaller than the size of a soccer ball. "If that material was coming inward and coating the face of Iapetus, then maybe we could see the ring," Hamilton says. "Usually those things don't pay off, but this one did." Some of the cost of education in the 10-campus system has tripled over the last decade, and the board voted to raise basic fees by $2,500, to about $10,300, plus about another $1,000 for campus-based charges. Room, board, and books will add another $16,000 to the total cost.

– Paralyzed rats have regained the ability to squeeze out urine—a "very big deal," says one neurologist. The rats, who suffered severe spinal cord injuries, were able to squeeze out urine almost as well as healthy rats do, the New York Times reports. "This is the first time that significant bladder function has been restored via nerve regeneration after a devastating cord injury," says a co-author of the study, published in the Journal of Neuroscience. The researchers snipped out a healthy nerve bundle from between rats' ribs, graft it onto a damaged section of spinal cord, and add an enzyme that chews up scar tissue. In six months, the rats "kept going and going like little bunnies," says the study's lead author. "If we can show in a larger animal that our technique works and does no additional harm I see no reason why we couldn't move rapidly in humans." The process could also help paralyzed people detect and avoid bedsores, and it could restore sensation to the skin, which could help paralyzed people avoid bedsores.

But the withdrawal of all NATO troops from Afghan ministries is likely to be temporary. "This is not going back to business as usual," an Army officer working as an adviser in Kabul tells the Post. "The threat is still higher than normal."

– A new federal report warns that climate change is here, and it's going to get much worse if we don't curb greenhouse gas emissions, the Los Angeles Times reports. The report, the third from the National Climate Assessment, says that there's "unambiguous evidence" that climate change is caused by humans, and that it's getting worse. "Certain types of weather events have become more frequent and/or intense, including heat waves, heavy downpours, and, in some regions, floods and droughts," the report says. "Sea level is rising, oceans are becoming more acidic, and glaciers and arctic sea ice are melting." If global emissions are cut sharply after 2050, the report says temperatures could rise as much as 5 degrees Fahrenheit. "This could help restart a national conversation about climate change," says a scientist with the Union of Concerned Scientists. "It gives us a road map for climate change. And the road is much bumpier if we continue along a higher emissions pathway."

– Cuba is famous for its cigars, rum, and baseball, but it also has some of the best and most inventive biotech and medical research in the world. That's especially notable for a country where the average worker earns $20 a month and the average Cuban lives on par with the average American. Cuba spends a fraction of the money the US does on healthcare per individual, yet the average Cuban has a life expectancy on par with the average American. Last month, during New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo's visit to Havana, Roswell Park Cancer Institute finalized an agreement with Cuba's Center for Molecular Immunology to develop a lung cancer vaccine and begin clinical trials in the US. Essentially, US researchers will bring the Cimavax vaccine stateside and get on track for approval by the Food and Drug Administration. "The chance to evaluate a vaccine like this is a very exciting prospect," says CEO Candace Johnson. She's excited, most likely, because research on the vaccine so far shows that it has low toxicity, and it's relatively cheap to produce and store. – It's not often that the leader of the free world gets to play hockey, but that's exactly what Vladimir Putin did in Sochi yesterday. The Russian president donned the No. 11 jersey and took part in the All-Russia Festival of Night Hockey League, playing alongside former Soviet hockey legends like Pavel Bure and Vyacheslav Fetisov, reports the Daily Mail. Putin missed several goals by a whisker, but his teammates nudged the puck in the right direction for him, and he eventually scored. The Week notes that the league, created in 2011, has grown to 108 teams from 11 countries and is attended by thousands of fans. "There are no winners or losers here," Putin told the crowd. "This is a friendly game. All this [the Night Hockey League] was invented to give an additional boost to the development of sports and physical culture."

– Spectacles, Snap Inc.'s smart glasses that record video and share them with the Snapchat app, are now available for purchase online. The company, which plans to go public later this year, made the glasses available through a temporary pop-up store in New York City and a Snapbot vending machine last fall, but they were limited to just six pairs and had to be found in random places around the country, TechCrunch reports. Now that they're available online for $129.99—and households can only buy six pairs at a time—the company says it wants to prove to investors that Spectacles can actually make money. "We're now happy to be able to make Spectacles more readily available—especially for those in the US who have not been able to make it to a Snapbot," a Snap rep tells TechCrunch. Snap admits in its IPO filing that "the launch of Spectacles ... has not generated significant revenue for us," and production and operating costs are expected to "exacerbate the related revenue in the near future," the Wall Street Journal reports. (Gizmodo notes that one of the glasses melted.)

– Facebook is working on a music platform that will integrate Spotify, MOG, Rhapsody, Slacker, and Rdio, sources tell Reuters. The music platform is expected to be unveiled at Facebook's developer conference on Sept. 22. Music is said to be just one aspect of the strategy to improve Facebook's 'stickiness,' and it is also expected to partner with other media content owners like movie studios. "They are working on a platform for music where the goal is to create a connective tissue for fans," said one source. Mashable, which first reported rumors of the music platform, says Facebook will not directly host or stream any music but will rely on partners to provide the content. "Facebook's plan is to become a platform for media content in the same way it is a platform for applications and games," said one source.

– Russian hackers broke into the White House's unclassified computer system last year and were able to access President Obama's daily schedule and other sensitive information, officials tell CNN. The White House has said the breach only affected an unclassified system, but the hackers had access to sensitive information such as real-time non-public details of the president's schedule. Officials say the Russian hackers first broke into the State Department's network and were able to get back into the White House system by sending a phishing email from a State Department account, the Hill reports. The White House says it does not believe its classified systems were compromised. "We're constantly updating our security measures on our unclassified system, but we're frankly told to act as if we need not put information that's sensitive on that system," deputy national security adviser Ben Rhodes tells CNN. "In other words, if you're going to do something classified, you have to do it on one email system, one phone system. Frankly, you have to act as if information could be compromised if it's not on the classified system." The FBI, Secret Service, and US intelligence agencies are investigating the breach, which they consider among the most sophisticated attacks ever launched against US government

The Turanor PlanetSolar crossed the Atlantic and the Pacific, passed through the Panama and Suez canals, and stopped in Miami; Cancn, Mexico; Brisbane, Australia; Singapore; Abu Dhabi and many places in between. PlanetSolar is the brainchild of Raphael Domjan, who is Swiss and a former ambulance driver and mountain guide. He enlisted enough sponsors to finance the creation of the surreal vessel. The goal, he said in a telephone interview this week from aboard the ship, was to spread the message that solar power can be harnessed for far more than it is doing now. That is admittedly not a super-fast pace. But there were stops along the way to promote solar power and even an encounter with pirates. There was also some waiting for the sun to come up to power those lithium batteries. Trump will be visiting the homelands of all three Abrahamic faiths— Judaism, Christianity, and Islam—before heading to Europe for meetings with Pope Francis and NATO leaders. "No President has ever visited the homelands and holy sites of the Jewish, Christian, and Muslims faiths all on one trip," says National Security Adviser HR McMaster. Trump will deliver an "inspiring yet direct" speech to leaders of 50 Muslim countries on Sunday in an effort to "unify the broader Muslim world against common enemies of all civilization," according to the White House. He'll also be in the Holy Land for meetings with Israeli and Palestinian leaders, as well as visiting the Western Wall. "What President Trump is seeking is to unite peoples of all faiths around a common vision of peace, progress, and prosperity," McMaster says. – Jeb Bush is officially a candidate for president, but he's got a long way to go before he can say "Jeb, Jeb, Jeb." The former Florida governor formally announced his candidacy today in Miami, reports Politico. "I'm running for president of the United States, and I'm running to be president of the United States," he said. "And I'm going to fight for the United States. And we're going to win." But he's got a long way to go before he can say "Jeb, Jeb, Jeb." The Washington Post has a lengthy look at Bush's campaign so far, which it says has been "torn between factions and more haphazard than it appeared on the surface." "This operation stopped a major terrorist attack from taking place," says a Belgian federal magistrate. "You could say a second potential Paris has been averted." According to Belgian media, the suspects were planning to kill several police officers in the street. "This operation was meant to dismantle a terrorist cell and also the logistic network behind it," says the magistrate. The raids were carried out in multiple cities, including Brussels and Paris. Two men were killed in the Verviers raid, and another was wounded. All three were Belgian nationals who are believed to have recently returned from Syria, the Guardian reports. Authorities found explosives, weapons, and "a significant amount of money" at the Verviers address, according to the magistrate. – A hydroelectric dam collapsed in southeastern Laos, leaving an unknown number of people dead and hundreds missing, state media said Tuesday. Rescue efforts were underway as top government officials rushed to the site and public appeals were launched for aid, the AP reports. The official Lao news agency KPL said the Xepian-Xe Nam Noy hydropower dam in Attapeu province collapsed Monday evening, releasing large amounts of water that swept away houses and made more than 6,600 people homeless. The dam was constructed by a joint venture led by South Korean companies, with Thai and Lao partners. The project was still under construction, KPL reported. It described the portion that collapsed as a "saddle dam," which is an auxiliary dam used to hold water beyond what is held by the main dam. Prime Minister Thongloun Sisoulith "suspended the planned monthly meeting of the government for August and led his Cabinet members and other senior officials to Sanamxay (district) to monitor rescue and relief efforts being made for flood victims," KPL said. Many areas of Laos have recently been hit by floods from heavy seasonal rains. – The Golden Globes nominations were announced Thursday morning, and the biggest surprise was that none of the nominees for best comedy series were in the running for the top prize. That honor went to The Good Place, which finally got a nod after more than a decade on the air, per the Hollywood Reporter. Other big winners included Bodyguard, which got a best drama series nod, and Who Is America?, which got a best comedy series nod. On the TV side, the biggest surprise was that HBO's Westworld, which racked up four wins at the Emmys, was left out of the best drama category. Other big misses included Hulu's The Handmaid Tale, which was nominated for best drama series last year, and Netflix's Atlanta, which was nominated for best comedy series last year but was left out this year. On the movie side, surprise nominees included If Beale Street Could Talk, A Star is Born, and Bohemian Rhapsody, which was nominated for best comedy series, best picture, drama, and best actor, best picture, drama, for star Rami Malek. On the film side, surprise nominees included Black Panther, which was nominated for best picture, best picture, drama, and best actor, best picture, comedy, for star Matt Damon.

Scott Shellenberger, the state's attorney for Baltimore County, tells the AP that the teen has been charged with murder as an adult. The Baltimore County Police and Fire Department tweeted Tuesday that the teen was arrested shortly after the female officer was fatally injured Monday. The enormous manhunt was continuing unabated in the suburban community of Perry Hall, where witnesses reported hearing a pop before seeing a Jeep run over the officer Monday afternoon. – The length of the day may be a well-known indicator of human health, but it's a little less well-known indicator for animals. Specifically, the length of the day is linked to the production of melatonin, a hormone produced at night in most vertebrates that is linked to the production of sex hormones, per a press release. But scientists had long wondered how melatonin affected the area of the pituitary gland that controls sex hormones, and a new study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences provides the answer. It turns out that the region of the pituitary gland that detects melatonin is separate from the area where sex hormones are made, and that a protein called vascular growth factor (VEGF) produced there helps control the production of two types of VEGF that are found in the area of the pituitary where sex hormones are made, per the Guardian. This allows VEGF to act as a messenger to control sex hormone-producing cells and fertility—the first time that the molecule linking long winter nights to sex hormones has been found. The department store's Twitter account tweeted, "Who kkmew theis was ghiong tob e a baweball ghamle. #lowsscorinh 5_0" last night, and it's since been taken down, the Huffington Post reports. The company's Twitter account has been inactive since last night. "Umm,@jcpenney, the intern you have doing your tweets is drunk," tweeted one user. – Jane Austen is coming to Britain's bank notes. The Bank of England announced today that the Pride and Prejudice author will replace 19th-century prison reformer Elizabeth Fry on the 10-pound note starting in 2017, reports the BBC. Austen is "one of the greatest writers of our time," said Bank of England Gov. Mark Carney. "We’re very certain that she will prove a popular choice." The choice was met with applause at a news conference at Austen's home in Hampshire, reports the Los Angeles Times. "We've listened, and we fully understand the concerns that were raised by many people," said Carney. "We believe that our notes should celebrate the full diversity of British historical figures and their contributions in a wide range of fields." The move is a reversal for the Bank of England, which in April announced that Winston Churchill would replace Fry on the five-pound note.

– President Obama's approval rating has sunk back to 50%, according to a new Washington Post/ABC News poll. That's down 5 points since January, and it's the first time he's fallen below the 50% mark in the poll's history. His approval rating is also lower than any of the seven second-term presidents since Harry S. Truman, and only George W. Bush has scored lower at this point in his second term. The Post notes that Obama's approval rating among Democrats is even lower at 34%, and his approval rating among Republicans is even lower at 80%. Obama's approval rating among independents is also at an all-time low, and his approval rating among women is at an all-time low. Overall, the poll "contains ample evidence of the disillusionment voters feel toward both sides amid a sense of continuing dysfunction in Washington," writes Chris Cillizza. Still, "large majorities expect that the sequester will eventually damage the economy, the military, and the government’s ability to provide basic services."

– Joe Biden will be in attendance at Antonin Scalia's funeral Saturday, but President Obama won't be. The White House says Obama will pay his respects at the Supreme Court on Friday before joining first lady Michelle Obama at the Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception for Scalia's funeral Mass, NBC News reports. "The president, obviously, believes it's important for the institution of the presidency to pay his respects to somebody who dedicated three decades of his life to the institution of the Supreme Court," White House press secretary Josh Earnest said Wednesday, per Politico, which notes that four of the past seven funerals for Supreme Court justices have seen the president or vice president in attendance. (Bill Clinton attended the funerals of Justice Warren Burger and Justice William Brennan but did not attend the funerals for Justices Harry Blackmun or Lewis F. Powell Jr.)
