– Trayvon Martin's body showed no apparent injuries before he was killed, the funeral director who prepared his burial says. "We could see no physical signs like there had been a scuffle [or] there had been a fight," Richard Kurtz tells CBS. "The hands—I didn't see any knuckles, bruises, or what have you. And that is something we would have covered up if it would have been there." The lawyer for Martin's parents, meanwhile, says surveillance video shows Zimmerman "was beating Trayvon Martin for more than one minute," CNN reports. "Look at that video. Do you see any blood on his head? He said he broke his nose. Look at that video. And look at how easy he walks out of the car." Zimmerman, meanwhile, showed no obvious head or face injuries in the hours after the shooting, according to police reports.

– Neanderthals weren't all bad. A new study finds they may have contributed to everything from allergies to depression. Researchers at Vanderbilt University looked at the genomes of 28,000 people whose medical records they had linked to electronic health records and found Neanderthal DNA was linked to a wide range of physical traits, including skin color, allergies, and depression, the Guardian reports. "We discovered associations between Neanderthal DNA and a wide range of traits, including immunological, dermatological, neurological, psychiatric, and reproductive diseases," senior author John Capra says in a press release. The study, published in the journal Science, also found Neanderthal DNA was associated with increased risk of nicotine addiction, as well as increased risk of developing sun-induced skin lesions called keratosis, which are caused by abnormal keratinocytes. "The brain is incredibly complex, so it’s reasonable to expect that introducing changes from a different evolutionary path might have negative consequences," says researcher Corinne Simonti, who adds Neanderthal DNA may have provided modern humans with "adaptive advantages" 40,000 years ago when they migrated from Africa. But the study, which Capra says "establishes a new way to investigate questions about the effects of events in recent human evolution," suggests many of the Neanderthal traits may no longer be beneficial in today's environment,

– The comet lander Philae has been stuck in a spot on comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko since landing on the comet Wednesday, and now it's running out of juice. The European Space Agency announced yesterday that it was preparing to "hop" the lander, hoping to get enough sunlight to charge its batteries and keep its systems running, the Guardian reports. But the lander's legs have a built-in spring, and the lander has been stuck in a spot on the comet since landing, with only a sliver of light reaching one of its solar panels. "I just started lifting myself up a little and will now rotate to try and optimize the solar power!" the lander tweeted early today. "First comet drilling is a fact!" But the lander's manager says that while 80% of the science the lander was supposed to deliver has been achieved, it is now running out of battery power, the BBC reports. "We juggled everything so that every instrument got to do a measurement, so we are very happy with the mission so far," he says. The comet is currently out beyond the orbit of Mars, heading for its closest approach to the sun in August 2015.

– Matthew McConaughey is returning to his alma mater, the University of Texas at Austin, to teach a film class this fall. The San Antonio Express-News reports the 46-year-old actor will be joined by Hunger Games director Gary Ross in teaching the upper-level class "behind the scenes" of his new movie, Free State of Jones. The class is an upper-level division course, so freshmen and sophomores won't be able to register, but there are no prerequisites or fees to take it, Us reports. McConaughey taught a similar class for students during the spring 2016 semester, but since Free State of Jones hadn't been released at the time, students had to sign a nondisclosure agreement.

A veteran hotel security officer says he witnessed the former governor using California Highway Patrol officers and vehicles to ferry scantily-clad women into his hotel room at the Sacramento Hyatt Regency where he and Maria Shriver often stayed. "It makes me very angry just to think of what was going on at that time," the former security officer tells the National Enquirer. – Dawn Wells, best known for playing Mary Ann Summers on Gilligan's Island, is in need of financial help, TMZ reports. Dugg Kirkpatrick, a friend of the 79-year-old Wells, recently started a GoFundMe page to raise money for her. According to People, the page claims Wells lost her life savings and her home during the 2008 financial crisis and has been struggling to make ends meet ever since. The page claims Wells needed to be hospitalized for two months after an "unexpected accident" and needs $194,000 to cover her hospital costs and "alleviate penalties by the IRS." Kirkpatrick says Wells broke her knee this year and is recovering from complications. He says she wants to be moved to an assisted living facility specifically for the film and TV industry, but was denied because of her debt. He says Wells has no family and has lost her home. "Debaltseve was under our control, there was no encirclement, and our troops left the area in a planned and organized manner," Petro Poroshenko said in a statement, per the BBC. He called for "a firm reaction from the world to Russia's brutal violation of the Minsk agreements, the ceasefire regime, and the withdrawal of heavy weaponry." Poroshenko visited troops who had left the town of Artemivsk and promised that they would be honored to shake hands with "Ukrainian heroes," the AP reports. The president's office says 22 Ukrainian soldiers have died in the past three days in Debaltseve, though the bodies of 25 have been brought to a morgue in Artemivsk, the BBC reports. A rebel spokesman says Debaltseve is fully under rebel control and conditions in the city are dire, with no electricity or a shortage of food and water. He says rebels are sharing their rations with the remaining civilians.

– A 23-year-old Michigan man is suing three celebrities who mocked him for having a rare genetic disorder, the Detroit Free Press reports. Jahmel Binion has hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, which reduces his ability to sweat and can cause facial deformities. In April, Binion took a selfie and posted it to Instagram and Twitter with the caption, "Smile today." It is based on a list that built during more than 30 years of archival research. "The world justice system has failed and I'm doing what a historian should do: expose the responsible individuals as war criminals," Lasik said. Up to 200 former guards at the German death camp could still be living, he said. Historians estimate that some 12% of Auschwitz guards were tried by courts in Poland and elsewhere. – Dietary supplements are often touted as a way to boost a person's health or sex drive, but a new study finds they can also be dangerous—especially to kids, NBC News reports. Researchers looked at 275,000 calls made to poison control centers between 2002 and 2012 related to exposure to all kinds of dietary supplements, and found that the most common cause was exposure to yohimbe tree bark extract, which has been used for centuries to treat everything from leprosy to fever and is now used to treat erectile dysfunction in men and women. The study, published in the Journal of Medical Toxicology, found that 80% of yohimbe exposures occurred in children under 6, and that 3.2% of cases were serious and one death was reported. "Many consumers believe dietary supplements are held to the same safety and efficacy standards as over-the-counter medications," says the study's senior author. "However, dietary supplements are not considered drugs, thus they are not required to undergo clinical trials or obtain approval from the FDA prior to sale, unless the product is labeled as intended for therapeutic use." Kristopher Oswald was on his lunch break early Sunday when he heard a woman screaming and a man hanging onto the hood of her car, WXYZ reports. Oswald asked her if she needed help, and when he approached, the man started punching him in the head, yelling, "I'm going to kill you." Oswald was able to get on top of the man, but two other men jumped him from behind. Livingston County sheriff's deputies arrived and stopped the fight. Oswald had worked for Walmart for about seven weeks and said he would not have been considered a permanent employee until after his 180-day probation ended. "The last thing I expected was to not have a job," Oswald said. "I will always do the right thing." Walmart has policies against workplace violence to prevent employees from assaulting co-workers or tackling a shoplifter, but it appears that nothing allows for them to assist in situations of imminent danger and self-defense, Oswald said. Now that he's out of a job, Oswald says, "I don't even know what to put on an application about all of this.

– The death toll in the devastating mudslide in Washington state has risen to 16, with another eight bodies found in the debris, officials say. The number of people unaccounted for is still at 176, but the county emergency management director says he's hopeful for a miracle, the Guardian reports. "I think that speaks for itself," he says. Two more bodies were found on the property of Navy Cmdr. John Regelbrugge yesterday, his brother-in-law says. His wife, Kris Regelbrugge, a mother of five, was later found. One of the rangers, a 46-year-old sergeant who has been on the job for 20 years, was stabbed in the abdomen and is in surgery at Massachusetts General Hospital; the other ranger, a 23-year-old who joined the force just last month, is in stable condition at Tufts Medical Center with less serious wounds. Witnesses say that before police chased Hutchinson into the Public Garden, where they arrested him, he told them to shoot him. Police recovered a knife they believe was used in the attack from a pond nearby. Hutchinson has an open warrant for his arrest on charges of assault and battery on a police officer. He was arrested in February of last year.

– Scientists have been keeping a close eye on Antarctica over the last two decades, and they've been shocked to find that the continent is losing more ice per year than it's holding—and that's causing sea levels to rise, the BBC reports. A new study in Nature finds that between 1992 and 2017, Antarctica lost about 200 billion tons of ice per year, a three-fold increase over the previous assessment in 2012. "A three-fold increase now puts Antarctica in the frame as one of the largest contributors to sea-level rise," says lead researcher Andrew Shepherd. "It's like applying the brakes on a bike," adds a scientist from Durham University. "Friction on the bottom of the ice, which was floating but has now grounded again, everything and changes the whole dynamic upstream. We do think the rebound (in the future) will be fast, but not fast enough to stop the retreat we've kicked off with today's warming." The melting is happening mostly in the West and Antarctic Peninsula, and the loss there is largely due to the collapse of floating ice platforms in front of glaciers, allowing ice behind to flow faster. North Korea fired five short-range projectiles into the sea an hour before Francis arrived, a South Korean defense official says, though it's not clear what the projectiles were. The trip is the first for a pope since John Paul II went to India in 1999, the AP notes, and it will be the first time a pope has spoken in English during a trip to Asia.

– A potentially deadly strain of E. coli has sickened 38 people in 20 states and prompted General Mills to recall three brands of flour, Food Safety News reports. According to the Minneapolis-based company, state and federal authorities have been investigating an E. coli O121 outbreak related to a specific type of flour that has sickened people in 20 states. "While attempting to track the cause of the illness, CDC [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention] found that approximately half of the individuals reported making something homemade with flour at some point prior to becoming ill," Food Safety News quotes a press release from General Mills. "Some reported using a General Mills brand of flour." The CDC found that half of the people who fell ill used General Mills flour. The affected brands are Gold Medal All Purpose Flour, Signature Kitchens All Purpose Flour, and Gold Medal Wondra Flour. They were sold to retailers including Safeway, Albertsons, Jewel, Shaws, Vons, United, Randalls, and Acme. No illnesses have been reported in connection with the flour.

– If you thought the lawsuit against Taco Bell over what it calls "100% USDA inspected beef" was going to blow your mind, think again. The fast-food chain says the beef in question is actually at least 88% meat, and it plans to take legal action against the lawyers who filed the "bogus" suit, reports the Los Angeles Times. "The lawyers got their facts wrong," says a statement on the company's website. "We take this attack on our quality very seriously and plan to take legal action against them for making false statements about our products." The lawsuit claims that only 36% of the beef in Taco Bell's "seasoned beef" is meat, and the rest is "extenders" that can be added to the product to make it seem more meat-heavy, notes the Huffington Post.

– The co-creator of Occupy Wall Street has a message for today's activists: Stop whining and start innovating. In his new book, The End of Protest, Micah White argues that protest is over and that activists must start innovating to create the next generation of social movements, the New York Times reports. "The end of protest is the beginning of the spiritual revolution within ourselves, the political revolution in our communities and the social revolution on Earth," White writes. " Rigorous, original, and compelling, The End of Protest is an exhilarating vision of an all-encompassing revolution of revolution." In the book, White lays out eight principles of innovation, including: Participatory Democracy: "Participatory democracy is the process by which people work together to make their voices heard," White says. "It's not a political movement. It's a movement of people coming together to make their voices heard." For more on White and his ideas, click here.

– The Road, a Cormac McCarthy adaptation, tells the story of a man and his son who survive a post-apocalypse after their mother is killed. Critics are divided on the film: "The Road is a depressing disappointment," writes AO Scott in the New York Times. "Despite numerous strong areas, including fine acting by Viggo Mortensen and young Kodi Smit-McPhee as father-and-son survivors of an unnamed apocalypse, what we've been given is no more than a reasonable facsimile, an honorable attempt at filming an unfilmable book." "The movie is in need of a finer sensibility, and that is simply not on offer," writes Roger Ebert in the Chicago Sun-Times. The film "turns out to be good at shocking and upsetting us, but it lacks the compensating emotional heft that would make absorbing those shocks worth our while," writes Betsy Sharkey in the Los Angeles Times. It's "for the most part profoundly depressing," she writes, but it's also "a vision of a world largely without us that completely chills the soul."

The decision came in a lawsuit brought by two nurses who challenged the law, which defines marriage as between a man and a woman. April DeBoer and Jayne Rowse have raised three special-needs children they adopted as individuals. "This is a happy day," DeBoer says. "We don't want to speculate. "It's like having a personalized gym and tracking system in the palm of your hand," the site notes. – Bad weather may have played a role in the crash of AirAsia Flight 8501, Indonesia's weather bureau says—and it could have caused ice on the plane's engines. "Based on the available data on the last received location of the aircraft, the weather was a factor in causing the accident," the weather bureau says, per Reuters. The search for the wreckage of the plane, which crashed into the Java Sea yesterday with 162 people on board, has found four large parts on the sea bed, says the head of Indonesia's search-and-rescue agency, per Reuters. "We've found four big parts from the plane we're looking for," he says. "The visibility is only 2 meters. It's cloudy, making it difficult for the cameras to detect." The plane's black boxes—the voice and flight data recorders—may be located tomorrow if the weather improves, officials say. Meanwhile, authorities say that AirAsia violated the terms of its license for the Surabaya, Indonesia, to Singapore route by flying on a Sunday, the day the Airbus A320-200 plunged into the Java Sea, and that they will investigate the carrier's other schedules.

– A 14-year-old oil leak in the Gulf of Mexico could be the biggest in US history, the New Orleans Times-Picayune reports. According to the Washington Post, the Taylor Energy platform was destroyed by Hurricane Ivan in 2004, and oil has been leaking from the seafloor ever since. The Coast Guard believes the leak is up to 29,000 gallons of oil per day. The Coast Guard has ordered Taylor Energy to figure out a way to contain the leak and stop it before it's too late. The Coast Guard estimates the leak is between 10,500 gallons and 29,000 gallons per day. That's five to 13 times more than the government's previous estimate. The Coast Guard believes the leak is coming from two sources: the seafloor and drilling fluid on the water's surface. Taylor Energy says the drilling fluid is coming from sediment that's "heavily contaminated" with oil. The company claims the oil is bubbling up from the seafloor and isn't leaking from the wells. The Coast Guard says the company must find a way to "eliminate the surface sheen and avoid the deficiencies associated with prior containment systems." Taylor Energy is suing the federal government for the remaining $432 million it was required to create to pay for the leak

– Police in Alabama are investigating the death of a 42-year-old mother of a 12-year-old girl as a homicide, AL.com reports. Kathleen Dawn "Kat" West was found dead outside her home in Calera on Jan. 13. Her husband, a campus police officer, was briefly on the scene, but police have not made any arrests and have not disclosed a cause of death. West, who also went by the name Kitty Kat West, had a subscription-only adult website and social media accounts under the name Kitty Kat West. Police have not said whether they believe her adult website, which included revealing photos of West, played a role in her death. In a statement, West's mother says it "seems so impossible for the extreme sadness and grief we feel as the loss of our beautiful daughter Kat to ever diminish orease." She adds: "The Lord is our hope and our salvation, and he can turn our mourning into comfort. God wants to encourage us and relieve our suffering if we will just go to him at all times. And his word is powerful enough to bring healing and solace even during our darkest hours." A GoFundMe campaign has been set up to help pay for West's funeral.

– The US has handed over the last of its detainees in Iraq to the Iraqi government, the Washington Post reports. Hezbollah operative Ali Mussa Daqduq is accused of kidnapping and killing five US soldiers in 2007, and the US had been trying to extradite him to the US for trial. But the Iraqi government wouldn't let him go, and the US legally had to transfer him to Iraqi custody under the security agreement negotiated by the Bush administration in 2008. “Coming on the heels of the Administration's failure to maintain a small American military presence in Iraq to support the fragile peace there, this failure to keep a committed murderer of Americans in US custody sends exactly the wrong message to our allies and enemies in the region,” said a statement from John McCain, Mitch McConnell, Joe Lieberman, and Lindsey Graham, who called the move "disgraceful." Daqduq will be tried in an Iraqi court, a US official tells the Wall Street Journal.

– British police have warned about people in clown outfits acting suspiciously and sometimes wielding knives as they follow people, the AP reports. The warning Saturday follows a string of incidents in recent days in an apparent effort to copy clown-related threats in the United States. Police in Gloucestershire said there have been six reports of clowns acting suspiciously and sometimes in a threatening way. Police say no arrests have been made because the people dressed as clowns have left the scene before police arrived. The incidents in Gloucestershire followed earlier reports of disturbances in other parts of Britain. Police said a masked man with a knife jumped out and threatened children in Durham on Friday and that several people dressed as clowns chased a young boy the day before in Suffolk. Police said a masked man with a knife jumped out and threatened children in Durham on Friday and that several people dressed as clowns chased a young boy the day before in Suffolk. "While we appreciate Halloween is just a short time away, scaring people—especially children and vulnerable people—in this way is completely unacceptable and could constitute an offense," a police spokesman said. "Anyone who sees any suspicious activity, or who has been intimated or upset by this behavior, should call Cheshire police immediately on 101."

"I am very impressed with myself," she said. "Way to go, girl." Some reactions to her last show: "She might have been the first late-night host who got it. She got that we're tuning in to her show bleary-eyed and exasperated before bed. She got that we wanted idle chatter about the world's most base-level news: celebrity gossip. She got that we carried a little bit of shame about having that craving, and she not only internalized some of that shame, but openly admitted it, even mocking herself for making money by telling jokes about Paris Hilton and Honey Boo Boo. She seemed like she couldn't believe that this was her job for seven years, to joke about Kardashians and Biebers and Lohans. And that's precisely why we loved listening to her talk about them. She took those things just about as seriously as we do—which is to say not very—but understood that, for some reason we can't explain, we still lived for talking about them

– More advertisers are deserting Rush Limbaugh's radio show after his "slut" attack on law student Sandra Fluke. Online florist ProFlowers is the seventh to pull its ads, reports the Los Angeles Times. "Mr. Limbaugh’s recent comments went beyond political discourse to a personal attack and do not reflect our values as a company," it said in a statement. Quicken Loans, Sleep Train, Sleep Number, Citrix Systems Inc., Carbonite, and LegalZoom also have suspended their ads, according to the AP. "No one with daughters the age of Sandra Fluke, and I have two, could possibly abide the insult and abuse heaped upon this courageous and well-intentioned young lady," said Carbonite CEO David Friend in a statement. "Even though Mr. Limbaugh has now issued an apology, we have nonetheless decided to withdraw our advertising from his show."

– Asiana Airlines is "reviewing taking legal action against both KTVU-TV and the NTSB" after the Bay Area news station mistakenly named the pilots of Asiana Flight 214 as "Fuk" and "Fook," reports the San Francisco Chronicle. The NTSB has apologized for the "inaccurate and offensive names," but says the station's summer intern "acted outside the scope of his authority when he erroneously confirmed the names of the flight crew." The NTSB says it didn't release the pilots' names to the media, and KTVU says it didn't confirm with the NTSB before airing the names. The NTSB says KTVU is reviewing its procedures to make sure this doesn't happen again. Asiana Airlines says the incident "had been seriously damaged by this report," SF Weekly reports. "The reputation of the four pilots and of the company had been seriously damaged by this report."

– A UK woman who killed her kitten by putting it in a microwave because she thought it had attacked her goldfish has been sentenced to 14 weeks in jail. Laura Cunliffe, 23, put the four-month-old kitten into the microwave and turned it on for five minutes, the Telegraph reports. She took it out about a minute later and realized what she had done, but the kitten died. Cunliffe pleaded guilty to "utterly horrendous cruelty" and was sentenced by a judge who told her, "This was an act of utterly horrendous cruelty on your part on an animal that, as far as I could see, had come to trust you and rely on you." A member of the public shouted in court, "She doesn't know what's happening—she hasn't clue." Cunliffe has been sectioned 20 times under the Mental Health Act and her lawyer says she suffers from depression. – If you're going to steal nearly $200,000 worth of quarters, you might as well do it while you're working at Brink's, the armored transport company where you're a money processing manager. That's what allegedly happened to Stephen Dennis, 49, of Harpersville, Ala., who has been charged with bank theft for the 2014 theft, AL.com reports. Federal investigators say Dennis made off with 784,000 quarters—about the weight of a hippo—between Jan. 1, 2014, and Feb. 20, 2014, his last day of employment at Brink's. According to an FBI press release, an April 2014 audit of Brink's coin storage found that four of the bags held beads, but only $1,000 worth of quarters. Dennis placed the beads in the bags so they'd be visible through a plastic window. He then allegedly stole $196,000 worth of quarters. "This defendant may have thought he had quite a haul, but now he carries a heavier load," US Attorney Joyce White Vance says in the press release. "He must repay the money and face a federal sentence." Dennis has agreed to plead guilty to the bank theft charge and to repay the $196,000. The maximum penalty for bank theft is 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine

– Mitt Romney released his 2011 tax return today, revealing that he paid $1.94 million in federal taxes on income of $13.7 million, for an effective tax rate of 14.1%. Most of his income came from investments, the Romney campaign said, and the majority of the income came from his wife's charitable donations, the Wall Street Journal reports. The effective tax rate is a far cry from the 15% he paid in 2009, according to the campaign, which says his effective tax rate in 2011 was 14.1%. The campaign also released tax filings from 1990 to 2009 that show Romney and his wife paid 100% of the federal and state income taxes they owed, and that their average annual effective federal tax rate was 20.2%, CNN reports. Romney's campaign says he paid $1.94 million in federal taxes in 2011, and gave $4 million to charity.

– A Vermont woman learned the hard way not to turn around too quickly when her GPS told her to do so. Nabila Altahan was driving on Route 4 in Mendon Wednesday night when her Toyota Corolla got directions that it had passed its destination, state police tell WCAX. She quickly left the road and her car ended up suspended on a telephone pole. Altahan and her passenger were not injured, police say.

– After a four-week hiatus, a solar-powered plane has taken off from Japan in an attempt to become the first to fly around the world without a drop of fuel. The Solar Impulse 2 took off from Nagoya Airport this morning after a last-minute decision to fly directly to Hawaii's Kalaeloa Airport, where it will spend five days and five nights crossing the Pacific Ocean, the BBC reports. "We are very, very happy," a project spokeswoman tells the AP. "We have now packed the hangar up. We are just doing the last logistical operations." The journey to Hawaii is expected to take about 120 hours, and the plane's Swiss pilot, Andre Borschberg, will have no choice but to turn around if the weather changes, the BBC notes. Borschberg, who has been taking turns flying the plane, is aiming to become the longest-duration solo flight in aviation history, as well as the furthest distance flown by a craft that is powered only by the sun. The journey to Hawaii is the eighth leg of Solar Impulse's journey around the world. It started in March in Abu Dhabi.

A spokesperson for McConnell says the senator "is not alleging the administration has threatened or pressured the sports leagues," but a spokesman for the NBA says the league has made no "substantive details" with the administration.

Ross Ulbricht, 30, was accused of creating the underground site, which allowed users to buy drugs using the digital currency bitcoin. He was also accused of commissioning the murders of five people he thought were threatening his business. Ulbricht's lawyer says his client wasn't the site's creator, but had turned it over to others before being lured back into running it with the help of federal agents. – Syria's second-largest city, Aleppo, is bracing for a major assault by government troops, reports the New York Times. Rebels are reportedly massing on the city's southern outskirts, and fighting has reportedly broken out on the city's streets. “We are terrified,” says one resident. The Syrian military, meanwhile, appears to be waiting for reinforcements before ordering an attack. The US is concerned about the possibility of a massacre, says a State Department spokeswoman, but “we do not think pouring more fuel onto the fire is going to save lives.” Aleppo has long been a strategic rebel stronghold, and it's not clear whether the regime will be able to hold it without exacting a heavy toll on civilians. “This used to be a restless city,” one resident tells the Times. “Now it’s the opposite.”

It's a key moment in the civil rights movement, and the film has been in the works for years. Here's what critics are saying: The film "transcends ordinary biopics," writes Manohla Dargis in the New York Times. It's "both a sweeping epic and an intimate personal portrait" that shows King in a "new way—not as a forbidding icon or flawless secular saint, but as a cannily strategic player who equalled Johnson move-for-move in a high-stakes bout of political gamesmanship." Oyelowo is "terrific" as King, and the film as a whole is "fascinating," writes Rafer Guzmn at Newsday. But it's DuVernay and Oyelowo who "get the most out of the film's power to tell King's story in a way that is authentic and moving." – Arguably the greatest director of all time, Bernardo Bertolucci, has died at the age of 73. Bertolucci had been suffering from a herniated disc for 10 years and was told by doctors he would never walk again, the Guardian reports. He spent years feeling "very negative," he says. "The total frustration of not being able to move. Not being able to do anything for myself. As far as I was concerned, I was finished." But then he read a novel and decided to make a film of it. "Immediately, it awoke ... my desire, you know. I soaked it up like a sponge," he says. "At that moment, it really felt as if my life depended on that book. And the whole process of making the film was the most fantastic therapy for me. I directed this film with the same passion I’ve directed all my other films."

– Sen. Bill Nelson says he's going for a recount in the Florida Senate race, which Rick Scott declared victory in last night's election. "We are proceeding to a recount," the Democrat said in a statement early Wednesday, per Politico. "This race is over. It's a sad way for Bill Nelson to end his career," said a Scott spokesman. "He is desperately trying to hold onto something that no longer exists." Under state law in Florida, a recount is mandatory if the winning candidate's margin is less than 0.5% of the total votes cast. The first unofficial returns are due Saturday, and 67 county supervisors of election have until noon Saturday to recheck their counts. If the recount comes up with a margin of one-half of 1% or less, the counties have until noon Nov. 10 to request a recount, reports the Washington Post.

Abzhanov says he's seen examples of two-headed creatures in his lab, including a two-headed bull shark foetus found in the Gulf of Mexico and conjoined dolphin offspring found on a Turkish beach. – At least 40 people were injured, five of them seriously, when two commuter trains collided head-on in western Switzerland last night, CNN reports. One driver is missing, and search crews are trying to pry open the train's crushed cab. The crash happened late last night on a regional line about 30 miles southwest of the capital, Bern. The two regional trains locked together but still on the tracks, the AP reports. The crash will interrupt train service between Payerne and Lausanne, a city on the shores of Lake Geneva, until at least midnight.

– A deadly explosion at an Iranian military base last week appears to have been far more destructive than authorities have described, according to a private group's analysis of satellite images. "It was pretty amazing to see that the entire facility was destroyed," the report's author tells the New York Times. "There were only few buildings left standing." The Institute for Science and International Security released the satellite images Monday along with an analysis of the damage. The destruction at the base, which was used to develop missiles, appears to have been far more extensive than authorities have described, according to the report. The institute discounted the possibility that the explosion was the result of a simple accident or sabotage, but noted that it is possible that pieces of heavy equipment from Iran's missile program may have gone missing after the blast.

According to WKMG, some of the overdose victims are in their 20s, 30s, and 40s, while others are in their 60s, 70s, and 80s. In Cedar Rapids, Iowa, heroin overdoses have soared over the past five years, KCCI reports. "It's a serious issue—not just the presence of heroin, but the effects that heroin is having on the users," Cedar Rapids' police chief says. – The Legos have officially taken over from Barbie as the world's biggest toymaker. The Danish company says revenue jumped 11% in the first six months of this year, thanks in large part to the success of the Lego Movie, reports the AP. "We are thrilled by the reception of the Lego Movie products," says the company's chief financial officer. The Lego Group—which is still owned by the same family that founded it in 1932—says sales were strongest in Europe, the Americas, and Asia, and it hopes the momentum will continue into the holiday season, reports CNNMoney. The Lego Movie has made more than $260 million so far, notes the Wall Street Journal, and a new set featuring female scientists sold out on the Lego website over the weekend.

– Kids who regularly eat at fast-food restaurants are more likely to be overweight or obese than kids who don't frequent fast-food restaurants, according to a new study. Researchers found that kids who eat at fast-food restaurants but don't eat at fast-food restaurants at all are 1.5 times more likely to be overweight or obese than kids who don't frequent fast-food restaurants, the Los Angeles Times reports. "Our findings suggest that the location where foods are obtained may not be as important as the nutritional quality of the foods consumed," the authors wrote. The study, which looked at data from nearly 4,500 kids between 2 and 18, also found that kids who follow a "prudent diet"—eating more fruits and vegetables, leaner proteins, and less added sugar and saturated fat—were significantly less likely to be overweight or obese. "Just because children who eat more fast food are the most likely to become obese does not prove that calories from fast foods bear the brunt of the blame," the study author tells RedOrbit.

– Snakes don't need to be on a plane to fly—they can soar 100 feet or more in the tropical forests of Southeast Asia, and scientists have figured out how they do it. The mystery? The snakes flatten out in a shape that resembles an alien's flying saucer from the side, reports LiveScience. "The shape is unusual," says a researcher at Virginia Tech. "You never find this kind of shape in any other animal flyer; you don't find it in engineered flyers. We didn't know if that was a good shape to have." The finding could help explain why the snakes undulate from side to side once they're airborne, and why they appear to glide even better than other gliding animals, such as squirrels and ants. The researchers printed a 3-D rod with the UFO-like cross section, then placed it in a tank of water that flowed over it to measure how the current moved it. The results, published today in the Journal of Experimental Biology, showed that at most angles, the snake model's shape generated enough lift to account for the animal's ability. Real flying snakes appear to glide even better than the model would suggest.

"At the minimum, it's a tax increase for families who choose to adopt. But at maximum, it could have a chilling effect on adoption." Sims says the credit was included as an example of things that could be eliminated as part of tax reform, but it was "positively took my breath away" when she saw it in black and white. – Scientists have discovered that tadpoles of a species of horned frog emit a "brief, clear, and very audible metallic-like sound" when they're in distress. It's the first time any vertebrate larva has been found to use sound to communicate underwater, the BBC reports. The "scream" comes from the tadpoles of the Argentine horned frog, a species that's famously aggressive and carnivorous, often eating the tadpoles of other frogs. Researchers were studying the mating calls of adult frogs when they caught a horned frog tadpole in a pond using a hand-held net. "We heard a brief, clear, and very audible metallic-like sound," one of the researchers says. The tadpoles emit the sound by pushing air out of their lungs, which develop very early. The discovery raises the possibility that other tadpoles may produce sound. It's possible, however, that the scream is mainly emitted when another horned frog tadpole moves to attack it as a measure to avoid cannibalism.

– If you've ever wondered what a cow is, what a sloth is, or what a Chewbacca is, Wolfram Alpha has just the thing for you. The new website lets you upload a photo and get a computer-generated guess within seconds, Fast Company reports. "It won’t always get it right, but most of the time I think it does remarkably well," CEO Stephan Wolfram writes in a blog post. "And to me what’s particularly fascinating is that when it does get something wrong, the mistakes it makes mostly seem remarkably human." Wolfram's system was trained with tens of millions of images, he says, and was able to identify things like a cow as "black angus" and two cups of ice cream as "frozen yogurt." But it couldn't identify Chewbacca, and it couldn't identify cats wearing spacesuits, sloths wearing party hats, or even Chewbacca. It still can't identify specific people, art, or things that aren't "real everyday objects," Wolfram says, but it's collecting the images to keep training its system, so be mindful of what you send in. The site is currently only available in the US, but Wolfram says he plans to expand to Europe

– Omran Daqneesh, the 5-year-old Syrian boy whose haunting photo of him in the back of an ambulance following an airstrike in Aleppo became an iconic image of last year's civil war, has appeared in footage for the first time since the attack, the BBC reports. In the video, Omran and his father, Mohammed Daqneesh, tell a reporter from Iran's Al-Alam TV that they're still living in Aleppo and that Omran doesn't want to leave the country. The video was posted on the social media account of a pro-Syrian government television presenter and appears to show Omran in good health, though it's not clear whether the family was coerced into taking part, the Thomson Reuters Foundation reports. In interviews with pro-government journalists, Mohammed Daqneesh complained that the Syrian opposition and international media had wanted to use Omran to attack President Bashar al-Assad. "They wanted to trade in his blood and published his photos," he said. Omran's older brother, Ali, died from his injuries after the airstrike, and Mohammed Daqneesh said he had cut his son's hair and changed his name to protect him from being kidnapped by rebels.

– Ron Paul's declaration that "we are all Austrians now" has set off a wave of conspiracy theories, including this one from New York Times columnist Nicholas Kristof. Kristof thinks Paul was talking about the views of the Austrian school of economics, a branch of free-market thinking that's at odds with the mainstream economists he admires. The school was founded by Ludwig von Mises and his student Murray Rothbard in the 1960s, and its views are very different from the views of most libertarians, writes Kristof. For one thing, they don't believe that low interest rates cause economic booms. Instead, they believe that artificially low interest rates spur "malinvestment" in unworkable enterprises that crash when the stimulus is withdrawn. "This is an emotionally appealing idea, positing that the suffering of a bust is a kind of cosmic payback for the boom," writes Kristof. "But it doesn’t make much logical sense. For one thing, as George Mason University economist Bryan Caplan, who’s ideologically sympathetic to the Austrians, points out, it’s hard to understand why businesspeople would be so easily duped in this way." Click for his full column.

– The Department of Labor has slapped the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints with $1.9 million in fines for allegedly employing children as unpaid pecan harvesters. The DOL says it found 175 children under the age of 13 working at two church-owned properties in Utah and Arizona, reports the Salt Lake Tribune. The church is a fundamentalist Mormon group, and the children were pulled from school for weeks at a time to work in the fields, according to lawsuits filed this week. "These children worked for the defendants in agriculture performing various job duties, including but not limited to: pruning trees, mowing fields, maintenance duties, picking and bagging pecans, shaking trees, driving equipment, cleanup work, and preparing pecans for commerce," says one of the lawsuits, per the Deseret News. "Defendants knew that they were employing these children during school hours without pay." The DOL has also filed a lawsuit seeking back wages for the 1,400 workers, and is trying to hold church leaders in contempt of court for violating a 2007 court order barring them from employing children.

Russia's Micex stock index is down 13% this year, and the ruble is the second-worst performer against the dollar among 24 developing-market currencies. "We're witnessing the start of a new geopolitical and economic Cold War and I think it will take at least two to three years to establish some sort of equilibrium," says Romania's government representative for diplomacy and economic projects. "The ones who'll pay the bill for this aggression, no matter how popular and patriotic it looks, will be the Russian people because there's a huge difference between the economic force of the EU and the US and that of Russia." Russia's central bank has unexpectedly raised its benchmark interest rate by 150 basis points after the annexation triggered a rout in the ruble. Russia's economy was facing the weakest growth since a 2009 recession as consumer demand failed to make up for sagging investment, and the current situation "bears clear signs of a crisis," says the deputy economy minister.

– Home values are falling at an accelerating rate in many cities across the US, according to the Wall Street Journal’s latest quarterly survey of housing-market conditions. Home values dropped in all of the 28 major metropolitan areas tracked during the fourth quarter when compared to a year earlier. The size of the year-to-year price declines was greater than the previous quarter’s in all but three of the markets, the latest indication that the housing market faces considerable challenges. Inventory levels, meanwhile, are rising in many markets as the number of unsold homes piles up. Home values dropped the most in cities that have already been hard-hit by the housing bust, including Miami, Orlando, Atlanta, and Chicago, according to data from real-estate website Zillow.com. But price declines also intensified in several markets that so far have escaped the brunt of the downturn, including Seattle and Portland, Ore.

– Ireland's parliament today passed a bill that will allow abortions when the mother's life or health is in danger, the AP reports. The bill allows abortions in cases of rape, incest, and when the mother's life or health is in danger from the fetus, the Guardian reports. Abortion is already legal in Ireland, where the only time it's illegal is when the mother's life is in danger from the fetus. The new law will also criminalize abortion if the mother's life is in danger from the fetus, and anyone who procures an abortion in Ireland will face up to 14 years in prison. The bill passed after 24 hours of intense debate in the Dil, the Guardian notes.

The study, published in the journal Nature, suggests humans interbred with Neanderthals in Europe as well as in the Middle East, not just in Africa. The hunter-gatherer, known as Oase 1, was from a "pioneer population" that entered Europe but didn't contribute much to the population as a whole. – It's called a "Frankenfish," but the FDA just gave the green light to one: AquAdvantage, a salmon engineered by AquaBounty Technologies, is the first genetically modified animal approved for consumption in the US. It's a Chinook salmon that has a growth hormone from a Chinook salmon and a gene from the ocean pout, an eel-like fish. The result is a fish that is large enough for consumption in about a year and a half, rather than the typical three years, reports the Washington Post. The Massachusetts-based company says its fish are all female and sterile, making it impossible for them to mingle with wild Atlantic salmon, which could lead to decimation of wild populations. The FDA says it found no difference in nutritional value between normal Atlantic salmon and AquAdvantage salmon, and that the fish is "as safe to eat as any non-genetically engineered (GE) Atlantic salmon, and also as nutritious." But critics, including salmon fishermen and environmental groups, say AquAdvantage salmon could wreak havoc on the ocean ecosystem. The company says it will begin selling the fish in 2017, and the Post reports that the FDA's approval was "based on sound science and a comprehensive review" that took years to complete.

– The number of confirmed cases of a rare condition that causes paralysis of the brain and spinal cord has soared this year. The Washington Post reports there have been 32 cases of acute flaccid myelitis, or AFM, confirmed across the US so far this year, compared to just seven cases by this time last year. Most cases have occurred between August and December, with a peak in October. The condition, which causes paralysis after a fever or respiratory illness, usually affects children, though it can occur in adults as well. “CDC is looking at these trends very carefully,” a CDC official tells the Post. “We have sent out several health alerts to states to let them know we are seeing an increase in reporting and to encourage them to communicate with doctors to report these cases in a timely fashion.” The chief of the section of the nervous system at the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke tells the Post she's worried this could be a repeat of 2014, when AFM hit the US at the same time as a much larger outbreak of polio. “You hate to be an alarmist, but there’s reason to have some concern,” she says. “What we don't know is where are these cases. – Blood-testing startups have been making a name for themselves in the medical world with their promise to detect a wide range of diseases using a single drop of blood. But new research out of Rice University suggests that using a single drop of finger-prick blood may not be as accurate as previously thought, reports the New York Times. In a study published in the American Journal of Clinical Pathology, scientists took seven drops of blood from 10 people, and found that results varied widely from drop to drop. "These data suggest caution when using measurements from a single drop of fingerprick blood," the researchers write. For the study, researchers averaged six to nine drops of blood from each person, and found that results varied widely from drop to drop. (Blood-testing startup Theranos has had a rough few months.)

– Astrophysicists using NASA's Cassini spacecraft have found new evidence that one of Saturn's other moons is, in fact, the most life-friendly habitat ever discovered outside of our own planet. Enceladus is the sixth-largest moon in the solar system, and last year scientists discovered a 6-mile-deep ocean, believed to contain many of the chemicals necessary for life, at the moon's southern pole, reports Space.com. Now researchers say they've found evidence that the ocean is also hot, possibly capable of supporting life. "This is yet another discovery in a series of really remarkable findings that have come one by one, to tell us that this may be the place to go look for life in the outer solar system," says a planetary scientist at Cornell University, who wasn't involved in the new research, per NPR. The researchers believe the ocean's temperature must be higher than 190 degrees Fahrenheit, which is cooler than many hydrothermal vents on Earth, and silica particles detected by the Cassini spacecraft could only have come from the ocean. The theory is that silica formed beneath Enceladus' icy crust and then dissolved in seawater before ending up in Saturn's magnetosphere, where it was detected by the Cassini spacecraft.

– A ship searching the Indian Ocean for the missing Malaysia Airlines plane has detected two more "pings" consistent with signals from flight recorders, reports the Sydney Morning Herald. The Australian vessel, which is towing a US pinger locator, picked up the first ping on Saturday and the second on Tuesday afternoon. "The analysis determined that a very stable, distinct, and clear signal was detected at 33.331 kilohertz, and that it consistently pulsed at a 1.106-second interval," says the head of the search's Joint Agency Co-ordination Center. "They believe the signals to be consistent with the specification and description of a flight data recorder." The signals were picked up over a smaller area this time around, but search chief Angus Houston says "there's no second chances," reports CNN. "We're either a long away from it or in my view more likely the batteries are starting to fade."

Police have taken Dillard-Bothuell into custody, and she could be charged with child abuse, reports WXYZ. The boy's father, Charlie Bothuell IV, is expected to face child abuse charges in the next couple of days, reports Fox 2 Detroit. Police say the boy was home-schooled and home-schooled severely, and he was beaten with a PVC pipe often with blood on it. The pipe was taken from the home as evidence, and sources say blood was found in the boy's room and on some of his clothes.

LaBeouf " profusely apologized in an odd rant," but the manager had enough and told him to get out. The restaurant tells the gossip site that the two had words, and LaBeouf "is officially persona non grata." Ri Yong Ho, speaking to Russia's state-run TASS news agency, says Trump's words "lit the fuse of war against us." "We need to settle the final score, only with a hail of fire, not words," he says. According to USA Today, Ri has previously called Trump "President Evil." Ri's comments come a day after the US military flew two B-1B Lancers over the Korean Peninsula as part of a training mission with military allies Japan and South Korea near the Sea of Japan. The US military says the mission was to ensure a quick and efficient response to threats in the area.

The Boston bombing suspect wanted to honor a Dagestan rebel fighter killed by Russian forces in 2009, law enforcement officials tell the Los Angeles Times. "He said, 'The Russian people have been terrorizing my home country for all these years.' This is why he needed to come back to America and help,'" one official says. Tsarnaev signed the form at a federal immigration office in the Boston area three months before the bombing and was advised to take an oath of allegiance to the US, including serving in the military. "Maybe he thought because he could not get accepted over there, maybe he could do something here." Tsarnaev's lawyers say he was radicalized during a trip to Dagestan in 2012 and that he returned to the US feeling pressure from the FBI to become an informant, the Times notes. The brothers' lawyers say the FBI interviewed Tsarnaev multiple times after the Russian government asked it to check on him in 2011.

– Peanut allergy is the No. 1 cause of anaphylaxis, a life-threatening allergic reaction, and one of the most common causes of death from food allergy. Now Australian researchers say they've found a long-term cure that will allow children with peanut allergies to eat peanuts without fear, the Guardian reports. In a clinical trial involving 42 children, 82% of those given a combination of the probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus with peanut protein were found to be tolerant to peanuts at the end of the trial in 2013. Four years later, 80% of the cured children were still showing no sign of an allergic reaction to peanuts. "These findings suggest our treatment is effective at inducing long-term tolerance, up to four years after completing treatment, and is safe," says lead researcher Mimi Tang. "It also suggests the exciting possibility that tolerance is a realistic target for treating food allergy. This is a major step forward in identifying an effective treatment to address the food allergy problem in Western societies." The treatment combines a high dose of the probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus with a small amount of peanut flour, which encourages the immune system to gradually tolerate larger and larger doses of peanut flour, the AAP reports. – Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel will face a runoff election in April after failing to get a majority of the vote in today's mayoral election, Reuters reports. Emanuel, who raised more than $15 million for his campaign, needed to get at least 50% of the vote to avoid a runoff; with 98% of precincts reporting, he had 45.4% of the vote and Jesus "Chuy" Garcia, a Cook County commissioner and progressive Democrat, had 33.9%. Garcia, 58, a former state senator and alderman, had the support of the powerful Chicago Teachers Union and its president, who recorded an endorsement for him the week he announced his bid for mayor. The run-off election will be held on April 7. "We have something to say," Garcia said to his euphoric supporters. "We want change." Garcia, who held a low public profile before entering the race, has argued that Emanuel paid more attention to the city's upper class and downtown than to the poor and communities outside the commercial center. Emanuel, 55, won the mayoral seat outright when he first ran in 2011, but controversial decisions to close 50 public schools and continued high crime helped send the Chicago mayoral election into its first run-off since the city started holding nonpartisan elections in 1995.

"Please help if you can and pray for my family. I'm sorry I never said anything sooner and that I'm suddenly asking for help. I love you guys so much," Bartell wrote on Twitter. She was wearing a tight white dress with a plunging neckline, and the Electoral Commission says the dress distracted attention from important issues, the BBC reports. His whereabouts are unclear today, with some saying he’s holed up in a hotel in the city, where his hold on power is not as strong as in the capital, Tripoli. “It seems that security forces in Libya do not feel there are limits on how far they can go in suppressing protests,” said a researcher for Human Rights Watch in Cairo who has been in contact with residents and doctors in Benghazi. The government has viewed the situation in Benghazi as so precarious that Colonel Qaddafi sent his son, Saadi, to the eastern Libyan city last week in an attempt to mollify resentment, residents said. In a speech Wednesday, Saadi promised reform, but his overtures were seen as condescending, several said. “We don’t trust the regime anymore,” said one Benghazi protester.

– Egyptians are voting today in the third and final round of parliamentary elections since Hosni Mubarak's ouster, and analysts expect Islamist groups to consolidate their gains, Bloomberg reports. "The third phase will not change much the nature of the upcoming parliament," says a Cairo-based analyst. "It will likely underline the control of Islamists." The Muslim Brotherhood's Freedom and Justice party has taken the lead in the first two rounds of voting, and analysts say the party could easily win a clean majority in the 150-seat final round. But it's not clear how the new parliament will be formed, and it's not clear whether the military will cede power before presidential elections are held in June. Protesters are preparing to mark the anniversary of the mass rallies that drove Mubarak from power on Jan. 25.

– A 51-year-old woman in Orange County, Calif., is lucky to be alive after getting stuck on a cliff while trying to rescue her kitten, reports the Orange County Register. Sara Beebe climbed up a 50-foot slope behind her Silverado Canyon home to get her adopted black cat down after it ran off Monday morning. "Because it's so dry and steep, she started trying to climb down and she slipped and continued sliding down about 50 feet," says Orange County Fire Authority Capt. Steve Concialdi. She twisted her ankle and was scraped during her fall and couldn't climb up or down. A firefighter rappelled down from a helicopter and pulled Beebe onto the aircraft to safety. Beebe said first she screamed for her young daughter and then yelled for her neighbors to call 911. "I did ask her how she got to where she was. She had told me that she had gone up to rescue a cat," says Jeff Shelton of the Orange County Fire Authority. Beebe says she will do things differently next time. "I am going have to start letting the cat be a little more independent when I get it out and just put my prayer into it that it get back home," she tells CBS Los Angeles.

– The scandal over rigged Libor rates may have started years before the financial crisis, with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York raising concerns to British authorities as early as 2007, reports Reuters. The New York Fed says it received "allegations" of "problems with Libor" in 2007 and 2008 from Barclays, and "shared our analysis and suggestions for reform of Libor with the relevant authorities in the UK." It didn't say when the communication took place. The Fed's role in the scandal is likely to raise questions about whether authorities took enough action to address concerns they had, or whether their struggle to keep the banking system afloat through the financial crisis meant the issue took a backseat, says Reuters. Rep. Randy Neugebauer, chairman of a subcommittee of the House Financial Services Committee, sent a letter to the New York Fed earlier this month asking for transcripts of any "communications with Barclays regarding the setting of interbank offered rates from August 2007 to November 2008." In his letter, Neugebauer asked New York Fed President William Dudley to provide transcripts by Friday.

Now, the 56-year-old has been charged with their murders, and police are searching for the body of his wife, who disappeared after Oner discovered she was having an affair. Police say Oner has saved thousands of documents, including maps of his parents' garden, detailing his movements over the years. Among the notes, police say: “What am I going to do with these now?” and “I dug my dad’s garden, I am very tired.” Oner fled Turkey for France in the 1980s after killing a friend, and Interpol issued a warrant for his arrest. He found a job at a bank, married his wife in 2008, and moved in with his parents

– Four of the women who have received womb transplants in Sweden have had embryos transferred into them in an attempt to get pregnant, the AP reports. "We have already begun transferring embryos into four of the women and plan to make attempts with the others when they are ready," says Dr. Mats Brannstrom, who is leading the research. Brannstrom predicted that three or four of the seven women might successfully give birth. "One or two more will perhaps get pregnant and miscarry, and one or two won't be able to get pregnant," he says. There have been two previous attempts to transplant a womb—in Turkey and Saudi Arabia—but both failed to produce babies. Brannstrom says any woman in the study who does get pregnant will be on a low dose of drugs to keep from rejecting the transplanted uterus and will be monitored as a high-risk pregnancy. The transplants are intended to benefit women unable to have children because they lost a uterus to cancer or were born without one. Some doctors said women who got pregnant with a new uterus would have to be watched carefully for how the womb progresses throughout pregnancy. – The heirs of a famous German Jewish art collector are suing the German state of Bavaria for the return of eight paintings they say were looted by the Nazis. Alfred Flechtheim fled Berlin for Paris in 1933 to escape the Nazis, and his heirs say the paintings by Max Beckmann, Juan Gris, and Paul Klee were taken from him, reports the New York Times. Flechtheim was one of the most important art collectors in Germany in the early 20th century, and his heirs say some of the paintings may have been sold by the Nazis to dealer Hildebrand Gurlitt, Reuters reports. Gurlitt was one of four dealers the Nazis allowed to sell "degenerate" art, and his cache of 1,400 paintings was discovered in his apartment in Munich in 2012. Flechtheim's heirs say the state has refused to return the paintings, which are currently on display in Munich's Pinakothek der Moderne museum. "The state-level program of Aryanizing Jewish businesses made the confiscation possible," their lawyer says. "The paintings would have remained accessible to Flechtheim but for the climate at the time." – A police officer in St. Louis is facing animal cruelty charges after leaving his K-9 police dog, Bo, in the back of his SUV for hours on a hot day, the St. Louis Post-Dispatch reports. The dog, who died of heat-related symptoms last week, wasn't the only animal to die in a police vehicle over the past eight years. According to BuzzFeed, more than two dozen police dogs have died of heat-related symptoms since 2007. "It is a painful, horrible death," a veterinary specialist tells BuzzFeed. "Once a dog's temperature goes above 105 or 106 degrees, their cells start dying, and they can start going into seizures or have mass organ failure." Police departments across the country have been taking steps to prevent such deaths, including setting up air-conditioning sensors in police vehicles, according to the Post-Dispatch. But it's not just police dogs who are at risk. Two police dogs in Texas died after being left in a police vehicle for 30 hours in August. Sasha, a police K-9, died in Georgia after being left in her handler's SUV for three days in August. A police officer in Warwick, Georgia, resigned after burying the dog's body in his backyard. The company says it will also launch a national smoking cessation program to help people quit smoking, USA Today reports. "Ending the sale of cigarettes and tobacco products at CVS/pharmacy is the right thing for us to do for our customers and our company to help people on their path to better health," says CVS CEO Larry Merlo. "Put simply, the sale of tobacco products is inconsistent with our purpose." The company estimates that it will lose $2 billion in revenues from tobacco sales this year, according to a press release.

– The world's oldest library is set to reopen after years of restoration, and the Guardian takes a look at Khizanat al-Qarawiyyin, located in the old medina of Fez in northern Morocco. It was founded in the ninth century by a woman, Fatima al-Fihri, and is believed to be the oldest library in the world. The library's treasures include a ninth-century copy of the Qur'an written in the Kufic script on camel skin, as well as works by Moses Maimonides, Ibn Khaldun, and Leo Africanus. "The people who work here jealously guard the books," says one of the caretakers. "You can hurt us, but you cannot hurt the books." After years of restoration, the library has a new sewerage and underground canal system to drain away moisture that had threatened to destroy many of its prized manuscripts—plus a lab to treat, preserve, and digitize the oldest texts. Digital scanners identify tiny holes in the old paper rolls, and a preservative machine moistens the manuscripts to prevent cracking. – A new survey from Transparency International finds that more than a quarter of people around the world have paid a bribe in the past year. The annual survey from the anti-corruption group polled 114,000 people in 107 countries, and found that police and the judiciary were the most corrupt institutions, the Wall Street Journal reports. In Liberia and Mongolia, for example, more than 75% of respondents said they'd been asked to pay a bribe in the past year. But two-thirds of respondents said they wouldn't do it. The survey also found that political parties were the most corrupt, with political parties in more than 50 countries scoring a 4.8 on a scale of 1 to 5, the Journal notes. The US came in dead last, with just one in 10 people saying they'd been asked to pay a bribe.

Ford, who has been away from City Hall for weeks as he undergoes chemotherapy, says he's been told he has liposarcoma, a rare and aggressive form of cancer. Ford, who is now a candidate for city council while he is being treated, says cancer has been the "worst event" of his life. "Some nights, I just cry myself to sleep," he says. "It's explaining to my kid what a will is. Stephanie's 10 and Dougie's seven—they know what's going on at 10 and seven, and it's heartbreaking at times ... They say stuff like, 'Who's going to tuck me in at night? Who's going to put me to sleep?'" Ford says he is not sure if he will be able to participate in any all-candidates debates in his old council seat,

The investigation found that pimps and sex buyers are using the bail bond system to find women in prisons and jails across the country and force them into prostitution. "Sometimes women are released not knowing who bonded them out or why, or what they've gotten into, and now they're being coerced," says Diane Checchio, a former prosecutor in Florida. "They come out of jail and there's someone waiting saying: 'I posted your bond—now you owe me' ... [They will] threaten to rescind that bond if the girls don't do what they're asked or told to do. Over the course of the investigation, the Guardian spoke to more than 20 trafficking survivors in 11 states, as well as correctional officers, convicted sex traffickers, law enforcement officials, lawyers, prosecutors, and frontline workers. The agency says the deaths are about three times the historical average for the region, the AP reports. The agency says it will work with colleagues in Canada, where six large whales have died off the coast of British Columbia since May. Officials have only been able to get samples from one of the 30 whales. Teri Rowles, NOAA Fisheries' marine mammal health and stranding response coordinator, tells reporters during a teleconference yesterday that large-scale whale deaths are among the toughest to investigate, partly because the carcasses often are floating, rarely beached, and difficult to access for examination. Police say two men broke into the home of Ayvani Perez early Tuesday and asked her mother for money and jewelry. When she refused, the men kidnapped Ayvani and drove off with her, say police. She has been reunited with her family and is in good health, reports WSB-TV. Miller is expected to join former deputy prime minister John Prescott and others in asking the courts for a judicial review of the police’s conduct of the case. – With California in the grip of a historic drought, Gov. Jerry Brown has issued an executive order calling for a 25% cut in state water use by 2013. "We're standing on dry grass," Brown said, as per the Los Angeles Times. "We should be standing on five feet of snow." Under the order, cities must stop watering median strips that run down the middle of roads and homeowners must replace grass with drought-tolerant landscaping. Golf courses, campuses, and cemeteries must cut their water use and new developments must install drip or microspray systems if they irrigate with drinking water. State agencies will create a temporary rebate program to encourage homeowners to replace water-guzzling appliances with high-efficiency ones. Water agencies will discourage water waste with higher rates and fees. Some critics of Brown's order said it didn't do enough to address agricultural uses. "The governor must save our groundwater from depletion by directing the state water board to protect groundwater as a public resource," said the director of Food & Water Watch California.

It's not actually blue, but the second in a month is what's known as a blue moon, and it's the third of four full moons in a season, according to the US Naval Observatory. The last one, in 1950, was caused by "moon light traveling through a cloud of particles from forest fires in Canada," the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration explains. The phrase "blue moon" has its roots in a 1943 edition of Sky and Telescope, which used the phrase "the third full moon to in an astronomical season in which four full moons fall" instead of "the third full moon to in an astronomical season in which four full moons fall," according to Space.com. The Maine Farmer's Almanac, which is unrelated to the more famous Farmer's Almanac, came up with a much more complicated definition in 1937: "seven times in 19 years there were—and still are—13 full moons in a year." Breyer, a retired tool-and-die maker, had claimed he was unaware of the mass slaughter at Auschwitz, but "the German allegations belie his claims," the judge wrote. – For the first time, astronomers have detected the filaments of dark matter that make up the "cosmic web" of matter and energy that surrounds our universe, the BBC reports. Cosmologists have long believed that galaxies are part of this web, which is made up of dark matter and ordinary matter. Until now, scientists have been able to detect dark matter using "gravitational lensing," in which light from distant galaxies is bent by the force of gravity. But using a quasar, 10 billion light-years away, astronomers were able to detect the filaments using glowing hydrogen gas. "The light from the quasar is like a flashlight beam, and in this case we were lucky that the flashlight is pointing toward the nebula and making the gas glow," says Sebastiano Cantalupo of the University of California, Santa Cruz, lead author of a study in Nature. "This is a new way to detect filaments. It seems that they have a very bright quasar in a rare geometry," says a scientist from ETH Zurich not involved in the study. "If indeed gravity is doing the work in an expanding Universe, we expect to see a cosmic web and it is important to detect this cosmic web structure."

– Archaeologists in Greece have uncovered what they say is the largest ancient tomb to have been discovered in the country—and they believe it's the final resting place of a senior ancient official, the AP reports. The tomb at the site of Amphipolis, about 65 miles northeast of Thessaloniki, appears to have two headless, wingless sphinxes guarding its entrance, as well as walls covered in frescoes. It's also surrounded by a long, 497-foot-long marble wall, which experts believe once held a giant stone lion sculpture that was part of a tomb monument that crowned the hill. "It is certain that we stand before an especially significant finding," says Prime Minister Antonis Samaras. "The land of Macedonia continues to move and surprise us, revealing its unique treasures." Alexander the Great died in 323BC in what is now Iraq, and his burial place has yet to be determined. "It looks like the tomb of a prominent Macedonian of that era," a culture ministry official tells Reuters, but there's no evidence yet to suggest a link to Alexander.

The Israeli military says it's still trying to destroy a network of Hamas-built tunnels running from Gaza into Israel, the AP reports. In other developments: The UN Security Council has called for an immediate ceasefire, "in order to bring an end to the hostilities and to enable the delivery of humanitarian aid and other assistance to the civilian population in the Gaza Strip," according to a statement. But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says he won't negotiate until the tunnels are destroyed, and Israel's defense minister says the military "will not hesitate to expand our operation," the New York Times reports. The Israeli military says it has hit more than 200 tunnels since the conflict began, but so far they've only destroyed a small fraction of them. In one incident yesterday, an Israeli airstrike hit a house in Gaza City's Jibaliya refugee camp, killing at least six people, including four children, the BBC reports. – Whale sharks, which can reach 47,000 pounds in weight and reach up to 41.5 feet in length, are becoming more frequent visitors to the Azores, a central North Atlantic island nation off the coast of Portugal, a new study finds. Researchers looked at 16 years of data on whale shark sightings collected by tuna fishing boats, and found that the giant fish became more frequent around the Azores in 2008—the year the area was the hottest it's been on record, LiveScience reports. The area in which they were spotted "is 1 million square kilometers [386,000 square miles], easy," the study's lead author says, and it's located along the colder northern edge of the waters where whale sharks used to prefer to live. Researchers say the findings could shed light on how climate change might affect the behavior of fish around the world. The study also found that higher water temperatures around the southern Azores Island of Santa Maria were associated with more whale shark sightings, as were underwater hills and mountains, which are associated with large amounts of photosynthetic organisms that feed the creatures the whale sharks eat. (In other oceanic news, click to read about how the world's oceans are becoming more "unsinkable.")

Trump began his Friday on Twitter, saying Democrats and Republicans "MUST come together, finally, with a major Border Security package, which will include funding for the Wall." He says it's "time for action," even though the idea is opposed by many Democrats, who recently won control of the House. Trump also calls on Congress to pass criminal justice reform legislation. He says Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and Democratic leader Chuck Schumer "have a real chance to do something so badly needed in our country." But Trump tweeted at the wrong account, tagging a Schumer fan instead of the senator. For Thanksgiving, Trump called troops, answered reporters' questions, visited a Coast Guard station, and had dinner at his Mar-a-Lago club, the AP reports. Trump has kept the door open to a potential government shutdown if an upcoming deal to fund parts of the government does not include funding for a border wall. Congress has until Dec. 7 to fund the rest of the government after lawmakers punted on seven of the 12 individual funding bills before the end-of-the-fiscal-year deadline. – There's a little food war going on in New York City, and it involves a croissant and a pretzel. The Cronut, popularized by chef Dominique Ansel, is a croissant-doughnut that's deep-fried. But Maury Rubin's take on the "pretzel croissant"—a combination of croissant, pretzels, and salt—is a hit, and lines start forming at both Rubin's City Bakery and Ansel's SoHo bakery at 5am. "Oblivious of the peril, we wake and find ourselves in an age of mutated pastry, cross-bread, trying to be two things at once," writes Daniel D'Addario in the New Yorker. " Doughnuts cross with croissants, croissants cross with pretzels; Montreal bagels are made puffier for New York tastes, and New York bagels are made as thin and sweet as the ones in Montreal. The Crumbs Bake Shop chain, having almost gone bankrupt pushing cupcakes, comes back to life to push the 'baissant, a bagel-croissant chimera.' Let us look, then, at these case studies of how stale bread becomes fresh and familiar sweets take mutant forms."

Faisal Mekdad also said the government is "100% sure" that rebels were behind the chemical attack that killed hundreds of people last summer, and that it's confident it's now in control. Mekdad did, however, acknowledge that Syria's religious leaders and community leaders have ties to the rebels, which the Times sees as "a subtle shift in tone from the government's portrayal of the armed rebellion as a foreign-led conspiracy." The Times notes that Mekdad's comments represent "a subtle shift in tone from the government's portrayal of the armed rebellion as a foreign-led conspiracy."

But as the 24-year-old crossed Bayshore Boulevard, Raubenolt was struck and killed by a car as she pushed the stroller across the northbound lanes, reports the Tampa Bay Times. Police say Raubenolt was crossing legally at an intersection when she was hit by a black Mustang driven by 18-year-old Cameron Herrin. Herrin and 17-year-old John Barrineau were allegedly street racing nearby, and witnesses say they heard the engines of the two cars rev before the crash. Raubenolt was thrown into the air, and Lillia died Thursday. Herrin and Barrineau, who graduated from Tampa Catholic High School on Monday, were charged with vehicular homicide and street racing; Herrin's 20-year-old brother, Tristin, was charged with racing but not vehicular homicide. "We hope something good will come of this foolish accident," says Raubenolt's uncle, John Reisinger. "That's what Jessie would want."
