– Argentina is the third-largest soybean producer in the world, but farmers there have been complaining for years about the dangers of Monsanto's popular Roundup, the AP reports. Residents say they've been exposed to dangerous levels of the chemicals, which are applied by hand, in close proximity to homes and schools. Now, a new study finds that children in Argentina have been found to have been exposed to "extremely high" levels of glyphosate, the key ingredient in Roundup, the New York Times reports. The study's lead author, a pediatrician, says glyphosate has been linked to a wide range of health problems, including cancer, autism, and learning disabilities. But Monsanto says there's no evidence the chemicals pose a health risk, and that farmers only use the chemicals when necessary. "We believe that the vast majority of Argentines are perfectly willing to accept the risks associated with Roundup," says a Monsanto spokesman. "We believe that there is no link between the use of Roundup and health problems in Argentines."

A new report from the UK's Action on Sugar found that many hot drinks contain as much sugar as a can of Coca Cola—and up to 25 teaspoons of sugar per serving, which works out to more than three times the maximum daily intake of sugars recommended for an adult. Costa Coffee's Chai Latte (large) is even worse, with 20 teaspoons of sugar and is topped with a cinnamon stick and orange. Action on Sugar says 98% of the 131 hot flavored drinks it analyzed would receive a "red" label for excessive levels of sugars. And 35% of the drinks contained the same amount or more sugar as Coca Cola. "No wonder we have the highest rates of obesity in Europe," the group's chair says. – Today's closing arguments in the Supreme Court's ObamaCare case have wrapped up, and the consensus seems to be that the health care law is all but certain to be struck down: "The verdict is in: The individual mandate at the heart of President Obama's healthcare law is not long for this world," writes Jeffrey Toobin at CNN. Toobin was among the pundits who declared the law dead before the arguments had finished. "If the justices decided the constitutionality of laws on performance, ObamaCare would go down like a flaming zeppelin," tweeted Mother Jones' Adam Serwer. "The stakes in this case and the court's notorious opacity encourage tea leaf-reading and overreaction," writes Mike Sacks at the Huffington Post. "It's noteworthy that they (and Kennedy in particular) exhibited such aggressive skepticism." The court's conservative majority, meanwhile, "appeared to have little sympathy for the individual mandate," writes Eugene Robinson at the Washington Post. "If the justices decided the constitutionality of laws on performance, ObamaCare would go down like a flaming zeppelin."

– A gunfight at a wedding party in Afghanistan has left 21 people dead and eight wounded, an official says. Most of the dead were wedding guests and at least two of the wounded were younger than 18 years old, the AP reports. Abdul Jabar Perdili, police chief of Baghlan province, said a gunfight broke out between two groups attending the wedding in Dih Salah district late Sunday. He said that most of the dead were wedding guests and at least two of the wounded were younger than 18 years old. Perdili's spokesman, Jaweed Basharat, had earlier said that 10 people were wounded. Conflicting accounts are common in the chaotic aftermath of violent incidents. Baghlan and other provinces of the north have been plagued by insurgent attacks since the US-led invasion in 2001 that toppled the Taliban. However, the war is often used as a cover for criminal activity and personal feuds. The police chief of Dih Salah, Col. Gulistan Qasani, said hostility between the two groups involved in the gunfight had been simmering for many years. "The clash broke out after a relative of a provincial police official was assassinated during the wedding party," he said. A district police chief says the armed men traded verbal barbs before the gunfight

– The Backstreet Boys haven't released a new album since 2013's In a World Like This, but that's about to change. The boy band dropped a new single Thursday, "Don't Go Breaking My Heart," Billboard reports. "The minute we heard this song, we knew it was special," Kevin Richardson says in a statement. "I hooked out over the piano synths. ... When that groove drops on the second verse ... great melodies. Just makes you geek over and over again." The band, which celebrated 25 years together last month, has announced 21 new Las Vegas shows from July 25 to Nov. 17. "We're definitely going to keep trying to let the Vegas show grow," Richardson says.

According to a sheriff's office report, 30-year-old Schaquana Spears ordered her sons to return property that belonged to the neighbor, then whipped them with an RCA cord as punishment. – The Department of Veterans Affairs is teaming up with IBM to use its Watson supercomputer to help 10,000 veterans with cancer over the next two years, the AP reports. The goal is to use the technology to help doctors make more-informed treatment decisions. "Genetic alterations are responsible for most cancers, but it remains challenging for most clinicians to deliver on the promise of precision medicine due to the sheer volume of data surrounding each decision that needs to be made," VA Under Secretary for Health Dr. David J. Shulkin says in a press release. "By applying Watson to this problem, we see an opportunity to scale access to precision medicine for America's veterans, a group most deserving of the best care in the world." Under the partnership, VA doctors will sequence cancer patients' DNA, then feed that data into Watson, which will analyze it to identify cancer-causing mutations and possible treatment options. "The power of cognitive computing is its ability to ingest, understand, and find patterns in massive volumes of disparate data—which is one of the fundamental barriers to precision medicine today," an IBM VP says in the press release. – Ruth Bader Ginsburg is in the hospital after falling and fracturing three ribs in her office Wednesday night, the Supreme Court says. The 85-year-old justice was admitted to the hospital early Thursday for observation and treatment, USA Today reports. "She went home, but after experiencing discomfort overnight, went to George Washington University Hospital early this morning," the court said in a statement. "Tests showed that she fractured three ribs on her left side and she was admitted for observation and treatment." The court's oldest member, Ginsburg has survived multiple bouts with cancer and had a heart stent placed in her right coronary artery in 2014.

– Steve Bannon's Breitbart News has been rejected for press credentials to cover Congress, the New York Times reports. According to USA Today, the Capitol Hill Standing Committee of Correspondents rejected the news outlet's application to join the Senate Daily Press Gallery on Tuesday, citing concerns about the organization's editorial independence. Breitbart had been trying to join the gallery for years, but it was rejected in part because it didn't have an office in Washington. The site had operated out of Bannon's home for years, despite the fact that the building was not zoned for commercial activity. The committee had also been concerned about Breitbart's inconsistent answers to questions about its masthead and office space. The temporary press credentials Breitbart had been using for more than two years will expire at the end of May. The committee said Breitbart could reapply, but only if it addressed the concerns.

– A Manhattan judge has ruled that Twitter must turn over three months' worth of tweets sent by an Occupy Wall Street protester charged with disorderly conduct, reports the New York Times. "The Constitution gives you the right to post, but as numerous people have learned, there are still consequences for your public posts," wrote the judge. "What you give to the public belongs to the public. What you keep to yourself belongs only to you." Twitter had argued that it was under an undue burden to turn over the messages, but the judge noted that laws regarding social media were evolving and that public speech, regardless of the forum, did not enjoy the same protections as private speech. The case raises important questions about the growing use of social media by law enforcement, notes the Wall Street Journal. In the first six months of this year, Twitter received 849 law enforcement requests for user information, 63% of which were from US law enforcement, compared to 40% from other countries. American law enforcement accounted for 80% of the requests, while US officials made 679 requests.

Mediaite spotted a Craigslist ad for a "new and exciting online news publication covering news on politics, US, international, media, sports, and other general news" called the Huckabee Post, which already has offices in New York City and Washington, DC. The ad doesn't say anything about a subscription service, though Mediaite points out that Glenn Beck has started the TheBlaze, and Andrew Sullivan launched The Dish earlier this year. Huckabee has been making noises about a 2016 run in recent days, the Hill reports. "I didn’t want any misinformation that I’ve told people I’m running—that’s not the case," Huckabee told Josh Feldman last week. "I wanted to be honest and say, sure I’m looking at it."

– An early warning system that might have prevented some deaths in the tsunami that hit an Indonesian island on Friday has been stalled in the testing phase for years, the AP reports. The high-tech system of seafloor sensors, data-laden sound waves, and fiber-optic cable was meant to replace a system set up after an earthquake and tsunami killed nearly 250,000 people in the region in 2004. But inter-agency wrangling and delays in getting just $69,000 to complete the project mean the system hasn't moved beyond a prototype developed with $3 million from the US National Science Foundation. It is too late for central Sulawesi, where walls of water up to 20 feet high and a magnitude 7.5 earthquake killed at least 832 people in the cities of Palu and Donggala, tragically highlighting the weaknesses of the existing warning system and low public awareness about how to respond to warnings. "To me this is a tragedy for science, even more so a tragedy for the Indonesian people as the residents of Sulawesi are discovering right now," says Louise Comfort, a University of Pittsburgh expert in disaster management who has led the US side of the project, which also involves engineers from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute and Indonesian scientists and disaster experts. Merriam-Webster released the sixth edition of The Official Scrabble Players Dictionary on Monday, four years after the last freshening up. The company, at the behest of Scrabble owner Hasbro Inc., left out one possibility under consideration for ew after consulting competitive players who thought it potentially too contentious, reports the AP. There are some sweet scorers now eligible for bizjet, and some magical word dumps, such as arancini those Italian balls of cooked rice. – An elderly Pennsylvania woman was surprised to find a man living under her roof after her daughter paid a visit. The woman, who is in her 80s and lives on the first floor of her two-story home, has a caretaker, but she was limited to the second floor due to mobility issues, NBC News reports. When her daughter went upstairs to check on her, she heard a noise and found Mark Potts, who had been hiding out in an upstairs closet for weeks. "He didn't bring in new furniture but he was living there," a local DA says. "This guy put this woman in fear and he probably killed any future feelings of security and we are going to make sure he is held accountable for that," the DA says. Potts, who had suitcases and a handgun on him, faces criminal trespassing charges. The caretaker, who has not been named, is expected to face charges as well.

– An explosion rocked Japan's Dai-ichi nuclear plant today, in the wake of yesterday's failure of the plant's cooling system. The explosion may have been caused by a buildup of hydrogen, the New York Times reports, but the plant's operator says it wasn't inside the reactor itself. Instead, the blast tore a roof and a wall off the building housing the reactor's No. 1, but the reactor's steel containment was still in place, the AP reports. The Japanese government has told people to stay indoors, and officials are distributing iodine to help protect thyroid glands from radiation. The explosion occurred in a building housing reactor No. 3, which has a separate containment that's still in place, officials say, but the explosion may have been caused by steam or hydrogen.

– Scientists at the Georgia Institute of Technology have created a tiny replica of the world's most famous painting, the Mona Lisa, using a new process they say could be used to create much larger works. The "Mini Lisa" measures just 30 millionths of a meter, or one-third the width of a human hair, and each pixel is spaced by 125 nanometers, reports the Christian Science Monitor. The researchers used a new process called ThermoChemical NanoLithography, which involves heating a cantilever and tip of an atomic force microscope, then lowering them to the desired location of a pixel. The heat of the cantilever triggers a chemical reaction and graying as heat produces a greater local concentration of new surface molecules. Less heat produced the darker shades of her dress and hair seen when the molecular canvas is visualized using fluorescent dye. Each pixel is spaced by 125 nanometers, and the overall image has 240 x 320 pixels. "We envision TCNL will be capable of patterning gradients of other physical or chemical properties, such as conductivity of graphene," the study's lead author says in a press release. – Scott Kelly returned to Earth on Thursday after a record-breaking year in space, and he arrived to find that he's now just 2 inches taller than his twin, Mark. The Washington Post reports that's a "weird but temporary side effect of spaceflight": Astronauts get taller in space as the spine elongates, but "they return to preflight height after a short time back on Earth," a NASA rep tells CNN. Mark Kelly was the first Earthling Scott saw when he arrived in Houston, the AP reports. The two are due to stand side-by-side for the first time in nearly a year on Friday. Scott Kelly spent 342 days on the International Space Station to help scientists study the effects of long-term spaceflight on the human body. The study is the first attempt to really study the effects of such a long stay in space. NASA hopes to put astronauts on Mars in the 2030s.

– Joan Fontaine, the Academy Award-winning actress best known for her roles in Suspicion and Rebecca, has died at age 96. She had been living at her home in Carmel, Calif., according to the Hollywood Reporter. Fontaine was the daughter of a patent lawyer and a stage mother who encouraged her acting career. But she was best known for a sibling rivalry with Olivia de Havilland, which the New York Times describes as "one of the longest-running sibling feuds on record." De Havilland won an Oscar in 1946 for her leading role in To Each His Own. Fontaine won an Oscar of her own six years later for her role in Suspicion, opposite Cary Grant. But her relationship with de Havilland was strained from the get-go. Fontaine once said that when she congratulated her sister at the Oscars, "She took one look at me, ignored my hand, clutched her Oscar, and wheeled away." The sisters broke up after their mother's death in 1975, and they had to be separated by a room at a memorial service in 1979. Fontaine said she threatened to leak the news to the press unless she was permitted to attend with members of her family.

– President Obama will deliver a prime-time speech tonight outlining his ISIS strategy, and a new poll by NBC News and the Wall Street Journal finds that nearly half of Americans think the US is less safe now than it was before 9/11. That's the highest percentage since the 9/11 attacks, and it's even higher than last year's 28%. The same poll found that just 26% thought the US was safer than before 9/11. "A very war-weary country ... seems to have woken up to the real threat that ISIS may present," says Republican pollster Bill McInturff. "The beheadings are so chilling to the American public. The only things I think of equal impact are the self-immolations back in Vietnam." More than six in 10 respondents believe that taking military action against the Islamic militant group ISIS is in the nation's interest, and a whopping 94% say they've heard about the beheadings. The numbers come as Obama is considering airstrikes in Iraq, and the AP reports that the president is expected to outline his strategy tonight.

Now I live in Los Angeles, where I'm a freelancer whose meetings mostly take place over coffee and whose friends are more likely to suggest we go for a hike than a cocktail. – Some 200,000 Salvadoran immigrants living in the US will lose the right to stay in the country in 2019, the Trump administration announced Monday. The immigrants have been granted temporary protected status (TPS) since two devastating earthquakes in El Salvador in 2001 left hundreds of thousands homeless, reports Reuters. The decision to end TPS for Salvadorans is part of the administration's broader push to tighten immigration laws and expel those living in the United States illegally. The move was heavily criticized by immigrant advocates who said it ignored violence in El Salvador and gave the Salvadorans few options but to leave the United States or remain illegally. "This is a real blow for everyone," says a 53-year-old woman who runs a construction business with her Honduran husband in North Carolina. "Most of us pay taxes, we're not living off the government, we're not criminals." The US Chamber of Commerce had urged the administration to extend TPS protections for Salvadorans, Haitians, and Hondurans, saying "the loss of employment authorization for these populations would adversely impact several key industries," including "construction, food processing, hospitality, and home healthcare services." – Leona Helmsley died nine years ago, but her estate is still embroiled in a legal battle. The New York City real estate mogul was known as the "Queen of Mean" for her business acumen, and she left behind a fortune estimated at $200 million, the Wall Street Journal reports. But two of her grandchildren, who are executors of her estate, want $100 million from the trust to cover their legal fees. New York's attorney general says that's "astronomical" and should be cut by about 90%, the New York Daily News reports. The grandchildren say they're entitled to part of the money because Helmsley left them nothing from her estate when she died. The battle over her estate is now in the hands of a New York judge, who has the power to order the executors to drop the fee.

– Congress wrapped up its lame-duck session with a flurry of legislation—including the repeal of Don't Ask, Don't Tell and the New START nuclear arms pact with Russia—before the House and Senate adjourned for the year last night. President Obama signed the repeal into law. "This has been a season of progress for the American people," Obama said. "This has been the most productive post-election period we've had in decades, and it comes on the heels of the most productive two years that we've had in generations." Congress passed an $814 billion economic stimulus, a massive health care overhaul, and new regulations on Wall Street trading and consumer credit cards, the Washington Post reports. The list grew longer during this month's frenetic lame-duck session: tax cuts, a nuclear arms treaty, and a repeal of the "Don't Ask, Don't Tell" policy on gays in the military. But the 111th Congress will also be remembered for endless filibuster threats, volcanic town hall meetings, and the rise of the Tea Party. All were symbols of a dissatisfaction that peaked on Nov. 2, with a Republican rout in the midterm elections. "This is the most dysfunctional political environment that I have ever seen,"

– If you've ever wanted to explore the ocean's mysteries, the X Prize Foundation has just the thing for you. It's offering up to $7 million to the team that can create a high-resolution map of the deep sea, take high-definition photos of objects, and sniff out their chemical and biological compounds, Fast Company reports. "Our oceans cover two-thirds of our planet's surface and are a crucial global source of food, energy, economic security, and even the air we breathe, yet 95% of the deep sea remains a mystery to us," says X Prize head Peter Diamandis in a press release. "The Shell Ocean Discovery X Prize will address a critical ocean challenge by accelerating innovation to further explore one of our greatest unexplored frontiers." The three-year competition, which is being funded by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and Shell Oil, is part of the foundation's "Ocean Initiative," which has already offered prizes for oil-spill clean-up and ocean pH sensors, Fast Company notes. The top team will get $4 million, with another $1 million going to the second-place team, Ocean Science Radio reports. The top 10 teams will get $1 million each. – The North American Aerospace Defense Command is ditching Google for Microsoft Bing to track Santa's progress this year. Norad, NORAD's predecessor, has been tracking Santa since 1955, and for the past five years, Google used Google Maps to provide updates on Santa's progress. But Norad says the split was "a mutually agreed-upon split," PC World reports. Norad will still provide updates on Santa's progress via its Santa Tracker website, a new Chrome extension, an Android app, and Google+. You can also call NORAD's 1-877-Hi-NORAD for live updates. "While we’ve been tracking Santa since 2004 with Google Earth, this year a team of dedicated Google Maps engineers built a new route algorithm to chart Santa’s journey around the world on Christmas Eve," says a Google Maps VP. "On his sleigh, arguably the fastest airborne vehicle in the world, Santa whips from city to city delivering presents."

– A 39-year-old woman from the Bronx is accused of getting married to 10 men between 1999 and 2010, all without ever changing her name, reports the New York Post. Liana Barrientos is currently married to four people, but authorities believe she was marrying men to get them into the country and never bothered to legally change her name. "This is a huge breach in security," says a national security expert. "If someone could remarry 10 times without bringing it to the attention of the authorities, potentially an al-Qaeda plant could come in, marry this woman, and be in this country illegally, plotting, recruiting, perhaps even executing a terrorist attack." Barrientos has been arraigned on charges of filing a false instrument and trespassing, reports DNA Info. She and her niece were arrested after walking through the gate of a subway station without paying their fare.

– The Texas woman who inspired the 1958 Buddy Holly song "Peggy Sue" has died at a Lubbock hospital. Peggy Sue Gerron Rackham of Lubbock died Monday at University Medical Center, according to UMC spokesman Eric Finley. She was 78. The family gave the hospital permission to confirm the death, but asked that no additional information be released, Finley said Tuesday. Peggy Sue Gerron in 2008 released her autobiography, Whatever Happened to Peggy Sue?: A Memoir by Buddy Holly's Peggy Sue, to mark the 50th anniversary of the song. Gerron, while promoting her autobiography, said material for the memoir came from about 150 diary entries she made during the time she knew Holly. "I wanted to give him [Holly] his voice. It's my book, my memoirs," she said about her book, according to a 2008 AP story. "We were very, very good friends. He was probably one of the best friends I ever had." She married drummer Jerry Allison, from Holly's rock 'n' roll band The Crickets, and they later divorced. Her son-in-law, Tom Stathos, on Monday reminisced and told KCBD-TV in Lubbock that the song "Peggy Sue" initially had a different name. "

– The town of Cerro Gordo, located in the Inyo Mountains near Death Valley in California, means "fat hill" in Spanish. It also means "ghost town," and the latest owner says he plans to keep it that way. Brent Underwood bought the town for $1.4 million after it was put on the market in June, CNN reports. The asking price for Cerro Gordo was $925,000. "We really didn't expect the activity we had," says Jake Rasmuson, a real estate agent who sold the town. "There were other offers, but Mr. Underwood's plan was beneficial to the preservation and public use of the property." Underwood and his business partner, Jon Bier, plan to "renovate a select number of the existing buildings to a point we'd be comfortable hosting people for long periods of time," Underwood says. They plan to bring "high level programming in forms of writing, music events, dining experiences, photo shoots, theater, special events, and more," Underwood tells the New York Times. Cerro Gordo has 22 buildings, including a saloon, church, bunkhouse, and superintendent's house, and Rasmuson says he hopes to find someone who can use the superintendent's house, which has a bloodstain under

– Get Out is the feature debut of writer-director Jordan Peele, who worked with Keegan-Michael Key on the hit Comedy Central show Key & Peele. The film follows a young black man as he makes new friends in a mostly white neighborhood. Here's what critics are saying: Get Out is "so truly, madly, mercilessly entertaining, even when it makes you want to jump out of your skin," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Times. "It is small-c catholic in its tastes, liberally sampling elements of Guess Who's Coming to Dinner, Rosemary's Baby and Invasion of the Body Snatchers before morphing into the most potent racial revenge fantasy since Django Unchained." It's "as much a triumph of craft as of inspiration," she adds. " Peele's handheld camera in these scenes keeps the anxiety high. It's rare to find a first-time director so fully in command of his tone." " Peele's movie is as much a triumph of craft as of inspiration," writes Rafer Guzmn at Newsday. – It Gets Better is a nonprofit organization dedicated to ending bullying of gay, lesbian, and transgender youth, and it's got a new project in the works. The group is putting out a book, It Gets Better: A Story of Hope for LGBT Youth, and it's looking for volunteers to help with the project, the New York Daily News reports. The book will include stories from some of the group's volunteers, as well as those who've experienced bullying, suicide, or other types of bullying. "We want to make sure that the bullying doesn't happen again," says the project's executive director. "We want to make sure that LGBT youth know that it gets better."

– When it comes to long-distance air travel, jet lag is one of the biggest headaches. But with the new Airbus A350 XWB—the first aircraft to land in the US last week—the airline says it has found a solution, Wired reports. "The design process was about optimization, pushing the constraints, and opening up the box of solutions," says Alain De Zotti, chief engineer of the A350 XWB program. Among the improvements: The plane's wings are 20% bigger, 10% wider, and 50% of the structure is carbon fiber-reinforced plastic, which is less susceptible to corrosion than aluminum, Wired reports. The material has been used in aircrafts in the past, but not in such large proportions. The A350 also features Rolls Royce engines, which, according to Wired, "result in fuel economy that is 25% better than similarly sized planes from competitors." The A350 XWB also features a pressurized cabin that's an inch wider than its predecessor, and LED lights that change color to mimic the sun's natural glow. The filtering system changes the air in the plane every two to three minutes to keep air from stale. The plane is pressurized to 6,000 feet, which, according to Wired, makes it more comfortable for passengers

– The UK is planning to ban the sale of new gasoline and diesel cars in Britain by 2040, the BBC reports. "We can't carry on with diesel and petrol cars," environment secretary Michael Gove says. "There is no alternative to embracing new technology." According to CNN, air pollution is responsible for 40,000 deaths in Britain each year. It's also linked to strokes, cancer, asthma, and heart disease. "Air pollution is one of the biggest public health issues we face," Gove says. The plan also calls for 80% of new cars to be electric or plug-in hybrids by 2050.

– A Jewish professor at Columbia University says her office was vandalized with swastikas and anti-Semitic slurs, the New York Times reports. "I was in shock," Elizabeth Midlarsky says. "I stopped for a moment, because I couldn't believe what I was seeing." According to the Columbia Spectator, Midlarsky discovered the graffiti in her office Wednesday afternoon. The NYPD is investigating the incident as a hate crime. Midlarsky says the swastikas were painted in red and the slur "Yid" was written in black marker. Midlarsky, who's worked at Columbia for 28 years, says the swastikas almost passed out when she opened the door. Midlarsky says it's the second time her office has been vandalized with swastikas. In 2007, her door was spray-painted with a swastika and anti-Semitic flyers were left in her mailbox. No arrests were made at the time. Midlarsky says this time the swastikas appear to be the result of a rise in anti-Semitic crimes across the country. – Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell says he believes the women who accuse Alabama Senate nominee Roy Moore of pursuing sexual relationships with them when they were teenagers and he should step aside from the race, CNN reports. "I believe the women, yes," McConnell told reporters in Kentucky. "I think he should step aside." Moore, who has denied the allegations against him, responded to McConnell's comments by tweeting, "The person who should step aside is @SenateMajLdr Mitch McConnell. He has failed conservatives and must be replaced. #DrainTheSwamp." The National Republican Senatorial Committee has already cut its ties with Moore.

– President-elect Donald Trump took to Twitter on Tuesday morning to issue a warning to anyone who wants to burn an American flag. "Nobody should be allowed to burn the American flag - if they do, there must be consequences - perhaps loss of citizenship or year in jail!" he tweeted. The Supreme Court has struck down laws against the burning or desecration of the flag, most recently in 1990, because they violated the First Amendment of the Constitution, which protects freedom of speech, Politico reports. A 1958 Supreme Court decision rejected the practice of stripping US citizenship as a form of criminal punishment, on the grounds that it violates Eighth Amendment protections against "cruel and unusual punishment." In a 5-4 decision in 1989, the Supreme Court upheld the right of protesters to burn the flag, with the late Justice Antonin Scalia siding with the protesters. He later said he based his ruling on a "Sen" reading of the Constitution. "If it were up to me, I would put in jail every sandal-wearing, scruffy-bearded weirdo who burns the American flag," Scalia said in 2015 in Philadelphia. "But I am not king." E! reports that the socialite's fashion line, Paris Hilton's Closet, was a "complete disaster" from the get-go. The line featured mostly one- and two-piece bathing suits, as well as clothing featuring Hilton's face, but it was a complete failure from the get-go, with E! noting that Hilton was "caught off guard" by the success of the line. Trump touched down Wednesday evening in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, and headed to a local community college, where he got a look at agriculture technology innovations before leading a campaign rally. He reveled in Georgia Republican Karen Handel's congressional victory in an election viewed as an early referendum on his presidency. "We're 5-0 in special elections," Trump said in front of a boisterous crowd that packed a downtown arena. "The truth is, people love us ... they haven't figured it out yet." He also applauded Republican Ralph Norman, who notched a slimmer-than-expected win in a special election to fill the South Carolina congressional seat vacated by Mick Mulvaney, and mocked Handel's challenger, Jon Ossoff, saying the Democrats "spent $30 million on this kid who forgot to live in the district." Trump, no stranger to victory laps, turned his visit to a battleground state he captured in November into a celebration of his resilience despite the cloud of investigations that has enveloped his administration and sent his poll numbers tumbling. – Clint Eastwood's American Sniper held onto first place for the third weekend in a row, with $30.7 million in ticket sales, according to studio estimates today. That's a tiny fraction of the record-breaking Super Bowl weekend gross of $31.1 million, held by Hanna Montana/Miley Cyrus: The Best of Both Worlds Concert Tour. But it was enough to propel Sniper to a $247.98 million domestic tally, notes the Hollywood Reporter. Project Almanac, meanwhile, a "found-footage thriller," opened at No. 2 with $8.5 million, and Black or White, starring Kevin Costner and Octavia Spencer, took No. 4 with $6.5 million. Rounding out the top five were The Boy Next Door at No. 5 with $6.1 million, and The Loft at No. 10 with $2.9 million.

– David Petraeus is about to face felony charges over his affair with Jill Kelley. Federal prosecutors have recommended that the former CIA director be charged for mishandling classified information, sources tell the New York Times. No charges have been filed yet, but prosecutors have recommended that Petraeus be charged with mishandling classified information, which carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison, according to the sources, who say the leak is an attempt to put pressure on Eric Holder to bring charges, especially given that other, lower-level government officials have been charged with leaking classified information. The investigation into the case has been going on for more than a year, the Times notes, and Holder has declined to comment publicly on the case. President Obama said at a press conference shortly after Petraeus' resignation that he had no evidence that the general had disclosed classified information "that in any way would have had a negative impact on our national security."

– If you're looking for a pickup truck that can tow up to 30,000 pounds, Ford's new F-Series Super Duty Limited is the truck for you. It starts at $32,890 for the base F-250 and goes up to $94,455 for the F-450 with the 6.7-liter Power Stroke diesel engine, reports Motor1. The Limited also comes with features such as adaptive steering, cruise control, lane keeping, and a 360-degree camera to help you with things like reversing and parking. The engine is rated at 440 horsepower and 925 pound-feet of torque, and it's paired with a six-speed manual or a six-speed automatic. It's not the first time Ford has offered such a truck, but it's the first time it's available with a diesel. The F-Series Super Duty line has long been seen as the go-to truck for those looking to make a buck on the ranch, but the popularity of the diesel model has led to a boom in sales of luxury-oriented Super Duty models, reports the Los Angeles Times. The 2017 F-Series Super Duty Limited will be offered this winter in either single or dual-rear-wheel configurations.

– Former Trump aide Sebastian Gorka is wanted in Hungary on a weapons charge, according to an arrest warrant seen by BuzzFeed and local outlet 444. The warrant, which was issued in September 2016 and was issued during Gorka's entire seven-month stint in the White House, is for "firearm or ammunition abuse," though details of the charge are scarce. The Hungarian police's website only notes the date of the warrant, and that it was filed with the Budars police station in Budapest. 444 notes that the charge could have resulted from an incident as far back as 2009. Gorka, born in the UK to Hungarian-born parents, has a longstanding interest in guns and told Recoil magazine earlier this year that his "everyday carry" includes two pistols, a knife, a tourniquet, and a copy of the US Constitution. He declined to comment to the Guardian, saying, "Since I moved to the US in 2008 ... More #FAKENEWS."

– Target knew it had been hacked nearly two weeks before it finally informed customers of the massive security breach, according to a scathing report from Bloomberg Businessweek picked up by Gawker. The report says that months before the hack, the retailer installed a $1.6 million malware detection tool from a firm called FireEye and had security specialists in Bangalore monitor the system at all hours. On Nov. 30, the firm informed Target's security team in Minneapolis, but "for some reason, Minneapolis didn’t react to the sirens," the report says. Target's security team apparently disabled an option on FireEye's system to delete malware as it's detected, according to the report. The breach could have been stopped without human intervention if Target's security team "had that last decision point of 'what do I do,'" the chief information security officer for Bombardier Aerospace tells Bloomberg. "Typically, as a security team, you want to have that last decision point of 'what do I do,'" he says. "What this points to, in the end, is inaction on the part of Target and a clear effort by FireEye to shore up its reputation."

– It's called a "meal appeal" spectrum: foods that are easy to eat, hard to eat, or just plain boring. And for people who suffer from swallowing disorders called Barrett's esophagus, the "arch-enemy of all foods to swallow," bread is one of the most difficult to chew, reports the Guardian. But Japan's EN Biotsuka Pharmaceutical Co. Ltd. has come up with an engineered substitute called iEat Bread, which is being marketed directly to consumers and is being studied for its ability to absorb saliva that would otherwise lubricate the throat and form sticky balls that can prevent the smooth journey on to the esophagus. Unadulterated white bread purée, for example, looks a bit like cereal left overnight in a bowl of milk and tends to be the low end of what researchers call the "meal appeal" spectrum. The new bread is reformulated with enzymes to alter its physical properties, and although it looks and tastes like real bread, it is easily mashed up by the tongue and is only one-fifth as sticky as normal bread, reports the Independent. It's not the first time iEat Bread has been studied for its ability to absorb saliva. In fact, it's just one of a number of advances in the

– Just hours before a July 1 deadline set by the Obama administration, the Pentagon announced Friday it will delay allowing transgender people to join the military, USA Today reports. "Secretary Mattis today approved a recommendation by the services to defer accessing transgender applicants into the military until Jan. 1, 2018," Pentagon spokeswoman Dana White said in a statement. "The services will review their accession plans and provide input on the impact to the readiness and lethality of our forces." The Army and Marine Corps both sought a delay. The Palm Center, which studies sexuality in the military, says the move will force transgender people to lie about their identity in order to join the military. "That makes no sense because, as predicted by all of the research, transgender military service has been a success," the center's director says. "It has been unequivocally proven that allowing qualified transgender people to serve openly strengthens our military and creates a more inclusive and diverse force. The issue has been thoroughly studied and moving forward with this new recruitment policy is imperative in order for the military to be able to recruit the best talent our nation has to offer." Rep. Vicky Hartzler, a Republican from Missouri, said allowing transgender troops to serve openly is "ill-conceived and contrary to our goals of increasing troop readiness."

– The Harvard professor who first presented the so-called "Gospel of Jesus' Wife" is out with a new paper in the Harvard Theological Review that supports her theory that the ancient papyrus refers to Jesus being married. Carbon dating, microscopic imaging, and other tests have all backed up Professor Karen King's theory, reports the New York Times. But they don't prove the text was written in ancient times. For one thing, it's not clear how a modern forger would have gotten the right kind of ink and applied it to a blank piece of ancient papyrus, explains the Boston Globe. It's possible, however, that the ink could have been applied in modern times. King's theory is that the text was part of a larger debate among early Christians about the role of women, family, and celibacy. “I’m basically hoping that we can move past the issue of forgery to questions about the significance of this fragment for the history of Christianity, for thinking about questions like, ‘Why does Jesus being married, or not, even matter?’” she says.

– Mark Zuckerberg is donating another $1 billion worth of stock to the Silicon Valley Community Foundation, "by far the largest gift in our history," says the foundation's CEO. It's part of the Facebook founder's pledge to spend more than half of his wealth on philanthropy, the San Jose Mercury News reports. Zuckerberg is selling $2.3 billion worth of Facebook stock to cover taxes, and donating 18 million shares to the foundation. "We believe this gift will immensely improve the lives of people here and elsewhere," says the foundation's CEO. Zuckerberg and his wife, pediatrician Priscilla Chan, have pledged to donate at least half their wealth to philanthropic causes, the Mercury News notes.

– Beto O'Rourke's chances of unseating Sen. Ted Cruz in Texas appear to be growing slimmer by the day. A new Emerson College poll released Monday has O'Rourke leading Cruz 38-37, the Hill reports. That's within the poll's margin of error of 4.4 percentage points. Meanwhile, the Cook Political Report has shifted the race from "likely Republican" to "lean Republican," and an NBC News–Marist poll released last week had Cruz leading O'Rourke by 4 points. President Trump weighed in on the race Monday morning, tweeting: "Texas just re-elected Ted Cruz, a man who has been fighting hard for us. Beto O'Rourke wants to raise your taxes, opposes Border Security, wants to raise the minimum wage. Vote for Ted Cruz, a man who has been fighting hard for you!" (The last time a Democrat was elected to the Senate in Texas was in 1982.)

– The world's most expensive home is going to a 22-year-old British heiress. Candy Spelling has agreed to sell her 57,000-square-foot Los Angeles mansion to Petra Ecclestone, daughter of Formula One racing boss Bernie Ecclestone, the Wall Street Journal reports. The sale price was not disclosed. The 57,000-square-foot mansion, built by Spelling and her late husband Aaron, has a double staircase inspired by Gone With the Wind, a bowling alley, a beauty salon, gift-wrapping rooms, and parking for 100 cars. Ecclestone will be splitting her time between London and Los Angeles after her August wedding to entrepreneur James Stunt, according to a spokeswoman.

He praised Black Lives Matter and "black Twitter" activists for their efforts, but said activists must be willing to sit at the table with their opponents, the Guardian reports. "You consolidate your gains and then you move on to the next fight from a stronger position," he said. Black Lives Matter leader DeRay Mckesson tells the Guardian that activists must be willing to engage in policy changes that don't align with their goals. "Without the pressure from all of us being in the streets, there would have been no 21st-century taskforce on policing, so this is a 'both-and,' not an 'either-or,' situation," he says. April Reign, a prominent black Twitter voice and the originator of the #oscarssowhite hashtag, tells the Guardian that the speech was inspiring and important. "Now that he's got his second-term swag on, he's able to let loose a little bit," she says. "I think he hit a lot of the right marks and I think it's one for the ages

But the Department of Homeland Security turned down the request, citing the Jones Act, which requires that all cargo and passengers be transported on American vessels. "We were pursuing a waiver, but we've been advised we wouldn't get one," a DOT spokesman tells the Washington Free Beacon. "It seems unlikely we will get it." With a waiver, the state would have made just one trip to get the salt from Searsport, Maine. "The supplies are tight. We have enough for another storm or two," the spokesman says. With a waiver, the state would have been able to move the salt quickly, but it will "take us a longer time," he adds. Municipalities in the past have been able to access the state's stockpile of salt if needed, but the shortage has made that impossible. "If a county ran out in the past, we would share salt. – The explosion that injured 29 people in New York City's Chelsea neighborhood on Saturday may have been caused by a compound called Tannerite, which is easy to find online and can be bought on its own, CBS New York reports. The compound is sold as a mix of two chemicals and it creates high explosives when combined. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives defines binary explosives as pre-packaged products consisting of two separate components—typically an oxidizer like ammonium nitrate and a fuel like aluminum or another metal. The ATF doesn't regulate the compound because separately, the chemicals don't meet the definition of explosive. In response to the Chelsea explosion, Tannerite Sports said it is working to determine if their product was definitely used in Saturday's explosion. “As far as our knowledge and independent testing results show, our product can only be set off by a successful high-power rifle shot directly to the target; and in addition that once done it vaporizes as it is an end product,” the company said in a statement. – John Daly says President Obama is "pretty good" when it comes to golfing, but he's not holding his breath waiting for the commander in chief to up his game. "He's pretty good, but he doesn't hold a candle to the all-time GOAT presidential links master, George HW Bush," the golfer tells TMZ. "I mean, he's not as good as Bush, but he's pretty good." Daly—who has a history of making anti-Obama statements—adds he's "not a big fan" of the president's golf swing. "I don't think he's very good at it," he says. "I mean, he's got his hands all over the place."

Police never found his mother, never identified him, and never charged anyone in his death. But every year since 1988, they've come here to pay their respects and remember. "It shows our commitment to the baby and to the children that we represent every day in the community," says a police lieutenant. – The first action sports athlete to be diagnosed with chronic traumatic encephalopathy has been identified as Dave Mirra. The 41-year-old, who died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound in February, showed signs of the degenerative brain disease, USA Today reports. "I started to notice changes in his mood. And then it quickly started to get worse," his wife, Lauren Mirra, tells ESPN. "He wasn't able to be present in any situation or conversation, so it was hard to be in a relationship with him to any degree. He was lost. I looked straight through him on a few occasions. And I was like, 'Where are you? Where are you? What is wrong?'" The disease, which has been found in the brains of dozens of football players, is linked to repeated head trauma and can lead to dementia and depression. Mirra, who competed in everything from rallycross to triathlon and held the record for the most X Games medals with 24, suffered a fractured skull at 19 and dabbled in boxing after his retirement from BMX. – In an interview set to air Sunday on Dateline, Marcia Clark—the prosecutor who tried OJ Simpson for the murder of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ron Goldman—says she's at fault for the case's outcome. "At the end of the day, we really ... there was no way to reach that jury," she tells Dateline. "There was no way to make them believe. There really wasn't." A preview of the interview released Tuesday notes that Clark also says she was against Simpson trying on the gloves, which police said the killer left behind, during the trial. "That was not my call. That was not my call," she tells Dateline. "I did not want him to try on the evidence gloves. I never did." Clark says that co-counsel Christopher Darden apologized to her for the huge blunder. "And I said, 'It's OK. If that lost the case for us, we were never going to win anyway,'" she says. Dateline airs at 9pm Eastern Sunday.

– A video of a fox in the Chernobyl exclusion zone carving up a sandwich has gone viral, and it's not because it's tasty. It's because it doesn't seem to care that it's being fed by journalists. The fox was found by journalists near the Chernobyl nuclear disaster zone, which was abandoned by humans after 1986 and has since seen an increasing population of foxes, wolves, and bears. According to the BBC, a radio crew gave the bread and meat to the animal, and the video has gone viral with more than 1 million hits on social and news media sites. The area was abandoned by humans after the disaster in 1986. There now appears to be an increasing number of foxes, wolves, and bears in the zone. The fox shows no fear of humans, stacking up meat and bread like a sandwich, which it carries off for later.

– President Obama took to Twitter last night to offer his condolences to the victims of the Boston Marathon bombing. "My thoughts and prayers are with the victims and their families," he tweeted. "This was a terrible tragedy, and we will do everything in our power to help. #Boston." The White House says Obama also wants to thank the first responders and first responders' families, the Boston Globe reports. The marathon bombing killed Tamerlan and Dzhokhar Tsarnaev and injured more than 100 others. The White House says Obama also wants to thank the first responders and first responders' families for their "extraordinary service."

– The California man accused of shooting and killing a sheriff's deputy earlier this month has been charged with attempted murder. Jack Lee Breiner, 47, was charged with first-degree murder in the death of Modoc County Sheriff's Deputy Jack Hopkins, who was killed Oct. 19 while responding to a disturbance call at a rural property near Alturas, reports the Redding Record Searchlight. Police say Breiner shot and killed the deputy as he entered the property, then exchanged fire with another deputy as he fled. The second deputy was shot and wounded. Breiner, who was wounded in the exchange of fire, has been charged with murder, attempted murder, and other crimes. The Modoc County Sheriff's Office says Hopkins, a 26-year veteran of the force, leaves behind a wife and two children. The Alturas Police Department has offered its condolences to the deputy's family in a Facebook post.

– Sarah Palin's year ended with a whimper: Lisa Murkowski has been elected as a write-in candidate in Alaska's Senate race, reports the Financial Times. It's "a blow to Mrs. Palin, who presented herself as a political kingmaker this election season, with decidedly mixed results," writes John Dickerson. "If there were any race in which Mrs. Palin's influence should have tipped the scales, it would have been this one." Palin endorsed 60 candidates this year, but only 15 of them won, notes Politico. "Mrs. Palin undermined her potential credibility by focusing on politics rather than policy, by gambling on a slew of high-profile endorsements (which kept her on television, at campaign events) rather than trying to find and nurture a handful of intellectual or philosophical protegees," writes Dickerson. – If you're like most of us, you probably have at least one copy of the online privacy policy and terms of service (TOS) you've just signed up for—and you're probably not reading them. So say researchers out of the UK's Exeter University and the University of California-Riverside, who set up a fake social media site called NameDrop, where 543 people signed up, then had open-ended questions about the privacy policy and terms of service for the fictional site, Ars Technica reports. The privacy policy and TOS were checked in at about 8,000 and 4,000 words, respectively, but the study found that 98% of participants didn't even realize there were "gotcha" clauses in the policies, such as users agreeing to "immediately assign their first-born child" to the site and agreeing to be "enforceable until the year 2050" if they didn't have children. The study, published in the open-access PeerJ journal, notes that users were most likely to have ignored the privacy policy and TOS if they had just signed up for the site and clicked the "quick join" clickwrap. The average time it took to read the privacy policy was 73 seconds, and the TOS was 51 seconds

– A Florida man who is challenging the state's ban on gay adoptions has won the right to adopt his two foster brothers, the Miami Herald reports. Martin Gill and his partner have been raising the boys, now ages 4 and 9, for the past four years. Florida's ban on gay adoptions dates back to 1977, when Gov. Rick Scott signed a bill allowing gay couples to serve as foster parents. Gill and his partner have been fighting the ban with the help of the ACLU, and a juvenile court judge approved the adoption in November. The state's attorney general immediately appealed the decision, and the brothers remain in Gill's care. "It's hard to imagine that a 4-year-old boy and a 9-year-old boy would be removed from your life and thrown in a children's home," Gill tells the Herald. "But that's exactly what happened to them." "I have every intention of working with our international partners in lawless areas around the globe to make sure that we're keeping the American people safe," Obama told People in an interview picked up by Reuters. "The same is true in Somalia, another country where there are large chunks that are not fully under government control and al-Qaeda is trying to take advantage of them," the president said. – The parking garage in Arlington, Va., that played a key role in the Watergate scandal will be demolished as part of a development project, the Washington Post reports. The garage, built in the early 1960s, was where reporter Bob Woodward met "Deep Throat," later revealed to be FBI official Mark Felt. The information Felt passed on to Woodward helped expose the Watergate scandal, which led to the resignation of President Richard Nixon in 1974. A historical marker marking the location of the garage was erected by Arlington County in 2011. Monday Properties, which plans to tear down the two aging office buildings in the Rosslyn neighborhood, says it hopes to preserve the marker. "We obviously think the location where Mr. Woodward and our friend Mark Felt met is certainly an integral part of a much broader historical event," says Monday executive vice president Tim Helmig. "The garage is at the end of its useful life, and with the redevelopment the configuration of the garage itself is going to change." He says he doesn't expect work to start until 2016 or 2017.

– Two Syrians were arrested in Geneva on Friday on suspicion of making, concealing, and transporting explosives and violating a Swiss law against al-Qaeda and the Islamic State, the BBC reports. Geneva has been on high alert since the Paris terror attacks last month, and the two men were arrested after traces of explosives were found in their car. They "were stopped by Geneva police ... because of the increased vigilance required from the police force," the BBC quotes Geneva's attorney general as saying. "These people, because of their behavior and nationality, were subject to more careful checks, and these checks revealed traces of explosives in the car they were using." The two men were arrested on the day they arrived in Switzerland, according to the BBC. Geneva prosecutor Olivier Jornot says the men—who can't speak French—only "recently arrived" in Switzerland and had Syrian passports. Jornot says the car they were driving was at one point used to transport explosives, but it's not clear if it was them who did so. Swiss media reports the arrests were the result of a tip from the US.

– Austin Pledger, an autistic boy from Alabama, took the anti-psychotic drug Risperdal as an 8-year-old, and by the time he started taking it in 2002, he was already size 46 DD breasts. Now 20, Pledger has been awarded $2.5 million in damages for Johnson & Johnson's failure to warn about the drug's side effects, reports People. Pledger's mother didn't know about the side effects until after he started taking the drug, and she testified that when she looked at her son's breasts, "he would smash them on a table. And that when he gets out of the shower he covers himself in a towel before he looks at himself in a mirror." Risperdal's maker, Janssen, is "disappointed" by the verdict and may appeal. "Risperdal has improved the lives of countless children and adults throughout the world," said a spokeswoman. "We firmly believe this verdict should be overturned." Pledger's case is the first of more than 1,200 filed in Philadelphia over Risperdal to be settled, according to his lawyer.

The Sydney Morning Herald reports the Year 1 student was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes at age 3 and attended a course taught by Hongchi Xiao, a Chinese-born self-described "healer" who describes himself as a "registered nurse" and as having treated thousands of people in his homeland with his own version of paidalajin, which combines fasting, stretching, and slapping the skin to treat diabetes. The course ended when the boy was found unconscious at a hotel after leaving the course on April 30, 2015. Police say Xiao, who left Australia days after the boy's death, denied the boy food and medicine, the Sydney Morning Herald reports. The boy's parents, both 41, were arrested at their home Tuesday and charged with "gross negligence" in the boy's death. They face up to 25 years in jail if convicted. Xiao, who left Australia in the days after the boy's death and is still on the run, has been charged with manslaughter in the death of a 71-year-old diabetic woman he was treating in England last year. She died suddenly during a retreat he ran.

The nonprofit that owns it has reached its $100,000 fundraising goal, but it needs $60,000 a month to keep the rehabilitation project afloat. The ship, which set a new transatlantic speed record at the time of its launch, was originally intended to be turned into a museum and mixed-use destination. But costs have skyrocketed as the ship, which is still covered by a life insurance policy, has been unable to stay out of the water. The ship "has sat idle for over 40 years against all odds, and it would be a crime on many levels to see her disposed of," the SS United States Conservancy said in a press release last month. – A new species of centipede has been discovered in Croatia's Velebit Mountains, where it calls home in the world's deepest cave. Geophilus hadesi—named for Hades, the " invertebrate king of hell"—is one of only two species of centipede that never leave its underground home, reports LiveScience. The new species has a long, flattened body, 33 pairs of legs that are "unusually long," and a pair of "exceptionally elongated" antennae and furlike body hair that allow it to detect prey in total darkness, says the lead author of the paper on the new species in ZooKeys. Jeff Hall, 32, who ran for a local water board last year and served as regional director for the National Socialist Movement, was shot in the head, the Press-Enterprise reports. Two handguns were recovered from the home, and police are investigating whether the shooting was intentional or accidental. The boy has been booked at juvenile hall for investigation of murder, police say. Neighbors say they were shaken by months of intimidation by Hall and other members of the neo-Nazi group. "Honestly, I feel like it's over," says a neighbor who lives across the street. "It was scary here. Hopefully we'll never see any of them again."

Police were analyzing security cameras to find how the 196 lapel pins ended up in a flowerbed of a hotel close to Incheon International Airport, just west of Seoul, according to a local police officer who requested anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak to the media on the matter. He gave no further details, but South Korean media said police were looking at a possibility that the lapel pins may have been carried by propaganda balloons that North Korea floated across the border. The possession of such lapel pins would be illegal in South Korea, where praising North Korea is punishable by up to seven years in prison. All North Koreans must wear lapel pins carrying the images of both Kim Jong Il and his father Kim Il Sung or the images of either of them. – President Trump is blaming "bad environmental laws" for California's wildfires, which have killed at least nine people and destroyed more than 1,000 homes. "California wildfires are being magnified & made so much worse by the bad environmental laws which aren't allowing massive amount of readily available water to be properly utilized," he tweeted Sunday. "It is being diverted into the Pacific Ocean. Must also tree clear to stop fire spreading!" The tweet has left experts scratching their heads, the Hill reports. "On the water side, it boggles the mind," UC Merced professor and wildfire specialist LeRoy Westerling tells the San Francisco Chronicle. "We do manage all of our rivers in California, and all the water is allocated many times over. So I'm not sure what he was recommending. Even if we eliminated all habitat for riparian species and fish, and allowed saltwater intrusion into the delta and set up a sprinkler system over the state, that wouldn't compensate for greater moisture loss from climate change." A California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection spokeswoman tells the Chronicle that she's not aware of water shortages, but "that doesn't mean it's not happening."

– If you suffer from lactose intolerance, you're not alone: About 30% of Americans have it, the Washington Post reports, and it can cause stomach cramps and diarrhea within 30 minutes of eating dairy products. Now, a study in Annals of Family Medicine finds that people who drink raw milk don't seem to be any better off. "These data do not support the widespread claim that raw milk confers benefits in reducing the discomfort of lactose intolerance," write the researchers. The study looked at 16 adults with confirmed lactose intolerance and lactose malabsorption, each of whom drank three types of milk for eight days: organic whole raw milk, organic whole pasteurized milk, and plain soy milk. They also had a "washout" phase, during which they avoided dairy and lactose-containing products. The results: "Raw milk failed to reduce lactose malabsorption or lactose intolerance symptoms compared with pasteurized milk among adults positive for lactose malabsorption," the researchers write. "Although other health benefit claims for raw milk are plausible, such claims remain similarly anecdotal and unsubstantiated and should be subjected to appropriately designed controlled trials." In other lactose-intolerance news, the Guardian reports on the discovery of a milk-eating Mesolithic hunter-gatherer who had dark skin and blue eyes.

Her lawyer says she will file for Chapter 7 relief, which would allow her to sell the house and pay child support, the AP reports.

– First-time moms may have a harder time getting pregnant than their male counterparts, according to a new study published in the journal Radiology. Researchers at a fertility center in Barcelona, Spain, scanned first-time moms' brains before, during, and after their attempts to get pregnant, then again six months and 12 months later. Of the 25 women who had the MRI before and after trying to get pregnant, five were still pregnant six months later, LiveScience reports. The study's lead author says the brains of first-time moms were similar to those of women who'd had previous pregnancies, but the difference in brain activity between the two groups wasn't statistically significant, according to a press release. The lead researcher says it's not clear why the difference exists, but it's possible it has to do with the fact that first-time moms tend to have more gray matter in their brains than women who've had previous pregnancies, LiveScience reports. The study's authors say more research is needed to see if the same thing happens for women who've had multiple pregnancies or for first-time moms who've had more than one. (MRIs can reveal more about a woman's brain than blood tests can.)

– Christine Lagarde's Guardian interview has not gone over well in Greece. The IMF chief has been pilloried for blaming Greeks for the country's economic woes and saying that she has more sympathy for children in sub-Saharan Africa than those in Athens. "I think more of the little kids from a school in a little village in Niger who get teaching two hours a day, sharing one chair for three of them, and who are very keen to get an education," she tells the paper. "I have them in my mind all the time. Because I think they need even more help than the people in Athens." In response, the Greek prime minister called Lagarde's remarks "insulting," the New York Times reports. "Greek workers pay their taxes, which are unbearable," said a lawmaker from the far-left Syriza party. A French government spokeswoman described Lagarde's remarks as "a bit of a caricature," while a French lawmaker called for her to resign.

Strampel's arrest comes the day before a press conference from an investigator hired by Schuette to investigate MSU's handling of the Nassar scandal. More than 150 women and girls, including Olympic gymnasts, spoke at Nassar's sentencing hearings in Michigan.

– At least two animals were killed and 14 people injured when baseball-sized hail pummeled the Cheyenne Mountain Zoo in Colorado Springs on Monday, the Denver Post reports. "It was hail the size I've never seen before," the zoo's marketing director tells the Post. "Basically chunks of ice ... It's frightening." At least 3,400 people were at the zoo when the hail hit, shattering windows and damaging cars in the parking lot. A 13-year-old caped vulture and a 4-year-old duck were killed in the storm. A third animal was initially reported dead, but later turned out to be severely injured. Animals and humans scrambled for cover from the sudden barrage, visitor Jesse Barkalow says. The zoo will be closed Tuesday while it assesses the damage, marketing director Jenny Koch tells CNN. Five injured people were taken to a hospital and nine more were treated on the scene.

– The State Department today announced the closure of all embassies and consulates in the Middle East and North Africa due to an al-Qaeda threat, reports CNN. embassies from Bangladesh to Libya were also closed. The news comes a day after the US recalled all its personnel from Benghazi, where an attack last month killed the US ambassador and three other Americans. "As a precaution, the State Department has ordered the closure of all embassies and consulates in the region," says the department in a statement. "These closures are out of an abundance of caution and are due to al-Qaeda's ongoing efforts to engage in acts of terrorism." The threat is specific to Yemen, reports the AP, but it also applies to other countries in the region. The travel alert applies only to the US, and it's not clear how long the closure will last.

– A new spider family has been discovered in a part of the world that's been crawling around without humans for thousands of years. The spider, which lives in coastal forests from California to British Columbia and is about the size of a half-dollar coin when its legs are extended, has large raptorial claws that suggest it is a fierce predator, reports the Los Angeles Times. The species has been named Trogloraptor, or "cave robber," and researchers say it's the biggest arachnid ever found in the West. The spider was spotted by scientists and spelunkers who found it hanging from the roofs of caves in the Klamath-Siskiyou region of Oregon and California, according to a study in the journal ZooKeys. It's not clear exactly how the spider mates or what it eats, but captive specimens have so far refused to eat a variety of prey provided in the lab, reports the Washington Post. "If such a large and bizarre spider could have gone undetected for so long, who knows what else may lurk undiscovered in this remarkable part of the world," the study said. (Earlier this year, scientists discovered a new kind of dinosaur in the Pacific.)

– Women who give birth in their 30s are more likely to have smart kids, a new study suggests. Researchers at the London School of Economics looked at data from the Millennium Cohort Study, which tracks the development of 18,000 British children for an "extended period of time," and found that kids born to women in their 30s scored higher in cognitive tests and were more likely to be intelligent, the Times reports. "First-time mothers in their 30s are, for example, likely to be more educated, have higher incomes, are more likely to be in stable relationships, have healthier lifestyles, seek prenatal care earlier, and have planned their pregnancies," says a researcher. But the study also found that women who give birth in their forties didn't play with their kids as much, and their kids were more prone to be obese, the Stir reports.

They scheduled emergency surgery, but when the London man went in, they were "very surprised to see blood coming from the liver," Dr. Joshua Luck, a resident surgeon at North Middlesex University Hospital, tells Live Science. Doctors even thought they might have injured a blood vessel during the surgery because the blood was coming from the abdominal cavity. But when they opened the man's liver, they discovered the cause of the injury was actually liver damage caused by being hit by a paintball pellet two days earlier. "This represents the first report of paintball-related blunt traumatic injury to the liver," the doctors write in BMJ Case Reports. "Solid organ injuries of this nature have only been reported three times previously." The man had been hit twice on the lower right hand side by a paintball pellet and had to have his liver packed or put pressure on it overnight. The dogs were on display at a traveling circus near Brescia, with children posing for photos next to them, paying a fee for the "panda" privilege. "Unfortunately, the rules passed by City Council don't allow true ridesharing to operate," Lyft said, adding it will suspend operations in Austin as of Monday. The loss could prod other cities to require fingerprint criminal background checks, encouraged that they can survive a bruising electoral battle with the ride-hailing services, analysts said.

– How did Hurricane Irma manage to get from Cuba to the Florida Panhandle? Well, scientists say it probably got stronger over time—because it had too much wind shear. In other words, "it had too much wind shear," a researcher tells the Miami Herald. Wind shear is the difference in wind speed between the top of the tropics' troposphere and the bottom of the troposphere. It's the difference between the speed of wind at the top of the troposphere and the speed of wind at the bottom of the troposphere that is the most important factor controlling a hurricane's formation and destruction, explains Weather Underground. "When one hears the phrase, 'wind shear is 20 knots over the hurricane,' this typically refers to the difference in wind speed between 200 mb (the top of the troposphere, 40,000 feet altitude) and a layer where a pressure of 850 mb is found—about 5,000 feet above the surface," writes Weather Underground. "This wind shear is computed over a large area—a circle of 700 miles in diameter centered on the hurricane." – Facebook's new patent deal with Microsoft is being widely hailed as another salvo in the social network's feud with Yahoo. "This is almost certainly a move against Google," says an analyst at Altimeter Group. "Microsoft is simply less concerned about the threat of social to its business than Google is." The deal will help Facebook beef up its intellectual property portfolio before its IPO next month, and it will also give Facebook more ammo in its patent feud with Yahoo. The deal comes less than two weeks after Microsoft bought 925 AOL patents for $1 billion and sold 70% of them to Facebook for $550 million. In a second deal, Microsoft said it had turned around and sold 70% of those same patents—about 650 in all—to Facebook for $550 million. While Facebook and Microsoft have not yet determined precisely how they are going to divvy up the patents, it is expected that Facebook will end up with a range of patents involving mobile, Web and instant messaging technologies. Microsoft is likely to keep AOL patents involving search, among other things.

Lawrence sold the gold to Ottawa Gold Buyers for between $6,800 and $9,500 each between 2014 and 2015, the Ottawa Citizen reports. He was also found to have set off the mint's metal detector more often than other employees, but security cameras didn't catch on. Prosecutors had sought an 18-month sentence. Lawrence's lawyer argued his client should only have to pay back $130,000—the amount he made selling the 17 pucks—or be sent back to jail for another three years. But Ontario Court Justice Peter Doody said the evidence was mostly circumstantial, and no one actually saw Lawrence taking the gold. Lawrence was also found to have Vaseline and latex gloves in his locker at work. Records show Lawrence set off the metal detector more often than other employees, but checks with a wand didn't set off alarms.

The small white dog, Soshe, became separated from her owner during the storm and was stuck in her Pender County home for nearly a week. Rescuers say it took three trips by boat to identify Soshe's home, which was submerged by floodwaters so deep they couldn't see roofs. They finally reached it after paddling half a mile. To test this, Thorstenson's team had people watch a sad movie clip, then another sad movie clip and another sad movie clip. The "sadness" group was then asked to look at red, yellow, green, and blue patches that had been desaturated of color and muted to gray. "Some of the patches are pretty difficult [to discern]," Thorstenson says. The team also had people watch a neutral desktop screensaver and perform the same tasks. – The situation at Japan's Fukushima Dai-ichi nuclear plant is worse than officials have acknowledged—and it's getting worse by the hour. In a desperate attempt to cool the overheating reactors, officials have resorted to seawater, a desperate measure that a US expert called "a Hail Mary pass" because of the volume of seawater and boron being used. It's not clear whether the seawater will be able to cool the reactors as effectively as it did, or whether it will even be able to distribute the seawater to the reactors' cooling systems, the AP reports. In other developments: The situation is worse than officials have acknowledged—and it's getting worse by the hour—because the plant's power supply has been cut off and its cooling systems failed, causing radioactivity to leak from the reactors. The situation is worse than officials have acknowledged—and it's getting worse by the hour—because officials knew the risks were high when they decided to vent radioactive steam from a severely overheated reactor vessel. They knew a hydrogen explosion could occur, and it did. The decision still trumped the worst-case alternative—total nuclear meltdown. Japan has a total of 55 reactors, and the situation is getting worse by the hour.

"Although Fitch continues to believe that the debt ceiling will be raised soon, the political brinkmanship and reduced financing flexibility could increase the risk of a US default," the agency said in a statement. The US is the most heavily indebted country in the world, and its 'AAA' rating is supported by its "highly productive, diversified, and wealthy economy," Fitch says. The US economy is expected to grow 2.6% in 2014 and 3% over the next few years, according to Fitch's forecast. But the country's medium-term debt burden is expected to rise to around 110% of GDP by the end of the decade, Fitch warns.

– Scientists have discovered a vast reservoir of melt water hidden beneath Greenland's ice sheet—and it's growing. The water is stored in the air space between ice particles, like juice in a slush drink, researchers say, but they don't know where it ends up, the BBC reports. "This discovery was a surprise," says the lead researcher. "Instead of the water being stored in the air space between subsurface rock particles, the water is stored in the air space between the ice particles, like the juice in a snow cone." The water is prevented from freezing by the large amounts of snow that fall on the Greenland ice sheet late in the summer. This insulates the water from the air temperatures that are below freezing, allowing it to persist as liquid all year. The aquifer covers an area the size of Ireland, and the researchers believe it holds 140 billion tons of melt water, which is the equivalent of 0.4 millimeters of sea level rise per year. "It's massive, it's a new system we haven't seen before—we need to understand it more completely if we are to predict sea level rise," says the lead researcher.

– A 14-year-old boy in Cuba who underwent a risky surgery to remove a 10-pound tumor from his face died Friday, USA Today reports. Emanuel Zayas was born with a condition called polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, which caused his body to develop scar-like tissue instead of bone. Zayas and his family traveled from Cuba to the US in hopes of having the tumor removed. The surgery was scheduled for last month. "I am saddened by the fact that we are losing him and that the physiological stress of surgery was apparently too much for his compromised anatomy," says Dr. Robert Marx. "Our hopes of saving his life, and with that allowing him a better quality of life, were not realized." Zayas' family plans to donate his body to science to learn more about the condition.

It is also common on temples and houses in India and Indonesia. The understory fires were found to be more common in 2005 to 2010—the years when Amazon deforestation hit its highest rate ever, according to the study, published in the Journal of Geophysical Experiment. "The human presence at the frontier where there is no indigenous reserve where there is no water storage leads to a risk of burning, with or without deforestation, in the region when climate conditions are dry," study author Yang Chen says. – California's San Jacinto fault, which runs from Imperial County to the San Bernardino Valley, is part of the larger San Andreas fault, which is responsible for 80% of the slippage along the Pacific and North American plates.
