– Astronomers have found the first comet with ocean-like water in a major boost to the theory that the celestial bodies were a significant source of water for a thirsty early Earth. The intense heat of the planet immediately after it formed means any initial water would have quickly evaporated and scientists believe the oceans emerged around 8 million years later. The puzzle is where the water, which is vital for life on Earth, came from. Past analysis of water-ice from far-flung comets suggested they could have delivered no more than 10% of today's oceans because the chemical "fingerprints" did not match up. But research from Paul Hartogh of Germany's Max Planck Institute for Solar System Research and colleagues published on Wednesday showed a comet called 103P/Hartley 2 has the same chemical composition as the Earth's oceans. The finding substantially increases the amount of water that could have originated from comets, which are made up of rock and ice with a characteristic tail of gas and dust. Previous models of the early Earth implied most water came from asteroids. In the case of Hartley 2, researchers using infrared instruments on the Hershel Space Observatory found that ice on the comet has a near identical "D/H" ratio to seawater.

– Japanese researchers have successfully repaired the hearts of monkeys with lab-grown heart cells from a donor chosen to be a good genetic match for the recipient, the Guardian reports. Heart attacks are the leading cause of death in the developed world, and while 70% of patients survive, many are left with tissue damage that stops their hearts from working properly. One idea to treat heart attack survivors is to take skin cells from the patient and convert them into pumping heart cells. The advantage is that the heart cells will not be rejected by the immune system, but the procedure is time consuming and expensive to do for individual patients. In the latest work, researchers in Japan induced heart attacks in five macaques and then treated the damage with heart cells created from the skin of a donor monkey. The donor was selected to be a close genetic match, but the recipients still need drugs to stop their bodies rejecting the cells. Yuji Shiba and others at Shinshu University injected the monkeys with 400m lab-made heart cells and found that they replaced about 16% of the damaged tissue. The new cells were wired up with healthy ones in the heart and over 12 weeks started to help the organ to pump more strongly. Tests revealed, however, that all of the monkeys developed unusual heart rhythms after the therapy.

Two empty vodka bottles were found on the floor of her bedroom in London. – The historic Berkeley City Club was evacuated yesterday afternoon after an elderly woman killed herself with a toxic chemical in her room, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. The San Jose Mercury News reports that the woman was in her 80s. The building was closed for several hours while hazardous materials crews and bomb squad technicians investigated. Berkeley Police Sgt. Joe Okies tells the East Bay Times that police, fire, and police departments from around the country were all involved in the effort. "The known quantity of what appeared to be a hazardous material has been removed," he says.

– Conventional wisdom says that if you put solar panels on your roof in the Northern Hemisphere, you should point them within 30 degrees of true south to generate the most energy in the course of a year. But a new study by Pecan Street Research Institute, an Austin, Texas-based research and development organization, suggests that most people may do better at covering their own electrical use and reducing stress on utility grids during summertime peak demand periods if they aim the panels westward instead. The study analyzed 50 homes in the Austin area, looking not just at the amount of electricity generated by the panels, but at the impact on homeowners' electricity use and the utility grid during periods of summer peak electrical demand, which generally occur between 3pm and 7pm. Homes with west-facing solar panels produced 2% more electricity during a normal day than homes with south-facing panels. Beyond that, they produced 49% more electricity during peak demand hours of 3pm to 7pm. "Those are pretty extraordinary peak reductions," the study co-author tells Green Tech Media. "It seemed like the child wanted to continue driving, he was trying to merge on the middle lane of the highway," Rubio says. – China on Sunday began a suspension of all coal imports from North Korea for the rest of the year as it increases pressure on its communist neighbor to give up its nuclear and ballistic missile programs. The ban is in line with UN Security Council sanctions imposed in November in response to North Korea's fifth nuclear test two months earlier, the Commerce Ministry said in an online statement Saturday, per the AP. China had already banned coal imports from North Korea in April last year, but those restrictions allowed some imports for civilian use. China is North Korea's largest source of trade and aid and Sunday's suspension will deprive Pyongyang of an important source of foreign currency. Beijing has come under pressure from President Trump to lean harder on Pyongyang, but Beijing says its influence is limited. However, it has grown increasingly frustrated with North Korea's defiance of the UN demands that it end missile tests and development of nuclear weapons. North Korea launched its latest ballistic missile test a week ago. Coal is North Korea's main export and an important source of foreign currencies for its fragile economy. Most of North Korea's exported coal is shipped to China, its only major ally on the global stage.

– The New York Times' David Remnick has returned from a rare trip to Iran, where he found a nation that's much more pro-American than he'd previously seen. "I encountered many Iranians—especially in the countryside—who strongly support the Iranian authorities and resent what they see as American government bullying," he writes in the Times. He encountered people who passed "Death to America" signs, but they kept giving him presents or inviting him into their homes. The FAA order will focus on the 737-300, 737-400, and 737-500, models that have taken off and landed more than 30,000 times. The airline has returned all but 14 of the jets to service. The tear in the plane, which lost cabin pressure and had to make an emergency landing, occurred in an area that was not considered high risk. "This could change the conversation regarding the risk of aging aircraft," said the president of the Flight Safety Foundation. The FAA last year toughened the standards for aging aircraft, but the latest discovery could lead to even broader requirements for costly inspections, Voss said. – The 112th Congress is on track to have the least productive two-year stretch since the end of World War II, according to a USA Today analysis of records kept by the House Clerk's office. So far this year, 61 bills have been introduced, or less than 2% of all proposed laws. In 2011, after Republicans took control of the House, Congress passed just 90 bills. The only other year in which Congress failed to pass at least 125 laws was 1995. Not even the 80th Congress, which President Truman called the "do-nothing Congress" in 1948, passed as few laws as the current one, records show. The difference between 1995 and now is that Republicans rebounded in the second year of the 104th Congress in 1996, churning out 245 laws with a Democratic president, including a tax cut package, a minimum wage increase, an overhaul of the nation's welfare system, and requiring law enforcement to disclose where sex offenders live. A spokesman for House Majority Leader Eric Cantor defended the chamber, citing over 30 economic measures the House has passed that have fizzled in the Democratic-run Senate "at the behest of a president who is presiding over the worst economic recovery in history."

– People around the country are dropping off their urine for a good reason: The stuff could be used as fertilizer, reports the Burlington Free Press. A group called Rich Earth is collecting the urine and sending it to farms to be tested on crops. The idea is to see if urine can be used as a replacement for conventional fertilizer, and the Vermont group has collected about 6,000 gallons so far. “We’ve given volunteers a few things to make it easier—some funnel devices and things like that,” says the group's administrative director. Urine contains nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium—essential plant nutrients that are usually mined from the earth or the air for agricultural use. In collecting human urine, Rich Earth is diverting the same chemicals from waterways to farms, making a potentially harmful substance a boon to crop production. The group knows of only one other such project in the US, in Sweden, and it's not clear whether it will get the EPA's OK. But the Swedes tested urine as a fertilizer in the 1990s and concluded that it could be used to grow 50% to 100% of the food requirement for another person. Other studies have shown that urine can be used as fertilizer in China and Mexico, though none as detailed as the Swedish one.

– The "blackest" name in the US is George Washington, according to an AP article by Jesse Washington ahead of the first president's birthday tomorrow. The Census counted 163,036 people with the last name Washington, 90% of whom were black. Williams was the blackest name, with 46% of all Washingtons, but Washington is by far the most popular, with 716,704 black Williamses. "There is no direct evidence," says an expert on black genealogy. "As far as I'm concerned it's a coincidence." Washington speculates that Reconstruction-era blacks might have chosen the name to show pride in the nation's history, or as a way to maintain ties to plantation owners. Or it could have been a way to keep the name in the public eye, as George Washington was still hugely popular at the time. "It's a myth," writes Washington, "that most enslaved blacks bore the last name of their owner." The president, however, owned hundreds of slaves and was "leading this schizoid life," biographer Ron Chernow tells the Huffington Post. "In theory and on paper he was opposed to slavery, but he was still zealously tracking and seeking to recover his slaves who escaped."

– Sea ice is disappearing faster than ever in the Arctic, and scientists say a new culprit is to blame. In a study published in Science, researchers say warm currents in the Atlantic Ocean are causing sea ice in the Arctic to melt faster than ever before. The Atlantic currents are delivered by an offshoot of the Gulf Stream, and they have long been known to prevent sea ice from forming north of Scandinavia on the western side of the Eurasian basin, where sea ice is more prevalent, reports the New York Times. But since 2002, they've been gathering data that shows the Atlantic currents have been mixing with surface waters in a way that is causing sea ice to melt faster on the eastern side of the basin, which is north of Europe and most of Asia. "Previously this monster, Atlantic warm water, was well covered from the surface" on the eastern side of the basin, says lead researcher Igor Polyakov of the University of Alaska in Fairbanks. "The new data show this layer has disappeared in winter." The Atlantic currents were found to be about 4 degrees Celsius warmer than surface waters at their deepest point, and they were causing sea ice to melt faster on the eastern side of the basin than on the western side, where sea ice is more prevalent. – "The power of social media is out of this world," Clare Shaw tells the Epoch Times. For hours, the family searched for Ryder, but they couldn't find him. The report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change warns that we'll need to curb carbon emissions by another 15 years or so, to 2070, if we want to avoid the worst effects of climate change, the New York Times reports. The problem, the report warns, is that governments are spending far more money to subsidize fossil fuels than to reduce emissions, which are growing in fast-growing countries like China. The report also finds that the Kyoto Protocol has "not been as successful as intended," the Times reports. The treaty, meant to limit emissions, was rejected by many countries, including the US, because it didn't apply to developing countries. A new treaty is now underway, but it's not supposed to take effect until 2020, and it's not clear whether countries will agree on ambitious goals to reduce emissions. The report will be presented to ministers at a UN meeting in Bangkok next week, the AP reports, and it's expected to be a major topic at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, next week. – Superheroes ruled the box office this weekend, with Thor: The Dark World pulling in $38.5 million—a 55% drop from its opening weekend, the LA Times reports. But that was enough to propel it to No. 2, with $30.5 million, followed by The Best Man Holiday ($20.1 million), Nebraska ($140,000), and Hunger Games: Catching Fire ($6.3 million), according to studio estimates. The Best Man Holiday is a sequel to 1999's The Best Man, which opened to $34 million. "There’s no crystal ball in guessing this stuff," says a Universal exec. "It was fair to think this film—where 87% of the audience was African American—would open in the high teens." Rounding out the top five, per the Hollywood Reporter: Avengers: Age of Ultron ($17.5 million), The Call ($13.3 million), and Battleship ($8.5 million).

– The European Organization for Nuclear Research (EoNR) is home to the world's most powerful particle accelerator, the Lagre Hadron Collider, and it's home to a giant statue of a Hindu deity. It's also home to a prank video that's gone viral, the Independent reports. In it, hooded figures appear to perform a human sacrifice under the statue. A woman is stabbed at the end of the video. EoNR says it's investigating the incident, which took place on its premises, but so far no one has come forward with any information about the perpetrators. The Independent notes the video was apparently recorded by scientists at the lab, though it's not clear who recorded it.

– A 16-pound turkey, rolls with butter, peas, cranberries, a relish tray of carrots and celery, pumpkin pie with whipped cream, and beverages of coffee and milk will set you back $49.04 for a Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation's annual informal survey. That's down from $49.48 last year, and it's the lowest cost since the survey began in 1950, the Los Angeles Times reports. "There's no inflation on the table," says an AFBF rep. The biggest cost-reducing item: the 16-pound turkey, which dropped from $21.76 last year to $21.76 this year. That's down about 3 cents per pound, or 47 cents per whole turkey, the Times notes.

Kristin and Candace Hermeler wrote two letters to Brooks Brown, a student at Columbine High School who was targeted by one of the Columbine gunmen, months after the massacre in 1999, CBS Denver reports. "As someone who has been rejected, victimized and ostracized in their life, I would like to thank you for giving him that chance," Kristin wrote in one letter. It completely baffles me as to why anyone would hate someone when they don't know them, it sickens me." Brown tells the Denver Post that the letters were "a very sweet letter, very sad," adding, "It was her wanting to know why it happened, trying to understand."

– An Aeroflot flight from Moscow to Bangkok experienced severe turbulence just before landing in Bangkok early Monday, sending 27 passengers to the hospital—including one child—with injuries ranging from broken bones to spinal compression fractures, the Guardian reports. "We were hurled up into the roof of the plane, it was practically impossible to hold on," a passenger tells Russia's Rossiya 24 by phone. "It felt like the shaking wouldn't stop, that we would just crash." According to the BBC, clear-air turbulence is caused when air masses move at different speeds and can't be detected by the naked eye. The turbulence hit about 40 minutes before the Boeing 777 was due to land. Twenty-four of the injured passengers were Russian, while three were Thai. None of the injuries are believed to be life-threatening. Aeroflot says the turbulence was "impossible to predict" and the crew was unable to warn passengers to return to their seats. The airline says the pilot had more than 23,000 flight hours and had experienced clear-air turbulence around 750 times.

Two alternate jurors' names were not released, and reporters and a photographer have been knocking on doors in the county looking for them. The judge had postponed the release of their names for three months as a "cooling off" period, notes the Orlando Sentinel, and he expressed "significant concern over the safety of the jurors" in his order.

– It's been a rough year for the grapes used to make champagne, with this year's harvest down 40%, the worst in at least 40 years, according to the French Agriculture Ministry. Hails and wet weather are to blame, along with fungus, the Christian Science Monitor reports. "This is the lowest harvest in at least 40 years," says the ministry. Fortunately, there's more than a three-year supply of grapes waiting to be bottled, Businessweek reports, so champagne drinkers won't have to worry too much about shortages. "We built up reserves during the years when we had big harvests, which helps us deal with the caprices of nature," says a spokesman for the French champagne producers association. Still, the news comes at a bad time, with the French drinking less champagne—and the country as a whole, not just the big champagne producers, is suffering. Sales fell 2% last year, Bloomberg reports.

– Last July, an iceberg the size of Delaware broke off from the Larsen Ice Shelf in Antarctica, causing a dramatic change to the region's landscape. Now, for the first time in more than 120,000 years, an expedition is going to be able to explore the newly exposed seafloor, USA Today reports. "It's important we get there quickly before the undersea environment changes as sunlight enters the water and new species begin to colonize," says marine biologist Katrin Linse, who's leading the mission from the British Antarctic Survey. The 2,200-square-mile area was previously off-limits to humans, and researchers are going to be collecting water, plankton, sediment, and animal samples from the newly exposed seabed. "The calving of A-68 provides us with a unique opportunity to study marine life as it responds to a dramatic environmental change," Linse says in a press release. "Now is the time to address fundamental questions about the sustainability of polar continental shelves under climate change," the survey's science director adds. The researchers are hoping to learn what kinds of creatures can survive in the frigid waters, which USA Today notes are filled with huge chunks of ice. (The largest iceberg ever recorded broke off from the Antarctic last summer.)

Myrna Arias says she was a sales executive and account manager for money transfer company Intermex when she was told she had to use an app called Xora to manage her job, Courthouse News reports. According to her lawsuit, she and her co-workers researched the app and were told it would be used to monitor employees' movements while off duty. But Arias says she objected to the monitoring of her location during non-work hours and complained to her boss that the app was an invasion of privacy. He "scolded" her for uninstalling the app shortly after she did, according to her lawsuit. Her lawyers say she made $7,250 a month and "met all quotas" during a short stint with the company last year. "This intrusion would be highly offensive to a reasonable person," the lawsuit says. Her lawyers say the Xora app allowed her "bosses to see every move the employees made throughout the day." – Two more Democratic senators have come out in support of gay marriage, bringing the total to 50, reports the New York Times. North Dakota's Heidi Heitkamp and Indiana's Joe Donnelly join Bill Nelson and Tom Carper, both from states that voted for Mitt Romney last year. "I view the ability of anyone to marry as a logical extension of this belief," says Heitkamp. "The makeup of families is changing, but the importance of family is enduring." Both senators come from red states, notes the Washington Post, and neither will be up for re-election until 2018. Heitkamp's and Donnelly's support is especially notable because both came from states that voted for Democrats last year. "However, neither face reelection until 2018, and if public opinion continues its dramatic shift in favor of same-sex marriage, the issue may become less controversial," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. It's possible that senators are learning from each other's experiences, he adds.

Roberts, who underwent a bone-marrow transplant in September, was visibly happy to be back on the air, the New York Times reports. "Now, we can resume regular programming," she said. "There was no handbook for this, but I'm very pleased with how we handled it." ABC decided to make Roberts a part of the show even while she was in the hospital recuperating from the transplant. "This experience has reminded us to take nothing for granted, and, like Robin herself, in many ways we feel like we're just getting started," said the president of ABC News. "After 173 very long days, it's beautiful to get back to business as usual with our full team and two more wonderful regulars."

– New Mexico Gov. Susana Martinez says church-bombings will feel the "full pressure of the law" after back-to-back explosions at two Las Cruces churches Sunday morning, the AP reports. Police say the Calvary Baptist Church was hit by a mailbox bomb around 8am Sunday; parishioners were inside the church at the time. Less than half an hour later, police were called to Holy Cross Catholic Church, where an explosive device had gone off in a trash can near the entrance of the church, according to police. The service at Holy Cross had started, and parishioners were evacuated, police say. The churches remained closed Sunday afternoon while multiple law enforcement agencies are investigating the nearly-simultaneous blasts, according to police. "Just the fact that they were at churches the same day a half an hour apart or so, that leads us to believe it could be something related," police spokesman Dan Trujillo tells the Las Cruces News. Trujillo says police have advised other churches in the area "to be on the lookout for anything suspicious." No one was injured in either explosion, and damage to each church was "relatively minor," police say.

The study looked at 44,000 photos from 166 people, asking them to rate images on a scale of zero to five based on how likable, happy, interesting, and sad they were. Researchers then used an algorithm to analyze photos based on the number of faces in each photo, colorization, vividness, and brightness. They found darker, bluer, and more faded photos predicted depression, while the more comments a post received increased the likelihood of being posted by a depressed person; more likes, however, signified the opposite. depressed people were less likely to use filters like inkwells and Valencia, while healthy people used warmer tones and images with more people in them. – Cat Vasko is on a mission to save the planet, and she's found a way to do it in the most efficient way possible: She's turned chicken into something called a rotisserie chicken, reports Bloomberg View. Vasko, who works in a supermarket's "prepared foods" section, says the practice uses up all sorts of unsold produce and meat, and it's a win-win for the consumer and the supermarket: Customers get cheaper, fresh food at a lower price, and the supermarket gets a profit. "This is the sort of thing that no one talks about when they talk about innovation—and yet, it's a major way in which our economy has become more efficient over the last few decades," she writes. "It's a win for the grocer and the consumer." Read her full column here.

– ISIS militants may be able to use seized Syrian government assets to create fake passports that could be used to travel to the US, a federal official tells CNN. The militant group has access to passport printing machines and blank passport books, according to an intelligence report released to law enforcement last week by the Homeland Security Investigations agency, ABC News reports. "Since more than 17 months [have] passed since Raqqa and Deir ez-Zour fell to ISIS, it is possible that individuals from Syria with passports 'issued' in these ISIS-controlled cities or who had passport blanks, may have traveled to the US," the report says. A State Department spokesman tells Reuters that officials are "mindful" of the report's findings. "Obviously, it's something that we take seriously," he says. "It's obviously something, clearly that we're mindful of." Officials are also concerned about the possibility of identity theft caused by ISIS access to Syrian government buildings that hold valid biographical data and fingerprint information on Syrian citizens, the source says.

– The French Laundry in California's Napa Valley is known as one of the best restaurants in the world, but on Christmas Day, thieves made off with 76 bottles of wine worth an estimated $300,000, reports the San Francisco Chronicle. The heist occurred in the wine room just after the restaurant closed for the holidays, and the thieves made off with bottles from the estate Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, as well as from California's Screaming Eagle, reports the Los Angeles Times. “We are confident that if and when any of the stolen bottles appear in public, they will immediately raise questions and red flags among the wine knowledgeable," says French Laundry chef and owner Thomas Keller in a statement. "We look forward to rebuilding our cellar in the meantime and plan to get to the bottom of this disheartening act immediately." The stolen bottles range in value from $2,100 to $7,500 each.

– Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams has been released from police custody in Northern Ireland after four days of questioning about the 1972 murder of a widowed mother of three. The IRA abducted Jean McConville from her Belfast home, shot her in the back of the head, and buried her body on a beach in County Louth, reports the BBC. Adams, who has long been linked to the IRA, denies involvement. He says he contacted police two months ago about the McConville case. "I have never dissociated myself from the IRA and I never will," he said. "The IRA is gone. It is finished." The McConville family says it will continue its fight for justice, the AP reports.

"He turned in his strongest performance yet," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post, praising Bush's "remarkable takedown" of Donald Trump's plan to deport 11 million undocumented immigrants and his "remarkable takedown" of Ted Cruz's plan to make Mexico pay for a border wall. "It was Jeb Bush who rose to the occasion and turned in his strongest debate performance to date, but it was Marco Rubio and Ted Cruz who again outshined their rivals," writes Cillizza, praising Rubio's " mastery of the facts and ease under the bright lights" and Cruz's "remarkable takedown" of Trump's plan. "The two-hour debate, marked by a smattering of sharp exchanges but fewer fireworks than the three previous showdowns, is unlikely to dramatically alter the race as it now stands—and the status quo may hold through the end of the year, with the next GOP debate 35 days away and the month of December effectively a dead zone for campaign fundraising," writes Cillizza. – Shia LaBeouf has dropped out of a Broadway production over "creative differences," the New York Daily News reports. The Transformers and Indiana Jones star had been set to star in the revival ofphans with Alec Baldwin, but he won't start previews until April 7. No word on who will replace him. Earlier this year, LaBeouf said he was quitting Hollywood blockbusters for " riskier, indie-flavor projects." Tom Hanks, meanwhile, is making his Broadway debut in Lucky Guy, the story of New York tabloid editor Mike McAlary. "I told Nora that McAlary sounded like a real" jerk, Hanks tells the New York Times. "I told Nora that McAlary is pretty far from a predictable Tom Hanks part."

– Afghanistan has agreed to allow a Taliban office to open in Qatar, but foreign powers can't get involved in the peace process without its consent, the government's High Peace Council has told foreign missions. "The Islamic Republic of Afghanistan is in agreement regarding the opening of an office for the armed opposition, but only to move forward the peace process and conduct negotiations," the council said, according to a note obtained by Reuters. The US has held about half a dozen meetings with the Taliban this year to prepare for face-to-face talks with the Afghan government. The Afghan government would prefer an office in Saudi Arabia or Turkey, but it's not averse to Doha as long as the office is only for talks. "We are saying Saudi or Turkey are preferable, we are not saying it has to be there only. The only condition is it should be in an Islamic country," said a government official. The council also said that any peace process would have to have the support of Pakistan since Taliban members are based there.

– The Supreme Court ruled unanimously today that Indiana farmer Vernon Hugh Bowman violated Monsanto's patents by planting seeds from his second crop that he hoped would be resistant to Monsanto's patented Roundup Ready gene, the New York Times reports. The ruling has implications for many aspects of modern agriculture and for businesses based on vaccines, cell lines, and software. But Justice Elena Kagan, writing for the court, emphasized that the decision was narrow. “Our holding today is limited—addressing the situation before us, rather than every one involving a self-replicating product,” she wrote. “In another case, the article’s self-replication might occur outside the purchaser’s control. Or it might be a necessary but incidental step in using the item for another purpose.” Bowman bought seeds from a grain elevator filled with seeds typically used for food processing or animal feed. He planted them and sprayed them with Roundup. Many plants survived, and he replanted their seeds. Monsanto sued, and a federal judge in Indiana ordered Bowman to pay the company more than $84,000. The United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which specializes in patent cases, upheld that decision, saying that Bowman had infringed Monsanto's patents. – Facebook analyzed 1 million status updates from English speakers in the US and discovered some interesting habits: Old people tend to babble. Religion, social processes, and family were more common among older users Kids skip words—there was a strong correlation between age and the use of articles and prepositions. Younger users were also more likely to swear, express anger, and use the word "I." People are most positive in the morning—that's when status updates contained the most positive emotional messages. Negative emotions spiked after 10pm. References to time peak in the morning. This is probably people posting about how late they were up last night, how late they are for work, and so on. Updates with negative emotions receive more comments than those with positive emotions, probably as friends race to console each other. People tend to use the same kind of words in status updates as their friends—particularly if they're referring to their family, using religious words, or swearing.

– The opening ceremonies of the Sochi Olympics are tomorrow, but before they begin, Google is taking a stand against Russia's anti-gay laws, Mashable reports. The company's latest "doodle" features a quote from the Olympic Charter: "The practice of sport is a human right. Every individual must have the possibility of practicing sport, without discrimination of any kind and in the Olympic spirit, which requires mutual understanding with a spirit of friendship, solidarity, and fair play." Clicking on the image takes you to the search result of "Olympic Charter." Google isn't the only one taking a stand on the issue. American Apparel and AT&T, both Team USA sponsors, have spoken out against Russia's anti-gay laws. Coca-Cola, Visa, Samsung, McDonald's, Procter & Gamble, Omega, General Electric, and Dow Chemical have yet to do the same. Click for more.

– Nicole Bahret was on her way home from running errands in Georgia in mid-July when she came across a three-car crash just past the entrance to the Sawnee Mountain Preserve. "I knew when I saw his car," Bahret tells WSB-TV. "So, I actually pulled up to the scene. That's how I found out." Police say an SUV driven by 17-year-old Natalie D'Allen failed to yield the right of way and hit a Honda Accord driven by 18-year-old Mackean Robertson, who was killed at the scene, Fox News reports. "He actually asked and said, 'Can I hang out with some friends tonight?' And I was like, 'Yeah, that sounds great,'" Bahret tells WSB. Robertson's last conversation with his mother was an hour before the crash. "The day he died was probably one of the happiest days of his life because everything was going his way," Bahret says. "He was precious." A GoFundMe page set up for Robertson's family has raised more than $17,000 as of this writing. (A man was killed in a horrific car crash while trying to help a friend.)

– Ten people have been arrested in China for allegedly killing a wild giant panda and chopping it down to sell as meat, the AP reports. According to state media, the suspects—two brothers and eight others—were hunting for an animal that had killed their goat when they found the panda in a tree. They allegedly shot it dead when it climbed another tree, the New York Times reports. Police say they found the panda's body, its skin, bones, and 22 pounds of meat in a raid on a home in Yunnan province in December. The suspects allegedly sold the panda's paws and meat for $820 to one buyer, and the parts were sold again to others, the Times reports. Poaching pandas is rare, the AP reports, but panda parts are prized on the black market because of their rarity. According to state media, there are only about 1,800 wild pandas left in China.

– Want to know someone's personality? Just sniff their white cotton t-shirts, a new study suggests. Researchers in Poland asked 100 men and 100 women to sniff white cotton t-shirts worn for three consecutive nights, MyHealthNewsDaily reports. Raters were then asked to evaluate the donors' level of extroversion, neuroticism, and dominance based on five personality traits, on a scale of one to 10. The matches were not perfect, but the raters were able to accurately predict how outgoing, anxious, and dominant the donors were based on their body odor. The findings are preliminary and more studies need to be done, but researchers say the results suggest that people use more than their eyes and ears when determining a person's personality traits, suggesting that men and women are using more than their eyes and ears when choosing a potential mate. Personality traits may also be linked with the secretion of hormones that could alter a person's scent. People who are high in dominance may have higher levels of testosterone, which in turn may modify their sweat glands, the researchers said. – Taylor Swift is back on social media, three days after she mysteriously deleted her Twitter, Instagram, and Tumblr accounts, USA Today reports. On Monday, Swift posted a 10-second clip of a snake on Instagram and Twitter. On Tuesday, she posted a 10-second clip of the snake's tail. On Wednesday, she posted a 10-second clip of the snake's head. On Monday, Swift's music director, Joseph Kahn, replied to Swift's video clip with a smiley face and wrote, "In 30 minutes, as a show of power, @taylorswift13 will blot out the sun." Kahn is the man who directed Swift's 2015 video for "Bad Blood," Us Weekly reports.

– Los Angeles is bracing for what's being dubbed "Carmageddon"—the massive traffic jams that are expected when a 10-mile stretch of Interstate 405 is shut down this weekend. "It will be an absolute nightmare," Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa said at a press conference last month. "Avoid the area, or stay home. Go on vacation that weekend." To ease the panic, local businesses are offering discounts, the Wall Street Journal reports. One pet photography company is offering 20% off all pets. And a helicopter company is offering $150 charter flights over the closed 405. "We're trying to make something good out of this," says the chief pilot of Briles Wing & Helicopter. "You've got to be crazy to try to drive anywhere."

– The Occupy Wall Street movement will mark its two-month anniversary today with a day of protests across New York City, the Wall Street Journal reports. Protesters plan to start at 7am with a march to Wall Street; others will gather in Zuccotti Park. They're urging people to gather at transit hubs in each of the five boroughs in the afternoon. Then protesters plan to take trains to Foley Square, in Lower Manhattan. At Foley Square, plans call for a large rally that is being backed by some of the city's largest unions, one of which has obtained a permit for the rally. Protesters then plan to march across the Brooklyn Bridge's pedestrian path. It's not clear how disruptive demonstrators plan to be, or what kind of police response they'll face. City officials on Wednesday said they're expecting problems and police are prepared to handle them. "Everything that we have seen and heard suggests that we may have tens of thousands of people tomorrow protesting," Deputy Mayor Howard Wolfson told reporters. "The protesters are calling for a massive event aimed at disrupting major parts of the city."

– A man who was gored by a bison at a California campground Saturday is lucky to be alive, police say. The man was sitting on a log at the Little Harbor Campground on Catalina Island when the animal approached, the Los Angeles Times reports. "When the man saw that the (animal) was getting closer to him, he got up and tried to move away," a sheriff's sergeant tells the Daily Breeze. "That's when (it) charged him and gored him in his left arm." The man was airlifted to a nearby medical center. Bison are common on the island, but they are "very rare for them to attack," the sergeant says. "People even forget sometimes that they are wild because they appear domesticated."

– A North Carolina man serving a life sentence for the murder of Michael Jordan's father is seeking a new trial, according to court documents obtained by the Charlotte Observer. Daniel Green was convicted in 1996 of shooting Michael Jordan's father, James, during a robbery. Green's accomplice, Larry Martin Demery, said he and Green planned to rob James Jordan as he slept. But Green's attorneys say Demery pulled the trigger and Green wasn't at the scene, the AP reports. According to court documents, the jury forewoman said she investigated the murder on her own, against the judge's orders. A former newspaper editor also signed an affidavit saying Demery admitted to killing James Jordan. A state forensics expert also said Jordan's blood was found in Green's car, but Green's attorneys say there's doubt about that evidence. The state has until the end of April to respond to Green's request for a new trial.

– Former Rhode Island Gov. Lincoln Chafee ended his long-shot bid for the Democratic presidential nomination on Friday, CNN reports. "I have been campaigning on a platform of Prosperity Through Peace," Chafee said at the Democratic National Committee's Women's Leadership Forum in Washington, DC. "But after much thought I have decided to end my campaign for president today. I would like to take this opportunity one last time to advocate for a chance be given to peace." Chafee said Hillary Clinton had a "good week" in the debates, Jim Webb dropped out of the race, Joe Biden declined to run, and she did well in the Benghazi hearing. "Obviously it was a good week for Secretary Clinton," Chafee said. "She did well in the debates and then Senator Webb got out, Vice President Biden declined to join the race, she did well in the Benghazi hearing, and Gov. Chafee got out of the race." According to the New York Times, Chafee's campaign raised just $30,000 in the first six months of his campaign and he was polling at zero in the latest CNN/ORC poll. Chafee was an anti-war candidate who opposed the Iraq war. He was scheduled to speak at the DNC forum Friday morning.

Here's what the pundits are saying: Will Ryan go for the jugular? – On a February day in 1944, a French police officer in the village of Gemeaux snatched two Jewish sisters, ages 10 and 9, from their school and threw them to the ground as they were about to be deported to Auschwitz. The girls never returned. Now, more than 70 years later, they've been reunited with their family. On Sunday, teacher Frédérique Gilles presented the dolls to the Holocaust museum in Paris, the Telegraph reports. Gilles' grandmother took them in after the officer left them lying in the street; a shopkeeper picked them up and gave them to Gilles' grandmother, who looked after them for three generations. "I never thought I'd see them again," says Gilles, who now lives in the town of Evreux. "It's a great honor." The Lévy sisters' parents, grandparents, aunt, and uncle were among those who lined up with the girls in the snow to await their deportation, the Telegraph notes.

– The Nebraska football team opened its season against Fresno State last night with a moment of silence for Sam Foltz, its late punter who died in a car accident in July. The team sent out 10 men in punt formation on its first drive, and after a minute or so, they punted the ball away, reports Big Ten Network. Foltz and former Michigan State punter Mike Sadler died in a Wisconsin car accident in July.

Seth Rogen tweeted yesterday that the movie "kind of reminds me of the movie that's showing in the third act of Inglourious Basterds," referring to Quentin Tarantino's WWII drama in which a German sniper kills Allied soldiers from a clock tower, USA Today reports. Michael Moore, who famously criticized the Iraq War in his 2003 Oscar acceptance speech, also took to Twitter yesterday to call snipers "cowards" and to say, "But if you're on the roof of your home defending it from invaders who've come 7K miles, you are not a sniper, u are brave, u are a neighbor." Taylor Armstrong, 40, filed for divorce in July, citing irreconcilable differences. Russell Armstrong, a successful venture capitalist, had been married to her for six years and had a 5-year-old daughter with her. He had also been involved with the Real Housewives of Beverly Hills. The coroner's office is still conducting an investigation, the Christian Science Monitor reports, but it does appear to be a suicide.

– A new study has linked a common chemical found in head lice treatments to behavioral problems in children, Yahoo Beauty reports. Pyrethroids work by damaging the nerves of insects, and scientists wanted to see if they had a negative impact on children as well. (Permethrin, an active ingredient in most popular drugstore lice treatments, is a pyrethroid.) For the study, researchers measured levels of five pyrethroid metabolites in the urine of women in the early stages of pregnancy and later in their 6-year-olds to see if there was a link between being exposed to the chemical in utero and childhood, and behavior that could suggest neurodevelopmental damage. Nearly 300 women filled out a questionnaire about socioeconomic factors, lifestyle, their child’s behavior, and various things their child had been exposed to. Psychologists visited the families at home to do behavioral assessments of the children, and also took urine and dust samples. Behavior was rated using the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, a validated behavioral screening test for children, with a focus on altruism (how social children are), internalizing disorders (the inability to share problems and ask for help), and externalizing disorders (being defiant and disruptive). – A new study finds that antibiotic-resistant MRSA bacteria are much more difficult to kill when exposed to cigarette smoke, Medical Daily reports. "We already know that smoking cigarettes harms human respiratory and immune cells, and now we've shown that, on the flipside, smoke can also stress out invasive bacteria and make them more aggressive," Dr. Laura Crotty Alexander of the University of California, San Diego School of Medicine says in a press release. Researchers tested two groups of MRSA bacteria—one exposed to cigarette smoke extract and one not—byinfecting immune cells with both types of MRSA. MRSA exposed to the extract was four times more resistant to macrophage killing than non-exposed MRSA. MRSA exposed to smoke extract was also more resistant to antimicrobial peptides, another line of immune defense used to make holes in bacteria and cause inflammation. "Now we have evidence that cigarette smoke-induced resistance in MRSA may be an additional contributing factor," Crotty Alexander says in the press release. The study is similar to one published last year that found MRSA becomes more resistant when exposed to e-cigarette vapors.

– A South Carolina woman has been charged with attempted murder after giving birth to a baby boy and dumping him in a trash can, the Greenville News reports. According to police, Sharon Lenise Ferguson, 28, gave birth to the baby boy on or about April 21 and then put him in a plastic grocery bag and wrapped him in a pink blanket. She then put him in the trash can in the family's backyard and "willfully abandoned him," police say. The baby was found by a neighbor who had followed a trail of blood, the Los Angeles Times reports. He was hospitalized and is now in foster care. "I was upset," a neighbor tells WYFF. "I saw the baby after they had pulled it out of the trash can and the fire department got here and I saw that the baby was moving." Ferguson has a "diagnosed mental illness" and was homeless, a family spokesperson says, and the family doesn't believe she knew she was pregnant or knew what to do.

Perdue's office says he didn't actually recite the psalm, but the crowd laughed and he added, "In all seriousness, I believe that America is at a moment of crisis." A spokeswoman for Harry Reid says Perdue "left the impression he was praying for the death of President Obama." But a Harvard Divinity School professor says the psalm is "one of the best examples of an extended series of calling upon God to punish or curse one's enemy." – Chris Christie is expected to make a big announcement soon about whether he's going to run for president. The New Jersey governor spent much of the weekend considering a late entry into the race, insiders tell the Wall Street Journal. Christie is expected to make an announcement within days, the sources say, though he hasn't said whether he'll do so today or tomorrow. The Journal notes that the crowded field of candidates could make an 11th-hour announcement difficult, but adds that the consensus is that Christie will enter the race.

– The House today overwhelmingly passed a bill that would let insurance companies keep offering health plans that were already canceled under ObamaCare, despite the White House's threat of a veto. The vote was 261-157, with 39 Democrats joining Republicans, the Hill reports. Only four Republicans voted against the "Keep Your Health Plan Act." The vote is a further blow to Obama, who was forced on Thursday to admit that new standards under the health care law are forcing millions into new and often more expensive health insurance plans. Obama had promised to let people keep their plans if they liked them, but he now says he will let insurers keep selling plans that don't meet ObamaCare standards for another year. The White House said Obama would veto any bill that allowed insurers to keep selling plans that don't meet ObamaCare standards, the New York Times reports. "The president has said from the start that if you like your health care plan, you will be able to keep your health care plan," the White House said in a statement. "He has also said that if you like your health care plan, you can keep your health care plan."

– Facebook is rolling out its own mobile app store, similar in concept to Apple's App Store, CNET reports. The "App Center" will be available only to US users starting today, and will feature 600 apps, including games and lifestyle apps like Pinterest and Draw Something. "The App Center gives you personalized recommendations, and lets you browse the apps your friends use," a Facebook rep says. "It only lists high-quality apps, based on feedback from people who use the app." The store will be available on Facebook's iOS and Android apps, as well as on the main website. Users will be able to send apps to the store via the website or through their mobile devices. Paid apps will also be available. The store is designed to keep Facebook users on the site for longer, but it's likely to draw criticism from those who see it as harmful to the future of the open web, the Independent notes.

Toronto Police Inspector Dominic Sinopoli said the teens, who are all 14 and 15, are from St. Michael's College and were charged with assault, gang sexual assault, and sexual assault with a weapon. Sinopoli said the school failed to notify police immediately and police became aware of the sexual assault through the media. Those arrested are young offenders and cannot be named. They appeared in court Monday and received bail. St. Michael's has expelled eight students and suspended another in connection with at least two other incidents that allegedly took place on campus and were captured on video. "These incidents are clearly indicative we have a problem. We need to do much better at our culture and our student's ability to talk to us." On Sunday, the school said it was conducting an independent examination into the "underlying attitudes and behaviors" that it said were inconsistent with the school's culture. – General Motors is recalling 1.02 million vehicles worldwide, including 1.02 million in the US, because of a problem with the power steering that has been linked to 30 crashes and two injuries, Reuters reports. "This was so extraordinary that at first I questioned the result: was this real or was it due to a data error?" one scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory tells the Los Angeles Times. Scientists believe the thaw was caused by a heat dome over the island, which allowed unusually warm air to rise onto the ice sheet. "What we are seeing at the highest elevations may be a sort of sign of what is going on across the ice sheet," says another scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center. "At lower elevations on the ice sheet, we are seeing earlier melting, melting later in the season, and more frequent melting over the last 30 years and that is consistent of what you would expect with a warming climate." Greenland returned to normal temperatures by the end of the week, but scientists warn that the thaw could have far-reaching consequences, including higher sea levels, reports AP.

The reason for the darkening is a complex series of physical processes, one of which can't be seen with the naked eye, according to the study published in The Cryosphere. As snowpack melts and refreezes, ice grains get larger, which in turn absorbs more solar energy. This effect is strongest in the infrared range, which is invisible to human eyes but can be seen with satellites. – Pregnant women who take acetaminophen are more likely to have children with ADHD, according to a new study. The FDA has asked drug companies to limit how much acetaminophen they put into products, the Los Angeles Times reports, but the new study doesn't say acetaminophen should be avoided during pregnancy. "We aren't saying if you take one Tylenol once it will give your child hyperactivity," one epidemiologist says. "You should just avoid chronic or long-term use." The study, which looked at 64,000 Danish children and their mothers, found that women who took acetaminophen frequently during pregnancy were 29% more likely to have children with ADHD and 37% more likely to have a diagnosis of hyperkinetic syndrome, the Washington Post reports. "We know that there are genetic and environmental and possibly prenatal (factors) but we know that none of them on their own cause ADHD," a doctor not involved in the study says. Researchers say it's possible that women who feel pain more acutely, and take painkillers more often, may have a genetic predisposition to ADHD. The FDA has asked drug companies to limit the amount of acetaminophen in products.

– The White House is working on a plan that would allow President Obama to close Guantanamo Bay and transfer its prisoners to US prisons around the country, the Wall Street Journal reports. Congress has banned the transfer of Guantanamo detainees to US soil, but the president could circumvent that by using an executive order. The move would be "the latest and potentially most dramatic use of executive power by the president in his second term," says the Journal's story, which notes that such a move "would likely provoke a sharp reaction from lawmakers, who have a history of blocking the president's efforts to close the detention facility." A Gallup poll finds that 29% of Americans support closing Guantanamo Bay and moving its prisoners to US prisons, while 66% oppose the idea.

– The University of New Hampshire will be the first state university in the US to accept results from China's standardized entrance exam, the BBC reports. Approximately 10 million Chinese students took the Gaokao high school entrance exam last week. According to the New York Times, the Gaokao is similar to the SAT in the US, but it takes place over two days, instead of the typical two. The Gaokao is seen as a "life-defining" test for millions of Chinese high school seniors who may not get into a top university or any school at all. Approximately one-third of all international students enrolled in US universities are from China. The University of New Hampshire will be accepting results from the Gaokao in an effort to attract "outstanding Chinese high school graduates," the BBC reports. According to the Times, the University of New Hampshire will be accepting results from the Gaokao in January, allowing Chinese students to start classes early. The University of New Hampshire had 781 international undergraduate and graduate students on campus last fall. About half of those foreign students—357—came from China. "This initiative is part of UNH's commitment to attracting more and stronger applicants from around the world," the BBC quotes a UNH spokesperson as saying

– The APOE gene is a known risk factor for a wide range of conditions, including Alzheimer's, and a new study suggests it may also play a role in age-related macular degeneration. In the study published in the New England Journal of Medicine, researchers looked at the health histories of more than 5,600 people from 10 countries and found that those with at least one copy of the gene variant were more likely to suffer from macular degeneration, which is a leading cause of vision loss in older people. They also found that those with at least one copy of the gene variant were more likely to have plaque in their brains, which is a sign of dementia, reports the Los Angeles Times. The researchers say the findings suggest that people with at least one copy of the gene variant may be able to delay the onset of the eye disease, which is a leading cause of vision loss among older people, while having at least one copy may increase the risk of the disease or cause symptoms to appear earlier. The researchers say more research is needed to clarify what role, if any, the gene variants play in the development of age-related macular degeneration. (A new drug could help prevent Alzheimer's, but there's a lot of red tape.)

– Scientists are still trying to figure out what's causing so-called "intersex" fish in the Chesapeake Bay watershed, but one thing is clear: Most male smallmouth bass in the region are developing "characteristics of the opposite sex," the Washington Post reports. That includes 90% of fish in some West Virginia waters and 50% to 100% in the southern stretch of the Potomac River. All of the affected fish had eggs where their testes should be, according to previous studies. "In the case of this specific study, we’re getting a better handle on how widespread [the problem] is," says a US Geological Survey researcher. "We’re seeing this signal at national wildlife refuges, ... evidence that in areas that are managed for animal health, stuff is going on behind the scenes." Scientists suspect prescription drugs, flushed down toilets, and chemical pesticides are to blame. The Post notes that smallmouth bass are "like the canary in the coal mine" because they are a sanctuary for 1,000 fish species, 700 bird species, and 200 species of mammals.

– When a 43-year-old man in Italy went into a coma after a car accident two years ago, he was in a "minimally conscious state." He remained there for 40 days before doctors decided to perform a CT scan. They gave the man a mild sedative called midazolam, which is normally given to patients in intensive care units to help them sleep before surgery, reports Live Science. The scan revealed that the man's brain had been affected by the drug, which may have caused him to wake up, say researchers from the University Hospital of Pisa. Within minutes, he was able to talk, recognize the road leading to his home, and calculate simple math problems, among other things. "This is the first report of midazolam having an 'awakening' effect," one of the researchers tells Live Science. The man, who did not remember the accident, began to exhibit "aimless, repetitive behaviors, such as clapping," the researchers write in the case report, but it's not clear whether the drug played a role in the man's condition or whether he simply suffered from catatonic symptoms, such as unresponsiveness to stimuli associated with schizophrenia, the researchers say. – Women tend to live longer than men, but why? Researchers at the University of Southern California are reporting in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences that a "twentieth-century surge of excess adult male mortality" may have had something to do with it. As LiveScience reports, the male-female gap in life expectancies began as early as 1870, but it began to fade around the turn of the 20th century. Specifically, women born after 1880 saw a 70% drop in death rates from males over the age of 40, while men saw a 40% drop. But heart disease was the leading cause of excess deaths in men over 40 after 1890, and only 30% of the difference in deaths between the sexes after 1890 was attributed to smoking. "We were surprised at how the divergence in mortality between men and women, which originated as early as 1870, was concentrated in the 50 to 70 age range and faded out sharply after age 80," study co-author Eileen Crimmins says in a press release. The study looked at people born between 1800 and 1935 in 13 developed nations, and while smoking was the leading cause of deaths in men over 40, it was not the leading cause of deaths between the sexes after 1890. Researchers say more study is needed

– Wine lovers, rejoice: A scientist at Brandeis University has invented a wine bottle that doesn't drip when poured. Daniel Perlman, a biophysicist, says he studied slow-motion videos of wine being poured to figure out why wine drips down the side of the bottle and onto anything below. He figured out that by adding one small groove around the lip of the bottle opening he could change the behavior of the liquid at the end of the pour. Instead of hugging the bottle, the wine fails to bridge the gap and simply falls directly into its intended vessel until it stops coming out entirely. The grooved tip is just 2 millimeters wide, but a video showing Perlman's alteration in action shows just how well it really works in comparison to the original, very basic wine bottle design. Perlman is currently shopping his invention to wine bottle manufacturers who may adopt the idea. For some reason, wine dripping down the side of the bottle when you pour it has become as accepted an inevitability as death and taxes (both of which some people probably consider preferable to dripping wine). Wine accessory companies sell products specifically built to address this problem. Even highly-trained sommeliers resort to wrapping a bandana around the bottle's neck as if that Cabernet Sauvignon is some Wild West outlaw up to no good

Since then, she's endured more than 40 surgeries, the Chicago Tribune reports, and she still hasn't been able to play the violin again. "It's never over, just because of the complicated nature of the combination of my injuries," she says. "If I didn't get to play with those kinds of orchestras, I would be heartbroken." Pine is now 33, and she's performing with less-heralded ensembles around the country. But she still hopes to play with the world's greatest orchestras, she says. Cruz's campaign is offering to donate $1.5 million to charities that help veterans if Trump will debate Cruz head-to-head before the Iowa caucuses, the AP reports. The political action committees Keep the Promise I and II are proposing a one-hour debate to be held in Iowa on or before Jan. 31, the day before the caucuses, with a moderator chosen by the candidates. Cruz himself sent a letter to Trump Wednesday inviting him to debate in Sioux City, Iowa, on Saturday night. The Cruz campaign suggested conservative radio hosts Mark Levin, Sean Hannity, and Rush Limbaugh as possible moderators. Trump dismissed Cruz's proposal earlier Wednesday. – China is planning to make history by becoming the first country to land a probe on the dark side of the moon. Zou Yongliao of the Chinese Academy of Sciences' moon exploration department told state broadcaster CCTV on Wednesday that the Chang'e 4 mission is planned for sometime before 2020, the AP reports. Zou said the mission's objective would be to study geological conditions on the moon's far side, also known as the dark side. That could eventually lead to the placement of a radio telescope for use by astronomers, something that would help "fill a void" in man's knowledge of the universe, Zou said. Radio transmissions from Earth are unable to reach the moon's far side, making it an excellent location for sensitive instruments. China's next lunar mission is scheduled for 2017, when it will attempt to land an unmanned spaceship on the moon before returning to Earth with samples. If successful, that would make China only the third country after the United States and Russia to have carried out such a maneuver. China's lunar exploration program, named Chang'e after a mythical goddess, has already launched a pair of orbiting lunar probes, and in 2013 landed a craft on the moon with a rover onboard. China has also hinted at a possible crewed mission

"We don't know what happened after they left the dinner party," DEC Police Maj. Scott Florence tells ABC News. "Some things at the scene raised a lot of questions." For example, a kitchen table on the boat had come apart, and Becker's uniform tie was found on the floor, suggesting a struggle. "It leads you to believe the tie was pulled off and the table was broken," he says. The case is getting renewed attention now, in advance of the 35th anniversary of the drownings, because Florence says it's time to "find out the missing pieces." Police say homicide detectives are "open to receiving any new information anyone had to provide." – Puerto Rico's official death toll from Hurricane Maria has long stood at 64, but a new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine puts the figure at closer to 5,000. Researchers from the Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health conducted a survey of 3,299 households in the island's most remote areas and found that there was a 50% increase in the annual mortality rate from September 2017 to December 2017, when the storm passed, from an average of 8 per 1,000 households to an average of 8 per 1,000 households. The study's lead author, Dr. Ricardo Rossello, tells NPR that the new figure is "a substantial underestimate." The death toll includes people who died in the immediate aftermath of the storm, as well as those who died in the months after the hurricane but were still alive at the time. The researchers say the new figure is likely much higher than the government's. Puerto Rico's official death toll for 2016 was just shy of 2,000, and the New York Times reports that the hurricane's death toll was much lower than the official estimate. The Times notes that the new study is based on a population estimate, not a death count, and the researchers say there are many possible reasons for the higher death toll

– A graffiti protest in Cambridge, England, is getting a lot of attention—but is it really a protest in Latin? The phrase " Locus in domos loci populum" ("The place into homes, the people of the place") is painted across four new homes, and it's not Latin, reports the Telegraph. "But anyone with a smattering of Latin will see the bigger problem: however construed, the Latin is nonsense—'the place into homes, the people of the place'. Even as a ten-pinter, that is not going to wash as a slogan," writes Martin Daubney in the Daily Beast. "The interesting thing is not how the Latin is wrong but that it is totally wrong: every word misfires. With a little reflection on this genuine curiosity, the culprit's profile starts to gain color. What then? A set of slips from whirring brain or adrenalin-riddled hand beneath the blanket of night? No, its uniform appearance twice on the walls puts paid to that. Or maybe a sign of the debasement of linguistic precision—even in Latin—in these Twitter-fuddled times?"

– A gunman who got into a deadly shootout with police, then took dozens of people hostage at a Los Angeles supermarket has been arrested on suspicion of murder, authorities said Sunday. Gene Evin Atkins, 28, was being held Sunday morning on $2 million bail, according to Officer Drake Madison, a Los Angeles police spokesman. It wasn't clear if he had an attorney and a message left at a number listed for Atkins in public records wasn't immediately returned. A woman was shot and killed when Atkins ran into the Trader Joe's supermarket in Los Angeles' Silver Lake section on Saturday, but no hostages were seriously hurt before the man handcuffed himself and surrendered about three hours later, police said. Coroner's officials identified the woman Sunday as 27-year-old Melyda Corado. Her brother, Albert Corado, said on Twitter that she worked at Trader Joe's. "I'm sad to say she didn't make it. My baby sister. My world," he tweeted. Atkins' grandmother was hospitalized in critical condition after the shooting and police had no update on her condition Sunday. Authorities said Atkins shot his grandmother seven times and wounded another woman, whom he forced into a car, at a South Los Angeles home around 1:30pm, police said

– Bernie Sanders gave a major speech at Georgetown University on Thursday in which he tried to dispel the notion that he's "radical," reports the Hill. "I don't believe government should own the means of production," he said. "I believe government should create an economy that works for all, not just the very wealthy." But he also stressed the importance of economic rights. "Democratic socialism means that we must reform a political system which is corrupt, that we must create an economy that works for all, not just the very wealthy," he said, per USA Today. "It is a vision that we have not yet achieved, and it is time that we did." The Vermont senator also called for a new international organization similar to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization that would allow NATO partners, Russia, and members of the Arab League to work together to fight terrorism, reports the Washington Post. "We need to develop a political movement which, once again, is prepared to take on and defeat a ruling class whose greed is destroying our nation," he said. "The billionaire class must be told loudly and clearly that they cannot have it all." He also called for paid family leave, free college tuition, a living wage, and public funding of elections, reports the Hill

– The Metropolitan Opera's new production of The Death of Klinghoffer has been met with protests from both Jewish and non-Jewish groups, the New York Times reports. The opera is based on the 1985 hijacking of the Achille Lauro cruise ship by the Palestinian Liberation Front, in which the four hijackers kill retired American Jew Leon Klinghoffer and demand the release of 50 Palestinians held in Israel. Jewish groups protested the Met's decision to go ahead with the production, but the Anti-Defamation League brokered a deal in which the Met dropped plans to show it in movie theaters and allowed Jewish leaders to attend the show. Protesters gathered outside the Met before the show. "By putting this on a stage in the middle of Manhattan, the message is, 'Go out, murder someone, be a terrorist, and we’ll write a play about you,'" one protester told the Times. A counter-protester held a sign that said, "A work of art about a subject is not a work in favor of that subject." The Met's general manager, Peter Gelb, addressed the performers and musicians at Friday's final dress rehearsal to tell them about enhanced security measures.

– The search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 is officially over, but that doesn't mean it's over. Officials are meeting in Canberra, Australia, today to plan the next phase of the search, which will involve combing a "staggering" 4.6 million square miles of the Indian Ocean, CNN reports. "We know very clearly the area of the follow-up search will be even broader, with more difficulties and tougher tasks," China's Transport Minister Yang Chuantang says. The search area has now been expanded to the north and east, but officials say it's too early to say whether the area will be expanded to the south, where the plane is believed to have crashed, the New York Times reports. The new phase will involve an analysis of the data collected so far, as well as the resources needed to search the new area, CNN reports. "It will also look again at the satellite information that's been accumulated so that we can make sure that it's been accurately interpreted," Australia's Deputy Prime Minister Warren Truss says. Officials will meet with relatives of the passengers and crew members, as well as Chinese and Australian officials, to discuss the next steps, the Times reports. The three countries will also hold a meeting in Beijing

– George Michael died of heart disease and fatty liver, according to a coroner's report. The senior coroner for Oxfordshire, England, says a post-mortem examination found the 53-year-old singer died of "dilated cardiomyopathy with myocarditis and fatty liver," reports CBS News. Dilated cardiomyopathy is a condition in which the heart's ability to pump blood is limited, while myocarditis is inflammation of the heart muscle. An initial autopsy failed to determine the cause of death. Salter said Tuesday that because Michael died of natural causes, no inquest will be held. (Michael had a life-threatening bout of pneumonia in 2011.)

– The white tiger that bit Siegfried & Roy's Roy Horn during a 2003 performance in Las Vegas has died. Mantecore, who was 7 years old when he bit Horn on the neck, died "after a short illness," according to a Siegfried & Roy press release. Though Horn suffered significant blood loss, it was a stroke and brain-swelling that ended Horn's stage career, the Las Vegas Review-Journal reports. He spent most of his remaining years alternating between the Siegfried & Roy Secret Garden attraction and Horn's estate. Even during the early days of his recovery, Horn was adamant in his wishes the tiger be spared, and has always argued with reports that he was "attacked" by the tiger. Siegfried & Roy have long contended Horn suffered a stroke onstage, and that the tiger punctured his neck while dragging him backstage as a protective response. "It was not an attack," Horn said as recently as his 69th birthday party last year. "It was his concern for my safety and well-being that caused him to act as he did on that night long ago."

– Author and actor Christopher Kennedy Lawford, who was born into political and Hollywood royalty, sank into substance abuse and addiction and rose to become a well-known advocate for sobriety and recovery, has died. Lawford died of a heart attack Tuesday in Vancouver, Canada, his cousin, former US Rep. Patrick J. Kennedy, tells the AP. He was 63. Lawford was in Vancouver living with his girlfriend and working to open a recovery center. He had been doing hot yoga, which he did often, but the strain of it "must have been too much for him at that point," Kennedy says. Lawford was the only son and oldest child of Patricia Kennedy—sister of John, Robert and Ted Kennedy—and Peter Lawford—the English actor and socialite who was a member of Frank Sinatra's "Rat Pack." – When the Cleveland Cavaliers won the NBA title last year, owner Dan Gilbert made a point to thank the city of Cleveland for its support. This year, he's going to do more of the same. Gilbert and his wife, Cathy, have committed to giving away $1 million in their lifetimes to groups that help the city's poor and disadvantaged, Cleveland.com reports. The Quicken Loans Arena, the Plain Dealer, and the Cleveland Cavaliers Foundation are among the dozens of groups that have pledged a total of $5 million. The giveaway will go to groups that help the city's homeless, the hungry, and the poor, as well as those that help the elderly and people with mental illness, the Plain Dealer notes. Gilbert says he wants to give back to the city that gave him "so much," the AP reports. "I want to give back to the community that has been so supportive of me," he says. "I want to give back to the city that has been so loving to me."

– When Casey Anthony was found not guilty this week in the death of her 2-year-old daughter, Caylee, one of the first things Michelle Crowder did was start a petition on Change.org to make it a federal offense and a felony for a parent or guardian to fail to report a child's disappearance to law enforcement. “When I saw that Casey Anthony had been found not guilty in the murder of little Caylee, and that she was only being convicted of lying to the police about her disappearance, I was sickened,” Crowder tells ABC News. “I could not believe she was not being charged with child neglect or endangerment, or even obstruction of justice.” If passed, “Caylee’s Law” would make it a federal offense and a felony for a parent or guardian to fail to report a child’s disappearance to law enforcement. The petition has so far received more than 25,000 signatures, making it the fastest-growing on Change.org. Another campaign on Facebook has more than 2 million people pledging to leave their porch lights on for Caylee.

– If you're an anti-vaccine parent, you might want to take heart: A new study finds that your child's vaccinations are as safe as they are beneficial. The study, published in Pediatrics, looked at 67 studies on vaccines and found that they cause "extremely rare" and "must be weighed against the protective benefits that vaccines provide," the New York Times reports. Among the worst side effects: a blood disorder called thrombocytopenicpura linked with the chickenpox and measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine, and a very rare intestinal blockage called intussusception caused by the rotavirus vaccine, USA Today reports. "Concerns about vaccine safety have led some parents to decline recommended vaccination of their children, leading to the resurgence of diseases," the study's authors write. "We found evidence that some vaccines are associated with serious adverse events; however, these events are extremely rare and must be weighed against the protective benefits that vaccines provide." The study was commissioned by the federal government as the US sees a resurgence of diseases like measles, whooping cough, and chicken pox, the Times notes.

– Scientists are virtually certain that California will be rocked by a strong earthquake in the next 30 years, the AP reports. A US Geological Survey report released yesterday raised the chance of a magnitude 8.0 or greater quake hitting the state in the next three decades from 4.7% to 7%. An 8.0 quake would be devastating—producing 89 times more energy than the magnitude 6.7 Northridge earthquake in 1994. Such powerful quakes are relatively rare—scientists believe the last mega-quake to hit Southern California was a magnitude 7.9 earthquake in 1857. Scientists in recent decades have begun to realize that earthquake faults are interconnected. In fact, earthquakes can begin on one fault and jump to another. Multiple faults can rupture in a simultaneous mega-quake. "A simplification we made in the past were these faults were separate and isolated. In other words, they couldn't link up together into truly large earthquakes," says the lead author of the report. But as scientists identified more faults in California, "it has become increasingly apparent that we are not dealing with a few well-separate faults, but with a vast interconnected fault system." Jan Tighe said Thursday. "We will look for a couple of things," Tighe told the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, per USNI News. "One, try to confirm cyber did not have anything to do with the collision and then how do we move forward in making sure these are a normal part of these investigations. It is something that we think about a lot and we have to have both the authorities and the human capital ready to respond." She said the Navy has set aside $1.5 billion over the next few years to improve its cybersecurity, though she added that the McCain's investigation will be the first to look into the possibility of a cyberattack on a ship's computer systems. US intelligence officials have warned in the past that hackers could manipulate a ship's computer systems to blind its commander by, for example, displaying an inaccurate location of the ship on its charts.
