– The so-called "Dark Web" is home to everything from underground drug markets and bitcoin exchanges to child pornography and child pornography sharing sites, according to a new study. Researchers from the University of Portsmouth ran 40 encrypted computers in the Tor network for six months, gathering data about the number of sites on the network and how many visits were made to them. They found that 83% of the visits to Tor hidden services were to child pornography sites, Wired reports. "It came as a huge shock to us," says researcher Gareth Owen. "I don't think anyone imagined it was on this scale." Owen's team found that more than four out of five Tor hidden services site visits were to sites with pedophilia materials. That's more than five times as many as any of the other categories of content they found in their Dark Web survey, such as gambling, bitcoin-related sites, or anonymous whistle-blowing. "Before we did this study, it was certainly my view that the dark net is a good thing," Owen says. "Looking back in the mirror, I saw her face turning red and drool pouring from her mouth," Joniec says. She pulled over and tried the Heimlich on her daughter, but "there was no resistance," she says. Britton told her mom she'd swallowed a metal bushing from a fidget spinner she'd bought, and her mom drove her to an urgent care center, where workers couldn't figure out whether it was lodged in her airway or her esophagus. She was then rushed to Texas Children's Hospital, where X-rays showed the nickel-size bushing was stuck in her esophagus. "The GI doctor was fascinated ... he'd only just learned of fidget spinners that morning when he was at the mall with his son, so it was a surprise to be faced with one in a case a few hours later," Joniec writes. Chestnut downed 70 franks and buns in 10 minutes last year, topping his record at the time and taking back the title from Matt "The Megatoad" Stonie. Stonie came in third on Tuesday, with 48 franks and buns. Miki Sudo won for the fourth year in a row in the women's division, downing 41 hot dogs and buns in 10 minutes. She beat Michelle Lesco, who downed 32 franks and buns. Women's record-holder Sonya "The Black Widow" Thomas came in third with 30. Thomas holds the women's record for the contest, at 45 hot dogs and buns. Thousands of people—many wearing hot-dog-shaped hats—gathered on Coney Island's famed boardwalk for the contest. – If the world wants to avoid the worst of climate change, it's going to have to ease up on the takeoffs. That's according to a new study in Climatic Change that finds rising temperatures will make it harder for some planes to take off in the hottest parts of the day. In fact, up to 30% of fully loaded planes will have to dump weight or wait for cooler temperatures to take place, reports the New York Times. "Our results suggest that weight restriction may impose a non-trivial cost on airline and impact aviation operations around the world," says Columbia University PhD student Ethan Coffel, who led the study. The problem is that air is getting thinner as it warms, and the weight of a plane's passengers, cargo, and fuel drop as the air moves along a runway. The authors of the study, which looked at 20 busiest airports in the US, Europe, the Mideast, China, and south Asia, say that by the year 2080, temperatures at these airports are expected to be up to 8 degrees Fahrenheit higher than they are today—and that's when takeoffs will be most affected. "This points to the unexplored risks of changing climate on aviation," says co-author Radley Horton of Columbia

– MTV is the latest network to allow vibrators to air in prime time—but only between 3:30am and 6am. Trojan's new ad for Tri-Phoria, which claims it's "like three massagers in one," was initially rejected by the network, the New York Times reports. "No matter how liberal you are, a little kid doesn’t need to hear the word 'vibrator,'" says an MTV exec. "At first there was a certain amount of trepidation that maybe the viewing public wasn’t prepared to see a commercial with vibrators, and we automatically put it in the overnight slot, but we opened it up because, instead of it being taboo, they got their point across subtly." A history of the vibrator dates back to the early 1900s, when it was advertised in women's magazines and the Sears catalog, but it was not until the 1920s that they started appearing in stag films. "The camouflage used to be a lot thicker, but there’s still a very thin layer of camouflage," says a vibrator expert. "The networks have moved to where they’re resigned to accept some sort of advertising—but they still require a fig leaf held up with suspenders."

Chua-Rubenfeld, who has applied to Harvard, Yale, and the University of Virginia, opened the speech with a joke about her mom's book, Battle Hymn of the Tiger Mother, says a source. "Instead of writing her own speech, she [told audience members] that she was going to read from her [favorite] book," the source says.

Jack McCullough was sentenced to life in prison in 2012 for the murder of Maria Ridulph, who was abducted from a street corner in Sycamore on Dec. 3, 1957. McCullough, a former security guard, has long insisted that he was 40 miles away in Rockford, Ill., at the time, talking to Air Force recruiters and trying to enlist, CNN reports. He says that when Maria was kidnapped, the telephone in his home was ringing. "And I was on the other end of that phone, in Rockford, three minutes before she was kidnapped," he says. "Try and make that happen. Only Scotty could make that happen, if he beamed me up." DeKalb County state's attorney Richard Schmack argued that McCullough's conviction was based on false testimony, improper legal rulings controlling the evidence presented, and a timeline that was tweaked some 50 years after the fact to rule out McCullough's alibi. – Reports that an explosion damaged Iran's Fordow nuclear site last week are "Western propaganda ahead of nuclear negotiations to influence their process and outcome," Iran's atomic energy deputy head said last night. "I deny an explosion at the Fordow site," Massoud Jazayeri was quoted as saying by Iran's ISNA news agency, according to Reuters. The 300-foot-deep bunker is immune to air strikes or bunker bombs, the Telegraph reports, and Tehran has blamed Israel for past explosive disasters. Israel, however, has been unable to confirm reports of an explosion at Fordow, and some Israeli officials believe Iran may have leaked false reports to prevent international inspectors from entering the site. "They [Tehran] are more than capable of inventing such a story—although if it's true, a damaged Fordow would definitely benefit Israel," an Israeli expert in Israeli foreign security policy tells the Telegraph. "Israel would do anything within its power to stop the Iranian nuclear program. This includes tactics that fall just short of, or substitute, a direct attack, such as the cyber war that has been raging for the past few years or acts of sabotage on Iran's nuclear facilities."

– North Korea's most powerful nuclear test yet may have just ratcheted up tensions on the Korean Peninsula. South Korean lawmakers say Pyongyang is moving an intercontinental ballistic missile, or ICBM, toward the North Pacific, possibly at a lower angle than its two nuclear tests in July, reports CNN. If true, that would make Sunday's test the third time Pyongyang has attempted to fire an ICBM toward the North Pacific, though it's not clear if the missile is capable of reaching the US. The revelation comes after US Ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley warned that the country has "basically slapped everyone in the face in the international community that has asked them to stop," and President Trump tweeted that the North "will be met with fire, fury and frankly power the likes of which the world has never seen before." A South Korean lawmaker who was briefed by South Korea's National Intelligence Service on Monday says Pyongyang is digging extra tunnels at its nuclear test site and could detonate another one "anytime," reports Reuters. (Analysts say Sunday's test was the biggest ever.)

– It's been 19 years since North Korea last broadcast a new year's message on state TV, but Kim Jong Un managed to pull off a rare feat today: He delivered it himself. In the speech, Kim called for a "radical turnabout" in North Korea's economy and said confrontation between the North and South should be removed, reports the BBC. The speech comes less than a month after South Korea's Park Geun-hye was elected president, and the speech comes as the UN Security Council debates how to punish Pyongyang for a recent long-range rocket launch. "The military might of a country represents its national strength," said Kim. "Only when it builds up its military might in every way can it develop into a thriving country." He also called for "anti- reunification forces" in South Korea to end their hostility toward the North, reports the AP, but he did not offer any specifics.

– Gas prices are finally on their way down, after 11 straight days of declines. The national average dropped to $3.72 yesterday, down from a summer peak of $3.87, the Christian Science Monitor reports. That's still a record high for this time of year, but it's expected to drop further. "If you're along the West Coast, specifically California, you have my sympathy," writes an analyst at GasBuddy.com. "Prices just aren't coming down fast enough—but at least they're coming down and not going up." The nationwide average is still 27 cents more expensive than it was one year ago, the AP reports. But it's expected to drop further as oil producers switch to cheaper winter-blend gas. And it could have a big impact on next month's election. "Certainly, lower gas prices are helpful in terms of consumer spending by increasing disposable income,'' an economist tells USA Today. "And if prices come down at a rapid rate in the next three weeks, that would tend to help the incumbent."

– North Korea is ratcheting up its war rhetoric again, issuing a warning to its military to be ready for an air raid on the US, South Korea's Yonhap News reports. The warning, issued this morning, said that "if the US dares to launch an air raid on the DPRK, the relevant units will be immediately retaliating with strong military counteraction," according to Pyongyang's official news agency, CNN reports. The US, meanwhile, is continuing its B-52 flights over South Korea as part of its annual military exercises with the South, the New York Times reports. Pyongyang had earlier warned that it would "take corresponding military actions" if the planes made more sorties.

– The father of a Pakistani woman who was bludgeoned to death by a mob in broad daylight after marrying the wrong man has been sentenced to death, along with three cousins and a former fiance, the BBC reports. Farzana Parveen's father was found guilty of her murder, as was a brother and two cousins, while a cousin was sentenced to 10 years in prison for his role in the attack. Parveen's husband, Muhammad Iqbal, was also sentenced to death. – A black man on North Carolina's death row has won the right to a new trial. A judge ruled today that Marcus Robinson, convicted of murdering a white teenager in 1991, was denied a fair trial, reports the AP. The jury that convicted Robinson had nine whites, two blacks, and one American Indian on it, and the judge ruled that race played a "persistent, pervasive, and distorting role" in the selection process. The case is the first of more than 150 to go to an evidentiary hearing under a 2009 state law that allows death row prisoners and capital murder defendants to challenge their sentences or prosecutors' decisions with statistics and other evidence beyond documents or witness testimony. "The Racial Justice Act represents a landmark reform in capital sentencing in our state," said the judge. "There are those who disagree with this, but it is the law." Robinson's case is the first of more than 150 pending cases to get an evidentiary hearing before a judge. Prosecutors said they planned to challenge the ruling. "Everybody is not guilty, everybody is not innocent, but at least be fair," said Robinson's mother. "It wasn't all about Marcus. It's about anyone who suffers discrimination."

– The winter solstice is upon us, and that means it's time to turn on the lights in the Northern Hemisphere. If you're in the Northern Hemisphere, that means you'll have the longest night of the year. But if you're in the Southern Hemisphere, that means you'll have the shortest days and longest nights, reports Time. The solstice occurs when the Northern Hemisphere is at its most tilted with the sun at its lowest point, meaning that the amount of sunlight the Northern Hemisphere gets varies from year to year. The Southern Hemisphere gets its longest days in June and its longest nights in December. The Washington Post explains why the winter solstice is the longest night of the year: The rotation of the Earth is slowing, and that means the length of a day increases by about 15 to 25 millionths of a second every year.

– A new poll from CBS News and the New York Times gives Hillary Clinton a slight lead over Donald Trump among likely voters, but it's not enough to give her the White House. The poll, which surveyed 1,753 adults from Sept. 9-13, has Clinton up 46-44 among those who support or lean toward a candidate. When Gary Johnson and Jill Stein are factored in, Clinton and Trump are even at 42%. The poll also found that more than four in 10 voters think both candidates should release more of their medical records. The poll was conducted before both candidates released their medical records. The poll also found that more than half of Trump voters and more than two-thirds of Clinton voters say they strongly support their candidate, though a quarter of Clinton voters say they're voting for someone else because they don't like their candidate.

– The child molestation and child pornography cases that have rocked Hollywood over the last decade are only getting worse, according to an investigation by the Los Angeles Times. At least a dozen child molestation and child pornography prosecutions have been filed in the entertainment industry since 2000. The cases include actors, managers, production assistants, and others who used the hopes of at least two girls who dreamed of careers in TV to sexually exploit them. "This is just like the Catholic Church pretending that priests never molested people in the past," says an expert on child sexual abuse. "What's surprising to me is why it hasn't come out even stronger and sooner." A bill that would require licensing and criminal background checks for those who work with actors under age 16 is expected to be filed this month in California. It would prevent registered sex offenders from being able to work with children.

– "Pharma bro" Martin Shkreli is in hot water again, this time for offering $5,000 to anyone who could "grab" some of Hillary Clinton's hair during her upcoming book tour. Federal prosecutors moved to revoke Shkreli's bail, arguing that his behavior shows he poses a "danger to the community," USA Today reports. "Shkreli's latest threat is concerning not only because it has required a significant expenditure of resources by the United States Secret Service, which is charged with protecting Secretary Clinton, but also because there is a significant risk that one of his many social media followers or others who learn of his offers through the media will take his statements seriously—as has happened previously—and act on them," prosecutors wrote in a legal motion. Shkreli, who was released on $5 million bail after being convicted on three counts of fraud last month, was back at it on Facebook after the motion was filed, saying the post was "just a prank, bro!" Shkreli could face up to 20 years in prison for the convictions. His defense lawyers also plan to appeal the convictions.

– The state of Louisiana's refusal to install air conditioning on death row has already cost taxpayers more than $1 million in legal bills, according to records obtained by the AP. The state could spend roughly the same money—and possibly much less—on an air conditioning system that would satisfy a federal judge's order to protect death-row inmates from dangerous heat and humidity inside Louisiana State Penitentiary at Angola. Instead, the corrections department and attorney general's office have accrued at least $1,067,000 in expenses fighting the 3-year-old lawsuit filed on behalf of three inmates with medical problems. This tally, based on state documents provided in response to the AP's public records requests, is the first public accounting of how much the case has cost taxpayers. Most of the money has gone to private attorneys on opposing sides of the case, which the judge said could ultimately cost many more millions of dollars. A list of expenses incurred by the prison itself adds up to more than $100,000, including an April 2014 payment of nearly $29,000 to a firm that was monitoring the heat and humidity every 15 minutes. Airing his frustrations last month, US District Judge Brian Jackson said the bill is "stunning," given the painful cuts lawmakers are making to balance the state budget

Grandview Aquarium in Guangzhou's Grandview Mall is home to wolves, beluga whales, walrus calves, and two polar bear hybrids. "Nowhere to hide from people taking photos—banging on the windows and shouting. In a court filing Monday, the Justice Department said it no longer needs Apple's assistance in unlocking Syed Farook's iPhone 5C and has asked a judge to vacate her order compelling Apple to assist in the case, the Los Angeles Times reports. The FBI hasn't said what method it used to access the data on the phone, which was used by Farook and his wife, Tashfeen Malik, in the December attack. Mariner Energy Inc.'s shallow-water platform wasn't covered by the moratorium put in place after the Deepwater Horizon spill, and the accident comes as the energy industry's effort to portray BP PLC's massive Deepwater Horizon oil spill as a fluke that shouldn't have provoked a drilling moratorium, some energy experts said. Mariner Energy has been involved in at least a dozen offshore accidents or pollution spills that were investigated by federal regulators, the Houston Chronicle reports. Possible violations were reported in at least six, and the company was fined three times.

"I'm not running for president," he said. "I'm running for governor." Bush, who was in town to speak at the National Conference of State Legislatures, said he's focused on being Florida's governor. "I'm here to tell you that I'm not running for president," he said.

– Three French workers who found 16 gold bars and 600 $20-gold coins buried in the ground at a property they were working on have been charged with theft, the BBC reports. The treasure may have been buried during World War II, according to a local newspaper. The workers, aged 20 to 40, decided to sell the treasure to a coin collector, but when the collector started depositing high-value checks into his bank account, tax officials were alerted, the BBC reports. The house's owner says she jokingly told the workers: "If you find any treasure, be sure to tell me!" They "had fun" with their new-found fortune, buying cars or motorcycles, but also investing in life insurance or in their homes, police say. The coin collector denies trying to conceal the theft.

– About half of Earth's water is older than the sun—and that's a good thing, scientists say, because it means we may have a lot more water to look for elsewhere in the universe. In a study published Thursday in Science, researchers found that heavy hydrogen levels on Earth are higher than they would have been in the protoplanetary disk, the same band of space dust around which the sun was formed, the Washington Post reports. That means some of our water must have predate the sun, when heavy hydrogen was in abundance. So, if water can survive a star's birthing process, and if other solar systems in the universe formed much like ours did, that means that water might be a common ingredient in the making of other planets far from our own. "By identifying the ancient heritage of Earth's water, we can see that the way in which our solar system was formed will not be unique, and that exoplanets will form in environments with abundant water," says study author Tim Harries. "Consequently," he says, "it raises the possibility that some exoplanets could house the right conditions, and water resources, for life to evolve." Last spring, scientists announced that there could be up to 11 billion exoplanets—

"Bobbi Kristina Brown passed away on Sunday, July 26, 2015, surrounded by her family. She is finally at peace in the arms of God," says a statement from the Houston family, per People. "We want to again thank everyone for their tremendous amount of love and support during these last few months." Bobbi Kristina, the 22-year-old daughter of Bobby Brown and Whitney Houston, was placed in a medically induced coma in January after her boyfriend, Nick Gordon, found her unresponsive. Officer Eric Parker's actions "did not meet the high standards and expectations of the Madison City Police Department," said Chief Larry Muncey, who apologized to 57-year-old Sureshbhai Patel and said the FBI was investigating the incident, AL.com reports. Patel, who arrived in the US a week ago to care for his son and daughter-in-law's 17-month-old child, was walking home from work Friday morning when he was approached by two officers responding to a call about a suspicious person. Patel underwent surgery the next day and is starting to regain feeling in his arms and one leg, according to a GoFundMe campaign.

The Android-powered device, which was unveiled in Barcelona on Tuesday, is HMD Global's attempt to revive the Nokia name and compete with the likes of Samsung and Apple, the Guardian reports. "We know that fans are creating and sharing live content more than ever before, with millions of photos and videos shared every minute on social media," says Juho Sarvikas, HMD's chief product officer. "People are inspired by the content they consume and are looking for new ways to create their own." The Nokia 8 has a 5.3-inch screen, two 13-megapixel cameras on the back, and spatial audio technology that can play back sound in multiple directions. The phone, which will go on sale in early September for 599, also has a front-facing camera for selfies. Mann's roommate, Steven Vander Briel, has been charged with first-degree murder in her death, though it's not clear whether the death was related to the harassment on Yik Yak. The group says it complained to the university's administration, but the staff told them to take up their case with Yik Yak. – Shares in Weight Watchers dropped to their lowest level since the company's 2001 IPO yesterday, after the weight-loss company reported a Q1 loss and warned that its turnaround would take longer than expected. The stock fell 35% to $11.33 on Friday in New York, the biggest drop since the company's initial public offering in November 2001, Bloomberg reports. The company forecast earnings of 40 cents to 70 cents a share for this year, missing the $1.43 average of seven analysts' estimates compiled by Bloomberg. "I am disappointed that we are not yet where we hoped to be and our turnaround will take longer than anticipated," Weight Watchers CEO Jim Chambers said Thursday on a conference call. The company's membership declined 15% in the past quarter, to 2.51 million active subscribers. While profit, excluding some charges, matched analysts' average estimate for 7 cents a share, revenue matched. The company has attempted to remake its image this year with a new ad campaign and redesigned magazine introduced in January. "They're struggling to keep pace," an analyst at Morningstar Inc. tells Bloomberg. "Its changes in marketing, product, and technology haven't connected with consumers."

– Mexico is sending thousands of troops and federal police to a dangerous stretch of the country near the US border in an attempt to drive out two drug cartels. The "Coordinated Operation Northeast" will boost forces in Tamaulipas and Nuevo Leon states, which have seen the heaviest fighting since the split of the Gulf and Zetas gangs, the AP reports. The Zetas and Gulf gangs have been fighting for control of the region for months, and authorities say the presence of federal and military forces will help. "These are geographic factors that have made the area a coveted route for organized crime in the trafficking of drugs and people and in receiving illegal money and arms coming into Mexico," said a spokesman for the federal police.

Singh, who is Sikh, suffered a fractured jaw and other injuries in the attack, which police are investigating as a hate crime. Singh was wearing a turban and beard, which "seems to be consistent with a national study released by Stanford University researchers less than two weeks ago, which shows that more than 50% of Americans associate the Sikh with Osama bin Laden than with any other figure," a friend of Singh's tells the Daily News. "Sadly, for many other Sikh Americans like Prabhjot, this is a story they have heard and experienced before."

"This has nothing to do with safety—95% of these inspections, searches, shoe removals, and pat-downs are ridiculously unnecessary." The only reason we continue to do this is that people are too cowed to even question the absurd taboo against profiling—when the profile of the airline attacker is narrow, concrete, uniquely definable and universally known. So instead of seeking out terrorists, we seek out tubes of gel in stroller pouches. The junk man's revolt marks the point at which a docile public declares that it will tolerate only so much idiocy." Click for Krauthammer's full column.

– Etta James is dying of leukemia and dementia, according to court documents filed as part of a legal battle over her health and financial affairs. The 72-year-old singer hasn't performed since early 2010 and hasn't been seen on stage since, the Press-Enterprise reports. Her husband, Artis Mills, is seeking control of James' money, and her son, Donto James, is asking the court to assign the duty to a third party "to avoid present and future family conflict and discrepancies." James gave power of attorney to Donto, her other son, Sametto James, and Donto's wife, Christy James, in 2008, according to court documents. Beyonce Knowles portrayed James in a 2008 film. Click for more.

– The latest development in the News of the World phone-hacking scandal comes via the New York Times, which reports that five senior police officers were aware their phones had been hacked shortly after Scotland Yard began its initial criminal inquiry in 2006. The investigators—the lead investigator, Andy Hayman; assistant commissioner John Yates; and two other senior officers—are now being grilled by Parliament about whether they were aware their phones had been hacked. The committee is also looking into whether the investigators had a conflict of interest because they were victims of the people they were investigating. Meanwhile, Rupert and James Murdoch have been called to appear before Parliament next week to answer questions about the scandal, Politico reports. The Murdochs and Rebekah Brooks, CEO of News International, will be questioned by the Culture, Media and Sport Committee on July 19.

– Just days after hackers showed off how they could "kill" a Jeep Cherokee at 70mph, Fiat Chrysler is recalling 1.4 million vehicles over a security issue, reports the Detroit Free Press. The recall affects 2013 to 2015 models of Dodge, Jeep, Ram, and Dodge Challengers, as well as the Chrysler 200, 300, and Charger, all of which have 8.4-inch touch displays on the inside of the car. The hack would allow hackers to control steering, brakes, and other functions from a laptop, Wired reports. The company says it has "applied network-level security measures to prevent the type of remote manipulation demonstrated in a recent media report," and customers whose vehicles are affected by the hack will get a USB device to update their software.

– President Obama's executive order to raise the minimum wage for federal contract workers to $10.10 an hour starts Jan. 1, 2015, and Gap is the first major retailer to announce a pay hike, reports the Wall Street Journal. The company says it will raise wages for about 65,000 employees to $9 in June 2014 and $10 in June 2015. "To us, this is not a political issue," says Gap CEO Glenn Murphy. "Our decision to invest in frontline employees will directly support our business, and is one that we expect to deliver a return many times over." Gap, which also owns Old Navy, Banana Republic, and Piperlime, says "the majority" of employees in stores, call centers, and distribution centers currently earn more than the federal minimum wage of $7.25 an hour, reports Reuters. Walmart, meanwhile, says it is "looking into the impact that this proposal will be on our business," but "we remain neutral. Our position has not changed," a spokeswoman tells Reuters.

The Salt Lake Tribune reports Alex Wubbels was arrested July 26 after she refused to let Detective Jeff Payne take a blood sample from a man who had been involved in a car crash that left him burned in the head. Video of the incident shows Payne telling Wubbels that he has the authority to draw a blood sample from a patient without a warrant unless there's a warrant or the patient is under arrest. Wubbels says she told him there was no warrant or consent from the patient. She says she was cuffed after consulting with hospital officials. "What I saw is completely unacceptable to the values of my administration and of the values of the Salt Lake City Police Department," says Mayor Jackie Biskupski. "I extend a personal apology to Ms. Wubbels for what she has been through for simply doing her job." The police department has placed Payne on administrative leave and is investigating. – It's official: Jennifer Aniston and Justin Theroux have moved in together, sources tell People. "They decided to rent a house together while they keep searching for the perfect [one] to buy," says one. Aniston, 42, and Theroux, 36, have been dating since last year. They met on the set of 2013's The Leftovers, which she also directed. Click for more.

– A New York City firefighter died Thursday night after a fire broke out on the set of a movie being directed by Edward Norton, NBC New York reports. Michael Davidson, a 37-year-old father of four, was battling the blaze at the five-story building in Harlem when he got separated from his group "inside the rapidly deteriorating fire conditions," Fire Commissioner Daniel Nigro says. He died of critical injuries at a hospital. Two other firefighters suffered serious burns. Norton, who was filming Motherless Brooklyn with Bruce Willis, Willem Dafoe, Alec Baldwin, Gugu Mbatha-Raw, and Leslie Mann, tweeted Friday that he was "deeply saddened" by the death. "My heart goes out to the brave men and women of the FDNY who put their lives on the line every day," he said. "I'm also deeply saddened by the loss of one of our own. It's hard to imagine what it's like to lose a loved one in the line of duty, and I'm sure it's hard to imagine what it's like to lose a colleague." (Last week, two firefighters died in a helicopter crash in Iraq.)

Gurriel hit a home run in the second inning against Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher Yu Darvish, and as he returned to the Astros dugout, he made a slant-eyed gesture and appeared to mouth the word "chinito"—a slur for Asian people. "I did not mean it to be offensive at any point," Gurriel said. "Quite the opposite. I have always had a lot of respect [for Japanese people]. ... I've never had anything against Darvish. For me, he's always been one of the best pitchers. I never had any luck against him. If I offended him, I apologize. It was not my intention." The 33-year-old Gurriel is a native of Cuba who played for the Japanese Central League in 2014. Darvish is of Japanese and Iranian descent. Gurriel said it's common in Cuba to use the word "chinito" to describe someone of Asian heritage, although he admitted he realizes it's considered offensive in Japan. – A wooden boat missing a rotor blade and navigational devices was found Sunday on a beach in northern Japan, the BBC reports. On Monday officials found the remains of eight people, some reduced to bones, while inspecting the boat. Kyodo news agency reported that the coast guard suspected the boat and its occupants had come from North Korea. The discovery is the latest in a string of similar incidents. On Friday, a wooden boat carrying eight men—alive and in reasonably good health— washed up at Yurihonjo city. The men said they were North Koreans fishing for squid, who had ended up drifting into Japanese waters when their boat experienced difficulties. Reuters news agency reported that two bodies were also found over the weekend at Sado island, with a pack of North Korean cigarettes and other belongings with Korean lettering. Japan regularly sees North Korean fishing boats straying into its territory, and its coast guard has occasionally had to rescue fishermen. The BBC's Celia Hatton says the appearance of "ghost ships" is thought to be a consequence of North Korea's attempts to satisfy hunger by demanding huge quotas of seafood. That forces fishermen to board aging ill-equipped vessels and to venture far out to sea, with no equipment to issue a distress call if their boats run into trouble.

– Mitt Romney found himself in a bit of a shouting match with hecklers at the Des Moines Register's booth at the Iowa State Fair today, reports the Hill. When one asked why he wouldn't raise the Social Security payroll cap or cut Medicare, Romney said, "If you want to speak, you can speak. But right now, it’s my turn. ... Corporations are people, my friend ... of course they are. Everything corporations earn ultimately goes to the people. Where do you think it goes? Whose pockets? Whose pockets? People's pockets. Human beings my friend." Democrats immediately pounced. "This is what Mitt Romney is going to run on? Corporations are people? Really?" said a DNC spokesman. "There's a great message for people struggling to get by and trying to make ends meet. Don't complain—corporations are people, too!" The Romney campaign, however, downplayed the incident. "Do folks think corporations are buildings? They're people who incorporate to conduct business. They create jobs and hire more people," said a spokesman.

Dianne Feinstein for releasing the transcript of an interview with the co-founder of a political opposition firm that commissioned a dossier of allegations about Trump's presidential campaign and Russia, the AP reports. Trump calls the California Democrat "Sneaky Dianne Feinstein" on Twitter Wednesday. He says she released the testimony "totally without authorization." Adds Trump: "Must have tough Primary!" Feinstein on Tuesday released transcript from the Senate Judiciary Committee's August interview with Glenn Simpson, of Fusion GPS. Feinstein had the ability to release the transcripts as the top Democrat on the committee, and her staff helped conduct the interview with Simpson. Trump also repeated that the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 US election is a "Witch Hunt" and says "Republicans should finally take control!"

– A bird called the chestnut-crowned babbler lives in the Australian Outback, but its calls are so social that they're hard to miss. That's why researchers say their new study in PLOS Biology could have a "potential early step in the emergence of the elaborate language systems we use today," the BBC reports. The birds make " discrete calls made up of smaller acoustically distinct individual sounds," says one of the researchers, who notes that unlike most songbirds, the chestnut-crowned babbler doesn't sing. "In contrast to most songbirds, the chestnut-crowned babblers do not sing," she says. "Instead, its extensive vocal repertoire is characterized by discrete calls made up of smaller acoustically distinct individual sounds." The researchers first noticed that the birds were rearranging two sounds—A and B—in different ways while engaging in behaviors. For example, they could tell which sounded was which by looking at the nests when they heard a feeding call and which sounded was a flight call while feeding chicks. "Doing so through combining two existing sounds is quicker than evolving a new sound altogether," says a co-author of the study, who adds that the findings could help in the understanding of how animals communicate. She's "still very relevant among Americans," says one of the young women behind the "Texts from Hillary" meme. Jay-Z, the leading nominee with eight, walked away empty handed Sunday—a year after his wife lost album of the year to Adele, causing fans and peers to criticize the Recording Academy for not properly rewarding Beyonce's bold Lemonade project, the AP reports. And though Kendrick Lamar won five awards, he lost in the top categories, marking another year where rappers were restricted to wins in the rap categories, instead of earning coveted prizes like album of the year. Mars picked up album of the year for 24K Magic, record of the year for the title track, and song of the year—shared with seven co-writers—for the No. 1 hit, "That's What I Like." Jay-Z and Lamar could have become the first rapper to win song or record of the year, and the third rap-based act to win album of the year. But Mars' win still marked some growth for the Academy: His is one of the few R&B albums to win the top prize. He dedicated his win to songwriters who have made

– The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department is reopening the Natalie Wood drowning case based on new information, TMZ reports. The investigation was prompted by a book written by the captain of the boat Wood was on the night of Nov. 29, 1981, in which he claims she drowned after a fight with husband Robert Wagner and actor Christopher Walken. Wagner has said he and Walken had a heated argument after dinner on the boat, during which he smashed a wine bottle and yelled at Walken, “What do you want to do, f**k my wife? Is that what you want?” Walken returned to the boat, and Wagner says he heard Wood and Walken screaming and thumping sounds. The death was ruled an accident, but the book, Goodbye Natalie, Goodbye Splendour, by co-author Marti Rulli and Splendour Captain Dennis Davern, claimed Wagner refused to call the Coast Guard when the boat capsized. The sheriff’s department has not called anyone a suspect in the case yet, and it will take "a long time to complete," a source tells TMZ. Click for more on the new investigation.

– The world’s oldest known wild bird, a Laysan albatross known as Wisdom, has given birth to a chick at the Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge in the North Pacific Ocean. The 63-year-old mother and her newly hatched chick were spotted alive a week after Japan’s earthquake and tsunami, Reuters reports. US Fish and Wildlife officials estimate Wisdom has raised at least 30 to 35 chicks during her breeding life, though the number may well be higher because experienced parents tend to be better parents than younger breeders. Wisdom was first banded in 1956 as she incubated an egg, and was estimated to be at least 5 years old at the time. “It's a dangerous world out there, there's lots going on, so I would say she's very lucky,” a US Fish and Wildlife Service project leader says.

Monalisa Perez, of Halstad, was charged Wednesday with second-degree manslaughter in the death of Pedro Ruiz III. Perez, who is pregnant, was released on $7,000 bail. She says she fired from about a foot away. Hours before the Tuesday night shooting, Perez tweeted: "Me and Pedro are probably going to shoot one of the most dangerous videos ever. HIS idea not MINE." The complaint says Ruiz set up one camera on the back of a vehicle and another camera on a ladder nearby. Ruiz's aunt, Lisa Primeau, told the Star Tribune that her nephew was always chasing a thrill and "putting a dangerous twist on everything he did." According to USA Today, Dallas Bishop Edward Burns told parishioners at St. Cecilia Catholic Church over the weekend that the diocese has hired private investigators to find Rev. Edmundo Paredes, who is believed to have fled to the Philippines. "Now that we know of his criminal sexual acts, we want to get a handle on him," Burns said. Paredes was suspended from ministry and removed from St. Cecilia in June 2017 after admitting to stealing between $60,000 and $80,000 from the church over the course of his 27-year career. Burns says the diocese wasn't aware of the sexual assault allegation against Paredes until February this year. The diocese wasn't aware of the sexual assault allegation when Paredes was suspended, a diocese spokesperson says. "The allegations were found to be credible," Burns says. Paredes can no longer administer the sacraments or represent himself as a priest. Burns disclosed the allegations to parishioners Sunday after consulting with the Diocesan Review Board, a group of nonclergy Catholics who counsel the diocese on matters involving the sexual abuse of minors. – Eric Cantor arrived at the Capitol this morning to meet with his "kitchen cabinet" of allies, and the race to replace him as House majority leader is already under way, reports Politico. Texas Rep. Pete Sessions is in the running for the No. 2 spot, and he's been calling and emailing fellow Republicans seeking their support. Jim Jordan and Cathy McMorris Rodgers are also in the running for the No. 3 spot, and they, too, have been calling and emailing colleagues seeking their support. But it's not clear whether Cantor will stay in leadership for the duration of his term. House Majority Whip Kevin McCarthy is also in the running, but he won't launch a formal campaign until Cantor makes a decision. Cantor is expected to meet with his allies in the House this morning and decide whether to run for re-election in November, reports the Hill.

– Anheuser-Busch InBev's acquisition of Wicked Weed Brewing Co. this week has led to some fallout in the craft beer world. Two Colorado brewers have severed ties with the company, citing "deep and serious issues with many of ABInBev's business strategies, mission, and overall ethics as they relate to craft beer in America," per a blog post by James Howat and Sarah Howat of the Black Project. "We truly believe that ABInBev intends to systematically destroy American craft beer as we know it." Howat and Howat say they have two collaboration beers in the works with Wicked Weed, one at their facility, and one at Wicked Weed's, but "we don't feel that having any connection with ABInBev is something we can do while still maintaining our mission, values, and core beliefs." They add that they won't be attending Wicked Weed's upcoming Funkatorium Invitational in July because "we will not be able to lend our name to the unfinished collaboration beer currently aging in Asheville, NC." The Huffington Post notes that the Black Project's blog post is notable because it's the first time a craft brewer has made such a public statement about a beer brand owned by a major beer company.

– The Oscar Pistorius murder trial is coming to a close, with the judge in the case telling both sides to make their closing arguments by the end of the day. "Unless, of course, you want to work on a Saturday and perhaps Sunday, after church," said the judge, smiling, reports AP. Prosecutor Gerrie Nel told the court that the defense's attempt to "falsify the facts" had been a "blunt instrument for digging up the truth," but that they had offered "two defenses that you can never reconcile," including the possibility that Pistorius wasn't criminally responsible for shooting Reeva Steenkamp through the bathroom door because he was "startled." The defense, for its part, countered that the athlete shot Steenkamp through the door in self-defense, fearing an intruder was in the house, but that he had been "startled" and fired through the door because he thought he was about to be attacked, reports the BBC. "It's two defenses that you can never reconcile," said Nel. Pistorius faces 25 years to life in prison if convicted of premeditated murder, or if he made a tragic error and should be acquitted. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges.

– A Florida man has been charged with murder after police say he pocket-dialed 911 and told someone else he was going to follow a victim home and kill him, the Sun Sentinel reports. Police say 24-year-old Scott Simon got into a fight with 33-year-old Nicholas Walker at a Waffle House early May 5 and shot him multiple times while Walker was driving on Interstate 95. Walker's Buick crashed into a guard rail, and he died at the scene from gunshot wounds. Police say Simon told someone else on a recorded 911 call just minutes before the shooting that he was going to follow Walker home and kill him. "This is a first for me," a Broward Sheriff's Office spokeswoman tells the South Florida Sun Sentinel. "Criminals say crazy things all the time, but I’ve never seen anyone call a recorded line." Simon was arrested Tuesday and charged with first-degree murder. Police say they don't think Simon was the shooter, but he coordinated the attack. They're still looking for the person who pulled the trigger. Walker's mother tells the Sun Sentinel that she's "very happy" Simon was arrested. "I want them to catch them all," she says.

– Australia's 2Day FM has suspended all advertising until tomorrow in the wake of the royal prank phone call that ended in the suicide of the nurse involved. The station's owner held an emergency board meeting yesterday, but made no comment afterward, the BBC reports. It has suspended all advertising on the station until tomorrow, while DJs Mel Greig and Michael Christian are on indefinite leave. The pair are said to be in a fragile condition and receiving "intense counseling" because of the hostile reaction to their prank. Scotland Yard has been in contact with Australian authorities, and an inquest into the apparent suicide is due to open this week. Legal experts say that Greig and Christian won't be prosecuted at home or in the UK because they didn't show "guilty intent." However, they may have violated the Surveillance Devices Act in New South Wales, which prohibits broadcasting of private conversations using a "listening device." The Australian Communications and Media Authority is investigating whether the station breached its license conditions or industry rules.

– The US is cutting off aid to Uganda and imposing visa restrictions on Ugandans it says are involved in human rights violations, including gay rights, in response to the country's harsh anti-gay law. The law, signed by President Yoweri Museveni in February, makes homosexual sex with a minor punishable by life in prison; it also criminalizes lesbianism for the first time and makes it a crime to help individuals engage in homosexual acts, Reuters reports. Western donors, including the US, had halted or re-directed about $118 million in aid to the east African nation's economy before today's announcement. The US will impose visa restrictions on Ugandans it believes have been involved in human rights violations, including gay rights. The US will halt $2.4 million in funding for a Ugandan community policing program in light of a police raid on a US-funded health program at Makerere University and reports of people detained and abused while in police custody. In addition, Washington will shift some funding for salaries and travel expenses of Ugandan health ministry employees to non-governmental agencies involved in health programs. – Sally Yates, the former acting attorney general who warned the White House about Michael Flynn's conversations with the Russian ambassador before he was fired, testified before a Senate panel Monday—and President Trump didn't waste any time making fun of her, the Guardian reports. "Holy cow. This is ACTUALLY DONALD TRUMP'S NEW TWITTER BANNER," tweeted Tom McKay. "This is like when the old guy gets a convertible to convince you he's young, except instead of age it's treason." Trump also changed his header to include a tweet denying Russia collusion with his campaign, the Daily Beast reports. Yates testified that she told White House counsel Donald McGahn in January that Flynn had been "compromised" by Russia and could be a target for Russian blackmail. She said she warned McGahn that Flynn's conversations with the Russian ambassador were "unfair to the United States," CNN reports. McGahn didn't fire Flynn until 18 days after she warned him that he had lied to Vice President Mike Pence about his conversations with the ambassador. She said she didn't know why it took so long for McGahn to fire him. "I don't know the answer to that," she said.

– A 12-year-old boy in Australia managed to drive all 2,700 miles of his intended journey alone, the New York Times reports. According to the Guardian, the boy was stopped Saturday morning by police in Broken Hill, an isolated mining city in New South Wales, after they noticed his car's bumper dragging on the road. Police believe the boy had driven from Kendall, on the east coast, to Perth, which is 2,700 miles away. The journey from Kendall to Perth is a grueling 40 hours in length by car, and involves driving through the Outback desert of Nullarbor Plain, which is four times the size of Belgium. Police say the boy had a clear plan for his journey, but it's unclear how he managed to drive so far without being noticed. The boy was arrested and taken to a police station in Broken Hill, where he spent a night alone on the road before being released into the care of his parents on Sunday. Police say they hope to speak with him and his parents on Monday.

Wilbert Carter, 31, told police he had been drinking and had no memory of leaving Leasia Carter in the car Sunday night, when the temperature was around 90 degrees, the Baltimore Sun reports. Carter, who had sole custody of his daughter, has been charged with second-degree murder and child abuse, the Sun reports. Neighbors say Carter had another child with him when he went looking for Leasia. "It never crossed my mind that something like that would happen," Leasia's great-aunt tells WBAL. – Archaeologists in Bulgaria have made "one of the most important discoveries in the history of the [Burgas Regional History] Museum," says the museum's director. What they found during excavations at a medieval fortress in the Black Sea city of Burgas: a lead tube with ashes from the grave of St. John the Apostle, one of Jesus' 12 apostles, Ancient Origins reports. The tube, which is less than an inch long, is decorated with crosses, and Milen Nikolov says early Christians would have believed it held healing powers. "Probably a pilgrim from the Foros Peninsula (Cape) went on a pilgrimage to Ephesus, and came back here with this relic which was then donated to the basilica on Foros," Nikolov says, per local news site Gramofona. The relic is named for John, who is also known as St. John the Theologian in Bulgarian (Eastern) Orthodox Christianity, Ancient Origins notes. John's grave in Turkey was also a pilgrimage site for early Christians seeking healing, Ancient Origins reports. – Archeologists in Austria have unearthed a rare find: the remains of a 17th-century camel, LiveScience reports. The skeleton was found in a cellar in the city of Tulln, which was under attack by enemy troops during the second Osmanic-Habsburg war. The find is "unprecedented" for Central Europe in that it's the only complete camel skeleton ever found, according to a study published in PLoS One. The skeleton shows "a few but characteristic pathological changes ... revealing not a beast of burden but probably a valuable riding animal," the study states. Researchers believe the skeleton belonged to a Bactrian camel that lived in the area in the late 17th century. It's also the first evidence of a dromedary camel ever found in Central Europe, according to a press release. Researchers believe the skeleton belonged to a man who lived in the area in the late 17th century and was killed by enemy troops during the second Osmanic-Habsburg war. The study states the skeleton shows "a few but characteristic pathological changes" that suggest a hybrid between the camel in the maternal line and the Bactrian camel in the paternal line. – The Los Angeles Times today profiles Gabino Zavala, the former auxiliary bishop for the Archdiocese of Los Angeles who resigned yesterday after the Vatican learned that he is the father of two teenage children. Zavala, 60, had been known by his first name, and the Times describes him as "popular and approachable." But the Vatican's announcement that Zavala, who is not celibate, had fathered the children came as a shock to many. "He is the father of two minor teenage children, who live with their mother in another state," Archbishop Jose Gomez wrote in a letter to his flock. "Let us pray for all those impacted by this situation and for each other." Zavala, who is no longer in ministry but remains a priest and bishop, could not be reached for comment. – The Greenland Ice Sheet may be the world's oldest, but it's probably not the oldest—at least in terms of how long it's been there. The oldest soil ever found is 2.7 million years old and lies thousands of feet below Summit, the island's highest point, according to a study published Thursday in Science. That's a lot of time—200,000 to 1 million years—before the ice sheet began covering the island. "There was a really stable landscape on Greenland before the ice sheet came," lead study author Paul Bierman tells Live Science. "This landscape has been preserved from beyond the dawn of humankind." The soil was found in 1993 during a deep-drilling project to reach the bedrock beneath Summit. It was dated using a technique called beryllium-10 dating, which reveals the age of rocks and soil at the surface by counting the number of beryllium-10 isotopes in those rocks and soil exposed at the surface. Bierman says he was "totally surprised" by the high levels of beryllium-10 in the soil from the Greenland Ice Sheet. "Our eyes just lit up," he says. "It was completely unexpected and one of the few times I've been totally surprised in my career." The soil also contains Pollen and Plant DNA

– Our last universal common ancestor, LUCA, lived 4 billion years ago and may have been a heat-loving microbe that thrived in a world without oxygen, according to a study published today in Nature Microbiology. It's been long theorized that life formed around hydrothermal vents, but geneticists have been unable to pin down how and where LUCA lived. To do so, they analyzed nearly 2,000 genomes of modern microbes. They found that only 355 of those genes were shared by all modern organisms, so they could be tracked from ancestral species through all its descendants. That made LUCA a likely candidate for the "last universal common ancestor of all cells," as Science puts it. LUCA likely lived in an anaerobe-like environment that lacked oxygen, according to a press release. It also likely produced hydrogen gas, which is what most cells today need.

– If you've ever had a sibling who was your mom's favorite, Purdue researchers have some bad news: You may be more likely to suffer from depression, Medical News Today reports. "Adult children who reported that they were most emotionally close to their mothers also reported higher depressive symptoms," the researchers write in the Journal of Gerontology: Social Sciences. "Depressive symptoms were also higher when respondents identified themselves as being the children with whom their mothers had the greatest conflict, and in whom the mothers were most disappointed." The researchers looked at data from 725 adult children in 309 families in which mothers were between the ages of 65 and 75 when the study began in 2001. They found that the children who believed they were closer to their mother than their siblings and the children who believed they were the sibling their mother was most disappointed reported the highest levels of favoritism and disfavoritism. "What we found suggests that the black offspring were particularly distressed when they, as opposed to their siblings, were the children in whom mothers were most disappointed," says one of the researchers.

– The German battleship Tirpitz, described by Winston Churchill as "the beast," spent most of World War II hiding out in Norway's fjords, where it produced vast amounts of chemical fog to keep Allied bombers at bay, Phys.org reports. But the smoke didn't escape, and Allied planes couldn't see the ship until late 1944, according to a study published Wednesday in the European Geosciences Union. "The story was in the tree rings," researcher Claudia Hartl tells AFP. "We got back to the lab and measured the tree rings, and saw that they were very narrow—in some cases nearly absent—for 1945," she says. "We got back to the lab and measured the tree rings, and saw that they were very narrow—in some cases nearly absent—for 1945," she adds. "Of course we wondered, why is that?" Hartl and her team set out to find out, and found that 60% of the trees near where the Tirpitz once lay had virtually no growth from October 1944 to late 1944. All of them were severely affected, taking an average of eight years to fully recover. "You don't normally see trees in this region without rings," researcher Scott St. George tells AFP.

– Women with early-stage breast cancer who have their axillary lymph nodes dissection (also known as "sentinel lymph node dissection") removed are less likely to survive five years than women who don't have the procedure, according to a new study. The American College of Surgeons report in the Journal of the American College of Surgeons that 445 women with breast cancer who had no palpable adenopathy were randomly assigned to ALND or no further axillary treatment, while 446 women with metastatic breast cancer who had 10 or more axillary nodes were randomly assigned to ALND or no further axillary treatment. Five years after the procedure, 91.8% of women who had ALND had survived, compared to 92.5% of women who didn't have the procedure, the New York Times reports. "This is the first study to show that ALND does not improve overall survival in women with early-stage breast cancer," the study's lead author tells the Times. "It's also the first study to show that there is no difference in survival rates between the two groups."

– A British escape artist lost consciousness during a stunt Saturday and had to be pulled out of a six-foot-deep grave at the end of a festival in West Yorkshire, the Guardian reports. Antony Britton was handcuffed and buried with his hands tied behind his back in what he hoped would be a feat similar to that of Harry Houdini in 1915. But he failed to emerge for nearly nine minutes. "I was just seconds away from death," he says. "It was scary. The pressure of the soil was crushing around me. Even when I found an air pocket, when I exhaled the soil around me was crushing me even more. I could feel myself losing consciousness and there was nothing I could do about it. I was pretty much dying." Britton was given oxygen before being taken by ambulance to a hospital, where he's recovering from scratches and a cracked rib. He's only the third person in 100 years to attempt the Buried Alive escape, and the first since British master of the craft Alan Alan tried it in 1949, the Telegraph reports. Britton says he'll take a few weeks to recuperate before deciding on another attempt. "I gave it my all, but it just wasn't my day," he says.

Rosenbaum grew up in a Jewish home, where he didn't talk about the Holocaust. But one night when he was a child, he tuned in to a reenactment of the Auschwitz trial. – David Welch left his home in Kansas on Sept. 2, hopped in his van, and drove hundreds of miles—and weeks—without telling anyone where he was going. Then, on Oct. 18, a hitchhiker spotted Welch's overturned car in a deep ravine along a desolate stretch of Interstate 70 in Utah, reports the Salt Lake Tribune. For weeks, the 54-year-old sat in his car, writing his last letters to his family. He was found dead in the car on Oct. 26. Police believe Welch fell asleep at the wheel in early September, sending his vehicle into the ravine, CNN reports. It's not clear how long he was trapped in the car, but nights became days, then weeks, police say. The notes have been handed over to Welch's family. Welch's family reported him missing four days after he left home, but there was no sign of him until his body was found.

– A US Air Force serviceman who disappeared 40 years ago was found living a double life in Florida last week, the Independent reports. According to WFTV, Jeffrey Michels, 64, disappeared from the Minot Air Force Base in North Dakota on July 6, 1977. Michels was arrested Thursday in Sanford, Fla., where he had been living with his wife and two children under the name Jeffrey Lantz for years. Michels was charged with desertion and will stand trial in a military court. There is no statute of limitations for desertion, and the military rarely gives deserters the highest sentence possible: a dishonourable discharge, which can range from two to three years, up to the death penalty. However, even at the height of the Iraq war fewer than 1% of deserters served prison time, New York reports. It's unclear if the Air Force opened an investigation into Michels' disappearance after a photo of him was posted to the Facebook group "Veteran Doe" in July. The post was deleted after Michels was discovered.

– If you're tempted to indulge in a few glasses of wine and a beer on the same night, you're not alone: A new study finds that those who both smoke and drink are twice as likely to develop esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, a type of cancer that starts in the esophagus, as those who only smoke, LiveScience reports. "Our study suggests that not only do alcohol and tobacco play an important role in the development of esophageal cancer, the combination of their use markedly increases their potency as carcinogens," says the lead author of the study, published in the American Journal of Gastroenterology. "As a result, we as physicians should focus efforts directed at controlling the burden of esophageal cancer on those who consume both of these substances." The researchers reviewed studies on ESCC and found that both alcohol and tobacco are linked to an increased risk of the disease, which the National Cancer Institute estimates will result in more than 18,000 new cases and more than 15,000 deaths in the US this year. (In other booze-related news, a new study suggests that mixing booze doesn't always lead to a hangover.)

Hasan is acting as his own attorney but declined to address jurors after prosecutors wrapped up their closing argument. When the judge told Hasan he could begin, he said: "The defense chooses not to make a closing statement." – The West Antarctic Ice Sheet is the last ice sheet on Earth resting in a deep marine basin and is the most likely player in any future rapid sea-level rise. If the grounding zone is retreating or primed to retreat, rapid changes in ice behavior could follow over the next century. Scientists are using a variety of tools and techniques to explore the subglacial environment, and this season's target is the grounding zone, where the ice sheet atop land meets the Ross Sea. Radar and seismic equipment is used to profile the overlying ice sheet and the underlying water, sediments, and rock, while GPS stations accurately track ice movement. This season's target is the grounding zone, where the massive West Antarctic Ice Sheet atop land meets the Ross Sea. In topographic depressions there are hundreds of lakes, both large and small; some are isolated, but many are interconnected by water channels and large areas of saturated sediments, the water eventually running out into the Southern Ocean as the ice sheet becomes a floating ice shelf. The conditions below that Antarctic ice sheet have certain characteristics in common with known places on other worlds in our solar system, leading many to wonder if life might be more inevitable in those distant locales than previously thought. – Cows, goats, deer, and sheep produce a lot of methane, a greenhouse gas with a global warming potential 25 times greater than that of carbon dioxide, Grist reports. Cows and other ruminant animals, like sheep and goats, use between 2% and 10% of their energy to produce the gas, according to the University of Aberdeen, which is leading a $10 million study on how to make them more efficient. Preliminary findings from the study show that methane production is consistent in each animal, which should allow researchers to breed animals that release methane at continually lower levels, the Verge reports. The study is part of a $10 million project to make these animals more efficient, which, in turn, would lower feed costs. "Methane production is important for cattle and sheep farmers because if the amount of methane produced can be lowered then there are benefits for the environment, production, and profitability," says the lead researcher.

– The DEA has asked the FDA to take a second look at marijuana's status as a Schedule I drug—the one with the highest potential for abuse, no "current accepted medical use," and a high risk of abuse. The FDA is reviewing the medical evidence surrounding the drug's safety and effectiveness, a process that could lead to the drug being downgraded, the Huffington Post reports. A Schedule I drug has a high risk of abuse, no "current accepted medical use," and little scientific evidence of its pharmacological effect. A lower classification could ease restrictions on research into the drug and make banks less wary of doing business with state-legal marijuana businesses. It could also allow those businesses to make some traditional tax deductions. "While DEA is the lead federal agency responsible for regulating controlled substances and enforcing the Controlled Substances Act, FDA, working with NIDA, provides scientific recommendations about the appropriate controls for those substances," an FDA deputy director testified during a House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform hearing on Friday. "To make these recommendations, FDA is responsible for preparing what's called an eight-factor analysis, which is a document that is used to assess how likely a drug is to be abused." The FDA hasn't said how long the review will take.

– A fruit fly's brain is the size of a salt grain, but that doesn't mean it can't fly like a fighter jet, according to a new study. Researchers at the University of Washington found that the insects can pitch their bodies like a plane in less than one-hundredth of a second, 50 times faster than we blink, reports LiveScience. "One of the fastest things a fruit fly does is take information from its eyes and react accordingly," says a co-author of the study, which will be published in the journal Science. "They do this with remarkably subtle changes in wing movement." The researchers used high-speed cameras to capture the behavior of the fruit fly, Drosophila hydei, in a flight arena. "These flies normally flap their wings 200 times a second and, in almost a single wing beat, the animal can reorient its body to generate a force away from the threatening stimulus and then continues to accelerate," says the study's lead author, Florian Muijres. "They do this with remarkably subtle changes in wing movement." – Nobel Prize-winning DNA scientist James Watson is back in the US, having apologized "unreservedly" for comments he made about black people in a British magazine. Watson, who was in the UK to promote his new book, canceled his remaining engagements there after the magazine quoted him as saying he was "inherently gloomy about the prospect of Africa" because "all our social policies are based on the fact that their intelligence is the same as ours— whereas testing says not really." Watson, 79, is "less an arrogant bigot than an enthusiastic if misguided old man, someone who does not quite understand that people won't always take his provocative remarks as innocently as he intended," writes Mary Elizabeth Williams in Salon. "And on that much at least, he's right. For one thing, science has no agreed-upon definition of 'race': however you slice up the population, the categories look pretty arbitrary. For another, science has no agreed-upon definition of 'intelligence' either—let alone an agreed-upon method to test it."

– Sales of Whitney Houston's records have soared since her death, with seven of her records currently in the top 10 on Amazon.com's best-seller list. Apple, meanwhile, has been accused of cashing in by raising the price of Houston's greatest-hits album on iTunes just hours after her death, the Guardian reports. Sony Music, which owns the rights to much of Houston's back catalog, increased the wholesale price of The Ultimate Collection at 4am California time on Sunday. This automatically boosted the retail price of the popular album, although Apple is responsible for setting the price paid by music fans. Music fans described the move as a cynical attempt to capitalize on Houston's in-demand greatest hits records.

General Mills says it "made no assertion non-GM ingredients were 'more wholesome.' That is simply mistaken." Researchers looked at 8,207 deaths in 24 states over a 10-year period and found that 74% of the younger victims were sharing a bed at the time of their death, while 58% of the older victims were sleeping on an adult bed or on someone's lap, LiveScience reports. Babies as old as 4 months were most likely to die from objects in the sleep environment, such as blankets or stuffed animals, while older infants were most likely to die from suffocation or strangulation, according to the study, published in Pediatrics. The study states its "objective was to determine any associations between risk factors for sleep-related deaths at different ages," but it makes clear that it hasn't found any clear cause and effect, the Los Angeles Times reports. Most of the students were suspended for a term, but at least 43 were given the option of dropping their scores by a letter grade. – If you've ever wondered why so many people don't follow a vegetarian or vegan diet, you're in good company: A new study finds that 2% of Americans are currently vegetarian or vegan, while 10% have never been, and 88% have never eaten meat, LiveScience reports. – The Justice Department and the FBI are launching a massive review of thousands of criminal cases dating back to at least 1985 because of shoddy forensic evidence, reports the Washington Post. The undertaking is the largest post-conviction review ever done by the FBI. It will include cases conducted by all FBI Laboratory hair and fiber examiners since at least 1985 and may reach earlier if records are available. In addition, prosecutors did not notify defendants or their attorneys even in many cases they knew were troubled. The new review will include help from the Innocence Project, a New York-based advocacy group for people seeking exoneration through DNA testing.

– Looking at someone who's shivering can cause your own body temperature to drop, according to new research out of the UK's Brighton and Sussex Medical School. The scientists watched eight videos of people putting their hands in either warm or cold water, and the temperature of their own hands was measured at the same time. When watching the "warm" videos, the temperature of subjects' right hands fell an average of 0.1 degrees Fahrenheit, and the temperature of their left hands fell 0.4 degrees, Science Daily reports. The study, published in PLoS ONE, suggests that humans are susceptible to "temperature contagion," in which two people mimic each other's feelings and reactions. "Humans are profoundly social creatures and much of humans' success results from our ability to work together in complex communities—this would be hard to do if we were not able to rapidly empathise with each other and predict one another's thoughts, feelings, and motivations," the lead researcher says in a press release. "Mimicking another person is believed to help us create an internal model of their physiological state which we can use to better understand their motivations and how they are feeling," he adds. (Another recent study found that people are more sensitive to cold than hot.)

– There's a reason some cheeses melt perfectly on the grill while others don't—and the American Chemical Society wants to help you solve that mystery. In a new Reactions video, the group explains how casein proteins clump together into spheres called micelles, which are held together by calcium and are full of fat. The surface of a micelle is negatively charged, so usually the little balls would bounce away from each other. But when lactic acid gets involved, the micelles smack into each other and create chains that trap water and turn into a mess of cheesy goo. Cheeses that age longer contain more lactic acid, lowering their pH. That means sharper cheeses have a lower pH than their counterparts, which don't age as long. If you're choosing between mild and sharp gruyére or manchego, go with mild—it has the texture you want, and won't break down like its sharp counterpart. "The ideal pH level for a cheese used to make grilled cheese is perfectly balanced between 5.3 to 5.5," the group explains. "If you want suggestions on how to cook that grilled cheese once you've selected which variety you want, check out our somewhat scientific We Tried It investigation."

For example, some say they can be disturbing, while others say they can be friendly. Others say voices are part of their personalities, while still others say they can be troubling, but also friendly. "We call into question the presumed auditory quality of hearing voices and show that there is an unrecognised complexity in the 'character' qualities of some voices," says lead researcher Angela Woods of Durham University in a press release. – The sun is about to turn its magnetic field in a big way—a reversal that will have " ripple effects throughout the solar system," says a NASA scientist. The sun's magnetic field will turn from the north to the south in the coming months, marking the peak of the sun's 11-year solar cycle and the halfway point in the sun's solar weather cycle, Space.com reports. "The sun's polar magnetic fields weaken, go to zero, and then emerge again with the opposite polarity," says a Stanford scientist. "This is a regular part of the solar cycle." The sun's magnetic field has already changed sign, but the south pole "is racing to catch up," says the scientist. "Soon, however, both poles will be reversed, and the second half of solar max will be underway." The change in polarity can stir up some stormy weather on Earth, but the sun's magnetic field can also provide extra protection from high-energy particles that zip through the universe at nearly the speed of light. The sun's magnetic field is a regular part of the solar cycle, notes a NASA scientist.

– Archaeologists digging for World War II soldiers in Poland have instead stumbled on a set of vampire graves, the Telegraph reports. The graves contained the remains of skeletons whose heads had been decapitated and whose legs had been placed on them—a sign that they had been buried as part of a ritual to make sure they remained dead. The practice was common in Slavic countries during the early Christian era, when pagan beliefs were still widespread, and the bodies had to be decapitated before burial to make sure they didn't decompose. LiveScience points out that the definition of a vampire in the Middle Ages was far broader than the classic Bram Stoker image of a blood-sucking aristocrat. "Even people who abided by old pagan customs and left food on the graves of dead relatives could fall foul of accusations of vampirism, and suffer a prompt execution," writes Benjamin Radford. "These processes are well understood by modern doctors and morticians, but in medieval Europe were taken as unmistakable signs that vampires were real and existed among them."

They really have nothing to be concerned about."

– A 44-year-old Canadian man is lucky to be alive after a three-month ordeal in the wilderness in which he killed his dog and ate it, reports the Montreal Gazette. Marco Lavoie got stranded in the Canadian wilderness after a bear ate his food and ruined his equipment. The bear didn't attack, but he left Lavoie without the tools or resources to survive, and he had to make a heartbreaking decision: He killed his dog, then ate it. "Hunger squeezes you so much that you would accept food that's not normally possible," a survival expert tells the newspaper. "You can crave slugs and bugs." Lavoie lost about 90 pounds in the process. "Other adventurers have gone there over 20, 30 years and never came back," says the expert. "He survived because he made the heartbreaking decision to kill and eat his dog." The dog did not survive, notes CNN. "Up there, in the Canadian shield, there's little plant life to live off, so he would have been slowly, painfully dying when they found him," says a police spokesman.

– Robin Williams' brain disease was "one of the worst pathologies they had seen," his wife, Susan Schneider Williams, writes in an open letter to neurologists published in the New Yorker. "He had about 40% loss of dopamine neurons and almost no neurons were free of Lewy bodies throughout the entire brain and brainstem." The disease, known as diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma, is caused by a buildup of a protein in the part of the brain known as the amygdala that regulates fear and anxiety. When symptoms first appear, they can be temporary. But they can become permanent. "How I wish he could have known why he was struggling, that it was not a weakness in his heart, spirit, or character," Schneider Williams writes of her husband, who died of suicide in 2014 at the age of 63. After his death, Schneider Williams learned that her husband had been diagnosed with LBD. "Not only did I lose my husband to LBD, I lost my best friend," she writes. But a study published last month in Teaching and Teacher Education has a different view. "We have to treat people as human, cognitive learners, and stop considering one specific group to have special powers," Paul Kirschner, a co-author of the study, tells Discover. "We have to stop thinking of people as one group." The study, co-authored by Kirschner of the Open University in the Netherlands, says there's no evidence that millennials, Gen Xers, or baby boomers are any more tech-savvy than previous generations, nor are they better at multi-tasking or listening than previous generations.
