– A dentist at the Tomah VA Medical Center in Wisconsin may have exposed nearly 600 veterans to HIV, hepatitis, and other diseases by reusing his equipment, the Washington Post reports. According to WEAU, the dentist used his own equipment to clean and sterilize his instruments from October 2015 to October 2016. That's a violation of VA regulations. The dentist was removed from patient care and is now working in an administrative role. The Tomah VA says it's working to notify 592 patients who received care from the dentist between October 2015 and October 2016. If they test positive for HIV, hepatitis, or other diseases, the VA will provide free screenings and treatment. The Tomah VA has been under investigation in the past for improper prescriptions and other medical practices.

The messages were allegedly left by William on his then-girlfriend's phone, the Telegraph reports. "Hi, baby. It's me," begins one of the messages. In another, he calls her "babykins." "I really miss you," he says. "Hopefully I'll see you very soon you big hairy fat ginger." The messages were allegedly left by Glenn Mulcaire, a private investigator who has pleaded guilty to hacking into the phones of royal aides. The trial also heard today that Andy Coulson, who became Prime Minister David Cameron's communications chief after the scandal broke, was warned about the risks of acquiring phone directories, which could be used to hack phones. "These people will not be paid in anything other than cash because if they're discovered selling stuff to us they end up on criminal charges, as could we," Goodman allegedly wrote to Coulson, in an email read in court.

– Oxytocin, the so-called "love hormone" that makes women more maternal and men less shy, may help people with autism improve their social skills, according to a new study. Researchers in France administered oxytocin, also known as the "cuddle chemical," to 13 adults with either high-functioning autism or Asperger's syndrome. They found that those given the hormone made more eye contact and responded better to social stimuli, the Los Angeles Times reports. "This is the first study that looked at whether oxytocin has an effect on social behavior, which is a major deficit in autism," the lead author says. "It looks like it could be very helpful." The study could lead to the first effective treatment for the central problems affecting people with autism, experts say. "It adds another brick in the wall that suggests there may be an opportunity to develop treatment for one of the core symptoms of autism," the director of the Stanford University School of Medicine tells the Washington Post. "That's been the brass ring."

– Labor Day weekend is right around the corner, which means it's time for Target's latest offering: a $5 bottle of wine. The discount retailer announced Monday that California Roots, its new line of California-grown grapes wines, will be on shelves at all 1,100 Target stores nationwide starting Sunday, the Los Angeles Times reports. There will be five different blends: chardonnay, pinot grigio, moscato, cabernet sauvignon, and a red blend. "We're out to give our guests even more reasons to love Target, including exclusive products they can't find anywhere else," Jeff Burt, senior vice president of food and beverage, says in a press release. "And we think they're going to love California Roots. These wines are just the right blend of incredible quality and amazing value that guests can only get at Target." Wine, beer, and other adult beverages are "among Target's fastest-growing categories," the retailer says. Trader Joe's, meanwhile, has been selling its Charles Shaw Wines for $1.99 a bottle for more than a decade, the Orange County Register reports. The California Roots wines will be sold in Target's traditional and small-format stores as well as online.

– Divers in Mexico have made an incredible discovery: the world's biggest flooded cave. The Gran Acuifero Maya (GAM) says the 215-mile-long cave system near the city of Tulum on the Yucatan Peninsula is connected to the larger Dos Ojos system some 52 miles away, making it the world's longest flooded cave, National Geographic reports. "This immense cave represents the most important submerged archaeological site in the world, since it has more than a hundred archaeological contexts, among which is evidence of the first settlers of America, as well as the extinct fauna and, of course, of the Maya culture," says GAM director and underwater archaeologist Guillermo de Anda, per Reuters. "It allows us to appreciate much more clearly how the rituals, the pilgrimage sites, and ultimately the great pre-Hispanic settlements that we know emerged," he says. The cave system is home to hundreds of archaeological sites, including evidence of America's first settlers, Mayan culture, and extinct animals. The discovery was made after 14 years of searching by GAM director Robert Schmittner and a team of divers. – Starting next week, Saudi Arabia will move its weekend to Friday and Saturday, a move that will make it a lot easier for foreign investors to get in on the country's $400 billion stock market, Bloomberg reports. Saudi Arabia's stock exchange, the largest in the region with a market value bigger than those in Turkey and Ireland combined, may open to foreigners as early as next year amid rising demand for assets. Such a move may attract as much as $30 billion of inflows. “Investors can read between the lines and see this as another step towards opening up the market,” says a fund manager at ING Investment Management in Dubai. “It’s not official, but this is one of the things Saudi needed to do to open the markets for foreign investors.”

– Barnes & Noble is giving up on its Nook tablets after sales fell 34% in the latest quarter. The company will continue to sell the e-readers in stores, but it plans to partner with a third-party manufacturer to make Nook HD tablets, reports the Wall Street Journal. Eventually, future Nooks might have Barnes & Noble's name on them as well as the Barnes & Noble logo. "We are 100% not exiting the device business," says the company's CEO. Microsoft already owns a 17% stake in Barnes & Noble's Nook business, and is rumored to be interested in buying it out.

– When Stefanie Gordon boarded her flight from New York City to Palm Beach, Fla., to visit her parents, the captain told her there was a chance passengers would witness the space shuttle Endeavour's last launch during the flight. As the plane descended toward Palm Beach and the Endeavour's launch became visible, Gordon pulled out her iPhone and snapped a few photos and a short video. On the ground, she posted one of the photos to her 1,800 Twitter followers. In a few hours, she was fielding phone calls from ABC, the BBC, and CNBC. She had accumulated about 1,000 new Twitter followers, and she had to turn the @mention push notifications off on her phone so they wouldn't drain the battery. "I don't have that many Twitter followers, and I basically tweet about sports," Gordon tells Mashable. "I really didn't expect it to go as viral as it did."

– The White House didn't know the full extent of the IRS scandal until May 10, when the agency admitted it had targeted conservative groups, insiders tell the Washington Post. The story says that when White House counsel Kathryn Ruemmler learned of an inspector general's report on the matter, she briefed Chief of Staff Denis McDonough and other top aides, but that they decided to wait until the report was finished and made public to protect President Obama from being accused of meddling in an investigation. The story says the White House's handling of the situation has left it looking like it didn't know what its agencies were up to—and it's been struggling to explain why it didn't learn of the scandal until May 10, when the media started focusing on the details. "It's become a Washington spectacle," says David Plouffe, who left the White House in January. The Post's sources say that Ruemmler didn't know the full extent of the scandal until after the inspector general's report had been completed, and that she didn't know whether the IRS had targeted only conservative groups or was politically motivated.

– The Danish inventor charged with murdering a Swedish journalist aboard his submarine says she died in an accident and he "buried" her at sea. Copenhagen police say Peter Madsen "told police and the court that there was an accident on board the sub that led to the death of Kim Wall, and that he subsequently buried her at sea in an undefined location of the Koge Bay," about 30 miles south of Copenhagen, the BBC reports. Police say they can't release any more information at this time, and the search for Wall's body is continuing. Madsen, who was rescued after Wall was reported missing on Aug. 10, has been charged with negligent manslaughter, which carries a sentence of up to eight years in prison, and aggressive manslaughter, which carries a sentence of up to 10 years. Police believe Madsen deliberately sank the UC3 Nautilus submarine.

– A 55-year-old Oregon man will spend 60 days in jail for harassing a bison in Yellowstone National Park. Raymond Reinke pleaded guilty in federal court Thursday to harassing wildlife and was sentenced to 60 days for interfering with law enforcement and 10 days for disorderly conduct, Fox News reports. Reinke was caught on video earlier this month aggressively provoking a bison. "I'm sorry to the buffalo," Reinke said in court. "He didn't deserve what I did to him. I'm sorry, I really didn't mean to hurt that buffalo." The bison didn't attack Reinke, but the judge said he was lucky the animal didn't kill him. "You chased and hounded the bison," he said. "You're lucky the bison didn't take care of it, and you're standing in front of it." The judge also banned Reinke from entering Yellowstone, Grand Teton National Park, and Glacier National Park for five years after he completes treatment for alcohol abuse.

– Police in California are looking for a woman they say beat up a teen and stole her phone—and they think she took selfies with the phone. The El Cerrito Police Department says the victim was walking to class when a car rolled up and two women got out, demanded her phone and backpack, and then punched her in the head after she refused, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. Police say the woman took several selfies with the phone and then uploaded them to iCloud, where they were later found by the victim. "I don't think she knew it was being uploaded to the cloud. I think they were assuming it was on the factory default settings," Sgt. Ian Wong tells ABC 7. The victim, who suffered minor facial injuries in the attack, found the selfies on her iCloud account and recognized the woman as her attacker. "I wonder if she's still smiling now that @ElCerritoPD has put her picture out there?" a Twitter user asks.

– The owners of a teriyaki restaurant in Sedro-Woolley, Wash., say they've received death threats after the owner asked four sheriff's deputies not to eat there, the AP reports. According to the Skagit County Sheriff's Office, four deputies were eating at Lucky's Thursday when two of them went to pay their bill. As they were paying, the owner told them "other customers didn't like law enforcement there anymore," Sheriff Will Reichardt says in a Facebook post. The owner repeated the request, Reichardt says, and asked "that we spread the word to other law enforcement that they were no longer welcome either." The sheriff says his chief deputy called the owner later and says the request was confirmed. Calls to Lucky's were met with busy signals, and the Sedro-Woolley Police Department said on Facebook it's interested in responding to the owner's request. Lucky's owners tell KOMO that they feel terrible about the incident and are inviting members of law enforcement to come eat there for free on Monday. They say they've received death threats online and over the phone.

QVC has announced that it is "taking a pause" in its relationship with the celeb chef and will " phase out her product assortment on our online sales channels over the next few months," reports Fox News. Deen's publisher has also backed out of a book deal, reports the AP. Ballantine Books had planned to release Paula Deen's New Testament: 250 Favorite Recipes, All Lightened Up in October.

– Colorado police are trying to find out if there's a connection between the murder of Jessica Ridgeway and an attempted abduction in May. In a press release, authorities say they're looking into the possibility that the two crimes are related, the Denver Post reports. On May 28, a 22-year-old woman says she was jogging near Ketner Lake in Westminster when a man grabbed her from behind and tried to put a chemical-soaked rag over her mouth. The woman was able to escape and call 911, and police have no description of the man's vehicle. "Police are trying to determine if there is any connection between the two cases," the press release says. "Several metro area law enforcement jurisdictions are working other cases of attempted abductions and various vehicle or suspect descriptions have been provided." Police are also looking for someone who may carry or wear a "cross like this," which matches the suspect's description from Ketner Lake. They're also asking the public to call if they know of someone whose behavior has been unusual.

Luis Walker was found guilty on all 28 counts he faced, including rape, aggravated sexual contact, and multiple counts of aggravated sexual assault at Lackland Air Force Base in San Antonio, Texas, the AP reports. Walker is one of 12 Lackland instructors investigated for sexual misconduct toward at least 31 female trainees, and among the six charged on counts ranging from rape to adultery. Several of Walker's alleged victims testified during his court-martial, including one who described how Walker lured her into an office and sexually assaulted her on a bed, ignoring her pleas to stop. The women told jurors that Walker gained their trust to get them alone in his office or an empty dormitory, where he then forced them into kissing, touching, or intercourse. The alleged sexual misconduct among instructors at the base apparently began in 2009, but the first woman didn't come forward until last year. The women who testified against Walker said they didn't tell anybody at first because they feared being booted from the Air Force. According to prosecutors, Walker had sexual intercourse with 4 of the 10 female recruits. He was also accused of making flirtatious or sexually suggestive

– Artist Ryan Mendoza has spent more than $130,000 repairing and rebuilding Rosa Parks' old Detroit home, and he now wants to bring it back to the US, the Detroit Free Press reports. Mendoza, who lives in Germany, saved the home about a year ago when it was threatened with demolition, and he plans to put it on display in Berlin and then return it to the US. But so far, Mendoza says, Detroit's cultural institutions are hesitant to bring it back to the city, and he wants it instead to end up in a museum or other venue elsewhere in the US. “If you look at the current situation in America, you have all of these monuments to the Confederacy—which are monuments to slavery,” Mendoza says. “There are very, very few monuments to the civil rights movement, which is antithetical to that.” Parks lived in the old house for a time after leaving the South in 1957. She was arrested in 1955 for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger, and the bus has since been restored and now sits at the Henry Ford Museum in Dearborn, Mich. “Her memory, her legacy will never die,” Parks' aunt, Rhea McCauley, told the Free Press last year. “It is an important lesson for the entire country

– Scientists in Japan have created an ear out of human stem cells and implanted it on the back of a rat, the Telegraph reports. The researchers at Kyoto University and the University of Tokyo used induced pluripotent stem cells, or iPS cells, which can be turned into any kind of cell in the human body. In this case, the stem cells were turned into cartilage balls the size of a human ear. The researchers say they hope to use the technology to treat people born without ears or with small ears, and they plan to start a clinical study on humans in five years. The team created the ear by taking stem cells from a patient and turning them into cartilage balls, the Japan Times reports. The balls were then implanted into the rat's back. After two months, the balls dissolved, leaving behind what looked like a human ear. Induced pluripotent stem cells could grow into various human tissues and they are considered promising in the field of regenerative medicine. In other stem cell news, scientists in the US are working on an artificial kidney that could be powered by human kidney cells.

– The Bramble Cay melomys is Australia's most isolated species of rodent, found only on the tiny coral cay of Bramble Cay in the Great Barrier Reef—and it's now believed to be the first mammal ever to go extinct due to climate change, Live Science reports. According to the Guardian, the rodent was discovered on the cay by Europeans in 1845, but the last known sighting was in 2009. Since then, the cay has been inundated by rising sea levels caused by climate change, which researchers say "point to human-induced climate change being the root cause of the loss of the Bramble Cay melomys." Researchers set out to find the melomys after a 2014 study found no evidence of the rodent at all. They set out to do just that with the help of traps, cameras, and even a helicopter, but they were unable to find a single melomys, according to a government and University of Queensland report published Wednesday in Scientific Reports. The report states the loss of Bramble Cay melomys habitat was "almost certainly" the result of ocean inundation caused by climate change. The only hope for the Bramble Cay melomys is that another population of the rodent exists on neighboring Papua New Guinea.

– China's economic growth slowed to a three-year low of 7.6% in the second quarter, the government announced today, and analysts aren't sure whether the slowdown is a sign of official corruption or a sign of a more troubling trend—or even a sign that the economy is in serious trouble. "But the system isn't good at measuring how many nights people have had karaoke or restaurant meals they have had." Other problems include a lack of accurate measuring devices for the service economy and for consumption by the middle class. "If you look at the number of cars produced in China, you will probably get a more or less accurate number," says a Standard Chartered economist. – It's that time of year again: time to reflect on the meaning of Thanksgiving and what it means to be an American. Here's what you need to know: The first Thanksgiving wasn't really a national holiday. That honor goes to the Pilgrims, who gave thanks for the harvest and honored the Wampanoag king, but it wasn't a national holiday across the country. Many of the early celebrations included turkey, and Alexander Hamilton famously said, "No citizen of the US shall refrain from turkey on Thanksgiving Day." The Pilgrims probably had plenty of venison, but it's not clear they even had an oven that could bake pumpkin pie, Mental Floss reports. The Wampanoag king gave the pilgrims five deer, but it's not clear they had any venison at all. cranberries were a rare luxury at the time, and it's not clear cranberry sauce was ever invented. The pilgrims probably didn't have an oven to bake pumpkin pie, and it's not clear they even had an oven in which they could have baked it. Pumpkin pie became a popular dish on 17th-century American tables, though, and it might have shown up for Thanksgiving as early as the 1623 celebration of the holiday.

– Beacon Island off Western Australia is best known as the site of one of the darkest episodes in Australian maritime history—the 1629 sinking of the Batavia, a Dutch East India ship that went down with more than 300 people on board. The survivors made it to the island, but about 40 died, including 30 women and children who were raped by the ship's undermerchant commander, Jeronimus Cornelisz, the BBC reports. – Paul Krugman and Ben Bernanke are locked in a "battle of the beards" over economic policy, writes Robert Samuelson in the Washington Post. The Nobel laureate wants the Fed to push for higher inflation, which would spur growth and job creation. Bernanke, on the other hand, thinks higher inflation is "reckless" and would hurt the economy. "What we should have learned since 2008 is that the Federal Reserve can’t do everything and overambitious goals guarantee disappointment," writes Samuelson. "People often don’t act according to academic theories. There isn’t a proper policy response for every need." At the Wall Street Journal, Dean Baker agrees. "Krugman’s theory could be right," he writes. "It responds to an understandable urge to do something about the feeble recovery and the millions left without work and hope. But in this debate, I side with Bernanke." Click for Baker's full column, or Samuelson's.

Other charities, he writes, "are more above-board about their financials and activities, probably should not be classified as charities. ... opera companies, charities which exist primarily for the benefit of their donors!" Miguel Solis and Alexander Rivas were found guilty of attempted murder and ordered to pay $10,000 in damages to the two photographers, the Telegraph reports. According to court documents, Solis and Rivas were among a group of men who confronted two photographers who were taking pictures of the wedding at a seaside home. The bodyguards demanded they hand over their camera memory cards and at least one of the men opened fire as the photographers drove away.

"The AP's servers got hacked. People quickly figured that out ... see how temperamental the market is? The age of social media, if you're allowed to monitor Twitter feeds like we are, we see that right away," says one analyst. The AP's corporate communications account quickly confirmed the hack, and the White House quickly dismissed the story. "The president is fine," said spokesman Jay Carney. "I was just with him." Prosecutors said the couple's African grey parrot, Bud, seemed to replay the murder by mimicking what sounds like an argument between a male and female. In a video, the family said it took several weeks after the incident for Bud to say, "Don't f---ing shoot."

Here's what they're saying: "Yes, of course, presidents have no direct control over gas prices. But the American people know something about this president and his disdain for oil. Obama's veto of the Keystone pipeline "gave away the extent of Obama’s antipathy to nearby, abundant, available oil," Grunwald writes. Deterred? Hardly. Our undaunted seer of the energy future has come up with his own miracle fuel: algae."

– With the search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 now in its fifth week, the Washington Post takes a look at the science of Bayesian inference, a type of statistical analysis that's been used in the search for sunken treasure, for men overboard, and for plane-crash debris. In short, Bayesian inference "formally formalizes what will seem, to many unfamiliar with it, like common sense," explains the paper's lead author. "Their founding principle is that most new situations can be assessed and assigned probabilities: How likely is this restaurant to be good? How likely is this cough to be a cold? How likely is Duke to win the NCAA title? Our first estimate of these probabilities may be no better than an educated guess." The Post explains that Bayesian inference "can help refine and focus the hunt for the plane and for a solution to the deepening mystery of its March 8 disappearance." Among the uses of Bayesian inference in the search for Flight 370: refine the probability of finding the plane at any given location based on new information, update the probability of finding the target in any latitude-longitude combination, and account for depth in the water. – The fossil of a dinosaur's brain has been found in the UK, more than a decade after it was discovered by a fossil hunter. It's the first example of fossilized brain tissue from a dinosaur, and researchers say it's an "astonishing" find, Phys.org reports. "The chances of preserving brain tissue are incredibly small, so the discovery of this specimen is astonishing," says a co-author of the study, published in the Geological Society of London. The fossil, found by Jamie Hiscocks in Sussex, was likely from a species related to Iguanodon, a large herbivorous dinosaur that roamed the early Cretaceous Period about 133 million years ago. Meninges—tough tissues surrounding the brain—as well as tiny capillaries and portions of adjacent cortical tissues have been preserved as mineralized "ghosts." The brain was likely "pickled" in a acidic and low-oxygen body of water, similar to a bog or swamp, so that the soft tissues could be mineralized before they decayed away completely. – Joe's Crab Shack is testing a no-tipping policy at 18 of its 131 restaurants in an effort to raise wages for its workers. "I personally believe tipping is an antiquated model," CEO Ray Blanchette told investors last week, per the Los Angeles Times. "We believe that the no-tipping service model gets us above the fray with regards to the increased minimum wage conversations that seem to be happening all over the country." The Houston-based Ignite Restaurant Group is testing the policy at restaurants in Utah, Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Illinois, Michigan, Nebraska, and Kansas. Joe's Crab Shack isn't adding service charges to checks at the 18 locations, though there have been small increases for menu items. Blanchette says the fixed hourly rate for test workers has been raised from $2.25 to $14, which is the same as a state model that allows employers to pay tipped workers below the federal minimum wage as long as their tips make up the difference. Joe's Crab Shack is the second major restaurant chain to test a no-tipping policy. – A new species of prehistoric cockroach has been discovered in what is now Myanmar, and it looks a lot like a crane fly, a praying mantis, and a cockroach, reports the BBC. It's about the size of a puppy, and it lived about 100 million years ago. “This little monster was a solitary hunter, able to run very fast, with a body unlike the vast majority of cockroaches living today, it posed high above ground, frequently taking flight when necessary, and seizing its prey with strong short spines developed on its extremely long feet,” says one of the scientists who found it. The creature, named Manipulator modificaputis, belongs to an ancient family of cockroaches called the Manipulatoridae, and it's the biggest of its kind ever found. It lived about 480 million years ago in a shallow sea in what is now the Sahara Desert. "It is one of the biggest arthropods that ever existed, far bigger than any arthropod today," says a Yale paleologist who helped find it. The creature had two appendages in the front of its mouth that were used to grab prey like worms and mollusks, but it modified them to create spikes that allowed it to catch rapidly diversifying plankton. – The "connected car" is expected to dominate this week's International Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas, and General Motors and Audi are among the companies showing off how they're going to make their cars Internet-ready. They're unveiling plans to equip their cars with 4G technology, which would allow them to access the Internet while on the road, the Wall Street Journal reports. They're also working with Google to add Android software to their vehicles. The move is part of Google's Open Automotive Alliance, which is made up of some of the world's biggest automakers, as well as tech companies like Nvidia and Honda. "We want to make the Android operating system available in hundreds of millions of cars around the world," says a Google exec. The move is part of Google's plan to get into the car business, and the Verge notes that it's a big change for the auto industry, which for decades has shied away from "stable, proven technology."

– Skywatchers are in for a treat on Jan. 31. For the first time in 150 years, the Pacific Ocean will be directly toward the moon at the same time it coincides with a blue moon eclipse, Space.com reports. In other words, the second full moon of the month will be a blue moon. The eclipse will take place at 4:51am PST on the West Coast, and the total phase will begin at 4:51am PST for Alaska, Hawaii, and northwestern Canada. The eclipse will last 77 minutes, with the total phase ending at 6:48am PST for the rest of North and Central America. The eclipse will also be visible in Europe, the Middle East, and parts of Asia, including Indonesia, New Zealand, and most of Australia, according to the Virtual Telescope Project.

The disease, which has killed millions of corals, is believed to be the result of an outbreak that began in 2014 off the coast of Key Biscayne. It has since spread to more than 50 miles of reefs in the Florida Reef Tract, which stretches from the Atlantic to the Gulf of Mexico, per a DEP release. "While disease outbreaks are not unprecedented, this event is unique due to the number of coral species affected across a large portion of the Florida Reef Tract, and the ongoing nature of the event," the release notes. "The exact cause and contributing factors for this event will likely take years to identify; however, addressing other known coral stressors (i.e., water quality, turbidity, and sedimentation, etc.) will increase the ability of the corals to recover." Those stressors include human-made pollutants in the water, as well as rising sea temperatures, UV radiation, and water quality issues, the release notes. – Verizon has announced a deal to buy Yahoo for $4.83 billion in cash and stock, the Wall Street Journal reports. The all-cash deal includes Yahoo's real estate, but not its stakes in Alibaba and Yahoo Japan. Yahoo will be left with its stakes in Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. and Yahoo Japan Corp., with a combined market value of about $40 billion. Verizon will add Yahoo web services that still draw 1 billion monthly users, including mail, news, and sports content, and financial tools. The company's market capitalization is $229 billion. While AOL chief Tim Armstrong has been a key part of Verizon's Yahoo pursuit, the driving force on the Verizon side is his boss, longtime Verizon executive Marni Walden. The career cellphone executive has been leading the company's moves beyond telecommunications, particularly its expansion into video and advertising, and was instrumental in the acquisition of AOL. "People are surprised about Verizon getting into the content space," Walden told Recode last year. "I think that's really important to bring eyeballs and audience. Our media business will play a much more significant role in the Verizon of the future."

– Edvard Munch's "The Scream" sold for a record $119,922,500 at Sotheby's last night, reports AP. The 1895 pastel image of a man screaming under a streaked, blood-red sky is one of four versions of the work by the Norwegian artist. The previous record for an artwork sold at auction was $106.5 million for Picasso's "Nude, Green Leaves, and Bust," sold by Christie's in 2010. The image has become part of pop culture, "used by everyone from Warhol to Hollywood to cartoons to teacups and T-shirts," says a London art adviser. "Together with the Mona Lisa, it's the most famous and recognized image in art history." The buyer's premium paid by Norwegian businessman Petter Olsen—whose father was a friend, neighbor, and patron of the artist—made the price the highest ever paid for an artwork at auction.

The strike took place in North Waziristan, one of the militant network's main strongholds. "The drone fired two missiles at the compound. We believe it was being used by militants," said one of the Pakistani officials. Yesterday, four suspected militants were killed in the same region. The US has been pressuring Pakistan to crack down on militants in North Waziristan, but that appears unlikely, given the country's ongoing feud with the US over the accidental killing of 24 Pakistani soldiers in a drone strike last year. In other US-Pakistan news: John McCain and Carl Levin today called the sentence of the Pakistani doctor who helped the US find Osama bin Laden "shocking and outrageous," the AFP reports. They urged Pakistan to pardon and free Shakeel Afridi "immediately."

– Ukraine's president has called off a trip to Turkey because of the "sharp aggravation" of the situation in his country's east, where pro-Russia separatists have entered from Russia. "I have made a decision to cancel my working visit to the Republic of Turkey due to sharp aggravation of the situation in Donetsk region, particularly Amvrosiivka," Petro Poroshenko said in a statement, per the BBC. "The president must stay in Kyiv today." He added that a meeting of the National Security and Co-operation Council will be held today "to elaborate further plan of actions." Poroshenko said that Ukraine will ask the UN Security Council to convene an emergency meeting. "The world must provide assessment of sharp aggravation of the situation in Ukraine," he said. Ukraine says Russian forces have crossed the border and are supporting the rebels, but Moscow denies that, reports the New York Times. A rebel leader in eastern Ukraine says some 4,000 Russian citizens are fighting in the separatists' ranks, and many of them are former servicepeople who are on leave, the AP reports.

– The Salvation Army in Tega Cay, SC, is asking for the public's help in finding the person who dropped a $1,200 coin into one of its red kettles. The Herald Online reports that an anonymous donor dropped the coin into a red kettle during a fundraiser held at a Tega Cay Walmart. An appraisal was performed at a local jeweler, and the coin is likely to be sold.

– "Loose tweets destroy fleets." That's the Air Force's message to servicemembers in the wake of recent threats from ISIS sympathizers, the Air Force Times reports. "There is sometimes a fine line between letting your friends see what you're up to and providing an adversary critical information about your connection to the military and its mission," Capt. Jonathan McDonald, the Air Force's Force Protection chief, says in a press release. "So not only is it important to not post vital mission related information, but it's also important to not post detailed personal information to keep yourself and your loved ones safe." The release includes a photo of a fleet of F-16 fighter jets parked on a runway at Al Udeid Air Base, Qatar, along with the message: "Loose Tweets Destroy Fleets." The phrase is a modern-day twist on the WWII propaganda poster "Loose Lips Sink Ships," the Times notes. The Navy and Army have used the slogan on social media in the past, but the Air Force is the first to use it publicly. – "Arbeit macht frei"—"Work sets you free"—is a phrase that has stood at the entrance to the Dachau concentration camp in Germany since it was stolen in 2014. It's "highly likely" that gate has now been found in Norway, police say. "The gate is in OK condition and will be returned to German authorities as soon as practical," police in Bergen say, per Reuters. Authorities say they received an anonymous tip and found the gate propped up in a store room, though it was mostly black with some flaking paint, CNN reports. German authorities made a replica of the gate and installed it at Dachau last year to mark the 70th anniversary of the camp's liberation.

– "It was a great shock but everyone responded, both our staff and volunteers and members of the public. They raised a cry and he did not get away." So says the dean of Salisbury Cathedral in England, after a man allegedly tried to steal one of the country's most important legal documents. The Magna Carta was on display in the cathedral's Chapter House when "someone manually started the fire alarm to alert others to the incident," a witness tells the BBC. "It looked like some men 'play-fighting' but as they got through the gates we got some shouting and kicked it into the road whilst another man held on to him. They then held onto him with hands behind his back whilst they picked him up." Police say a 45-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of attempted theft, criminal damage, and possession of an offensive weapon. The 1215 document is one of four original copies of the Magna Carta still in existence, the BBC reports. It's believed to be one of the most important legal documents in the world and was signed by King John in 1215, according to the Salisbury Journal. – Minnie Driver, who was once Hollywood's hottest young thing, has never gone the way of Kate Winslet or Catherine Zeta-Jones. "I can't believe you've got me doing this," she tells the Guardian in an interview about her new movie, Hunky Dory. "I just read the script and I could see the movie." Driver, 42, is still a fine actor working steadily in film and television but she has never quite graduated to the leading-lady status that she seemed set to attain. Her latest film, Hunky Dory, a small British indie from Jon Finn, the producer of Billy Elliot, is a sweet if slightly odd high-school musical set in Wales during the heatwave of 1976. Her performance is brilliant, as angular and Welsh. "I just don't feel I've totally ticked off the singing movie," she says. "Oh, I've been trying to get on that show since, well... God knows. I know, I'm not scared to say it! Gwyneth Paltrow completely stole my thunder!"

Border Patrol Agents: Colorado Voters Disenfranchised," the Drudge Report's latest headline reads. The Drudge Report's anti-Cruz attacks are "breaking through on social media in a significant way," according to the Post, which notes that the Drudge Report is named for Matt Drudge, who broke the story of Bill Clinton's affair with Monica Lewinsky. In a radio interview yesterday, Cruz said the Drudge Report has "basically become the attack site for the Trump campaign." "Most days they have a six-month-old article that is some attack on me, and it's whatever the Trump campaign is pushing that day will be the banner headline on Drudge," he said. Critics are split on whether it's worth the price of admission: "The Other Guys is one of the funniest movies of the year, if not the funniest movie of all time," writes Peter Travers in Rolling Stone. It's "a goofballs'-and-fireballs comedy that has the effect of dissolving, rather than piquing, whatever worldly anger or frustration you may be harboring." It's "anarchic" and "highly disciplined," writes AO Scott in the New York Times. " Ferrell uses his big body, his quick mind, and his infinitely fungible voice to disparate and ridiculous traits into a brand new and yet instantly archetypal comic character." The movie's plot is "neither the movie’s point nor its most memorable feature," writes Roger Ebert in the Chicago Sun-Times, but it's "most authentically itself when it indulges in a free-form but nonetheless highly disciplined silliness that has the effect of dissolving, rather than piquing, whatever worldly anger or frustration you may be harboring." – An Egyptian pop singer has been sentenced to two years in prison for "inciting debauchery." Shaimaa Ahmed, 25, appeared in a music video that showed her dancing in her underwear before appearing in front of a classroom of adult men, pouring milk over a banana, licking an apple, and tasting chocolate cake, per the BBC and New York Daily News. The video, titled I Have Issues, drew more than a million viewers in a few days, but it also sparked controversy among conservatives for the strong sexual gesturing in the video. Ahmed was arrested Nov. 18 before she could be referred to the prosecution for investigation. She denied the accusations, saying the director included the controversial scenes without her consent. The director of the video was also sentenced to two years in prison, but in absentia.

– A New Hampshire woman who became stuck in a swimming pool after the ladder broke turned to Facebook to ask for help getting out, the AP reports. Sixty-one-year-old Leslie Kahn was swimming in her pool Aug. 11 when the ladder broke, leaving her stranded. She said she didn't have the strength to pull herself. No one else was home and her cellphone was inside. She used a pool pole to drag the chair her iPad was on and posted in a community Facebook page, asking for help. She said she labeled the post "911" to get people's attention. A woman who lived nearby showed up, followed by police and a neighbor. Kahn, a breast cancer survivor, tells WMUR-TV that sometimes you help others and other times, you ask for help. "I was thinking I might be here a while because my tenants were out, nobody was home," she says. But her old iPad was on a chair on the small pool deck, but it was out of reach. Then, ingenuity. "So then I grab the pole. Hooked the leg of the chair. Dragged it over, and got online," she says. She posted her 911 on "Epping Squawks," a community Facebook group.

– The Federal Reserve's stress tests on the nation's 19 biggest banks haven't been kind to Citigroup. The bank failed to meet minimum standards, and CEO Vikram Pandit says the company will work with the Fed to figure out a way to return "meaningful capital" to shareholders, Bloomberg reports. The Fed objected to Citigroup's capital plan, which may have included a request for a higher dividend. "We will work with the Federal Reserve to formulate a plan that returns meaningful capital while satisfying our regulators," Pandit said in a memo to employees. The Fed said Ally Financial, SunTrust Banks, and MetLife also fell short of minimum standards. The tests were designed to see how banks would fare in a second recession and a deep economic slump. Most of the banks passed, but Ally, which received $17.2 billion in federal aid, may have to delay its initial public offering, the Wall Street Journal reports.

Booker will be only the fourth African-American elected to the Senate, and he'll be only the fourth mayor of a major US city to do so, notes the New York Times. "People who know nothing else about Cory Booker know that the 44-year-old Newark mayor is going big places," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. "The next big entry on his résumé will very likely be junior US senator from New Jersey, after Booker easily won Tuesday's Democratic primary for the special election to replace the late Sen. Frank Lautenberg." Given that he'll be running against a Republican who promises to run a "line-in-the-sand campaign between a conservative and an extreme liberal," that will probably rankle a good number of liberals, Cillizza notes. But not everyone on the left is against Booker. "My grandfather being in the military, it hit home for me as well, and specifically it's the veterans," he says. Kaepernick is expected to sit during the national anthem when the 49ers take on the Seahawks on Sunday. – For more than a decade, Delphine Boel has been trying to prove that she is, in fact, the biological father of the 84-year-old former king of Belgium. On Monday, a Brussels appeals court ruled in her favor and ordered King Albert II to take a DNA paternity test, reports Reuters. If he doesn't do so within three months, Boel will be legally presumed to be Boel's father. Albert, who abdicated in favor of son Philippe in 2013, had been refusing to recognize Boel as his daughter, notes the Telegraph. He has acknowledged that he had an extra-marital relationship with his Italian wife, Queen Paola, in the 1960s.

– Democrat Jon Tester has won a hard-fought race for Montana's open US Senate seat, reports the Missoulian. The incumbent led Republican challenger Denny Rehberg by 16,000 votes late yesterday, with some votes still to be counted in four counties. Libertarian Dan Cox, who ran as a third-party candidate, got 6.5% of the vote. Tester, a 56-year-old farmer, is the state's first openly gay senator. “The outside money that’s coming in (to politics) is bad for democracy," he said. "We’ve got to get some transparency in this process, at a minimum ... so we know who’s footing the bill. It shouldn’t be about someone who has a ton of money, trying to buy an election.” The race was the most expensive in Montana history, with Tester and Rehberg each spending about $20 million of their own money.

– Pro-independence Democratic Progressive Party candidate Tsai Ing-wen took a commanding lead in Taiwan's presidential election results late Saturday evening, and the candidate for the China-friendly Nationalist Party conceded a massive loss. Tsai had about 60% of votes while Nationalist Eric Chu had about 30%, with about half of votes counted, the AP reports. "We failed. The Nationalist Party lost the elections. We didn't work hard enough," Chu said before a thin crowd of a few hundred supporters at his campaign headquarters. He followed his concession speech by making a long bow. "As the Nationalist Party chairperson, I need to pay the highest level of responsibility. Dear all friends, Eric Chu apologizes to everyone. I'm resigning as party chief," he said. Outgoing Nationalist President Ma Ying-jeou has served eight years and is constitutionally barred from another term. The outcome of the contest for a majority in the 113-seat legislature remained uncertain, with independents and smaller parties posing a threat to both the Nationalists and the DPP. Tsai has pledged to maintain the status quo of de-facto independence for the island of 23 million, although she has refused to endorse the principle that Taiwan and China are parts of a single nation to be unified eventually. – The driver of a Spanish train that derailed last night, killing at least 80 people, has been placed under police guard and formally investigated, reports Reuters. Francisco Jose Garzon Amo, 52, had been a train driver for 30 years and had only been driving the eight-carriage train for a year. He told a station radio station that the train entered a curve at 120mph, well over the speed limit, reports the BBC. "We're only human! We're only human!" he said. "I hope there are no dead, because this will weigh on my conscience." At least 94 people were injured, 35 of them in serious condition, reports AP. The crash occurred on the eve of a major Christian festival in the northwestern city of Santiago de Compostela.

– A 22-year-old Disneyland employee has been arrested on suspicion of possessing a destructive device after a "dry ice bomb" exploded in the park's Toontown section Tuesday evening. Christian Barnes, who worked as an outdoor vendor, is being held on $1 million bail, the Los Angeles Times reports. Police believe Barnes placed dry ice inside a water bottle in a trash can where it exploded. No one was injured in the blast, which forced the evacuation of Toontown. "You wouldn't expect situations like that coming to a place like this," says one visitor. "That is crazy, that's wild." Police say the incident is an "isolated incident with unanticipated impacts," but they don't think it's connected to recent dry-ice explosions in Anaheim.

– The US and four other countries dropped humanitarian aid to a besieged Iraqi town last night as part of an effort to protect its minority Yazidi population, reports CNN. The airdrops came as the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported that the Islamic State had "distributed" 300 Yazidi women to its ranks, some of whom had converted to Islam so they could be married off to ISIS fighters. The women were kidnapped in Iraq before being taken to Syria, and the SOHR says it could confirm at least 27 cases in which women were "sold and married" for $1,000 each. Amerli is home to many of Iraq's Shiite Turkmen, and the UN high commissioner for human rights warns of an "imminent massacre" if aid doesn't reach the town, reports Reuters.

– A college student who caused a stir on Broadway by plugging his phone into a fake outlet during a performance of Hand to God apologized at a press conference yesterday, the New York Daily News reports. "I downed a few drinks, and I think that clearly impaired my judgment," Nick Silvestri, 19, said. "I guess I wasn't really thinking." Silvestri said he didn't realize the stage was off-limits to cell-phone users. "I've learned a lot about the theater in the past few days—theater people are really passionate and have been very willing to educate me," he said. "I would like to sincerely apologize to the Broadway community." Silvestri's stunt was staged by the producers of Hand to God to draw attention to the issue of cell-phone use during shows, the New York Post reports. "I am so defeated by this issue that I seriously question whether I want to work on stage anymore," star Patti LuPone said after the incident at Shows for Days earlier this week. "Now I'm putting battle gear on over my costume to marshal the audience as well as perform." Silvestri's phone was returned to its owner after the show.

– Four pit bulls slipped through a hole in a backyard fence and attacked and killed a Texas family's 10-year-old beagle, the Houston Chronicle reports. “They busted through, attacked my dog, and shook her like a rag doll and chewed on her until she bled out,” 13-year-old Brittany Baker’s father tells the Texas City Daily News. Police and animal control officers arrived within minutes. “They spend about 45 minutes trying to get the dogs back on her property,” Steve Baker says. “The lady in the house tried to prevent this attack with everything she could,” Steve Baker says. “She was trying to break it up, but what it comes down to is she couldn’t control them.” The city has a dangerous dog ordinance, and the dogs' owners must be registered annually. “The damages are really limited,” Steve Baker says. “It’s not like I want to put any real pain on them for this. A dog’s value to a family is priceless—you can’t replace that.”

"He looked dead, he looked like a corpse," said State College Police Detective David Scicchitano, describing sophomore Tim Piazza's appearance in footage showing frat brothers carrying him upstairs the morning after a pledge event that involved heavy drinking. Scicchitano spoke at preliminary hearing at a courthouse near campus that will determine if there's enough evidence to send the case to court for trial, the AP reports. Video shot inside the Beta Theta Pi house was being shown from the night the pledge was ordered to drink and then fatally injured in a series of falls. Piazza consumed what prosecutors said was a life-threatening amount of alcohol during a hazing ritual on Feb. 2 in State College, Pa., and he died two days later. Fraternity members didn't call 911 until nearly 12 hours after his first fall. Scicchitano said the footage shows Piazza was clearly injured after his first serious fall, at 11:22pm. – Hawaii's Big Island was shaken by its strongest earthquake in 37 years Friday, with a magnitude 6.9 temblor hitting the state, the Washington Post reports. The quake was one of more than 110 that hit the island in 24 hours, according to the US Geological Survey. The quake struck in the Leilani Estates area, where residents have been ordered to evacuate as lava has burst through cracks in the ground. USGS volcanologist Sally Sennert says the quake was among the strongest to hit the island in 37 years. "It was strong enough to shake houses hundreds of miles away," Sennert tells the Post. "It was felt as if the shaking was very strong." USGS says the quake was among the strongest to hit the island since a magnitude 4.5 quake on May 3, CNN reports. Sennert says the quake caused widespread power outages and damaged buildings, but there have been no reports of deaths or major injuries, the AP reports. The USGS says the quake was centered near the Pu'u O'o spatter cone, which is part of the Kilauea volcano, and not far from the area where lava has been spurting from fissures.

– The Mega Millions jackpot has climbed to an estimated $502 million—the fourth-largest in the game's 16-year history, USA Today reports. The numbers drawn Tuesday night were 7, 25, 43, 56, and 59, with a gold Mega Ball 13. No tickets matched all six numbers, pushing the estimated prize for the next drawing to $502 million, according to lottery officials. "Jackpot rolls are always exciting, but surpassing the $500 million mark for only the fourth time is a historic milestone," Mega Millions lead director Gordon Medenica said in a press release Wednesday morning. "Large jackpots like this one capture everyone's attention, and it would be great to see the roll go on for a while longer. But at the same time, we can't wait to see someone win." The flick starring Ethan Hawke, Willem Dafoe, and Claudia Karvan is "a balls-out, R-rated movie about bloodsuckers that doesn't spare the gore so little girls won't cry into their Twitpics of Rob Pattinson," writes Joe Neumaier in the New York Daily News. Daybreakers is "a nifty genre piece from Aussie twins Michael and Peter Spierig (Undead) who put some oomph into an overworked theme," writes Peter Travers in Rolling Stone. – Danish inventor Peter Madsen has been sentenced to life in prison for torturing and murdering Swedish journalist Kim Wall on his private submarine. Judge Anette Burkoe at the Copenhagen City Court said she and the two jurors agreed Wall's death was a murder, saying Madsen didn't give "a trustworthy" explanation. Madsen, 47, had denied murder and said Wall died accidentally inside the submarine, but he has confessed to cutting up her body and throwing the body parts into the sea, the AP reports. "This is a cynical and pre-planned sexual assault of a particularly brutal nature on a random woman who, in connection with her journalistic work, accepted an invitation for a sailing trip on the accused's submarine," Burkoe said, explaining the rare decision to hand down Denmark's most severe sentence. Prosecutor Jakob Buch-Jepsen has claimed Wall's murder was sexually motivated and premeditated because Madsen brought along tools he normally didn't take when sailing. He has sought a life sentence for Madsen. Madsen's defense lawyer has said he should only be sentenced for cutting Wall into pieces. The cause of death has never been established. Madsen stood quietly listening as the judge read out the verdict Wednesday.

– One person is dead and eight others injured after a Chicago Transit Authority bus jumped a curb during rush hour today in downtown Chicago, reports NBC Chicago. The accordion-style bus was heading east on Lake Street when it stopped at a red light and proceeded through the light, hitting four cars and two pedestrians, reports the Chicago Tribune. It then jumped the curb and came to rest on the sidewalk. "People were screaming and running towards the bus," says a witness. "The bus driver was hurt. The windshield of the bus was out." Aimee Coath, a 51-year-old pedestrian, was pronounced dead at Northwestern Memorial Hospital. The bus driver and six others were hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries. Investigators are reviewing surveillance video from the bus.

– When Kelly Tousley and Curtiss O'Rorke Stedman of Juneau, Alaska, bought a utility trailer in June, they didn't set out on a vacation. Instead, the couple, who met while working with autistic kids, decided to hit the road for a year to build a tiny house and tour the US. The 98-square-foot trailer they bought cost $8,600—less than half the cost of a typical tiny house—and they've already traveled from Alaska to Montana and Michigan. "We had the conversation of, if we're living in this and this is our house, we don't want to be sitting on milk crates with cushions on top of them and feeling like we're going to get slivers in our fingers when we touch the walls," Tousley tells MLive.com. The couple, who are traveling with their two dogs, have a small bathroom separated by a curtain and a kitchenette, but no running water. They also have a queen-sized bed, a bench that folds out into a queen-sized bed, and solar panels. They're not the first to travel the US in a tiny house. The death toll is expected to rise as outlying areas are reached. "We spent the night in the car here. But I won't leave until I see him. When they told me he was still alive I couldn't believe it. – The Mars rover Curiosity is scheduled to touch down at 1:31am ET today, and if everything goes according to plan, NASA will know within two hours whether it's safe, reports the New York Times. If it's not, engineers on Earth will have to wait for two to eight hours. The rover will use an X-band radio to send simple messages to Earth, but the landing site will rotate out of view within minutes, meaning that a NASA orbiter will have to relay those messages to Earth in real-time. If anything goes wrong with the communications, then silence will follow. The rover will also use a UHF antenna to send data, but it's not powerful enough to be picked up by an Earth antenna. NASA's Mars Odyssey orbiter has had a problem with one of three spinning wheels, so a spare wheel was put into operation. If Odyssey misses Curiosity's messages, a second orbiter, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, will also be listening. But Reconnaissance Orbiter will be recording the data, not relaying it, and engineers on Earth will not get to sift through that information until hours later. – Dilma Rousseff is no more. Brazil's Senate on Wednesday voted 61 to 20 to convict the country's first female president of an impeachment charge and remove her from office for the rest of her term, reports the New York Times. She will now be replaced by interim President Michel Temer, who will be in charge until a new president is elected next year. NPR reports that Rousseff, who was suspended from office in May on charges of illegally borrowing money to pay for presidential expenses, wept in the Senate chamber after the vote. "I'm not a thief," she said. "I'm the president of the people." She has the right to run for office again, but the Senate didn't actually vote on an impeachment ban that would have kept her from doing so for the next eight years. Instead, it held a second vote and failed to get the necessary 42 votes.

The find suggests that Homo sapiens or their relatives began to spread out and acquire smaller tools as the climate changed, reports the New York Times. “Social networking during a long period of climate variability was a key to success for early Homo sapiens,” says paleoanthropologist Rick Potts of the Smithsonian Institution. “Greater mobility encouraged thinking about how to acquire resources for early Homo sapiens.” The discovery of the 320,000-year-old tools is the oldest of their kind, and they show that Homo sapiens or their relatives began to downsize their tools as the climate changed. – Fish that live in the frigid waters of Antarctica have developed antifreeze proteins that keep their blood from freezing—but those proteins also prevent the fish from ever ridding themselves of ice in their veins, according to a study published Monday in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Marine biologists studying the notothenioid, a bony fish that thrives on anchor ice that exists on the sea floors of the Antarctic region, discovered that the antifreeze proteins help the fish survive in frigid waters by binding to ice crystals and preventing them from growing. But the fish also carry ice crystals around with them for most of their lives, a risky proposition that could help them stay cool under pressure but could also cause a life-threatening traffic jam inside small capillaries, reports UPI. "Since much of the ice accumulates in the fishes' spleens, we think there may be a mechanism to clear the ice from the circulation," says study author Paul Cziko of the University of Oregon's Institute of Ecology and Evolution. "This is just one more piece in the puzzle of how notothenioids came to dominate the ocean around Antarctica." Job growth is likely to rebound in the coming months as businesses in the area reopen and construction companies ramp up repair and renovation work. Last month's drop was driven by huge losses in restaurants and bars, which shed 105,000 jobs, a sign of the damage to Florida's tourism industry. Roughly 1.5 million people were unable to work last month because of the weather, the government said, the most in 20 years. Hourly workers who couldn't work and missed a paycheck were counted as not working, which lowered September's job totals. The unemployment rate fell because it is calculated with a separate survey of households. That survey counted people as employed even if they were temporarily off work because of the storms. Dakota Layers had taken "extensive biosecurity measures" over the last two months to prevent the virus from spreading, but "even our extraordinary measures proved ineffective," says the company's CEO. – The UN's highest court has dismissed Croatia's claim that Serbia committed genocide against its ethnic Serbs during the 1990s war for independence. The International Court of Justice ruled today that there was no evidence that the "specific intent required for acts of genocide" took place, the BBC reports. Croatia had filed the case in 1999, accusing Serbia of targeting ethnic Croats during the war, in which about 20,000 people died. Serbia counter-sued in 2010, accusing Croatia of ethnic cleansing by forcing 200,000 Serbs from their homes, the New York Times reports. "What is generally called ethnic cleansing does not constitute genocide," Judge Peter Tomka said in his ruling. "Acts of ethnic cleansing may be part of a genocidal plan, but only if there is an intention to physically destroy the target group." Croatia's prime minister said his country was "not satisfied with the court's ruling, but we accept it in a civilised manner."

– Scientists have laid bare the DNA of a kangaroo species for the first time, and identified a gene responsible for the kangaroo's hop. The tammar wallaby (Macropus eugenii) is only the third marsupial to have its genome sequenced. Making up the trio are the Tasmanian devil and the South American opossum, the BBC reports. Tammar wallaby young are only the size of a grain of rice when born. They spend the next stage of their development in their mother's pouch, feeding on her milk. The pouch is external to the mother's body and therefore the developing animal comes under attack from many pathogens. Antibiotics in the mother's milk are key to the survival of the offspring. This is only the third marsupial genome to be sequenced. "It's always really valuable to look at an organism that is a bit different to understand how humans and other mammals have evolved," one researcher says. "It gives you a perspective on mammalian evolution by looking at mammals that have diverged fairly early on, like the kangaroo."

The company said in a public statement that an initial flyover of the platform did not reveal any spilled oil. Photos from the scene showed at least five ships floating near the platform. Researchers at Ohio's Nationwide Children's Hospital looked at 100 breast milk samples purchased on a milk-sharing website and compared them to milk donated to a milk bank, USA Today reports. The researchers found that 75% of the breast milk purchased online was contaminated with high levels of bacteria, including staphylococcus and streptococcus, which have been linked to illnesses in infants. The study's lead author says it is "totally normal" for certain bacteria in breast milk to have high levels of bacteria, but the researchers believe the contamination is likely the result of poor collection, storage, and shipping practices, along with the use of unclean containers or breast milk pump parts. – A simple blood test can detect Alzheimer's disease up to 20 years before symptoms set in, according to researchers who say it could be used to screen thousands of people for the disease. The test measures the levels of beta-amyloid, a plaque that builds up in the brains of people with Alzheimer's, New Scientist reports. Researchers compared the levels of two types of beta-amyloid in the blood of 41 people with Alzheimer's to PET scans, which show how much of the plaque is in the brain. A positive test for amyloid doesn't mean a person has Alzheimer's, but the presence of the plaque is a sign that they are at risk for developing the disease. A negative test, however, means a person doesn't have Alzheimer's. "This kind of test could be used to screen many thousands of patients to identify those at risk for Alzheimer's disease, and to start treatments before memory loss and brain damage," says researcher Randall Bateman. The Alzheimer's Association is "very positive about the test, but would like to see it validated," a spokesman says. The survey sent to Windsor Elementary School students was conducted by WISE, a nonprofit domestic violence prevention and advocacy group, WPTZ-TV reported. A notice was sent to parents allowing them to opt their children out of the survey, but parent Vanessa Beach said she never received it. While she doesn't oppose topics on gender identity and sexuality being discussed, Beach said she feels the survey questions were inappropriate for her daughter's age group. "My daughter is 10. So are all the other kids who took this," Beach said. "A sexual partner at 10 years old would be called sexual abuse." A WISE representative said the survey questions were created with University of New Hampshire researchers with whom the group is sharing the collected data. Beach said she told the school and WISE about her concerns. School administrators and WISE officials said they are working to address parents' complaints. Students are told that they are not required to take the test and can choose not to, a WISE official said. Beach said she appreciates other work WISE does to raise awareness about domestic violence.

Police say that after the man drove by Officer Nic Abts-Olsen with his headlights off, Abts-Olsen stopped him to check his license and registration, then walked back to his car to see how he was doing, the Seattle Post-Intelligencer reports. When Abts-Olsen knocked on the driver's window, the man opened it, spilled a glass vial of cocaine, and tried to snort it. "Are you kidding?" Abts-Olsen can be heard asking the man, who eventually admitted to having "vitamins" in his possession. He was arrested and booked into King County Jail on a narcotics possession charge, KOMO News reports.

– Cops in Freeland, Pa., wanted to track down a 35-year-old suspect who had been on the lam since last summer, so they posted a mugshot of him on their Facebook page. But Anthony Lescowitch quickly reposted the post on his own page, the Times Leader reports. "CAPTURED!!!!!! SHARES OUR STATUS ON FACEBOOK ABOUT HIMSELF, CAPTURED 45 MINUTES LATER," read the post. Police say they noticed Lescowitch's post minutes later, and figured out he was the guy who'd reposted it. They then set up a fake Facebook profile of an attractive woman to talk to Lescowitch about his wanted picture. He agreed to meet them at an undisclosed location, and they arrested him without incident. Lescowitch is being held on $25,000 bail.

– When a Connecticut man was arrested last year in connection with a series of burglaries in which expensive golf equipment was stolen, he was also charged with wearing a stolen sweatshirt in his booking photo, the Smoking Gun reports. The homeowner of a Glastonbury residence who was burglarized in July 2014 contacted police two months ago to report seeing the mugshot, which contained the logo for Coco Libre, a "pure organic coconut water." Police say that "a subsequent investigation linked Benson to the burglary." The 30-year-old is being held on $125,000 bond on burglary, larceny, and criminal mischief charges.

– The iPhone 4S will hit the Chinese market a week from today, making it the fastest iPhone launch in Apple's history and one of the fastest in the company's history, Computerworld reports. The iPhone 4S will also be available in more than 20 other countries, including Bolivia, Dominican Republic, Jamaica, and Senegal. China Unicom, the only Apple-sanctioned carrier in the People's Republic of China, will start selling the iPhone 4S on Jan. 13. Apple has not revealed prices for the iPhone 4S in China, but most experts believe it will cost about the same as the iPhone 4 did in the US with a two-year carrier contract. "We believe the demand for the iPhone 4S in Mainland China to be unprecedented," says a Ticonderoga Securities analyst.

He buried the gold in various locations around the Bay Area, but he lost most of it when he died in 1875 and forgot where he'd buried it all, the Chronicle reports. In 1903, a worker in Sonoma County found $7,000 in gold in Swift's $50 slugs. A year later, $30,000 in gold was found in a chimney hiding place on Swift's old ranch near Sears Point. – Move over, "Gangnam Style." YouTube has a new top-viewed video of all time. Wiz Khalifa's video for "See You Again" featuring Charlie Puth became the site's most-watched video Monday and has more than 2.896 billion views as of Tuesday, the AP reports. That's about 2 million more than the video for Korean rapper Psy's 2012 smash "Gangnam Style," which held the most-viewed title for five years, YouTube said. Justin Bieber's "Sorry" sits in third place, more than 250 million views behind the leaders. Puth reacted with surprise on Twitter, noting that he joined YouTube in 2007 hoping to make a video that would hit 10,000 views. Puth also earned a congratulatory message from YouTube star Tyler Oakley, who called the feat "legendary & epic." Wiz Khalifa said in a statement that he's happy the song has been able to "inspire and impact so many lives." "See You Again" was released in 2015 as a tribute to late Fast and the Furious star Paul Walker.

– "Clearly they knew that what they were doing was wrong," the superintendent of Michigan's Anderson High School tells CBS Detroit. "I'm a little disappointed that they would choose to not only take a picture of an answer key but then share it globally." The superintendent says two students snuck into the classroom and took photos of the exam's answer key while the teacher was in the hallway. They then texted the photos to a number of students who may or may not have been taking that exam. The teacher noticed some unexpected grades—everyone had perfect scores—and alerted the administration. Now, the entire class must go back to school to retake the exam while other students are enjoying their summer break. "Consequences are forthcoming," the superintendent says. "Because our disciplinary matrix is progressive in nature, one of the things that we always do is to determine whether or not a student may or may not have been involved in similar activity prior to this, and that may change their particular consequences." WXYZ reports that about 30 students were taking the exam.

– The SEC is planning a major crackdown on high-speed trading, which has been blamed for everything from theflash crash of 2010 to the European debt crisis, reports Bloomberg. Under the plan, all proprietary traders using algorithms to buy and sell stocks would have to register with the SEC. “The SEC should not roll back the technology clock or prohibit algorithmic trading, but we are assessing the extent to which specific elements of the computer-driven trading environment may be working against investors rather than for them,” SEC chief Mary Jo White told a conference yesterday. Other parts of the plan include increased oversight of stock exchanges, and monitoring of so-called "dark pools," venues that don't publish bids and offers. The SEC also plans to review the dozens of order types on exchanges, which it says can "create conflicts of interest and raise serious questions about whether such conflicts can be effectively managed." New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman is investigating whether HFT gives firms an unfair advantage.

– "This is absolutely appalling," says Ina Rogers, speaking out about the "absolutely appalling" conditions in which she and her husband, Jonathan Allen, allegedly abused their 10 children. "My husband has a lot of tattoos. He looks like a scary individual, and that's why people are so quick to judge him. But my husband is an amazing person. I am an amazing mother." Rogers was speaking after Allen was charged with nine felony counts of child cruelty and seven felony counts of torture following a six-week investigation, ABC 7 reports. Police say the children, ages 4 to 14, described incidents of intentional abuse resulting in puncture wounds, burns, bruising, and injuries consistent with being shot by a pellet or airsoft gun. "Not only do I have 11 children and I'm 30 years old, but I also homeschool all of my children and people don't agree with that lifestyle and so I've had many people question my right to parent and I just feel like this whole situation was exploded," Rogers said. Allen was arraigned Monday afternoon in a Solano County court. He is being held on $5.2 million bail. The children have been placed in the custody of Rogers' sister and mother in the Bay Area.

– New parents will soon be able to take unlimited maternity or paternity leave from Netflix. The streaming service announced the policy Tuesday in a blog post by Tawni Cranz, its chief talent officer. "We want employees to have the flexibility and confidence to balance the needs of their growing families without worrying about work or finances," Cranz writes. "Each employee gets to figure out what’s best for them and their family, and then works with their managers for coverage during their absences." The company will "keep paying them normally," eliminating the hassle of having to switch to disability leave, Fortune reports. Netflix has an unlimited time-off policy, but "today’s policy update is a clear reminder that the company wants the best talent," writes Brian Barrett at Forbes. "Especially when and after they become new parents." (Netflix shares hit an all-time high Tuesday.)

– The size of the oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico has tripled in just a day or so, growing from a spill the size of Rhode Island to something closer to Puerto Rico, according to images collected from mostly European satellites and analyzed by the University of Miami. On Thursday, the size of the slick was about 1,150 square miles, but by Friday's end it was in the range of 3,850 square miles, said Hans Graber, executive director of the university's Center for Southeastern Tropical Advanced Remote Sensing. That suggests the oil has started spilling from the well more quickly, Graber told the AP. "The spill and the spreading is getting so much faster and expanding much quicker than they estimated," said Duke University biologist Larry Crowder. "If it gets into the Keys, that would be devastating." The environmental mess could eclipse the Exxon Valdez disaster, when an oil tanker spilled 11 million gallons off Alaska's shores in 1989. BP suggested in a 2009 exploration plan and environmental impact analysis for the well that an accident leading to a giant crude oil spill—and serious damage to beaches—could be averted. President Obama planned a Sunday trip to the Gulf Coast to see the damage himself.

– A hiker in Yosemite National Park fell to his death while climbing the iconic granite cliffs of Half Dome in rainy conditions, authorities said Tuesday. The National Park Service said the accident occurred Monday at about 4:30pm in the Northern California national park. The hiker's body was recovered Tuesday afternoon. NPS spokeswoman Jamie Richards said the man and a companion were scaling the steepest part of the trail where rangers recently installed cables to help hikers to climb the steepest part of the 4,800-foot ascent. Richards said the companion was helped from the trail and was unharmed. Richards said hikers can clip safety harnesses to the cables, but the vast majority don't. Richards said investigators are still trying to determine how the fall occurred. She said it's unclear if the hikers were climbing in the rain, but that the well-worn trail over smooth rock was wet. The NPS declined to release the man's name pending notification of his family. The NPS said it's the first fatal fall from Half Dome since 2010. NPS requires hikers to obtain permits to hike the popular trail to avoid overcrowding during the peak summer season. Half Dome is one of the symbols of Yosemite, and the trail to the top is one of the most popular routes in the park, requiring reservations to prevent overcrowding.

– A Silicon Valley clean-energy startup has just unveiled its first product—a "server" capable of generating electricity using natural gas or biogas, the AP reports. But Bloom Energy is keeping key details under wraps, including the life span of the server, how much downtime it will have, and whether it will be used in homes. "The Bloom Energy Server is certainly an exciting development, but that excitement should be tempered by the challenges it faces, and the likelihood that another company has something at least as exciting in development," writes David Coursey of Tech Insider. "My takeaway is that energy problems may be more easily solved that previously imagined."

– Netflix has renewed the watercooler hit 13 Reasons Why for a second season, the AP reports. The streaming service announced Sunday that it has picked up the series revolving around the suicide of a high school girl. Season two will debut on Netflix next year. While Netflix doesn't release ratings information, 13 Reasons Why has proven a conversation-starting drama. Some have criticized the show for glorifying suicide, which led to Netflix adding an additional warning ahead of the series. The Selena Gomez-produced 13 Reasons Why is based on Jay Asher's young adult best-seller. The second season will also be 13 episodes long.

The researchers looked at Medicare beneficiaries who went to the ER for non-life-threatening conditions between 2008 and 2011, and found that those who saw doctors for less-life-threatening conditions were more than twice as likely to be prescribed opioids for chronic pain than those who saw doctors for less-life-threatening conditions. The researchers also found that people who saw doctors for less-life-threatening conditions were more than twice as likely to be prescribed opioids for chronic pain than those who saw doctors for less-life-threatening conditions.
