– Amazon will open its first brick-and-mortar store in the middle of New York City this holiday season, reports the Wall Street Journal. The "mini-warehouse" on West 34th Street—across from the Empire State Building and home to Macy's flagship store—will serve as a place for customers to return and pick up their online orders, as well as offer same-day delivery. An analyst tells USA Today that Amazon will likely focus on its Kindle e-readers and tablets, as well as the struggling Fire set-top box and Fire smartphone. "There's still a segment of the population that's touchy-feely," says the analyst. "They want to see the product up close, and have it shown to them."

– Mark Sanford’s campaign has been in a bit of a tailspin lately, so he decided to step up and debate Nancy Pelosi instead of his opponent, Elizabeth Colbert Busch. “Since Elizabeth won’t debate, I’m allowed to debate Nancy,” he said at a press conference, before posing a question to a cardboard Pelosi cutout. The move is “seemingly ripped from the political playbook of Clint Eastwood, who famously delivered a rambling address at the Republican National Convention to an empty chair meant to represent President Obama,” writes Ben Smith at Politico.

Al-Ansi added that many of those who didn't die in the explosion were seriously injured by shattered glass falling from the mosque's windows. – India has chosen an "untouchable" president in the country's first contest since the country gained independence from Britain in 1947. Ram Nath Kovind, a 72-year-old lawyer and governor of the eastern state of Bihar, was the clear favorite in Thursday's election, but he was defeated by Meira Kumar, a former parliament speaker from the lower rung of the country's caste system, NBC News reports. Kovind is not the first president to be "Dalit," a term that means "oppressed" in Sanskrit and refers to members of the lowest caste. Kocheril Raman Narayanan took office in 1997 more than half a century after Gandhi pledged to end the country's ancient system of discrimination. One-fifth of all parliamentary candidates must be Dalit under decades-long affirmative-action laws introduced to improve representation and outlaw discrimination. Dalits are also guaranteed a proportion of college places and government jobs. But while social mobility has improved, particularly in India's fast-growing cities, rural areas still often witness members of lower castes forced to live in separate areas or prevented from using communal facilities such as water fountains. – "Athena" is a humanoid robot, but she's also a paid passenger on a Lufthansa flight from Los Angeles to Frankfurt, making her the first such robot to fly on a commercial jet, the LA Times reports. The robot, which has a white head, hands, and legs, was accompanied by two scientists who will be transporting her to Germany for research. "We don't want humans to go there and sacrifice their lives," one of the scientists tells Reuters. "I would like to have a robot achieve the same task, such as opening up doors and cleaning up." Right now, Athena is strapped into a seat like a regular passenger, but she'll be put in the off position during flights so she can be more dangerous for humans. The scientists "wanted to see how humans responded to a robot sitting in a plane," says an airport spokeswoman. "It's cheaper to get a seat." The robot was also treated to a cut on the front of the ticket line in first-class, and TSA had a special pat-down waiting for her, the Times notes. (Earlier this year, a flight attendant had a baby inside a baby carriage.)

– Archaeologists digging under Cambridge University's Old Divinity School have uncovered what they say is "one of the largest medieval graveyards in the UK," the Independent reports. The graveyard, which had been known to historians since the mid-twentieth century, contained about 1,300 burials—including 400 complete skeletons—and had been pre-dug in anticipation of winter deaths, according to a report in the Archaeological Journal. "This suggests that some, but not all of the graves may have been dug in advance of being needed," the report says. "One possibility is that this occurred prior to the winter, when ground conditions would have potentially made digging graves considerably more difficult." The hospital cemetery dates from the 13th to 15th centuries and was used by the "poor scholars and other wretched persons" who lived in Cambridge at the time, the Telegraph reports. Most of the bodies were buried without shrouds or coffins, and there were few women or children among them. Grave-goods, such as jewelry and a crucifix, were found in only a handful of graves. – For more than a century, the story of Vincent Van Gogh's decision to cut off his ear has been linked to a falling-out with fellow artist Paul Gauguin. But a new book suggests the famous artist may have actually done it on his own brother's orders. In Studio of the South, Martin Bailey finds evidence that Van Gogh learned of his brother's engagement the same day the razor cut off his ear, reports the Guardian. The brothers had been working together in Provence, and on the night of Dec. 23, 1888, Theo delivered a letter to Van Gogh's rented home in Arles containing the news that his brother had engaged in a whirlwind romance with another artist, Jo Bonger, and had agreed to marry her. Van Gogh had met Bonger just two weeks earlier, and the news of Theo's engagement could have caused him to lose his close relationship with his brother, who was unable to fund a struggling brother. Theo died the following year, and his widow inherited the bed Van Gogh used in his famous The Bedroom, but it was donated to a museum in the Netherlands and destroyed in WWII. – Five Republicans on the House ethics committee issued a statement today calling on Democrats to schedule ethics trials for Reps. Charlie Rangel and Maxine Waters before the November elections, Politico reports. “It is in the best interests of the transparency and fairness to the American people, Representatives Charlie Rangel and Maxine Waters, and other Members of the US House of Representatives, that the House Ethics Committee stop stalling the resolution of the Rangel and Waters matters and complete those public trials prior to the November elections,” said the statement from ranking Republican Jo Bonner and four other GOP members. Democrats were furious with the statement, with one Democratic aide saying, “The whole ruse of it being a bipartisan, non-politicized committee has blown up in their face. The fact that they can put out this statement shows how damned partisan it is.” Both Rangel and Waters have called for the trials to take place before the elections, and they've been frustrated with the ethics committee's inability to set a trial date.

– The $43,000 phone booth installed by then-EPA administrator Scott Pruitt in his office lasted just five minutes, according to newly released records from the agency. The Washington Post reports the records were released in response to a lawsuit filed by the Sierra Club, an environmental advocacy group. The records don't show how many incoming calls Pruitt received from the White House in the soundproof booth, which he installed last year. In April, Pruitt told Congress he used the booth "for confidential communications, and it's rare." He said the booth was necessary for him to be able to do his job. "Cabinet-level officials need to have access to secure communications," Pruitt told the House Energy and Commerce Committee in December. "It's necessary for me to be able to do my job." The new records don't show how many calls Pruitt received from the White House in the booth. The EPA identified two phone lines associated with the booth, according to correspondence between EPA attorneys and Sierra Club lawyers. The phone numbers released through billing records for the booth involve calls technicians made to test the lines, EPA lawyers said. The EPA voluntarily provided billing records for the booth through June 20, just two weeks before Pruitt resigned his post, that show no other outgoing calls from the booth

– The Colorado man bitten by a great white shark off Cape Cod last week says he wishes there had been shark warnings in place. "I have deep puncture wounds on both of my legs that required stitches. I had 47 stitches," Christopher Myers tells the Denver Post. "I had a couple of severed tendons in my left ankle and so I'm feeling very pleased to be here and walking." Myers says he and his 16-year-old son were swimming about 400 yards off Ballston Beach when "something very heavy had a very hard grip" on his leg. "I didn't feel pain from the lacerations. I'm not quite sure it pulled me under," he says. "Some people said they saw my head go under. I don't remember that." Myers says he kicked in the shark's snout and it let go of his left foot. "I've got a lot of lacerations on my right foot where I kicked at it, and I imagine I kicked its teeth and it let me go," he says. "I imagine it must have been the snout I was kicking." The attack, the first on Cape Cod in 76 years, is believed to be the work of a great white shark, state officials say

– A man who urged an end to violence in Oakland after gunfire killed his son and grandson as they slept three years ago became a victim himself this week as he drove near a street memorial for his slain family. Melvin Johnson, 39, was shot and killed Tuesday on the east side of the San Francisco Bay Area city, not far from the shrine for his 16-month-old grandson and 20-year-old son, who were fatally shot in August 2013, the East Bay Times reported Thursday. Police have made no arrests and released no motive for Johnson's killing. They have not said if the shooting was random or if Johnson was targeted. He died at a hospital. "In three years and four months, three generations of one family has been lost to gun violence in the streets of Oakland," community activist Sherri-Lyn Miller, a friend of Johnson's, told the AP. "Melvin Johnson was a giant teddy bear, and the loss has not only devastated the Johnson family, but all that knew him." Johnson had moved his son, Andrew "Drew" Thomas, and grandson, Drew Leon Deon Jackson, to the central California city of Fresno to get them away from Oakland's street violence, but they were slain while in town for a birthday party.

– Mexican drug kingpin Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman has been moved from a maximum-security prison to a medium-security facility in Ciudad Juarez, across the border from El Paso, Texas, a Mexican law enforcement source tells CNN. "Due to the proximity (to the US), it makes it easier to extradite him," the official says. The source says Guzman was transferred to the prison "with full respect for the human rights of the inmate." Officials say renovations to the Ciudad Juarez facility are to improve security, but it's not clear when Guzman will be extradited to the US, the AP reports. Last July, Guzman escaped from the same prison through a hole in the floor of his cell's shower stall. He was recaptured in January after hiding out in the town of Los Mochis in Sinaloa state. Guzman's lawyers say he wants to be extradited "as soon as possible" to stand trial in the US, but it's not clear when that will happen. His transfer to a medium-security facility will send him to Brooklyn to stand trial on federal drug trafficking charges, CNN reports. His lawyers say he will plead guilty to those charges as long as he's allowed to see his family.

Prosecutors disclosed Wednesday that two more women—one he was convicted of raping and another he attempted to kidnap and rape in Germany while in the US Army in the 1970s—may testify during the penalty phase. The Department of Interior announced Friday that it's canceling two upcoming lease sales in the Beaufort and Chukchi seas, as well as denying requests from Shell and Statoil to extend their existing leases, NPR reports. "In light of Shell's announcement, the amount of acreage already under lease and current market conditions, it does not make sense to prepare for lease sales in the Arctic in the next year and a half," Interior Secretary Sally Jewell said in a statement. The announcements come after Shell announced last month that it had found "disappointing" results from its Arctic drilling, the BBC reports. The company spent about $7 billion on Arctic drilling, but it said last month that it would stop the project for the "foreseeable future." Environmentalists are celebrating the government's decision to back away from Arctic drilling. Garcia Zarate, a 45-year-old Mexican citizen who had been deported five times to the US, was in the country illegally when he shot Steinle, 32, with a .40-caliber handgun as she and her father walked on a San Francisco pier, CNN reports. Garcia Zarate had been released by San Francisco officials before the shooting, despite a warrant for his arrest for felony re-entry to the US. – Two rare tiger cubs have been born at the National Zoo in Washington, DC, after their 4-year-old mother, Damai, went into labor last week. The zoo's curator tells the Washington Post that he and his fellow keepers had been watching the tiger's progress via a webcam because they knew the gestation period was just over 100 days, and because Damai had refused food over the weekend. On Monday, she finally gave birth. "How many people on the planet have seen this kind of thing happen before?" he asks. "You count yourself lucky to be a part of it." He says the birth was a "pretty powerful scene to watch" and that it was a relief when the surviving cub, which had been sick, came around. The cubs were sired by the zoo's male Sumatran tiger, 12-year-old Kavi. The cubs are the first born for Damai and Kavi, and the zoo says they are doing well. The cubs will not go outside for four to six weeks, and will be examined when they are able to lure their mother outside or into a separate enclosure. They will then be given a physical.

– A George Mason University professor was pepper-sprayed in the face while teaching a class on "vigilant justice" yesterday, but he refused medical treatment and returned to teach today, the Raw Story reports. Police aren't sure why the professor, economist Tyler Cowen, was targeted, but commenters on the school's Facebook page speculate that it could be because of his libertarian beliefs. Cowen is a well-known blogger at the conservative site Hot Air, and he has advocated for the idea of "self-defense"—or, as he put it in a recent post, "the act of self-defense by a stranger."

– The end of an era has arrived in the UK, where Blockbuster has gone into administration, putting more than 3,000 jobs at risk. The DVD rental chain, which announced last week that it would be shuttering its remaining 300 stores, tweeted a celebration this morning, complete with a photo of a smiling customer who rented This Is the End at 11pm Saturday, the last day for in-store rentals, the BBC reports. Seth Rogen also got wind of the news and tweeted that customers who rented movies before the last day for rentals can simply drop their movies off at any Blockbuster drop-off location. A Dish Network spokesperson tells Business Insider that customers who rented movies before the last day can drop them off at any of the chain's drop-off locations.

– JK Rowling is the author of the crime novel The Cuckoo's Calling, the Sunday Times reported today, in a scoop that sent the book's sales skyrocketing. The book sold more than 48,000 copies in the US in its first 24 hours after the news broke, CNN reports, while Amazon and Barnes & Noble both said it was No. 1 on their best-seller lists. Publisher Mulholland Books initially described the author as a former member of the Royal Military Police named Robert Galbraith. "I hoped to keep this secret a little longer, because being Robert Galbraith has been such a liberating experience!" Rowling said in a statement. Rowling will publish a second book in the series next summer.

According to NJ.com, police were recently provided with video footage of the alleged attack. All five players were team starters before the charges were filed. The team was scheduled to play Norfolk State in its season opener on Saturday.

– Greece's three-party coalition government has agreed on most of the austerity measures demanded by its creditors, but is now considering further pension and wage cuts as it scrambles to find $1.5 billion in savings, a source close to the talks tells Reuters. "The political leaders don't disagree on anything, there are just alternative proposals being discussed to protect those with low pensions or incomes in the public sector," the source says. "We need measures worth 1.5 billion euros to finalize the 11.5 billion euro package." Creditors—who are due to leave Athens at the end of the month, but will now stay until the savings plan is finalized—are increasingly impatient with Greece's progress. "We want to help and we will stay as long as it takes and until the plan is finalized," an IMF mission chief has told the Greek finance minister, according to a Greek official. Greece is expected to need another $11 billion in aid, and Deputy Finance Minister Christos Staikouras says the country is "taking extra care in managing our cash."

– A new law in Utah could make it illegal for women to have an illegal abortion or a miscarriage without a doctor's supervision. The bill passed the state legislature last Thursday and still needs final approval by the governor, but it's getting attention this week for its unusually restrictive language. It doesn't address legal abortion, but allows punishment up to life in prison for an "intentional, knowing, or reckless act" that leads to a miscarriage or abortion without a doctor's supervision. Especially concerning to some Utah Democrats and many women's rights activists is the word "reckless"—writing for RH Reality Check, Rachel Larris says, using the legal standard of "reckless behavior" all a district attorney needs to show is that a woman behaved in a manner that is thought to cause miscarriage, even if she didn't intend to lose the pregnancy. Drink too much alcohol and have a miscarriage? Under the new law such actions could be cause for prosecution. Women might also make themselves open to prosecution if they failed to wear a seatbelt and got in a car accident, if they stayed with an abusive partner, or even if they fell down the stairs, like a woman in Iowa who found herself jailed on suspicion of "attempted feticide."

– Pakistan is in the midst of a power crisis that has left the country sweltering in 100-degree heat, the New York Times reports. "Everyone is affected," says one resident in Karachi. "I can't pay my salaries. How can I if we can only work a few hours every day?" The country is $5 billion in "circular debt"—that's unpaid bills from government departments, wealthy politicians, slum dwellers, and more, leaving power providers with no money to pay for fuel, so their plants shut down. "This is not like finding a cure for cancer—people know what needs to be done," says the director of the Asia program at the Woodrow Wilson International Center, who has written a book on the power crisis. "The problem is implementation, and finding the political will." The country's last prime minister, Raja Pervez Ashraf, lost his parliamentary seat in a crushing defeat over allegations that he had taken kickbacks from foreign companies on power projects. One prominent candidate in this election—Nawaz Sharif, a former steel baron—has been closely identified with the power crisis.

Prosecutors haven't said why the students allegedly targeted the chapel, or how they got in. At a bond hearing on Saturday, Cook County Judge Peggy Chiampas told the teens, "These allegations are disgusting to me. I don't know if any of you know how lucky you are to be at Northwestern University."

Other first-time astronauts have described the smell of space as something akin to gunpowder or ozone, and Space.com has details on how NASA recreates the smell on Earth for training purposes.

– Three people are dead, including the suspected shooter, after a shooting Thursday morning at a Rite Aid distribution center near Aberdeen, Md. Harford County Sheriff Jeffrey Gahler says the suspect was a 26-year-old temporary employee who showed up for work at the facility, CNN reports. Gahler says the suspect used a 9mm Glock pistol and brought several magazines for the gun, which was hers and was purchased legally. The sheriff says the three people killed were shot outside the building and on the warehouse floor. Three others were shot and injured. The suspect died at a nearby hospital after shooting herself in the head, Gahler says. The shooting comes a day after two other mass shootings in the US, one at an office complex in Middleton, Wis., and one at a municipal center in Pennsylvania.

According to BuzzFeed, the class-action lawsuit alleges that the Wen products "contain a caustic ingredient that causes a chemical reaction and damages hair and follicles." Lead counsel for the plaintiffs, Amy Davis, tells CBS Los Angeles, "What we understand about the product and how it causes hair loss is it contains virtually no cleanser. It's like using lotion to wash your hair, so instead of removing the product, when you rinse it off, it just becomes impacted in your hair follicle." Davis says her firm hired chemists to test the Wen products and found that they contain hydroxycitronella, a chemical banned in the EU, Vox reports. According to the lawsuit, hydroxycitronella can cause irritation and damage to hair follicles. The Wen products in question—including a cleansing conditioner, deep conditioner, and leave-in conditioner—all contain water, glycerin, cetyl alcohol, and cetearyl alcohol, the first four ingredients in many Wen cleansers. The 18-year-old Hernandez was recently identified through fingerprints, Los Angeles County coroner's spokesman Ed Winter said Friday, per the AP. Hernandez died of "inhalation of smoke, soot, carbon monoxide and thermal burns," Winter said. His body was found May 2, 1992, inside an auto parts shop that was set ablaze during the riots in South Los Angeles. Investigators have said they were able to lift a single fingerprint from Hernandez's left middle finger. The coroner's office did not immediately respond to questions Friday about whether Hernandez's fingerprints had been run through databases previously. Attempts to reach Hernandez's family members on Friday were unsuccessful. The looting and violence that would turn into one of the deadliest race riots in American history was sparked after a jury acquitted four white police officers in the beating of black motorist Rodney King. Video shot by a citizen captured officers repeatedly striking, kicking, and using a stun gun on King, even after he was on the ground. A total of 53 people were killed and more than 2,000 injured during several days of violence.

The suit, which was filed Wednesday in federal court in Manhattan, says the league has "subjected and continues to subject its players to the imminent risk of head trauma and, as a result, devastating and long-term negative health consequences," the New York Times reports. Some of the plaintiffs were brawlers, like Jack Carlson, who racked up 1,111 penalty minutes in the league and the World Hockey Association. The suit, which is more graphic than similar ones filed by former players, also mentions movies like The Last Gladiators and the Broad Street Bullies of the 1970s. The plaintiffs are Michael Peluso, 48; Tom Younghans, 61; Allan Rourke, 34; Richard Brennan, 41; Brad Maxwell, 56; Dan LaCouture, 36; Jack Carlson, 59; and Scott Bailey, 41. Fernando de Noronha island, which is located in the Atlantic Ocean and has a population of just over 3,000, doesn't allow births because there's no maternity ward. – For the first time in 27 years, the definition of Alzheimer's disease has been updated. The new guidelines from the Alzheimer's Association and the National Institute on Aging reflect the growing evidence that the disease begins years before symptoms develop, reports the New York Times. “We’re redefining Alzheimer’s disease and looking at this in a different way than had ever been done,” says the director of the National Institute on Aging. “I think we’re going to start to identify it earlier and earlier.” The three stages of Alzheimer's are mild cognitive impairment, moderate cognitive impairment, and full-blown dementia, reports the Wall Street Journal. The latter stage is when no symptoms appear, but changes are brewing in the brain. biomarkers, proteins and other molecules in patients' blood and tissue, are key to earlier diagnosis, and the new guidelines call for more research into them.

Demonstrators chanted "Death to America," "Death to Christians," and "Death to Karzai," the latter referring to Afghan President Hamid Karzai, in the biggest protests since unrest erupted last week over plans by a US pastor to burn the Koran. "There are more than 10,000 of the demonstrators and some of them are waving the Taliban flag," a police officer tells Reuters. The protests come three days before a parliamentary election which the Taliban have vowed to disrupt. The election is a key test of stability in Afghanistan before US President Obama conducts a war strategy review in December. They follow three days of protests at the weekend over plans by an obscure US pastor, which he later abandoned, to burn copies of the Koran to mark the anniversary of the September 11, 2001, hijacked airliner attacks on the United States.

– Frances Bean Cobain has a great voice, but it’s not like she’s following in her parents’ musical footsteps. “She's got a great voice,” says Amanda Palmer, who recorded Cobain as a guest vocalist on her new album. “But she's a really good visual artist. She's really interested in graphic novels.” Palmer and fellow musician Jason Webley were inspired by conjoined twins Evelyn Evelyn, who share three legs, two arms, three lungs, two hearts, and a single liver. Evelyn Evelyn is the story of Eva and Lyn Neville— conjoined twin sisters who fell in love with the Andrews Sisters and Joy Divison and started a ukulele club. “Despite such obviously campy origins, the sisters' music often manages to rise above mere spectacle, their back-story flavoring oddball tracks such as 'Chicken Man' and 'Elephant Elephant' with surprising gravity, elevating the songs above mere musical curiosity,” writes Jon Caramanica in the New York Times.

– Ivins Rosier shot and killed Florida Highway Patrol Trooper Robert Boody's retired police dog Drake in November 2012, and now Rosier is going to prison. Rosier, then 16, confessed to shooting the 5-year-old German shepherd, but he was charged as an adult and tried this week, the Palm Beach Post reports. He was found guilty yesterday on charges of cruelty to animals with a firearm, burglary of a dwelling with a firearm, and shooting into a building, and sentenced to 23 years in prison. His lawyers plan to appeal, arguing that the case should have been tried as a juvenile, the Sun-Sentinel reports.

– The top House and Senate Democrats said Wednesday they had reached agreement with President Trump to protect thousands of younger immigrants from deportation and fund some border security enhancements—not including Trump's long-sought border wall. The deal announced by Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic Leader Nancy Pelosi following a White House dinner would enshrine protections for the nearly 800,000 immigrants brought illegally to this country as kids who had benefited from former President Barack Obama's Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, program, the AP reports. Trump ended the program earlier this month and had given Congress six months to come up with a legislative fix before the statuses of the so-called "Dreamers" begin to expire. "We agreed to enshrine the protections of DACA into law quickly, and to work out a package of border security, excluding the wall, that's acceptable to both sides," Pelosi and Schumer said in a joint statement. It was the second time in two weeks that Trump cut out Republicans to reach a deal with Pelosi and Schumer. A person briefed on the meeting, who demanded anonymity to discuss it, said the deal specifies bipartisan legislation called the DREAM Act that provides eventual citizenship for the young immigrants. "They did a very lousy job building their platform. I got their entire user base," Raja Bhatia wrote to Noel Biderman, CEO of Avid Life Media, which owns Ashley Madison and other dating sites. "Also, I can turn any non-paying user into a paying user, vice versa, compose messages between users, check unread stats, etc." Bhatia, who was no longer with Avid Life Media at the time, posted a sample of the stolen database to a GitHub account and discussed whether he should tell Biderman about the vulnerability, Wired reports. If he did hack Nerve and exfiltrate its database, he could be criminally charged with unauthorized access under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, Gizmodo notes. – The nation's public university presidents made an average of $441,392 last year, up 4.7% from the previous year, according to the annual compensation report by the Chronicle of Higher Education. But the highest-paid one was Penn State's Graham Spanier, who got $2.9 million, including $1.2 million in severance pay and $1.2 million in deferred compensation, the New York Times reports. "The fact that Graham Spanier turns out to be the highest paid president in the country says something about the nature of compensation packages for people who leave under a cloud," says the Chronicle reporter who worked on the survey. "Severance agreements are often very lucrative." Three other public university presidents made more than $1 million, including Ohio State's Gordon Gee, who made $2,542,865. The median total compensation for public university presidents was $441,392, up 4.7% from the previous year. The median base salary was $373,800.

– Stonehenge may be England's most famous monument, but it's not the oldest settlement in the country—at least not according to the Guinness Book of Records. Archaeologists have determined that the settlement of Amesbury, which includes the ancient monument, is Britain's oldest, having been continually occupied for each millennium since 8,820BC, the BBC reports. Thatcham, 40 miles west, was previously thought to be the oldest settlement in the country, but Amesbury has been continually occupied since 8820BC, researchers from the University of Buckingham say. "The site blows the lid off the Neolithic revolution in a number of ways," says the dig's leader. "It provides evidence for people staying put, clearing land, building, and presumably worshipping monuments. The area was clearly a hub point for people to come to from many miles away, and in many ways was a forerunner for what later went on at Stonehenge itself. The first monuments at Stonehenge were built by these people." Carbon dating of aurochs, the cattle twice the size of today's bulls, found at the dig site also revealed that people in Amesbury were eating frogs' legs 8,000 years before France, the Guardian reports.

– It's one of the most popular hikes in Shenandoah National Park—and one of its most dangerous. That's why park officials are warning hikers to plan ahead and make sure they're physically able to complete the 9-mile circuit hike on Old Rag Mountain in the Virginia park, per the National Park Service's website. "There is a significant elevation change and a strenuous rock scramble that requires good upper body strength," it says. "Often, children and shorter adults need assistance navigating the scramble. Take at least 2 quarts of water per person. Dehydration is one of the most prevalent issues. Wear sturdy shoes that will support your ankles and allow you to get a foothold without slipping." Old Rag is located near the park's eastern boundary, and the NPS notes that the parking lot can become "full and there will be long lines and substantial waits at some of the narrow passages." There are no pets allowed on Old Rag for their own and hikers' safety.

– If your city is hit by a small-scale nuclear blast, Michael Dillon has some advice: Stay in your building for at least 30 minutes. That's according to a new mathematical model he created to figure out the "optimal shelter exit time" in the event of a low-yield detonation, the AFP reports. Buildings that are lightweight or lack a basement are more likely to be penetrated by radioactive dust in a nuclear attack, so Dillon created the model to help emergency planning officials decide when and how far to go in search of better shelter. His model estimates that 10,000 to 100,000 people could be killed in a single low-yield blast, LiveScience reports. People living within 20 miles of a nuclear attack have up to a half-hour to seek better shelter, Dillon says, as long as that shelter is no more than 15 minutes away. If the better shelter is only five minutes away, people should head there immediately.

– The Islamic State has killed 1,878 people in Syria over the past six months, most of them civilians, according to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights. Of those, 930 were members of the Sheitaat tribe, a Sunni Muslim tribe that fought ISIS for control of two oilfields in eastern Syria in August, the group's head tells Reuters. The rest were soldiers and pro-regime militiamen, mostly for trying to flee to their home countries, the group says. Most of the victims were shot dead, beheaded, or stoned to death, the New York Times reports. The Islamic State has also executed 120 of its own members, most of them foreign fighters trying to return home, the group says. The Observatory says the real number of ISIS victims is higher than the 1,878 it has documented because hundreds of people are still missing and imprisoned in the group's jails, as well as because there are dozens of Kurds still missing since the beginning of ISIS attack on the countryside of Ayn al- Arab "Kobani."

– President George HW Bush has died at the age of 94, reports the Wall Street Journal. He had been hospitalized in Houston with congestive heart failure. His wife of 73 years, Barbara, died earlier this year at the age of 92. Here's a look at some of the coverage of the 41st president, who was the only American president to serve in both the Cold War and the Gulf War: The New York Times looks back at Bush's presidency, from his victory in the Gulf War to his defeat in 1992 to son George W.'s election to a second term. The Washington Post has a profile of Bush's life, from his humble beginnings in Texas to his decision to leave Wall Street for an oil-field supply business instead of a career on Wall Street. The AP has a profile of Bush's life as president, from his Navy service during World War II to his decision to run for president in 1980. He had a reputation for being "unpredictable" and "arrogant," but the AP says he was actually "the most impressive man in the White House." He was "a steady hand on the tiller," helping President Ronald Reagan navigate the economic crisis and the Korean War. The Washington Post has a profile of Bush

– The bodies of three missing Israeli teenagers who had been missing for more than two weeks were found in the West Bank last night, and Israeli forces launched more than 30 airstrikes in response to a barrage of rockets from the Gaza Strip, the BBC reports. At least four people were wounded in Gaza as air strikes hit sites belonging to Hamas and Islamic Jihad. "Hamas is responsible and Hamas will pay," Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said. "Now is the time for actions, not words." Israeli forces raided the homes of two Hamas suspects, killing one and blowing up the home of the other, the New York Times reports. The bodies of Naftali Frenkel, Gilad Shaar, and Eyal Yifrach were found under a pile of rocks near the West Bank town of Halhul, and an Israeli official says they appear to have been murdered soon after they were kidnapped, the BBC reports. Israel says it has identified two of the suspects and is seeking a third, the AP reports. The bodies will be buried today, and Israel has closed off the West Bank town of Halhul, the Times reports.

– A diet rich in fruits, vegetables, fish, nuts, olive oil, and plenty of sleep may help keep you younger than your years. So say researchers out of Boston in the British Medical Journal after looking at the health of nearly 5,000 nurses over more than a decade. They found that those who largely stuck to the Mediterranean diet had longer telomeres, which protect the ends of our chromosomes from cell division, reports the BBC. The researchers say the findings support the notion that dietary interventions may lead to "substantial improvements in health." The diet was not the only factor associated with longer telomeres. The researchers also found that the more sleep participants got, the longer their telomeres were. "Our findings suggest that the benefits of the Mediterranean diet extend to telomeres at the ends of chromosomes," the lead researcher says in a press release. " Telomere length has been associated with a wide range of age-related diseases, including heart disease, cancer, and multiple sclerosis." The researchers aren't saying that the Mediterranean diet is the reason for the longevity benefits, but they say it's important to have a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, fish, nuts, olive oil, and plenty of sleep. – With more than 20,000 absentee and questioned ballots still to be counted in Alaska, Joe Miller’s lead over Lisa Murkowski stands at 1,668 votes, the Anchorage Daily News reports. But Murkowski’s campaign manager says “any speculation about anything else is absolutely premature.” Miller, meanwhile, says he has no intention of dropping out. “If Sen. Murkowski is going to keep her word, she’s going to get out—if the voters decide that in fact I prevail in this primary election,” he tells the Washington Post. “She said at the Kenai forum on Friday that she would respect the will of the Alaskan voter and we’re going to hold her to it.” There is a chance Murkowski could run as a Libertarian in the November general election. The Alaska Libertarian Party is discussing the possibility, and its Senate candidate, David Haase, has said he is open to talking to Murkowski about him stepping aside.

– A new study suggests that cats aren't necessarily tied to their owners in the same way that dogs are. Researchers at the University of Lincoln in the UK say that even when left alone by their owners, cats tend to show signs of distress and are more vocal when the owner leaves them with a stranger than when they're left with their own owner. "Our findings don't disagree with the notion that cats develop social preferences or close relationships, but they do show that these relationships do not appear to be typically based on a need for safety and security," researcher Daniel Mills says in a press release. "For pet dogs, their owners often represent a specific safe haven; however it is clear that domestic cats are much more autonomous when it comes to coping with unusual situations," he adds. The study looked at 20 cat-owner pairs and used the Ainsworth Strange Situation Test, which has been used to test the "secure attachment" of children and dogs with their parents. It found that cats tended to be more vocal when the owner left them with a stranger than when the owner stayed with them, but there was no sign that the cats of owners who considered them highly attached showed any other signs of attachment. – Police have identified the driver who plowed into a crowd of pedestrians at the South by Southwest festival in Austin, Texas, yesterday, killing two, as Rashad Owens, a 30-year-old from Killeen, the AP reports. Police say Owens fled a police checkpoint after driving through barricades set up for the festival. Owens was charged yesterday with two counts of capital murder; his bail was set at $1 million, the Austin American-Statesman reports. Twenty-three people were injured in the crash, some critically.

– When David Cameron announced his resignation as British prime minister Monday, he was heard saying "right" and removing the microphone that had recorded his private moment. Some thought it sounded like the start of the West Wing theme, others thought it was a Winnie the Pooh-style hum, and still others thought it was Beethoven-esque. The Washington Post rounds up some of the reactions to the hum, which came as Cameron handed over the microphone to his successor, Theresa May. Here's what people are saying: "Somebody's happy to be done with this country," reads one tweet. "David Cameron humming to himself after press conference," reads another. "And this is roughly what we think he was humming: Understandably, the media have jumped on this surprising musical act, but we've investigated further," writes a post at the Guardian. "There is a theory that the soon-to-be-former PM is actually humming the opening of the Fifth Symphony—of which more here." Classic FM calls the hum "Wagnerian, Beethoven-esque harmonic doubt and then a strange contemporary flourish at the end," while the BBC's political editor thinks it's a Winnie the Pooh style hum as Cameron says his goodbyes.

– Martin Scorsese is returning to the director's chair for the first time since The Wolf of Wall Street. Leonardo DiCaprio will star in The Devil in the White City, an adaptation of the Erik Larson book that has been in the works for more than a decade, sources tell Deadline. The film will focus on serial killer HH Holmes, who murdered as many as 200 people in and around the 1893 Chicago World's Fair. It's expected to be the next collaboration between DiCaprio and Scorsese, who also worked with DiCaprio on The Wolf of Wall Street. The Devil in the White City was first put in development in Hollywood by Tom Cruise and Paula Wagner through their Cruise/Wagner banner, but the option lapsed in 2004. Paramount reacquired the film rights in 2007 and DiCaprio first joined the project in 2010. The project has been in development for more than a decade, but it was put on hold when Warner Bros. let the rights lapse a month ago.

When asked why she was there, Thompson said she was there to see Tebow. When asked why she wanted to see him, Thompson said she and Tebow were in a relationship. The officer asked her what kind of relationship she was in with Tebow, and Thompson said she didn't feel it was appropriate to answer that question. – Samsung and Google today unveiled the Galaxy Nexus, a smartphone running on a new version of Android. The launch comes just days after Apple unveiled its new iPhone 4S in several markets across Europe, the US, and Asia on Oct. 14. Samsung and Google originally planned to launch the device in San Diego on Oct. 11 but the event was postponed, the Wall Street Journal reports. The Galaxy Nexus will go on sale in the US on Oct. 25 for $200 with a two-year contract from AT&T or Verizon. In other Android news: There's a new Facebook app for the Galaxy Nexus, VentureBeat reports. Facebook's new app, called Cover, allows the phone to show your Facebook posts on a map. It also allows you to add photos to the page. The phone has a 4.8-inch screen, resolution of 1920 x 1080, and runs on a new version of Android known as "Gingerbread." There's also a camera capable of taking photos and video. The phone will be available in 16GB and 32GB models.

The film features no sex, nudity, or violence and is unlikely to be seen by children, critics say. "Not only is there nothing violent in Love Is Strange, there's not even anything explicit," writes Stephen Whitty of the New Jersey Star-Ledger. "It's a simple human story. And it is very hard to imagine that—if it starred, say, Robert Duvall and Jane Fonda as a similar long-time couple suddenly facing homelessness—it would be lumped in with movies crammed full of queasily stylish sexism and sickening torture porn." The MPAA ratings are supposed to provide information on a movie's content, so parents can decide whether or not it's suitable for their children. But what kind of information are they really providing? And what are they assuming we want to protect our children from? "If there's an equivalence among these three films, and their equal unsuitability for anyone under 17, it's lost on me—and, I suspect, on anyone but the censors at the MPAA," Whitty writes. – For the first time in four decades, limited cobalt production started in the US last year, and mining companies are now staking claims in Idaho, Montana, and Alaska in search of the precious metal, the BBC reports. "Miners like us have never actually gone looking for cobalt," says First Cobalt's CEO. "There's a lot of cobalt in the world. As miners, we're behind." Cobalt, which is used in lithium-ion batteries in electronic devices and electric cars, is expected to increase its consumption by between 8% and 10% a year as a result of increased demand. The price of cobalt has risen above $40 a pound this year, compared with $20 in 2011. The Democratic Republic of Congo is the world's top producer of cobalt, while China is the world's leading producer of refined cobalt, the BBC reports. Concerns about corruption and child labor at cobalt mines in the DRC are increasing pressure on buyers to find new sources of supply. "There's a few places where you can get ethically mined cobalt, and we want to be one of them," the CEO of Missouri Cobalt says. "We would like to think that that gives us an advantage." – Two capybaras—the world's largest rodents—have been missing from Toronto's High Park Zoo for more than three weeks now, and the public is getting increasingly desperate to track them down. The CBC reports one capybara was spotted in the city on June 5, but the other hasn't been seen since May 24, when it escaped as workers were moving a third capybara into its enclosure. The zoo set traps the next morning, but it's been more than two weeks since anyone has spotted the missing capybaras, which have been dubbed Bonnie and Clyde by the public. On Friday, a TV cameraman spotted one of the missing capybaras in the city's High Park, the National Post reports. "She was right there! And she was ninja-still. It looked like a log," Breakfast Television cameraman Bertram Dandy says. Capybaras can reach up to four feet in height and weigh as much as 140 pounds, according to the Guardian. They don't like children, and the zoo could face charges under the Ontario Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, an animal welfare group tells the CBC. (This capybara was found thanks in part to a Good Samaritan.)

– Want to be a teacher but can't afford to graduate from a four-year college? Consider National Louis University, which is offering a three-credit teaching course for the low, low price of $950 via Groupon, reports the Chicago Tribune. The deal—which will be available until Wednesday or until it sells out—is the first time an academic university has used the website as an effort to boost student interest. "We'd like (potential students) to understand what the realities are, whether you are committed to this profession ... and see if you have what it takes," says a university exec. The course is open to anybody with an undergraduate degree, notes Groupon, which sees the move as an experimental step in the right direction. "National Louis joins an innovative list of merchants who were the first in their industry to experiment with collective buying power, and do it on Groupon," says a spokeswoman.

– Former President Obama has broken what's known as an "unwritten rule" of former presidents not to criticize the current one. In a statement released Monday, a spokesman for Obama said the former president "fundamentally disagrees with the notion of discriminating against individuals because of their faith or religion," CNN reports. The spokesman said Obama is "heartened by the level of engagement taking place in communities around the country," adding that the protesters are "exactly what we expect to see when American values are at stake." The statement came as protesters took to the streets across the country to protest Trump's executive order banning travelers from seven Muslim-majority countries. Meanwhile, the Washington Post takes a look at how Trump's executive order differs from Obama's in two ways: The Obama administration's action was limited to one country in response to a specific threat, while Trump's is much broader and applies to visitors from seven countries without a history of terrorism. Trump's chief strategist, Stephen Bannon, said Sunday that the order is "not about religion—this is about terror."

– The number of violent crimes reported in the US last year was up 3.9% from 2014, according to an FBI report released Monday. The agency says there were an estimated 1,197,704 violent crimes reported around the country in 2015, compared to 1,165,164 in 2014, the New York Times reports. The violent crime rate—which includes murder, rape, assault, and robbery—was 372.6 incidents per 100,000 people, up from 361.6 in 2014. The report says the increase was most pronounced in big cities, where the violent crime rate was more than twice as high as in the West, the Midwest, and the Northeast, Reuters reports. There were an estimated 15,696 murders last year, up from 14,164 in 2014. The murder rate in Chicago, the country's most dangerous city, jumped 13% from 2014 to 2015, with 54 more people killed in the city last year than in the previous year, the Chicago Tribune reports. The report says the increase in violent crime was caused by a "chill wind" of criticism of police tactics. "We're just beginning to see a shift in mentality in law enforcement from a warrior mentality ... to a guardian mentality," Carter Stewart, a former prosecutor in Ohio, tells Reuters. – If you're in one of the 35 US cities where flu season is upon you and you don't want to drive yourself to the doctor, Uber is here to help. The ride-sharing service is partnering with Passport Health to offer on-demand flu shots Thursday, the Washington Post reports. Customers who request the shot using Uber's app will get a $10 " Wellness Pack," which includes a water bottle, tissues, hand sanitizer, lollipop, and recyclable trash can. They can also request up to 10 free shots from a nurse who will show up at their home or office. Last year, Uber teamed up with Boston Children's Hospital to offer flu shots for a day in Boston, New York, Washington, and Chicago. That effort was so successful, the company is planning to do the same in more cities this year. The CDC recommends flu shots for everyone six months and older, but only 50% of adults get them, according to a press release.

– Michelle Hui was devastated when she had a miscarriage six weeks into her pregnancy. But 10 days later, when she went back to the hospital to have a final procedure to clear her uterus, doctors discovered she was actually pregnant with twins—and one of those twins had survived both the miscarriage and the abortion, the Mirror reports. Hui, 31, had taken the abortion pill mifepristone to make sure nothing was left behind to cause infection, but a pregnancy test revealed that blood clots had remained in her uterus and doctors deemed her dead. So Hui took a pregnancy test that revealed the pregnancy and was sent to the hospital for a surgical procedure to remove the uterus' contents. But 10 days after her miscarriage, doctors found Megan's heartbeat on a scan. "They said that with all the blood and clots it must have created shadows so they couldn't see her," Hui says. "I couldn't believe it. Neither could the doctors. But as happy as I was, I was angry they had missed her on the scans." Hui gave birth to Megan on Feb. 25 at 18 weeks. She weighed under 6 pounds and now has a 4-year-old sister and a 2-year-old brother. "She is just a big healthy pudding of a baby

– The US has officially recognized the newly-formed Syrian opposition coalition as the "legitimate representative" of the Syrian people, President Obama announced in an ABC News interview today. "It's a big step," he said of the move, which follows Britain and the European Union's recognition of the coalition last month. But the US won't be sending weapons to the coalition, and Obama made clear that the US won't be supporting extremist groups that seek to overthrow Bashar al-Assad. "Not everybody who's participating on the ground in fighting Assad are people who we are comfortable with," he said. "There are some who, I think, have adopted an extremist agenda, an anti-US agenda, and we are going to make clear to distinguish between those elements." The US had been holding off on formally recognizing the coalition because it wanted to encourage it to form a more inclusive government, notes the New York Times.

In a video posted to Facebook Wednesday, a man identified as Kino Jimenez can be seen in the video throwing a drink at a group of teens and yelling a racial slur. In a statement to Business Insider, Whataburger says it was "shocked" to see the video and "certainly don't condone this type of customer behavior in our restaurants." The San Antonio Police Department says Jimenez, 30, was arrested at his home Thursday and charged with theft. In the video, the man can be seen taking the hat from Hunter Richard and throwing it in his face. The teen's mother, Patricia Spittler, posted the video to Facebook asking for help identifying the "scum bag of the year." "His friend was wearing a patriotic hat, and this happened!" she wrote. "It would be nice to know who he is for someone to let him know his actions are not okay! Real tough guy ... approaches a group of teenagers minding their own business just having a burger! The US Marshals Service reports that 59-year-old James Robert Jones was arrested Thursday morning when he showed up for work in Pompano Beach. Jones had been listed as one of the US Army's 15 Most Wanted for escaping from a federal prison in Fort Leavenworth, Kan., in 1977. As a private in 1974, Jones was sentenced to 23 years in prison for premeditated murder and aggravated assault. Authorities say Jones obtained a fraudulent Florida driver's license in 1981 and used the name Bruce Walter Keith. He had been living at a home in Deerfield Beach since at least 2005. In January, the Army requested assistance from the US Marshals Service in finding Jones. In January, Army investigators, believing Jones to now be living in Florida, contacted the US Marshals' office for assistance. Marshals ran a prison photo of Jones through a database, and it matched closely with the photo on a Florida driver's license first issued in 1981. Authorities began observing the man they thought to be Jones, now living under the false name Bruce Keith, and on Thursday morning, arrested him outside his work location in nearby Pompano Beach. "It is in our national security interest to stop the use of chemical weapons by the Syrian regime," Trump said in a statement issued early Friday. "The regime's use of chemical weapons against its own people has no place in the 21st century." He said the strike was in response to Tuesday's chemical attack, which killed dozens of people, including many children. The strike hit the Shayrat air base southeast of Homs, a small installation with two runways, where aircraft often take off to bomb targets in northern and central Syria, the AP reports. The Syrian military says at least seven people were killed and nine wounded in the missile strike. The British-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, an opposition monitor, also put the death toll at seven, including a general and three soldiers. The Kremlin said President Vladimir Putin believes the US strike is an "aggression against a sovereign state in violation of international law." – Last year, a janitor for San Francisco's Bay Area Rapid Transit raked in $271,000 in salary, overtime, and benefits, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. Now, KTVU has obtained surveillance video that shows Liang Zhao Zhang entering a storage closet at the Powell Street station multiple times a day for hours at a time. – President-elect Donald Trump has announced that he will nominate attorney David Friedman as US ambassador to Israel, selecting an envoy who supports Israeli settlements and other changes to US policies in the region, the AP reports. Friedman said he looked forward to carrying out his duties from "the US embassy in Israel's eternal capital, Jerusalem." Friedman, who has no diplomatic experience, has said that he does not believe it would be illegal for Israel to annex the occupied West Bank and he supports building new settlements there, which Washington has long condemned as illegitimate and an obstacle to peace. Lee is also accused of giving millions to the daughter of Choi's friend to help her equestrian career.

– The White House has walked back President Trump's statement that he won't sign a bipartisan immigration bill set for a House vote next week, Politico reports. According to the Washington Post, White House spokesman Raj Shah said Friday that Trump misunderstood a question he was asked on Fox & Friends Friday morning, when he said he wouldn't sign a "moderate" immigration bill. Shah says the president "fully supports" both the House leadership bill and a conservative DACA plan that's expected to fail next week. Trump's apparent embrace of the bill is a boon to House leaders hoping to pass the text next week. Conservatives need the president to give them cover to vote for a bill that includes a pathway to citizenship for young undocumented immigrants who came to the US as children. But Trump's apparent criticism Friday morning would have led to an embarrassing spectacle in which only a few dozen lawmakers supported the plan, some leadership sources speculated. Trump's earlier comments Friday might still spook skittish lawmakers, making passage difficult. The president has big-footed senior White House officials before, catching them off-guard and reversing official White House positions without so much as a warning. Republicans will spend all next week fretting about a repeat of such a situation.

– A consumer advocacy group says two fidget spinners sold at Target have "extremely high levels of lead" and should be taken off shelves, CBS News reports. US Public Interest Research Group tested 12 fidget spinners found in children's toy aisles at Target stores across the country and found two of them contained levels reaching 33,000 parts per million. That's 300 times higher than the legal limit for children's products. "They should take these toys off the shelves," says US PIRG's toxics program director. "The reason that lead is a large concern—especially in children's products—is that when children are exposed to high levels of lead they can experience things like memory loss, learning disabilities." US PIRG tested for 33,000 ppm of lead in the center circle of the "Fidget Wild Premium Spinner Brass" and 22,000 ppm of lead in the arm of the "Fidget Wild Premium Spinner Metal." The fidget spinners are marked for ages 14 and up, but Target and manufacturer Bulls-i-Toy say the products aren't required to meet children's product standards. "The products in question are clearly labeled 'ages 14+' ... there are no mandatory CPSC (Consumer Product Safety Commission) requirements for it," the company says.

Haig's death was announced by the White House, and he will be laid to rest in Washington on Sunday, reports the AP.

– A new survey from PayScale finds that women make 79% of what men do in a year for the same full-time job, the New York Times reports. And that's not counting part-time work and hours. The survey of 1.4 million full-time employees found that women make only 81% of what men do in a year for the same full-time job in the US. And that's not even taking into account part-time work and hours. The survey also found that women make less in every industry and job, and even in areas where one might think the gap would be nonexistent. "It's not really a wage gap, it's a jobs gap," PayScale's lead economist tells Bloomberg. The president of the Institute for Women's Policy Research says the gap isn't due to women taking time off to have kids and returning to work with less specialized skills. Instead, she says, it's because female-dominated jobs, like teaching and nursing, tend to be less specialized, so they don't demand the string of promotions and pay premiums that firms typically use to keep their best performers around. Meanwhile, the wage gap is highest between married men with children and married women with children. The Times

"It was my fault. I should have looked at those guys working, and I didn't," Ronald Wagenhoffer said in the video. "When I saw it was too late. I should have parked my truck and went over there, but I didn't. I'm sorry." Wagenhoffer, 52, was found dead of an apparent suicide Wednesday night less than a mile from his home. In the video, Wagenhoffer says he couldn't sleep and blamed himself for the tragedy. "This man did nothing wrong," says the deputy mayor. "The department did what it was supposed to do under the code that existed at the time." But the mayor's press secretary has disputed the video's authenticity. "NBC10 falsely stated that L&I inspector said of collapse—'It was my fault.' That is a total lie," he tweeted. "We have seen the video. We are standing behind our journalism."

Medicaid expansion will proceed in Virginia, one of the latest states to accept that option. But Republicans, still stinging from their loss of the House in the midterm elections, are facing a fresh political quandary after US District Judge Reed O'Connor said the entire 2010 health law was invalid. – BP's board is considering suspending payment of the company's next dividend, sources tell the New York Times, as the company searches for a way to satisfy President Obama and the US government. The board is looking at three options:  suspending payment of the dividend for two quarters, paying the dividend in bonus shares, or escrowing the amount of the dividend while paying for the cleanup. Obama is expected to outline in his speech a plan to legally compel BP to create an account to compensate businesses and individuals for their losses from the oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico. The company's $10.5 billion annual dividend has become a point of contention as President Obama has said BP should not be paying stockholders when fishermen, oil workers, and small business owners are saying they cannot get the company to pay their loss claims. BP has said it does not expect to announce decisions about its dividend until after its chairman and chief executive speak with Obama at a meeting he has called for midweek. The visit is part of a week of activities intended to convey presidential command of a crisis that continues to test both the government and BP, which said yesterday that its costs of responding to the spill had risen to $1.6 billion.

The vote was sparked by 24-year-old Stella Harville and 28-year-old Ticha Chikuni, who plan to marry in July. "In addition to communicating the contents of one's mind, like specific thoughts and beliefs, a person's speech conveys their fundamental capacity to think—the capacity for reasoning, thoughtfulness, and intellect," says lead researcher Professor Nicholas Epley, per Phys.org. "When conveying intelligence, it's important for one's voice to be heard—literally." In an initial experiment, a separate group of evaluators judged a short pitch created by MBA student job candidates. – UCLA geochemists say they've found evidence of life on Earth some 400 million years earlier than previously thought—and 300 million years earlier than previously believed. The findings suggest that life may have started on the planet about 4.1 billion years ago, after it formed 4.54 billion years ago, the Los Angeles Times reports. "Twenty years ago, this would have been heretical; finding evidence of life 3.8 billion years ago was shocking," says Mark Harrison, a co-author of the study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. "Life on Earth may have started almost instantaneously." The findings are based on the analysis of 10,000 ancient zircons found in Western Australia. Zircons are heavy, durable minerals that can serve as time capsules, Reuters reports. They were formed from molten rocks, and the researchers believe one found in Western Australia contains a carbon deposit that is 4.1 billion years old, give or take 10 million years. "Its complete encasement in crack-free, undisturbed zircon demonstrates that it is not contamination from more recent geologic processes," the researchers say. "Its 12 C-rich isotopic signature may be evidence for the origin of life on Earth by 4.1 Ga." (Click to read about how life on Mars may have started earlier than thought.

– Bradley Manning's alleged accomplices include a number of MIT students and at least one other Boston-area resident, Army officials tell the Boston Globe. “These are people that knew him and might know things about what he may have done,” says a Pentagon official. The Globe spoke to Adrian Lamo, a former hacker who exchanged emails with Manning and later turned him in. Lamo, who was convicted of hacking into the computer system of the New York Times in 2003, says Manning was motivated by ideology and by his access to Julian Assange. “He was opposed to what he saw happening on the ground in Iraq and, and I think WikiLeaks played on his ego,” Lamo says. “He had access to a special server that allowed his leaks jumped to the top of the queue. I think he was made to feel special.’’ Lamo says he knows people who work for WikiLeaks, but he has never met or corresponded with Assange. “It’s impossible to be in this community and not know people in WikiLeaks,’’ he tells the Globe.

– If you're one of the 465,000 people in the US who have pacemakers, the FDA has issued a warning that they're at risk of being hacked. Abbott, which makes pacemakers under the St. Jude Medical brand, says there's a "risk of patient harm due to potential exploitation of cybersecurity vulnerabilities," and it's issuing a software update to the devices, the Wall Street Journal reports. The company says the update, which will be pre-loaded in the pacemakers, will make the devices more secure and "essential, life-sustaining features" will remain available. The FDA says there are no known cases of patient harm caused by the vulnerabilities, and Abbott says replacement pacemakers aren't recommended. But a study published last month by Johns Hopkins researchers found that third-party programmers were able to remotely access pacemakers, and that doctors' monitoring systems didn't require log-in names and passwords when the devices connect to them, Ars Technica reports. The researchers also found unencrypted patients' data stored in the tools, including SSNs, names, phone numbers, and medical conditions. "It's still ideal to make cardiac devices more secure as cyberattacks become more common, elaborate, and sophisticated," Gizmodo states.

That's the question posed by two physicists and a food anthropologist in a paper published earlier this year in the journal arXiv, Live Science reports. Varlamov and Glatz traveled to Rome, where a pizzaiolo—an Italian for "dude who makes pizzas"—had a personal pie of tomato, mozzarella, and basil prepared and then baked in a brick oven heated to 625 degrees Fahrenheit. Under ideal conditions, the authors found that a Margherita pizza could be cooked to perfection in just two minutes in an electric oven. The authors found that a pizza cooked in an electric oven could achieve the same conditions by turning the heat down to 450 degrees F for 170 seconds. The authors determined that a pizza cooked in an electric oven could leave the oven longer, as the pizza will return more heat to the oven via evaporation. – Scientists have long debated what Dickinsonia is—a flattened, ribbed oval that can grow over four feet across and a distinct ridge down its center. Some have called it fungi, others protists, and now a new study in Science concludes that it was an animal. "This was already actually one of us," says study author Jochen Brocks of Australian National University. "It was an animal." Dickinsonia was found in the Ediacara hills in what is now South Australia around 570 million years ago, and it's one of the earliest life forms ever found. More than 50 types of Ediacarans are now known, and more than 50 types of Dickinsonia are believed to have existed. The new study focused on molecular biomarkers known as sterols. Animals make a version known as cholesterols, "like we find in chicken McNuggets," says Brocks. These chemical compounds actually play an important role in the membranes of the cells of virtually all animals, helping to regulate what goes in and out. "In this case, what you get is an average composition of the ecosystem that was living there," says lead author Ilya Bobrovskiy. – Gatorade is introducing a zero-sugar version of its classic sports drink in a bid to stay on top in a changing market. Bloomberg reports the 53-year-old brand, which accounts for more than 70% of the US sports drink market, saw sales fall  0.5% last year to $5.9 billion. "The same trends that emerged within soft drinks in the last decade are revealing themselves in the sports drink market," Pepsi CEO Indra Nooyi told analysts in April. "A growing number of consumers are moderating their sugar intake, and some don't want sugar at all." Gatorade Zero, which comes in orange, lemon lime, and glacier cherry flavors, is priced in line with the brand's classic drink. It's the first no-sugar product introduced in Gatorade's history. "We worry that Gatorade's artificial and sugary ingredient profile (plus lack of awareness on low-sugar versions) has caused its brand image to shift toward being less healthy than alternatives," Barclays analyst Lauren Lieberman said in an April research report. Gatorade Zero will take on Coca Cola's Powerade Zero for the first time. Coke launched Powerade Zero a decade ago, and it has been a bright spot in the sports hydration market.

– Gov. Rick Scott has declared a state of emergency in two Florida counties due to an algal bloom that's sickened swimmers, boaters, and beachgoers. The governor made the declaration in Martin and St. Lucie counties, citing "the inaction and negligence of the federal government not making the needed repairs to the Herbert Hoover Dike and Florida can no longer afford to wait," reports the Palm Beach Post. He's also calling on the federal government to "quickly approve permits for our dispersed water management programs," per a press release. The algae—which can cause rashes, vomiting, nausea, and abdominal pain—has been spreading from Lake Okeechobee to the St. Lucie and Caloosahatchee estuaries, where it's been found in local waterways. The governor's declaration allows the South Florida Water Management District to "store additional water north of Lake Okeechobee in the Kissimmee Chain of Lakes" and redirect it to address the problem, reports CNN. He's also asking the Florida Department of Environmental Protection and the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission to set up a hotline for residents to report algal blooms. The algae is caused by large amounts of water being dumped into the lake by the US Army Corps of Engineers, which blames mismanagement of the water system.

– The star of HGTV's Fixer Upper has reached a settlement with the Environmental Protection Agency over alleged violations of federal lead paint rules, the AP reports. The EPA says Magnolia did not comply with the rules, including getting certification from the EPA before performing renovations covered by the RRP Rule and providing homeowners or occupants with an approved pamphlet about lead-based paint hazards prior to the renovation. Magnolia says it has already taken steps to ensure compliance, including getting certification and training for its staff. The EPA says Magnolia will also host a video to discuss lead paint safety on social media.

– Margaret Thome Bekema was supposed to graduate from Catholic Central High School in Grand Rapids, Mich., in 1936. – Mike Dubke, President Trump's communications director for the past three months, has resigned, Axios reports. Dubke says he offered to stay through Trump's first foreign trip to ensure a smooth transition, but Trump accepted the resignation immediately. Dubke tells Politico that the reasons for his departure were "personal" but that "it has been my great honor to serve President Trump and this administration." Dubke, a veteran GOP strategist, joined Trump's campaign in 2015 and worked on his transition team. He joined the Trump administration as communications director in January and was named deputy chief of staff for social media earlier this year. Dubke's resignation comes as the White House considers a shakeup of its senior staff amid multiple scandals.

– Three-term incumbent Sen. Pat Roberts has fended off a Tea Party challenger in Kansas' GOP primary, reports the AP. It's the third time in four years that a GOP senator has defeated a Tea Party challenger, but this time it was Roberts himself who came out on top, 48% to 41%, reports Politico. Tea Party groups backed radiologist Milton Wolf, a distant cousin of President Obama, but he didn't have an easy time of it in the state's 1st Congressional District, which includes Kansas City. The National Republican Senatorial Committee played a big role in Roberts' win, sending six workers to the state in the final weeks to get out the vote. "Senator Roberts has served as a diligent check on Democrats’ push for ever expansive government and is a true conservative voice for our state," said his colleague, Sen. Jerry Moran, who chairs the NRSC. In another closely watched race, Tennessee's Lamar Alexander is expected to win the Republican nomination and thus avoid a 2016 primary challenge, reports the Hill.

– Michael Moore thinks it's wrong to support Julian Assange because of the rape allegations against him, but he's not backing down: "For those of you who think it’s wrong to support Julian Assange because of the sexual assault allegations he’s being held for, all I ask is that you not be naive about how the government works when it decides to go after its prey," he writes in his latest blog post. "Please—never, ever believe the 'official story,' despite the fact that Assange’s people have been caught lying—it turns out there is no such crime as 'sex by surprise' in Sweden as Assange’s lawyer Mark Stephens alleged, it is not worth a fine of $715 because it doesn’t exist, and there is also no Swedish law against having sex with a broken condom."
