– Wade Michael Page, the Army veteran who killed six Sikh temple members in Wisconsin on Sunday, was a neo-Nazi, a white supremacist, and a murderer, law enforcement sources tell the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. The sources say Page, who killed himself as a police officer closed in, was a long-time supporter of the KKK and other white supremacist groups. The sources say Page visited the white supremacist website KKK.com at least 20 times in the last two years. Page was a 40-year-old Army veteran of a special unit who had been fired from his job as a truck driver. He served in Fort Bragg, North Carolina, from 1992 to 1998, and was assigned to psychological operations, specialists who analyze, develop, and distribute intelligence. Page's stepmother says he was a "precious child" who grew up in a normal, loving family. "Where he changed and where this came from, we have no idea," she tells the Los Angeles Times. She says she last saw him three weeks ago, when he called her to say he had been fired from his truck job.

– A gunman opened fire at Los Angeles International Airport today, killing a TSA officer and wounding at least two other people, NBC Los Angeles reports. The shooter was shot multiple times by airport police and is in critical condition, the Los Angeles Times reports. Police have identified the alleged shooter as 23-year-old Paul Ciancia of Los Angeles, according to the AP. The slain TSA officer has been identified as 39-year-old Gerardo Hernandez, who was the first TSA employee killed in the line of duty in the agency's 12-year history. Two other people were injured, one of them critically. The gunman entered Terminal 3 this morning and opened fire on a TSA officer before being chased by police into restaurants near the terminal, law enforcement sources tell NBC Los Angeles. The mayor says the shooter had "more than 100 more rounds that could've literally killed everybody in that terminal today." The FAA has grounded all flights in and out of the airport.

– Lori Cichewicz always planned to have a child, but in 2008, her doctor found that her fallopian tubes were blocked and told her she didn't need to take birth control, the Detroit Free Press reports. Cichewicz went to get a permanent birth control procedure, but three years later she got pregnant and gave birth to a daughter with Down syndrome. Now Cichewicz, 50, is suing her doctor for "wrongful conception," which she says is basically negligence, WXYZ reports. "I'm older, I don't know, will I see her graduate college? Will I see her get married? Will I see her graduate high school? All this is going through my mind," Cichewicz says of her 5-year-old daughter, Reagan. "She's full of life, loving, kind, sweet, everything you could ever imagine," Cichewicz says. "I mean, I can't imagine life without her now. When they say having a child with special needs is a gift, it's a gift." A Michigan appeals court ruled this week that Cichewicz can seek financial damages for the emotional distress of knowing she would have a child with Down syndrome. "That's advice that misled Lori

– Uber is teaming up with Carnegie Mellon University to build a robotics research lab to develop a fleet of self-driving taxis, TechCrunch reports. Sources say the company has hired engineers from the university's Robotics Institute, including lead engineering and commercialization experts. The partnership will also include funding from Uber for faculty chairs and graduate fellowships, recognizing and supporting Carnegie Mellon's world-renowned faculty, and attracting the best and brightest graduate students. "As a global leader in urban transportation, we have the unique opportunity to invest in leading edge technologies to enable the safe and efficient movement of people and things at giant scale," Uber's chief product officer said in a blog post. "This collaboration and the creation of the Uber Advanced Technologies Center represent an important investment in building for the long term of Uber." But not everyone is excited about the partnership. "Finding new sources of capital shouldn’t be too difficult in Silicon Valley, but there’s no good substitute for Google Maps—MapQuest and Apple Maps are crap," writes Adam Clark Estes at Gizmodo. "And playing catch-up on self-driving vehicle tech won’t be easy for Uber, either."

– Three crocodiles that can grow to 18 feet long and weigh as much as a small car have been captured near Miami and confirmed to be invasive species in the wild, the Miami Herald reports. "They didn't swim from Africa," University of Florida herpetologist Kenneth Krysko tells the Herald. "But we really don't know how they got into the wild." According to a study published in the Journal of Herpetological Conservation and Biology, the crocodiles were captured between 2000 and 2014. Researchers believe they were brought to Florida illegally by an unlicensed reptile collector who either didn't contain them properly or planted them in the Everglades in an attempt to multiply. "My hope as a biologist is that the introduction of Nile crocodiles in Florida opens everyone's eyes to the problem of invasive species that we have here in our state," Krysko tells the Herald. "Now here's another one, but this time it isn't just a tiny house from Africa." The Nile crocodile—which can be found in sub-Saharan Africa where it's believed to be responsible for at least 480 attacks on people and 123 fatalities between 2010 and 2014—can survive in Florida and may even thrive there, the study states. – The refrigerated train carrying the bodies of the victims of Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 arrived in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv this morning, after being held up at the crash site for five days. A government spokesman says Ukraine "will do our best" to send the bodies to the Netherlands, the AP reports. Of the 298 people who died aboard the Amsterdam-to-Kuala Lumpur flight, 193 were Dutch citizens. The crash site itself, in farmland held by the pro-Russian separatists who the West accuses of shooting down the plane, remained unsecured five days after the disaster—another source of frustration for officials around the world eager to establish the facts of the case. In some places, the smell of decay and flies suggested the presence of remains under the wreckage, and observers said Monday that not all bodies had been recovered. British Prime Minister David Cameron said Monday that the jet's destruction on Thursday has drastically changed the situation, and that the Russians cannot expect continued access to European markets and capital if they continued to fuel a war against another European country. Lithuanian Foreign Minister Linas Linkevicius blamed "terrorists supplied by Moscow" for shooting down the airliner, killing all aboard. He said he hoped the EU will impose more sanctions in response to the disaster

– The House intelligence committee has voted to release a Democratic rebuttal to a GOP memo on the Russia investigation, the AP reports. The panel vote was unanimous to make the classified Democratic document public. It now goes to President Trump for a five-day review, and he will decide whether to allow its release—as he did with the Republican document last week. The Democratic document aims to counter the Republican document, which accused the FBI and Justice Department of abusing their authority in monitoring a onetime Trump campaign associate. A White House spokesman says Trump will "consider" the Democratic memo's release the same way he considered the Republican document. Politico reports the panel rejected a request to release their rebuttal memo when the GOP-led House Intelligence Committee meets late Monday afternoon. The committee rejected that move last week. Rep. Adam Schiff, the top Democrat on the House intelligence panel, responded to Trump on Twitter Monday after the president called him one of the "biggest liars and leakers in Washington." Says Schiff: "Mr. President, I see you've had a busy morning of 'Executive Time.' Instead of tweeting false smears, the American people would appreciate it if you turned off the TV and helped solve the funding crisis, protected Dreamers or ... really anything else

– Police are investigating after swastikas were found etched onto the faces of two New York City subway riders on Saturday, the New York Times reports. "Jews are a virus" and "Hitler is a dog" were written on the faces of two men, identified only as Nied and Locke. "I've never seen so many people simultaneously reach into their bags and pockets looking for tissues and Purell," Locke wrote in a Facebook post about the incident. "Within about two minutes, all the Nazi symbolism was gone." Nied, a sous-chef, says he asked if anyone had hand sanitizer. "A light bulb went on, and I just asked, 'Does anyone have hand sanitizer?'" he tells the Times. Locke, who took photos of the incident, says he returned a bottle of hand sanitizer to one of the riders, apologizing for having used most of it. "We sat down and glanced around at each other and settled back into the commute," he tells the Times. "I understand the criticism, but unfortunately, I don't have an answer for it." In Chicago, a synagogue was vandalized with swastikas early Saturday, the Chicago Tribune reports. Police are investigating as a hate crime.

– A Facebook board member has apologized for apparently supporting "Internet colonialism" in a series of tweets after India banned Facebook's Internet access program, the Wall Street Journal reports. After India's telecom regulatory authority banned Facebook's "Free Basics" Internet access program Monday, Marc Andreessen tweeted: "Anti-colonialism has been economically catastrophic for the Indian people for decades. Why stop now?" According to Quartz, Andreessen went on to call the ban "morally wrong" and say he was withdrawing his comments "in full and without reservation." Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg responded to Andreessen's tweets Wednesday, saying the comments were "deeply upsetting" and that they "do not represent the way Facebook or I think at all." A Facebook spokesperson also said the company "strongly rejects the sentiments expressed by Marc Andreessen last night regarding India." The Free Basics Internet access program was introduced by Facebook and other tech companies to bring the Internet to areas of India where it wasn't available. It was banned after India's telecom regulator found that Facebook was violating net neutrality principles by picking which websites people could access for free. "Anti-colonialism has been economically catastrophic for the Indian people for decades. Why stop now?" Business Insider quotes Andreessen.

– At least one country will leave the euro area this year, according to the Center for Economics and Business Research. “It now looks as though 2012 will be the year when the euro starts to break up,” the London-based CEBR said in a statement. “It is not a done deal yet—we are only forecasting a 60% probability—but our forecast is that by the end of the year at least one country (and probably more) will leave.” CEBR says the likelihood of a euro breakup in the next decade has increased to 99%. European leaders return to work this week seeking to buy time for the Spanish and Italian governments to wrest control over their debt and rescue the euro from fragmentation in its 10th anniversary year. Ten years after euro bank notes replaced national currencies on Jan. 1, 2002, the euro has for the first time recorded two consecutive annual losses against the US dollar while plunging to a record low against the yen. That raises the pressure on leaders as they struggle to hold the monetary union together in the face of credit downgrades, European Union splits, and a looming recession that might compound rising debt. The crisis may force “most of the French and German banking systems” to seek bailouts to compensate for writedowns on their holdings of sovereign debt,

– For the first time in eight years, not a single woman was included on Forbes' list of the 100 highest-paid athletes in the world, NBC News reports. The list, released Tuesday, shows Floyd Mayweather as the highest-paid boxer with $275 million in earnings in 2018. NBA players make up a majority of the list, followed by football and baseball players. But the list also contains a notable first: Serena Williams, who had a baby last year, didn't make the list. She was the top-earning female athlete in 2018 at $18 million, but fell nearly $5 million short of the $22.9 million cutoff for the top 100. "This is very sad.... and ppl say we are winning the war on equality, opportunity, and there is no such thing as a pay gap," tweeted tennis legend Billie Jean King. "Hopefully [gender inequity] can become a global conversation so we can hold people accountable, and we can create change."

On Monday, she received her birth record in the mail from the Ohio Department of Health, including her mother's name— Francine Simmons. "It's just amazing that all this time we're thinking about her and trying to find her and she was trying to find us, too," says Mitchell-Clark's sister, Maisha Cummings. The two women live just six minutes apart, but "we've got a bigger extended family where we can just be together," says Simmons. The 32-year-old immigrant from El Salvador, who pleaded guilty to sexually assaulting his female roommate in 2014, will be sentenced to three years in state prison under a deal overseen by Judge Aaron Persky, who is facing a recall campaign in the wake of the Stanford case, the Guardian reports. Persky oversaw the sentencing of Ramirez, who pleaded guilty to a felony of sexual penetration by force, and the assistant district attorney says the judge agreed with prosecutors that Ramirez should receive a state prison sentence. Ramirez, who has no criminal record, had his bail set at $200,000—significantly higher than the $150,000 set for Turner, who was convicted of assault with intent to commit rape of an intoxicated woman, sexually penetrating an intoxicated person with a foreign object, and sexually penetrating an unconscious person with a foreign object. Court documents show that Ramirez had a very different experience in court than Turner, who was convicted of assault with intent to commit rape of an intoxicated woman, sexually penetrating an intoxicated person with a foreign object, and sexually penetrating an unconscious person with a foreign object. – Vicki Gardner, the third victim and sole survivor of yesterday's on-air shootings in Virginia, is in stable condition in the hospital, NBC News reports. The Smith Mountain Lake Regional Chamber of Commerce executive director was shot in the chest during an interview and went through emergency surgery. "She's doing pretty well," her husband, Tim, tells the Roanoke Times. "She's got a gunshot wound to her chest, but she's doing pretty well." Alison Parker and Adam Ward, both of WDBJ-TV, were being interviewed at Bridgewater Plaza, a shopping center near the resort town of Smith Mountain Lake, when shots rang out. Police say gunman Vester Lee Flanagan, who died after being taken to the hospital, was wearing a wig, six magazines of ammunition, a to-do list, 17 stamped letters, and a briefcase with three license plates in his rental car, according to a search warrant.

– Nevada is the land of slots and casinos, but it's also the home of the world's biggest public pension fund. That's because the state's pension funds—with $35 billion to its name—have for the last two years been investing all their money in stocks and bonds that track market indexes, the New York Times reports. That's a big change for a fund that used to be heavily invested in index funds that tried to beat the market. But the state's chief investment officer, Steve Edmundson, and his predecessor, Ken Lambert, say they've found that index funds aren't the answer. "You have to trade active managers," Lambert tells the Times. "Not only do you have to believe that they can beat the market, but you must spend time hiring and firing them." The state's pension funds have saved $4 million in fees per year thanks to the change, and Edmundson says they're confident they'll save even more in the long run. "If we are freaking out about what is happening tomorrow or what happened last quarter, then we're not doing our jobs," he says.

Rasmussen is one of two editors of the Royal Shakespeare Company's edition of Shakespeare's complete works, and he and Jonathan Bate have just announced that they're convinced that Shakespeare is the author of the 1602 Additional Passages to The Spanish Tragedy. They're citing a 2012 article in the History of the Bard journal that cited linguistic patterns that suggested the passage was written by Shakespeare himself, and they're planning to include it in their new edition of Shakespeare's complete works coming out in November. "We don't have any absolute proof, but this is as close as you can get," says Rasmussen. "It has his fingerprints all over it." The Additional Passages were added more than a decade after Christopher Kyd wrote the original, and they include a "Hamlet-like scene of a grief-maddened father discoursing on the death of his son," reports the New York Times. – President Trump says he's looking at the possibility of meeting with Vladimir Putin in July, and the White House says national security adviser John Bolton will be in Moscow next week to discuss the possibility. The meeting would come just before or after the NATO summit in Brussels on July 11 and 12, and it's not clear whether it would take place as planned or after the summit, Politico reports. The White House says Bolton will meet with US allies in London and Rome to discuss "national security issues" during his visit to Moscow. The timing of Trump's trip to Russia—he's scheduled to visit Britain on July 13 and then visit Moscow on July 15—could be awkward, given that the NATO summit will be held just two days after the World Cup final in Russia's Luzhniki Stadium. "This is really what Putin sees as the benefit of the 2016 presidential election. He is out of isolation. He is an equal," says Heather Conley of the Center for Strategic and International Studies. "Russia and the United States will be seen as equals at the summit and that is exactly what President Putin desires."

– A gunman opened fire at a New York City hospital Friday, killing a woman and wounding at least six other people before killing himself, law enforcement officials tell CNN. The shooter was identified as Dr. Henry Bello, who previously worked at the Bronx-Lebanon Hospital, two law enforcement officials tell CNN. Police officers found the gunman, who was wearing a white lab coat and carrying ID, dead on the hospital's 17th floor. He died of what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound, New York City Police Commissioner James O'Neill said at a news briefing. The body of a woman who was shot was found near his body, O'Neill said. Six people were wounded on the 16th floor, and five of those are in serious condition from gunshot wounds, O'Neill said.

The forms allow public officials to list their assets in broad ranges, the AP reports, so it's not clear exactly how much the couple is worth. Most of the president's income came from royalties from his three books—Dreams From My Father, The Audacity of Hope, and Of Thee I Sing—which totaled between $70,000 and $165,000 last year, down from $250,000 to $2.1 million in 2011. The forms also show the largest jointly owned assets by the president and the first lady were Treasury notes worth between $1 million and $5 million. While the value of their assets is certainly higher than that of most Americans, their mix reflects the financial demands of a 50-something couple with two daughters. Their assets include Vanguard retirement funds and college savings plans. The Obamas also have a 30-year mortgage on their Chicago home worth between $500,000 and $1 million with an interest rate of 5.6%. – Marcia Strassman, who played Gabe Kaplan's wife, Julie, on the 1970s sitcom Welcome Back, Kotter, has died. She was 66. Strassman died at her Sherman Oaks, Calif., home on Friday after battling breast cancer for seven years, her sister, Julie Strassman, said Sunday. "They gave her 2 12 years to live but she lasted much longer," she said. "She was very courageous." Strassman had numerous roles on television and in film during her five-decade career. She played nurse Margie Cutler on the first season of M.A.S.H. before her breakout role in Welcome Back, Kotter. The show was about a teacher returning to the tough high-school of his youth to teach a classroom full of misfits, including future movie star John Travolta. She also played Rick Moranis' wife in the Disney hit movie Honey I Shrunk the Kids and its sequel, Honey I Blew Up the Kids. Strassman was active in fundraising for various progressive and social causes, including breast cancer research and treatment even before she was diagnosed, her sister said. – The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences has promised to double the number of women and minorities in its ranks by 2020. But the Los Angeles Times reports that four years later, the organization's membership is still overwhelmingly white: 91% white and 76% male. Blacks are up from 2% in 2012 to 3% today; Asians are up from 2% to 2%; and Latinos are up from 2% to 2%. The academy has invited more women and minority members over the last four years, but with its 6,261 voting members appointed for life, the organization's ranks were on track to remain overwhelmingly white and male for decades. Under fire for nominating an all-white slate of actors for two years in a row, the academy last month vowed to double the number of women and minority members by 2020. It also adopted controversial new rules that will allow it to take away voting rights from inactive members. "Our goal is to make sure that we are active in bringing in different voices regardless of gender or race or sexual orientation," academy President Cheryl Boone Isaacs says. Mashable reports on the newest addition to the "Dabbin" dance craze: the "Dab on them folks" or "Dab on them dabbing" celebration, in which a person places their head into the bent crook of an arm while raising the opposite arm out straight. The move has been used by everyone from Justin Bieber to Jay-Z to James Corden, and it's been used by everyone from Hillary Clinton to the president of Kenya. It all started in the Atlanta hip-hop scene in the 2010s, according to the Verge, with artists such as Migos and Skippa Da Flippa being mentioned as possible dab originators. American rapper Bow Wow claimed to have invented the dance in 2012 but was met with backlash from other rappers who said they didn't even know how to do it, according to the Huffington Post. – Joy Covey, who rose to prominence as chief financial officer of Amazon.com at the time of its IPO, was killed on her bike in California on Wednesday. The 50-year-old was riding in Woodside when she was hit by a van that turned in front of her, the San Jose Mercury News reports. Covey, who was the treasurer of the Natural Resources Defense Council, served as a director of the group. In an interview with Harvard Business School last year, Covey said that in the tech world, "it's easy for talented people—whatever their gender, age, or race—to rise up and succeed. In fact, in my career, during the time I spent working in larger companies or, for a brief time, at an East Coast company, age would have been more of an impediment than gender." "But on the West Coast, in high tech, people simply wanted to find the most talented person," she continued. "And someone who was a young, really energetic person was viewed as an ideal candidate."

– Facebook's IPO didn't quite live up to expectations today, with shares closing at $38.23 on the Nasdaq, about 23 cents below the IPO price, reports MarketWatch. The company raised $18.4 billion with the sale of 421.2 million shares, which values the company at $100 billion. It's the second-largest IPO in US history, notes the Wall Street Journal, but investors and analysts weren't exactly blown away by the performance. "Facebook debuted at a inopportune time, as the recent stock market swoon clearly pressured the shares," said one IPO analyst. "Had the company gone public a couple of weeks earlier, first day performance would likely have been much better."

– The trial of two Americans arrested last year on suspicion of crossing the border from Iraq to Iran has been delayed, reports Reuters. A spokesman for Iran's judiciary says the trial of Shane Bauer and Josh Fattal has been pushed back to next week because of the absence of a third American arrested with them, Sarah Shourd. "Due to the absence of the third person, the court has delayed the trial time so that in between this time the third person can return to Iran or, in the event of her refusal to appear, her case be dealt with differently," said the judiciary spokesman. The delay comes as the US and other powers are trying to prod Iran to return to talks about its nuclear activities, which they fear are aimed at making an atomic bomb. Iran, which says its nuclear ambitions are peaceful, has said it is ready to restart the talks which stalled last year, but has yet to agree a date and has even suggested the talks should not address the nuclear issue.

– The Panama Papers have revealed the offshore holdings of many of the world's richest people, but it's China's elite that are taking the biggest hit. The Guardian reports that eight members of the country's top political body, the politburo standing committee, have been linked to offshore companies set up by law firm Mossack Fonseca. Among them is Xi Jinping's granddaughter, Jasmine Li, who became the sole shareholder in two British Virgin Islands companies when she was just a teenager. The company was set up by Li's grandfather, Jia Qinglin, who was at the time China's fourth-ranked politician, the BBC reports. Other members of the politburo linked to the offshore companies include the son-in-law of Zhang Gaoli, another member of the politburo standing committee, and the daughter of Li Peng, who oversaw the Tiananmen Square crackdown. Chinese censors have been blocking coverage of the scandal on social media, and some media outlets including CNN say parts of their websites have been blocked, the Guardian reports. – Police in Mexico found 513 migrants crammed into two trailer trucks bound for the US—some suffering from dehydration after hours clinging to cargo ropes strung inside the containers to keep them upright, the AP reports. The trucks had air holes punched in the tops of the containers, but migrants interviewed at the state prosecutors' office said they lacked air and water. The trucks were bound for the central city of Puebla, where the migrants said they had been told they would be loaded aboard a second set of vehicles for the trip to the US border. "We were suffering, it was very hot and we were clinging to the ropes," said a 23-year-old Honduran migrant who identified himself only by his first name, for security reasons. Mexico's National Human Rights Commission says thousands of undocumented migrants are kidnapped and held for ransom by drug gangs in Mexico each year. None of the migrants would say whether any drug gang had been involved in the mass smuggling scheme broken up early Tuesday when Chiapas state police discovered the migrants while using X-ray equipment on the trucks at a checkpoint in the outskirts of city Tuxtla Gutierrez. The migrants said the smugglers were charging them about $7,000 apiece to get them into the US. An agent for the National Immigration Institute who was not authorized to be quoted

– When Oklahoma mom Coty Vincent went to the Enterprise Rent-A-Car in Tulsa last week to pick up her 11-month-old twins, she didn't have a double stroller with her. So she asked 25-year-old employee John Goodlett if he could help her out. "He grabbed one of the boys out of his car seat and I grabbed the other and we went inside," she tells Today. Instead, Goodlett headed straight for the counter and began processing her order. "So I kind of moseyed on over to where he was working, playing with one son while he had the other one," Vincent says. "He was working away, holding him like a champ, like he’s done it his whole life. I can’t even multitask that good." That's when Vincent snapped a photo of Goodlett holding one of the boys and posted it to Facebook. "While he helped me with my rental due to a hit-and-run accident, he held one of my twin sons as I don't have a double stroller," she wrote in the caption. "One of the most compassionate and caring people I've ever met. We need more people like John who go that extra step. Be a John."

Benavidez, a third-grade teacher, was about to give birth in the car when a car pulled up behind her. The driver told Trooper Miguel Rincon that her granddaughter was about to give birth and that they needed an ambulance. But the baby couldn't wait. Benavidez gave birth in the car. – If you're a football fan, you can now buy a stake in one of your favorite players. A new company called Fantex has announced a deal with Houston Texans running back Arian Foster in which fans will receive stock linked to his future earnings, the New York Times reports. Fantex will pay Foster $10 million in stock upon consummation of the deal, and he'll also receive 20% of his future earnings. "Fantex represents a powerful new opportunity for professional athletes, and I wish it were available during my playing days," says former Denver Broncos quarterback John Elway, a member of Fantex's board. But if you're worried about losing your money, you're not alone. "You are potentially one hit away from losing your money," a sports management professor tells the Times. "On any given Sunday, anything can happen to any player."

– Melania Trump's parents became US citizens Thursday in a private ceremony in New York City, the AP reports. Immigration lawyer Michael Wildes says Viktor and Amalija Knavs, originally from Slovenia, have lived in the US for more than a decade and gained permanent legal residency during that time. Wildes says the couple "have travailed a wonderful journey like millions have, in getting citizenship and waiting the requisite period of time." He says the Knavses "are very grateful and appreciative of this wonderful day for their family." A source tells CNN that Melania Trump sponsored her parents for their green cards, a status that allowed them to live and work in the US indefinitely and paved the way for citizenship. The White House declined to comment on the Knavses' new citizenship status, saying they were "not part of the administration and deserve privacy." The Knavses are "very grateful and appreciative of this wonderful day for their family," Wildes says.

– CIA chief John Brennan defended the agency's use of waterboarding and other "enhanced interrogation" techniques at a news conference today, saying they provided vital intelligence that helped kill Osama bin Laden. But he also admitted that some CIA personnel used techniques that "had not been authorized, were abhorrent, and rightly should be repudiated by all," reports the New York Times. The CIA "did a lot of things right during this difficult time to keep this country safe and secure," he said. "They did what they were asked to do in the service of our nation." At another point, he said, "There is a lot of exaggeration, misrepresentation of the facts, and therefore I think certain agendas are being pursued." He declined to say whether he supported the release of the Senate report, notes Politico. "I think there is more than enough transparency that has happened over the last couple of days. I think it's over the top."

– CNN'sParker Spitzer has been axed after four months on the air and replaced with an ensemble show called In the Arena. Co-host Kathleen Parker has left the show, and Eliot Spitzer will stay on as host, reports the New York Times. The show was never able to gain much traction in the ratings, and Parker says she is returning to her syndicated newspaper column “to focus more on my syndicated newspaper column and other writings.” It's not clear what role, if any, Parker will have with the show.

– It's been a brutal winter in the northern hemisphere, with record low temperatures in many parts of the US and Canada. In the UK, meanwhile, things have gotten so bad that climate experts are blaming global warming. "We are being asked to commit ourselves to the wilful stupidity of extrapolating a long-term trend from a single event," writes Martyn Brown in the Express. "It has clearly made a calculated decision in recent months that climate scepticism plays to its readership—and therefore shifts papers—just as the daily drip-feed of conspiracy theories about Princess Diana and Madeleine McCann has done in the past." At the Guardian, Andrew Revkin sees it as "as predictable a feature of the British winter as log fires and roasting chestnuts: a national outpouring of idiocy."

– Chelsea Manning's first public appearance since she was released from prison in May is here. The 29-year-old, who was sentenced to 35 years in prison for passing classified documents to WikiLeaks, appears on the cover of Vogue's 125th anniversary September issue in a red swimsuit by photographer Annie Leibovitz, the Guardian reports. " guess this is what freedom looks like," Manning tweeted alongside the photo. In an interview with the magazine, Manning says she decided to enter the military in the hope that it would help her "figure [herself] out." "I think it's important to remember that when somebody sees government wrongdoing—whether it's illegal or immoral or unethical—there isn't the means available to do something about it," she says. "Everyone keeps saying: 'You should have gone through the proper channels!' But the proper channels don't work." Manning is the first transgender woman to appear on the cover of a major fashion magazine. French Vogue featured a trans woman on the cover of its March issue, the first time a trans woman has done so.

– The bittersweet romantic musical Once was the big winner at the Tony Awards last night, taking home eight awards, including best new musical. The musical is based on the 2006 documentary-style 2006 film about an unlikely love affair between a Czech flower seller and an Irish street musician in Dublin. Both the film and musical use songs by Marketa Irglova and Glen Hansard, including the sublime, 2007 Oscar-winning song, "Falling Slowly." It stars Steve Kazee and Cristin Milioti. It beat out Newsies, 'Nice Work If You Can Get It," and "Leap of Faith," the AP reports. Once also won awards for actor Steve Kazee, director John Tiffany, and playwright Enda Walsh, who wrote the book for the musical. Host Neil Patrick Harris kicked off the show with a performance from Bonnie & Clyde, which won best new musical. Click for the full list of Tony nominees.

– The 25-year-old man mauled by a tiger at the Bronx Zoo yesterday has a broken arm and leg, but is expected to survive, reports the New York Daily News. The tiger, Bashuta, will not be euthanized, says the zoo's director. "The tiger did nothing wrong in this episode." The attack occurred in the Wild Asia exhibit, where visitors glide over the Bronx River and through a tiger enclosure. The man jumped from a moving monorail train and plummeted over a protective fence, reports the AP. He was alone with Bashuta for about 10 minutes before he was rescued by zoo officials, who used a fire extinguisher to chase the animal away. "When someone is determined to do something harmful to themselves, it's very hard to stop that," says the zoo director. "The tiger did nothing wrong in this episode."

– Nora Ephron, who has died at the age of 71, was an essayist, writer, director, and screenwriter who made her mark with films including You've Got Mail, When Harry Met Sally, and Sleepless in Seattle. She was also a rare "triple-hyphenate"—a woman in the male-dominated movie business, a writer, director, and producer, the New York Times reports. Ephron was a social confederate of New York playwrights, filmmakers, and wits, including Mike Nichols, Woody Allen, and Calvin Trillin; Washington journalists including former Post executive editor Benjamin Bradlee and his journalist wife, Sally Quinn; and a Hollywood coterie that included Rob Reiner, Tom Hanks, Steve Martin, and Steven Spielberg. As a writer and director, Ephron was regarded as a keen cultural barometer. She repeatedly channeled her interest in the zeitgeist to the screen. Her last film, Julie & Julia, starring Meryl Streep as the French-cooking apostle Julia Child and Amy Adams as a modern disciple, explored the trendy fascination with blogging and gourmet cooking. – Joe Paterno's name is back on the Big Ten's list of coaches banned from college football for life over their response to the Jerry Sandusky sex abuse scandal. Paterno's name has been on the list since before the scandal broke, but now it's back in the spotlight, thanks to a blog dedicated to exposing what it calls the "Framing" of the former Penn State coach. The Big Ten announced today that its members will no longer be allowed to recruit or coach against Paterno, who won more games than any other coach in college football history, reports the Wall Street Journal. Paterno's name will remain on the Big Ten's list until the end of the season, but the conference will have to find a new coach to replace him. The Big Ten said it made the decision based on an analysis of the facts, not on Paterno's status as the winningest coach in college football history.

– All women who have breast implants should discuss the possibility with their doctors that they may cause an extremely rare type of cancer, the FDA said today. Anaplastic large-cell lymphoma is usually a systemic disease, but in some cases it has developed in the capsule of scar tissue around the implants, the New York Times reports. The risk is small, the FDA says, but it is not comfortable recommending specific treatment for the disease, which is treatable. So far, the FDA says it knows of about 60 cases worldwide, a tiny number compared with the 5 million to 10 million women who have implants. But even that small number appears to be an excess of cases when compared with the usual incidence of the disease: This type of lymphoma in the breast is normally found in only 3 in 100 million women who do not have implants. Because the risk appears to be so small, the drug agency says “the existing data support the continued marketing and use of breast implants.” But it also said that women considering implants should first discuss the information with their doctors.

– Nevest Coleman spent 23 years behind bars for a crime he didn't commit. But on Monday, the 49-year-old Chicago man was back at his old job, working as a groundskeeper for the Chicago White Sox, CBS Chicago reports. "I was proud to come back here," Coleman says. "I love the atmosphere." Coleman was released from prison in November after DNA evidence cleared him of the 1994 rape and murder of Antwinica Bridgeman. "It took a lot of weight off my shoulders," Coleman says. "Just to look around and be on my front porch. Take a shower, sit in a tub. I take it one day at a time. Now, I just have to enjoy life." He says he's been able to support himself since being released by having the support of his family and friends. "If I'm miserable, that means everybody else around me will be miserable," he says. "So if I'm happy, everybody else will be happy. I don't have time to be miserable, you know?" Coleman says he hopes to eventually become a full-time groundskeeper. "I hope we win a World Series because I'm out now," he says.

– The man who led police on a high-speed chase and barricaded himself in an armored van outside Dallas police headquarters has been identified as James Boulware of Carrollton, Texas, reports the Dallas Morning News. Police say Boulware, a 35-year-old with a history of mental health and family violence problems, told negotiators that he had planted bombs near police headquarters and planned to drag officers to their deaths, the AP reports. "He blames the police for taking his son away from him," Boulware's father tells the Morning News. "I tried to tell him that the police are just doing their job." Police say Boulware's motive isn't clear, but he blamed police for losing custody of his son, a 12-year-old boy. "He's blaming the police for taking his son away from him," says Jim Boulware, who last saw his son Friday night. "I tried to tell him that the police are just doing their job." Police say the suspect's body has been taken to a medical examiner to be positively identified.

– Monsanto's genetically modified corn was supposed to do two things: It would make it easier for farmers to get rid of pesky rootworms that have developed resistance to some pesticides, and it would make it resistant to weeds that have developed resistance to the company's herbicide, Roundup. But as the Wall Street Journal reports, the pests have been eating the modified seeds, and scientists fear that if the bugs develop resistance to the corn's toxin, farmers will have to revert to using pesticides. "The western corn rootworm is one of the most significant insect pests of corn in the United States and has a potential to become a very significant insect in Europe," a University of Illinois crop scientist tells AFP. The resistant rootworms have been found in four Iowa fields that had been planted with the genetically modified seeds for at least three years. The problem is that farmers are supposed to plant 20% of their fields with corn that doesn't have the genetic modification, so that if the resistant bugs develop they will end up breeding with non-resistant rootworms drawn to the unprotected plants and lessen the chance of passing resistance on to the next generation. Monsanto is taking the study results "seriously," but a spokesman says there is no reason for farmers to stop using the current seeds. Click

"Jefferson asked, 'Can the liberties of a nation be secure when we have removed a conviction that these liberties are the gift of God,'" said Trump. "Among those freedoms is the right to worship according to our own beliefs." But opponents of the amendment say repealing it would open the door to a flood of money into politics through unregulated, tax-free churches. – Poland's deputy defense minister isn't holding back when it comes to his country's relationship with France. The BBC reports Bartosz Kownacki recently took issue with the French pulling Poland's invite to an international defense fair in Paris. "The French side officially invited us a long time ago and now they are showing us the door," Kownacki said. "But these are the people we taught to eat with a fork a couple of centuries ago, which may explain their behavior today. This is obvious history, and I invite you to read up on that." He went on to say the French "are a people who learned to eat with a fork from us a few centuries ago. So maybe this is why they are behaving in this way now." Kownacki's remarks have been condemned in Poland, with a rep for the ruling Law and Justice party calling them "unfortunate" and "not very diplomatic." France pulled Poland's invite after the country scuttled a deal to buy 50 Airbus helicopters. Airbus is threatening to sue, and the BBC notes that Kownacki's remarks are just the latest in a long line of controversies for Poland's Law and Justice party, which took power in November. – Standard & Poor's knocked Italy down a notch in its credit rating today, citing the country's weak economic outlook and political dysfunction, reports MarketWatch. The agency also said the outlook for Italy's ratings is negative, meaning a further cut is possible. “Just when everyone was waiting for Moody’s to downgrade Italy, S&P gets in first with what is a much more damaging downgrade as its rating of Italy was already the lowest of the three agencies,” said one London-based fixed-income expert. Italy is the third-largest economy in the euro zone, and its bond market is the third-largest in the world. “These upcoming bond auctions could become the true test of the country’s credit strength and, if investors balk at rolling over its debt, the downward pressure on the euro could quickly accelerate,” said one currency research analyst at GFT. But Silvio Berlusconi's office issued a statement today saying the government had a solid majority in Parliament and was working to lift growth. “The evaluations of Standard & Poor’s seem dictated more by behind the scenes reports in newspapers than reality and seems influenced by political considerations,” the statement said.

– One of New York City's most high-profile restaurateurs is changing the name of his restaurant because of a racist past. "In the mid-1800s, the building where the Beekman [ restaurant] stands housed the offices of Fowler & Wells, a pair of publishers and phrenologists," chef Tom Colicchio said in a statement, per the Guardian. Phrenology is the study of skull size and structure to determine mental abilities, and was often used as a justification for discrimination and slavery. After picking the name, Colicchio and his team "dove more deeply into the works of Fowler & Wells" and "discovered facts about their beliefs that go against everything we stand for," the chef said. The restaurant will now be known as Temple Court. Colicchio's statement didn't specifically mention Fowler & Wells by name, but it made clear that the owners of the now-defunct Beekman Hotel were Fowler & Wells publishers and phrenologists, and that the name change was in response to their racist past, the New York Daily News reports. The restaurant has been open since 2009, and Colicchio said in the statement that he's been "proud to serve people from all walks of life from all over the world" at Beekman,

– Disgraced Chinese politician Bo Xilai has been kicked out of the Communist Party and will "face justice," Chinese state media announced today, following months of speculation that the move was imminent. Bo, the former Communist Party chief of Chongqing, is accused of taking huge bribes, abusing power, and engaging in improper sexual relations with several women, the Wall Street Journal reports. He will also be expelled from the party, and the 18th Party Congress, which will begin the process of transferring power to a new generation of leaders, will convene on Nov. 8. China's leadership is trying to send a strong message to the public that it will tackle the issues at the heart of the Bo scandal—corruption, abuse of power, and the decadent lives led by some members of the party elite. That represents an acknowledgment that growing public anger over those issues constitutes a grave threat to the party's future grip on power. Bo, the son of a fabled revolutionary, was a rising star in Chinese politics before the scandal broke. He was a front-runner for a spot on the powerful Politburo's Standing Committee.

– The top US military officer doesn't want to be "complicit" in an Israeli attack on Iran, reports the Guardian. "I don't want to be complicit if they choose to do it," said Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Martin Dempsey. "I don't know Iran's nuclear intentions, as intelligence did not reveal intentions." He added that such an attack would "clearly delay but probably not destroy Iran's nuclear program." Iran, meanwhile, issued a warning of its own today, reports Reuters. "The Zionist regime separated from America has no meaning, and we must not recognize Israel as separate from America," said a naval commander. "On this basis, today only the Americans have taken a threatening stance towards the Islamic Republic. If the Americans commit the smallest folly they will not leave the region safely."

– Celebrities are continuing to show their support for Texas victims of Hurricane Harvey. On Monday, Kevin Hart launched the Hurricane Harvey Relief Challenge, urging his fellow celebrities to donate $25,000 to the American Red Cross to help those affected by the storm. He donated $25,000 and asked Beyonce, Dave Chappelle, Jay-Z, Dwayne Johnson, Chris Rock, Jerry Seinfeld, and Justin Timberlake to match his donation, CNN reports. "Keep your head up Houston and keep your faith," Hart wrote Tuesday. "I love you all and my prayers are with you!" Hours earlier, Kim Kardashian and the rest of her family donated $500,000 to the Red Cross. E! reports that Sandra Bullock donated $1 million to the cause. "I'm just grateful I can do it," Bullock said in a statement. "We have to take care of one another."

– It's official: Ryan Seacrest is Live!'s new co-host, CNN reports. "Today, the next chapter of the Live' story is about to be written," Kelly Ripa said on Monday's show. "They are a part of the Live family forever." She and Seacrest then broke the news to the audience. Seacrest has been a guest co-host on Live! five times since ABC started its search for a replacement for Michael Strahan. He will also be an executive producer on the show, according to the Hollywood Reporter, giving him at least nominally the same level of power over it that Ripa herself has. The beloved talk show airs in many markets at 9am, directly against the third hour of NBC's Today. In the fall NBC is introducing a new 9am show led by Megyn Kelly, who recently jumped from Fox News to NBC.

The new offer values the 61% stake in the company at about $9.4 billion, but BSkyB says the price is still "significantly undervalued," the Guardian reports. BSkyB's independent directors have called for talks "with the objective of achieving an agreed proposal for the mutual benefit of all shareholders," but say they have been unable to reach a "mutually agreeable price at the current time." News Corp. says it plans to fund the deal with a "significant portion" of its cash reserves. "We believe that this is the right time for BSkyB to become a wholly-owned part of News Corporation with its greater scale and broader geographic reach," says Chase Carey, News Corp's deputy chairman.

– Little Caesars is hoping to cash in on America's love of bacon with its new Bacon Wrapped Crust DEEP!DEEP! Dish pizza, which comes topped with pepperoni and 3 1/2 feet of bacon wrapped around the crust, USA Today reports. "Every time you take a bite out of the crust, you'll get bacon," says Little Caesars CEO David Scrivano. "This is a more indulgent offering for a demographic that craves premium quality." According to CBS Detroit, the chain's R&D team came up with the idea after one of its employees ordered a bacon-wrapped filet. The $12 pizza will be available for a limited time at participating locations.

– Germanwings co-pilot Andreas Lubitz suffered a "serious depressive episode" six years ago and received treatment for a year and a half, according to a report in Germany's Bild newspaper picked up by Reuters. The report doesn't say why the treatment was necessary, only that the relevant documents will be passed to French investigators once they have been examined by German authorities. Lufthansa CEO Carsten Spohr has said that Lubitz took a break from training six years ago but returned after being cleared again. "Six years ago there was a lengthy interruption in his training. After he was cleared again, he resumed training," Spohr said. "He passed all the subsequent tests and checks with flying colors. His flying abilities were flawless." Lubitz, who is believed to have locked his captain out of the cockpit and steered the plane down on Tuesday, was treated for depression after finishing training in 2008, reports the BBC, which notes that it's not clear whether the episode was related to his current mental health problems. A police spokesman says investigators have found "a very significant clue as to what has happened" at Lubitz's parents' home in Montabaur, but he didn't specify what that was.

– Vitamin B12 is found in multivitamins, but a new study suggests that too much of it could cause acne. Researchers at UCLA found that skin bacteria known as Propionibacterium acnes—which causes pimples in some people but not in others—changes its gene expression when too much of the vitamin is present, reports LiveScience. This could lead to inflammation, which is a key step in acne development. "There's still a lot to be studied in order to really understand if B12 causes acne," says a co-author of the study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. "This study does present some compelling evidence suggesting that supplementation with B12 can cause or exacerbate acne in a subset of individuals," says a doctor not involved with the study. But it's too early to say that people suffering from acne should stop taking B12 supplements, he adds. "Proof of a causative effect of B12 supplements on acne development will require randomized control trials with enough subjects to see a significant effect."

Airbnb is giving away a one-night stay for two in the Catacombs catacombs in Paris on Oct. 31, UPI reports. "Before bedtime, a storyteller will have youbound with fascinating tales from the catacombs guaranteed to produce nightmares. Finally, enjoy dawn with the dead as you become the only living person ever to wake up in the Paris catacombs," the contest description reads. The contest is open to "couples and friends" and there are no pets allowed, but "you can be assured there will be a monster under your bed," the description says. The friend pulled Ransom out of the water and tried to give him chest compressions, but he was dead before they got to shore. Authorities have yet to identify the shark, but they believe it was a great white. "It takes a shark of massive size and jaw to inflict that kind of injury," says a shark expert. Great whites seek prey at the water's surface and attack with enormous ferocity from underneath. After they bite, it's too late. "It may be mistaken identity," says the expert. The last fatal shark attack in California was in 2008.

– A World Series of Poker player says he hit an "emotional jackpot" thanks to an Uber driver who returned his $7,000 ante, the AP reports. Earlier Friday, the FBI was investigating a business deal involving Nojay and the city's $1.3 billion school modernization program, which Nojay played a central role in. – Bloomberg has apologized to clients after it emerged that some of its reporters were spying on them on the company's desktop computers. The New York Post reports that "several hundred" reporters were using a technique called the "Z function" that allowed them to access lists of clients' subscribers on the company's desktop computer. The Federal Reserve is now investigating whether its employees were similarly spied on, the New York Times reports. A Bloomberg spokesman says both of the functions used by reporters have been disabled in the newsroom. The practice was discovered after Goldman Sachs complained last month that Bloomberg reporters were also spying on its traders, the Post reports. Bloomberg CEO Daniel Doctoroff says the "limited customer relationship data previously available to our reporters never included access to our trading, portfolio, monitor, blotter or other related systems or our clients' messages." He says the company has taken steps to make sure the practice doesn't happen again.

Two officials said an announcement on Shulkin could happen this week, subject to Trump's final decision as the White House hones in on possible replacements to head the Department of Veterans Affairs. One of the officials rated Shulkin's chances of being pushed out in the next day or two at "50-50." The three officials demanded anonymity to discuss a sensitive personnel matter. Trump, who spent the weekend at his Mar-a-Lago estate, told associates that he would keep two other administration officials who had been under fire: White House chief of staff John Kelly and Housing Secretary Ben Carson. "He did say that he's expecting to make one or two major changes," said Newsmax CEO Chris Ruddy, a Trump confidant who spoke with the president over the weekend. "Now, other White House sources, not the president, tell me that Veterans Affairs Secretary David Shulkin is likely to depart the Cabinet very soon." – A Southwest Airlines flight bound for Dallas had to return to Seattle on Sunday because someone forgot to unload a human heart on board, the Seattle Times reports. According to KOMO, the heart was supposed to be unloaded after an earlier flight from Sacramento. But after the pilot took off for Dallas, he realized the heart was still on the plane. "We made the decision to return to Seattle to ensure the shipment was delivered to its destination within the window of time allotted by our cargo customer," the airline said in a statement. The heart, which was supposed to be used for a heart transplant, was unharmed and reached its intended destination on time. Southwest says it's unclear what the heart was intended for. Passenger Andrew Gottschalk calls the incident a "horrific story of gross negligence," KOMO reports. According to the Times, passengers were shocked to find out the heart was still on the plane. But they were happy to save a life. Southwest says it was “absolutely necessary to deliver the shipment to its destination in the Seattle area as quickly as possible.” It's unclear whether anyone's life was ever in danger because of the heart.

– Sarah Palin's visit to Paul Revere's house this week has led to a new account of the famous midnight ride—and it turns out Revere was actually warning the British. "He who warned, uh, the the British that they weren’t gonna be takin’ away our arms, uh, by ringin’ those bells and, um, by makin’ sure that as he’s ridin’ his horse through town to send those warnin’ shots and bells that, uh, we were gonna be secure and we were gonna be free and we were gonna be armed," Palin said, according to ABC News. "Had he used bells, or had he warned the people with whom America was at war, Palin's tour bus might have chugged through the northeast on the left side of the road," writes Steve Kornacki at Salon. "Perhaps this week's lesson in the annals of American history was necessary for Sarah Palin," he concludes.

In addition to the Macron campaign, the German political group Konrad Adenauer Stiftung, associated with Angela Merkel's Christian Democratic Union, Friedrich Ebert Stiftung, associated with the Social Democratic Party, and others were also targeted by Fancy Bear. "Most espionage groups have tradecraft to stay low and slow, and remain in a system as long as possible," Ed Cabrera, Trend Micro's chief cybersecurity officer, says. "This group is loud and fast." The Trend Micro report states the Fancy Bear group has been making "these types of attacks for a long time," and the number of command-and-control servers it has used to carry out attacks has increased from five in late 2013 to 26 in early 2016. – A right-wing think tank has pulled a billboard featuring Unabomber Ted Kaczynski and Charles Manson after a barrage of criticism. The billboard was part of a campaign by the Heartland Institute to convince people that global warming is a hoax perpetrated by liberals and the United Nations, the Chicago Tribune reports. The billboard also featured tyrant Fidel Castro and mass murderer Osama bin Laden. "These rogues and villains were chosen because they made public statements about how man-made global warming is a crisis and how mankind must take immediate and drastic actions to stop it," the think tank said in a statement. "The people who still believe in man-made global warming aren't scientists. They are murderers, tyrants, and madmen." The billboard was paid for by the think tank, which is known for promoting climate skepticism. "What on earth were they thinking?" asks Joseph Bast at Reason. "The point is that believing in global warming is not 'mainstream,' smart, or sophisticated. In fact, it is just the opposite of those things."

– The Coast Guard is considering setting the growing oil spill off the Louisiana coast on fire, CNN reports. The Coast Guard has deployed fire-proof booms to contain the oil, which is still leaking at a rate of 42,000 gallons a day from a well that exploded last week. If the slick does reach land, it could take more than two months to clean up. "If we don't secure the well, this could be one of the most serious oil spills in US history," said the Coast Guard's Rear Admiral Mary Landry. The Coast Guard is considering setting the oil slick on fire as early as tomorrow, but officials warn that setting it on fire could cause more harm than good. The Coast Guard has deployed nearly 50 vessels to contain the spill and clean it up.

– A band called Vulfpeck has released a new album, Sleepify, but it's made up entirely of songs that aren't being played. The idea is that people will stream the songs on Spotify, and the band will get a cut of the proceeds. "We've only played twice in three years," band member Jack Stratton tells Wired. "We're trying to raise money so we can go on tour." The band says it's made between $6,700 and $9,400 from Spotify streams of Sleepify's 10 tracks, though it won't say for sure. A Spotify spokesperson tells Wired that the album is "clever," but adds, "We prefer Vulpeck's early albums. Sleepify seems derivative of John Cage's work." Stratton says Spotify does a great job of presenting his music to fans, but "frankly, we make less on YouTube." He adds that the silent tracks have inspired a lot of traffic to the band's actual music, and Spotify seems to be enjoying it, too, with the spokesperson noting, "We prefer Vulpeck's early albums. Sleepify seems derivative."

– The body of a former White House chef who went missing while hiking in New Mexico's Sangre de Cristo Mountains was found Sunday night, the AP reports. Walter Scheib, 61, had been missing for more than a week after he set out for a four-mile hike June 13. He was last heard from on June 13, when his girlfriend reported him missing; his vehicle was found June 14 near a trailhead in the Taos area. Scheib served as White House chef for 11 years under presidents Bill Clinton and George W. Bush. After leaving the White House, he started his own private chef business and co-authored a book, White House Chef: Eleven Years, Two Presidents, One Kitchen. "The search has been a little slow-going because of the terrain, but it is ongoing," said New Mexico state police spokeswoman Sgt. Elizabeth Armijo, according to NBC News. Scheib, who has two sons, recently moved to New Mexico and had been living in Taos.

"Corporations are not people," he told Stephen Colbert this week, according to the Huffington Post. "They do not have freedom of expression rights in terms of buying elections."

– CNN's prime-time viewership has sunk to its lowest level since the first Gulf War, according to new ratings. The network's average of 446,000 viewers in the second quarter is down 35% from a year ago, and it was CNN's worst performance ever for a second quarter, the New York Times reports. MSNBC and Fox News were down 18% and 14%, respectively, while CNN's decline was more than twice that of the other two networks. CNN's prime-time programming is considered too liberal for advertisers, and the network is struggling to find an answer to what to do when news is light, Politico notes. Piers Morgan's 9pm show was the network's worst ever, with 137,000 viewers in the coveted 25-to-54 demographic.

No one was injured in the attack on the A6 highway connecting Paris and Lyon, and the drivers of the two vans were left at the scene unharmed, reports the AP. The jewels remain missing and it's unclear where the attackers were heading. After hours of searches failed to locate them, another police official said authorities were concentrating efforts on the investigation into the attack, which was handed to the French police agency overseeing organized crime. No possible suspects have been named in Wednesday's theft, although the case was reminiscent of heists by the Pink Panther gang of jewel thieves. The male student has been identified as a student at the school, which is about 12 miles southeast of Charlotte, the AP reports. Police say the shooting happened during an argument, and they have not released the names or ages of the two students involved. – Andy Roddick announced today that he's retiring from tennis after this year's US Open, reports USA Today. "I just feel like it's time," said the last American man to win a major at the 2003 US Open. "I don't know that I'm healthy enough or committed enough to go another year." Roddick, who turned 30 today, said he made the decision after his last loss at Wimbledon this summer, notes Bleacher Report. "It's probably the first time in my career that I can sit here and say I'm not sure that I can put everything into it physically and emotionally," he said. "I don't know that I want to disrespect the game by coasting home." Roddick faces Australia's Bernard Tomic in the second round tonight.

– The federal government shut down at midnight after Republicans and Democrats failed to reach an agreement to fund it. The shutdown means 800,000 federal workers will be furloughed, national parks will close, and most federal offices will be closed, the Washington Post reports. Some services will continue, but others will be shut down entirely. Here's what you need to know: The White House has asked agencies to "execute plans for an orderly shutdown due to the absence of appropriations," the New York Times reports. John Boehner says the House will pass a "clean" spending bill to reopen the government, but Harry Reid says he won't accept it unless Republicans drop their attacks on ObamaCare. "The responsibility for this Republican government shutdown will rest squarely on his shoulders," Reid said. The GOP plan to delay ObamaCare's individual mandate for one year and wipe out long-term government health benefits for members of Congress and their aides failed in the Senate, the AP reports.

– At least 6 people were killed by tornadoes that ripped through the South and Midwest yesterday, and the death toll is expected to rise. Hundreds of homes and other buildings were destroyed and dozens of people were injured in Arkansas, Missouri, and Mississippi as the unusually warm weather wreaked havoc. "I wanted to see the end coming. You're only going to see it one time and I thought that was it," a survivor in the small town of Cincinnati, Ark., tells the AP. "It takes more than a tornado to get me." Three people died in the northwestern Arkansas hamlet of Cincinnati when a tornado touched down just before sunrise yesterday, and three others died when a storm spawned by the same weather system ripped up the Missouri countryside near Rolla. Early today, two people were injured in central Mississippi and several homes were damaged by a storm in Attala County. Tornado watches were in effect for parts of Mississippi, Alabama, and Louisiana. Click here for more on the tornadoes.

– Harry Reid named three senators today to the 12-member "super committee" tasked with finding $1.2 trillion in budget cuts by the end of the year. Democrat Patty Murray of Washington will serve as co-chair, while Montana's Max Baucus and Massachusetts' John Kerry will be named as co-chairmen of the House panel, Politico reports. House Speaker John Boehner will pick two members from each side of the aisle, and Nancy Pelosi and Mitch McConnell will each pick three members from their own party. Republicans are calling on Reid to withdraw his pick for co-chair, saying it's a political move designed to fill coffers for the Democratic campaign committee. “The select committee is no place for someone whose top priority is fundraising and politics,” RNC Chairman Reince Priebus said.

– Harvard has the highest graduation rate of any US research university, with 98% of its 2002 enrollees graduating by 2008, according to a new report from the Chronicle of Higher Education. The University of Virginia, meanwhile, had the highest graduation rate among public research universities at 93%. The Chronicle compared graduation rates at public and private research universities in 2002 and 2008, surveying students who enrolled in 1996 and 2002. Among private research universities, Yale and Notre Dame had high graduation rates of 97% and 96%, respectively. Click here for the full list.

– The Internet's "godfather" has a warning for future historians: Our digital age could turn out to be a "digital Dark Ages," he warns. "If we're thinking 1,000 years, 3,000 years ahead in the future, we have to ask ourselves, how do we preserve all the bits that we need in order to correctly interpret the digital objects we create?" asks Vint Cerf, Google's VP. "We are nonchalantly throwing all of our data into what could become an information black hole without realizing it." Cerf, speaking at the annual meeting of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in San Jose, likened the digital age to the post-Roman era, notes the BBC. "Historians will tell you that sometimes documents and transactions images and so on may turn out to have an importance which is not understood for hundreds of years," he said. "So failure to preserve them will cause us to lose our perspective." One possible solution is what he calls "digital vellum," a concept being explored by computer scientists at Carnegie Mellon University. – Google's new social networking service, Google+, is off to a slow start, according to new numbers from research firm Experian Hitwise. Google+ visits fell 3% in the week ending July 23, and the average time spent on the site was down 10% to 5 minutes and 15 seconds, Bloomberg reports. Google+ has more than 10 million users, less than three weeks after its launch. " phase one of G+ was clearly a success," writes Adam Clark Estes at Gizmodo, but "now comes the hard part. Keeping those users around and engaged." He notes that traffic is down week to week, and that "almost everything shared remains about Google (or worse, Google+ itself)." At All Things Digital, Kara Swisher agrees that "the new car smell is wearing off," but adds that "user retention is a bitch." Click for more.

– Two servers are suing Hard Rock Cafe, alleging that the restaurant ripped them off by taking their tips and divvying them up among its kitchen staff. That's illegal, their lawyer says, because it's not allowed for servers and bartenders to retain all their tips or for Hard Rock to pool their tips among employees "who customarily and regularly receive tips." "In this economy, servers and bartenders need all the tips they can get," the lawyer says in the Orlando Sentinel. "Hard Rock should have known that a tip-sharing arrangement that included kitchen staff violated Florida and federal law." Click for more on the lawsuit.

– Scientists have discovered a new source of water on the moon, and it's a pretty nifty one: solar winds. The wind carries hydrogen and oxygen from the sun into the moon's soil, where it reacts with oxygen present on the moon's surface, according to a study published in Nature Geoscience. "Now we have ready sources of water that can not only be consumed by plants and humans, but also electrolysed into its constituent elements—hydrogen and oxygen—to make rocket fuel," says lead author Yang Liu of the University of Tennessee at Knoxville, per Phys.org. Liu's team discovered the source while studying glass-like grains of soil on the moon's surface brought back by the Apollo missions, reports the Sydney Morning Herald. It's not clear how much water is in the soil, but "it's very hard to generalise from a couple of grains of sand—or glass, which is essentially what they have," says a planetary scientist from Australia's National University. "What they're working with is a tiny fraction of lunar soil brought back by the Apollo missions, so it's very hard to generalise from a couple of grains of sand—or glass, which is essentially what they have."

Tim Scott tweeted, "We are Americans from all walks of life, working towards the American Dream. Nowhere in that dream is there room for racism." Democratic Sen. Chuck Schumer called Trump's remarks "very, very wrong," the Washington Post reports. "When David Duke and white supremacists cheer your remarks, you're doing it very, very wrong," Schumer said. "Great and good American presidents seek to unite, not divide. Donald Trump's remarks clearly show he is not one of them." White House

The message on the jersey will be "I AM Paris" and "nothing else," the team says in a statement. The jerseys will be worn during a match against Malmo in the Champions League on Wednesday and a match against Troyes on Saturday. According to the AP, the Paris soccer team has been a kind of "national figurehead" in the wake of the attacks.

Video of the moment shows people ducking and screaming, with one attendee tweeting that it was "EXTREMELY irresponsible and distasteful to end songs w the shot gun sound effect." A military official in the pro-Assad alliance says the evacuation will start at 5am, while the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights says it's likely to be delayed until Thursday. The evacuation is part of a ceasefire brokered by Turkey and Russia, but Iran-backed militias on the ground are preventing civilians and opposition fighters from leaving the besieged district. "The sectarian militias want to resume the massacre in Aleppo and the world has to act to prevent this sectarian slaughter led by Iran," says Bassam Mustafa, a member of the political council of Noureddine Zinki, one of the main rebel groups in east Aleppo. "The opposition will continue to abide by the agreement." The Syrian military initially said it had no knowledge of the deal before backtracking and saying the evacuations would begin at 5am Aleppo time. – The complete genome of the cannabis plant has been sequenced for the first time. A company called Medicinal Genomics released the raw sequence of Cannabis sativa on Amazon’s EC2 public cloud computing service last night, Wired reports. The company hopes the information will help scientists explore the plant’s therapeutic benefits, including fighting cancer, and perhaps guide plant breeding programs to generate new strains. “This is the beginning of a more scientific approach to the genetics of the species,” the director of the Human Genome Sequencing Center at Baylor College of Medicine tells Bloomberg. “This is not really about marijuana; it’s about pharmacology.” The company’s founder, 38-year-old Kevin McKernan, worked on the Human Genome Project from 1996 to 2000, and started a commercial laboratory with his two brothers called Agencourt Bioscience, which was sold to Beckman Coulter Inc. in 2005. A spin-out of Agencourt that made sequencing technology, called Agencourt Personal Genomics, was acquired by Applied Biosystems Inc. in 2008 to become Carlsbad, California-based Life Technologies. Life Technologies bought Ion Torrent last year for $375 million in cash and stock.

– Justin Timberlake opens up about his past relationships—with Jessica Biel and Britney Spears—in the latest issue of Vanity Fair, calling Biel “the single-handedly most significant person in my life.” “In my 30 years, she is the most special person, OK?” he continues. “I don’t want to say much more, because I have to protect things that are dear to me—for instance, her.” Of marriage, Timberlake says, “As little as six months ago I wouldn’t have even thought about that, but now it feels like a closer planet orbiting around.” Click for more from the interview, including Timberlake’s thoughts on ex-girlfriends.

– Alaska will become the 30th state to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act after Gov. Bill Walker announced today that he will do so on his own, the Anchorage Daily News reports. Walker, an independent, says he has decided to expand the state's version of the health care program for the poor without the help of state lawmakers, who he says have blocked the expansion several times. "I have concluded that the only option left is to expand Medicaid in Alaska," Walker said, per the Washington Post. "The federal government has made it clear that they will not stand in Alaska's way." Walker says the move will bring in $146 million in new federal funds for the first year and cover 20,000 Alaskans, Reuters reports. The expansion would cover people who make up to three-quarters of the state's poverty level. "We appreciate the swift action by the local authorities, and the patience and professionalism of all the employees who were impacted." The New York Police Department tweeted that the threat was not substantiated.

– The US has poured more than $90 billion into Afghanistan over the past decade, but a new report from the special inspector general for Afghanistan reconstruction finds that many of the projects are behind schedule and may not even help turn the tide of war, the Wall Street Journal reports. The $300 million "Kandahar Bridging Solution" project, which was supposed to boost electricity in the war-torn city, is behind schedule because the US won't be paying for the diesel needed to run the city's turbines for at least two more years, the Washington Post reports. "While the Kandahar Bridging Solution may achieve some immediate [counter­insurgency] benefits because—as stated by USAID officials—'people like having their lights on,' the US government may be building an expectations gap that cannot be met in a timely manner," the report states. The US embassy defends the projects, saying they "have signaled to Afghan populations the US government's long term commitment to Afghanistan." But the inspector general's office used to be more interested in contracting waste and fraud, and the report raises serious questions about the strategic rationale of the US spending so much money in a country that has little infrastructure, the Post notes.

– Massive flooding in southeastern Louisiana could bring an increased risk for the Zika virus, an expert in tropical medicine said Sunday. Strong floodwaters often wash away mosquito eggs, which would be good news. But mosquito eggs already laid in containers, such as empty buckets or tires, could be protected from surging water and then be stimulated to hatch after the flooding recedes, Peter Hotez, dean of the National School of Tropical Medicine at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston, tells USA Today. "We could be seeing an increase number of Aedes aegypti now in the coming weeks," he says. "This is crunch time." Ben Beard, deputy incident manager for the Zika outbreak program at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, agrees. "I wouldn't say right off that there's reason to believe that (the flooding) would have significant impact," he tells the Times-Picayune. But he adds that there could be an increase in other types of mosquitoes, and the Zika-carrying species is smaller and more easily washed away by floodwaters. Hotez says there could be cases that have gone unreported in Louisiana, but he says there could also be cases that have gone unreported in Florida, the only state where Zika was contracted locally. Pete Sessions announced last night that he's dropping out of the race, leaving McCarthy as the only candidate, reports Reuters.
