– It's not every day that a marriage proposal is featured in a crossword puzzle, but that's exactly what happened in Britain this week. Matthew Dick, a 38-year-old lawyer from London, used the Times newspaper's Tuesday crossword to ask his girlfriend, Delyth Hughes, to marry him, the BBC reports. "I underlined the words 'will you marry me' which appeared in the clue, and the answer was proposal," Dick tells the Times. "My hands were shaking and I put my hands in my pocket to get the ring to propose." He says Hughes, 39, "looked so surprised and didn't say anything for about 30 seconds, before then saying 'No,' which she thought was hilarious. But she did then say 'Yes' and I had to tell her this was the real Times crossword, not something I had printed out myself." Times crossword editor Richard Rogan says he believes it's the first time the newspaper has included a proposal in a puzzle. "It's so special and such a geeky way of doing it," he says. "We won't be doing it again."

China's military is firmly in control of its Korean policy, and it doesn't want to be seen as abandoning its ally. "One nuclear test will not make China’s new administration decide to ‘abandon North Korea,’ but it will definitely worsen China-North Korea relations," says a Peking University professor. "North Korea’s nuclear test will make the new Xi Jinping administration angry, and give China a headache." Meanwhile, the US and South Korea are discussing a common strategy for dealing with the North, the Washington Post reports. The two countries will likely meet in person at a military forum in South Korea next week, and President Obama is expected to raise the issue with South Korea's president.

That raised the prospect of still more declines, which would help struggling Chinese exporters at the expense of foreign competitors and might shore up flagging economic growth. On Wednesday, the yuan dropped another 1.6%. In theory, it could drop 2% every day given it can trade 2% around a rate that is set based on the previous day's closing value, reports the AP. Until now, China has set the yuan's value each day based on a basket of currencies that is believed to be dominated by the US dollar. That meant the yuan rose as the dollar jumped over the past year, hurting its exporters and raising the threat of politically dangerous job losses. Exports in July plummeted by an unexpectedly steep 8.3% from a year earlier. The People's Bank of China promised yesterday to keep the exchange rate "basically stable," but today's decline prompted suggestions the yuan is likely to fall further. Kernes, a wealthy businessman and former supporter of the ousted pro-Russia president, is in stable condition after surgery to repair chest and abdomen damage, but his life is still in danger, his office says. The list of targets includes two members of Vladimir Putin's inner circle, 17 companies linked to Putin's "inner circle," and a number of Russian state-owned banks.

Salim Saleh has spent his entire life in the bush with his father's force and had been in charge of security, but he now has "an added responsibility of field command" and is the "most influential person after his father," says the head of the Ugandan mission searching for Kony. The previous record was 69 degrees in Ketchikan. Other high temperatures in southeast Alaska on Thursday included 65 degrees in Ketchikan, 57 degrees in Yakutat, and 64 degrees in Juneau, the Alaska Dispatch News reports. March 2016 was the warmest month on record for Juneau, Sitka, Klawock, Haines, Petersburg, Skagway, and Ketchikan.

– Rupert Murdoch is giving up full control of News Corp's three Chinese TV channels to a Beijing-based private equity fund. The sale of a controlling stake in Xing Kong, Xing Kong International, Channel [V] Mainland China, and the Fortune Start Chinese film library to China Media Capital is a "clear sign that they aren’t interested in China any more, but they can’t say that," an industry executive tells the Financial Times. News Corp will retain a "significant stake" in the business. The sale is the most significant step so far in a gradual retreat by News Corp from China, where the government insists on maintaining tight controls.

– A zookeeper in Japan is dead after a rare white tiger attacked him, the BBC reports. Akira Furusho, 40, was found bleeding from the neck in the tiger's cage at Hirakawa Zoological Park in Kagoshima on Monday. He was taken to a hospital and pronounced dead. The 5-year-old male tiger, Riku, was sedated with a tranquilizer before rescue workers and police arrived. "We plan not to kill Riku and continue to keep it because the bereaved family asked us to do so," says a zoo official, per AFP. The attack is believed to have happened as Furusho went to clean the tiger's enclosure. Tigers are normally removed from the display pen to a separate area before staff enter. Police are investigating how the zoo looks after the four white tigers it keeps. (A zookeeper in the US was mauled by a tiger and survived.)

– A Hillary Clinton speech in Las Vegas got a little more high-profile today when a woman jumped up and threw a shoe at the former secretary of state. Clinton was speaking to more than 1,000 people at the Institute of Scrap Recycling Industries convention at Mandalay Bay when the woman, wearing sandals, chucked her shoe and some papers, the Las Vegas Review-Journal reports. "Thank goodness she didn't play softball like I did," Clinton quipped to the crowd after the incident. The woman, who was not affiliated with the institute and was not credentialed for the event, was escorted out by convention center security and Secret Service officers, and police will be called, the Review-Journal reports. Clinton, who didn't use the stage to announce her plans for the 2016 presidential race but did mention her upcoming book, spoke about international trade, the civil war in Syria, and US relations with Russia during the speech, the AP reports.

– A federal law enforcement officer accused of killing his estranged wife and wounding two other people in a Maryland shooting spree was arrested Friday in the same shopping center where the DC Beltway sniper attacks began more than 14 years ago, the AP reports. Police say 62-year-old Eulalio Tordil was taken into custody without incident at the Northgate Shopping Center in Bethesda, where he had been spotted walking into a Dunkin' Donuts, Fox 5 reports. "We had him under surveillance and he was walking from store to store and at no point was it safe to take him into custody until we did," says Montgomery County Police Chief Tom Manger. Police say Tordil shot and killed his estranged wife Thursday night outside a Beltsville, Md., high school. He was also charged with assault for shooting a man who tried to intervene, the Washington Post reports. Two people were killed and two others wounded in two separate shootings Friday morning, police say. One of the victims is in critical condition, and the other is in stable condition with non-life-threatening injuries, police say.

– It's been more than two years since China sent its first unmanned lunar probe to the moon, and the country's National Space Administration has just released hundreds of high-resolution photos taken by the Chang'e-3 lunar lander and rover. CNN calls it a "rare show of openness for the country's usually secretive space program." The photos, which can be seen here, show the moon's surface in vivid detail. China's National Space Administration made the images, video clips, and scientific data available on its website in a rare show of openness for the country's usually secretive space program. China sent its first unmanned lunar probe, the Yutu, or "Jade Rabbit," to the moon in 2013 as part of its Chang'e-3 mission, becoming only the third nation after the US and Russia to land on the moon's surface. Despite a rocky start, Jade Rabbit is still working and sending images and data back to earth.

– The aurora borealis, aka the Northern Lights, should light up the night sky over much of the US and Canada Sunday night into Monday morning, USA Today reports. According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the lights should be visible in states such as Montana, the Dakotas, Minnesota, Wisconsin, northern Illinois, Michigan, northern New York State, and much of New England. Viewers in cities such as Minneapolis, Chicago, Detroit, Buffalo, Syracuse, Albany, and Boston should have a good chance of seeing the lights. The aurora forms when particles from the sun get caught up in the Earth's magnetic field. The particles interact with molecules of atmospheric gases to cause the famed glowing red and green colors of the aurora. The lights are visible in both the far northern and southern parts of the world. The southern lights are known as aurora australis. NOAA has issued a geomagnetic storm watch for the event and expects a "moderate" storm, a 2 out of 5 on its severity scale. Sunday night's aurora borealis should be visible almost as far south as the yellow line on this map.

– Texas executed Cameron Todd Willingham in 1996 for the murders of his two young daughters—and last night at the GOP debate, Brian Williams tried to hold Rick Perry accountable for it. When Perry was asked if he had ever struggled with the idea that someone who was executed was innocent, Williams simply asked: "If you come into our state and you kill one of our children, you kill a police officer, you're involved with another crime, and you kill one of our citizens, you will face the ultimate justice in the state of Texas, and that is, you will be executed." Perry's response: "No, sir. I've never struggled with that at all. The state of Texas has a very thoughtful, very clear process in place in place of which—when someone commits the most heinous of crimes against our citizens, they get a fair hearing, they go through an appellate process, they go up to the Supreme Court of the United States, if that's required. But in the state of Texas, if you come into our state and you kill one of our children, you kill a police officer, you're involved with another crime and you kill one of our citizens, you will face the ultimate justice in the state of Texas

– A UPS driver in Missouri is being hailed as a hero after he spotted a message scrawled on a package—"Contact 911"—and called police. Authorities say the driver was on his way to a Robertsville home to pick up a package yesterday when he spotted the message and called police, CNN reports. The woman who had given the package to him managed to talk to the driver while standing behind her with a gun, according to court documents. Authorities say the woman's husband, 33-year-old James Jordan, had been holding a gun to her head and threatening to kill her, then himself, when the UPS driver arrived. He was arrested after a SWAT team was called in because Jordan was refusing to cooperate with police, KTVI reports. Jordan has been charged with domestic assault, sodomy, felonious restraint, unlawful use of a weapon, and endangering the welfare of a child. Police say the woman's 3-year-old son was home at the time of the incident but was unharmed.

– Brad Pitt premiered his new movie, Moneyball, last night in Oakland, but he still had time to clear up some comments he made about ex-wife Jennifer Aniston. "I don't know what was pieced together or put together," he told Matt Lauer on Today. "All I know is that my point was, the best thing I'd done as a father is be sure that my kids have a good mother. That's all I was, or am, trying to say. It has no reference to the past. And I think it's a shame that I can't say something nice about Angie without Jen being drug in. You know, she doesn't deserve it." He added that Aniston didn't respond to his comments after they were published, the Los Angeles Times reports. "That was never my intention for it to be spun that way," he said. "People read things into it that just weren't there." Click for more from the premiere, including Pitt's thoughts on Derek Jeter's broken bat.

– A woman in Jerusalem has been arrested after allegedly setting a gas station pump on fire because a man wouldn't give her a cigarette, the Times of Israel reports. According to the Jerusalem Post, the unidentified woman approached the man filling up his car Tuesday and asked for a cigarette. He said no, and she allegedly pulled a lighter out of her pocket and set the pump on fire. CCTV footage shows the man running away as the pump goes up in flames. He pulled the pump away from his car, but it was too late: The car was completely on fire within seconds. The woman was arrested soon after the incident and denied any involvement, but a court has extended her arrest by five days and sent her for psychological evaluations. The man's brother was in the car at the time, but was unharmed.

– The latest craze in kids' toys is the Rainbow Loom, a device that combines a crochet hook with rubber bands to create colorful bracelets. But two New York City schools—one Upper West side and one in Brooklyn—have banned the bracelets because they say they're taking away recess time, DNA Info reports. The schools say the bracelets are causing conflict between students who have the looms and those who don't, and they've banned bracelet-making kits and "related paraphernalia" as well. "I think it's a complete overreaction on the part of the administration," says one Upper West side mom. But a Brooklyn dad says the bracelets are "hard enough to control a class of 9-year-olds as it is." The schools aren't the first to ban the bracelets, but they're the first to do so in New York City, reports Today Moms. "As far as I know, the ( Rainbow Loom) bracelets aren't banned in our schools at the moment," says one parent. "But I don't think most teachers permit the student to bring the loom and a gazillion bracelets into class, although they can wear them."

– "Perhaps I am going to lose fame but I accept it, I assume it." That's the plea of Sébastien Bras, one of only 27 French chefs with three Michelin stars, reports the Guardian. Bras' restaurant, Le Suquet  Laguiole, in central France, has had three Michelin stars since 1999. But the 46-year-old chef says he's tired of the pressure that comes with being one of France's most celebrated chefs and wants to be allowed to "redefined what is essential" in a way that won't put pressure on his restaurant, per the Telegraph. "Today, at 46 years old, I want to give a new meaning to my life ... and redefine what is essential," he says in a Facebook video. Bras says he'll continue to cook good food at Le Suquet "without wondering whether my creations will appeal to Michelin's inspectors," but he wants to be able to do so without fear of being judged. "You're inspected two or three times a year, you never know when," he tells AFP. "Every meal that goes out could be inspected. – LinkedIn may have been hit by a much bigger security breach than previously thought. Security researcher Troy Hunt says a hacker has posted data including email addresses and passwords for up to 117 million LinkedIn accounts on the dark web for $2,200, reports the Verge. The data was apparently stolen in a 2012 breach, according to LeakedSource, a site that maintains a database of more than 1.25 billion compromised accounts. LinkedIn confirmed the hack and says it is "taking immediate steps to invalidate the passwords of the accounts impacted, and we will contact those members to reset their passwords." The company says it has "no indication that this is a result of a new security breach." Motherboard reports that 123456 is the most common password in the leaked data, followed by linkedin, 12345678, and 111111. "It is only coming to the surface now. People may not have taken it very seriously back then as it was not spread," one of the people behind LeakedSource tells Motherboard. "To my knowledge the database was kept within a small group of Russians." The data was advertised on a dark web site called The Real Deal, according to posts on social media. It's not clear whether LinkedIn was aware of the high number of accounts affected by the 2012 hack when

– President Obama's budget is expected to include a fee on banks to help taxpayers recoup the cost of the AIG bailout, sources tell Bloomberg's Morning Money blog. The move would stop short of a financial transactions tax, but the administration has decided that a tax on compensation packages would be too easily evaded. The sources say the final approach has not been locked down. Meanwhile, New York Fed general counsel Thomas C. Baxter wrote to Darrell Issa, ranking member of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, clarifying that emails relating to AIG securities law disclosure were not brought to the attention of Tim Geithner. “In my judgment as the New York Fed’s chief legal officer, disclosure matters of this nature did not warrant the attention of the president,” he wrote. “Further, Mr. Geithner played no role in, and had no knowledge of, the disclosure deliberations and communications referenced in those emails.”

– Ruth Bader Ginsburg says she plans to stay on the Supreme Court until she's 90. "I'm now 85," Ginsburg told a crowd in New York on Sunday, per the Guardian. "My senior colleague, Justice John Paul Stevens, he stepped down when he was 90, so think I have about at least five more years." The 85-year-old, who has been on the court since 1993, added that she has already hired law clerks for at least two more terms, CNN reports. Ginsburg spoke after a performance of The Originalist, a play about her former colleague and friend Antonin Scalia, who died in 2016. "If I had my choice of dissenters when I was writing for the court, it would be Justice Scalia," Ginsburg said, saying that the back and forth would help her form her arguments. "Sometimes it was like a ping-pong game." She added that she is a "flaming feminist" and that "one change in my life is I am now recognized."

– "We hard for a big one for 2 days and finally got on this group. Made a perfect 200 yard shot." That's how Larysa Switlyk described her recent hunting trip to Scotland, where she posted photos to Instagram showing her holding up the head of a wild goat she'd killed, reports the New York Times. The images were decried as "disgraceful" and "sickening" by critics on social media, and Scotland's first minister promised to review the country's hunting laws. Meanwhile, Switlyk, a former accountant who hosts an online hunting show, defended her trip. "I was in Scotland over a month ago and will be without service for two weeks," she wrote on Instagram. "Hopefully that will give enough time for all the ignorant people out there sending me death threats to get educated on hunting and conservation." She added: "How does 'connect with nature' for a lot of service longer than that???" (This hunter received death threats after killing a giraffe.)

– A well-known drummer who's performed with A-list artists including Paul Simon, David Bowie, Diana Ross, Tupac, Dr. Dre, Daft Punk, and Johnny Cash has been charged with embezzling hundreds of thousands of dollars from a charity concert for homeless and displaced children in the world's conflict zones, NBC News reports. Robin DiMaggio, 47, was arrested Friday on a single felony charge of wire fraud. According to CBS Los Angeles, DiMaggio promised to help the Peace for You Peace for Me Foundation, a Bulgaria-based nonprofit, with organizing a charity concert in the Bulgarian capital of Sofia that was designed to raise money for and raise awareness of homeless and displaced children from conflict zones throughout the world. "He took the money, deposited it into his own account, never put it in an escrow account, and then spent the money on cars, living expenses, and purchasing a home for his ex-wife," Assistant US Attorney Poonam Kumar says. DiMaggio allegedly told the foundation's financial sponsor that he would be able to secure several celebrities to perform at the charity concert. In August 2016, the foundation's financial sponsor allegedly wired $750,000 to a DiMaggio-controlled account as a guarantee for future payments related to artists

Tallahassee Mayor Andrew Gillum, an unabashed progressive, won the Democratic primary, moving him a step away from becoming the state's first black governor. He'll face off against Trump-backed Republican Rep. Ron DeSantis, the AP reports. DeSantis gave Trump credit for his victory, saying that with one supportive tweet, the president "kind of put me on the map." Gillum is his party's third black gubernatorial nominee this year, along with Stacey Abrams in Georgia and Ben Jealous in Maryland. The results immediately transformed the Florida race into one of the most closely watched gubernatorial campaigns in the country. Gillum's primary victory could help Democrats boost enthusiasm among minorities who often don't vote in large numbers in years when a presidential candidate isn't on the ballot. Meanwhile, DeSantis will test Trump's grip on a crucial state he won in 2016 and wants to keep in his column in 2020. In Arizona, primary contests were shadowed by the death of Sen. John McCain. – The relatives of a family killed in a Toyota crash that prompted a recall of millions of cars are suing the automaker. The lawsuit, filed yesterday, accuses Toyota of producing a “ fatally flawed vehicle” that led to the deaths of California Highway Patrol Officer Mark Saylor, his wife, their daughter, and his brother-in-law, Reuters reports. The family's 2009 Lexus ES350, which Saylor had taken out for service the day of the crash, “began to accelerate on its own,” the lawsuit says. Saylor, who was an experienced driver, tried to stop the car, but was unable to do so, the lawsuit says. Investigators found that a wrong-sized floor mat that trapped the accelerator was the cause of the crash. The lawsuit also names the El Cajon dealership that loaned the car to Saylor, according to the AP.

– At least five people have been killed and more than 1,000 injured in two days of protests against Egypt’s military leaders. Security forces and police stormed Cairo’s Tahrir Square yesterday, firing tear gas and birdshot in the second straight day of clashes, the Los Angeles Times reports. Protesters numbered as many as 20,000 before midnight. “We are on the brink of danger. Those asking for the government to fall are asking for the state to fall,” said Gen. Mohsen Fangary. But at times the military appears in denial, as if the deepening discontent against it can be placated or ignored in the run-up to next week’s parliamentary elections. The military is not ready to cede the country's future to an array of political interests, including remnants of the old regime and the dominant Muslim Brotherhood. These forces mistrust one another but they—along with thousands of idle, angry young men—have banded against what they all regard as the larger enemy in the ruling Supreme Council of the Armed Forces. But political parties, especially Islamist groups, face a dilemma: They want to tap into the spirit of the protests but do not want violence to jeopardize the country's first significant elections in decades. – If you’ve ever wondered what it’s like to be a hipster, check out Hipster Puppies and Hipster Kitty. They’re both “cute animals” that combine two of the Internet’s favorite things: cute animals and making fun of hipsters, Time reports. “Hipster Puppies proves that you don't need an original idea to create a popular blog; you simply need to combine two things that people love—and sometimes love to hate,” writes Mary Elizabeth Williams.

– The owner of the convenience story that sold the only winning ticket for the $758.7 million Powerball jackpot says she is happy and emotional after learning her store sold it. Kamaljeet Kaur, who owns Handy Variety in Watertown, Mass., says she was getting ready to come to work Thursday morning when her husband told her. Reporters descended on the store hours before it opened around 6:30am, the AP reports. The jackpot is the largest grand prize won by a single lottery ticket in US history. Watertown is the suburb to which the Boston Marathon bombers fled. Tamerlan Tsarnaev was killed in an ensuing gunbattle with police, and his brother Dzhokhar was captured hiding in a boat in a Watertown man's backyard. The Massachusetts State Lottery announced around 2:30am Thursday that a convenience store in Watertown, near Boston, had sold the winning ticket. But shortly before 8am, the lottery said it had made a mistake, and that the winning ticket was sold across the state at the Pride Station & Store in Chicopee, in Western Massachusetts. The lottery did not say how the error was made. It said the store in Watertown did sell a ticket that won a $1 million prize.

– Michigan's Republican Party is apologizing after a mailer directed voters to a phone number under a Democratic candidate's name, MLive.com reports. "Tell him hard-working Michiganders are being hurt by ObamaCare and the health care policies (Democrats) support," read the mailer, which was paid for by the Michigan GOP. The number is registered under the name of 64-year-old John Fisher, who's running for the state House, but is actually a direct line to his 91-year-old mother's room at a nursing home. "To direct people to call a suffering woman who deserves peace and comfort is beyond the pale," Fisher said in a statement. "Their lack of ethics and contempt for personal privacy is just another reason for people to question what—or better, who—the Republican Party stands for, so that they can make a wise decision at the ballot box on Nov. 4." Fisher's Republican opponent, Kalamazoo County Commissioner Brandt Iden, says he doesn't condone "negative campaign tactics," but he hopes Fisher will do the same. "I'm doing it in part to point out the lack of responsibility and thoughtfulness which is what I'm running against," Fisher tells Newschannel 3.

– The origins of the AIDS pandemic have long been a topic of debate, and a new study in Science sheds light on the origins of the virus. Researchers say it started in the Democratic Republic of Congo's capital, Kinshasa, in the 1920s, thanks to a "perfect storm" of factors, including a sex trade, rapid population growth, and unsterilised needles in health clinics, the BBC reports. Kinshasa was part of the Belgian Congo at the time, and the "perfect storm" conditions lasted just a few decades, but by the 1940s, the virus was already spreading around the world, thanks in large part to the city's railways. The study, which analyzed HIV's genetic code, found that a mutated version of a chimpanzee virus made a number of jumps from infected blood while handling bush meat, ultimately jumping to humans. The virus was eventually found in humans in the late '20s in two cities in the southeastern part of the country, likely aided by the "extensive rail system" that then existed, the researchers say. "It does seem an interesting study demonstrating very elegantly how HIV spread in the Congo region long before the Aids epidemic was recognized in the early 80s," one infectious diseases expert tells the BBC. – A tetraplegic man in England was left brain-damaged after a nurse switched off his ventilator by mistake, the BBC reports. Jamie Merrett, 37, has been cared for at home since being left paralyzed from the neck down in a 2002 road accident. He had become increasingly concerned about the care he was receiving, his sister says, but health bosses did not act on emails he sent complaining about nurses operating his ventilator. In January 2009, he arranged to have a camera installed in his room. Within days, it captured Violetta Aylward switched off the ventilator, leaving him brain-damaged. A confidential report by Wiltshire social services into the incident concluded the agency agency was fully aware it was required to supply a nurse with training in use of a ventilator, but the company did not have adequate systems in place to check what training their staff had received. The BBC reports that Aylward has been suspended pending an investigation.

– Kim Jong Un is now North Korea’s “supreme commandership” of the army, state media announced today, according to CNN. The younger Kim was made “supreme leader” of the North Korean army on Oct. 8, at the request of his father, Kim Jong Il. The news comes a day after North Korea said a change in leadership would not mean a change in policy. “We solemnly declare with confidence that the South Korean puppets and foolish politicians around the world should not expect any change,” the country’s National Defense Commission said in a statement. The North blasted South Korea for “culminated in its act of blocking south Koreans who wanted to visit Pyongyang to mourn the demise of leader Kim Jong Il.” The North also criticized the South for allowing a select group of South Koreans to visit Pyongyang to pay their respects to Kim Jong Il. The North “will have no dealings with the Lee Myung-bak group of traitors forever,” the statement said.

– Sam's Club is closing 19 stores across the US, including three in Indiana, in what CEO John Furner calls a "difficult but necessary" decision. Per USA Today, the stores being closed are in Alaska, Arizona, California, Connecticut, Florida, Idaho, Michigan, Minnesota, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas, and Wisconsin. Walmart, which bought Sam's Club in Sam's Town in 2000, says it will offer severance packages and job training to affected employees, the Wall Street Journal reports. "Transforming our business means managing our real estate portfolio—we need a strong fleet of clubs that are fit for the future," Furner wrote in an email to employees Thursday. "After a thorough review, it became clear we had built clubs in some locations that impacted other clubs, and where population had not grown as anticipated. We've decided to right-size our fleet and better align our locations with our strategy."

– Police accidentally wounded nine bystanders yesterday when they opened fire on the gunman outside the Empire State Building, the New York Daily News reports. Commissioner Ray Kelly says the two officers confronting Jeffrey Johnson shot 16 rounds, but they hit "flowerpots and other objects around, so ... their bullets fragmented and, in essence, that's what caused the wounds," he said today. Investigators believe at least seven of those 16 rounds struck the gunman, according to NYPD spokesman Paul Browne. Browne stressed that the officers were justified in using deadly force though: “They were approaching this man with a gun, and he turns on them, and he is eight feet away, pointing a gun right at them.” You can see surveillance video of the two officers confronting and shooting Johnson here.

– Every year for the past 50 years, a local pilot has flown a plane over Yellville, Ark., and dropped turkeys from it as part of the annual Turkey Trot festival, which has drawn opposition from animal-rights activists. But while turkeys can slow a fall by flapping their wings, they can't do it forever, Michael Habib, a professor of anatomy at the University of Southern California, tells Live Science. "A lot of flightless birds have wings that can produce lift; it's just not enough to fly," he says. Domestic turkeys can't fly, but wild turkeys can, and like other birds in their order, they can slow a fall by using their wings to break it down. Habib says the turkeys dropped from the plane are too heavy and shapely for this to work, and that's why two of the dozen turkeys that were dropped last year died on impact. The turkeys are so heavy because their wings are too small and relative to their body size to generate lift, Habib says. – The US government's push to go "paperless" is taking a toll on seniors and others who don't have Internet access, two members of Congress write in the Washington Post. The Treasury, Social Security, and other agencies are trying to do away with paper services, but "millions of seniors remain uncomfortable with technology—and even more cannot even access it—should stop," write Rep. Sean P. Duffy, a Republican, and Rep. Michael H. Michaud, a Democrat. "Government agencies shouldn't be rushing to make these changes, and Congress should have proper oversight of such significant shifts in policy that negatively affect our seniors and all Americans." Indeed, a recent poll found that 73% of Americans think it's wrong to expect people without Internet access to interact with government agencies online, and 85% say federal decisions on paper-based services should be handled by Congress. The push to go paperless is "dis disenfranchising millions of seniors and other vulnerable Americans, and making the digital divide even deeper," the lawmakers write. "Our job is to serve the American people. That means maintaining and protecting access."

– Google wants to take 90% of Microsoft Office users away from Microsoft, and it's not just Office users who it's targeting. "Our goal is to get to the 90% of users who don’t need to have the most advanced features of Office," a Google exec tells Forbes. Google has been working to woo business customers away from Microsoft's office productivity suite by offering its own online productivity suite, Google Apps. When Google Apps first launched, they were free to use, but recently Google has started charging users to access the apps. "While Google knows there are gaps between its features and features that Microsoft offers, it's continually adding features and improvements to its service in an attempt to win the 90% of Office users," the exec says.

– Bai Yun is known to spend up to 12 hours a day munching on bamboo at the San Diego Zoo. On Wednesday, she had to go to the dentist. The 23-year-old mother of six had a dental procedure to fix a chipped canine tooth, the San Diego Union-Tribune reports. Pandas use their teeth to chew and break apart bamboo, which is their primary source of nutrition. A bad tooth can be hard on any animal. But pandas are particularly vulnerable to damaged or worn down teeth. The problem is that bamboo is chewy and not particularly nutritious. To get enough nutrition, giant pandas need to eat a lot of bamboo and they spend a lot of time chewing and breaking it apart. Bai Yun has been known to spend up to 12 hours a day dining on bamboo.

– The five-second rule is a bunch of boloney, according to Clemson University food scientist Paul Dawson, who stirred up the long-debated issue in this month's National Geographic. Though previous research has shown we may have up to a minute to rescue certain types of spilled food before it becomes contaminated, Dawson and his students made a strong case for the "zero-second rule." They found that salmonella and other bacteria can live up to four weeks on dry surfaces and be immediately transferred to food. The zero-second rule is alive and well at Illinois same-day surgery centers, according to the AP, despite the findings of two Connecticut College student researchers who sprinkled apple slices and Skittles candies in the college dining hall and snack bar for five, 10, 30 and 60-second intervals. The apple slices picked up bacteria after one minute; nearly five minutes before the Skittles attracted any. Then there were the University of Maine undergraduates who concluded that using the five-second rule could reduce food waste and possibly improve children's immune systems. Still, most researchers agree that the critical thing is not time, but location. It's OK to brush off the bagel that fell from the stroller onto the sidewalk and give it to your screaming child, for example,

His family will sell the photo at a sale of militaria in Bristol on March 29. The UK Intellectual Property Office ruled this week that Scottish craft brewer BrewDog must change the name of its 2015 Elvis Juice IPA after receiving a copyright infringement notice from the estate, Munchies reports. BrewDog co-founders Martin Dickie and James Watt changed their names to Elvis in response to the notice, saying Elvis wasn't the only Elvis out there and suggesting the estate "divert its attention to another potential source of quick remuneration: a brewery that calls itself 'The King' of beer." The hearing officer agreed, saying most consumers "on seeing the name Elvis alone, are likely to conceptualise that on the basis of Elvis Presley." BrewDog now has to change the beer's name or ask the Presley estate for "official permission" to use the name, the Guardian reports.

Twenty years later, his death is being honored as one of the most heinous hate crimes in American history—and one that led to the passage of the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act, which expanded federal hate crime laws to include attacks motivated by a victim's gender or sexual orientation. "It's meaningful to process how much time has gone by," Jason Marsden, Shepard's executive director of the Matthew Shepard Foundation, tells the New York Times. "Obviously, now, we are in a very different position with same-sex marriage being legal nationwide." But, he adds, "a tremendous amount of work remains to be done." Anti-gay or anti-LGBT attacks accounted for the most frequent types of hate crimes in the 10 largest US cities in 2017, according to a report by the Center for the Study of Hate & Extremism at California State University, San Bernardino. – John Kerry arrived in Pakistan today on the first visit by a high-ranking US official since the raid that killed Osama bin Laden, and emerged with a series of promises to repair relations between the two countries, reports the Washington Post. Hillary Clinton will visit soon, he said, "a sign of confidence in the relationship." Kerry also announced that Pakistan would return the tail of a damaged US helicopter that had to be destroyed during the bin Laden raid, reports the Los Angeles Times. Kerry said the two countries had agreed to "specific series of steps" to improve relations, but didn't specify what those steps were. He also defended the US decision not to tell Pakistan in advance of the raid. "When I spoke with the leaders of Pakistan last night and today, I explained that the extreme secrecy surrounding every aspect of the raid in Abbottabad was essential to protecting the lives of the professionals who were involved and ensuring they succeeded in capturing or killing the man responsible for so much death in so many places."

– It's not too late to get a flu shot, health experts say—but if you don't get one before this year's flu season kicks in, you may not be as protected. CBS Chicago reports that eight Chicago-area hospitals have had to turn away emergency room patients this week because of the flu. "Emergency departments are getting overrun with people with respiratory illness," an Illinois health official tells the Chicago Sun-Times. "We are seeing an increase in influenza cases." The University of Chicago Medical Center's emergency room has seen 166 flu cases this season, compared to 43 last year. And CVS pharmacies have been flooded with flu patients, CBS reports. "It takes about two weeks between when you get the flu shot and when you're protected against the flu," says one doctor.

Seven more were killed in the western province of Herat, two more in eastern Khost province, and one in northern Baghlan province, health and local officials say. In Herat, around 500 men charged at the US consulate, throwing rocks and opening fire. The US embassy in Kabul tweeted that Americans should "please be safe out there," and Germany announced that it was pulling out of a small base in the northern Takhar province over security concerns.

In a blog post, the scientist who first proposed the theory in 1974 calls it "wildly implausible" and says it would be impossible to produce such an effect using radar or a commercial microwave generator. "To induce such an effect, one could cobble together a device from a military radar set or a commercial microwave generator, such as the one I used in my original experiments, and then direct a beam at a distant target," writes Chen Yan. Putin appeared on a music channel to hand out an award, but instead of receiving it he rapped and spoke out against drugs and vodka. "Rap, even urban rap and street rap, is kind of crude, but is already filled with social content and addresses the problems of youth," he said. "Graffiti is becoming a real art form— refined and polished. Break dancing is something completely unique." One Moscow newspaper called the move a "desperate move" to appeal to the nation's youth, notes the Independent.

– A team of explorers has re-enacted Ernest Shackleton's 1916 voyage to raise the alarm about the sinking of his ship, and they've made it across the Antarctic despite a blizzard that stranded most of their support team. "It was epic, really epic, and we've arrived here against the odds," expedition leader Tim Jarvis tells the Global Post. He says he and fellow climber Barry Gray had more than 20 crevasse falls up to their knees during the 2,950-foot climb over the interior of South Georgia, requiring their one-man support crew to help pull them free. "These early explorers were iron men in wooden boats, and while modern man mostly travel around in iron vessels, I hope we've been able to emulate some of what they achieved," he says. "There's no doubt in my mind that everyone has a Shackleton double in them and I hope we've inspired a few people to find theirs." The journey from Elephant Island to Stromness, South Georgia, took 12 days, with Jarvis and Gray re-enacting Shackleton's journey in a spartan lifeboat from Elephant Island to South Georgia, along with four other members of the British-Australian team.

– Could Apple be preparing to go head-to-head with Google for street-level mapping? A number of cars have been spotted in San Francisco driving around with cameras and scanning equipment registered to Apple, the Guardian reports. A New York-area blog also spotted a similar vehicle last year, and a video posted on YouTube in September shows a similar Dodge minivan in New York with the same LIDAR camera system, which Google and other companies have used to create Street View imagery. Apple hasn't commented on the mystery vehicles, but an update to its maps app for the iPhone and iPad, iOS 9, is expected to debut in the summer and include street-level photography. "A test in New York and San Francisco isn't enough to map all of the world's streets," the Guardian notes. "Google also uses LIDAR cameras to help power its self-driving cars. In the video published on YouTube, you can see a spinning camera system at the rear of the vehicle."

– President Trump signed an executive order Thursday that could roil the Affordable Care Act insurance markets—and he tweeted about it Friday morning. "The Democrats ObamaCare is imploding. Massive subsidy payments to their pet insurance companies has stopped," he tweeted. "Dems should call me to fix!" The Washington Post reports that Trump's move to stop paying subsidies could cause premiums to rise for people currently covered under the ACA. The subsidies are paid out in monthly installments to insurers, which in turn lowers the cost of coverage for those who buy it. Trump's order would allow the sale of "short-term" plans that don't meet the ACA's requirements on benefits and costs. The New York Times reports that the move could cause a spike in premiums for people currently covered under the ACA. The president's order also could make it easier for small businesses to band together to buy insurance, which is a goal of Trump and many Republicans. Politico reports that Trump's move to stop paying the subsidies could be a "double whammy" for the Affordable Care Act markets.

Those are the words of Susan Yanow, a spokeswoman for Women Help Women, which this week launched a website to help US women perform their own abortions, the Guardian reports. The website, Self-managed Abortion, Safe and Supported, or SASS, connects US women with counselors who are trained by medical professionals to walk them through the process of using misoprostol, an abortion-inducing drug that can be purchased over the counter in many Central American pharmacies. – The brother of tennis star Andy Murray has become the youngest person to reach the South Pole on a solo trek. Scott Sears, a lieutenant in the First Battalion Royal Gurkha Rifles, pulled a sled and supplies for 38 days through 150mph winds in temperatures of -50 degrees before reaching his destination on Christmas Day, the BBC reports. The Guinness Book of Records has yet to confirm whether the 27-year-old's feat will make it into the record books. "I've never experienced anything like it, I would take a couple of steps and just stop, everything was just saying 'no more, not one more step,'" Sears wrote on his blog after hitting a wall on Christmas Eve. "It was bizarre as I've genuinely been feeling pretty good." Sears, who spent five weeks negotiating 700 miles of Antarctic plateau, crevasse fields, and glaciers on his own, hung his socks up as makeshift stockings but reached the pole in blue skies the next day. Sunder Raj, 48, and Pandit Tiwari, 52, of the Sentinelese tribe were fishing for mud crabs on North Sentinel Island on Jan. 25 when their open-topped boat apparently got stuck in the mud, reports the Independent. – A new study finds that people with the highest levels of optimism are twice as likely to be in ideal cardiovascular health as their pessimistic counterparts. "This association remains significant, even after adjusting for socio-demographic characteristics and poor mental health," says the lead author of the study, published in the journal Health, Behavior, and Policy Review. Optimists also had significantly better blood sugar and total cholesterol levels than their counterparts, and they were more physically active, had healthier body mass indexes, and were less likely to smoke, reports the New York Times. "It’s incentive to try to be optimistic, which is oftentimes difficult in the times we live in, in the world we live in and the sad news all the time," one physician tells CBS New York. "But if you knew that you could actually save your life, I think that’s a pretty good prescription." The study looked at more than 5,100 adults and found that happiness and optimism were linked to lower heart disease and stroke risk, though it's not clear whether a positive outlook directly protects health, or whether people who are generally in good health simply have more reason to be happy and optimistic.

– A "cloud of radioactive pollution" over Europe appears to have been caused by an accident at a nuclear facility in Russia or Kazakhstan in the last week of September, the French nuclear safety institute IRSN says. The institute says it measured high levels of ruthenium 106, a radioactive nuclide that is the product of splitting atoms in a nuclear reactor, in the atmosphere of most of Europe between Sept. 27 and Oct. 13. The institute ruled out an accident in a nuclear reactor, as that would have led to contamination with other radionuclides, and also ruled out the crash of a ruthenium-powered satellite as an IAEA investigation has concluded that no ruthenium-containing satellite has fallen back on Earth during this period. IRSN estimates that the quantity of ruthenium 106 released was major, between 100 and 300 teraBecquerels, and that if an accident of this magnitude had happened in France it would have required the evacuation or sheltering of people in a radius of a few kilometers around the accident site. The ruthenium 106 was probably released in a nuclear fuel treatment site or center for radioactive medicine, Peres says

According to the study, 14% of high school seniors in Southern California reported smoking cigarettes or e-cigarettes in the previous 30 days in 2014. That's the same rate as in 1995, when 12th-grade smoking rates were 19%, the Times reports. The study found that all of the teenagers expected to be smoking cigarettes in 2014 are now using e-cigarettes, and there's also a new group of teens using e-cigarettes "on top of that." E-cigarettes contain nicotine and flavorings, and the study found that most teens were using nicotine-infused liquid in their e-cigarettes. – A comprehensive study of 408 men in their mid-30s has cast doubt on the notion that chronic marijuana use is linked to mental and physical health problems down the road, reports Medical News Today. "What we found was a little surprising," says lead researcher Jordan Bechtold of the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center. "There were no differences in any of the mental or physical health issues." The study, published in the American Psychological Association journal Psychology of Addictive Behaviors, tracked the men for 20 years starting when they were in their teens. Researchers found that men who used pot regularly as teens were no more likely to suffer health problems in their mid-30s than men who rarely or never used the drug, men who took up the habit in adulthood, or men who became chronic pot users as they grew up, reports the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette. "This is the first study to show that chronic marijuana users were not more likely than late increasing users, adolescence-limited users, or low/nonusers to experience several physical or mental health problems in their mid-30s," says Bechtold. "In fact, there were no significant differences between marijuana trajectory groups in terms of adult health outcomes, even when models were run without controlling for potential confounds." – A new study suggests that babies who start looking at other people's eyes as early as two months old may be at higher risk for developing autism later. The research, based on eye-tracking data on 110 babies, suggests that the earliest sign of autism may be the decline in attention, the New York Times reports. "This paper is a major leap forward," says a pediatrician not involved in the study. "Documenting that there’s a developmental difference between 2 and 6 months is a major, major finding." The study, published in Nature, found that the babies who looked at other people's eyes the most—10 times in two months and 10 times by age 3—developed the most severe form of autism. "Kids whose eye fixation falls off most rapidly are the ones who later on are the most socially disabled and show the most symptoms," says one of the study's authors. "These are the earliest known signs of social disability, and they are associated with outcome and with symptom severity. Our ultimate goal is to translate this discovery into a tool for early identification" of children with autism, he adds.

– The hackers who got into Target's system did so as far back as July, and the breach was not fully contained until Sunday, sources tell the New York Times. Neiman Marcus, meanwhile, says that some customers' credit card numbers were used fraudulently after making purchases at its stores. The company says it has "no knowledge of any connection" between the two breaches, though it did tell credit card companies around Christmas that some cards had been used to make fraudulent purchases, according to the Times' sources. Neiman Marcus says it will provide one year of credit monitoring for all affected customers, similar to what Target is offering, NBC News reports. The security breach at Target was caused by malware similar to a computer virus placed in a store's point-of-sale systems, according to a 17-page report filed to the Secret Service by computer firm iSight. "While some components of the breach operation were technically sophisticated, the operational sophistication of the compromise activity makes this case stand out," the report states.

– Vincent Van Gogh's paintings are so saturated with color that it's hard to believe they were created more than a century ago. But a new exhibit at the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam reveals that some of the artist's favorite paints have faded, making his works " milder, more empty, less exquisite in their use of complementary colors than they were when he painted them," reports the Guardian. The exhibit also reveals that Van Gogh reused his canvases, sometimes painting on the back to keep them fresh, and that he was friends with artists such as Gauguin and Toulouse-Lautrec, who bought their works at the same shop. "Normally, the idea is these paintings are there for a hundred years, or five hundred years, and they’re static—nothing really changes," says Koen Janssens of the University of Antwerp in a press release. "But the opposite is actually true when you look in detail." Janssens and his colleagues used X-ray technology to study a wheat stack painted under a cloudy sky in Van Gogh's 1889 work "The Yellow House." – Kanye West spent his Labor Day weekend in Kazakhstan, where he performed a private concert for the country's president's grandson, sources tell TMZ. It's not clear how much West was paid, but the sum was probably in the millions, the gossip site says. Kazakhstan's president, Nursultan Nazarbayev, is said to be worth billions, and the country is near the bottom of the world in terms of corruption, according to Complex. West's performance, of course, included "Can't Tell Me Nothing," and one of the wedding guests posted a video of him on stage.

– Last month was so hot in Death Valley, Calif., that it set a record for the hottest month in US history, USA Today reports. According to the National Weather Service, the average temperature in July was 107.39 degrees. That beats the previous record of 107.2 set in 1917. And it didn't drop below 89 degrees for all but three days of the month. The hottest day of the month was July 7, when it was 127 degrees. Death Valley is the hottest, driest, and lowest of all US national parks. It has no permanent residents.

– A bag carried to the moon aboard the Apollo 11 spacecraft and used for the first sample of lunar material is at the center a legal fight after the government mistakenly sold it during the criminal case against the former director of the Kansas Cosmosphere and Space Center. The white bag—which was flown to the moon on Apollo 11 in June 1969 and has lunar material embedded in its fabric—is "a rare artifact, if not a national treasure," the government said. The dispute is the latest legal twist in the case of Max Ary, the founder and longtime director of the Cosmosphere in Hutchinson who was convicted in November 2005 for stealing and selling museum artifacts. At issue in his prosecution were hundreds of missing space artifacts and memorabilia. The lunar bag was discovered in 2003 during the execution of a search warrant in a box located in Ary's garage. The US Attorney's Office asked a federal judge to set aside the final forfeiture order and rescind the bag's sale, saying that the National Aeronautics and Space Administration was not properly notified of its forfeiture because the bag was misidentified. The bag was sold at a government auction on Feb. 15, 2015 for $995 to Nancy Carlson in Inverness, Illinois. NASA learned the Apollo 11 bag had been sold without notice or permission

– Medicaid expansion is on the ballot in Maine on Nov. 7, and if voters approve, 70,000 low-income residents will gain access to free health care. Gov. Paul LePage, a Republican, has been one of the most vocal opponents of the Affordable Care Act's Medicaid expansion, which would cover an additional 70,000 low-income Maine residents. But the New York Times reports he's not on board with the expansion, which he says would be "pure welfare" and cost Maine taxpayers more than $500 million over five years. On Friday, he attacked hospitals that support the referendum, saying they "do not care about taking resources away from our most vulnerable Mainers—including our elderly and intellectually and physically disabled people—just so they can give free, taxpayer-funded healthcare to adults who should be working and contributing to the cost of their own health insurance." Maine Medical Center's CEO agrees, saying in a hospital newsletter that "it's obvious the CEO of Maine Med and other hospitals do not care about taking resources away from our most vulnerable Mainers," per the Portland Press Herald. The expansion would also create 4,000 jobs, improve health and access to preventive care, and reduce the state's uninsured rate, which is 9.1%, according to Gallup polling.

The company has filed for a patent on a system that uses its Autopilot technology to detect when it's time for a driver to activate his or her turn signal and put the signal on for him or her, Electrek reports. "An embodiment includes a method of automated turn signaling, the method comprising: determining, via the processor, that a vehicle will cross a lane line or turn based on a measured steering angle value that is within a value range stored in a memory," the patent application reads. "And activating, via the processor, the turn signal source based on the determination that a vehicle will cross a lane line or turn." The patent application doesn't say when the system will be available in Tesla's vehicles, but the Verge notes that it's "surprisingly" sound like it's not for self-driving cars. – Skin cancer is the No. 1 cancer in the US, but it's also one of the most expensive: A study published Tuesday in the Journal of Cancer Policy estimates indoor tanning beds are responsible for $343 million in medical costs per year. That's on top of the $127 billion the cancer will cost over the lifetime of people currently diagnosed with melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and basal cell carcinoma caused by using tanning beds, Reuters reports. "We already knew that the use of indoor tanning devices is damaging to health and can cause cancer, but we did not have a comprehensive documentation of the health impacts at the population level or an estimate of the costs of health care to treat these conditions," says Hugh Waters, a study co-author and an epidemiologist at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Researchers looked at 2015 data on indoor tanning use in the US and estimated 263,600 cases of skin cancer caused by the beds that year. They also looked at the prevalence and risk of melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and basal cell carcinoma, as well as the costs for treating them. "I believe you are a good person, but I do not believe that this film is a good film," Assange writes. "Your skills play into the hands of people who are out to remove me and WikiLeaks from the world. ... I believe that you should reconsider your involvement in this enterprise." The Hollywood Reporter has the full letter, in which Assange accuses the movie of being based on "a deceitful book by someone who has a vendetta against me and my organization." – Twitter CEO Dick Costolo is known for his work ethic and sense of humor, but he's also a firm believer in privacy. In a New York Times profile of the 38-year-old, the paper notes that he's often criticized for the company's aggressive defense of user privacy, including its fight with the Justice Department to keep the identities of WikiLeaks supporters secret. "No one wants a pen that’s going to rat them out," Twitter's chief lawyer says. "We all want pens that can be used to write anything, and that will stand up for who we are." Costolo, who moved to California with his wife and two children in 2009, is known for his quick decision-making and his work ethic—"he tends to bang his fingers on a tablet as if he’s playing an imaginary piano that won’t make any sounds," notes the Times—which has come to permeate the company's culture. "He’s had a dramatic impact on the company and the culture," co-founder Jack Dorsey said in a statement. "He’s questioned everything we started with and made it better."

– Women 15 and older will be able to buy the Plan B morning-after pill without a prescription starting next Monday, the FDA announced today. But they'll have to show a government-issued ID in order to do so, and the pill will be packaged with an age-verification code, the Washington Post reports. The move is partially in line with a judge's order earlier this month that the over-the-counter contraceptive be made available to all women, not just those with a prescription. "The data reviewed by the agency demonstrated that women 15 years of age and older were able to understand how Plan B One-Step works, how to use it properly, and that it does not prevent the transmission of a sexually transmitted disease," said FDA Commissioner Margaret Hamburg in a statement. But the Center for Reproductive Rights says it's not satisfied. "Lowering the age restriction to 15 for over-the-counter access to Plan B One-Step may reduce delays for some young women—but it does nothing to address the significant barriers that far too many women of all ages will still find if they arrive at the drugstore without identification or after the pharmacy gates have been closed for the night or weekend," the group said in a statement.

The document was filed in response to Cohen's request to prevent federal prosecutors from using records seized in Monday's FBI raids of his home and office, ABC News reports. Prosecutors say previous search warrants allowed them to search multiple email accounts, but they found that Cohen had done "little to no legal work, and that zero emails were exchanged with President Trump." Prosecutors say Cohen has told at least one witness that his only client is Trump, CNN reports. They say Cohen has not turned over any documents to Robert Mueller's Special Counsel investigation. Prosecutors say they've set up what's known as a " taint team" to review the records seized so nothing they seized is used improperly or breaches client confidentiality. Once they've reviewed the records, the filter team can give to the investigators communications "between Cohen and persons with whom Cohen undisputedly does not have an attorney-client relationship." – Mike Pence's "ignorant and stupid remarks gushing from the mouth of the US vice president" could lead to a "nuclear-to-nuclear showdown," says North Korea's vice minister of foreign affairs. Choe Son Hui made the warning in state news Thursday, days after Pence warned that North Korea "may end like Libya," where then-leader Moammar Gadhafi was killed by rebels in 2011, the BBC reports. "As a person involved in US affairs, I cannot suppress my surprise at such ignorant and stupid remarks gushing from the mouth of the US vice president," Choe said. She added: "Whether the US will meet us at a meeting room or encounter us at nuclear-to-nuclear showdown is entirely dependent upon the decision and behavior of the United States." Analysts say Choe's statement will have been sanctioned by Kim Jong Un, the AP reports. (President Trump has suggested the planned June 12 summit with North Korea could be delayed.)

– The man arrested for breaking into Sandra Bullock’s home may have been obsessed with the actress, law enforcement sources tell the Today show. Joshua Corbett, 39, may have even kept a diary about Bullock, the sources say. Corbett was arrested on suspicion of burglary after rummaging through Bullock’s personal belongings. Bullock was home with her 4-year-old son at the time of the break-in, People reports.

– Attorneys who contended "junk science" was used to send a father to death row for killing his 2-year-old daughter 14 years ago have won a reprieve blocking the Texas inmate's execution set for next week, the AP reports. Robert Roberson III, 49, was set to die Tuesday for the February 2002 death of his daughter, Nikki Curtis, at his home in Palestine in East Texas. But the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals sent his case back to his Anderson County trial court late Thursday to review claims he is innocent of capital murder. There is no timetable for the appeal to be resolved. One judge on the nine-member court, Lawrence Meyers, voted to refuse the reprieve and dismiss the appeal. Lawyers argued Roberson's conviction was based on "junk science" and "false, misleading, and scientifically invalid testimony" and that new scientific evidence establishes he would not have been convicted. The child had serious head injuries, and Roberson contended she accidentally fell from a bed. Medical staff at a Palestine hospital called police because they considered the injuries suspicious. Physicians who examined her said bruises to her chin, cheek, and jaw and a subdural hematoma—bleeding outside her brain but inside her skull—likely were intentional and no accident. – A Massachusetts woman was able to escape her home before it exploded Sunday afternoon after she removed the valve on a gas-fueled hot water heater, police say. Laurie Beliveau, 52, was attempting to repair the heater when she removed the valve and gas poured into the basement, where it was ignited by an unknown ignition source, according to a statement from the state fire marshal and Taunton fire chief. "Everything caved in. It's just a pile of lumber," the deputy fire chief tells ABC News. "Nothing is salvageable." A neighbor tells ABC that he and his son got Beliveau a pair of sandals and a glass of water as she ran down the street screaming for help. "We, my son and I, got her a pair of sandals and a glass of water and within about five minutes the house was in flames and the windows exploded," the neighbor says. "She was hysterically talking to the fire department about a gas fire place." Authorities suspect a gas leak caused the explosion.

– President Trump slammed a judge's temporary restraining order on his revised travel ban as "an unprecedented judicial overreach" just hours after the order was issued. Speaking at a rally in Nashville Wednesday night, Trump said the order was "tailored to the dictates of the 9th Circuit's—in my opinion—flawed ruling," ABC News reports. "This ruling makes us look weak," he said. "We are going to fight this terrible rule," Trump said. "We are going to take our case as far as it needs to go, including all the way up to the Supreme Court. We are going to win. We are going to keep our citizens safe and regardless, we are going to keep our citizens safe, believe me." Earlier Wednesday, a federal judge in Hawaii issued a temporary restraining order against the revised travel ban. US District Judge Derrick Watson said the Trump administration failed to show the US would be harmed if the ban prevented travelers from seven Muslim-majority countries from entering the US, the Honolulu Star-Advertiser reports. He also said the administration failed to show the US would be harmed if the ban didn't apply to people who already have a visa. The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals declined to stay the ruling.

– German Chancellor Angela Merkel says President Obama took her concerns over US spying on European allies very seriously during a phone call last night. "I made clear spying on institutions within the European Union is not how we would expect those we consider friends to treat us," she said today, according to Reuters. "We are no longer in the Cold War." The White House says Obama and Merkel agreed to high-level talks on intelligence and privacy early next week. Meanwhile, Germany's interior minister will travel to the US next week to investigate reports that the NSA spied on EU institutions, an EU spokesman says. Meanwhile, the leader of Germany's SPD party is calling for the country to give Edward Snowden witness protection if he is reliable, CNN reports.

– A doctor's engagement photo on Facebook led to a murder-suicide at her wedding reception last night in India, the Hindustan Times reports. Jayshree Namdeo's first cousin, Anurag Singh, 31, allegedly entered the wedding hall in Bhopal with a country-made pistol and went on a shooting spree, killing the 26-year-old bride before being overpowered by guests. Namdeo's family disapproved of the relationship between Singh and the only child of her parents, a doctor at the Gandhi Medical College in Bhopal. "We had planned to convince Anurag after the marriage," a relative says. "In the past, Anurag would fight with anyone who tried to dissuade him and would threaten relatives. He once sent a threatening SMS to me." Singh allegedly bought the pistol a day before the wedding and planned the killing for 20 days, the Times of India reports. He told police he shot Namdeo after she changed her relationship status on Facebook to "just wait and watch." Singh was beaten by guests and is now in the hospital. Namdeo's father says he didn't invite her family to the wedding because he didn't think Singh would go that far.

– More than half of all births in Brazil are Cesarean sections, and the country's health minister has called them an "epidemic." The new rules, which went into effect Monday, are an attempt to reduce the rush for C-sections, which the World Health Organization says should only be performed between 10% and 15% of all births. Brazil still leads the world in C-sections, but with the new rules, doctors and hospitals are now required to give patients information on the number of C-sections they've already performed, and health insurance companies face fines of up to $8,000 if they fail to do so, AFP reports. The director of a specialized health ministry agency says the new rules will "be more sure in her decision regarding the delivery, choosing what's best for her health and for her baby's health." But pediatrician Luciana Herrero, author of a book on childbirth in Brazil, says doctors and hospitals are also to blame for the rush for C-sections. – An elderly Texas man is dead after he went back into his burning home to get his cell phone, reports CBS DFW. Rex Benson, 72, and another man escaped from the house when the fire started around 1am yesterday; the other man's roommate and Benson's adult daughter also made it out, but Benson had to go back in to call 911. "Nine people out of 10 that return back into a burning building don't make it out alive," says a local fire captain. "That's evident here and it's really tragic." Firefighters arrived three minutes after the first call came in and found the house "fully engulfed," says the fire captain. Benson was found dead inside, and his roommate survived. "Great guy, willing to help anyone who needed a hand; and to hear he made that big of a mistake and the loss of life because of something as simple as a cellphone seems sad," a neighbor tells NBC DFW. "This is a notch in the statistic on the wrong end." The cause of the fire is under investigation.

An arrest warrant was issued for Jayveon Caballero on a murder charge following the Sunday morning shooting in Montpelier, police said. Police said the bus was headed to New York City but had several intermediate stops where he could have gotten off. Caballero and Austin had been involved in an altercation outside Gustos bar in Barre earlier Sunday morning, police said. During the altercation Austin assaulted Caballero's girlfriend, witnesses said. Caballero later confronted Austin outside Austin's apartment and shot him, police said. – The Wall Street Journal's take on Apple's firing of iOS chief Scott Forstall is pretty straightforward: It's because Steve Jobs was too proud to sign the company's apology for Maps. Forstall had called the product "fantastic" in his presentation of it, but he neglected to make sure it had enough geographical data to be useful, and he didn't warn Apple users that the software wasn't quite ready. "I suspect that’s why Cook’s tossed Apple’s powerful iOS chief, Scott Forstall, out the frying pan, reportedly because Jobs’ golden child was too proud to sign the company’s apology over the Maps affair," writes David Pogue at the New York Times. "Apple may be working away at its pride problem, after all," he writes. Forstall's ouster is a sign that Tim Cook is serious about turning Apple into a software company, not a hardware one, writes Farhad Manjoo at Slate. "Apple is a software company. It’s hardware may be good, but it is the software that defines the user experience. At best Apple is all about focus: focus on the customer; focus on the products; focus on the company." Click for his full column.

– Pope Francis wasted little time in making good on his promise to spread the faith to the world's outcasts, telling tens of thousands of people gathered in St. Peter's Square today that "we must not forget that hatred, envy, and pride defile our lives," reports the New York Times. "We must not be afraid of goodness or even tenderness," he said during his inaugural Mass. Francis, the son of Italian immigrants to Argentina, is the first pope from Latin America, and the first Jesuit pope, notes CNN. He spoke of the "poorest, the weakest, the least important, those whom Matthew lists in the final judgment on love: the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the sick, and those in prison," reports AP. He received two symbolic symbols from the Vatican: a fisherman's ring and a pallium, a white woolen vestment.

– The Weinstein Company has filed for bankruptcy, months after its co-founder, Harvey Weinstein, was accused of sexual harassment and assault by dozens of women. The company's board says it has entered into a "stalking horse" agreement with an affiliate of private equity firm Lantern Capital Partners to buy substantially all of the company's assets, the Guardian reports. "Today, the Company also takes an important step toward justice for any victims who have been silenced by Harvey Weinstein," the company said in a statement. "Effective immediately, those 'agreements' end." New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman, who filed a lawsuit against the company last month on behalf of its employees, praised the move. "The Weinstein Company's agreement to release victims of and witnesses to sexual misconduct from NDAs will finally allow voices that have too long been muzzled to be heard—something my office has sought from the start," Schneiderman said in a statement. "No one should be afraid to speak out or coerced to stay quiet. The Company thanks the courageous individuals who have already come forward. Your voices have inspired a movement for change across the country and around the world." The bankruptcy filing lists $500 million to $1 billion in liabilities and up to $1 billion in assets, Variety reports.

– North Korea has reportedly executed two senior officials with anti-aircraft guns. If the report in South Korea's JoongAng Ilbo is true, it would mark the first time Kim Jong Un has ordered an execution from outside his party or military, Bloomberg reports. The two men were reportedly arrested for dozing off during a meeting with Kim, possibly education minister Ri Yong Jin. The former agriculture minister, Hwang Min, was reportedly killed for proposing a project that would have challenged Kim's leadership. "Kim is continuing to replace the old guard of his father's regime with loyalists," a political science professor at South Korea's Pusan National University tells Bloomberg. "The charges are obviously trumped up, and this is how promotion or demotion often works in totalitarian states without legitimate venues for opposition." The executions could be a response to recent high-level defections from North Korea, including that of Thae Yong Ho, the country's deputy ambassador to the UK, the Guardian reports. North Korea has denounced Thae as "human scum."

– Disney lost one of its great songwriters this week with the death of 86-year-old Robert B. Sherman in London, reports the Los Angeles Times. Sherman and his brother Richard won Oscars for best score for Mary Poppins and for "Chim Chim Cher-ee," among other things. They also wrote the most-played song on Earth, "It's a Small World (After All)," notes AP. "What seems so simple is really very complex," says Sherman's son, Jeffrey. "He was a very simple guy—complex but simple. If you ever want to know about my Dad, listen to the lyrics of his songs."

– For the first time in 88 years, a sitting US president will visit Cuba, ABC News reports. According to CNN, President Obama announced the trip Thursday. "14 months ago, I announced that we would begin normalizing relations with Cuba—and we've already made significant progress," he tweeted. "Our flag flies over our Embassy in Havana once again. More Americans are traveling to Cuba than at any time in the last 50 years." The last sitting US president to visit Cuba was Calvin Coolidge in 1928. Obama will meet with Cuban President Raul Castro during the trip, which will also include a visit to Argentina. "There is much more that can be done—by the United States, and by the Cuban government—to advance this opening in ways that will be good for Cubans, and good for the United States," Deputy National Security Adviser Ben Rhodes writes on Medium. Obama will be joined by Michelle Obama and the first family during the trip.

But a survey by the nonprofit America Saves—which polled 1,000 people three times a year for its Personal Savings Index—also found that September's numbers were "new highs," with savings interest up from 63% to 75%, effort up from 58% to 65%, and effectiveness up from 55% to 62%.
