– Andre Davis was just 19 when he left Chicago for Rantoul, Ill., to learn the business of his father, a disc jockey. Thirty years later, the young man's body has been found in an alley in the town of 20,000, the Chicago Tribune reports. Davis, who was known as "Crazy Legs" for his nightclub dance moves, had been shot three times in the face, neck, and torso, and was stabbed twice in the torso. His body was discovered on Oct. 26. Police have charged Andre's uncle, Andre Davis, 52, with his murder, and say he admitted to witnesses to cutting the throat of his nephew, Jamal Harmon, after an argument over a dice game, NBC Chicago reports. The two men had been at a party when Harmon got into an argument with Andre's nephew about losing money in the dice game, prosecutors say. A witness says Harmon was still alive after being shot, and Davis ordered another person to help him move the body. Davis drove away with Harmon in the trunk and witnesses say he told them he was going to find somewhere to dump Harmon's body. He has been charged with murder and kidnapping, prosecutors say.

– Antibiotic-resistant bacteria is on the rise, and the CDC wants people to know that it's time to stop taking them when they shouldn't. A new study published in the CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report finds that among all conditions and ages combined, 12.6% of people who visited an outpatient clinic for an acute respiratory condition were prescribed an antibiotic, reports the New York Times. That's about 34 million prescriptions per year, and researchers say it's not enough to just cut that number in half: It's necessary to cut overall antibiotic use by 15%. The study looked at 184,032 outpatient visits from 2010-2011, and found that 56 of those were for sinusitis, 47 for ear infections, and 43 for pharyngitis, reports Pharmacy Times. "Health professionals generally know when antibiotics are and are not needed," says lead author Katherine Fleming-Dutra. "Often, clinicians are worried about patient satisfaction. They think that a patient wants antibiotics ... sometimes leading them to prescribe when they shouldn't." The CDC wants to cut antibiotic use by 50% by 2020, but the new study suggests that a 15% reduction is necessary. (President Obama signed an executive order last fall calling for a 50% reduction.)

– Ten of the Nigerian schoolgirls who managed to escape Boko Haram's clutches after being kidnapped in April will be getting an education, a human rights group says. Jubilee Campaign USA, which supports religious freedom and human rights, is trying to raise $125,000 by Aug. 14 to send the girls to " specialized boarding schools where their traumatic experiences may be transformed into empowering triumphs over evil," a rep tells CNA. "These rescued girls are living in constant fear of Boko Haram's further vengeance and need your help," the group says on its website. "Through this campaign, these girls who due to cost, environmental threats, or ongoing Boko Haram violence in Nigeria, would otherwise be out of school and thus their future potential and healing neglected, will be able to enroll in a school where she will grow in wisdom and stature while gaining mental and emotional support." The group has also hosted a "100 Days of Captivity Rally" to mark 100 days since the girls were kidnapped, urging the Nigerian government to do everything it can to find and return them.

– Militants from the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria posted photos online last night of what they said were mass executions of 1,700 captured Iraqi soldiers in Tikrit, reports the New York Times. The militants said the executions took place at seven sites, and if true, it would be the largest slaughter in the region since the poison gas attack in Damascus last year. The captions read, "The liquidation of the Shiites who ran away from their military bases," and "This is the destiny of Maliki's Shiites," referring to Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki. The Times notes that the captions are " tailor-made to ignite anger and fear among Shiites," and it's not clear whether the number of victims is actually large enough to confirm the claims. But if true, the killings would mark a significant increase in the number of people ISIS has killed since it launched a major offensive earlier this month. The group has also killed dozens of civilians in Tikrit, and it is believed to have burned the city's police headquarters and government buildings.

– Japanese fishermen have begun the slaughter of more than 200 bottlenose dolphins in a cove in Taiji, and conservationists say many of the animals are stressed and bloodied. Twenty-five dolphins were taken to "to a lifetime of imprisonment" on Saturday, and another 12 were taken yesterday, according to the Sea Shepherd Conservation Society. Two dolphins have died in the process, CNN reports. The dolphins will spend a third night without food or rest before the fishermen begin the slaughter today. "Many of the 200+ Bottlenose dolphins who are in still the cove are visibly bloody & injured from their attempts to escape the killers," tweeted the conservation group. "Dolphin slaughter in Taiji continues because of the captive trade. Please do not support aquariums & parks with marine mammals." US Ambassador to Japan Caroline Kennedy tweeted that she is "deeply concerned by inhumaneness of drive hunt dolphin killing." The slaughter is a major event in the dolphin-hunting season in Taiji, and the Sea Shepherd Conservation Society has been live-streaming the event.

Prince William and wife Kate will be in the stands to support Phillips as she competes in today's cross-country competition, USA Today reports.

– The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is warning people to be on the lookout for Candida auris, a fast-spreading yeast infection that's resistant to common drugs used to treat it. The fungus, which can be spread through direct contact with an infected person or through contaminated food or water, can cause abscesses that can lead to kidney failure and, in rare cases, death, the Washington Post reports. It's especially dangerous to people with weakened immune systems, the elderly, or people who've had close contact with recently ill people, according to the CDC, which warns that people should follow "common-sense precautions" to prevent infection. " Candida auris is an emerging fungus that presents a serious global health threat," the CDC states. "It is difficult to identify with standard laboratory methods, and it can be misidentified in labs without specific technology. Misidentification may lead to inappropriate management. It has caused outbreaks in healthcare settings. For this reason, it is important to quickly identify Candida auris in a hospitalized patient so that healthcare facilities can take special precautions to stop its spread."

– The last jobs report before the election is in the books, and it shows that the US economy added 214,000 jobs in October, well below the 233,000 economists expected, reports the Wall Street Journal. The unemployment rate, however, ticked down from 5.9% to 5.8%. It's the lowest it's been since July 2008, notes the AP. The 214,000 is the ninth consecutive month that at least 200,000 jobs have been added, the longest such stretch since 1995. The last three months have seen job gains of at least 250,000. "The labor force participation rate, which measures the participation rate of people who are working and those who are out of the work force, remained unchanged at 62.8%," notes the Journal. But it's down from 62.9% a year ago. "The labor force participation rate has not been this low since early 2009 during the depths of the recession," writes Steven Russolillo at the Journal. "That said, the labor force participation rate is still below the levels that are typical of a healthy economy, which is a good thing."

– When a 7-year-old girl died of an allergic reaction at a Virginia school in 2013, the FDA made it legal for the EpiPen to be sold to anyone at risk of an allergic reaction, even if they'd already been prescribed the device by a doctor. That same year, drugmaker Mylan acquired the device, and since then, it's become a $1 billion-a-year business, Bloomberg reports. "They have done a tremendous job of taking an asset that nobody thought you could do much with and making it a blockbuster product," says a Leerink Partners analyst. But EpiPen's price has gone up about 400% since Mylan bought it in 2007—from about $57 per EpiPen to an average of $415 for a two-pack—and that's left many families with kids with severe allergies struggling to afford the life-saving injections. "It's become unaffordable for a lot of families," says the father of a 4-year-old boy with severe allergies. "It's not just for the kids, it's for the entire family." – The Supreme Court has ruled that public schools in the US don't have to tell parents when their kids are being paddled, hit with metal objects, or otherwise disciplined with physical force. The decision was 5-4, with Justice Anthony Kennedy writing for the majority, reports the AP. The ruling came in a case out of Florida in which a teen was paddled for refusing to take a test, reports the Miami Herald. The boy's parents sued, but the case ended up in the lower court, where a judge ruled that school officials had to tell the parents before using any kind of corporal punishment. The Supreme Court overruled that. "The history of the Eighth Amendment and the decisions of this Court make it clear that the prohibition against cruel and unusual punishment was designed to protect those convicted of crime," writes Kennedy. "There is no need to wrench the Eighth Amendment from its historical context and extend it to public school disciplinary practices." The high court has previously ruled that school officials can't be held liable for a child's punishment without a hearing.

– Rapidly losing and gaining weight—or "yo-yo" dieting—may increase the risk of heart attacks and strokes in people with stable coronary artery disease, according to a new study. Researchers followed 9,509 men and women with CHD for an average of 4.7 years, during which time they recorded their weight an average of 12 times a year, Medical News Today reports. Those with the largest weight fluctuations were 117 percent more likely to have a heart attack, 136 percent more likely to have a stroke, and 124 percent more likely to die, the New York Times reports. Those with the smallest fluctuations were only 2 pounds less likely to have a heart attack and stroke. "It’s important to lose weight," says the lead author. "But this data says you have to keep it off. Many times people are motivated until they lose the weight, and then they feel they can take it easy. Maybe this information can be used as motivation to keep the weight off."

– The FDA is investigating reports of seizures in infants and children who've taken "natural" homeopathic teething products, the agency announced Sept. 30. In a statement, the FDA warns that "consumers should seek medical care immediately if their child experiences seizures, difficulty breathing, lethargy, excessive sleepiness, muscle weakness, skin flushing, constipation, difficulty urinating, or agitation" after taking the products, Live Science reports. The FDA says it's not aware of any proven health benefit of using the products, which are not regulated as drugs by the FDA. Homeopathy is an alternative medicine practice based on the idea that "like cures like." In homeopathy, extremely minute concentrations of toxic substances are used under the idea that they could cure the symptoms that they would cause at higher doses. The FDA issued a safety alert about a homeopathic teething tablet that contained belladonna, a poisonous plant. Belladonna—also called deadly nightshade—is a poisonous plant that contains a chemical called atropine. In homeopathy, it is used to treat redness and inflammation. The company that made the teething tablets, Hyland, subsequently recalled the product. Instead, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends teething rings or hard, unsweetened teething crackers. Do not use frozen teething toys because they can cause more discomfort

– Last year, Apple recycled more than 61 million pounds of steel, aluminum, glass, and other materials, including 2,204 pounds of gold, the Verge reports. According to Fairphone, an activist group focused on electronics supply chains, the average smartphone uses 30 milligrams of gold, mostly in circuit boards and other internal components. And Apple pays to recycle millions of iPhones and other computers that have tiny bits of gold in them.

They say that while whale-watching is "not as bad as whaling," dolphins and whales are being killed by boats and stressed out by the activity, which has expanded from 4 million in 31 countries in 1991 to 13 million in 2008, the most recent year for which full data are available. The International Fund for Animal Welfare estimated the value of the industry at $2.1 billion in 2008. In Iceland, for example, researchers found that minke whales there responded to whale-watching boats as they do to natural predators by increasing their speed and respiring more heavily, but it's not clear whether this was a direct result of the boats. In New Zealand, researchers found that bottlenose dolphins there could be driven to extinction in the next 50 years thanks to the large number of whale-watching trips in Doubtful Sound. – If you're tired after a long day at work, take a break—but do it right, according to a new study in the Journal of Applied Psychology. Researchers at Baylor University surveyed 95 employees over a five-day workweek and asked them to document every break they took during the workday, from lunch to personal email to bathroom breaks. They found that employees who took breaks earlier in the day had more energy, concentration, and motivation, while those who took breaks later in the day had less, the Dallas Morning News reports. "We found that when more hours had elapsed since the beginning of the work shift, fewer resources and more symptoms of poor health were reported after a break," the study says. "Therefore, breaks later in the day seem to be less effective." The study debunks other break-time myths, including the belief that doing non-work-related things is better than work-related things, and that longer breaks are better than short ones. John McCain announced that he would not support the legislation, the White House announced that the ObamaCare website would be down from noon to 12pm every Sunday during next year's open enrollment period, the Washington Post reports. – Pizza Hut has launched an online service that allows customers to customize their pizzas and have them delivered to their homes in as little as 30 minutes, reports the Santa Cruz Sentinel. Customers use PizzaNet to create a menu, enter their personal information, and choose their toppings. The data is then transmitted to a central server at Pizza Hut headquarters in Wichita, reports Gizmodo. Customers can then call the restaurant to verify the order and pay with their credit card. "The hardest part was to get the Internet connection in," says a Pizza Hut exec. "Otherwise, this was very easy to execute ... almost routine."

– A fire official says about 10 people were sickened by a suspicious package in the mailroom of a sprawling IRS building in downtown Kansas City, Mo., the AP reports. Kansas City Fire Department spokesman James Garrett says 10 people complained of feeling ill, including vomiting and sweating, after the package arrived at the building Friday. He says two people were taken to a hospital. St. Luke's Hospital spokeswoman Laurel Gifford says those victims are in good condition. Garrett says the Fire Department was checking for gasses and fumes but hasn't determined the package's contents. He says the package was isolated from the public. The building was not evacuated and has returned to business. Garrett says the investigation has been turned over to the IRS and other federal authorities.

– Chemotherapy is often given to terminally ill cancer patients months before death so they can palliate their symptoms and improve their survival. But a new study finds that those who receive palliative chemotherapy are more likely to die in an intensive care unit in the last week of life, and are also more likely to die at home, the New York Times reports. The study, published in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute, looked at 386 adult patients who had at least one chemotherapy regimen but were deemed terminally ill at study enrollment and who died. The researchers found that those who received palliative chemotherapy were more likely to die in an intensive care unit (11%) than those who didn't (9%). They were also less likely to die in their preferred place (66% vs. 80%) and more likely to receive hospice care (at least one week before death vs. one week before death). But they found no difference in survival rates between those who received chemotherapy months before death and those who didn't (6.2% vs. 6.2%, respectively). – For the first time in almost half a century, fewer than half of Americans support the death penalty, according to a Pew Research Center poll released Wednesday. The poll found that just 49% of Americans back capital punishment, down seven points from last year and the lowest level of support since support hit 80% in 1994. Support for the death penalty has been declining every year since 1994, when it peaked at 80%, according to the poll. The decline in support may be due to the popularity of lethal injection drugs, which have been involved in multiple botched executions in the US. Support for the death penalty declined across all groups in the Pew poll, but it was especially pronounced among independents (down 16 points) and those who lean toward the Democratic Party (down 14 points). Support for the death penalty fell across all political parties, but it fell the most among independents (down 16 points) and those who lean toward the Republican Party (down 10 points). Support for the death penalty is now at its highest level since 1972, though support for capital punishment is still lower than it was in the mid-1990s, when eight in 10 supported it and fewer than two-in-10 opposed it. The Supreme Court will hear the first of two death penalty cases this year, CNN reports.

– If you eat meat, you may want to steer clear of the southeastern US. That's where the Lone Star Tick lives and where thousands of people have developed a life-threatening allergy to meat, reports Wired. The problem is that meat contains a sugar called galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose, or alpha-gal, and the body's immune system reacts badly to alpha-gal. The body releases histamines to deal with the allergen, but they also cause the rest of the body to swell up, leading to sweating, itching, difficulty breathing, and, in some cases, even death, Wired reports. The allergy was first identified in the 1990s by immunologist Thomas Platts-Mills, who noticed that people in the region were 10 times more likely to be allergic to a cancer drug called cetuximab than people elsewhere. Since cetuximab and mammal meat both contain alpha-gal, and since alpha-gal antibodies are present in affected blood, Platts-Mills hypothesized that the sugar was behind the allergy. – Brown University has punished two fraternities for hosting unregistered parties that "facilitated sexual misconduct," reports the Providence Journal. Phi Kappa Psi, for instance, was accused of serving a drink that contained a date-rape drug at an unregistered party in October, and one student reported "an incident of non-consensual sexual contact that did not happen within the fraternity’s facility nor did it involve a member of the fraternity, but its occurrence was a result of the student’s incapacitation." Sigma Chi, meanwhile, was accused of having an unregistered party in the basement of its residence in October and one student reported "an incident of non-consensual contact of a sexual nature that occurred as students were exiting the crowded basement." – Edward Snowden's father is in Russia today to meet his son, who has been granted temporary asylum. Lon Snowden arrived at Moscow's Sheremetyevo airport today and was met by his son's Russian lawyer, Anatoly Kucherena, the BBC reports. "I am his father, I love my son, and I certainly hope I will have an opportunity to see my son," Lon Snowden told reporters. He said he had no direct contact with his son for months, but felt "extreme gratitude that my son is safe and secure and he's free." He added that he was "not sure my son will be returning to the US again," Reuters reports. Kucherena later said Lon Snowden would meet with his son for a few days, but that he would have to travel "quite a number of kilometers" to get there.

– Michelangelo's David has been the victim of violence before. In 1527, his arm was smashed by rioters; in 1991, a man attacked his toe with a hammer. Now, Italy's culture minister says the 16-th-century statue has suffered his "greatest indignity to date" by being shown in an ad for an American-made AR-50A1 rifle, the Independent reports. "We will take action against the American company which must immediately withdraw the campaign," Dario Franceschini tweeted. The 60-year-old Illinois-based small-arms engineering company is part of its "Work of Art" campaign, which also includes an ad showing the Mona Lisa with a gun pointed at her head. The director of the Accademia Gallery, where David is on display, says the ad is both "bad taste" and "completely illegal," AFP reports. A city councilman in Florence, where the statue is located, says the depiction of David holding the rifle is "an act of violence towards the sculpture; like taking a hammer to it and perhaps, actually, even worse," according to La Repubblica. An art critic, however, says certain cultural icons " belong to everyone and no one."

– North Korea is set to begin fueling its long-range rocket this week, a South Korean official tells Yonhap News. Pyongyang has completed the installation of three stages of boosters on the launch pad and is expected to start fueling the rocket this week, considering it typically takes two to three days to complete the fueling. North Korea says the rocket will be launched between April 12 and 16 to mark the 100th anniversary of the birth of founder Kim Il Sung. But the US, Japan, and South Korea say the launch is a cover for a missile test, and Japan says it will shoot down any part of the rocket that enters its territory. North Korea allowed foreign journalists to tour the launch site yesterday, CNN reports. "If you look for yourselves with your own eyes, then you can judge whether it's a ballistic missile, or whether it's a launch vehicle to put a satellite into orbit," said the head of the launch site. "That's why we've invited you to this launch site."

– Skywatchers are in for a treat today: a "Blue Moon," the second in a row and the 13th of this year's, Space.com reports. It's not actually blue, of course, but the second full moon in a month is called a blue moon because it follows the second full moon in a calendar month. In other words, a blue moon occurs about once every 2.7 years, notes Space.com. Today's full moon coincides with the blood moon, a rare "supermoon" that happens when the moon is at its closest point to the Earth and the sun at the same time, National Geographic reports. The next blue moon won't happen again this year, but if you miss it today, you can still catch one in August.

– The MV Akademik Shokalskiy was on its way to the spot where Sir Douglas Mawson first set foot in Antarctica when it ran into bad weather and got stuck in the ice, with the 50 or so passengers and 20 crew members on board. "We've been in touch with the master of the vessel, who says they are beset by ice," a rep for the Australian Maritime Safety Authority tells ABC News. "They are basically trapped or stuck in the ice and can't move." Rescue ships are at least two days away, though the Shokalskiy isn't far from land. "We're in the ice like the explorers of old! All are well and spirits are high. Happy Christmas," tweeted Australian professor Chris Turney, who was on the cruise, per the Guardian. "On Christmas Eve we realized we could not get through, in spite of being just 2 nautical miles from open water. We hoped the conditions would change but we have experienced several low pressure systems over the last few days which have held the ice fast."

– Nintendo is having a very bad year. The company yesterday slashed its annual sales forecast for the Wii U console by a third, to 2.8 million units, and warned that it will end the year in the red for the third straight year, Bloomberg reports. The news sent the company's American depositary receipts down 17%, the biggest drop since 2001. "The revision is much worse than expected," says an analyst. "It’s going to be a third consecutive annual operating loss and that raises a serious management issue." The company is also considering a new business model, says its president. "Given the expansion of smart devices, we are naturally studying how smart devices can be used to grow the game-player business," he said. "It’s not as simple as enabling Mario to move on a smartphone." Nintendo's shares have lost 80% of their value since the original Wii came out in 2007.

– Mark Pincus is leaving his post as CEO of Zynga, the company he founded, to be replaced by the head of Microsoft's Xbox business. Don Mattrick, 49, will take over next week, and will also join Zynga's board, the company announced today. Pincus, who has held the top job at Zynga since the company's founding, will continue as chairman and chief product officer. "I’m confident that Don is that leader." Pincus has been struggling to turn Zynga around since its IPO last year, and sources say he decided the company needed a top manager to focus on creating hit games and other products. Mattrick has been at Microsoft for five years, after 15 at Electronic Arts, where he was president of its worldwide studios. "Don is unique in the game business," Pincus said in a statement. "He deeply understands the value of a network and the importance of creating lifelong consumer relationships." Zynga shares rose about 9% after the news broke.

– The comet currently being studied by the Rosetta probe smells like rotten eggs, horse pee, alcohol, and bitter almonds, scientists say. "If you could smell the comet, you probably wish that you hadn't," the team writes on the European Space Agency's website. The comet, 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, is currently 400 million miles from the sun, but the team has been analyzing the comet's "coma," the fuzzy head surrounding its nucleus, using one of the instruments aboard the European spacecraft Rosetta, which is preparing to land a lander on the comet on Nov. 12, the Christian Science Monitor reports. "The perfume of 67P/C-G is quite strong, with the odor of rotten eggs (hydrogen sulphide), horse stable (ammonia), and the pungent, suffocating odor of formaldehyde," the lead researcher says. "This is mixed with the faint, bitter, almond-like aroma of hydrogen cyanide. Add some whiff of alcohol (methanol) to this mixture, paired with the vinegar-like aroma of sulphur dioxide and a hint of the sweet scent of carbon disulphide, and you arrive at the 'perfume' of our comet."

The "total fertility rate," or the number of babies a hypothetical group of 1,000 women would have over their lifetime, fell to 1,764.5 births per 1,000 women in 2017, a 3% drop from 2016, according to the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics. The boy was taken to Arkansas Children's Hospital, where a statement released this morning says he's "stable and is expected to improve."

– Jay Z may not be a household name, but he's still got a stake in the music streaming service he launched two years ago. Sprint announced Monday that it's buying a 33% stake in Tidal for an undisclosed amount, reports the New York Post. The deal will make Tidal available to Sprint's 45 million customers, and the two companies plan to create a "dedicated marketing fund" that will spend $75 million a year to promote Tidal exclusives and content from its artists, reports Billboard. – A 38-year-old upstate New York man has confessed to strangling an 82-year-old nun, then stabbing her to death, the Albany Times Union reports. Michael Briggs, who was out on parole at the time, pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and attempted burglary on Monday. He'll be sentenced in June to 30 years to life. Prosecutors say Briggs met Mary Greco on Dec. 27, 2012, when he offered to shovel her car out after a snowstorm. She paid him in cash and cookies. Days later, he returned after half a foot of snow had melted, and she called her neighbor to ask if she wanted him to shovel her car as well. The neighbor declined. Briggs had shoveled snow for Greco around the time she was killed, prosecutors say. His fingerprints were lifted from the toilet's handle, and fingerprints from a mug on the kitchen counter and a glass in the sink were found in Greco's apartment. He had served 10 years in prison for a robbery in which he tied up a 12-year-old boy and sexually assaulted him. He was wanted for the murder at the time, but was being sought by authorities.

– The 10-year-old son of Denmark's Crown Prince Frederik and Princess Mary was saved from the surf by an Australian lifeguard on Thursday, the Guardian reports. According to the Brisbane Times, Prince Christian was swimming between the flags at Mermaid Beach on the Gold Coast on Australia's east coast when he was swept out to sea by a rip. "The rip was pretty strong so he [Nick Malcolm] only had to paddle [33 feet]," the Gold Coast's chief lifeguard says. "He said, 'Do you want a lift in?' and the boy jumped on and away they went." Malcolm was unaware he'd saved a member of the Danish royal family until a fellow beachgoer told him. "He didn't know who it was until someone said, 'Oh that was the royal family from Denmark,' and Nick said, 'Oh OK,' and Nick said, 'Oh, OK.'" The boy was fine and his parents thanked the lifeguards as they left the beach. Malcolm, a New Zealand native who trains as a lifeguard on the Gold Coast, was also credited with saving a 68-year-old man who went into cardiac arrest at the same beach two years ago, 7 News Queensland reports.

– The long-awaited white iPhone 4 is here, Apple announced today. “The white iPhone 4 has finally arrived and it’s beautiful,” said Philip Schiller, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Product Marketing. “We appreciate everyone who has waited patiently while we’ve worked to get every detail right.” The phone will be available tomorrow from Apple, Verizon, AT&T, and other resellers for $199 and $299 with a two-year wireless contract, Time reports. Apple also released a Q&A on the controversy over location data on its devices. The company says it has never tracked the location of a customer’s iPhone and will never do so, but it did identify several “bugs,” and will release a free iOS software update in the next few weeks that will reduce the size of the Wi-Fi hotspot and cell tower database on the iPhone.

– The remains of 42 children and 76 llamas have been found in a mass sacrifice in Peru dating back 600 years, National Geographic reports. "This is unusual, and not what we've seen before, especially on the coast of Peru," Tulane University physical anthropologist John Verano tells the magazine. He and Peruvian archeologist Gabriel Prieto dug up the remains of the children in 2011, but Verano and Prieto expanded the dig this year. They believe the children were sacrificed as an offering to the sea, or as a response to severe flooding brought on by El Nio. "It's not a place where you'd think to look," Verano tells National Geographic. "But it is an exciting discovery." Researchers are analyzing the bones and teeth found at the site, which sits on a sandy ridge 100 yards from the beach in the coastal village of Huanchaquito. The area was part of the Chim state, which ran from 1100 to 1470 AD, when it was conquered by the Inca empire.

– Archaeologists have uncovered a stone tool at an ancient rock shelter in the high desert of eastern Oregon that could turn out to be older than any known site of human occupation in western North America. The find was announced Thursday by the US Bureau of Land Management, which controls the land on which the site was found. University of Oregon archaeologist Patrick O'Grady, who supervises the dig, says the Rimrock Draw Rockshelter outside Riley has not been fully excavated. But the tool, a hand-held scraper chipped from a piece of orange agate not normally found in eastern Oregon, was found about 8 inches below a layer of volcanic ash from an eruption of Mount St. Helens that has been dated to 15,800 years ago. The depth was about 12 feet below the surface. Bureau of Land Management archaeologist Scott Thomas said that if the age of the site holds up to scrutiny, it would be the oldest west of the Rockies, and another predating the so-called Clovis culture, once generally believed to be the first people to migrate from Asia into North America. The earliest Clovis artifacts, known for distinctive and elegant stone points, are dated to about 13,000 years ago. She called 911, and Paige was given CPR for about an hour before her heart started to beat again, reports KTLA. She was rushed to the hospital, where she died on Nov. 30. "We're trying to get the word out that journalism is important, and that journalists should be rewarded for doing their jobs." AFAJP is asking supporters to sign the petition at its website.

The structures were made from hundreds of pillar-shaped mineral deposits, called stalagmites, which were chopped to a similar length and laid out in two oval patterns up to 16 inches high. They were discovered by chance in 1990 after a rockslide had closed the mouth of the cave at Bruniquel in southwest France. While previous research had suggested the structures pre-dated the arrival of modern humans in Europe around 45,000 years ago, the notion that Neanderthals could have made them didn't fit long-held assumptions that these early humans were incapable of the kind of complex behavior necessary to work underground. Using sophisticated dating techniques, a team led by archaeologist Jacques Jaubert of the University of Bordeaux, France, found that the stalagmites must have been broken off the ground around 176,500 years ago "making these edifices among the oldest known well-dated constructions made by humans." – Those airport security plastic trays are the most germ-filled spot in the world, according to a new study. Researchers from the University of Nottingham and the Finnish National Institute for Health and Welfare swabbed surfaces at Helsinki-Vantaa airport in Finland during the winter of 2016 and found 10% of them harbored respiratory viruses, CNN reports. The most common virus found was rhinovirus, which causes the common cold, but the swabs also picked up the influenza A virus. Interestingly, no respiratory viruses were found on toilet surfaces. "People can help to minimize contagion by hygienic hand washing and coughing into a hankerchief, tissue, or sleeve at all times but especially in public places," says Professor of Health Protection Jonathan Van Tam. "These simple precautions can help prevent pandemics and are most important in crowded areas like airports that have a high volume of people traveling to and from many different parts of the world." The study, published in the BMC Infectious Diseases journal, was part of a larger EU-funded research project called PANDHUB, which explored the role of airports and other traffic hubs in the spread of serious infections. – The heirs of Walmart founder Sam Walton are in a legal fight with the widow of a photographer who shot hundreds of photos of the family over the years. The family is suing Helen Huff to get the negatives, proofs, and prints she still has, reports the Washington Post. Huff says her husband and father-in-law, who both died in 1994, were independent contractors who used their own equipment, lenses, lights, and backdrops to take the photos. The family, however, says the photos were created as a “work-for-hire.” Without a written contract, the Waltons have to show their relationship with the photography studio was like an employer-employee relationship in which the family was boss, the Arkansas Times reports. Huff counters that the photographers used their own equipment, lenses, lights, and backdrops, controlled the positions of their subjects, chose and developed the film, and provided a copyright notice to the Walton family notifying them that they owned ‘exclusive rights to reproduce’ the pictures. The case will be heard by a federal judge on July 7.

West was born with sacral agenesis, meaning his legs crossed below the pelvis. Doctors amputated both of his legs when he was 5, but he has led a normal life ever since. Zimmerman was required to stay in Seminole County except to visit his attorneys in a neighboring county. Under the terms of his release on $1 million bond, Zimmerman was required to stay in Seminole County except to visit his attorneys in a neighboring county. Next year, fines will kick in. “It's hard to grab somebody when you're in a marked squad car,” says one deputy. “In your own personal car, you can see it going down the road—how many people are doing it.”

– The Senate passed a stopgap spending bill today that will keep the government running—but it does not defund ObamaCare. The bill is expected to pass the House tomorrow, but John Boehner has already vowed that the House will not accept it, the Hill reports. Conservatives are pressuring Boehner to reject the bill, and Tea Party groups are ramping up their lobbying efforts against him. "He's going to be threatened," says Brent Bozell of ForAmerica. The bill funds the government through Oct. 1, but it doesn't include language defunding ObamaCare or prioritizing debt payments in the event of Congress fails to raise the debt limit. "The House will take action that reflects the fundamental fact that Americans don't want a government shutdown and they don't want the train wreck that is ObamaCare," says Boehner's spokesman.

– Amazon is trying to get even more of a leg up on its competitors this holiday season by offering a $5 off deal to shoppers who download its Price Check app. To take advantage of the deal, which starts Saturday and runs through Dec. 10, you'll need to be in a brick-and-mortar store, Mashable reports. Just download the Price Check app to your iPhone or Android, scan the bar code on the product you're looking to buy, and place it in the app's virtual basket. The discount will be applied to the item within 24 hours. "With just weeks until the holiday shopping season kicks off, Amazon clearly wants to be your shopping source, and they’re better equipped to roll-out pricing changes and promotions than any B&M store," writes Ryan Singel on PC World.

– An annual three-day festival that would have seen thousands of dogs slaughtered and eaten has been canceled after a furious online campaign by animal rights activists. Officials in Jinhua, in eastern China, said they were canceling the festival "in full respect of the public's opinion," reports the New York Times. The move came after images of bloody dog carcasses circulated on popular microblog platform Sina Weibo. “I once had a pet dog, and I’m not a huge fan of dog meat,” said a 36-year-old man credited with starting the campaign. “The reason why I posted that message online is very simple—that is, I don’t want to see dog lovers’ feelings get hurt.” Dog meat is popular in China because it is believed to have warming properties. Practitioners of Chinese traditional medicine say that dog meat imbues the eater with energy and strength. The annual three-day festival was scheduled to begin Oct. 18.

– The leaders of North and South Korea will meet in Pyongyang in September for the third time this year, CNN reports. The announcement came after high-level talks between officials from the two Koreas at the Demilitarized Zone on Monday. "What's very important is that both governments do all they ought to do regarding progressing all the issues on the agenda," says Ri Son Gwon, North Korea's point man for inter-Korean relations. "If the issues that were raised in the inter-Korea talks and individual meetings are not resolved, then unexpected problems could arise and all the items on the agenda could meet obstacles." Ri didn't say exactly when the summit would take place, but South Korean President Moon Jae-in will be the first South Korean president to visit Pyongyang in more than a decade. He and Kim Jong Un met for the first time in person in April, and they held an impromptu meeting in May.

The Planter was built in 1860 and used as a supply and transport ship and as a cotton cargo hauler. – A renowned jockey who was among the best in Pennsylvania history died Thursday of injuries suffered in a racing accident, the AP reports. Parx Racing announced the death of Jose Flores, 56, who was racing Monday at the suburban Philadelphia track when his horse went down and Flores was thrown off. The jockey hit the ground headfirst and suffered a massive trauma. He was removed from life support Thursday afternoon. Flores won 4,650 races in a career that spanned more than three decades. He was the top career earner at Parx, formerly known as Philadelphia Park. "It's unbelievable, just sickening," Scott Lake, the top trainer at Parx, who has known Flores since 1991, told the Philadelphia Inquirer. "He was just tremendous, a nice guy, always a professional." Flores' mounts earned $64 million in nearly 29,000 career starts, according to the Equibase thoroughbred database. Parx called Flores an "outstanding jockey" and expressed condolences to his family. The Jockeys' Guild said Flores is the 157th jockey to die in a racing accident in unofficial records going back to 1940. The group said that before Flores, it had no record of a jockey ever being killed in an accident at a Pennsylvania track.

The sources say Avicii broke a bottle and used the glass to cause massive bleeding that led to his death. The sources say the point of injury was Avicii's neck but another strongly denies that. Avicii battled alcohol problems for years, and his friends worried those issues would eventually kill him. Avicii's family released a statement that included the clear message it was suicide. The tax break was set to last until March next year, but it has now been capped at $112,500 for private EVs. That means first-time owners in Hong Kong can no longer get a tax break on an electric car. Quartz reports there were 2,939 first-time Tesla registrations in March before the tax break went into effect, five times more than there were in February. A Tesla spokesperson says the company expects the Hong Kong market to continue to be "very strong." But Quartz reports Tesla CEO Elon Musk called Hong Kong's tax break for electric vehicles "excellent" in April.

The company says it learned a lot from the uproar over the proposed new logo, which was panned by thousands of Facebook and Twitter users, and will not be using it, CNN reports. "We've heard loud and clear that you don't like the new logo," the company said in a Facebook post. "We've learned a lot from the feedback. We only want what's best for the brand and our customers." The company had planned to crowdsourcing the new logo, but that idea didn't work. "We've learned a lot in this process," the company said. "And we are clear that we did not go about this in the right way. We recognize that we missed the opportunity to engage with the online community. This wasn't the right project at the right time for crowdsourcing." Gap Inc. did not respond to requests for comment.

– OJ Simpson has been permanently banned from the Cosmopolitan Hotel in Las Vegas, TMZ reports. The former NFL star and convicted murderer had been frequenting the hotel's bars since his release from prison last month. A patron at the hotel's bar tells ABC News that Simpson arrived around 10:40pm Wednesday, about 10 minutes after others in his party had consumed wine. He stayed at his table for the duration of the time he was at the bar, the patron says. Simpson, who is allowed to consume alcohol as part of his parole, abstained from wine, the patron says. But he was drunk and became "extremely unruly," the patron says. Hotel staff tells TMZ Simpson was angry at staff and glasses broke at the bar. Security removed Simpson from the hotel, though TMZ says he was nice to security guards. Simpson's lawyer, Malcolm LaVergne, says his client was not drunk and did not become belligerent, contrary to media reports. LaVergne says Simpson was at the Cosmopolitan to eat chicken wings and was at the hotel to socialize. He says the hotel-casino decided before Simpson's visit to trespass him from the property. LaVergne says that Simpson is a social drinker, meaning he usually orders one drink and sips on it

– The death toll from yesterday's violent storms in Oklahoma has risen to nine, including two children who were killed when a tornado hit the suburb of El Reno, reports CNN. The other seven victims in Canadian County, which includes Oklahoma City, have not been identified. At least 104 people were injured in the storm, and 11 of them are still being treated in Oklahoma City-area hospitals, the health department says. "We're all pretty shook up," says a man who was in an oil field repair shop when the tornado hit. "Surreal, really no other way to explain it."

– Donald Trump's surprise visit to Mexico City Wednesday was "great honor," he said after meeting with President Enrique Pea Nieto at the president's official residence in Mexico City. Pea Nieto told reporters following a closed-door meeting that "misinterpretation or assertions" had negatively impacted perceptions of Trump's candidacy. He added that, the "Mexican people have been hurt by the comments that had been made." But he said he's sure that Trump is genuinely interested in building a relationship that will benefit both countries, the AP reports. Pea Nieto spoke in Spanish throughout. After meeting with Mexican President Enrique Pea Nieto, Republican nominee Donald Trump says that both countries must respect the others' right to build a border wall on their soil to stop the movement of people, illegal drugs, and weapons. Trump says he and PeaNieto discussed his call for a border wall during their meeting, but did not talk about Trump's insistence that Mexico pay for it. He says, "that'll be for a later date." Trump says that having a secure border is a sovereign right and mutually beneficial. Mexicans have been outraged by the proposal. Trump called his surprise visit to Mexico City Wednesday a "great honor."

– "The thought of Donald Trump becoming president nauseates me in a big way," Hustler publisher Larry Flynt tells HOSS magazine. "I don't know, maybe move to Canada." Flynt, a longtime Democratic supporter, says he's "embarrassed" by the prospect of a Trump presidency. "I wish I didn't," he tells the magazine. "I don't know why I let it obsess me the way it does." He adds that he'd be "doing a great service to our country." Flynt's company has produced X-rated videos like Asian Fever 12, Barely Legal 151, and The Porn Identity, and the Cape Breton If Donald Trump Wins website says the Canadian island is the perfect place for Trump haters. "If me winning means Rosie O'Donnell moves to Canada, I'd be doing a great service to our country!" the site says. Fox News rounds up more celebrities who've said they'll leave America if Trump is elected.

– A new drug that reduces the urge to drink is now available in the UK, and it's designed for people who "probably don't even recognize themselves as an alcoholic," a health official tells the Guardian. Nalmefene, which costs about $5 a day and can be taken once a day, can be prescribed to people who drink at least half a bottle of wine or three pints a night. The drug reduces the urge to drink and can be prescribed alongside counseling support, experts say. About 35,000 people are expected to be prescribed the drug in the first year, though the actual number may be lower, the Guardian notes. "Many people have a difficult relationship with alcohol even though they have a very stable lifestyle, maintain jobs and a social life and would not automatically assume they have a problem," a health official says. "But regularly drinking over the recommended daily amount of alcohol can seriously damage your health."

– Donald Trump may have won Arizona's March 22 presidential primary—but there's still a chance the results could be challenged. Secretary of State Michele Reagan certified the official canvass of the election Monday and said she had no authority to do anything except sign off on the election, the AP reports. She says anyone who wants to sue over the results now has five days to file a court challenge. Maricopa County records show that five polling places in metro Phoenix still had voters in line after midnight, including one location where the final ballot was cast at nearly 1am. The US Justice Department is inquiring about the lines and other problems to evaluate whether the largest county in the state complied with federal oversight. The frustrating waits come after the Arizona Legislature slashed funding last year for counties to carry out the presidential election. Election officials in Phoenix responded with scaled-back polling, citing a lack of money and the belief that people would vote by mail. Despite the investigation, Arizona Secretary of State Michele Reagan on Monday certified results of the presidential primary, which Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton won. As the state's top election official, Reagan didn't have the ability to reject the official canvass from the 15 counties, despite acknowledging problems that led some voters to be incorrectly left off rolls

– A New Mexico peanut-butter plant linked to a salmonella outbreak last year is being dumped in a landfill after Costco refused to sell it, the AP reports. Sunland Inc.'s bankruptcy trustee says he had no other choice after Costco refused to sell or donate the 950,000 jars of peanut butter, worth an estimated $2.6 million. "We considered all options," he says. "They didn't agree." The last of 58 truckloads of peanut butter was expected Friday. Sunland made peanut butter under a number of different labels for retailers like Costco, Kroger, and Trader Joe's, along with products under its own name. But the plant was shut down in September 2012 after its products were linked to 41 salmonella cases in 20 states. It later reopened for about five months, but shut down last October after the company's Chapter 7 bankruptcy filing. Sunland processed Valencia peanuts, a sweet variety of peanut that is unique to the region and preferred for natural butters because it is flavorful without additives. Sonya Warwick, spokeswoman for New Mexico's largest food bank, declined to comment directly on the situation, but she noted that rescued food accounted for 74% of what Roadrunner Food Bank distributed across New Mexico last year. – It's that time of year again: time for the Maine Department of Transportation to sift through the 2,000 or so entries it received in its "My Maine Sign" contest in an attempt to come up with the next tongue-in-cheek safety message to flash across the state's interstates, reports the Bangor Daily News. The tongue-in-cheek message had to be no more than 8 characters in length and focused on one of five safety themes: distracted driving, impaired driving, speeding, seatbelts, or wildlife winter driving events. DOT officials will pick their finalists by the end of the month, and the public will then vote on the winning message via the department's website. The winner will get his or her idea in neon lights but also a custom street sign from the state's sign shop. The six winning entries: "Put Down UR Cell—Or You May End Up In One," "Spend Money On Lobstahs—Not Speeding Tickets," "Little Known Fact—Snow Is Really Slippery," "A Cold Suppah Is Bettah Thana Hot Ticket," and "Keep In Mind—Moose Eyes Don't Shine."

– Police on Michigan's Mackinac Island say they're investigating a bar fight between aides for Marco Rubio and Rand Paul, CNN reports. John Yob, a Paul aide, says he was punched in the face by Rich Beeson, Rubio's deputy campaign manager. "He literally physically assaulted me by punching me in the face," Yob said in a Facebook post this morning. "The state police are looking for him. I have it on video, from multiple angles. This will play out in the national media in the next few hours." Yob says he has video of the alleged assault, which took place at Horn's Bar, the Detroit Free Press reports. "Any time you're at a bar past midnight things seem to get misconstrued as to what happened," the island's police chief says. "I'd really like to see this video." Police say they've forwarded the alleged assault complaint to the Mackinac County prosecutor. Whether charges will be filed "would be up to the prosecutor," the chief says.

– The mother of a 4-year-old girl whose photo appeared on an anti-abortion billboard targeting African Americans is suing the ad company, claiming it violated the terms of her contract. The billboard featured Anissa Fraser in a sun dress and the message, “The most dangerous place for an African American is in the womb,” Courthouse News Service reports. The mother, Tricia Fraser, says she never agreed to have her daughter’s image associated with “an offensive, defamatory, and racist statement.” She says she only signed a release allowing her daughter to be photographed for stock “family photos.” The photo was purchased by Heroic Media from Getty Images with the agreement that it would not be used “in connection with a subject that would be unflattering or unduly controversial to a reasonable person.” Fraser says the defendants used her daughter’s photo in “massive billboards on a busy street in Manhattan outside the entrance to the Holland Tunnel, and in Jacksonville, Florida.” The defendants operate out of Texas, and work “to discourage women from exercising their constitutional rights to reproductive freedom via messages in billboard advertising.”

– The Federal Reserve left its key interest rate unchanged today and signaled that it's ready to take action if the economy doesn't improve. The central bank said in a statement that growth had slowed recently, and it expected unemployment to "only slowly" decline over the next few quarters, the New York Times reports. The Fed said it would "provide additional accommodation as needed to promote a stronger economic recovery and sustained improvement in labor market conditions in a context of price stability," a stronger statement than it used in June, when it said it was "prepared to act." Analysts had expected the Fed to announce some kind of new action to boost the economy, like a bond-buying program, but MarketWatch notes that the Fed said it would likely hold its rate steady until late 2014.

– As part of its bailout of Cyprus, Britain has sent a plane to the island carrying $1.3 million in emergency loans for its military personnel. The defense ministry says the Royal Air Force flight left today "as a contingency measure to provide military personnel and their families with emergency loans in the event that cash machines and debit cards stop working completely," the BBC reports. Britain does not use the euro, having stuck with the pound as its national currency. "We're determined to do everything we can to minimize the impact of the Cyprus banking crisis on our people," says a ministry spokesman. Some 3,000 British troops are stationed at two military bases on the island, and the government says it is "proactively approaching personnel to ask if they want their March, and future months' salaries paid into UK bank accounts, rather than Cypriot accounts," AFP reports. The British government has also promised to fully refund any military or government personnel's deposits subject to a levy that was part of the bailout deal.

– People who drink five cups of coffee a day have a lower risk of heart disease than those who drink less, according to a study published Tuesday in the Journal of the American Heart Association. Dr. Gregory Marcus and his team at the University of California San Francisco—whose research was funded by the National Institutes of Health—examined 1,388 people with an average age of 72 and found no difference in the number of premature cardiac contractions (which are typically harmless) or the number of heartbeats associated with caffeinated products like coffee, chocolate, and tea, NBC News reports. "We may unnecessarily be discouraging consumption of items like chocolate, coffee, and tea that might actually have cardiovascular benefits," Marcus says in a statement. "Given our recent work demonstrating that extra heartbeats can be dangerous, this finding is especially relevant." The team measured instances of ventricular contractions and premature atrial contractions and did not ask about super-caffeinated energy drinks. They could not find any differences in 24-hour heartbeats. "Therefore, we are only able to conclude in general, consuming caffeinated products every day is not associated with having increased rates or arrhythmia but cannot specify a particular amount per day," Marcus and colleagues wrote in the study. – German prosecutors said Wednesday they have indicted two former Nazi SS guards in their 90s on charges of being accessories to murder while they worked at a World War II concentration camp. Both men served as guards at the Stutthof concentration camp, located near what is now the Polish city of Gdansk, Dortmund prosecutor Andreas Brendel told the AP. The indictments were filed against a 93-year-old man from Borken who served in Stutthof from June 1942 to September 1944 and a 92-year-old man from Wuppertal who was there from June 1944 to May 1945. The charges were filed last week at the state court in Muenster but only announced Wednesday because the defendants first had to be notified. Both deny they had any knowledge of killings at the camp. About 65,000 people died at Stutthof. Some were put to death in gas chambers or shot, while others died from malnutrition or froze to death. During the time they were at Stutthof, hundreds of killings occurred. Members of the SS killed more than 100 Polish prisoners and some 77 Soviet prisoners of war in the camp's gas chamber in 1944. An unknown number of Jews also were gassed there in late 1944. Between June 1944 and April 1945, SS members also

– Police in Rome say they've cracked the code to a code-breaking document used by the 'Ndrangheta mafia to recruit new members. The document, found alongside weapons and ammunition during an investigation into a high-profile murder in the city last year, was deciphered by two policemen with a passion for crosswords, the BBC reports. "Its content is basically the formula that a person must recite to become part of the 'Ndrangheta," says the head of Rome's police rapid response team. "Finding such a document shows that even if they are projected towards big businesses and are a criminal group with a global presence, they still use archaic systems." The translated text describes how to recognize a mafioso—a so-called "Man of Honour"—by the signs around him. The 'Ndrangheta is now reckoned to be Italy's most powerful mafia, having overtaken Sicily's Cosa Nostra.

– A fire on an empty Ethiopian Airlines Boeing 787 Dreamliner at London's Heathrow Airport has shut down the airport for nearly 90 minutes and delayed flights for the second day in a row. No passengers were aboard the plane, which was parked on a remote stand after departing for Nairobi, the BBC reports. Fire-retardant foam was sprayed on the plane, and an area in front of the tail appeared to be scorched. The fire is being treated as unexplained, police say, and the airport's runways are now "fully open following an earlier fire on board an Ethiopian Airlines aircraft which the airport's emergency services attended," a spokesman says. "The aircraft was parked on a remote parking stand and there were no passengers on board. Arrivals and departures were temporarily suspended while airport fire crews attended to this incident. This is a standard procedure if fire crews are occupied with an incident." The Dreamliner was grounded for more than two months after a battery fire in Boston.

– Dylann Roof, the 21-year-old accused of killing nine people during a Bible study at a historic black church in Charleston, SC, has been charged with nine counts of murder, reports the Post and Courier. He was also charged with possession of a firearm during the commission of a violent crime and possession of a weapon during the commission of a violent crime. Roof was taken into custody during a traffic stop in Shelby, NC, about 250 miles from Charleston, reports the Washington Post. Police say he had a warrant out for his arrest for possession of a firearm during the commission of a violent crime and possession of a weapon during the commission of a violent crime. The victims in the Emanuel AME church ranged in age from 26 to 87. Police have not speculated about a motive, but the Post and Courier quotes Charleston Mayor Joe Riley as saying that "the only reason this is happening is because of hate." The victims include the church's pastor, Rev. Clementa Pinckney, 41; state Sen. Depayne Middelton Middleton-Doctor, 49; Myra Thompson, 59; and Daniel Simmons Sr., 74.

– The US flag will be carried by Bryshon Nellum at tomorrow's closing ceremony for the London Olympics, the AP reports. The 29-year-old, who won a silver medal in the 400-meter dash, was told by doctors in 2008 that he might never be an elite athlete again after he was shot in the legs while leaving a restaurant near Southern California. Nellum says he's "humbled by this incredible privilege." US Olympic Committee CEO Scott Blackmun says Nellum's courage "embodies the Olympic spirit." Meanwhile, the US is poised to finish atop the medals table for the first time in Olympic history, with a total of 94 medals and 41 golds, according to the AP. China is second with 81 medals and 37 golds.

– President Trump's choice to be secretary of the Navy, businessman Philip Bilden, said Sunday he was withdrawing from consideration for the post, citing concerns about privacy and separating himself from his business interests, the AP reports. Bilden's withdrawal raises similar issues to that of Vincent Viola, Trump's nominee for Army secretary who stepped aside earlier this month. Just last week, the Pentagon sought to tamp down reports that Bilden might pull out. Bilden was an intelligence officer in the Army Reserve from 1986-1996. He relocated to Hong Kong to set up an Asian presence for HarbourVest Partners LLC, a global private equity management firm. Bilden recently retired from HarbourVest Partners after 25 years. In a statement released Sunday by the Pentagon, Bilden said he determined that he would not be able to satisfy the Office of Government Ethics requirements without what he called "undue disruption and materially adverse divestment of my family's private financial interests." Defense Secretary Jim Mattis said in a statement that he would make a recommendation to Trump for a nominee in the coming days. Chauncy Jones Black met 30-year-old Tara Trammell at the Kroger, where he asked if he could take her groceries to her car in exchange for some donuts. "He had me at donuts," says Trammell. " lolWhat followed was perhaps one of the most cherished experiences of my life." The two went on a "fun-filled shopping spree" together, and now Trammell has created a GoFundMe page to raise money for Chauncy, who lives with his disabled mother. "He is a straight A student who is doing his best to make it in a world with no money and very few resources," writes Trammell. "He wants to work and help his mother financially. He wants to become a successful business owner and offer jobs and opportunites to others in his community. What so many can take for granted, he wants. – Lady Gaga’s new album Born This Way sold more than a million copies in its first week, making it the first album to ever sell more than 1 million copies in its first week, Nielsen SoundScan reports. Some 66% of those sales were digital downloads, the New York Times reports, making Born This Way the most popular digital album of all time. The record also outsold the next 42 albums on Billboard’s chart combined. “People lose sight of how an artist becomes successful in 2011,” says Billboard’s editorial director. “She could have sold 600,000 albums, or a million, or two million. But in terms of revenue that’s going to be a smaller piece of the pie.” Born This Way’s success is thanks in part to a year-in-the-making marketing campaign, the Times reports. Lady Gaga announced the title of the album at MTV’s Video Music Awards last September and gave the release date on New Year’s Eve. As the promotions piled up in recent weeks, she became inescapable. If you missed her HBO concert special or Saturday Night Live appearance, her GagaVille online game or fashion sale through Gilt Groupe, then perhaps you rode in one of the New York City subway cars decked out top to

– The deportation of Guadalupe Garcia de Rayos has set off a wave of anger and confusion in her hometown of Peoria, Ariz., and across the country, the Washington Post reports. Garcia de Rayos, a Mexican native who came to the US with her husband and two children when they were children, was taken from her home by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers on Thursday. She was at the border for a visit with her children when she was detained by ICE agents. She was then taken to a federal detention center, where she was told she was an undocumented immigrant and would be deported. Her lawyer says her children, who are US citizens, were not informed of her immigration status and were not informed she could be deported. The president of the National Council of La Raza tells the Hill the deportation "reinforces that when the Trump administration said they would go after criminals, they really meant everybody." She says the deportation of Garcia de Rayos is the first of many to come. "We want people to stay calm and we want to give them assurances, but we can't give them assurances," she says. "What we are asking of the community is to get more plugged into community organizations."

– Scientists say they've made a "big" breakthrough in the search for a cure for Alzheimer's disease, reports the Guardian. In a study published in Science Translational Medicine, researchers at the University of Leicester say they've found a way to stop the disease in its tracks in mice with prion disease, the best animal model of human neurodegenerative disorders. "It's the first time a substance has been given to mice that prevents brain disease," the lead researcher tells the Independent. "The fact that this is a compound that can be given orally, that gets into the brain and prevents brain disease, is a first in itself." The team used an enzyme called PERK, which is "very promising" and would "not be impossible" to develop a drug that protects the brain without side effects. The side effects included weight loss and mild diabetes, but the researchers say they're confident the same principles would apply in a human brain suffering from Alzheimer's or Parkinson's. "From finding the first effective drug in a mouse, to having an effective medicine in man, usually takes decades to bring to fruition, in the very few cases in which it is successful," says one expert. – If you've been thinking about moving to Canada in the event of a Donald Trump presidency, you're in luck: A new dating site called Maple Match is here to help you find your "ideal Canadian partner." "Maple Match makes it easy for Americans to find the ideal Canadian partner to save them from the unfathomable horror of a Trump presidency," the website reads. CEO Joe Goldman tells Global News that interest in the site has been "immense" and that signups have " surpassed our expectations." Interested? You can fill out a form to get on the site's waiting list, and Goldman tells Cosmopolitan that there's a waiting list, too. "People ask me all the time if Maple Match is joke," he says. "Donald Trump is a joke. Finding true love in a place where you can be happy is not a joke. Maple Match is very real."

The sources say prosecutors want to know what Trump knew about the meeting and whether he sought to conceal its purpose. The meeting occurred at Trump Tower in June 2016 and was attended by Donald Trump Jr., Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort, and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner. The meeting, which also involved Russian attorney Natalia Veselnitskaya and former Soviet intelligence officer Rinat Akhmetshin, was scheduled in order to convey damaging information about Hillary Clinton and her campaign. – There are only about 500 of what's called "Canada's panda"—black bears with white fur—on Earth, and they're found only in the Great Bear Rainforest, a Canadian wilderness area the size of Switzerland that's home to whales, wolves, and eagles, ABC News reports. But there's one thing the bears do have in common with pandas: They're very rare. "It's a magnificent bear," says the director of the nonprofit conservation group Pacific Wild. "The only thing that's standing between that is really the spirit bear, the concerted efforts from conservationists and the First Nation [native] people." That's because BC is preparing to allow the construction of an oil pipeline from Alberta to British Columbia, and the spirit bear is worried. "They want to bring Big Oil to this coast," he says. "The only thing that's standing between that is really the spirit bear, the concerted efforts from conservationists and the First Nation [native] people." Click here to see ABC's video of a photographer trying to capture one.

– Climate change is taking a heavy toll on Antarctica's emperor penguins, who are in danger of disappearing by the end of the century, according to a new study. The penguins, which can grow to 4 feet tall, breed on sea ice and are vulnerable to shifts in ice thickness, Reuters reports. "It's not happy news for the emperor penguin," says a co-author of the study in Nature Climate Change. "There is a goldilocks point for ice and emperor penguins. Too much ice means the females, which can travel 60 miles to the sea to catch fish, must waddle ever further. Too little ice means waves could break up colonies in spring. Too little ice means that emperor penguins could adapt by climbing onto land or higher ice." The study is the first to project the long-term outlook for Antarctica's largest penguins, and calls on governments to list the birds as endangered.

– More than 200 civilians fleeing fighting in Malakal, South Sudan, drowned yesterday when their boat capsized on the Nile, an army spokesman tells the BBC. "The reports we have are of between 200 to 300 people, including women and children," he says. "They all drowned. They were fleeing the fighting that broke out again in Malakal." The UN estimates that more than 350,000 people have fled their homes in the country's two-month-old conflict, which has pitted President Salva Kiir against former vice president Riek Machar. The rebels say they've captured Malakal, but the army says it's still marching on the state capital. "There is heavy fighting in Malakal," an army spokesman says. "This is not over yet. The fighting is ongoing." A rebel spokesman says they've "recaptured Malakal," but the army denies that.

– Just two weeks ago, Endemol Shine North America announced it was developing a TV series based on the relationship between Selena Quintanilla and her husband, Chris Perez. Now, Selena's father is suing to stop the series, TMZ reports. Abraham Quintanilla Jr. says Perez has violated a 1995 agreement between Perez and Selena's estate regarding the singer's estate. Quintanilla is the only person with ownership and all proprietary rights in Selena's name, voice, signature, photograph, and likeness, according to the lawsuit. "He doesn't have the rights to publish a book or produce a television series based in any part on Selena," says Quintanilla's estate attorney. Perez was married to Selena from 1992 until she was murdered in 1995. His best-selling book, To Selena With Love, tells the story of their relationship.

– The editor-in-chief of the New York Review of Books has been forced out over an essay he wrote about former Canadian broadcaster Jian Ghomeshi, who has been accused of sexual assault and harassment by at least 20 women. In the essay, Ian Buruma defended Ghomeshi, who was acquitted in 2016 of three counts of sexual assault and one count of choking involving three women, saying he wanted to give a more "nuanced" view of what had happened to the former radio host. Critics accused Buruma of being "publicly pilloried" and "convicted on Twitter," the Guardian reports. Buruma, who was only the third editor in the magazine's 53-year history, was removed from the post on Wednesday. In a statement, the New York Review of Books said it had "decided to remove Ian Buruma from his position as editor of the New York Review of Books, effective immediately, due to his editorial judgment regarding the #MeToo movement." The statement did not explain the reason for Buruma's departure. Ghomeshi, who was fired by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in 2014 after allegations of physical abuse were made against him, has apologized to all the women who accused him of sexual assault or harassment.

– Jodi Kantor's book on the Obamas has been called everything from "self-indulgent" and "self-aggrandizing" to "self-indulgent" and "self-absorbed" by critics. Now the New York Times Book Review is in hot water for one of its reviews. "Call it chick nonfiction, if you will; this book is not about politics, it’s about marriage, or at least one marriage, and a notably successful one at that," historian Douglas Brinkley wrote in his review. "His vaguely sexist-sounding characterization, in what was otherwise a quite positive review, immediately raised howls (and tweets) of protest," writes Jennifer Weiner on Salon. "It’s a little outside my ordinary purview—though Kantor, a New York Times reporter, is Jewish—but the line struck me as newsworthy, particularly given recent discussion accusing the Times Book Review of giving short shrift to woman authors," writes Weiner. "Here, that alleged lack of respect—and to call a book 'chick nonfiction' is to call it unserious—extends not only to the woman who is the author but also to the woman who is the subject." Click for Weiner's full column.

– Former FBI Director James Comey recorded a memo in which he said President Trump had asked him to stop investigating Michael Flynn, the New York Times reports. "I hope you can see your way clear to letting this go, to letting Flynn go," Trump said in the memo. "He is a good guy. I hope you can let this go." According to NBC News, the memo is the first confirmation that Trump asked Comey to stop investigating Flynn. It's also the first time Trump has publicly acknowledged asking Comey to stop investigating Flynn. The Washington Post reports Trump fired Comey over the FBI's investigation of Russian interference in the 2016 election and possible ties between Trump's campaign and Russia. The bill—which was first proposed in 2009—was dropped from an earlier version, and President Yoweri Museveni must now sign it into law. "This is a victory for Uganda. – A new species of praying mantis from Madagascar has been named in honor of Ruth Bader Ginsburg's "relentless fight for gender equality," per a press release. Scientists at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History say the new species of praying mantis is the first to be classified female based on its genitalia. "As a feminist biologist, I often questioned why female specimens weren't used to diagnose most species," says lead author Sydney Brannoch. "This research establishes the validity of using female specimens in the classification of praying mantises." The researchers say the new species of praying mantis reminds them of Ginsburg's famous lace collar, "which resembles the neck plate of the insect," per the Washington Post. The new species of praying mantis, which lives on leaves, was named Ilomantis ginsburgae (ill-oh-mantis ginnz-BURG-ee) in honor of the 83-year-old Supreme Court justice, reports the Cleveland Plain Dealer. The mantis is the first type of praying mantis to be classified female based on its genitalia, which is a first in the insect world, the researchers say. They also say it's the first new species of praying mantis to be named for a woman.
