– NASA's New Horizons spacecraft is hurtling toward Pluto at a million miles per hour as the space agency prepares to make history Tuesday by becoming the first spacecraft to fly by a dwarf planet. The New Horizons probe, which launched nine and a half years ago, will be within 7,800 miles of Pluto's surface when it makes its closest approach at 7:49am EDT, reports Space.com, which has a list of things scientists can learn from the flyby. "The science we've already made is mouth-watering," the mission's lead scientist tells the Guardian. "The Pluto system is enchanting in its strangeness and its alien beauty." Pluto was previously thought to be the ninth planet in the solar system, but new measurements reveal it is actually two-thirds the size of Earth's moon, per the Guardian. The New Horizons probe will take photos of the dwarf planet and its five moons, including Charon, Hydra, Nix, STyx, and Kerberos, NASA reports. It will take so much information from the flyby that it will take 16 months to send it all back to Earth.

– Mitt Romney cruised to an easy victory in Florida's GOP primary, reports AP, winning 47% of the vote to Newt Gingrich's 33%. Rick Santorum finished a distant third with 13%. Ron Paul won just 7% of the vote. Exit polls showed that Romney had a double-digit lead over Gingrich among voters seeking a candidate who could beat President Obama in the general election, and that he won by a wide margin among women, who overwhelmingly favored him over Gingrich. Gingrich vowed to stay in the race despite the one-sided result. "While we celebrate this victory, we must not forget what this election is really about: defeating Barack Obama," he said. The Florida results are a stinging setback for Gingrich, who had been leading in the polls until last week. Exit polls showed that voters were concerned about the economy in a big way, and that Romney was the candidate best able to fix it, notes Politico.

– "Julian Assange said 'a 14 year old could have hacked Podesta' - why was DNC so careless? Also said Russians did not give him the info!" That was Donald Trump's Wednesday morning tweet in response to Assange's claim that a 14-year-old could have hacked Hillary Clinton campaign chairman John Podesta, NBC News reports. "Also [Assange] said Russians did not give him the info!" the president-elect continued in another tweet. Assange on Tuesday told Sean Hannity that the source of Podesta's emails was "not the Russian government and it is not a state party" and that "a 14-year-old kid could have hacked Podesta." US intelligence officials have said Russia is to blame for hacking Democratic groups in an attempt to influence the election, CNN reports. According to NBC News, Trump has previously said it's "nearly impossible" to know who hacked what and when. Trump's Wednesday tweet was in response to Assange's comments.

– BP CEO Bob Dudley's $19.6 million pay package may not seem like much compared to the oil company's $5.2 billion loss last year, but it's actually quite a bit more than some shareholders would like to see. A leading shareholder advisory group has criticized the company's decision to award its top directors their maximum bonuses for 2015, despite the company's lackluster performance, and recommended shareholders vote against the payment plans, the Wall Street Journal reports. "We believe shareholders should question whether payouts were fully earned in respect of the past fiscal year relative to the company's performance," Glass Lewis said in a March report seen by the Journal. BP's compensation committee awards executive bonuses based on the company's performance in a number of strategic areas, including its safety record and internal targets for operational cash flow and underlying profits. "BP executives performed strongly in a difficult environment in 2015, managing the things they could control and for which they were accountable," a BP spokesman said, adding that "safety and operational risk performance was excellent and BP responded quickly and decisively to the drop in oil price." Dudley's pay was going to a non-binding shareholder vote on April 14, but on Thursday, angry shareholders protested at BP's headquarters in London, the Guardian reports.

The suspects—two of whom have confessed to the plot—were recruited online by an al-Qaeda operative in Gaza, who was in the midst of preparations to carry out large-scale bombing and shooting attacks on multiple targets in Israel, according to the Shin Bet security agency. One of the suspects, 23-year-old Iyad Khalil Abu-Sara, admitted to volunteering to carry out a "sacrifice attack" on an Israeli bus traveling between Jerusalem and Ma'aleh Adumim, the Post reports. In the planned attack, terrorists would have fired shots at the bus' wheels, causing it to overturn, before gunning down passengers at close range and firing on emergency responders. The men allegedly received bomb-making training from the Gaza operative via the Internet, and planned to bring a group of foreign terrorists to Israel using fake Russian passports to pose as tourists.

Several people were injured. The officers fired the rubber bullets while trying to clear protesters who were trying to prevent National Police cars from leaving after police confiscated ballot boxes from the voting center. The Spanish government has ordered police to stop the voting process, saying it's illegal. Catalan officials said 38 people were treated for mostly minor injuries. – Australia's Great Barrier Reef is in the midst of what could be the worst outbreak of coral-eating starfish in its history. Already, up to 12 million crown of thorns starfish—which feast on coral—have been found on the 1,400-mile-long reef. A new report commissioned by WWF-Australia predicts the starfish population could jump to 60 million by 2020. "It would be like a locust plague devastating vegetation," Glen Holmes, co-author of The Starfish That Eat The Reef, tells the Brisbane Times. The outbreak is believed to be the result of agricultural fertilizer flowing into the reef waters. "If we cut pollution we can starve the baby crown of thorns starfish and prevent the next outbreak before it happens," Holmes says. "This will give the reef a chance to rebuild its coral cover and grow again." The report warns that if the outbreak follows the patterns of previous ones, coral cover could fall to 10% of its original size.

– The photo of Lee Harvey Oswald holding the same rifle used to kill John F. Kennedy is authentic, according to a new study. Dartmouth researchers used a new digital image forensics technique and a 3-D model of Oswald to refute claims that the photo was faked, reports Highwire Press. "Our detailed analysis of Oswald's pose, the lighting and shadows, and the rifle in his hands refutes the argument of photo tampering," says senior author Hany Farid, a professor of computer science and a pioneering researcher in digital forensics. "With a simple adjustment to the height and weight, the 3-D human model that we created can be used to forensically analyze the pose, stability, and shadows in any image of people," says Farid. The study refutes claims that the photo was faked because Oswald's pose is physically implausible, but "more generally we believe that the type of detailed 3-D modeling performed here can be a powerful forensic tool in reasoning about the physical plausibility of an image," says Farid.

– Baltimore Mayor Stephanie Rawlings-Blake imposed a 10pm-to-5am curfew on the city today, a day after violence and looting erupted following the funeral of Freddie Gray, a 25-year-old black man who suffered a spinal injury while in police custody. The 10pm-to-5am curfew will be in effect for the rest of the week, reports Reuters. "We have no exceptions other than for medical or coming and going from work. We will be stopping people who are out after curfew. We are taking that seriously. We don't want to engage in any forceful action," said Police Commissioner Anthony Batts. The 10pm-to-5am curfew will apply to all adults in the city.

– The American Psychiatric Association has released its fifth version of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, and the big changes are in the categories of autism and ADHD. The big change in ADHD is that adults can now be diagnosed with the disorder as long as they meet one less symptom than children, reports Psych Central. The big change in autism, however, is that it now encompasses four separate disorders— Asperger's, autism spectrum disorder, childhood disintegrative disorder, and pervasive developmental disorder—all of which were previously classified as one disorder. The APA has published three drafts of the new book on its website, and has received more than 13,000 comments, reports the New York Times. The big changes include: The criteria for autism have been relaxed to include symptoms that appear before age 12, instead of before age 7, and the disorder is now called autism spectrum disorder ( ASD) instead of Asperger's. The criteria for ADHD have been strengthened to include several symptoms, instead of just one. Bereavement can now be considered a major depressive episode that lasts more than two months, instead of two years. She was one of the passengers on a Singapore Airlines flight that caught fire early Monday after returning to Changi Airport more than four hours after takeoff, CNN reports. The Boeing 777-300ER carrying 222 passengers and 19 crew had to make an emergency landing around 6am local time after an engine oil warning message was read over the public address system. "I could feel the vibrations," passenger Amit Jain tells Today. "There was a very strange sound, sort of like a slight screeching noise coming from the plane." Jain says he didn't notice anything unusual until he saw a convoy of fire engines racing toward the plane. "I saw the flames getting worse and worse," he says. "I could see the wing turn black from the heat." Passengers were not allowed to leave the plane as firefighters sprayed water and foam on the flames, Jain says. "The pilot came on the public address system a couple of times to tell passengers to stay calm and that fire was being put out," he says. The cause of the fire is under investigation.

Santorum, meanwhile, congratulated Romney but made clear that he has no intention of dropping out. He predicted a big win in Louisiana this Saturday, as well as a victory in Pennsylvania in five weeks, and said he was thankful for the delegates he did get in Illinois.

Scientists have long suspected a link between brain volume and IQ, but a new review of 88 studies involving more than 8,000 participants finds no causal link, reports Science Daily. "Although a certain association is observable, brain volume appears to be of only little practical relevance," says lead researcher Jakob Pietschnig of the University of Vienna in a press release. "Rather, brain structure and integrity appear to be more important as a biological foundation of IQ, whilst brain size works as one of many compensatory mechanisms of cognitive functions." What's more, the link between brain volume and IQ isn't predictive of how smart you are, but of how well you're able to process and use information, Pietschnig says. "While it is tempting to interpret this association in the context of human cognitive evolution and species differences in brain size and cognitive ability, we show that it is not warranted to interpret brain size as an isomorphic proxy of human intelligence differences," the researchers conclude in Neuroscience and Behavioural Reviews. (Want to boost your IQ? Take a IQ test.)

In one case, an undercover agent was stopped when he set off an alarm at a checkpoint but TSA screeners failed to find a fake explosive device taped to his back when he was patted down, officials tell ABC. "The numbers in these reports never look good out of context but they are a critical element in the continual evolution of our aviation security," Johnson says. "We take these findings very seriously in our continued effort to test, measure, and enhance our capabilities and techniques as threats evolve." – A new survey of doctors finds that most agree with parents who want to delay vaccinations for their children—but the doctors aren't happy about it, the New York Times reports. The survey of 534 primary care physicians found that 93% agree with parents who want their children to delay vaccinations, while 20% agree with them "often" or "always," and another 10% agree "sometimes." The doctors say it's important to build trust with families and avoid losing them as patients, but the study's lead author says that's not always the case. "It is sad that we are willing to let children walk out of our offices vulnerable to potentially fatal infections," he tells the Times. "There's a fatigue here, and there's a kind of learned helplessness." The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that children be vaccinated for 14 diseases before age 6, sometimes several shots at once. The doctors in the survey said they tried various strategies to persuade parents, like telling them they had immunized their own children, but they didn't think they were effective.

– Facebook researchers say they've figured out a way to predict whether a relationship is doomed by the shape of the social network—and it's pretty damn good at it. "A spouse or romantic partner is a bridge between a person’s different social worlds," one of the researchers tells the New York Times. The researchers looked at 1.3 million Facebook users and found that embeddedness—the number of mutual friends one has with the other—is a lousy predictor of romantic relationships. But dispersion—the number of friends from a couple's further reaches—is a much better predictor. They were able to identify a user's spouse 60% of the time, or better than a one-in- 50 chance. They also found that people who say they're in a relationship correctly identified their partners a third of the time, compared to one in 50 for guesswork. "So much of social-network analysis confirms what we already know. Relationships that last are ones in which the other person widens our world? Well, yes. Still, it’s kind of nice to have it confirmed with lots of data and algorithms."

– Al-Jazeera's long-awaited arrival in the US is finally here. The Qatar-based news organization will air at 3pm EDT today, replacing Current TV, reports the AP. The network has hired many veterans of US television, including John Seigenthaler, Joie Chen, Antonio Mora, and Sheila MacVicar, and is promising a meaty diet of news that it believes will contrast with the opinionated talk that dominates American news networks. The threats led to the evacuations of dozens of Jewish sites in 33 states. The ash cloud has already forced the cancellation of more than 6,700 flights in Europe so far, the BBC reports, and is threatening to disrupt air traffic to and from the US as well. The planes will fly over Iceland, Scotland, Norway, and Finland, as well as over parts of Iceland, the Faroe Islands, and Norway. The girl's mother, who searched for them for two days, believes the car was traveling no more than 100mph when it crashed. She believes a tire blew, not on the girl or her father, and that a half-dollar-sized hole in the car's right rear wheel is evidence of a blowout. Troopers believe a mechanical failure was not involved in the crash.

– An American Airlines flight en route from Phoenix to Boston had to make an emergency landing in Syracuse, NY, this morning after its captain fell ill, reports USA Today. The airline says the 57-year-old pilot, identified as Capt. Michael Johnston, died during the four-hour flight. "Unfortunately our pilot passed away. The flight, carrying 147 passengers and five crew members, had to make an emergency landing at 7:10am, about four hours into the flight. The FAA requires two crew members be in the cockpit at all times for commercial airliners, and former airline pilot John Cox tells Today in the Sky that Johnston would have been no more vulnerable than any other pilot.

Fossilized traces of the Saccorhytus coronarius, about a millimetre in size, are "exquisitely well preserved," researchers say, per the BBC. "To the naked eye, the fossils we studied look like tiny black grains, but under the microscope the level of detail was jaw-dropping," says a Cambridge professor. "We think that as an early deuterostome this may represent the primitive beginnings of a very diverse range of species, including ourselves. All deuterostomes had a common ancestor, and we think that is what we are looking at here." Saccorhytus was also covered with a thin, relatively flexible skin and muscles, leading researchers to conclude that it moved by contracting its muscles and got around by wriggling. It had a large mouth, likely to eat particles or other creatures, as well as conical structures on its body that might have allowed water to escape, the researchers say. Footage on state television showed them strewn across a snowy field with no buildings nearby. No on the ground casualties were reported. He did not give the number of people on board, but Russian news reports said the plane carried 65 passengers and six crew members. But scientists have now used a pig's own stem cells to rebuild a missing jaw, New Scientist reports. The researchers used stem cells from the pigs' backs to grow scaffolds out of cow leg bone, then sucked fat from the pigs' backs and isolated precursor cells that turned into bone. The scaffolds, carved with a pin to match the pigs' 3D images of their jawbones, shrank slightly over time but remained in place for six months, according to Science Translational Medicine. "You'd get something that looks like M&M candy," the lead researcher says. The researchers used the scaffolds on 14 pigs with facial bone damage. – New York City has been home to the world's richest people for seven years, but the city is no longer home to the world's richest people. A study published Thursday by research firm Wealth-X found that Hong Kong overtook New York as the planet's wealthiest city in 2017, with 10,000 people worth $30 million or more living in the Asian financial hub. The number of ultra-high-net-worth individuals (UHNWIs) in Hong Kong rose by a third last year to 10,000, knocking the Big Apple into the No. 1 spot for the first time, CNBC reports. New York had held the top spot since Wealth-X first started ranking cities with the highest number of UHNWIs in 2011. The firm defines a UHNWI as a person worth $30 million or more. Overall, the United States remains the preferred country for the world's richest and is home to almost a third of the world's ultra-high-net-worth individuals. But Asia, and China in particular, are catching up. Rising Asian wealth has been helped by increasing consumer spending, more investment in infrastructure, and economic reforms, among other factors, Wealth-X said. – Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is backtracking on controversial comments he made last week about a Muslim cleric who convinced Adolf Hitler to exterminate Jews, the New York Times reports. "I wish to clarify my remarks about the connection between the Mufti Haj Amin al-Husseini and the Nazis," Netanyahu wrote on his Facebook page today. "In no way did I intend to absolve Hitler of his responsibility for the Holocaust. Hitler and the Nazi leadership are responsible for the murder of six million Jews." Netanyahu had said Hitler "did not want to exterminate the Jews at the time—he wanted to expel the Jews," but instead convinced al-Husseini, then the mufti of Jerusalem, to convince him to adopt the "Final Solution," a plan that involved killing all European Jews. Netanyahu's original remarks had been denounced as Holocaust denial, and Germany's Chancellor Angela Merkel said today that it was Germany's responsibility, the AP reports. "All Germans know the history of the Nazis that led to the break with civilization that was the Holocaust," she said. "This is taught in German schools for good reason, it must never be forgotten."

– A simple blood test can detect early signs of cancer in as little as five minutes, according to researchers who say the technique could someday be used to screen for such cancers as breast, colorectal, ovarian, and lung cancers. In a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, scientists used a technique called targeted error correction sequencing to analyze circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) in the blood of healthy people and cancer patients. They were able to detect changes in the DNA of 16% of healthy people with cancer and 68% of cancer patients with early-stage disease, according to a press release. "Early detection and intervention are likely to be the most effective means for reducing morbidity and mortality of human cancer," the researchers write. "Early detection has generally been applied for the monitoring of patients with existing tumors. ... This approach has not been useful for early diagnosis of cancer because of insufficient sensitivity to detect really small tumors that only shed minute quantities of DNA into the blood, as well as difficulties with identifying cancer-associated genetic changes without knowing what mutations are present in the primary tumor." – Firefighters in Alberta used chainsaws and other tools Sunday to rescue 10 horses who had fallen through ice in a slough, CTV News reports. According to the Canadian Press, the horses were on a property near Grande Prairie when they wandered onto the ice. "With the warmer temperatures, the ice on the dugouts the horses are used to being on all winter is a lot thinner," Trevor Grant, a regional fire chief, tells the CBC. Firefighters and a search and rescue team were called to the scene, where they used chainsaws to cut a path through the ice so the horses could walk to safety. They then used slings and boards to melt the ice at the edge of the slough. All 10 horses were removed from the water by 6pm, but two horses died from exhaustion and one was injured after kicking other horses. Seven horses were saved. Grant says the rescue was "one of the more difficult ones that our crews have had to deal with." "They weren't domesticated," he says. "They were a wild broncing horse, used in rodeo. So they're not the horses that are standard riding horses."

DeAngelo, a former police officer, hasn't entered a plea.

Pinkus, who was discharged as Lee's agent last year, is still receiving royalties from the book as of this year, Lee's lawyer says. "Pinkus knew that Harper Lee was an elderly woman with physical infirmities that made it difficult for her to read and see," she says. Lee, who is 87 and living in an assisted-living facility, took legal action to get the copyright reassigned last year, but Pinkus was still receiving royalties.

– If you're an older person, your best chance of performing well on memory tests is in the morning, according to a new study. Canadian researchers who observed 16 younger adults between the ages of 19-30 and 16 older adults between the ages of 60 and 82 as they took part in a series of memory tests found that the older adults were 10% more likely to focus on distracting information in the morning than in the afternoon, Medical News Today reports. "Time of day really does matter when testing older adults," says lead author John Anderson. "This age group is more focused and better able to ignore distraction in the morning than in the afternoon." The older adults who were tested in the afternoon showed signs of "idling," which is when a person is resting or thinking about nothing in general. This could indicate that the adults were having a hard time focusing, because when a person is fully aiming their attention at something, resting state activations are suppressed. But there is a silver lining for older adults. When another group of 18 older adults was tested in the morning between 8:30 and 10:30 am, they performed significantly better. – The US embassy in Moscow was supposed to close its recreational facility in the Russian city of Yekaterinburg on Aug. 1. Instead, it's been locked down for two days, the BBC reports. "In line with the Russian government notification, the US Mission to Russia was supposed to have access to our dacha until noon on 1 August," the embassy said in a statement. – It's time to ditch the penny. The US Mint produced 8.4 billion one-cent coins last year, and between production and shipping, they cost $69 million—the highest amount in nine years, the Wall Street Journal reports. That's likely due to the rising cost of zinc, which is used in construction, machine and ship building, and steel production. Meanwhile, the price of copper has surged, which has put pressure on stainless steels. Fortunately, dimes and quarters are cheaper to make, costing less than their monetary value. So the Mint makes up the losses incurred on pennies and nickels with its 10- and 25-cent coins, and last year reported making $391.5 million in seigniorage. Time has a number of ways to save the penny: Get rid of it.

– For the first time, scientists have an accurate count of the world's lakes—and it's a good one. The high-resolution survey, published in Geophysical Research Letters, estimates that there are 117 million lakes on the planet. That's about 3.7% of the surface area of the Earth, reports LiveScience. "This is something one would have assumed had been done long ago, and was in a textbook somewhere," says an environmental scientist involved in the study from Sweden's Umea University. Previous estimates were based on the number of lakes in a parcel of land or on average lake size, and the new count takes into account lakes of all sizes. The biggest lakes, however, are in the Northern Hemisphere, with the Caspian Sea taking up about 143,000 square miles. Most lakes are in the Northern Hemisphere between 45 degrees north latitude and 75 degrees north latitude. "Most lakes are in the far North, and there's actually quite a few of them," says the Umea scientist. "Even if they're small and no one sees them, they are potentially important for global-scale environmental issues like the carbon budget." "The term dates back to medieval times and is based on the concept that fear or horror would 'run the blood cold' or 'curdle' blood." Researchers at Leiden University Medical Center in the Netherlands set out to find out if fear inspired by horror movies actually speeds up blood clotting, and they followed 24 healthy volunteers ages 30 and younger as they watched two horror movies—Insidious and A Year in Champagne—back-to-back. Insidious was more frightening than the documentary, and levels of the blood-clotting protein Factor VIII increased in 57% of viewers compared to 14% of viewers of A Year in Champagne. During the documentary, 86% of participants' levels decreased compared to 43% of viewers of Insidious. "We suspected that fear might speed clotting in the blood," researcher Banne Nemeth says in a press release. "Damaged tissue gives off tissue factor, which triggers the coagulation really, but that's probably faster if there are more clotting factors in the blood." – The link between marijuana and schizophrenia is well established, but a new study suggests that schizophrenia itself may also play a role in one's likelihood of smoking pot. Researchers at King's College London studied the genetic variants associated with schizophrenia, then compared those to the genetic variants associated with marijuana use. They found that people with schizophrenia were more likely to use cannabis, and to use it in greater amounts, than those with no schizophrenia risk genes. "There is a well-established link between people who use cannabis and schizophrenia," says the study's lead author, but "this study indicates 'that people who are at risk for schizophrenia are more likely to use cannabis, and in greater quantities,' which means the causal relationship might actually go both ways," he tells Reuters. "These findings are very valuable." The study looked at 2,082 healthy Australians, of whom 1,011 had used marijuana, and measured each participant's genetic risk profile—the number of genes related to schizophrenia each of them carried. The results "highlights the complex interactions between genes and environments," says the lead researcher. "Certain environmental risks, such as cannabis use, may be more likely given an individual's innate behavior and personality."

"No deal has been proposed," prosecutor Mark Lindquist tells KIRO-FM. "We are not offering any deal but if information is brought forward we would listen." The revelation comes after the police chief in West Valley City, Utah, said that Steven Powell was a "person of interest" in his daughter-in-law's disappearance. "Sure we can't prosecute Josh, but did somebody know anything? Did somebody help him? Those are all the question that we need to resolve," the police chief told a Utah TV station. Susan Powell was reported missing in 2009 after she failed to return from a weekend camping trip with her two sons. Steven Powell was arrested in Washington state last year on charges that he took thousands of photos of women without their knowledge.

– If you're a regular at a strip club in Knoxville, Tenn., you may want to steer clear of the Rock Church's new billboard. It's a three-dimensional image of a bare-chested man with the words, "Strip for me, Jesus Christ." It's a play on the Bible's lectionary reading, "Let us strip off every weight that slows us down, especially the sin that so easily trips us up," according to the church's website. The billboard, which has been up since last month, is meant to draw attention to the church's "discernment and discipline" for its members, the church's marketing director tells the Knoxville News Sentinel. He says it's not meant to be controversial. "It's not meant to be controversial," he says. "It's meant to draw attention to what the Bible says about God's love for us."

In a letter to Mitch McConnell, the RSC warns that the Senate bill could lose support in the House if it doesn't keep four key provisions, including the phasing out of extra federal funding for Medicaid in 2020, the Hill reports. The group also warns that the Senate bill may remove language defunding Planned Parenthood or barring tax credits from being used to "federally fund abortions." The letter comes as Senate Democrats plan a late-night talk-a-thon on the Senate floor Monday to protest the secretive process being used to craft the bill, the Washington Post reports. Sen. Mike Lee, Sen. Ted Cruz, and Sen. Rand Paul have all said they won't support the bill unless states are allowed to opt out of ObamaCare's "community rating" and "guaranteed issue" mandates, which require insurers to cover people with pre-existing conditions. Sources tell the Post that McConnell has so far refused to promise the states will be exempt from either requirement, or to allow states to opt out of the community rating requirement entirely. According to the Washington Post, the 33-year-old Republican from Illinois recently redesigned his office to look like the dining room of Downton Abbey—a show he repeatedly voted to end federal funding for PBS. The office's decorator, Annie Brahler, says she wasn't paid for her work, which is against House rules. “Perhaps it’s not totally surprising that the same congressman who spent campaign money on P90X workout DVDs wanted to create a more picturesque setting in which to be photographed, but the rules clearly require him to pay for those renovations himself,” the executive director of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington says in a statement. “Again and again, Rep. Schock’s seeming obsession with his image impedes his ability to conduct himself in ethical manner.” Schock, who has stepped down from his House seat, hasn't commented on the ethics complaint but has said he's not a Downton Abbey fan, the Post reports. – De La Soul is making its entire catalog available for free download from 11am to noon Saturday, marking the 25th anniversary of its debut album, 3 Feet High and Rising, Rolling Stone reports. "For Pos, Dave, and Maseo this giveaway celebrates the upcoming 25th anniversary of their legendary 1989 debut," the band says in a press release. "For the rest of us it’s just the best Valentine’s gift we’ll probably ever receive." The band— Pos, Dave, and Maseo—has given us such classics as "Eye Know," "Talkin' Bout Hey Love," "I Am I Be," "Betta Listen," and "More Than U Know," among others.

– Wang Qi says he was working as an army surveyor in China in 1963 when he "strayed erroneously" into Indian territory. "I was tired and hungry," he tells the BBC. "I saw a Red Cross vehicle and asked them to help me. They handed me over to the Indian army." For the next seven years, police took him to various jails, where he gave "false background and the circumstances" about his whereabouts, before a court ordered his release in 1969. He never left India, though he was given a Chinese passport in 2013, and on Friday, he flew out of the country. He was met by family members when he landed in Beijing and was met with banners reading "Welcome home, soldier, it's been a rough journey," the BBC reports. His wife, an Indian citizen, was sick and did not accompany him. It's not clear whether he'll return to India, where neighbors say he lived in "utter poverty."

– Man Haron Monis had been fighting his conviction for sending "grossly offensive" letters to the families of Australian soldiers killed in Afghanistan for more than a year when he took 17 hostages in a Sydney cafe on Monday. The siege ended with Monis' death just 17 hours later, the Sydney Morning Herald reports. The 50-year-old, who was convicted of the offense last year and sentenced to 300 hours of community service, had been " consumed by the fight over his conviction," the Herald notes. "This pen is my gun, and these words are my bullets," he had said outside a Sydney court after he was charged over the letters. "I'll fight with these weapons against oppression to promote peace." Monis argued that the offense in question, which he pleaded guilty to, infringed the implied freedom of communication on political and governmental matters in the Commonwealth constitution. But the High Court rejected his application to hear the case on Friday. "In our opinion it suffices to say that, having regard to the history of the matter, we do not think it appropriate to make [the order sought to hear the case]," the chief justice and another justice wrote in their decision.

– Rep. John Conyers says he won't attend Donald Trump's inauguration because the president-elect "has demeaned and insulted the African-American community," the New York Times reports. "I will do everything in my power to ensure that accountability is brought to bear on the administration and that the Constitution and our nation's laws are adhered to, as no one is above the law," the Hill quotes Conyers as saying in a statement. He's one of 26 Democratic members of Congress who have said they won't attend Trump's inauguration on Friday. According to the BBC, Conyers says Trump "has demeaned and insulted the African-American community, and we are going to have to really raise our voices and resist this if these views are going to be reflected in his policies." Others skipping the inauguration include Rep. Barbara Lee of California, Rep. Ral Grijalva of Arizona, Maxine Waters of California, Luis V. Gutiérrez of Illinois, Katherine M. Clark of Massachusetts, William Lacy Clay of Missouri, Nydia M. Velzquez of New York, Marcia L. Fudge of Ohio, Earl Blumenauer and Kurt Schrader of Oregon, and Mark Pocan of Wisconsin. – BP's latest attempt to contain the oil spill hit a snag today when a diamond-edged saw became stuck in a thick pipe on a blown-out well at the bottom of the Gulf. Coast Guard Adm. Thad Allen said the goal was to free the saw and finish the cut later in the day. This is the latest attempt to contain—not plug—the leak, which is at least two months from completion. "I don't think the issue is whether or not we can make the second cut. It's about how fine we can make it, how smooth we can make it," Allen said. If the cut is not as smooth as engineers would like, they would be forced to put a looser fitting cap on top of the oil spewing out. This cut-and-cap effort could temporarily increase the flow of oil by as much as 20%, though Allen said officials wouldn't know whether that had happened until the cut could be completed. Officials may have to bring in a second saw awaiting on a boat, but it was not immediately clear how long that could delay the operation. – Hillary Clinton unveiled a plan Monday to tighten gun laws, including expanding background checks and revoking the licenses of gun dealers who sell to "straw purchasers," the New York Times reports. According to the Washington Post, Clinton wants to close the so-called "gun show loophole," which requires no background check for buyers at a gun show or online. It's unclear how Clinton plans to close the "gun show loophole," though her campaign says she plans to use executive action to close the loophole. Gun control advocates say the current definition of what it means to be "engaged in the business" of selling guns is too vague, so executive action might be the way forward. "By putting this idea forward, it is something of an implicit challenge to the current administration to move forward along these lines," an expert at the Center for American Progress tells the Post. Clinton's plan also includes repealing a law that protects gun manufacturers from liability for gun violence, the Times reports. According to the Post, Clinton's plan includes closing loopholes in the background check system and revoking the licenses of gun dealers who knowingly supply so-called "straw purchasers." Clinton's plan also includes repealing the ban on assault-style weapons and requiring background checks for all gun sales.

"I have a great relationship with the Mexican people. I have many people working for me—look at the job in Washington—I have many legal immigrants working with me. And many of them come from Mexico. They love me, I love them," he tells NBC News. "And I'll tell you something, if I get the nomination, I'll win the Latino vote." He says Hillary Clinton's immigration policy would "let everybody come in ... killers, criminals, drug dealers." "Hillary's weak on immigration," he adds. "I might be divisive on immigration, but she's weak on immigration, which is far worse." Trump—who says he'll build an "impenetrable" wall on the US-Mexico border and "get them to pay for the wall"—says he has a contractor that's "one of the biggest in the nation" and is doing a "very good job" at his hotel project in Washington, DC. – A van veered onto a promenade and barreled down the busy walkway in central Barcelona on Thursday, swerving back and forth as it mowed down pedestrians and turned a picturesque tourist destination into a bloody killing zone. Thirteen people were killed and 100 were injured, 15 of them seriously, in what authorities called a terror attack. The late afternoon attack in the city's Las Ramblas district left victims sprawled in the historic street, spattered with blood or writhing in pain from broken limbs. Others were ushered inside shops by officers with their guns drawn or fled in panic, screaming and carrying young children in their arms. "It was clearly a terror attack, intended to kill as many people as possible," Josep Lluis Trapero, a senior police official for Spain's Catalonia region told reporters late Thursday. The Islamic State group claimed responsibility, saying in a statement on its Aamaq news agency that the attack was carried out by "soldiers of the Islamic State" in response to the extremist group's calls for followers to target countries participating in the coalition trying to drive it from Syria and Iraq. – The House Benghazi committee released its final report today, and one nugget in particular is getting a lot of attention: During an emergency conference call on the night of the attack, State Department officials raised concerns about whether Marines should wear uniforms instead of their uniforms, the Washington Post reports. The military never deployed to Benghazi, and a commander told the committee that as they were readying themselves to deploy, they kept having to change in and out of their uniforms four times. The issue came up because, during the call, half of the action items people wrote down were about evacuation, and many of them were about the attack itself. "We are aware that the committee is critical of these issues, but we are not aware of any finding that they had any impact on the attacks or our ability to send help," a State Department spokesperson said in a statement. "The fact is, we did not cause a delay." The full report is here.

– Air Force One’s “absolutely impeccable,” Hillary Clinton tells the BBC, but “it’s a little challenging jet lag-wise, mileage, dehydration, all of the problems that come with spending a lot of time in the air.” So how does she handle it? “I’ve traveled with you quite a bit, and at the end of the trips, I’m exhausted and I take a few days off. You go back to the office the next day.” She does yoga, a special diet, and drinks a lot of water: “I know that some people think you should stay up for a certain period of time and not sleep on certain legs, but since I am perpetually tired, I figure make up for the lost hours of sleep while flying,” she says. “Also, I know very simple things—drink a lot of water, deep breathing, try to get a little bit of sunshine if you can every day. But I don’t know that there’s any magic formula. Because I, too, often am tired.”

– Japan's government and business groups are hoping a new initiative will cut down on suicides linked to overwork. The "Premium Friday" plan calls for companies to make employees leave work early on the last Friday of the month, starting in February, reports the BBC. The idea is that employees will be better able to spend time with family and friends after work, which is often the case in Japan, where some 22% of the population work more than 49 hours a week. " Japanese workers worry about letting down their colleagues," says an economist at the Dai-ichi Life Research Institute. "They have a strong sense of working as a team." A recent case of "karoshi," or overwork-related suicide, prompted Dentsu, Japan's biggest ad agency, to investigate the death of a woman who had been working more than 100 hours overtime a month, reports the Wall Street Journal. Her death was ruled to be a case ofkaroshi, and Dentsu's chief executive will resign while the company investigates. Japan has tried other ways to combat overwork in the past, including increasing public holidays and allowing government workers to work early in the summer. – A Swedish power plant is turning old coal- and oil-fired plants into cleaner ones, and it's using clothing from the likes of H&M to do so. "For us it's a burnable material," says a rep for Malarenergi, the utility that runs the 54-year-old Vasteras power station northwest of Stockholm. "Our goal is to use only renewable and recycled fuels." The coal- and oil-fired units at the plant, which burned as much as 650,000 tons of coal at its peak in 1996, will be replaced by a wood-fired unit by 2020, reports Bloomberg, which notes that Sweden is among the world's most carbon-free countries. Malarenergi has a deal with the city of Eskilstuna to burn some of the city's trash, including clothing from H&M's warehouses, reports the Local. H&M, which says it doesn't burn clothes that aren't safe to wear, isn't the first to try to make use of old plants and trash: The company runs a clothing recycling program at one of its stores in Sweden, per Quartz.

– President Obama has created two new national monuments—one in Utah and one in Nevada—in his final weeks in office. The Bears Ears National Monument in Utah will cover 1.35 million acres in the Four Corners region, the White House says. In Nevada, the Gold Butte National Monument will cover 300,000 acres near Las Vegas that includes rock art, rare fossils, and recently discovered dinosaur tracks, Reuters reports. "Today's actions will help protect this cultural legacy and will ensure that future generations are able to enjoy and appreciate these scenic and historic landscapes," Obama said in a statement. In Utah, Republican Sen. Orrin Hatch called Obama's move an "astonishing and egregious abuse of executive power" and vowed to work with Congress and the incoming Trump administration to undo it, the Salt Lake Tribune reports. But Navajo Nation President Russell Begaye called it an exciting day for his tribe and people of all cultures. "We have always looked to Bears Ears as a place of refuge," he said. "The rocks, the winds, the land—they are living, breathing things that deserve timely and lasting protection." The designation is "a victory for Native American tribes and conservationists," the White House says. "Today's actions will help protect this cultural legacy

– There's no evidence of foul play or violence in celebrity chef Anthony Bourdain's death in a French hotel room, a French prosecutor said Saturday. The famed cook, writer and host of the CNN series Parts Unknown killed himself Friday in a luxury hotel in the ancient village of Kaysersberg, Christian de Rocquigny, the prosecutor of Colmar in France's eastern Alsace region, told the AP in a phone interview. Rocquigny said there did not appear to be much planning in the television personality's suicide. "There is no element that makes us suspect that someone came into the room at any moment," he said, adding that a medical expert had concluded that there were no signs of violence on Bourdain's body. Rocquigny said toxicology tests were being carried on Bourdain's body, including urine tests, to see if the 61-year-old American took any medications or other drugs, in an effort to help his family understand if anything led him to kill himself. Olivier Nasti, the chef and owner of Le Chambard, the luxury hotel in Kaysersberg where Bourdain took his life, paid tribute to his colleague Saturday. – Cleveland has released a surveillance video showing the fatal police shooting of 12-year-old Tamir Rice—and it's not pretty. In the first two minutes of the 30-minute video, officers can be seen forcing Tamir's 14-year-old sister to the ground, handcuffed her, and placing her in the back of a police car less than 10 feet from her dying brother, the AP reports. An attorney representing the Rice family calls the video "shocking and outrageous" and says it shows officers showing "overwhelming indifference" to Tamir as he lay on the ground after being shot by officer Timothy Loehmann. An FBI agent who was in the neighborhood can be seen in the video administering first aid to Tamir, the AP reports. Cleveland Mayor Frank Jackson's administration initially refused to release the video, arguing it was part of an "open and ongoing investigation" and therefore not public viewing. The city agreed to release 15 minutes of footage after the Northeast Ohio Media Group filed a public-records request.

– A group of soldiers stormed the presidential palace in Mali's capital today and declared a coup, ousting President Amadou Toumani Toure just one month before he was due to step down. The soldiers announced that they were suspending Mali's constitution and dissolving its institutions. The soldiers complained that the civilian government had not done enough to combat a rebellion by the ethnic Tuareg separatists, who want to carve out a homeland in the country's northern desert. "The CNRDR representing all the elements of the armed forces, defensive forces, and security forces has decided to assume its responsibilities and end the incompetent and disavowed regime of Amadou Toumani Toure," they said, reading from a statement. "The objective of the CNRDR does not in any way aim to confiscate power, and we solemnly swear to return power to a democratically elected president as soon as national unity and territorial integrity are established." The West African regional bloc ECOWAS said it "strongly condemns the misguided actions of the mutineers." The US condemned the coup, the AP reports, calling it "all the more reprehensible, coming amidst the ongoing regional and international efforts to seek a peaceful solution to the rebellion in the north of the country

– If you've ever wondered what it would be like to relieve yourself in space, NASA has just the thing for you: It's offering $30,000 to the winner of its "Space Poop" contest to come up with a hands-free system that collects waste for up to six days, reports the Telegraph. "The old standby solution consisted of diapers," says NASA. "However, the diaper is only a very temporary solution, and doesn't provide a healthy/protective option longer than one day." Astronauts currently use a vacuum and tube to get their waste out of the International Space Station, but in weightlessness, fluids can blob up and stick to surfaces. "You don't want any of these solids and fluids stuck to your body for six days," NASA says, recalling how easy babies can get diaper rash. NASA plans to test three winning designs in the next year, then roll them out to astronauts in the next three, reports Space.com. (Click to read about NASA's new robot astronaut.)

– John Kerry was in Warsaw today for a joint press conference with Polish President Bronislaw Komorowski, and the secretary of state fell asleep just as Komorowski was beginning his response to a question from a reporter, ABC News reports. President Obama, who was also at the press conference, could be heard praising Poland's support of the US in the face of Vladimir Putin's aggression in Ukraine, CNN reports. Kerry, who was also at the press conference with Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, had a bit of a rest before meeting with NATO Secretary-General Anders Fogh Rasmussen, the AP reports.

– Janet Napolitano’s former top adviser on immigration has been placed on leave amid allegations of “lewd” behavior. Suzanne Barr, who stepped down last week as chief of staff for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, has been referred to the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General and ICE’s Office of Professional Responsibility for review, Fox News reports. Two new affidavits were submitted this week as part of a discrimination and retaliation lawsuit filed against Napolitano earlier this year by James T. Hayes Jr., head of ICE’s New York office. In one, an employee says Barr called him a “sexy” and asked, “How long is it anyway?” Barr was also present at a party in Colombia where she “offered to perform oral sex,” according to one affidavit. “People are coming out of the woodwork on this because this is such a serious matter,” the attorney representing Hayes tells the New York Times.

– Daivon Reeder's stepdad told him it was "pointless" to go to orientation at Eastern Michigan University. "I was like OK, I'll show you," the 22-year-old Detroit native tells Fox 2 Detroit. Four years later, Reeder is graduating with a major in criminal justice and a minor in military science—and his tweet about it has gone viral. "I looked at the picture and the emoji of me laughing I thought that was an ironic situation—we are in two different situations in our lives," Reeder says. "Look what you said and look where you are at." Reeder, who is the first in his family to go to college, says he lost a scholarship while attending EMU, had to go to basic training for the Army, and worked two jobs to support his family. But instead of being angry, he and nine students founded a mentoring organization to teach young boys what he had to learn the hard way. "Living our values—live, learn, teach, knowing I was living life making mistakes," he says. "But I was learning from them able to teach someone else."

– Reality Winner, the young woman accused of leaking classified information to the Intercept, is expected to plead guilty to charges related to that leak at a hearing Tuesday, the Washington Post reports. According to CNN, Winner, 22, is accused of providing information to the Intercept about the FBI's investigation into Michael Cohen, President Trump's former personal lawyer, who has pleaded guilty to lying to the FBI about his ties to Russia. Winner's lawyer says the charges against her will be laid at Tuesday's hearing. According to the Post, the charges against Winner include disclosing national security information to the Intercept and giving the Intercept information about the FBI's investigation of Cohen. Winner's mother says in a statement that she "will accept full responsibility for any wrongdoing and that she is ready and willing to face the consequences." She is the second person to plead guilty under the Trump administration's crackdown on leakers.

He added: "GQ editor: What you did was very offensive to Hugo Boss. Me: What Hugo Boss did was very offensive to the Jews."

– A ruling issued Tuesday by the New Jersey Supreme Court could cause more than 20,000 drunken driving convictions to be vacated, the AP reports. The justices unanimously found that criminal charges pending against a state police sergeant made breath-testing device test results from five counties inadmissible as evidence. Sgt. Marc Dennis was in charge of calibrating the devices, and authorities have alleged that he skipped a required step in the calibration process. Dennis has denied any wrongdoing and has alleged that he skipped a required step in the calibration process. The Supreme Court ruling does not automatically expunge all the drunken-driving convictions, but the justices did note that defendants tested by the affected breath machines could now seek to challenge their convictions. The decision also raises questions about cases that are still moving through the judicial system. "We'll be issuing guidance shortly for our county prosecutors and municipal prosecutors over how to handle those cases," Gurbir Grewal, the New Jersey attorney general, said at a news conference on Tuesday. NJ.com reports the ruling opens the floodgates for thousands of people to challenge DWI convictions that occurred over nearly a decade. – Bristol Palin’s time on Dancing With the Stars came to an end last night—for the first time ever—with Kirstie Alley and Maks Chmerkovskiy the latest to be eliminated. The audience vote saved Alley last week, but it wasn’t enough this time, PopEater reports. “I had an awesome time and an awesome partner and I wish everyone the best of luck,” Palin said before leaving the stage. Apolo Ohno and Karina Smirnoff were also in the bottom three, along with Alley and Chmerkovskiy, and Palin and partner Mark Ballas. The rest of the competitors will compete next week in a team freestyle dance and an individual dance to a guilty pleasure song.

– Mitt Romney's application to tear down a beach house in California and quadruple its size has been shot down by the man who owns it. "That was the wire story we had run the day before, and it was all over the Internet," New Hampshire Union Leader publisher Joe McQuaid tells Politico. "It’s not accurate, Romney said, simply. The application he made, two years ago, was to double the living space by turning one story into two. The 'quadrupling' was a measurement of added nonliving space, including a basement and garage. That sounds more reasonable, I said. Had he issued a statement to that effect? He shrugged his shoulders with a 'why bother?''' McQuaid, who says he's never met Romney, notes that the candidate "makes no bones about making a lot of money in the private sector." The full piece is in the Union Leader today.

– Texting $10 to 90999 to donate $10 to Haiti earthquake relief is proving to be a simple and effective way for hundreds of thousands of Americans to help victims of the devastating quake. Wireless carriers, including AT&T, Verizon, and Sprint, say they're waiving fees for the appeal, which has raised more than $3 million so far. AT&T and Sprint say they're not charging for the appeal, MSNBC reports, but T-Mobile and Sprint say you can just upgrade to an unlimited text package to make the donation. Sprint also says it's waiving fees, retroactive to Wednesday. "So many folks who are texting $10 now might not have been at a place to write a check, or call a toll-free number or send mail," says a Verizon spokesman. "This is a new stream of philanthropy."

– The Ukrainian government will restart cease-fire negotiations with pro-Russian insurgents in the country's east only once the rebels lay down their weapons, the defense minister said today. Valery Heletey's statement, posted on the Defense Ministry website, comes amid growing confidence among government forces after they drove the insurgent militia from their stronghold of Slovyansk. Last week, Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko promised cease-fire talks no later than that Saturday, but a series of military successes by the Ukrainian army may have changed minds in Kiev. Instead, on Saturday, Ukrainian troops routed the rebels in Slovyansk, forcing hundreds of militants to regroup in the regional capital, Donetsk—a rare and significant victory for Ukraine, which has often appeared helpless in the face of the spreading insurgency. On today, the mayor of Donetsk issued a statement after a meeting with Poroshenko, saying the president suggested talks could take place in Svyatogorsk, a town in the north of the region. The insurgents would be unlikely to agree to Svyatogorsk, which is controlled by Kiev. He said locations acceptable to the rebels include Donetsk, Russia, or Belarus. – Joe Biden arrived in Boston today to mark the first anniversary of the Boston Marathon bombing, and he praised survivors, first responders, and the city's resilience in a ceremony at the Hynes Convention Center. "This day will always be hard, but this place will always be strong," former Mayor Thomas Menino told an invitation-only audience of about 2,500 people, the AP reports. "We recognize the incredible courage and leadership of so many Bostonians in the wake of unspeakable tragedy," President Obama said in a statement. "And we offer our deepest gratitude to the courageous firefighters, police officers, medical professionals, runners, and spectators who, in an instant, displayed the spirit Boston was built on— perseverance, freedom, and love." The Boston Marathon is scheduled for Monday, and Biden said this year's race will "show the world the meaning of Boston Strong as a city chooses to run again." The family of Lingzi Lu, one of the three people killed in the bombing, was among those in attendance at the ceremony, the Boston Herald reports.

– Pope Benedict XVI made his first public appearance since announcing his resignation today, presiding over Ash Wednesday celebrations from St. Peter's Basilica. But as the Wall Street Journal reports, the real news out of the Vatican today isn't about the pope's appearance—it's about what he'll do once he steps down on Feb. 28. Benedict is expected to appoint the new chief of the Vatican bank, a move that would make the next pope the custodian of the secretive institution, leaving him with a just-picked man to run it. The pope has made it clear that he has no intention of interfering with his successor's work, and Vatican officials say he'll continue to be one of the church's leading theologians, an intellectual status that carries enormous weight. He'll continue to live inside the Vatican, where he'll write and pray, but he'll be whisked by helicopter to the papal summer residence, Castel Gandolfo, on the outskirts of Rome, where the Vatican is finishing up a recently renovated convent. – A UK mom of "miracle" triplets died suddenly at home on her first Christmas with the girls, the BBC reports. Rachel Park, 39, died Tuesday at the family home in Bransty, Whitehaven. Police say her death is "unexplained but not suspicious." Park gave birth to the girls, Poppie, Mollie, and Evelyn, in March, but they were born 14 weeks early and spent more than three months in the hospital. "They each took a turn at being quite poorly," says Park. "It was touch and go with all three at some point, but they're all out of hospital and fine now. We were told to prepare for the worst. They've had quite a tough journey but they're growing now and doing well. We're looking forward to Christmas—there are toys everywhere!" A family friend says Park "supported me through every step because she knew what I was going through. I wouldn't be where I am without her support." A GoFundMe page has been set up to help the family.

– The EPA is rolling out new air-pollution rules today that will slash the amount of sulfur in gasoline by two-thirds and put lower-pollution vehicles on the road by 2017, reports the Washington Post. The rules, which have been in the works since 2011, are seen as one of the Obama administration's most significant air-pollution initiatives, notes the Post. Automakers and their lobbying groups have been pushing for the tougher rules, and they met with White House aides last week to present their case, reports the Hill. Oil industry officials, however, say the rules will be costly and unnecessary, and they've been pushing the administration to delay them for a year to give them time to mature.

– Edgar Latulip was 21 years old when he disappeared from his home in Kitchener, Ontario, and police had no idea he'd been missing for three decades. But in January, Latulip told a social worker in St. Catharines, Ontario, that he had "effectively forgot who he was" after suffering a head injury when he moved to the city years ago, reports CTV News. Police were able to track him down thanks in part to a tip that he had been spotted in Hamilton, Ontario, years earlier. A DNA test confirmed his identity on Friday and police say they're now working to reunite him with his family. "I did speak with one of the family members yesterday and today, and ... they're obviously very happy about it, and they're making plans to get together with Edgar and speak with him further," says a police spokesman.

Even before polls opened in the former Soviet republic, the Central Election Commission announced that 36% of the 7 million registered voters had cast their ballots during five days of early voting. By 4pm on election day, the official turnout was nearly 75%, even though many polling stations in the capital and nearby villages were nearly empty, the AP reports. – If the US doesn’t raise its debt ceiling by Aug. 2, it won’t have enough money to pay its bills, according to an analysis by the Bipartisan Policy Center. The government’s savings account would be nearly empty, and the president would be forced to make “extraordinarily difficult choices” about what to pay or not pay, including Social Security, Medicare, unemployment benefits, student loans, and salaries for members of the military and veterans, administration officials and the former senior Treasury Department official in the George HW Bush administration tell the Washington Post. “You can move the chess pieces around all you want,” said Jay Powell, an author of the center’s report. “You’re going to lose.” The center estimates that if the debt ceiling isn’t raised, the US will have a $134 billion shortfall in August alone. It would also have to cut 44% of spending through August, according to the report. “You do not have to default and you don’t have to shut down the government if you choose not to,” said an economist. “They’ll never solve the problem, and we’ll end up like Greece.”

– When Ohio state troopers pulled over a rented Ford Expedition on Wednesday for following too closely, they say they were in for a big surprise—in the trunk and back seat, UPI reports. Troopers say a drug-sniffing police dog alerted them to 10 gift-wrapped boxes containing 71 pounds of marijuana, 360 THC pills, and a pound of hash wax oil. The haul was worth an estimated $330,000. Daniel Yates, 31, of Eureka, Calif., was charged with drug possession and trafficking, both felonies. He faces up to 16 years in prison and up to a $30,000 fine.

– Hurricane Irma made landfall in the Florida Keys early Sunday as a Category 5 storm, knocking out power to at least 850,000 people in Miami-Dade County, reports USA Today. The eye of the storm made landfall around 5am ET and was moving north-north-east at 12mph. It was centered about 30 miles north-northeast of Marco Island, reports the AP, and was expected to move over the southern tip of the Florida Keys early Monday and then hit Tampa as a Category 1 storm. It had maximum sustained winds of 100mph early Sunday but was expected to weaken as it moves over Georgia and South Carolina. "I can't tell you how bad this is," Florida Gov. Rick Scott said at a news conference. "We're going to get through this. We've got a lot of work to do." The death toll from the storm in Florida was at least three, including a sheriff's deputy and a prison employee killed in a car crash as the storm approached the state's east coast. Irma is expected to move over Georgia and South Carolina on Monday before reaching the Carolinas on Tuesday.

– Australian Prime Minister Julia Gillard is in the news today for what some are calling an "absurd" choice of hobby: knitting a baby kangaroo for Prince William's soon-to-be-born baby. "In terms of knitting for Kate's baby—I knit for babies, in part, because they are smaller projects," she tells Australian Women's Weekly. "I've got not that much time in my life. You can get them done and there's a sense of satisfaction in having completed it." Critics are calling it "contrived" and "remarkable," notes the Guardian. "We know the prime minister is good at spinning a yarn, now we have a picture to prove it," says a senior Liberal politician. But Gillard's press office says it wasn't a PR move: "I'm picturing a story that includes the patterns for the items the PM will knit so your readers can knit their own royal blanket or something."

– Joe McGinniss is no fan of Sarah Palin, and he's not happy about it. The journalist, who is feuding with Palin over his upcoming book about her, has shut down his email account, reports the AP. Palin has been posting nasty comments about McGinniss on Facebook, recruiting other right-wing figures to help her destroy him, and urging her followers to send McGinniss death threats. " McGinniss is a particular sort of journalist unfortunately not so in vogue anymore," writes Michael Wolff at Vanity Fair. "His own obsessiveness and personal involvement invariably become part of the story." "The campaign against McGinniss is a pretty stunning abuse of the kind of media access and power that Palin & Co possess—it’s crowd incitement," writes Wolff. "Not a lot of chance he’s going to be scared off. He’s Br'er Rabbit."

– Police in Denver say a 16-year-old girl killed her 7-year-old nephew, wrapped his body in a blanket, and hid it in a portable closet in her basement bedroom, the Denver Post reports. According to a probable cause statement, the girl was upset after having a fight with her girlfriend and told her nephew, Jordan Vong, to go upstairs to play video games on Aug. 6. Instead, he went to sit on her bed and she pushed him off the bed, the statement says. He hit his face on the floor and stopped moving for a few minutes. The teen "didn't tell any of her family what she had done to Jordan because she was afraid," the statement says. "Nor did she tell any of her family where she had hid Jordan." Police found Jordan's body on Aug. 6 after getting a search warrant for the home. The teen was arrested the next day and will be charged as an adult in Jordan's death, KDVR reports. "It was intentionally concealed, and it took some time to find it," a police spokesman says. The coroner's office has ruled Jordan's death a homicide.

– Far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon used 3D holograms to make his campaign launch—the same day far-right candidate Marine Le Pen held a rally in Paris. Melenchon used the technology to give a modern look to his campaign launch, which coincided with Le Pen's rally, Reuters reports. Le Pen, speaking in Lyon on Sunday, told thousands of flag-waving supporters "This is our country!" that she alone would protect them against Islamic fundamentalism and globalisation if elected president in May. There are some similarities between Melenchon's platform and Le Pen's, as both are skeptical of the EU and globalisation, but they differ sharply on other issues including migration. Melenchon mentioned the Socialist party's presidential candidate Benoit Hamon, who has called on left-wing forces to unite. "Everyone wants to abolish El Khomri (a labor law), including the Socialist candidate. I wonder what holds him back?" said Melenchon, who has between 11 and 11.5 percent support, according to Friday's BVA poll. The Socialists, weakened after the deeply unpopular presidency of Francois Hollande, have no chance of getting beyond the first round of the election in April, according to the latest polls.

– Tom Petty's family and former Heartbreakers members are releasing a four-CD box set of previously unreleased material in the late singer's memory. An American Treasure, which will include live recordings, deep cuts, and alternate versions of Petty's most popular songs, will be released Sept. 28, SiriusXM reports. It was produced by Petty's family and former Heartbreakers Benmont Tench, Mike Campbell, and Ryan Ulyate. A less expensive two-CD set will also be available for purchase. Petty was found unconscious at his home in Malibu on Oct. 2, 2017, and died hours later. A medical examiner ruled that he died of an accidental overdose.

Snap is planning to raise up to $3.2 billion with the IPO, and the Journal notes that at the top of the range, the company would be worth about $20 billion. "I'm old and they're older," one portfolio manager says. "Because of that lack of understanding, the first reaction is we'll steer clear until we see the dust settle."

That's 312 times the average CEO pay, reports the Guardian, which notes that the pay gap has risen dramatically since the 1990s. In 1965, the ratio of CEO to worker pay was 20 to one; by 1989, it had risen to 58 to one, and in 2000, it had hit 344 times. Last year, CEOs of the country's largest companies saw an average pay rise of 17.6%; the S&P 500 index of the country's largest companies grew 637% over the same period. The Guardian notes that the pay gap is skewed by tech companies, where the CEO founders may own a large chunk of the company but don't take home much in compensation. Amazon's Jeff Bezos was paid close to $82,000 last year, while the average Amazon worker earned $28,446—a ratio of 59 to one for his entire package and just three to one counting salary. – The "unicorn of the sea" has been washing up on beaches from British Columbia to Alaska in what the Guardian calls an "unprecedented, insane amount." Olivia Blondheim, a University of Oregon graduate student working with National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration biologist Rick Brodeur on a research expedition, tells the Guardian that pyrosomes have been washing up "as far as the eye can see" along the west coast of the US. "There were reports of some pyrosomoes in 2014, and a few more in 2015 but this year there has been an unprecedented, insane amount," she says. Pyrosomes are "tubular, gelatinous creatures that are actually moving colonies of tiny organisms," according to the NOAA. They're usually found far from the coast in tropical waters, but this year they've been spotted as far north as Sitca, Alaska, and they've been washing up on beaches from British Columbia to Alaska, the Washington Post reports. Kyl, a fellow Arizona senator and McCain's Senate colleague for more than 40 years, said McCain "did not like to quarrel. He did not like to argue. He was a man of great courage." – Two Ohio men wrongly convicted of a 1975 murder were freed today after 39 years behind bars, reports NBC News. Ricky Jackson, 57, served more time in prison on a wrongful conviction than anyone else in US history, and Wiley Bridgeman, 60, was the longest-held US prisoner to be exonerated, says the Ohio Innocence Project. The men were convicted based on the testimony of a 12-year-old boy, Edward Vernon, who recanted last year, saying he was coerced by detectives. "A lot of people think I should be mad," said Jackson after being released. "In '75, he was a 12-year-old-kid." Bridgeman's brother, Ronnie, was released from prison in 2003, and both men were on death row until Ohio declared the death penalty unconstitutional in 1978. "One of them came within 20 days of execution before Ohio ruled the death penalty unconstitutional," says the director of the Ohio Innocence Project. Jackson was originally sentenced to death, but that sentence was vacated because of a paperwork error, and he was sentenced to life in prison. Wiley Bridgeman was sentenced to death, but that sentence was vacated because of a paperwork error. The state is conceding the obvious, says Cuyahoga County Prosecutor Timothy McGinty.

– Investigators are looking into whether Prince died from an overdose and whether a doctor was prescribing him drugs in the weeks before he was found dead at his home in suburban Minneapolis, a law enforcement official told the AP on Thursday. The official said that among the things investigators are looking at is whether a doctor was on a plane that made an emergency landing in Illinois less than a week before Prince died. The official said investigators are looking at whether Prince overdosed on the plane and whether an overdose killed him, and at what kind of drugs were involved. One possibility is the powerful painkiller Percocet or something similar, the official said. Narcan can be used on people even if an overdose isn't confirmed because it wouldn't necessarily be harmful. The official also confirmed some details that have previously been reported by other media outlets, including TMZ. Prince's plane made an emergency stop in Moline, in western Illinois, on April 15 and he was found unconscious on the plane, the official said. The person said first responders gave Prince a shot of Narcan, which is used in suspected opioid overdoses. The official said the so-called save shot was given to when the plane was on the tarmac in Moline as Prince returned to Minneapolis following a performance in Atlanta.

– Ohio voters will get to decide in November whether to make their state the sixth to legalize marijuana for recreational use—and the first to do so for anyone over 21—with a constitutional amendment on the ballot, the Cincinnati Enquirer reports. A private investor group called ResponsibleOhio collected more than 321,000 signatures for the measure, which would allow Ohio to join Colorado, Washington State, Oregon, Alaska, and the District of Columbia in legalizing marijuana for both medical and recreational use. "It's time for marijuana legalization in Ohio, and voters will have the opportunity to make it happen this November—we couldn't be more excited," the group's executive director said in a statement after the state's secretary of state certified the signatures. "By reforming marijuana laws in November, we'll provide compassionate care to sick Ohioans, bring money back to our local communities, and establish a new industry with limitless economic development opportunities." The measure would limit commercial marijuana cultivation to 10 farms, which would be owned by a few, including Nick Lachey, Oscar Robertson, and a fashion designer, USA Today reports. If the measure passes, Ohio would be the first state to legalize marijuana for both medical and recreational use, though 28 states have medical marijuana programs.

– A Montana police officer who shot and killed an unarmed man during a traffic stop last year was justified in his actions, a jury decided today. Grant Morrison, a five-year veteran of the Billings force, testified that he thought 38-year-old Richard Ramirez was reaching for his waistband after the man dropped his left hand, the AP reports. "I knew in that moment, which later was determined to be untrue, but I knew in that moment that he was reaching for a gun," Morrison said. "I couldn't take that risk. I wanted to see my son grow up." Dashcam video of the shooting shows Morrison breaking down as colleagues try to calm him down, Mediaite reports. "I thought he was gonna pull a gun on me," he says. Ramirez's actions were not shown in the video, but Morrison said Ramirez dropped his hand out of the officer's view and "started to jiggle it up and down." The jury deliberated about an hour before delivering its decision. Yellowstone County Attorney Scott Twito said he does not expect to file any charges given the jury's decision. Ramirez's family said they were disappointed by the ruling and intend to file a lawsuit against Morrison and the Billings Police Department alleging excessive use of force

But China's state-run Securities Daily said last week that the 36-year-old X-Men: Days of Future Past star was "under control" and "will accept the legal decision," several news outlets including Taiwan News reported last week, per the Hollywood Reporter. It's not clear why Fan hasn't been seen in public since then, but the Epoch Times reports that rumors have circulated that she is living under house arrest. The rumors started in May when Cui Yongyuan, a former TV host with the state-owned China Central Television, posted purported contracts online that suggested Fan had received under-the-table payments. – The all-natural vanilla flavoring used in your brownies, cookies, and candy may actually come from the anal secretions of beavers, National Geographic reports. "I lift up the animal's tail, and I'm like, 'Get down there, and stick your nose near its bum,'" wildlife ecologist Joanne Crawford says. "People think I'm nuts. Beavers secrete a chemical compound called castoreum, which the FDA calls a "generally regarded as safe" additive, and it's been used in perfumes and foods for at least 80 years. – Scientists in Canada think they've figured out a way to fix heart disease without having to get up and go to the gym. They've found that a protein called cardiotrophin 1 tricks the heart into growing in a healthy way, reports Nature World News. The trick happens naturally during pregnancy and when the heart is still growing after a baby is born or an athlete stops exercising, explains the Ottawa Citizen. "This derives from simple, basic research on the cellular and molecular mechanisms that make heart muscle grow," says one of the researchers. "People hadn’t pushed to understand the process. "And although we have drugs that can reduce the symptoms of left heart failure, we can’t fix the problem, and left heart failure often leads to right heart failure over time."
