– Male black widow spiders aren't exactly known for being monogamous, but a new study in Biology Letters suggests they're getting a little carried away. Reporting in the journal Biology Letters, researchers from the University of Toronto Scarborough say they've found that a "significant" number of male widow spiders are engaging in sexual cannibalism with immature females, who are still too young to capture and consume their mate. These females have functioning reproductive organs, but their genitals are still internal and protected by a tough shell. Undaunted, the males penetrate right through this exoskeleton to deposit sperm. The young females, apparently not worse for wear, produce the male's offspring once they've matured. Normally, mature female widow spiders engage in sexual cannibalism—an evolutionary strategy that improves a species' reproductive fitness as a whole. But in this case, the male widow spiders, who are normally monogamous, have adopted a strategy that's allowing them to have sexual liaisons with multiple partners. It's a completely selfish act but also one that improves an individual male's reproductive success. – A rat-sized animal with a furry tail, a two-horned uterus, and a placenta that fed on insects has been named Protungulatum donnae, and it's the most common ancestor of the branch of the mammalian family tree known as the placental branch. The animal, which lived some 66 million years ago, is the ancestor of today's mammals, including humans, shrews, bats, whales, cats, and dogs, reports the New York Times. Protungulatum donnae, which lived in what is now North America, had the right features for full-term live births, including close contact with the placenta and membranes surrounding the fetus, as in humans. The animal's existence had long been a bit of a mystery, and scientists had been searching for a common ancestor of the many placental species since the end of the Cretaceous Period some 66 million years ago, when all non-avian dinosaurs died off. The Protungulatum species appears to be the first to appear on the mammalian family tree after the breakup of the supercontinent Gondwana around 120 million years ago, and the researchers say its presence suggests that 39 placental species survived to enter the post-extinction world. "We now have this finding in these high familial risk infants that we can predict 8 out of 10 that we think will get autism," psychiatrist Joseph Piven says in a press release. According to a study published in Nature, Piven's team scanned the brains of 106 "high-risk" infants at age 6 to 12 months, 42 of whom were diagnosed with autism at 24 months. They also followed 42 low-risk infants. The study found that the volume of the high-risk infants' brains grew faster between 12 and 24 months than the low-risk infants. Piven and his team believe the brain changes underlying autism begin much earlier—possibly in the womb—but behavioral assessments haven't been helpful in predicting who will get autism. – The race for the White House has tightened, according to Nate Silver's projection model, which puts Hillary Clinton's chances of winning at 74% and Donald Trump's at 70%. "The race between Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump has tightened," the model states. "Clinton, whose lead over Trump exceeded 8 percentage points at her peak following the Democratic convention, is ahead by 4 or 5 percentage points today, according to our polls-only forecast." If the race continues to tighten, FiveThirtyEight says it's possible Clinton's position in the swing states will protect her in the Electoral College. "But this is potentially mistaken," the site states.

Some 50 "deal vetters" have filed a class-action lawsuit against the company, claiming they didn't get overtime for working more than 40 hours a week, PaidContent reports. The suit follows one filed in August by more than 1,000 salespeople. Marchionne said the timing of the EPA's accusation was "very strange." The EPA says Fiat Chrysler installed illegal software in 104,000 diesel vehicles, including the Jeep Grand Cherokee and Ram 1500, that allowed the vehicles to pass emissions tests while emitting nitrogen oxide at rates up to 30 times what is allowed by the EPA. The EPA says Fiat Chrysler didn't disclose the software in the vehicles, which were also used in Volkswagen's emissions-cheating scandal, the New York Times reports. Marchionne says the use of the software in Fiat Chrysler vehicles is completely different from that in Volkswagen vehicles. He says the EPA's allegations are "without merit" and the company will "work with the Trump administration to present its case and resolve this matter fairly and equitably." But New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman says he is "deeply troubled" by the alleged violation of the Clean Air Act and will work with state and federal partners to resolve the matter.

– An Arizona mom is facing child abuse charges after her 2-year-old daughter allegedly ate THC butter while eating macaroni and cheese. According to a police report, 25-year-old Alaina Marie Limpert and her husband laughed about the "side effects" her daughter was having and "then proceeded to place her into their backyard pool to use the cold water to 'shock' her," KPHO reports. She was booked on one count of child abuse.

– If you're trying to lose weight, you might want to think twice about drinking diet drinks or eating artificial sweeteners. A new study finds no evidence that artificial sweeteners help people lose weight, and they're linked to weight gain and an increased risk of diabetes and high blood pressure, reports the CBC. Researchers from the University of Manitoba reviewed 37 studies involving more than 400,000 people and found no evidence that regular consumption of artificial sweeteners led to weight loss. "Surprisingly, given how common these products are, not many studies have looked at the long-term impact of their consumption," study co-author Meghan Azad tells CTV News. "And there was some evidence of long-term harm from long-term consumption." Azad says people should "maybe think twice about whether you really want to be consuming these artificial sweeteners, particularly on an everyday basis," because "really we don't have evidence to say for sure whether these are truly harmless alternatives to sugar." artificial sweeteners, including sucralose, stevia, and aspartame, are widely used in foods and drinks, including diet soda, yogurt, sauces, and dressings, and baked goods. – A Polish cybersecurity researcher says he's figured out a way to use club music to send hidden messages across an entire rave—without most people even noticing. In a paper published on arXiv preprint server, Krzysztof Szczypiorski says he used Balearic techno, a style of dance music born on the tropical shores of Ibiza, to hide messages hidden in nearly imperceptible changes in tempo. The basic system is this: letters are ascribed a dot-and-line series, but the "dot" is a slight increase in tempo, and the "line" is a slight decrease. By modulating the tempo ever so slightly, an entire sentence can be communicated over time. To decode the messages, you could use an algorithm that analyzes the beats per minute or simply listen very closely, if your ear is finely tuned enough. "It is very easy—it is just tuning the tempo which is visible as a curve in [Digital Audio audios like Logic]," Szczypiorski tells Wired. "The shape of this curve could be changed by a mouse and follow adopted Morse mode or any coding scheme." Szczypiorski used the system to hide messages at two separate raves. – British restaurant chain Pret a Manger says a second customer has died after eating a sandwich containing an allergen that was not noted on the label, the AP reports. The coffee-and-sandwich business has promised to improve its labeling following criticism at an inquest into the death of 15-year-old Natasha Ednan-Laperouse, who died in 2016 after eating a Pret baguette that contained traces of sesame. The company said an investigation was underway into a second case, in which a customer died in December after eating a supposedly dairy-free product that contained dairy protein. Pret a Manger blamed a supplier of its dairy-free yoghurt. The parents of Ednan-Laperouse, who are campaigning for stronger allergen warnings, said Sunday they were "incredibly saddened to learn of someone else losing their life from allergens in their food." – President Trump is hailing the passage of the Republican tax bill in the Senate early Saturday morning. "We are one step closer to delivering tax cuts for working families across America," Trump tweeted after the bill passed the Senate 51-49. "Massive tax cuts for the middle class, very good jobs for our country, very high taxes for the wealthy," he added. "Very unfair to the middle class," Sen. Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the tax-writing Finance Committee, said shortly before the bill passed, the Wall Street Journal reports. "Tonight, the Republican Senate betrays the middle class for the benefit of multinational corporations," he said. The bill slashes the corporate tax rate from 35% to 20%, reduces the number of tax brackets from seven to four, and generally raises taxes on the wealthy. It also reduces the number of tax brackets from seven to three. It repeals the ObamaCare mandate that people buy health insurance, Politico reports. Bob Corker was the only Republican to vote against the bill

– Northern California's Humboldt County was shaken by a 6.5-magnitude earthquake this afternoon, toppling chimneys and power poles and sending residents running out of their homes. No major injuries have been reported, but dozens of people have been taken to hospitals with minor injuries, reports the Los Angeles Times. The quake struck about 20 miles west-northwest of Ferndale at 4:30pm. "It was like the street was breakdancing," said a driver who was in his car when the quake hit. "We really felt it. It was pretty intense." The quake came a day after a 5.4-magnitude temblor hit the area, but there were no reports of major damage.

– A mountain lion that became trapped inside a Colorado home killed a house cat before police and wildlife officers were able to scare it out. Boulder police say the homeowner came back to the house late Thursday night and found the mountain lion inside. It appeared that it had pushed through a screen and couldn't get back out. The big cat roamed throughout two levels of the home for more than an hour before officers used non-lethal rounds to scare it out the front door and away from the neighborhood, which is just southwest of downtown Boulder, the AP reports. Police, who photographed the mountain lion lying down between a coffee table and a couch, called the break-in worrisome and asked residents to keep ground-level doors and windows locked at night.

– Rutgers University is raising tuition by $300 this fall—or about 2.3%. The typical in-state undergraduate student will pay $14,131 for tuition and fees, NJ.com reports. Once all of the costs are tallied, the average student living on Rutgers' New Brunswick campus will pay a total of $26,185—or $624 more than last year. The Board of Governors unanimously approved the tuition hike during a meeting on the New Brunswick campus. The board also approved a $3.8 billion budget for the 65,000-student university. Rutgers needs the tuition hike to cover several rising costs, including new contracts with various unions calling for a 2% raise for Rutgers employees and a 3.7% cut in state funding for Rutgers operations. "A lot of this is out of our hands," said Mark Angelson, head of the board's finance committee.

– Economists had expected the unemployment rate to hold steady at 5% in April, but instead it ticked up to 5%, the Wall Street Journal reports. The Labor Department issued a stronger-than-expected jobs report Friday: The US added 160,000 jobs in April, well below the 205,000 economists had predicted and the lowest gain since September. The unemployment rate for African-Americans, however, held steady at 6.8%. The AP notes that the labor force participation rate, at 62.8%, also held steady, at 62.8%. Over the past 12 months, employers have added an average of 200,000 jobs a month. Average hourly earnings in the private sector rose 4 cents to $26.92, while the average workweek held steady at 34.4 hours. The AP notes that the labor force participation rate has fallen to 62.8%, the lowest level since 2000. The report is seen as a key piece of data that will influence the Fed's decision on whether to raise interest rates later this year.

– An overturned oil tanker burst into flames in Pakistan on Sunday, killing 153 people who had rushed to the scene of the highway accident to gather leaking fuel, a hospital official said as the death toll continued to rise. Dr. Javed Iqbal at Bahawalpur's Victoria Hospital in south Punjab said the latest deaths occurred at a hospital in Multan where some of the 50 critically injured, many of whom suffered extensive burns, had been taken. The death toll could rise further as dozens are still in critical condition, said Dr. Mohammad Baqar, a senior rescue official in the area. There were dozens of other injuries of varying degree, he said. Local news channels showed black smoke billowing skyward and scores of burned bodies, as well as rescue officials speeding the injured to hospital and army helicopters ferrying the wounded. Saznoor Ahmad, 30, whose two cousins were killed in the fire, said the crowd of people screamed as the flames engulfed them. "The fire moved so fast," he said. When the flames subsided the field was strewn with bodies, and nearby were the charred shells of motorcycles and cars that the villagers had used to race to the scene. In a statement Monday, Munoz called the incident an "upsetting event" and apologized for having to re-accommodate the "disruptive and belligerent" passenger, the AP reports. – Visiting America's national parks could get a little more expensive starting in May. The National Park Service is proposing increasing entrance fees at 17 parks— Arches, Bryce Canyon, Canyonlands, Denali, Glacier, Grand Canyon, Grand Teton, Olympic, Sequoia & Kings Canyon, Yellowstone, Yosemite, and Zion—by $70 per vehicle, $50 per motorcycle, and $30 per person on foot, NPR reports. The money would be used to improve the parks' aging infrastructure, including roads, bridges, campgrounds, waterlines, bathrooms, and more. "Targeted fee increases at some of our most-visited parks will help ensure that they are protected and preserved in perpetuity and that visitors enjoy a world-class experience that mirrors the amazing destinations they are visiting," Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke says in a press release. "We need to have the vision to look at the future of our parks and take action in order to ensure that our grandkids' grandkids will have the same if not better experience than we have today," he adds. The NPS is accepting public comments on the proposal through Nov. 23 on its website.

– A paraplegic says he spent three days dragging himself along a dirt road in the New Mexico desert—without a wheelchair. Ricky Gilmore, 49, says he was dropped in the desert by a couple he met while hitchhiking, who threw him out of their truck when he refused to share his alcohol with them, the AP reports. Gilmore, who lives by himself and lost the use of his legs in a car crash years ago, says he didn't have a coat or a wheelchair to help him endure the desert. "It was dark and I was shivering and the wind was blowing so I just crawled to a bush and dug in right there. It was cold that night," he says. He spent a second night at the side of the road before he woke up sore and thirsty and didn't want to move. "I could have easily gave up and said 'Forget it,' but I said 'I'm not going to freeze out here' and I just kept on going," he says. On the third afternoon, a man in a blue pickup truck stopped and called for help. Gilmore said doctors told him his body temperature was 94 when he was found. "I don't think I would have made it another night," he says.

The director of Thailand's Wildlife Conservation Office, Teunjai Noochdumrong, says three tigers were tranquilized and transported Monday in an operation involving about 1,000 state personnel that is expected to continue for a week, the AP reports. The animals will be taken to three government animal refuges elsewhere in Thailand. The temple, a popular money-earning tourist attraction in the western province of Kanchanaburi, has been criticized by animal rights activists because of allegations it is not properly set up to care for the animals and flouted regulations restricting their trade. The monks resisted previous efforts to take away the tigers, and impeded the effort again on Monday morning despite the massive show of force by the authorities. They relented after police obtained a court order. More than 300 officials remained at the temple overnight to ensure the tigers remained safe. "When our vet team arrived, there were tigers roaming around everywhere," Noochdumrong tells CNN. "Looks like the temple intentionally let these tigers out, trying to obstruct our work." The temple recently made arrangements to operate as a zoo, but the plan fell through

The digital audio broadcasting (DAB) transition will save Norway an estimated $23.5 million per year, according to Quartz. But not everyone is onboard with the move. "We are simply not ready for this yet," MP Ib Thomsen tells Reuters. "There are 2 million cars on Norwegian roads that don't have DAB receivers, and millions of radios in Norwegian homes will stop working when the FM net is switched off. So there is definitely a safety concern." Those who don't already have a DAB-equipped car will have to buy a digital adapter, which costs about $176, reports Radio.no. The head of Digital Radio Norway says old radios will still emit the same frequency and transmit the original FM signal. DAB has 25 national radio channels, while FM only has five. "We're the first country to switch off FM but there are several countries going in the same direction," says Ole Jrgen Torvmark. "It was only five minutes and then my daughter was gone," Wang tells the West China Daily, per the BBC. For the next 24 years, the couple searched for their missing daughter—and on Tuesday, they were reunited with her. Wang became a taxi driver in 2015 and began handing out fliers in the hope that his missing daughter might see them. Over the years, Wang had been contacted by scores of women who thought they might be Qifeng, but DNA tests ruled them out. – The White House held a conference call with congressional leaders last night to make the case for military action against Syria, but the 90-minute meeting didn't produce any major surprises, reports the Wall Street Journal. Lawmakers emerged convinced that Bashar al-Assad was behind the chemical weapons attack, but they're not sure how—or when—the White House will push for international support. "The administration is figuring out the best way to do that and is seeking as much international support as possible, but won't let that dictate what our policy will be," says a Democratic aide briefed on the call. Lawmakers pressed the administration on how it would fund any military action, and the White House offered no answer, a congressional source tells Politico. Still, lawmakers emerged convinced that the Assad regime was behind the attack. "This is not a moment to look the other way, to blind ourselves to the horrifying images in Syria, and to send the dangerous message to the global community that we would allow the use of a chemical weapons attack to take place with impunity," says the ranking Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

– Scientists thought there were about 2.3 million Adelie penguins in East Antarctica—but a new study suggests there may be more than that. Using aerial and ground surveys, tagging, and automated camera images, researchers from Australia, France, and Japan estimate there are 5.9 million of the penguins on a 3,100-mile stretch of coastline, Phys.org reports. "Non-breeding birds are harder to count because they are out foraging at sea, rather than nesting in colonies on land," says Australian Antarctic Division seabird ecologist Louise Emmerson. "However, our study in East Antarctica has shown that non-breeding Adelie penguins may be as, or more, abundant than the breeders. These birds are an important reservoir of future breeders and estimating their numbers ensures we better understand the entire population's foraging needs." The findings could have implications for conservation, with more birds potentially interacting with humans in Antarctica and the Southern Ocean than previously thought, a researcher says. The study also estimated there are an estimated 193,500 tons of krill and 18,800 tons of fish eaten by the penguins during the breeding season, which will be used to set sustainable krill fishery catch limits, reports the Guardian. (Scientists have discovered a new penguin species.)

– Nicolas Maduro has been re-elected president of Venezuela with 67.7% of the vote, according to the country's electoral board, but the international community is not buying it. The election was boycotted by the opposition, which accuses Maduro of plotting to cling to power amid a worsening economic crisis, the Guardian reports. "We do not regonize this electoral process as valid," opposition candidate Henri Falcn said after voting Sunday. "As far as we are concerned there has been no election. There must be new elections in Venezuela." The US, meanwhile, says it will not recognize the result, Reuters reports. "We need to make sure we adhere to our goal which is to target corrupt regime officials and not the people of Venezuela," says US Deputy Secretary of State John Sullivan. "We don't want to damage the country in a way that makes it difficult to repair after democracy is restored." Sullivan says oil sanctions are "a very significant step" and a response to the election will be discussed at a G20 meeting in Buenos Aires on Monday.

– Violence is coursing through the world's newest country after its president claimed yesterday that his forces had defeated a coup attempt. The UN says at least 20,000 people have fled the capital, Juba, and it's worried about a "mass exodus" of civilians, the AP reports. Al-Jazeera reports that 10 top former government officials have been arrested, including six cabinet ministers, in the wake of the violence. President Salva Kiir, an ethnic Dinka, said yesterday that his forces had defeated supporters of former vice president Riek Machar, an ethnic Nuer, but details of the coup attempt remain murky. "The attackers went and [the] armed forces are pursuing them," Kiir said. "I promise you today that justice will prevail." Machar, who was fired by Kiir in July, is believed to be holed up in an army base in Juba. The two men have long been political rivals, and analysts say the violence could turn into a proxy war between them.

"For operational security reasons and to preserve the safety of our personnel and our Coalition partners, we will not discuss precise details on when and how this incident took place," the forces said in a statement, per the CBC. Military sources tell the Globe and Mail that the record-breaking shot took less than 10 seconds to hit the target from a high-rise. "This is an incredible feat. It is a world record that might never be equalled," one source says. The record was previously held by British sniper Craig Harrison, who shot a Taliban gunner with a 338 Lapua Magnum rifle from 2,475 feet away in 2009, the Globe and Mail reports. The record-breaking shot was verified by video camera and other data. Canadian Corporal Rob Furlong previously set the world record for the longest kill shot when he shot an Afghan insurgent at 2,430 feet away. (Canada has been conducting airstrikes against ISIS in Iraq and Syria.)

The Vail Daily reported Wednesday that 43-year-old Juan Jose Vidrio Bibriesca was standing next to two other defendants at an Eagle County District Court podium when he took his hat off and a square of folded paper fell out. A police officer watched the paper filled with cocaine fall to the floor, and after reviewing surveillance footage, authorities determined it fell from Bibriesca's hat. Bibriesca was then walked to the county jail. He was charged with narcotics possession and another bond violation.

– A class-action lawsuit filed against the Ulta Beauty chain alleges the company repackages and resells its customers' used beauty products, putting them back on the shelves as if they'd been purchased new, Consumerist reports. The lawsuit, which was filed by attorney Thomas Zimmerman Jr. on behalf of his client, Meghan DeVries, alleges that Ulta stores have a quota on the number of returned items that can be deemed "damaged" and thrown away, and store managers are given a quota as to the number of returned items that can be deemed to be resold. The lawsuit alleges that Ulta employees are instructed to clean and reseal used beauty products with cotton swabs before putting them back on the shelves. The lawsuit cites an undercover investigation that found used beauty products at Ulta were contaminated with harmful bacteria, including E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, "such that people could literally be applying and smearing someone else's fecal matter directly onto their lips," Zimmerman says in a press release. The lawsuit alleges that Ulta employees are also told to clean used beauty products with cotton swabs before putting them back on the shelves. A Ulta spokesperson tells Consumerist the company is "aware of the lawsuit, and intend to vigorously defend against the allegations."

Santorum was already trailing Mitt Romney in Ohio in the race for delegates, by a margin of 29% to 29%, according to Politico. If you're wondering how on earth such a civilization could possibly do this, Dan Hooper offers this: "Given the inevitability of the encroaching horizon, any sufficiently advanced civilization that is determined to maximize its ability to utilize energy will expand throughout the universe, attempting to secure as many stars as possible before they become permanently inaccessible." – A majority of Americans—60%—believe humans have evolved over time, according to a new Pew Research Center poll. But when it comes to those who don't believe in evolution, the number who say we've changed has gone from 54% in 2009 to 33% today, Reuters reports. The poll also found that the gap between those who believe in evolution and those who don't has widened, with 43% of Republicans versus 67% of Democrats saying we've evolved, compared to 54% and 64%, respectively, four years ago. "The gap is coming from the Republicans, where fewer are now saying that humans have evolved over time," says a Pew researcher. Among white evangelical Protestants, the number who think humans have evolved rose from 64% in 2009 to 66% today. Among other religious groups, the number who think evolution is caused by natural processes or by a "supreme being" rose from 31% to 24%.

– Two pilots in a helium-filled balloon on a record-setting journey across the Pacific Ocean entered the final leg of their trip today as they traveled along the California coast for an expected landing somewhere in Mexico. The pilots made history yesterday, first matching and then surpassing the 5,209-mile official world distance record for human flight in a gas balloon, reports the AP. Their next milestone is a 1978 duration record of 137 hours, 5 minutes, and 50 seconds in the air in a traditional gas balloon—a mark that's considered the "holy grail" of ballooning achievements. The Two Eagles pilots, Troy Bradley of New Mexico and Leonid Tiukhtyaev of Russia, are aiming to set both distance and duration records with their flight from Saga, Japan, which began shortly before 6:30am Sunday Japan time. The duration record was set in 1978 when Ben Abruzzo, Maxie Anderson, and Larry Newman made the first trans-Atlantic balloon flight. – Workers in the Spanish town of Cristovo de Cea thought they were fixing a broken picnic table when they poured concrete into a 6,000-year-old tomb and replaced it with a brand-new table, NPR reports. According to the Local, the tomb was supposed to be protected and marked as an artifact. But officials in the Galicia region weren't aware of the site. "No one told me, neither Heritage nor the environmental group," the mayor of Cristovo de Cea tells the Spanish Huffington Post. "The site wasn't even marked, and the logical thing would have been for them to get in contact with the local council so that we could have taken measures to protect the site." An archaeologist calls the destruction of the tomb a "monumental error." He says it's not representative of Spain, where monuments over 100 years old are "all preserved by law." But it's not the first time an archaeological mistake has been made. In 2007, a work crew in the ancient capital city of Nanjing unearthed and destroyed the burial sites of 10 noblemen from six dynasties. Last year, an ancient Native American burial ground and village in California was discovered and then razed in order to make way for multimillion-dollar homes.

– It's called a Moscow mule, and it's a drink so popular these days that Iowa's Alcoholic Beverages Division is warning people against using copper mugs for the cocktail, Live Science reports. The warning says copper can leach into acidic foods and drinks, and too much of it can lead to copper poisoning. Traditionally, Moscow mules contain vodka, ginger beer, and lime, and have a pH of well below 6.0, according to the advisory. Symptoms of copper poisoning include abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, and jaundice, the National Institutes of Health says. The Alcoholic Beverages Division says it issued the advisory because of the recent rise in popularity of Moscow mules, which has led to questions about the safety of copper containers for this beverage. But Moscow mule enthusiasts need not despair—you can still use a mug with a copper exterior, as long as the interior is lined with a different metal, such as nickel or stainless steel. Mugs with these interiors are safe containers for the cocktail, and are widely available.

– How much time do office workers spend on their phones at work each day? An average of 56 minutes, or nearly five hours per week, according to a survey of 600 office workers and senior managers by staffing firm OfficeTeam. That's 43% more time than managers say they actually spend on non-work activities, reports WTOP. The average employee spends another 42 minutes a day, or 3.5 hours a week, doing personal tasks, including errands. Personal email and social media make up the majority of the time spent on phones, and sports sites, mobile gaming, and shopping round out the top five in the wasted time category. More than half of the 600+ office employees surveyed said they used their phones to access websites blocked by company IT departments.

The last of the attackers was killed this morning as Afghan and NATO special forces stormed the building, the Washington Post reports. At least seven Afghans were killed in the attack, which a Taliban spokesman said was meant to remind Afghanistan's government and the US about the Taliban's power. "We have not run out of patience, and we want to fight to end their occupation," he said. "We have the ability to strike when we want." The US ambassador to Afghanistan downplayed the significance of the attack, saying it was "not a very big deal, a hard day for the embassy and my staff, who behaved with enormous courage and dedication. But look, you know a dozen RPG rounds from 800 meters away—that isn’t [the] Tet [offensive], that’s harassment."

– The well-preserved mummy of a hunter-gatherer who died atop a glacier in what is now Italy some 5300 years ago was already well-studied. Now, thanks to the 3D computer tomography (or CAT scan) used to examine his teeth, researchers report in the European Journal of Oral Sciences that tzi, as he was known, also suffered from severe gum disease and cavities. His teeth, back and front, were also heavily worn from chewing coarse grain and used as a "third hand" for gripping tools and cutting, reports Phys.org. One of his front teeth was killed in a fall or other accident, and he may have had a small stone that went unnoticed in his whole-grain bread, likely to thank for a broken molar, says geneticist Angela Graefen of the Institute for Mummies and the Iceman in Bolzano, Italy, one of the lead researchers on the paper. Graefen says that in the late Stone Age, humans were increasingly incorporating ground grain into their diets, and that could explain the increasing frequency of cavities in teeth since. (Click to read about how modern-day bears may have been better at hiding their teeth.)

– Ted Kaczynski’s infamous manifesto is worth a few thousand bucks, but his infamous sweatshirt is worth nothing. The US Marshall’s office is auctioning off the convicted Unabomber’s personal effects to pay off a $15 million restitution order for his victims, but so far only two items are garnering serious interest: his 35,000-word manifesto and his infamous sweatshirt, which is up for $20,025. The top bid for Kaczynski’s hand-bowed wood saw is $310, but handwritten letters to his aunt are only getting $250 bids, Aol News reports. “I hate to say it, but there is some collectibility in this auction,” an art historian says. “This is one of the most tragic events in US history and the manifesto has historical value as does the typewriter that he used to type his two manifestos. Zenimax, a video game developer, sued Oculus, Facebook's subsidiary that developed the virtual reality headset the Rift, claiming Oculus stole Zenimax's trade secrets when it launched the Rift in 2014, the BBC reports. On Wednesday, a jury in Texas awarded Zenimax the damages after three weeks of trial. The spokesperson says the company is "disappointed" with the ruling and will appeal. Facebook, which bought Oculus for $2 billion in 2014, says it is "disappointed" with the ruling and plans to appeal. Luckey was accused of stealing intellectual property belonging to Zenimax when he joined Oculus as its chief technology officer.

According to CNN, Gianforte was at a campaign event Thursday night when the reporter, Ben Jacobs, asked him a question about the GOP's health care plan. Gianforte grabbed Jacobs by the wrists and slammed him to the ground. Gianforte won the special election for Montana's at-large congressional seat in November. He has apologized to Jacobs and said he will donate $50,000 to the Committee to Protect Journalists. Gianforte was at the campaign event to stump for Republican Senate candidate Matt Rosendale. – The Washington state Department of Fish and Wildlife is pleading with fishermen to catch as many Atlantic salmon as they can after 3 million pounds of the fish escaped from a farmed pen and swam out to sea over the weekend. Cooke Aquaculture estimates between 4,000 and 5,000 of the nonnative fish made their way out of the pen when an anchor line broke Saturday on Cypress Island, near Bellingham, per KIRO-TV. The company says it's not clear how the fish survived the collapse of the net pen, which was holding 305,000 fish, but it appears "many fish are still contained within the nets," Cooke says in a statement. The public is being asked to catch as many fish as possible, with no limit on size or number. Cooke, which is considering a controversial net-pen operation in the Strait of Juan de Fuca near Port Angeles, says "exceptionally high tides and currents coinciding with this week's solar eclipse" are to blame for the damage to the pen, which was built to withstand high tidal movements. But environmental groups are skeptical. "If they can't be trusted in an accident like this how can they be trusted to tell the truth in the permitting process?" the executive director of Puget Soundkeeper tells KIRO-TV.

– A skier was killed in an avalanche in Alaska's Rainbow Mountains on Saturday, reports KTUU. State troopers say 63-year-old Michael Hopper was skiing with 35-year-old Eric Peterson when they heard a "whoomp" about 20 feet above them. "Hopper reported it took him 2-3 hours to dig himself out," troopers wrote in a dispatch. "Once he was free he located Peterson's glove and dug down and found Peterson deceased." – If you're charged with a drug offense in federal court, a new Human Rights Watch report finds that just 3% of defendants choose to go to trial instead of pleading guilty. That means they face an average of 11 years more behind bars than those who plead guilty, NPR reports. The problem, says the report, is that federal prosecutors have "essentially unchecked power" thanks to mandatory-minimum sentencing laws. "Prosecutors can say, 'Take these 10 years or, if you get a trial and are convicted, you’re going to look at life,'" says the report's author. "That’s a pretty amazing power that unfortunately they are more than willing to wield." In fact, the percentage of defendants who plead guilty has risen steadily since the mid-1980s. The report found that defendants who took the deal face an average of three times as many years in prison than those who take the deal—and the majority of those who take the deal lose at trial, the Washington Post reports.

– A new study suggests that people can accurately gauge a man's intelligence by looking at his face—but not women's. Researchers from the Czech Republic found that both men and women were able to accurately assess the intelligence of men by looking at their faces, they report in PLoS One. But the same can't be said for women, they say. "Our study revealed no relation between intelligence and either attractiveness or face shape," they write. "People can accurately judge intelligence by looking at faces of men, but not women." The scientists theorize that women's attractiveness clouds the judgment, and that "the strong halo effect of attractiveness may thus prevent an accurate assessment of the intelligence of women." The study recruited 80 students, who completed an IQ test and had their face photographed with a neutral expression. Another 160 students rated the 80 photographs in random order for either perceived intelligence or attractiveness. For women, however, the researchers found no statistically significant link between perceived intelligence and their actual IQ.

– Jeremy Lewis and Josh Potter lived within 75 miles of each other in Albertville, Ala., and were married with two kids about the same age. Both were injured on the job and lost limbs, but Lewis lived and worked in Alabama, which has the nation's lowest workers' comp benefits for amputations. Potter, on the other hand, lost his arm across the border in Georgia, which has the nation's more generous benefits for such catastrophic injuries, ProPublica and NPR report. "This disparity grimly illustrates the geographic lottery that governs compensation for workplace injuries in America," they write. Congress allows each state to determine its own benefits, with no federal minimums, so workers who live across state lines from each other can experience entirely different outcomes for identical injuries. Nearly every state has what's known as a "schedule of benefits" that divides up the body like an Angus beef chart. Workers are awarded a portion of their wages up to the state maximum for the specified number of weeks assigned to each body part. The loss of an arm is worth up to $48,840 in Alabama, $193,950 in Ohio, and $439,858 in Illinois. The big toe ranges from $6,090 in California to $90,401.88 in Oregon

– Saddam Hussein may be dead, but his name is still hurting one young man in India. Two years after graduating from Noorul Islam University in Jharkhand, Saddam Hussain says he's been denied 40 or so jobs by shipping companies because of his name, the Hindustan Times reports. "People are scared to hire me," he says. "Even Shah Rukh Khan gets detained at US airports. What is this Saddam in comparision?" Saddam, who says he was given his name by his grandfather 25 years ago, has been unable to obtain his educational certificates, passport, voter ID, and driving license under his new name, Sajid, because his university refuses to change it until he gets his Class 10 and 12 exam certificates changed first. He's also had to get a new passport and driving license under his new name. "I am an innocent victim of somebody else's crimes," he says. He has even taken to court to force authorities to change his name, but a judge last week set a May 5 date for a hearing, the BBC reports. "I am an innocent victim of somebody else's crimes," he says. (In the US, a man named Saddam was hanged in 2006.)

– A marketing major and a journalism major won the Hunger Games-themed contest to work for no pay at Emmis Digital this summer, the Chicago Tribune reports. More than 25 college students applied for the one internship available at the River North, Ill., office. The top 10 candidates were invited in for interviews, and the field was whittled down to three finalists—#TeamJake, #TeamKelsey, and #TeamKatie. Every day for two weeks, the three "tributes"—each assigned to drive social media for the company's websites—created a video explaining why they were worthy. "Once I knew it was a competition I knew I had to give everything," Jake Bouvy, a marketing major at Indiana University, tells DNAinfo. "I'm a competitive guy. I don't like to lose." "I've never had to do anything like this before." Emmis Digital's Rory Foster and Katlyn Hayes decided, "much like the Hunger Games," to keep both finalists.

"Now it's a search area hundreds of miles big," a US Navy commander tells CNN. More than 40 ships and dozens of planes from 10 countries are searching the area, but so far there's been no sign of the plane or its passengers. – This winter has been the snowiest on record in Chicago, with just a trace of snow on the ground in January and February, the Chicago Tribune reports. According to the National Weather Service, the last time the city didn't have snow on the ground in both January and February was in 1864, the AP reports. The last time there wasn't snow on the ground in both January and February was in 1925. "It's pretty impressive for any place in the northern part of the state to go both January and February with no snow on the ground," a University of Illinois climatologist says. Experts blame the lack of snow on warm air and ground temperatures. "The biggest issue is because it's been so warm all through the winter, it's really encouraging the trees and shrubs and perennials to come out a little bit too early for their own good," the Tribune quotes the climatologist as saying. "For example, we might have fruit trees that might be in dormancy right now, leaf out and their buds will start to swell and open and that makes them highly vulnerable to frost later on." And that's bad news for fruit growers, the AP reports. "It can really set an orchard back a couple years to get into this situation

Police are still searching for the thieves, who are believed to have used a secret pathway in the catacombs to reach the private cellar. According to the BBC, 200 of the party's 533 MPs voted in favor of May, while 117 voted against her. The vote was triggered by 48 Conservative MPs who called for a confidence vote in May over her Brexit deal with the European Union. – Two American economists have won this year's Nobel Prize in economics for their work in market design, focusing on how to fairly and efficiently match people with things—be they employers, schools, or donated kidneys—when pricing isn't involved. Their work led to systems used by school districts in New York City, Boston, and other cities to place students in high schools; by hospitals to match donated kidneys with patients; and by a program that assigns recent medical-school graduates to hospitals for residency programs. "Now we are able to see the fruits of this 50-year quest, if you wish, and these techniques—initially very much mathematical—are now directly affecting peoples' lives," a Boston College economist tells the Wall Street Journal. Harvard's Alvin Roth and University of California Los Angeles' Lloyd Shapley won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for their work in researching market design and putting practical applications in use.

Meanwhile, Boston University researchers are trying to obtain the brain of Junior Seau to see if it has the degenerative brain disease CTE, reports the Boston Globe. Seau killed himself last month.

– A 158-year-old colonial-era law has been struck down by India's top court, which says adultery is unconstitutional and discriminatory against women. A five-judge bench ruled unanimously that Section 497 of the Indian penal code, which made adultery a crime punishable by up to five years in prison, was arbitrary and violated women's rights, reports the Guardian. "The time when wives were invisible to the law, and lived in the shadows of their husbands, has long since gone by," said one of the two women on the court, per the BBC. The court—which earlier this month decriminalized homosexuality and will decide Friday whether women in their menstruating years can be restricted from entering a Kerala state temple—was unanimous in its decision. The adultery law had survived three previous legal challenges, the most recent in 1988. "It is time to say husband is not the master," said Chief Justice Dipak Misra. He quoted John Stuart Mill: "Legal subordination of one sex over another is wrong in itself." The decision was welcomed by the head of India's National Commission for Women. "It was an outdated law, which should have been removed long back," she says. "This is a law from British era.

– A school district in Mississippi has scrapped a policy that kept mixed-race students from running for some office, reports the Clarion-Ledger. The move came after a mother of four mixed-race kids got wind that her 12-year-old couldn't run for a sixth-grade class reporter position at her new school because she wasn't the right race. The policy had been in place for 30 years, and the Nettleton School District superintendent posted a statement on its website saying, "It is the belief of the current administration that these procedures were implemented to help ensure minority representation and involvement in the student body. It is our hope and desire that these practices and procedures are no longer needed." The policy had been in place so long that the local NAACP called for an investigation by the Justice Department. The school district acknowledged that diversity is no longer a black-and-white issue, and said it "acknowledges and embraces the fact that we are growing in ethnic diversity."

Trump called the deal the "worst deal ever" in a March tweet, and he's been trying for six months to change the terms of the deal. Iran, for its part, says it will remain in the deal. "We've known for months that President Trump wouldn't be committed to this deal," Iranian President Hassan Rouhani said Tuesday, per the AP. "The Iranian foreign ministry will continue talks with remaining countries in the deal."

– Eliot Spitzer is taking on the Wall Street Journal, and not in a good way. Marsh & McLennan Cos, the insurance broker Spitzer sued over an insurance bid-rigging scandal, is also suing Spitzer over the column, which appeared on Slate last August. Marsh says Spitzer's column "falsely accused" the company of wrongdoing, and "destroyed the company's reputation." Spitzer's lawsuit accuses the Journal of trying to "protect a particularly rabid, and ultimately damaging, anti-regulatory philosophy that has dominated the past 30 years," he writes on Slate. "By trying to rewrite the narrative of the economic cataclysm we have lived through, the deniers are attempting to challenge the common-sense conclusions that flow from an accurate understanding of history."

Police say they seized 247 pounds of marijuana, worth about $2 million, along with $11,000 in cash. "I've been out here 28 years and this is the biggest I've seen in our area," says West Manheim Police Chief Tim Hippensteel. "This is obviously a big operation," says Kearney. – The Senate today confirmed Sally Jewell to be the next secretary of the Interior, filling the post left empty by Ken Salazar's resignation. The vote was 87-11, with 11 Republicans joining Democrats in approving the 57-year-old REI chief, Bloomberg reports. Jewell, a former petroleum engineer and commercial banker, has worked with environmental groups to fight fossil-fuel mining and oil drilling on federal land. "Sally knows that business and environment both benefit when we are committed to protecting our national parks and national treasures," said Sen. Ron Wyden, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, before the vote. Jewell will head an agency that oversees 500 million acres of mineral-rich land, as well as the management of national parks and millions of acres of oil and gas drilling, the Hill reports.

– Easter Island is best known for its giant stone statues of full-body figures, many of which are buried up to their heads. But what happened to the thousands of islanders who arrived there 900 years ago and carved the statues? A new study published Monday in the Journal of Pacific Archaeology suggests that the islanders had a complex, collaborative society that included chiefs, priests, and guilds of workers who fished, farmed, and made the statues, reports CNN. "The idea of competition and collapse on Easter Island might be overstated," says lead study author Dale Simpson Jr., an archaeologist at the University of Queensland. "To me, the stone carving industry is solid evidence that there was cooperation among families and craft groups." Researchers used chemical analysis of fragments from 17 of the tools used to carve the statues to determine that most of them came from a single quarry. "Once the people found the quarry they liked, they stayed with it," Simpson says. "For everyone to be using one type of stone, I believe they had to collaborate. That's why they were so successful—they were working together." – Alan Rickman, who played Severus Snape in the Harry Potter film series, has died at the age of 69, the BBC reports. Rickman's production company, Rickman's World, announced his death Tuesday. "We are deeply saddened to announce that Alan Rickman has passed away," the company said in a statement. "He was a creative force and an inspiration to us all. He will be deeply missed." Rickman played Snape in the first seven Harry Potter films. He also starred in Alice in Wonderland and Inglourious Basterds, among other films.

– Taller people are more likely to get cancer, according to a new study that found the risk jumps by about 10% for every inch over an average height. "If you were comparing a 5-foot guy to a basketball player who's over 7 feet tall, then that basketball player has around twice the risk of cancer across the board," says Leonard Nunney, the study's lead author. Nunney, an evolutionary biologist at the University of California, Riverside, reviewed data from three large cancer studies—the Million Women study in the UK, the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer (EPIC) study in the US, and the Korean Cancer Study—as well as the American Cancer Society's Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) study. He found most cancer types increased with height, but there were a few that bucked the trend. For example, tall women were more likely to get thyroid cancer, while tall men were more likely to get melanoma. Nunney suspects the higher risk of thyroid cancer is due to the fact that taller women are more likely to be infected with a strain of HPV that causes cervical cancer. Acevedo says the city has gotten more than 3,000 calls for rescue since the storm made landfall early Sunday. The Coast Guard says it has gotten more than 1,000 calls per hour, including both air rescues and rescues using boats, the New York Times reports. Acevedo says the city is dealing with "catastrophic and life-threatening" flooding. He says some areas have received more than 40 inches of rain in a single day, and the National Weather Service is warning of "catastrophic and life-threatening" flooding through Friday in areas along the Texas coast and southwest Louisiana. – The Honda Accord is the most stolen car in the US for the fifth year in a row, according to a new report from LoJack, which notes that $121 million in stolen vehicles were recovered last year. The Honda Civic came in second, followed by the Toyota Camry and the Toyota Corolla, ABC News reports. The most expensive recovered vehicle was a $103,400 Porsche Panamera. A rep for the National Insurance Crime Bureau, which compiled its own list last year, says Accords "are very popular cars. Those things tend to be stolen anyway." The VP of law enforcement for LoJack says Accords "are a top seller at car dealerships throughout the United States for a variety of reasons, including their reliability. That means year after year there are more Accords on the road, getting into car accidents or needing parts for repair." He adds that because car parts are often interchangeable over multiple model years, thieves can get up to three times the value of the vehicle if they sell it for parts. (In other car-related news, check out the 10 most popular cars of all time.)

Protests have been simmering in Wukan, in Guangdong province, since September and escalated after the death of a village negotiator in police custody. Villagers had planned a march through police barriers on Wednesday. But a senior official met a village representative, and villagers said some demands had been met. The villagers say officials have sold off their land to developers and failed to compensate them properly. They also want an investigation into the death of Xue Jinbo, who died on 11 December while in the hands of local police. Police say he died of a "sudden illness" but his family say he was beaten to death. The villagers had planned to march through police barricades around the town to local government offices. Local authorities had urged them not to. Amid deadlock, deputy provincial Communist Party secretary Zhu Mingguo agreed to meet local leaders on Wednesday in the town of Lufeng. The BBC reports that a senior provincial official told him and another village representative in a meeting yesterday that four villagers being held by police would be released over the next few days and land from one development project would be returned to the villagers. – Students at Broad Run High School in Ashburn, Va., have a bit of relief after nearly a month of searching for SAT tests that never made it to the College Board. A sealed box with 236 answer sheets was found yesterday on the bottom shelf of a cart in the shipping area of the school, WTOP reports. The tests had been sent off via UPS, but school officials initially said that a UPS employee carried the box out of the building, according to WUSA9. But yesterday, the school said the tracking number for the box never entered UPS' system. "UPS did not lose this, and we apologize profoundly to UPS," a school spokesman says. The tests will be validated and the 200 or so affected students won't have to retake the exam, the Washington Post reports.

– Just knowing that you got a good night's sleep doesn't just make you feel better, it actually improves your cognitive abilities, according to a new study. Researchers at Colorado College studied 164 students who were split into "above average" quality sleep and "below average" quality sleep. They were also given a talk on sleep quality and given a five-minute session on how important REM sleep is for cognitive function. Students in both groups were then connected to a machine they were told would measure their brainwave frequency and show spreadsheets and formulas. Those in the "above average" sleep quality condition were told by researchers they had spent 28.7% of their total sleep time in REM sleep, whereas those in the "below average" sleep quality condition were informed that they had only spent 16% of their time in REM sleep. The students who were told they got a good night's sleep performed significantly better in the Paced Auditory Serial Addition Test, a cognitive exercise which measured their ability to listen and process information. The authors say what the students were told about their sleep is known as "placebo sleep." – A group of aviation enthusiasts spotted a B-2 bomber flying over Texas earlier this month, Fox News reports. "We looked southwest and there they were," says journalist Steve Douglass, who was part of the group. "We thought they were B-2s, but when we studied our pictures, we ruled that out." The silver-grey bomber had a smooth backside, and a distinct "W"-shaped back. "The trailing edge is wrong," Douglass shouted, according to his March 28 blog post. The photos "tell us more about what the mysterious stranger isn't than what it is," writes Bill Sweetman at Aviation Week, which first reported on the sighting. "If I had to guess, I'd say we took a picture of a stealthy transport aircraft." Douglass reached out to Whiteman Air Force Base in Missouri, which houses B-2s, to see if it flew that day, and got no response. But Aviation Week says that Douglass picked up some apparently related voice signals, which would indicate the aircraft had a pilot. "If I had to guess, I'd say we took a picture of a stealthy transport aircraft," Douglass says.

– Cuba's National Assembly will elect a new president on Wednesday and announce the replacement for Raul Castro the next day, an unusual two-day process that will install someone from outside the Castro family in the country's highest government office for the first time in nearly six decades. The Cuban National Assembly has generally met and selected the president in one day. Its votes are nearly always anonymous and seen as reflecting the will of the country's top leadership. Communist Party newspaper Granma says the congress will assemble at 9am and select leaders of the legislature before voting for the president and other members of the Council of State, the country's highest government body. Granma says state media will broadcast live "the most important moments of the unfolding of this transcendental session." The secret vote will be counted by the National Electoral Commission and announced Thursday, Granma says. The new president will take over for the 86-year-old Castro, who is stepping down after two five-year terms. His brother Fidel was prime minister and president from 1959 until he fell ill in 2006. – A doomsday cult leader in Utah has been sentenced to at least 26 years in prison for the rape of his 8-year-old child bride. Samuel Shaffer, 34, was sentenced Wednesday to 15 years to life for felony sodomy on a child, KUTV reports. He was co-leader of the Knights of Crystal Blade, which believes in polygamy and believes in doomsday prophecies, People reports. Police arrested Shaffer in December 2017 after his ex-wife called authorities to report that another man in the cult, 34-year-old John Coltharp, had kidnapped their four children and fled. Police say Shaffer told them he was married to Coltharp's 8-year-old daughter. Authorities found two of Coltharp's daughters— Shaffer's 7-year-old daughter and Coltharp's 16-year-old daughter—in empty 50-gallon water barrels about 1,000 yards from Coltharp's property. Police say the girls were "poor health" with signs of dehydration and "acting lethargic" when they were found. Coltharp pleaded guilty to charges of child sodomy and child bigamy last month and is scheduled to be sentenced Aug. 8.

Five more bodies were found today, bringing the total presumed dead to 36, police say, as toxic gases and ash from the still-erupting mountain forced rescue workers to halt efforts to recover the victims. Eight more bodies were airlifted off Mount Ontake before work on the ash-blanketed peak was called off around 1:30pm, a spokesman for the Nagano prefecture police tells the AP. Together with four victims brought down on Sunday, 12 bodies have now been recovered, leaving 24 near the summit. Exactly how they died remains unclear, whether from gases, suffocating ash, falling rocks, or other causes. Rescuers at the peak of Mount Ontake, now an eerie moonscape under a thick layer of grey ash, on today found five more victims of Saturday's eruption at Japan's second-highest active volcano but authorities did not immediately confirm them as dead. The eruption of the 10,062-foot peak, 125 miles west of Tokyo, took place as the hiking site was packed with climbers, including children, admiring autumn foliage under a brilliant blue sky. – A suburban Philadelphia transit worker who found $15,000 and turned it in to police has been given the cash since no one ever claimed it, the AP reports. Bob Tracey was driving home from work last March when he spotted a black bag in the middle of the road. When he opened it, he saw dozens of $100 and $20 bills and immediately called police. The Philadelphia Inquirer reports a judge on Monday ordered the money returned to Tracey. Upper Darby Police Superintendent Michael Chitwood said some people claimed the money was theirs, but they had no proof. He said it was unlikely the real owners would come forward since the bag also contained drug paraphernalia. Tracey had to petition the court under a law dealing with finders of lost property. Chitwood was so impressed by the good deed, he said at the time that he believed the money should go to Tracey, a SEPTA worker, if nobody claimed the cash. And this week—after more than a year—a judge agreed with him.

Trump was flanked in the larger meeting by chief of staff John Kelly, Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, and national security adviser John Bolton. They sat across the table from Kim and his team. Trump said Tuesday after meeting Kim that he's feeling "really great." He says, "We're going to have a great discussion and a terrific relationship." That decision has raised concerns about the risk of holding such a monumental meeting with barely anyone to bear witness. Trump has said he'll know within minutes whether a deal can be made.

Aaron Leider sued the zoo in 2007 over its treatment of elephants, claiming they were subjected to "cruel, abusive, and illegal treatment." According to the Los Angeles Times, Leider's lawsuit alleged that the zoo used chains, drugs, bullhooks, and electric shocks on the elephants to get them to exercise. He also alleged that the elephants were neglected and died prematurely. A judge ruled in favor of Leider in 2012, ordering the zoo to stop using bullhooks or electric shocks and to exercise the elephants regularly. A divided appeals court upheld that ruling. But on Thursday, the California Supreme Court ruled that Leider's lawsuit couldn't force the zoo to improve conditions for the elephants. According to the Times, the court found that the zoo and its director had violated criminal law by using public money to violate animal abuse laws. The court also found that Leider couldn't use the taxpayer-funded lawsuit to force the zoo to move an Asian elephant to a sanctuary. – The collapse of the Interstate 5 bridge in Washington state less than a month ago has renewed attention to the nation's infrastructure, and the number of bridges deemed "structurally deficient" by the feds is on the rise. The Federal Highway Administration says there are 66,405 of the nation's bridges deemed "structurally deficient," reports USA Today. That's 11% of the total, and it would cost $76 billion to repair them. That's a problem, because 260 million trips are made each day on bridges like these. "You're seeing the aging of the system," says a co-author of a new report from Transportation for America. "It really does parallel the (aging of) the Baby Boomers in a startling way." Fifteen states have seen an increase in their structurally deficient bridges over the past two years, and the report predicts that in 10 years, one in four will be 65 years old or older. Congress has cut funding for bridge repair, but "the upshot is that bridge repair now must compete with other transportation needs," the report says. Reason.com has a list of the nation's most dangerous bridges.

– People who sleep for more than eight hours a day are twice as likely to have a stroke, according to a new study out of the University of Cambridge. The study followed nearly 10,000 people over a decade, asking them in 1998-2000 and again four years later whether they slept well and how many hours on average they slept each day. Almost 70% of participants reported sleeping between six and eight hours per day, while one in 10 said they slept more than eight hours per day. Over the course of the study, 346 people suffered stroke, either non-fatal or fatal. Those who slept longer than eight hours were at a 46% greater risk of stroke than average, while those who slept less than six hours a day were at an 18% increased risk. "It's apparent both from our own participants and the wealth of international data that there's a link between sleeping longer than average and a greater risk of stroke," a researcher says in a press release. "What is far less clear, however, is the direction of this link, whether longer sleep is a symptom, an early marker, or a cause of cardiovascular problems." – Mad Men creator Matt Weiner has signed a deal that will keep the popular AMC series on the air for at least two more seasons, reports the New York Times. The first and last episodes of each season will run 47 minutes, the same length as previous seasons, but Weiner will be able to create a 45-minute version for AMC to televise and a 47-minute "final cut" that will be available in digital formats, like on iTunes. The deal is said to be worth $30 million, "one of the biggest payouts of its kind in cable television," notes the Times. Weiner said he expected the seventh season to be the show's last. "That’s how long the show is," he said. "I’m just thrilled I get to finish it." The show, which has won three Emmys, won't return for its fifth season until early 2012.

The Amsterdam will join the Independence on Saturday as part of a ceremony marking the 70th anniversary of the US entry into World War II. The USS Independence was commissioned in 1943 as the first of a new class of carriers, and it's believed to have been the first of its kind to be built on a cruiser hull. "There is an ongoing need for safety equipment along with prevention and treatment supplies," says Garrett Ingoglia of AmeriCares, which has provided protective gear and medical equipment to more than 100 health facilities in Sierra Leone, Guinea, and Liberia. – The Oregon chub, a tiny minnow native to the Willamette Valley, is set to become the first fish ever taken off the endangered species list. The US Fish and Wildlife Service announced yesterday that it was proposing that the Oregon chub be removed from the endangered species list, 21 years after it went on the list. The proposal will go through a 60-day public comment period before becoming final. The Oregon chub was placed on the endangered species in 1993 after the loss of floodplain habitats and predation by non-native fish. At the time, fewer than eight populations of Oregon chub existed, with fewer than 1,000 fish. A recovery plan to boost chub numbers was finalized in 1998, and thanks to the success of methods such as habitat restoration, education, and careful monitoring, the species was reclassified as "threatened" in 2010. Oregon chub numbers now exceed 150,000, across 80 different sites. If the chub is removed from the US endangered species list, it will join 26 animals, including the Steller sea lion and Gray wolf, that have had their populations re-grow following their classification as endangered. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is currently considering whether to remove the North Pacific humpback whale from the list of more than 2,000 plants and animal species currently considered endangered in the US and abroad.

– Tens of thousands of people fled into Thailand today as fighting erupted between Burma’s government and a splinter group of rebels, one day after the country’s first election in 20 years. At least three people were killed and 10 wounded in the border town of Myawaddy, where Karen rebels seized a police station and post office yesterday, al-Jazeera reports. The clashes broke out when a group of Democratic Karen Buddhist Army (DKBA) militia members, who had been employed as border security troops, revolted because Burma’s military was forcing people to vote at gunpoint. "In order to win votes in the elections, [the junta] is bullying and forcing people to vote. But the people want to boycott [the vote], so the soldiers are holding them at gunpoint and our troops had to intervene and take sides with the people," a DKBA faction head told a website.

– Data brokers are selling lists of rape victims, people with AIDS, and even people suffering from depression and cancer, according to a Senate report out today. The World Privacy Forum says it found lists of more than 30,000 police officers' home addresses, as well as those of seniors suffering from dementia and people with addictive behaviors, CNN reports. Data brokers are required by federal law to keep consumers' data private, but the World Privacy Forum says that's not enough. "Highly sensitive data are the frayed and ugly ends of the bell curve of lists, far from the center," says the group's executive director. "This is where predatory can work to remove unsafe, unfair, and overall just deplorable lists from circulation." The Senate Commerce Committee held a hearing on the data industry today, and privacy groups testified that the companies also sell lists of rape victims and people with HIV and AIDs. "These people are gullible. They want to believe that their luck can change," says the World Privacy Forum's executive director. The report calls for tighter government regulations and says nine of the biggest data brokers were cooperative with the committee, but not Equifax, which was singled out as particularly cooperative, Ars Technica reports.

– President Trump is in Finland for his summit with Vladimir Putin on Monday, but he's still in Scotland, where he sat down with CBS Evening News anchor Jeff Glor on Saturday for a wide-ranging interview. Some of the highlights: On the European Union: "I think we have a lot of foes. I think the European Union is a foe, what they do to us in trade. Now, you wouldn't think of the European Union, but they're a foe. Russia is foe in certain respects. China is a foe economically, certainly they are a foe. But that doesn't mean they are bad. It doesn't mean anything. It means that they are competitive," Trump said at his golf club in Turnberry, Scotland. "I respect the leaders of those countries. But, in a trade sense, they've really taken advantage of us and many of those countries are in NATO and they weren't paying their bills." On the Russia investigation: "I think it hurts our relationship with Russia. I actually think it hurts our relationship with a lot of countries. I think it's a disgrace what's going on. Nothing bad is going to come out of it, and maybe some good will come out."

– President Obama told Hamid Karzai today that he's ready to pull all US troops out of Afghanistan by the end of the year, reports the Washington Post. The move comes because Karzai hasn't yet signed a security agreement with the US that would keep troops in the country after the end of the year. “President Obama told President Karzai that because he has demonstrated that it is unlikely that he will sign the BSA, the United States is moving forward with additional contingency planning,” says the White House statement. (It adds that the two leaders spoke by phone.) It's not clear whether Karzai will sign before the end of the year, but it's clear that Obama is tired of sitting on his hands. “The longer we go without a BSA, the more challenging it will be to plan and execute any US mission,” says the White House statement. The Post sees the move as a "sharp break" with Obama's position a few months ago, when he said the US wanted to wait for a new president to be elected in Afghanistan before making any decisions about keeping troops in the country. The US, however, is increasingly exasperated with Karzai's dragging out of the process.

– US and Canadian fighter jets intercepted six Russian military planes that approached North American airspace this week, military officials say. Two F-22 fighter jets intercepted the planes about 55 nautical miles from the Alaskan coast at about 7pm Pacific time Wednesday, the AP reports. The Russian planes were identified as two IL-78 refueling tankers, two Russian Mig-31 fighter jets, and two Bear long-range bombers. They looped south and returned to their base in Russia after the US jets were scrambled. At about 1:30am Thursday, two Canadian CF-18 fighter jets intercepted two of the long-range bombers about 40 nautical miles off the Canadian coastline in the Beaufort Sea. In both cases, the Russian planes entered the Air Defense Identification Zone, which extends about 200 miles from the coastline. They did not enter sovereign airspace of the United States or Canada. A US official tells CNN that officials in Washington think the incidents were related to the visit by Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko, who talked to Canadian officials Wednesday and President Obama on Thursday. The United States promised Ukraine $46 million in nonlethal aid for its battle with pro-Russian militants. In the past five years, jets under NORAD's command have intercepted more than 50 Russian bombers approaching North American airspace.

– The US government has been paying researchers to study the body movements of Vladimir Putin and other world leaders in a bid to predict how he'll act in the wake of the Ukraine crisis, USA Today reports. The "Body Leads" project, backed by the Office of Net Assessment think tank, has paid at least $300,000 to experts to study Putin and other leaders since 1996, records show. An ONA official says the goal of the project is "to learn about the physical movements of national leaders and determine if these can be used to gain insight about a leaders' attitudes, mindset, etcetera." But, he adds, "ONA does not make policy recommendations, so we cannot assert with any certainty how the studies have been used by policy makers." The project's director, Brenda Connors, has acknowledged her work on Putin but declined comment. A Harvard expert on Russia has also been paid $113,915 since 2009 to study Putin's movements, according to military contract records. "He is like that ice skater who had a club foot and became an Olympic skater," Connors told the Atlantic in 2005. "It is really poignant to watch him on tape. This is a deep, old, profound loss that he has learned to cope with, magnificently."

"In the end we both thanked each other for our mutual displays of respect and agreed to take a 'selfie' together to help tell our story," Barnes writes. In the selfie, the officer is leaning in Barnes' car, smiling, and the man is sporting a similar grin. "Neither of us are the enemy," Barnes writes. "Neither of us are the enemy. We can continue to fight against each other until we are literally 'black and blue', or we can show one another the respect we inherently deserve, not as 'black man' and 'blue police officer,' but as humans. None greater, none less." Trooper Shawn Cosgrove, who took the selfie,

– Conjoined twins Knatalye Hope and Adeline Faith Mata are set to undergo a risky surgery later this year in Texas, and their parents are still holding out hope. "You can't have hope without faith and you can't have faith without hope," Elysse Mata tells KHOU. "And if one baby would have gone, the other would too. And that was a big fear." The girls, who were born at 31 weeks, share a liver, diaphragm, pericardial sac, intestines, and heart lining. They're joined at the chest and abdomen. "Will it be easy? No," the chief of neonatology at Texas Children's Hospital tells KHOU. "The best thing do is to do the safest thing do is grow them up, get them bigger, more healthy with great nutrition and great developmental care, and then separate them in a time which is as safe as possible." The surgery will be performed by two surgical teams, and the girls are expected to be between 6 and 8 months old when they're separated. The girls' father, Eric Mata, has been working in Lubbock, Texas, since their birth, so he's had to drive back and forth to Houston to be with the family.
