– Five years after Heath Ledger’s death, Michelle Williams still can’t find the meaning of his life. “I’ve found meanings around the circumstance but the actual event doesn’t have it, I can’t find it,” she tells ABC. “I can’t find a meaning for it.” Click here for more from the interview, including Ryan Gosling’s comment that she’s “like a sexy cowboy.”

– Humans have a tendency to kill each other, according to a new study that suggests lethal violence is part of our evolutionary history. Researchers in Spain looked at more than 1,000 mammal species and estimated that one in every 300 deaths in the ancestor of all mammals was caused by a fight between members of the same species, the Guardian reports. primates are particularly prone to such fights, and the rate of lethal violence among humans has fluctuated over time. "Lethal violence is part of our evolutionary history but not carved in stone in 'our genes,'" says a researcher. "At least to some extent, the way humans organize in societies influences our levels of lethal violence." The study, published in the journal Nature, also found that the rate of lethal violence among humans has fluctuated over time, with the number of deaths down to 2% in prehistoric man and below 2% in modern times. But it's unclear if the violence is due to genetics or other factors. "Not only genes are inherited from ancestors, also environmental conditions and ecological constraints," the researcher says. "Those are also probably influencing the human lethal violence in our evolutionary past." (Click to read about how modern humans are better at hiding their identities.)

– Yahoo announced today that it will be "freeing up" email addresses that have been inactive for a year or more. But it's not just deactivating these accounts, it's going to offer them to other people. In mid July, anyone can have a shot at scoring the Yahoo! ID they want. In mid August, users who staked a claim on certain IDs can come to Yahoo! to discover which one they got. Wired calls it a "spectacularly bad idea." It means that people will be able to claim Yahoo IDs and use them to take over other people's identities via password resets and other methods. For example, someone who uses a Yahoo email address solely as a backup for Gmail, and thus hasn't logged into it for a long time, would be vulnerable to having that address taken over by a malicious individual who only wanted to ultimately get into the active Gmail address. The bottom line is that unless it rethinks this policy, this is going to lead to a social engineering gold rush come mid-July."

– Hillary Clinton's campaign says she raised $28 million in the third quarter, while Bernie Sanders' campaign says it raised $25 million, reports CNN. Both campaigns will be required to release their third-quarter fundraising numbers next week, and while it's not a huge surprise that Clinton raised less than Sanders, it's a "surprising development that shows the insurgent candidate's strength while the former secretary of state struggles," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. Sanders' campaign says it has $25 million cash on hand, while Clinton's camp says it has $75 million. Clinton's campaign says 93% of her third-quarter donations came in increments of less than $100, while Sanders' camp says 93% came in increments of more than $100, Politico reports.

– A New Jersey dog was put on the wrong flight and ended up in Ireland, where he spent 24 hours stuck on a plane, the AP reports. The 6-year-old English Springer Spaniel, Hendrix, was traveling in cargo on United Airlines when he was put on the wrong flight from Newark to Phoenix. When the airline realized the mistake, "immediate steps were taken to return Hendrix to his owner," a spokeswoman tells CNN. United staff walked him and fed him until he arrived in Phoenix, where he was reunited with owner Edith Albach on Friday. "I felt like somebody punched me in the stomach. I mean, that's my dog. That's like my child," Albach tells KNXV. United offered a full refund and apologized, but Albach says she doesn't think her dog will fly again. "Obviously they take better care of people's bags than they do dogs. To them it's just an animal. What do they care?" she says.

The Wall Street Journal reports Amazon is offering makers of electronics a small chip that can be used to tell Alexa—Amazon's voice-activated assistant—to do things like turn the microwave on or off, add a potato, or make popcorn. The chips, which cost a few dollars each, will be available later this year for lower-end devices and will be part of Amazon's Alexa Connection Kit, which will also allow makers to add Bluetooth, WiFi, and other voice-control features. The microwave is Amazon's first product with Alexa capability, but other appliances with Alexa control are already available from companies like GE, Whirlpool, Kenmore, LG, and Samsung. A Romney ad supporting Mourdock began airing yesterday, and Democrats are calling on Romney to take it off the air, the AP reports. The National Republican Senatorial Committee is also calling on Romney to drop the ad, Politico reports. But a Romney spokeswoman wouldn't say whether the candidate would continue to support Mourdock. The comments from Mourdock—who also said that "life is that gift from God"—are "outrageous and demeaning to woman," said DNC chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz, calling on Romney to take the ad off the air. The DNC is also using Mourdock's comments as an opportunity to paint him as a "zealot," the Indianapolis Star reports.

The study found that 1.7% of women knew or suspected their best friend had ever self-induced an abortion, and 4.1% of those women said they'd tried to do so themselves. Most of the women who reported attempting to end their pregnancies with misoprostol said they didn't have the money to travel or pay for the procedure, their local clinic had closed, a close friend or family member had recommended self-induction, or they feared the stigma associated with going to an abortion clinic. – Baby Cearra Nicole Soper was born on Oct. 10, 2010, making her the third child in the Soper family to be born on a numerical anomaly. Her first was born on Aug. 8, 2008, her second on Sept. 9, 2009, and her most recent on Oct. 10, 2010, USA Today reports. Mom Barbara Soper says she and husband Chad weren't thinking about dates when their children were born. Their doctor had to give drugs to start labor for the couple's first daughter, Chloe Corrin Soper, who was born full term on Aug. 8 at Spectrum Health's Butterworth Hospital in Grand Rapids, Mich. "He wasn't a planned baby at all, he was a miracle," says Barbara Soper. He was due on Sept. 20, 2009, but because sister Chloe's birth had caused some hemorrhaging, their doctor, Andrew Van Slooten, suggested he come out a little early so he'd be smaller. Soper was started on drugs to induce labor on Sept. 8, but it took 24 hours before Cameron Dane Soper made his way into the world, arriving on 9-9-09. – A new Trojan is hitting Macs, and experts are warning users to make sure their computers have the latest software updates from Apple and Microsoft, and to use anti-virus software. Mac users who open a boobytrapped Word document "may be caught off guard," writes Graham Cluley of Sophos. "As a decoy, a Word document is dumped onto your drive and displayed—effectively acting as a camouflage for the Trojan's true intentions." The malware, called Sabpab, takes advantage of the same Java exploit used by Flashback, which infected up to 600,000 Macs. One version of Sabpab arrives in an email attachment called "10th March Statemnet," which is linked to the Dalai Lama. "The name of the file ("10th March Statemnet") is directly linked with the Dalai Lama and Tibetan community," says a researcher. "On March 10, 2011, the Dalai Lama released a special statement related to owning Windows machines around the world for the last few years, attackers in China now have taken up the challenge of going after Macs with the same kind of targeted attack tactics that have served them so well in the Windows world."

– Andreas Gursky's "Rhein II," a 1999 photograph of the Rhine river, sold for $4.3 million at Christie's yesterday, making it the most expensive photograph in the world, the AP reports. The German artist's genic color print face-mounted to acrylic glass had a pre-sale estimate of $2.5 million to $3.5 million. The buyer was not disclosed. The previous record for any photography sold at auction was Cindy Sherman's "Untitled," which fetched $3.8 million at Christie's in May. Gursky is known for his large, disorienting landscapes. At once majestic and alienating, they don't require a lot of explanation. This photo is meant to be stared at. Of his works, Gursky has explained: "Maybe to try to understand not just that we are living in a certain building or in a certain location, but to become aware that we are living on a planet that is going at enormous speed through the universe." Click for more.

The charges—the first levied in a probe that's expected to broaden—were filed against a pair of state Department of Environmental Quality officials, a state-appointed emergency manager, and two teachers who work for the department. The charges include official misconduct, evidence tampering, and neglect of duty, among other things. "The state of Michigan has been hit with a great injustice," AG Bill Schuette says. "The people of Flint have been hit with a terrible injustice." Snyder says he's "disappointed" in the charges, the Detroit News reports. "I'm not going to pay a penny more than what the people of Flint deserve," he says. "I'm going to get to the bottom of what's happened and make sure there's no repeat of this." He says he'll meet with Flint's mayor and other officials on Friday to discuss a deal that would send Flint's water to Lake Michigan. – Mitt Romney's April Fools' Day prank didn't go as well as he might have hoped. A blogger at Forbes.com declared that Romney had dropped out of the race and backed Rick Santorum, reports the Washington Post. The blog was quickly taken down, but not before it went viral on Twitter. “It was April Fools’ Day, and it was completely implausible. Nobody in the party would have said those things,” wrote Len Burman. “I don’t want to wait until 2020 to get my party back. I’m all about efficiency. Let’s get our butts kicked now and move on.” Burman, an economics professor at Syracuse, says he was trying to mock the "right wing" of the GOP. “I really thought the blog was my blog and as long as I didn’t do anything grossly irresponsible—and I don’t consider this to be in that category—I could do what I wanted with it.”

– Opioids like morphine and oxycodone may not be the answer for all chronic pain, according to a new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine. The study looked at 240 patients with moderate to severe chronic back pain or hip or knee osteoarthritis pain who weren't getting relief from painkillers. They were randomly assigned to one of two groups: opioids (e.g., morphine, oxycodone, or hydrocodone) or nonopioid drugs like acetaminophen (paracetamol) or a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug. The study found no difference in pain intensity between the two groups at a year. The New York Times reports the results are "troubling," as opioids have been shown to be more dangerous than other pain medications, and current guidelines discourage the use of opioids for chronic pain. The study's lead author, Dr. Nancy Baxter, tells the Times the results are "troubling" because the patients in the study were at high risk of overdosing on the opioids. She says the findings should be interpreted in the same way as other types of pain medication and should not be used to steer patients away from opioids. However, she says they should be used in patients who can't get relief from opioids and who are at high risk

– A Chinese farmer who needed seven hours of surgery after a wild panda bit him on the leg has won $83,000 in compensation from government officials, AFP reports. The farmer, identified only as Guan Quanzhi, says he was working on his farmland in Gansu province last year when a panda wandered onto it. "I saw a panda jump out in front of me, its body completely covered in mud," he tells a local newspaper. The panda bit Guan on the right leg and released its grip when another villager covered its head with a coat. Guan sued three government departments responsible for controlling wild animals, including the forestry bureau and the management bureau of the nearby Baishuijiang National Nature Reserve, which is home to more than 100 wild pandas. Officials agreed to pay the compensation. Guan's lawyer says he is "satisfied" with the amount, which will cover his medical bills.

"I have not made a decision about the use of military force," he says. "My decision has not been made." But he added that the use of chemical weapons would cross a "red line" for him and he would need to seek the approval of Congress. Biden said the US has been in "close consultation" with its foreign counterparts and that the administration's national security team has been in "close consultation" with its own national security team, the AP reports. The White House has been pushing hard for the US to take action, with Jay Carney saying today that "there must be a response," reports the Hill.

– If you're one of the 930 million passengers who flew out of a US airport last year, you're not alone. There's another group: industry experts who say flying has never been better. They say it's the cheapest it's ever been, affordable for the majority of Americans, and safer. Your bags are less likely to get lost. You're likely to have honest-to-god internet on a damn plane. So this is a conundrum. How can flying be both the best and the worst it's ever been? The experts are right. Saying that flying is the best it's ever been, of course, requires knowing what it used to be. Interior ministers in the country's 16 regions are meeting this week to discuss using software similar to Shazam, a mobile phone-based music identification service, to quickly identify neo-Nazi music. A regional police office has developed a prototype system of registering audio fingerprints from neo-Nazi rock. It has the advantage of "sparing resources and enabling very quick investigations," said an internal government assessment. The software would allow police to react instantly if neo-Nazi music is played on radio stations, at concerts, club nights, or demonstrations. "Music is indeed a weak spot through which young people can easily be recruited into neo-Nazi circles," a spokesman for the Network Against Nazis website tells the Guardian. "A song can plug teenagers straight into the ideology conveyed through the lyrics."

– Malaysia Airlines is "technically bankrupt" after last year's disasters—including the downing of Flight 17 over Ukraine and the disappearance of Flight 370—and it has decided to make drastic changes to get itself out of the red, the BBC reports. New CEO Christoph Mueller says the airline has "offered jobs" to 14,000 of the 20,000 employees it employs and plans to cut a third of its work force by the end of the year, the AFP reports. He says the changes will "stop the bleeding" and allow the airline to start growing again by 2017, the BBC reports. Analysts have long blamed the airline's failure to compete on poor management, unwise business decisions, government meddling, and unfavorable service and supplier contracts stemming from Malaysia's crony capitalism, the AFP notes. Mueller, who has previously worked at Aer Lingus, Belgium's Sabena, and Germany's Lufthansa, was hired by the Malaysian state fund Khazanah Nasional last month to lead the restructuring.

– As part of his push to reform the criminal justice system, President Obama plans to restore federal funding for college for prison inmates, the Wall Street Journal reports. Pell grants, the main form of federal aid for low-income students, have been banned for state and federal prisoners for 20 years. Education Secretary Arne Duncan is expected to announce the move Friday, and it could allow thousands of prisoners to enroll in college courses, the Journal reports. "A lot of my friends here in Washington have been talking about the need for debt-free degrees. And they're right," Duncan said during a speech at the University of Maryland yesterday, per Politico. "We want to do even more, developing experimental sites that will make Pell grants available to programs that award credentials based on demonstrated competency, to incarcerated adults seeking an independent, productive life after release, and to adult learners who enroll in short-term certificate programs that provide job-ready training."

Mariano Rajoy made the appeal in a tweet Friday, minutes after Catalonia's parliament approved a motion declaring the wealthy region a republic independent from Spain. The bill passed with a 7-2 vote Wednesday and now goes to Honolulu Mayor Kirk Caldwell, who is still weighing the pros and cons of the bill, which would fine pedestrians up to $99 for the first offense and up to $500 for a third offense. The bill doesn't prohibit audio equipment, so listening to music with headphones will still be allowed. Supporters of the bill say it will hold pedestrians and motorists responsible for actions on the road, while critics called the bill intrusive and "another attempt at local government overreach." The Honolulu Police Department has expressed support of the measure. If signed into law, enforcement could begin in October. (New York has banned texting while driving.)

The ideal candidate will have a clean driving record, be willing to work nights and weekends, and be able to commit to at least two weeks of work per week, per the post, which notes that the ideal candidate will have a clean driving record and be able to commit to at least two weeks of work per week. The two-minute spot, which is available on YouTube, is "a great homage to the original 1986 film," writes Andrew O'Hehir at Salon. "Broderick amazingly slips back into the role with ease," he adds. "And fans who've been grousing that the teaser wasn't for an actual sequel to the movie will be pleased to see that Broderick doesn't sully the original film's reputation here. – If you're going to spank bank employees, you might as well do it in front of 200 of them. That's what happened at a bank in China, and it's led to the suspension of the bank's president and a second executive, reports the South China Morning Post. The video shows eight employees of the Zhangze Rural Commercial Bank in Shanxi province being spanked by a man wielding a piece of wood. He asked why they ranked last in the day's training, and they listed reasons such as "failing to make a personal breakthrough" and "inadequate team cohesion." The man said, "Get your butts ready," and began to spank them in turn. The 75-second video went viral after an audience member recorded it, notes NPR. The trainer, identified as Jiang Yang of Shanghai's Hongfeng Leadership Academy, later apologized, saying physical spanking is "one of the most effective ways to raise consciousness," reports the Beijing Times. He also said 16 employees were forced to have their heads shaved that day. The bank says it has stopped the training session, asked the trainer to openly apologize, and suspended several managing personnels from the branch. Economic compensation is in discussion.

He will stand up there as a comedian and leave as a comedian.” Stewart's rally is being widely seen as a test run for the new role he's taking, in which he's shifting from an "outside figure" to a "mainstream political player."

– Fighter jets from the Royal Air Force in Britain were scrambled twice this month to intercept passenger planes flying over the country, the BBC reports. On March 22, two Typhoon fighter jets were scrambled from Coningsby in Lincolnshire after air traffic control picked up the words "ransom" and "hostage" from a United Airlines plane en route from New York to Frankfurt, Germany. Minutes later, a Delta Airlines plane en route from the US to Frankfurt made an "unusual request" to descend just as it was flying south of Reading, England. The fighter jets circled over Kent as the civilian flight cleared UK airspace. It was, thankfully, a false alarm. But the speed of the interception by the RAF Typhoons gives a sense of how seriously these incidents are taken. They are a reminder of the work the air force carries out to defend the homeland at a time when serious questions are being asked about the overall cost of the UK's defense budget. There will be a Strategic Defense Review after the general election to decide the future shape of the armed forces. Cuts are inevitable. The RAF, like the Royal Navy and the Army are engaged in their own PR battle to ensure they will not end up bearing the brunt of the costs. In another incident earlier this month

– An EgyptAir flight carrying 66 passengers and 10 crew from Paris to Cairo disappeared from radar early Thursday over the Mediterranean Sea, reports Reuters. EgyptAir initially reported that Greek authorities had found debris, including two life vests, near the Greek island of Karpathos. But an hour later, the head of Greece's Air Accident Investigation and Aviation Safety Board told state ERT TV that "an assessment of the finds showed that they do not belong to an aircraft." EgyptAir VP Ahmed Adel tells CNN that a statement he made earlier to the network was not accurate. "We stand corrected on finding the wreckage because what we identified is not a part of our plane," Adel says. "So the search and rescue is still going on." USA Today reports that Egypt's Civil Aviation Minister Sherif Fathi says the possibility of a terror attack being responsible for the crash is "higher than that of a technical error." French President Franois Hollande confirmed the disappearance of the flight but said it was too early to determine the cause.

A fourth child was critically injured and airlifted to a hospital. A Tippecanoe Valley School Corp. bus had stopped and lowered its stop-arm on the road near Rochester around 7am, just before a northbound pickup truck slammed into the children as they crossed the southbound lane, Indiana State Police Sgt. Tony Slocum said. Six-year-old twin brothers Xzavier and Mason Ingle and their 9-year-old sister, Alivia Stahl, died at the scene, he said. The rural Rochester residents were students at nearby Mentone Elementary School. The siblings' great aunt, Pamela Pugh, told the South Bend Tribune that she was stunned and shaken by their deaths. "I'm just trying to make sense of all of it. There are no words," she said. Slocum said an 11-year-old boy not related to the deceased siblings suffered multiple broken bones when he was also hit by the pickup. – At least 70 works of art from Cuba's National Museum of Fine Arts have gone missing, and a Miami art dealer says he knows where they are: in the US. Ramon Cernuda says he discovered the missing artworks after buying a painting for $15,000 from a dealer in Miami, CNN reports. He says the same dealer had 10 other Cuban artworks for sale in the city that appeared to have been cut from their frames. "It's an obvious tell that something is going on," says Cernuda. The UN yesterday released a list of the stolen artworks, which it says "threatens the integrity of the seized property," placing them "at the mercy of illicit trafficking of cultural assets at the national and international level," the Havana Times reports. Cernuda says the case is notable because art theft is relatively rare in Cuba. Museums are tightly guarded and artwork is usually inspected before it leaves the country. "The theft is so much more complicated than the smuggling out of Cuba," Cernuda says. "To just get the art out of the museum is very complicated." Cuban authorities haven't said whether any arrests have been made.

– Columbia University's student newspaper, Bwog, says it has found a fourth "rape list" of alleged rapists scrawled on bathroom stalls on campus. Bwog says it found the same four names in a stall on the second floor of a women's bathroom yesterday, hours after the first list was found in a stall on the third floor of a women's bathroom. The fourth list has been found in a stall on the fourth floor of a women's bathroom, Jezebel reports. Bwog says it is "incredibly disturbed that people think this is a legitimate way to deal with the issue," but it says publishing the list would violate Title IX and FERPA. "Perhaps writing this list (and publishing the work of a campus 'vigilante') is not the best way to create a safer campus environment for victims," the paper says. "We strongly encourage the prosecution through Columbia or the legal system of sexual assault perpetrators and taking all appropriate actions to 'cultivate a community that is hostile to perpetrators of sexual violence,' and we acknowledge the bravery of victims and faculty to help force change from the administration."

– People are better at empathy for abused puppies and dogs than people who have been abused themselves, according to a new study. Researchers surveyed 240 college students and asked them to read one of four versions of a fictional news article about a brutal beating. The wording was the same, except for the identity of the victim, which was either an infant, an adult in his 30s, a puppy, or a 6-year-old dog. Participants then rated their level of empathy for the abused child, puppy, and dog than they did for the abused adult, the study found. "Contrary to popular thinking, we are not necessarily more disturbed by animal rather than human suffering," one of the researchers said in a press release. "Our results indicate a much more complex situation with respect to the age and species of victims, with age being the more important component. In addition, it appears that adult humans are viewed as capable of protecting themselves while full grown dogs are just seen as larger puppies." Interestingly, the researchers found that the difference in empathy for children versus puppies was statistically non-significant.

– Starting next week, rush-hour riders on Chicago's train system will be asked to submit their bags for bomb screening—and if they refuse, they won't be able to get on the train, the Chicago Tribune reports. The city's police department will randomly select a rail station each day and have a mobile explosive screening team approach riders, who will be selected at random. Officers will swab bags and place the sample in a machine to check for explosive compounds. Bags will not be opened. "We know the fears and the possibilities. It’s going to take 20 to 30 seconds of someone’s time," a police spokeswoman tells CBS. "While we know our commuters’ time is precious, we think their safety is probably priceless." But some riders say they're skeptical about the plan, which is being funded with a $3.5 million federal anti-terrorism grant. "If they swab one random person's bag, what about the next person who might have something?" asks one rider. "I think it's just a waste of money and time." A transit expert says it's difficult to provide airport-level security. "We have hundreds and hundreds of access points to our stations."

– Police have identified the suspect in Norway's twin terror attacks as Anders Behring Breivik, a 32-year-old right-wing Christian, reports the New York Times. “We are not sure whether he was alone or had help,” said a police official. “What we know is that he is right wing and a Christian fundamentalist.” In a 1,500-page manifesto posted on the Internet before the attacks, Breivik claims to be part of a small group that intended to “seize political and military control of Western European countries and implement a cultural conservative political agenda.” He also calls for a Christian war to defend Europe against Muslim domination. “The time for dialogue is over. We gave peace a chance. The time for armed resistance has come,” reads the manifesto, which was signed Andrew Berwick. Breivik also posted a video on Friday summarizing his views, which a Norwegian terrorism expert says bears an eerie resemblance to those of Osama bin Laden and other al-Qaeda leaders.

– Investigators looking into the Dark Knight massacre in Aurora, Colo., say suspect James Holmes must have had a lot of target practice before the shooting, the Los Angeles Times reports. Based on what they call his "unusually high" hit rate, the officials say he practiced with an AR-15 assault-style rifle with a magazine that could hold as many as 100 rounds before the attack. He also practiced with a 12-gauge shotgun and a Glock .40-caliber pistol, authorities say. Investigators are searching Holmes' apartment for evidence of target practice, including a receipt, a brochure, related information he may have accessed on his computer, or phone calls he may have placed to a range. Such evidence would provide more evidence of premeditation and show that he deliberately planned the attack. The owner of a local shooting range says Holmes applied to join his club in June but never showed up. "It was this very bass, guttural, rambling, incoherent message that was bizarre, at best," he says. "Freakish, maybe."

– Texting while walking is so dangerous that police in Fort Lee, NJ, are going to start handing out $85 jaywalking tickets. "It's a big distraction. Pedestrians aren't watching where they are going and they are not aware," the police chief tells ABC News. He hopes the crackdown will make his town safer, but not everyone is on board with the idea of issuing $85 tickets. "When I walk I still look around. I'm not like constantly looking down the whole time," says one resident. Another complained about the tickets being "a lot of money." More than 117 tickets have been issued so far. Two professors at Stony Brook University in New York conducted a study on walking and texting. They found texters are 60% more likely to veer off line than non-texters. "We want to raise awareness that a real disruption occurs because of texting," Eric Lamberg, co-author of the study, told Long Island Business News. "Texting disrupts your ability much more than does talking." The study found "gait velocity is reduced when using a cell phone while talking or texting," that "navigational errors occur when texting while walking" and "texting while walking produces greater interference than talking on a cell phone."

– Sixteen US Postal Service letter carriers and clerks in Atlanta have been sentenced to between three and nine years in federal prison for taking bribes to deliver cocaine, CNN reports. According to a press release, the drug traffickers targeted postal workers because their jobs made them less likely to be caught by law enforcement. The workers were paid to deliver mail, "not drugs," says the US Attorney's Office in Atlanta. "This important operation identified and prosecuted 16 corrupt individuals who chose to abuse that trust and instead used their positions to bring what they thought were large amounts of dangerous drugs into those same communities for a quick payoff," US Attorney Byung J. "BJay" Pak says in the press release. The US Attorney's Office says a confidential source posed as a drug trafficker looking for postal workers to deliver packages of cocaine or marijuana. The workers were willing to accept bribes as low as $250 to deliver the drugs to designated addresses. The press release says the drug traffickers believed the postal workers were less likely to be caught by law enforcement because of their official jobs. All 16 postal workers were sentenced after pleading guilty to federal felony charges of accepting bribes.

– The Texas State Board of Education has told textbook publishers to clean up their act when it comes to Islam and Christian history. The board voted 7-6 to tell publishers that textbooks have been “tainted” with “gross pro-Islamic, anti-Christian distortions,” the Austin American-Statesman reports. The resolution claims that textbooks have glossed over events that occurred in Islamic history. “What we're trying to do is prohibit and send a clear message to the publishers that [the bias] should not happen in the future,” one board member said. The resolution was attached to an attachment that cited a past investment by the Dubai royal family in a major US textbook publisher. Opponents called the proposal a waste of time and a “narrow-minded resolution” that is biased. “We are allowing ourselves to be distracted by this narrow-minded resolution, which is itself biased,” said board member Rick Agosto. “We should have taken the higher ground on this.”

– If you want to live a long life, it might be best to give up marathons and triathlons, according to a new study in the Christmas edition of the British Medical Journal. Researchers looked at the mortality records of nearly 10,000 Olympic athletes who competed between 1896 and 1936, and found that those who engaged in cycling and rowing (high cardiovascular intensity) had no added survival benefit compared with playing golf or cricket, the Wall Street Journal reports. The study doesn't prove cause and effect, and the results are too "preliminary and controversial to trigger warnings against marathons and triathlons," writes Kevin Helliker at the Journal. That means the air molecules in the path of the meteor can be stripped of electrons, allowing the energy they release to light up the sky and leave trails of light and color. The bright meteors will appear to come from the constellation Aquarius.

– A new Washington Post/ABC poll has Mitt Romney and President Obama in a statistical dead heat, with Romney squeaking ahead 49% to 46% among registered voters. That's not a huge lead, but it's still within the poll's margin of error. Obama leads all other potential GOP candidates, including Sarah Palin, by the same margin. Palin, however, fares the worst: She trails Obama by 17 points among registered voters, and by a scant 41% among Republicans and Republican-leaning independents. Overall, 21% of leaned Republicans support Romney for the nomination, 17% Palin, with all others in single digits. What's more, just 22% of Americans (and 24% of leaned Republicans) are following the 2012 presidential election very closely. That's down from 43% in April. Also, ABC's Frustration Index stands at 68—essentially what it was going into the 2010 midterm elections. That's based on presidential approval, anti-incumbency, and dissatisfaction with the federal government.

Dianne Feinstein today accused the CIA of illegally searching a computer network used by the Senate Intelligence Committee as it investigated the CIA's use of waterboarding and other "enhanced interrogation" techniques. "The CIA just went and searched the committee's computers," the California Democrat said in a speech on the Senate floor, according to the AP. "I have grave concerns that the CIA's search may well have violated the separation of powers principles embodied by the United States Constitution, including the speech and debate clause," she said. "It may have undermined the Constitutional framework essential to effective congressional oversight of intelligence activity or any other government function." The CIA provided the computers to congressional staffers in a secure room at its headquarters so that the committee could review millions of pages of top secret documents, reports NBC News. The computers were provided by the CIA and housed at a separate facility in Virginia operated by an agency contractors. Feinstein confirmed that committee investigators had obtained documents detailing the interrogation policy, but said she confirmed that an internal agency investigation of the action has been referred to the Justice Department for possible criminal prosecution. She accused the CIA of violating the Fourth Amendment, various federal laws, and a presidential executive order that bars the agency from conducting domestic searches and surveillance. "I will be

– If you're like most of us, your plate is likely full of food you don't want to eat. That's the takeaway from a new study out of Cornell University that found adults eat an average of 92% of the food they put on their plates, regardless of gender or nationality. "If you put it on your plate, it’s going into your stomach," says lead researcher Brian Wansink. The study, published in the International Journal of Obesity, looked at 14 studies involving a total of 1179 diners. Wansink and co-author Katherine Abowd Johnson found that the results were nearly identical in the US, Canada, France, Taiwan, South Korea, Finland, and the Netherlands, reports Medical Daily. Kids, on the other hand, eat only 59% of the food they put on their plates. "This might be because kids are less certain about whether they will like a particular food," says Wansink. "Regardless, this is good news for parents who are frustrated that their kids don't clean their plate. It appears few of them do." The researchers say the findings can help people be more mindful of portion size. "Just knowing that you're likely to consume almost all of what you serve yourself can help you

– President Trump says he has a deal in place to put Chinese telecommunications giant ZTE back in business, Reuters reports. "I closed it down then let it reopen with high level security guarantees, change of management and board, must purchase U.S. intellectual property," Trump tweeted Friday night. "ZTE has a beautiful track record of being a very good and reliable source of information & jobs for our country." The deal involves the US government imposing penalties on ZTE for violating sanctions against Iran and North Korea. ZTE has 70,000 workers across 160 countries and supplies telecom networks for 80% of the world's smartphones, according to the New York Times. It has also been sued more than 100 times in the US for patent infringement, according to one Chinese tech publication. Democrats and Republicans have urged the Trump administration not to bend on ZTE, but Axios reports that the administration is considering a deal that would allow ZTE to buy component parts from the US without facing penalties. ZTE's behavior is "completely outside the norm," the Washington Post reports. "Despite what you may hear, some Chinese companies are actually good IP citizens—Lenovo for one," the Post states. "But ZTE is not one of them."

– "This may be the most ironic aspect of this case," says a judge in Canada. On Thursday, Anita Krajnc was found not guilty of mischief for giving water to pigs outside a slaughterhouse, the Toronto Star reports. The 49-year-old founder of the Toronto Pig Save group had pleaded not guilty to the charge, which stemmed from an incident in 2015. On June 22, 2015, Krajnc dumped liquid from a water bottle into a truck carrying pigs to Fearman's Pork Inc. in Burlington, Ontario. The pigs' owner, Eric Van Boekel, testified that he was concerned about contaminants in the water and that the slaughterhouse would turn the pigs away. Krajnc admitted to giving the pigs water, but said she was treating them as she would want to be treated. Justice David Harris found that Krajnc did not harm the pigs or cause the slaughterhouse to reject them, and that the prosecution "actually accomplished what they accused Ms. Krajnc of trying to do." He rejected the defense's argument that Krajnc's actions were in the public good and that she should be cleared because she was acting in the greater good. Krajnc says she hopes the ruling inspires other activists. "This is how social movements get their

– The Islamic State's new media arm has launched on social media, and it's already got guidelines for women who want to be "good wives of jihad," the Independent reports. The Zora Foundation has posted videos, tweets, and recipes on its Twitter account, all of which are in Arabic. "To the victorious supporters [of jihad] and the beloved muhajiraat [for example, women who go to Syria], may Allah bless their efforts and reward them accordingly, we dedicate this first recipe to the heroes on the front line," says the recipe. "It's kind of a guideline on how to be a good supporter of jihad and have the best role in supporting 'your mujahidin' as a woman," says a researcher at a counter-extremism think tank. "I haven't seen anything like this before," he adds. "There will probably be forums doing similar things online, but this is the first time I've come across an actual media organization giving guidance to women on their role."

– McDonald's Mighty Wings were supposed to be a hit when they debuted last year, but they didn't, and now the fast-food chain is offering them at a 40% discount. The bone-in chicken wings were originally priced at $1 per wing, but now a pack of five is $3—or about 60 cents per wing, USA Today reports. A McDonald's spokeswoman says the price was "not as competitive as it could have been" when Mighty Wings first launched, and consumers weren't happy with the amount of spice in the wings. But "there is more awareness that they have a spicy kick to them," the spokeswoman says. A restaurant analyst says McDonald's is "really the only sensible option at this point" because Mighty Wings will be sold at the discounted price "until supply runs out."

– Osama bin Laden's youngest son Hamza hasn't been seen since the US raid that killed the al-Qaeda leader, Pakistani security officials tell ABC News. Hamza, 19, has been dubbed the "Crown Prince of Terror" because of his prominence in al-Qaeda propaganda. He is believed to be the son of bin Laden's second wife, Khairiah Sabar. Pakistani officials say three of bin Laden's wives have told them one of his sons has not been seen since the raid. Another son, 22-year-old Khalid, was confirmed dead by the US military. He is believed to have been one of the men shown in graphic photos taken in the aftermath of the raid and released to Reuters last week. Pakistani security officials say the wives have told them one of Osama's sons has not been seen since the raid, the Daily Mail reports.

– Scientists have long wondered how much water was on Mars when it formed 4.5 billion years ago, and a new study in Science sheds new light on the planet's past. The findings suggest that the Red Planet once had a massive ocean that covered more than a fifth of its surface, more than the Atlantic Ocean, and was a mile deep in some places, reports the Guardian. "We now know Mars was wet for a much longer time than we thought before," says NASA scientist Michael Mumma. "Ultimately we can conclude this idea of an ocean covering about 17% of Earth's surface ... opens the idea of Mars as a more promising place for alien life to emerge." The findings suggest that water once trickled down streams, rivers, and lakes and eventually froze, reports the New York Times, which notes that the loss of the ocean means that Mars is no longer a warm-and-wet planet, as scientists had previously believed. The findings also suggest that the planet once had an ocean that was much deeper than the Arctic Ocean, which is only about a mile deep, reports the BBC. (Scientists have found evidence of ancient water on Mars.)

– Iran is in the midst of a "soft war" against Western culture, and morality police have decided to step in: They've banned the sale of Barbie dolls, Reuters reports. "About three weeks ago they (the morality police) came to our shop, asking us to remove all the Barbies," says a shopkeeper in Tehran. "We still sell Barbies but secretly and put these in the window to make the police think we are just selling these kinds of dolls." It's not the first time the doll has been banned in Iran. A range of officially approved dolls were launched in 2002 to counter demand for Barbie, but they haven't proven successful, says a Tehran toy shop manager. "My daughter prefers Barbies. She says Sara and Dara are ugly and fat," says one mother.

– Benjamin Netanyahu's concession speech today was short on specifics, but he made clear that he's sticking to his guns on two states for two peoples. "I don't want a one-state solution. I want a sustainable, peaceful two-state solution," he told MSNBC's Andrea Mitchell. "I haven't changed my policy." He added that he's "very proud" to be prime minister of "all Israel's citizens," reports the New York Times, and dismissed the criticism of his campaign stance from the Obama administration. "America has no greater ally than Israel and Israel has no greater ally than the United States," he said. "We'll work together. We have to." President Obama, meanwhile, called Netanyahu to congratulate him on his re-election victory and tell him that the US "will need to re-assess our options" in the wake of his comments on a two-state solution, reports CNN.

– A set of never-before-seen sketches by Vincent Van Gogh will be published for the first time this November, reports the Guardian. The publisher Seuil in Paris says the sketches are "stunning, dazzling" and were only recently discovered. No word yet on where the sketches came from or how they were found, but they will be published under the title The Fog of Arles. "Now that they've cast these drawings in a shroud of mystery and hype, those sketches better be pretty amazing," observes the Washington Post.

– A giant panda cub at the National Zoo in Washington, DC, has died just days after its birth, reports USA Today. Mei Xiang gave birth to twins Saturday night, but the smaller of the two cubs died today after struggling to breathe and spending the night with its mother. The zoo's chief veterinarian says that despite "extreme efforts on the part of our dedicated staff, we weren't able to change things." A necropsy will be performed to determine the cause of the cub's death.

– The death toll in the Algerian gas plant siege has risen to 32, with 25 more bodies found at the site today, reports the BBC. It's not clear whether they were captors or captives, but the dead include three Britons, a Colombian, and two Malaysians. Algeria's energy minister says the gas plant will resume production within two days. Meanwhile, five militants have been arrested, according to local media. Algeria's communications minister earlier said the militants were from six countries, "nationals of Arab and African countries, and of non-African countries," the AP reports. Meanwhile, the militants have released a video in which they vow to kill Western hostages if France intervenes in Mali.

– Pope Francis' much-anticipated environmental encyclical was just days away from its official release when it was leaked to an Italian newsweekly, the AP reports. Now the Vatican has indefinitely suspended the press credentials of L'Espresso's veteran Vatican correspondent, Sandro Magister, saying the publication had been "incorrect." Magister tells the AP he wasn't the one who leaked the 191-page document: "I just wrote the introduction," he says in a text message. "I promised the Vatican I wouldn't leak the document." But some Vatican experts believe the leak was timed to take the punch out of the encyclical ahead of its official release Thursday, in which Francis has lined up a Catholic cardinal, an Orthodox theologian, an atheist scientist, and an economist to discuss the contents, the AP reports. According to the New York Times, some Vatican commentators believe the leak came from "conservatives" inside the Vatican, who would like to derail Francis' reform plans. The Times reports Magister has been covering the Vatican for L'Espresso for more than 30 years and is considered one of the most reliable and respected Vatican reporters. He was once put on trial for stealing the pope's private papers and passing them to an Italian

– The Polish government is in damage-control mode after a series of tapes leaked this week allegedly show officials discussing payoffs to officials at the country's top central bank. The tapes allegedly show Interior Minister Bartlomiej Sienkiewicz and Finance Minister Jacek Rostowski talking to National Bank of Poland head Marek Belka, the BBC reports. Belka is heard calling for Rostowski to be removed in return for the bank's support in the event of an economic crisis. Sienkiewicz was replaced four months later, but Prime Minister Donald Tusk denies the tapes show Rostowski being asked to step down. A raid on the magazine Wprost, which published the tapes, has been criticized by the country's justice minister as "too far-reaching" and "legitimate concerns about breaching of journalistic confidentiality." A professor of international studies at Rhodes College says he's especially concerned about the timing of the tapes, which appear to have been going on for more than a year. "I am especially concerned about the lack of clarity as to who did the recordings," he tells the New York Times. "And also why they surfaced now, at a time of significant shifts in regional security, when Poland is making key decisions on defense, military modernization

– The FDA has issued a warning to consumers that some over-the-counter antibacterial soaps may be harmful. Specifically, the agency says it's banning ingredients such as triclosan and triclocarban from marketing in products that claim to be more effective than plain soap and water in preventing illness. The agency says there's not enough evidence to suggest they're safe for daily use, and manufacturers haven't shown they're any more effective than water or soap in preventing infections. "Following simple handwashing practices is one of the most effective ways to prevent the spread of many types of infection and illness at home, at school, and elsewhere," an FDA official says in a press release. "We can't advise this enough. It's simple, and it works." The FDA says manufacturers will be required to remove the ingredients from products within two years. The warning applies to products that have been in use for at least 10 years and are labeled as "antibacterial." The FDA says manufacturers will be required to provide data showing the ingredients are safe and effective for at least two years. "This demands a full investigation into what happened, why it happened, and what needs to be done to make sure it never happens again," he said on Fox News Sunday, per Politico. "There can be a lot of conspiracies against the president—a lot of very complex assassination plots. This is the most basic, the most simple type of procedure, and how anyone, especially in the days of [Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant] ... can actually get into the White House without being stopped is inexcusable." – A California lawyer has been given the green light to move forward with a ballot measure that would require gay people to be "put to death by bullets to the head or by any other convenient method." Attorney Matt McLaughlin paid $200 to file the "Sodomite Suppression Act" in February, and now state Attorney General Kamala Harris is bound by law to prepare a title and summary of the measure by May so that its sponsor can begin collecting signatures, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. The "Sodomite Suppression Act" would make it illegal for anyone who advocates gay rights to minors to stay in the state, and it would require sensitivity training for at least three hours a month and a $5,000 donation to a "pro-gay or pro-lesbian organization." Harris has no power to stop the measure, which is unlikely to get the 365,000 signatures it needs. But Slate reports that activist Charlotte Laws has filed the "Intolerant Jackass Act" with the California State Bar, and more than 3,800 people have signed a petition calling for McLaughlin to be disbarred. "A lawyer such as Mr. McLaughlin who actively pursues creating laws that permit genocide has no business practicing law in California or any other state," writes Mark Joseph Stern at the Daily Beast.

– The Sandra Bullock-George Clooney space drama Gravity rocketed to the top of the box office and into industry record books during its opening weekend, the AP reports. The film has been beloved by critics, notching a 98% fresh rating on Rotten Tomatoes. And those who saw the film this weekend— 59% of whom were over the age of 35—enjoyed it too, assigning the movie an average grade of A-, according to market research firm CinemaScore. The only other film that debuted nationwide this weekend, Runner Runner, fell short of even the lowest projections with a disappointing $7.6 million start. The opening weekend tally for Gravity—which includes the $1.4 million the picture grossed Thursday evening—marks the biggest October debut ever. Previously, 2011's Paranormal Activity 3 held that record with its $52.6 million opening. "This gives new hope to exhibitors who have been getting nervous about 3-D," a Warner Bros. exec tells the Los Angeles Times. "But you’ve got to be careful about which movies you release in the format. One that lends itself to the format like this doesn’t come along often, but when it does, it becomes a cultural phenomenon."

– In what is being described as a stunning upset in Britain, the Conservative Party appears to have won the most seats in the country's general election—but not enough to form a majority government, the BBC reports. According to the AP, the Conservative Party won 314 of the 650 seats in the House of Commons, while the Labour Party came in second with around 260. In order to form a majority government, a party has to get more than 326 seats. The Conservative Party appears to be on track to do that, though it will have to try to find support from other parties in order to do so. The Labour Party, meanwhile, is expected to try to form a coalition government with the help of the Scottish National Party, which has seats in both the House of Commons and the devolved Scottish Parliament. The Conservative Party is expected to stay in power until at least June 19, when a Queen's Speech will have to be presented to Parliament to determine whether May has the confidence of the House of Commons. If May can't form a majority government, she will be expected to step down as prime minister. Reuters reports that if she can't form a majority government, it will be Corbyn's party's turn to try to form one. The Labour

– A Pennsylvania woman died last week after apparently overdosing herself while cleaning up drug paraphernalia in her son's bathroom, WJAC reports. Theresa Plummer, 69, found her 45-year-old son, Ronald, passed out in the bathroom on Nov. 5. After he was hospitalized, Plummer went back to clean up the bathroom. She began having shortness of breath and was taken to the hospital, where she died Nov. 6. Her son died the next day. "This is a caution for safety, for anyone coming into contact with any type of powder substance," Cambria County Coroner Jeff Lees tells WJAC. "You should use extreme caution and notify the proper authorities." Officials believe Plummer absorbed a substance through her skin or had a reaction to the drug paraphernalia after handling it. They don't think she used the drugs—they think she accidentally touched something so strong it killed her. Toxicology results won't be back for six to eight weeks.

– The European Space Agency lost contact with its Schiaparelli probe just before it was scheduled to touch down on Mars on Wednesday, and now NASA has released images of what it believes is the probe's final resting place. The images, taken by the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, show what the BBC calls a "large dark patch in the robot's targeted landing zone consistent with a high-velocity impact." The MRO took the images on Oct. 20 as part of a mission to study the Red Planet's atmosphere and surface. The BBC notes the resolution is low—just 6 meters per pixel—but its context is compelling. The roughly 15m by 40m dark patch, which is probably dust and rock fragments thrown out from the impact, is sited some 5.5km west of Schiaparelli's expected touchdown point in the equatorial Meridiani Plain. Tellingly, the feature is not present in previous MRO pictures of the location. The clincher, though, may be the artifact 1km to the south of the patch. This white blob looks to be Schiaparelli's 15m-wide parachute which would have floated down behind the probe. Again, this was not present in earlier pictures. Engineers continue to analyze the telemetry the probe transmitted through

– The bodies of six Japanese World War II soldiers have been found in a sealed cave on the island of Palau, and their remains will be repatriated to their homeland before the end of the year, reports the BBC. The soldiers are believed to have died during the Battle of Peleliu, one of the fiercest battles of the war in which US Marines were pitted against Japanese troops who used the caves and underground bunkers as their base. More than 10,000 Japanese soldiers died in Palau, but the remains of 2,600 troops have never been found. Palau has agreed to open about 200 other sealed caves to allow experts to search for the soldiers' remains. "A lot of field caves will contain considerable quantities of human remains and as such you could designate them as graves and wouldn't be appropriate to use as tourist attractions," says the operations director of Cleared Ground Demining, which has been searching the caves for six years. The bodies of the six Japanese soldiers have been found in a cave with a 7-foot opening, and archaeologists found a set of bones while clearing the cave's entrance, a local journalist tells ABC Radio. "They found some bones while they were clearing the entrance of the cave," she says. "They did not use heavy equipment because they have to make

– The 18-year-old lesbian shot in the head along with her girlfriend in a park in Portland, Texas, over the weekend is making "amazing" progress, her brother tells NBC Latino. "Krissy's health—considering what happened to her—she's doing amazing," says Hilario Chapa, 32. "She's making a strong recovery. The doctors are amazed." Police say they don't know who shot Mary Kristene Chapa and Mollie Judith Olgin, 19, because they haven't gotten a name from the teen. "We don't know if it's a hate crime," says Chapa's brother. "We don't know who did it, we don't know if it's a hate crime." Police say the two teens were in a same-sex relationship, but there is no evidence that they were the victims of a hate crime, reports the Oregonian. Olgin's father says the family is touched by the outpouring of support from the gay and lesbian community. "I know she's looking down on us, in a better place," he says.

– A recent Dr. Phil interview with a mom of a 5-year-old boy who loves Barbies and plays with both girls and boys has prompted a debate among parents: Is it OK for parents to force their kids to be gender-nonconforming? "The conflation of gender expression and sexuality is so ubiquitous in our society that it was refreshing to hear our country's second-highest-rated talk show host giving the same message to millions of Americans that I've given to dozens (literally dozens!) of Random Moms on playgrounds across my fair city," writes Tracy Clark-Flory on Salon. "But really, haven't you met a guy like this, the one you think is gay when you first met him, but then realize that his sexuality doesn't match his gender presentation? And if you get busy thinking about femmy boys who grow up to be straight, you might also start thinking about butch boys who grow up to be gay, like all those bears and leather daddies I see walking around the Castro." Clark-Flory writes that she's "actually kind of a NO-saying badass" and tries to impose no harm on her son, but "as a mother, I'm too powerful. Or too

– A man set himself on fire outside the Georgia Capitol in Atlanta Tuesday morning in what authorities say was a protest against the Department of Veterans Affairs. John Michael Watts, a 58-year-old Air Force veteran, suffered burns over 85% to 90% of his body in the incident, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports. "He was strapped with some homemade incendiary devices (and) firecrackers, and doused himself with some kind of flammable liquid" before setting himself on fire, Georgia State Patrol Capt. Mark Perry tells WSB-TV. "He did indicate that he is disgruntled with the VA system and was seeking attention for that," Perry says, adding that a trooper quickly put out the fire after hearing several loud explosions. The state Capitol and judiciary buildings were evacuated as a precaution. The Georgia Bureau of Investigation has identified Watts as a man without a current address.

– Two Tibetan monks set themselves on fire in China today in the third such protest this year, reports Reuters. The 18-year-old monks, one of whom is related to a 21-year-old who set himself on fire last month, "shouted: 'We need freedom of religion,'" says an exiled Tibetan activist. "When they set themselves on fire, they shouted: 'We need freedom of religion,'" he adds. The activists say the monks belong to the Kirti monastery, which has been the site of protests against Chinese policies in recent years. China's official Xinhua news agency reported that the monks were in stable condition, and that the suicide attempt is being investigated.

– The woman killed in yesterday's shooting rampage at a Wisconsin salon was a "wonderful mom" who saved for a year to take her two daughters to Disney World, a friend of hers tells the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. Zina Haughton, 42, worked as a hair stylist at Azana Salon & Spa in Brookfield, but "never talked negatively about her husband," the friend says. "She did say she was exhausted because she was working so many hours, because this had been going on for years. He was in school and she was supporting the family." Haughton had been granted a restraining order against her estranged husband, Radcliffe Haughton, after he allegedly slashed her tires while she worked at the salon earlier this month. He was also in school at the time, the friend says. The couple's two daughters, ages 4 and 6, were reportedly with Haughton when she was killed. Four other women were injured in the shooting, all of whom are expected to survive, the AP reports.

– Google CEO Sundar Pichai is one of the world's highest-paid executives, having just been awarded $199 million worth of shares, the Guardian reports. According to a securities filing Friday, Pichai was awarded 273,328 shares of Alphabet, Google's holding company, on Feb. 3. The shares—which will vest in quarterly increments until 2019—bring Pichai's stake in Alphabet to $650 million, the Wall Street Journal reports. That's 14,440 times Pichai's median net worth of US citizens. But it's still a lot less than the fortunes of Google's founders, Larry Page and Sergey Brin, who are worth $34.6 billion and $33.9 billion, respectively. It's also a lot less than former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, who has shares worth $3 billion. Pichai, 43, was named CEO of Alphabet in October following the company's reorganisation into a holding company.

– "I've never been an advocate of the death sentence, but in this particular instance I would probably find an exception if this were a different state," says a judge in Michigan. Garry Cordell was sentenced to life in prison without parole Thursday for the murders of three people in April, the Detroit Free Press reports. Cordell, 46, and two co-defendants were charged in the deaths of Jody Hutchinson, Carrie Nelson, and Heather Aldrich. The victims' bodies were found in a burned car in the woods of Michigan's Upper Peninsula. Cordell pleaded guilty last week to two counts of murder. The second suspect, Kenneth Brunke, pleaded guilty to obstruction of justice and lying to a police officer in exchange for his testimony against Cordell and the late Marietta Carlson, who died of natural causes while in custody. "I didn't do this to hurt their family; no way ever will I ask for forgiveness," Cordell said at his sentencing. "I'm proud of who I am and what I did and what I stand for." Police say Brunke was angry that one of the victims, Aldrich, was spurning his affection, and had stolen drugs from him. The other two victims were killed, police say, because

– The world's most famous dodo, which inspired Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, met an untimely and murderous end, scientists have discovered. The Oxford dodo is the most well-preserved example of the extinct bird on Earth and still contains soft tissue and DNA which could be used one day to resurrect the species. It was always thought the Oxford dodo survived the fate of its kin, and was brought back alive from Mauritius, ending up as an exotic curiosity on the streets of London. The last of the dodos left this planet somewhere in the mid to late 17th century, brought to extinction by early European explorers and invasive species of animals introduced to its native island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean. The skull of the Oxford dodo, housed at the Oxford University Museum of Natural History in the UK, is one of the museum's most precious treasures because most dodo remains today are skeletons reconstructed from bones found on Mauritius. The mummified bird's skull and foot and even skin and soft tissue, making it the only specimen that retains any viable DNA. Now, using 21st-century forensic scanning technology, researchers have uncovered new evidence that shows the world-famous Oxford dodo had a violent death. "We noticed

– Blade Runner actress Sean Young was arrested outside the Oscars' Governors Ball after an alleged altercation with a security guard. Young, who didn't have a ticket to the party, says she was taking pictures with celebrities when the guard asked her to leave because she didn't have a ticket. "They said, 'No, you have to leave,'" she tells People. "I started to leave and [the guard] grabbed my arm and he started pulling me. And I turned around and I was pulling my arm away—and I struck him." Young, 52, was booked for misdemeanor battery but released after posting bail. She blames the Academy's lawyer for suggesting a citizen's arrest. "They need to make a public apology on behalf of their security guard," she says. Click for more on Young's arrest.

– The 2010 census counted 308,745,538 people, which is 1.3% less than the 2000 count and the smallest growth since the Great Depression. But the South and West continued their strong population growth, with the South growing 14.3% and the West 14.6%, according to the Census Bureau. The Northeast grew 3.2%, while the Midwest 3.9%. Michigan was the only state to see a decline, at 0.6%. Nevada had the largest population growth, 35.1 percent, followed by Texas (31.7), Georgia (31.7), and Florida (31.7), according to the AP. The 2010 count will determine which states getportions of the new congressional seats, and which ones lose them.

– Pope Francis has wrapped up the second day of World Youth Day in Brazil with what the Wall Street Journal calls the "strongest show of public support yet for the pontiff on his first overseas trip." More than 3 million Catholics crowded Copacabana Beach for an evening vigil with the pope, reports USA Today, which puts the turnout at more than 4 million. The pontiff addressed Catholic bishops in the cathedral of Rio de Janeiro, telling them to get out of their cathedrals and reach out to the less fortunate. "We cannot keep ourselves shut up in parishes, in our communities, when so many people are waiting for the Gospel," he said. "Let us courageously look to pastoral needs, beginning on the periphery (of where we live), with those who are farthest away, with those who do not usually go to church. They, too, are invited to the table of the Lord." The pontiff later gave a speech to political and business leaders in which he called for "social humility" and "dialogue, dialogue, dialogue" in a country rife with inequality.

– The leader of al-Qaeda's affiliate in Yemen has released an audio recording in which he describes President Trump as the "White House's new fool" and says a recent US raid against the group killed 25 people, including 11 women and children, the AP reports. Addressing his followers in the recording, which emerged late Saturday, Qassim al-Rimi says: "The White House's new fool has received a painful blow at your hands in his first outing on your land." – Three more women have come forward to accuse Bill Cosby of sexual assault, and they're being represented by attorney Gloria Allred, People reports. Beth Ferrier says she met Cosby through her then-agent in New York City in the '80s and was invited to one of his performances in Denver. She says she was drugged and woke up in her car "in the back of my car alone. My clothes were a mess; my bra was undone. My car was in the alleyway behind the venue. I felt confused and disoriented. I had no idea what happened to me. The last memory I had was drinking Mr. Cosby's coffee." She says two security guards drove her home at Cosby's request that same night. "Mr. Cosby's explanation for what happened was that '[I] had too much to drink.' I did not believe him. I had not consumed any alcohol that night," she says. "I believe that Mr. Cosby drugged or sexually assaulted me." The other two accusers, Therese Serignese and Janice Dickinson, say they met Cosby in the '70s or '80s and were sexually assaulted. Allred says Cosby should waive the statute of limitations and set up a $100 million fund for his alleged victims.

– A New Jersey mayor says one of five devices found in a backpack near a train station has exploded as a bomb squad robot was attempting to disarm it, NJ.com reports. Elizabeth Mayor Christian Bollwage says the blast happened around 12:40am Monday as the robot was cutting the device. He says no one was injured in the explosion. The mayor says two men discovered the backpack in a trash can about 300 feet from the train station around 8pm Sunday. He says they took it "because they thought it was of some value" and dropped it after seeing wires and a pipe. New Jersey Transit says service has been suspended on the Northeast Corridor and North Jersey Coastline commuter rail lines. "We apologize to our customers for the inconvenience and will resume service as soon as it is safe to do so," a transit agency spokesman says. The FBI is investigating.

– Mikhail Kalashnikov, the man who designed the AK-47 assault rifle, died last month at age 94, and before that he wrote a letter to the head of the Russian Orthodox Church expressing guilt over the many deaths his weapon caused, the BBC reports. "My spiritual pain is unbearable. I keep having the same unsolved question: if my rifle took away people's lives, then can it be that I, a Christian and an Orthodox believer, was to blame for their deaths?" he wrote in the letter, which was published in a pro-Kremlin newspaper. "The longer I live, the more this question drills itself into my brain and the more I wonder why the Lord allowed man to have the devilish desires of envy, greed, and aggression." Kalashnikov's daughter, Elena, says she believes a priest helped her father write the letter, but it's not clear how much of it he wrote himself, the BBC notes. In 2008, Kalashnikov said it was "painful for me to see when criminal elements of all kinds fire from my weapon." He also blamed the policies of other countries that bought his guns, the AP reports.

Authorities say an individual who met Dishman about five years after his escape told them where to find him, KTHV reports. Dishman was found after police received an anonymous tip. He was taken into custody by local law enforcement and Arkansas State Police.

– In 2013, a 4.7-magnitude earthquake hit near the town of Wind River, Wyo., which is located about 100 miles from the center of the US. The quake was so powerful it registered as the biggest temblor to hit the region in 60 years. Now, a new study published in the journal Earth and Planetary Science Letters suggests the quake was one of the deepest earthquakes ever recorded—one that occurred deep within the Earth's mantle, rather than within its crust, the BBC reports. The study's authors say the quake occurred "well within the mantle, and likely over 20km deeper than the base of the crust." That would make it among the three deepest earthquakes yet identified to have occurred in a region covered by a stable continental crust. It could mean the mantle is brittle. The authors say the quake may have been caused by tectonic forces rather than fluid or magma moving into the Earth's mantle. That could mean the mantle is brittle under the Wind River Craton, and it failed, producing the shock. But that doesn't match our current understanding of the forces needed to deform and break the mantle in such areas, say the researchers, leaving the true cause of the quake open to debate. – The humpback whale is back on the endangered species list, but the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration wants to take 10 of them off it, the Guardian reports. The agency has proposed dividing humpbacks into 14 population segments, and two of those populations—in the Arabian Sea and off Cape Verde and northwest Africa—would remain protected under the US Marine Mammal Protection Act. "As we learn more about the species—and realize the populations are largely independent of each other—managing them separately allows us to focus protection on the animals that need it the most," a NOAA official says. The public has 90 days to comment on the proposal, the AP reports. Humpback whales were listed as endangered in 1970, four years after the International Whaling Commission banned commercial whaling. The whales, which weigh up to 40 tons and can grow up to 60 feet long, have rebounded in the North Pacific since the listing, which requires federal approval for federally funded or authorized activities that could harm whales or their habitat. Last year, the state of Alaska filed a petition to remove some North Pacific humpback whales from protection under the Endangered Species Act. Environmental groups have said North Pacific whales continue to be vulnerable to factors including increased shipping, climate change, and ocean acidification, which affect the prey stock.

– Scott Kelly is on his second and final mission in space, and NASA wants to know what he ate while he was there. The results of the agency's "Twins Study" will be analyzed as he spends a year aboard the International Space Station, reports Space.com. The study has already revealed that Mark Kelly ate less than his twin brother, and the results could shed light on why. Scurvy—a blood infection caused by massive internal hemorrhaging near the brain and heart—often sets in after a few days in space and turns the skin black, reports LiveScience. The infection can be treated with blood transfusions or surgery, but in the case of Scott, the results could be life-saving. "Nutrition is vital to the mission," the manager of NASA's Nutritional Biochemistry Lab tells Space.com. "Without proper nutrition for the astronauts, the mission will fail. It's that simple." Scott and Mark will each provide blood and urine samples during and after their missions, and NASA will compare their results to those of other astronauts on previous missions. The results could help the agency plan for future missions beyond low-Earth orbit, such as a trip to Mars that could last as long as 30 months.

In a recording released yesterday, Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi says al-Qaeda in Iraq has been splitting funds with the Nusra Front, which has become one of the most effective and disciplined rebel formations in the Syrian civil war, the Wall Street Journal reports. Al-Baghdadi says al-Qaeda in Iraq has been sending money to the Nusra Front, which has launched more than 40 successful bombing attacks against government military targets, often using suicide bombers. The merger will be seized on by the Assad regime, which has consistently spun the uprising as a foreign conspiracy relying on terrorists and foreign Jihadist fighters, the Journal notes. Al-Baghdadi's remarks are likely to complicate the arming of Syrian rebels by Gulf powers, the Journal adds. Saudi Arabia and Qatar have increased significantly weapon supplies to brigades affiliated with the Free Syrian Army in the hope that the weapons would shift the balance of the war decisively and quickly in favor of the rebels. – A Los Angeles restaurant is offering customers a 5% discount on their bill if they check their phones at the door. Mark Gold, owner of Eva Restaurant, says distracted diners are a big problem. "It seems like every five minutes there's somebody calling, and it's still going on," he tells KPCC. "I'm guilty of it as well. When [my wife and I] go to dinner it seems like the cell phone is part of the table setting now. Every table you look at, it's a wine glass, the silverware, and the cell phone." So far, he says, "a little less than half" of diners have agreed to take advantage of the deal. "It's really not about people disrupting other guests," he says. "It's about two people sitting together and just connecting, without the distraction of a phone."

– The FAA has extended its ban on US flights to and from Tel Aviv for another 24 hours, after a Hamas rocket slammed into the roof of a building near the city's airport yesterday. The FAA says it's "working closely with the government of Israel to review the significant new information they have provided and determine whether potential risks to US civil aviation are mitigated so the agency can resolve concerns as quickly as possible," CNN reports. The decision came after the FAA banned American airlines from flying to Tel Aviv after a Hamas rocket slammed into the roof of a building near the city's airport yesterday. Lufthansa, Air France, and Germany's two largest airlines, Air Berlin and Lufthansa, have extended their cancelations through tomorrow, the AP reports. The European Aviation Safety Agency has also "strongly recommended" that airlines refrain from flying to and from Tel Aviv.

– The New York Jets have settled a class-action lawsuit brought by cheerleaders who claimed they were paid less than minimum wage, NBC New York reports. According to the New York Daily News, each of the 52 cheerleaders will receive $2,500 for each season they worked for the team. They're also eligible for an additional $400 payment per photo shoot. "When you look at the actual hours worked versus what Krystal was paid, she only made $3.77 per hour," the Daily News quotes a former cheerleader's attorney as saying. "When you factor in the required hair, makeup, and transportation expenses, the hourly rate goes below $1.50 an hour." The lawsuit was filed in 2014 by a woman identified only as Krystal C., who claimed the cheerleaders made only $150 per game and $100 for special event appearances. She also claimed they didn't receive compensation for weekly practices or time spent rehearsing. The Jets "deny the claims and the parties have agreed to a settlement to avoid the expense, time, and distraction of litigation," NBC quotes a joint statement from the team and the cheerleaders as saying. A New York state senator applauded the settlement, calling for the Buffalo Bills to do the same. (The Raiders and Bengals have also settled with their cheerleaders.)
