– The Great Pyramid of Giza, also known as Khufu's Pyramid, is the oldest of the seven wonders of the ancient world. It's also the first major structure discovered in its entirety since the 19th century. Scientists using sensors that detect particles known as muons say they've found a large cavity that extends more than 100 feet below the pyramid's grand gallery. "We know that this big void has the same characteristics as the grand gallery," says Mehdi Tayoubi of the HIP Institute in Paris, per the Guardian. "It's really impressive." The researchers, who found the cavity using a technique known as muon analysis, say they're not sure if it's a chamber or corridor, or whether it's a series of smaller cavities close together. "What we are sure about is that this big void is there, that it is impressive, and was not expected by any kind of theory," says Tayoubi, whose team is developing a tiny flying robot to explore inside the cavity. – Two Denver police officers were injured Friday night when a stolen tractor led police on a high-speed chase through the city, the Denver Post reports. According to KDVR, the tractor was pulling some kind of farm equipment when it was reported stolen from a Denver Water facility. More than a dozen police cars and a helicopter pursued the tractor through downtown Denver. Police say the tractor hit several cars and buildings as it led police on a chase that ended when a police cruiser rammed the tractor head-on. Witnesses say the impact was strong enough to make the police vehicle's airbags deploy. "It could've definitely been a lot worse, for sure," one witness tells Fox 31. The tractor driver was arrested and the two injured officers were treated and released. Police say they did not fire their guns at the tractor.

– The mountains on Oahu in the Hawaiian Islands are dissolving from within under the slow but inexorable onslaught of groundwater, researchers say. Sometime in the distant future the mountainous tropical island will be reduced to a flat, low-lying island similar to Midway, scientists at Brigham Young University reported Friday. While external erosion is the primary force that wears down mountains, that's not the case on Oahu, they said. "We tried to figure out how fast the island is going away and what the influence of climate is on that rate," BYU geologist Steve Nelson says. "More material is dissolving from those islands than what is being carried off through erosion." That was the result from comparing groundwater against stream water to see which removed more of the total quantity of mineral material mass that disappeared from the island each year, the researchers say. "All of the Hawaiian Islands are made of just one kind of rock," Nelson says, referring to the volcanic composition of the islands. "The weathering rates are variable, too, because rainfall is so variable, so it's a great natural laboratory." While Oahu is at present still growing, after about 1.5 million years the force of groundwater will eventually triumph and the island will begin its descent to a low-lying topography, the researchers say

– The Supreme Court wrestled with the future of the 1965 Voting Rights Act today, with its more conservative justices appearing to tip the balance in favor of striking down a key part of the law. If the law is struck down, nine states, mostly in the South, would no longer need to get permission from the federal government before changing their voting procedures. The justices heard 90 minutes of arguments, with the New York Times noting that the "sharpest exchange" took place when Sonia Sotomayor asked a lawyer challenging the law, "Do you think that the right to vote is a racial entitlement?" Justice Antonin Scalia responded that the law amounted to a "perpetuation of racial entitlement." The court's liberal justices, however, argued that Congress had the right to use a formula to determine which states and localities should remain subject to the law. "It’s an old disease," said Stephen Breyer. "It’s gotten a lot better. A lot better. But it’s still there." If the law is struck down, it would make it easier for Republicans in the nine states to enact their own voting rules, including tougher identification standards.

– The 29th Ig Nobel Prize ceremony is scheduled for Sept. 12 in Cambridge, Mass., and this year's winners have been announced. The prizes, organized by the magazine Annals of Improbable Research, are "intended to celebrate the unusual, honor the imaginative—and spur people's interest in science, medicine, and technology," per the Ig Nobel website. This year's winners, who will be presented with their prizes in a short ceremony that lasts just 60 seconds, include a team that determined that the shape of the human heart can be altered to make it more or less efficient at converting lactic acid into oxygen, reports NPR. The team's findings were published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology. The two runners-up: a team that determined that the shape of the human hand can be altered to make it more or less efficient at converting lactic acid into oxygen, and a team that determined that the shape of the human fist can be altered to make it more or less efficient at converting lactic acid into oxygen. The full list of this year's winners is here. (This year's Ig Nobel winner was the first woman to win.)

– Armed police and members of the military will be patrolling the streets of London over the next few days in the wake of Friday's Parsons Green subway bombing, Prime Minister Theresa May says. "For this period, military personnel will replace police officers on guard duties at certain protected sites that are not accessible to the public," she says, per the Guardian. "The public will see more armed police on the transport network and on our streets, providing extra protection. This is a proportionate and sensible step which will provide extra reassurance and protection while the investigation progresses." May says the UK terror threat level has been raised from severe to critical, indicating a further attack may be imminent, the BBC reports. Police say 29 people, including a child, were injured when a bomb partially detonated on a train at the busy station in west London. The bomb was packed in a white plastic bucket inside a Lidl supermarket bag, and the train is believed to have had onboard CCTV, and there are a large number of cameras covering the network. Islamic State claimed responsibility for the blast, the militant group's Amaq news agency said on Friday evening. Nobody suffered life-threatening injuries in the incident, the fifth terrorist attack Britain has suffered in less than six months. May condemned the attack as cowardly

Now Facebook users are calling for a boycott of the airline. The "Boycott Spirit Airlines" Facebook page has more than 18,000 likes as of this writing. It was started in 2010 when the airline announced it would start charging for checked luggage, and it has gained support from current military members and veterans. "I believe Spirit Airlines owes a debt to the Veteran and an apology," writes one commenter. "Being a good corporate citizen seems not to be in their culture. I will not fly them because of this. I am a proud US Navy Veteran." Another adds, "I will not fly them because of this. I am a proud US Navy Veteran." Spirit Airlines is also in the news for a new carry-on fee that starts Nov. 6.

– Police in Neustadt, Germany, are asking for the public's help in finding out who stole a trailer that contained more than 20 tons of chocolate, including Nutella, Kinder Surprise eggs, and other treats worth up to $80,000, NPR reports. "Anyone offered large quantities of chocolate via unconventional channels should report it to the police immediately," Neustadt police said in a statement. A police spokesman tells a German newspaper that the thieves would have needed a truck of their own to tow the refrigerated trailer, which was taken sometime between Saturday evening and Sunday afternoon, Deutsche Welle reports. Police are also looking into whether the theft of an empty trailer in Weimar, which was also stolen at the weekend, had any link to the Nutella theft. (Police in Schleswig-Holstein last week announced they were looking for 53g of chocolate believed to have been stolen.)

– An Air Algerie flight carrying 116 passengers and six crew has crashed in a remote part of Mali, reports the AP. The plane, an MD-83 owned by Spanish company Swiftair, took off from the Burkina Faso capital of Ouagadougou at 11:27am local time and was supposed to arrive in Algiers at 5pm local time. Instead, it vanished from radar about an hour after takeoff. "Everything must be done to find this plane," French President Francois Hollande told reporters. "We cannot identify the causes of what happened." He said France would use all military means to find the wreckage. The area where the plane is believed to have crashed is largely controlled by Tuareg separatist rebels, who briefly seized the northern Mali city of Gao last year, Reuters reports.

In the first, a 21-year-old student at Mississippi State University was shot in a dorm Saturday night. Three suspects fled the scene in a blue Crown Victoria, and police are still looking for them. In the second, a 19-year-old freshman at Jackson State University was shot in the face and killed at an off-campus apartment pool party. Details of what happened are sketchy, and no arrests have been made.

– Police say a 37-year-old man was far from lovin' it when workers at a McDonald's restaurant in Oregon refused to make him 30 double cheeseburgers and tried to destroy the golden arches, the AP reports. The News-Review reports that police arrested Jedediah Ezekiel Fulton on March 16 on suspicion of second-degree disorderly conduct, second-degree criminal trespass, second-degree criminal mischief, and harassment. Authorities say Fulton became upset when the fast food restaurant in the western Oregon town of Sutherlin declined to make his order. Police say he destroyed a banner and then attacked the arches. The Sutherlin Police Department says he also grabbed a person's shirt and that a witness afraid for that person's life pulled out a gun.

– A 4-year-old California girl may have saved the day for her mom, police say. When her mom saw an intruder enter her home through an unlocked door Monday night, she fled with her baby in tow—but left her little girl behind, police say. The girl went outside and told her mom that the intruder was in her closet, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. Police found the girl at the top of the stairs, but there was no sign of the intruder. The girl told her mom that her closet was where the suspect, 21-year-old Demaria Lopez, was hiding, police say. When officers went to check the girl's bedroom, they found Lopez hiding in the closet, but he wouldn't comply with their commands, police say. He was arrested and charged with burglary and resisting arrest.

– President Obama made a surprise appearance in the White House briefing room today to address the Trayvon Martin shooting and the acquittal of George Zimmerman, reports USA Today. "Trayvon Martin could have been me 35 years ago," said Obama. "And when you think about why, in the African-American community at least, there’s a lot of pain around what happened here, I think it’s important to recognize that the African-American community is looking at this issue through a set of experiences and a history that—that doesn’t go away." Obama spoke of his own experiences as a black man and of his daughters. "There are very few African-American men who haven’t had the experience of being followed in a department store. That includes me," he said. "And it's inescapable for people to bring those experiences to bear." Obama also said that "as difficult and challenging as this episode has been, things are getting better," reports the Washington Post.

– The FDA is proposing a ban on the use of indoor tanning beds for kids under 18. The agency says the move would help protect teens from the "known and preventable cause of skin cancer and other harms," reports USA Today. The ban would apply to beds and sun lamps, which can cause burns and eye damage, and would require users over 18 to sign a "risk acknowledgement" saying they had been made aware of the risks. The agency also wants tanning facility operators to have emergency shut-offs or "panic buttons" on the devices to reduce the risk of burns. The proposal is here.

– The annual A Capitol Fourth Fourth fireworks show in Washington, DC, was supposed to be live Monday night on PBS, but it turned out to be a bit of a mess. Viewers complained on social media that footage from previous years' shows had been spliced into this year's show, which was supposed to be held on the National Mall, NBC News reports. "Only in DC could a PBS show become a scandal," tweeted one viewer. "How is using stock video patriotic? If I wanted that, I'd watch YouTube," added another. The show's Facebook and Twitter pages later acknowledged that the footage had been cut from previous years' shows. "We showed a combination of the best fireworks from this year and previous years. It was the patriotic thing to do," the show tweeted. "Only in DC could a PBS show become a scandal." PBS didn't immediately return NBC's calls for comment. A Capitol Fourth host Tom Bergeron told the Washington Post before the show that he wasn't worried about the weather. "We've only had six tornado warnings," he said. "Everything else gets me here."

– Scotland Yard is "scoping" new information about the deaths of Princess Diana and Dodi Al Fayed and is "assessing its relevance and credibility," the BBC reports. The Metropolitan Police says it is not reopening the investigation into the 1997 car crash in Paris, which was ruled an accident by an inquest in 2008. The information is said to have been passed to police by an Army source, according to several British newspapers. The Metropolitan Police says it will "not discuss the source of the information" it is assessing, but Mohamed Al Fayed, Dodi's father, says he will be "interested in seeing the outcome."

– If you live in New York's Westchester, Rockland, or Putnam counties, you may have noticed that the Journal News has published the names and addresses of every licensed pistol permit holder in the area. The newspaper did so as part of a series of stories on gun control that ran last week, Talking Points Memo reports. The stories included a map created by the Talk of the Sound blog that showed the addresses of every Journal News employee in the tri-state area. The map has since been taken down, but you can see the full list of names and addresses here. The story that prompted the map was a piece on gun control by reporter Dwight Worley, who wrote that he was "troubled" by the map's invasion of privacy, the New York Daily News reports. He said he was "shocked" by the map's invasion of privacy, but added that he had no choice after the newspaper refused to remove the map. The Journal News, which is owned by the Gannett company, says the story was based on public records and that it had no choice but to publish the map. "We felt it was important to inform our readers and the community about the important role licensed gun owners play in our communities," the paper said in a statement.

– A toxin produced by a common foodborne bacteria may be linked to multiple sclerosis, according to researchers at Weill Cornell Medical College. The toxin, produced by Clostridium perfringens, is responsible for a million cases of food poisoning in the US each year, reports the Los Angeles Times. "What we've shown is the toxins target the cells that are targeted in MS," says a researcher, who presented her findings yesterday at a meeting of the American Society for Microbiology. "To me, if you were going to design a trigger for this disease, this would really fit the mold really well," says a National Multiple Sclerosis Society official. The researchers found that 13% of a small sample of food products they tested contained the toxin epsilon, and nearly 3% of the samples were positive for it. They also found that MS patients were 10 times more likely to have antibodies signaling they'd previously been exposed to the toxin. If the link is confirmed, it could lead to a vaccine or drug, or a probiotic treatment.

– An 11-year-old boy with autism was found dead in his family's home in Los Angeles last month, and authorities say he had been kept in a closet for years, the Los Angeles Times reports. According to CBS Los Angeles, the boy, Yonatan Daniel Aguilar, was often sedated with liquid sleep medication to keep him quiet. The boy's mother, 39-year-old Veronica Aguilar, has been charged with murder and child abuse causing death. Yonatan's stepfather, Jose Pinzon, says he didn't know the boy was living in the family's home. Aguilar told Pinzon Yonatan had died three years ago and sent him to Mexico to live with family, but he didn't know he was still living in the family home. Aguilar told Pinzon Yonatan was living in the closet because he was hoarding food. Aguilar allegedly kept Yonatan in the closet for three years and sedated him with liquid sleep medication to keep him quiet. Yonatan was found dead in the closet on Aug. 22. He weighed just 34 pounds and was covered in pressure sores. Aguilar allegedly told Pinzon Yonatan had died. He ran to a 7-Eleven and called police. – The man who hijacked an EgyptAir flight Tuesday and forced it to land in Cyprus has asked to be extradited from Egypt to face charges including air piracy, kidnapping, and threatening behavior, the BBC reports. Seif al-Din Mustafa appeared in court in Cyprus on Tuesday and gave a victory sign as he was driven away by police. The hijacking is believed to have been motivated by a row between Mustafa, 58, and his ex-wife, who lives in Cyprus. Cypriot authorities have said the hijacking was not terrorism-related. As more became known about the motive of the 59-year-old Egyptian who was taken into custody, authorities characterized the commandeering of the EgyptAir jetliner not as an act of terrorism but more like a "family feud" with his former wife. The aviation drama ended peacefully on the tarmac of Larnaca airport on the island nation's southern coast with the surrender of a man identified by Cypriot and Egyptian authorities as Seif Eddin Mustafa. The incident was likely to renew concerns about Egyptian airlines and airport security. CCTV footage released by the interior ministry shows Mustafa being frisked at two security checks and passing a slim bag through X-ray machines at Alexandria's Borg El Arab airport. – It's official: Florida has surpassed New York in population to become the third-most populous state in the nation, the AP reports. Figures released today by the US Census Bureau show that Florida has at least 19.9 million residents. The number is likely higher because the Census uses the population as of July 1 to create its estimate. New York had 19.7 million residents. Florida added almost 300,000 new residents from 2013 to 2014, or a little more than 800 new residents a day. By contrast, New York grew by only 51,000 over that time period. Florida likely reached the milestone sometime last spring, but it wasn't official until the Census said so. An AP analysis earlier this year showed that ex-New Yorkers represented about 1 in 10 new Florida residents. Migrants from other countries made up about a quarter of Florida's new residents. Florida has a way to go before it catches up with California and Texas, the largest and second-largest states. California has 38.8 million residents; Texas has 27 million residents. The other states rounding out the 10 largest in the nation are: Illinois, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Georgia, North Carolina, and Michigan. North Carolina slipped by Michigan for the ninth spot on the list. – A 19-year-old gunman who stormed the headquarters of Dutch national broadcaster NOS last night claimed to be from a "hackers' collective," according to a reporter who spoke to the man. The AP reports that NOS was off-air for around an hour. When it came back, it showed recorded footage of the young man, wearing a black suit, white shirt, and black tie, and carrying a pistol. Speaking calmly to someone off-camera, the man said, "We are hired in by intelligence agencies." Shortly after, police arrived with their guns drawn and ordered the man to drop his weapon and put his hands up. At least five police officers then ordered him to turn around and lie down, which he did and he was arrested without a struggle. Police said in a statement the man demanded airtime and threatened that bombs would go off at several locations around the Netherlands if his demand wasn't met. Nobody was injured and there were no reports of shots being fired. The suspect's name wasn't released by the prosecutor. Officials said they were still investigating the man's background and the seriousness of the threat he posed. "There is a major investigation underway to get clarity as quickly as possible about what happened here tonight," Bac said.

– Authorities say a man saw a doll inside a parked truck and called police about an unresponsive infant, leading to the recovery of stolen truck and real baby, the AP reports. Lumberton Police Department Capt. Terry Parker tells the Fayetteville Observer that a woman reported her pickup truck stolen and 3-week-old baby missing Monday. Parker says the woman was taking two other children inside a house when someone stole the vehicle and baby inside it. Police issued an alert, and Parker says the truck and baby were abandoned in a nearby parking lot minutes later. He says a man walking past the truck noticed a window was down and peered inside. Parker says the man saw a doll lying on the floor and called police. Parker says no arrests were made as of Tuesday.

– Customs officials at Los Angeles International Airport recently made a pretty big find: 67 live giant African snails. The mollusks, which can grow to be 8 inches long and live up to 10 years in the wild, arrived from Lagos, Nigeria, in two plastic baskets marked "for human consumption," CBS Los Angeles reports. They were headed for San Dimas, Calif., about 30 miles east of Los Angeles. Customs and Border Protection says the snails are a serious threat to US agriculture, the environment, and public health, Reuters reports. They can consume more than 500 types of plants, and will even eat paint and stucco off houses. They can carry several parasites that are harmful to humans, one of which can lead to meningitis. "It exemplifies how CBP agriculture specialists protect our nation's agriculture from the introduction of threatening foreign pests, plants, and diseases," says a CBP official.

– A Tennessee state senator has apologized for a joke he posted on his personal blog about the "evil" and "large-capacity" pressure cooker used in the Boston Marathon bombing. State Sen. Stacey Campfield's post, titled "Here comes Feinstein again," showed a pressure cooker with various parts labeled as weapons, the Raw Story reports. Campfield tells WVLT that he didn't mean to offend, but he added, "I say it's insensitive that people go after guns and Second Amendment rights after the Sandy Hook shooting." "If my post was inappropriate talking about 'crock pot control' then where is the outrage from the left when they push for gun control after the Sandy Hook shooting?" he wrote in a follow-up post. "Im [sic] sorry if I exposed your double standard.... Well, not really." Campfield has been in the news before for controversial comments. Earlier this month, he told TMZ that the "homosexual community gets AIDS at a 50 times higher rate than the heterosexual community." He also compared homosexuality to "shooting heroin."

– Two dogs in the Flint, Mich., area have tested positive for lead toxicity, the first such cases in the state in five years, reports the Detroit Free Press. One was a pet and the other a stray, and both are still alive. It's not clear whether the dogs were drinking the city's tap water or if they were poisoned by the water themselves. The state veterinarian says there's no regular testing for lead in dogs, but they are at a higher risk than other mammals for lead poisoning. “Dogs are at a higher risk amongst mammals for finding high lead levels, but it’s not that common," he tells CBS Detroit. "Typically for us when we deal with lead toxicity, we’re usually dealing with cattle. So, really this was a new instance for us." The state is advising people in Flint to get their water tested and to filter the water out of their pets' water.

– It's been more than 40 years since a back-of-the-envelope calculation was made of the world's groundwater, but a new study offers the first global estimate of how much we have and when it will run out. The study, published in Nature Geoscience, estimates that less than 6% of groundwater in the upper two kilometers of the Earth's landmass is renewable within a human lifetime. "This has never been known before," says the lead author from Canada's University of Victoria. "We're using our groundwater resources too fast—faster than they're being renewed." Modern groundwater is closer to the surface and is more renewable, but it's also more vulnerable to climate change and can contain arsenic and uranium, reports the Guardian. Most groundwater is found in mountainous areas and in tropical and mountainous regions, including the Amazon Basin, the Congo, Indonesia, and along the western borders of North and South America. The least amount is in arid regions such as the Sahara, reports the Thomson Reuters Foundation. (Click to read about how groundwater is becoming more important as the planet continues to warm.)

– A severed foot found in a boot at the base of Colorado's Eldora Mountain Resort in June didn't belong to a missing ski resort employee, the Boulder County Coroner's Office said Friday. The foot was identified as belonging to a 21-year-old man who went missing in January, the Daily Camera reports. Ryder Johnson was last seen leaving his job at the ski resort on Jan. 17, and his car was found later that day in a parking lot more than 20 miles from where he was last seen. Investigators say it's likely Johnson disappeared on his own. His father, Richard Johnson, is offering $100,000 for information that leads to an arrest in his son's disappearance. "Justice needs to be served, and I think it's time to bring him home," Richard Johnson says.

– On July 23, 1992, Morrad Ghonim's 17-year-old wife, Vicki, was shot in the head as the couple drove away from a park in La Mirada, Calif., with their 6-month-old son in the back seat. The night before, Ghonim, then a 19-year-old widower, had taken Vicki to the park to spend time with her and the couple's son, reports the Los Angeles Times. But when they arrived, Ghonim says he heard a group of people catcall Vicki, thought they were gang members, and ushered his family toward their car. As they settled in, he heard gunfire. The shooter had been hiding behind bushes, Ghonim said, so he never got a look at who had attacked his wife. The investigation went cold, and Ghonim fell out of touch with Vicki's family. But about a decade ago, the LA County Sheriff's Department received grant money to reopen old cases and look at DNA evidence. Leon Martinez, who was serving time for burglary at the time of Vicki Ghonim's murder, eventually admitted to shooting Vicki and told detectives he was Ghonim's hired hit man. "I was, like, 'Yo, this doesn't sound like anything that's in my life, anything that's me,'" the Pulitzer Prize-winning author says. Daz, who says he's "deeply sorry" for what he calls a "terrible mistake," says he's keeping his teaching job at MIT and his editing position at the Boston Review, despite investigations by the Review that found the accusations were not "the kind of severity that animated the #MeToo movement." – An Alabama man who posted videos of himself threatening to run over, run over, and run over a bunch of bicycle riders has been arrested and charged with reckless endangerment, reports the Anniston Star. "See what I was talking about?" Keith Maddox says in one video. "Look there! Look right there. I ought to run him in the ditch. Ride your little bicycle!" In another, he says, "Lord have mercy, I’m gonna hurt one of them one of these days. Can’t help myself, I’m gonna do it." The videos were discovered by cycling enthusiast groups online, who alerted the Calhoun County Sheriff's office to Maddox's threats. They arrested him and charged him with reckless endangerment, a misdemeanor charge, and released him on $3,000 bond. Maddox asked for forgiveness on his Facebook page with a note—since taken down—in which he apologized "to all people that I have offended over those absolute stupid videos that I posted ...anybody who knows me knows that I would never ever intensionally [sic] hurt anyone...those were in very bad taste and I especially want to apologize to the northeast Alabama bicycle association...I am truly sorry for Anyone I may have offended....and please everyone share the road and

– A new study says children living near the Fukushima nuclear meltdowns have been diagnosed with thyroid cancer at a rate 20 to 50 times that of children elsewhere, a difference the authors contend undermines the government's position that more cases have been discovered in the area only because of stringent monitoring. "This is 20 times to 50 times what would be normally expected," lead author Toshihide Tsuda tells the AP. The most recent statistics, released in August, show that thyroid cancer is suspected or confirmed in 137 of those children, a number that rose by 25 from a year earlier. Elsewhere, the disease occurs in only about one or two of every million children per year by some estimates. "This is more than expected and emerging faster than expected," Tsuda says. "This is 20 times to 50 times what would be normally expected." The study was released online this week and is being published in the November issue of Epidemiology, produced by the Herndon, Va.-based International Society for Environmental Epidemiology. The data comes from tests overseen by Fukushima Medical University. – The World Cup will not ban the annoying vuvuzela, despite complaints from players and fans. A World Cup spokesman insists the plastic horn is "ingrained in the history of South Africa" and will remain, the BBC reports. "Let us not make this a South Africa instrument alone," he says. "A vuvuzela is now an international instrument. People buy them and stuff them in their suitcase to go home." England defender Jamie Carragher says he bought two to take home to his children. "We in South Africa love them," he says. "You either love them or hate. We in South Africa love them."

– A 63-year-old deaf and mute man was held captive in the basement of a Philadelphia home for months, deprived of food and forced to urinate in a bucket, police say. The man was found locked inside the basement of a Southwest Philadelphia home on Sunday, CBS Philadelphia reports. Family members say the man was held captive by acquaintance Dwayne Young, 56, who cashed his victim's Social Security checks. "He was physically abused. No scars, but the body was being beaten," the man's brother says. "He said he was getting no food and he was urinating in a bucket." Police say the man was held against his will after he was abducted in April. The victim's cousin and caretaker, 46-year-old Regina Bennett, has been charged with terroristic threats, simple assault, public drunkenness, aggravated assault, unlawful restraint, false imprisonment, and related offenses. Police say they found the man in "unsuitable conditions" after responding to an "ongoing neighborhood dispute" at Bennett's home Friday night. – Police say a Pennsylvania man applying to become a state trooper has been arrested after saying during a polygraph pretest that he had sex with an underage girl four years ago, the AP reports. State police say 29-year-old Joseph Adam White, of Hartstown, was at the Meadville barracks Jan. 15 for his police cadet lie detector exam. They say during the pretest, he told the examiner he had consensual sex and other contact with the girl in 2011. She is now 19. Police say they charged White on Thursday with four counts of unlawful sexual contact with a minor and 10 counts of corruption of minors after interviewing the woman and corroborating that information. Needless to say, he won't be getting an interview.

– Prince William and wife Kate have released the third official portrait of Prince George ahead of a three-week tour of New Zealand and Australia. The image, taken by royal christening photographer Jason Bell, shows the 8-month-old in his mother's arms as William holds the family pet, Lupo, through an open window of Kensington Palace, the BBC reports. The family will be in New Zealand from April 7 to 25 and Australia from April 16 to 25. "George being just a little over eight-months-old by the time they travel, I'm sure you will appreciate that the couple will have to make a final decision on those moments much closer to the time," a palace spokesman tells CNN.

– A medieval well believed to have been used by religious pilgrims to wash away sins and heal diseases has been found buried on a private farm near Liverpool, England, the Telegraph reports. According to legend, the well was built to honor St. Anne, the supposed mother of the Virgin Mary, who was a cult leader in Britain during the late Medieval Period. The well was said to have been cursed, the Independent reports. "This well was probably a late Medieval foundation as the cult of St. Anne did not become widespread in England until after the end of the 14th century," archaeologist Jamie Quartermaine tells Seeker. The well was found with little to no sign of it on the surface, but archaeologists were able to identify it thanks to photos taken in 1983. The well had been on the Heritage at Risk Register since 2010, and was "clearly in need of help," a spokesperson for Historic England says. After two days of digging, archaeologists were able to replace stones that had fallen into the well, as well as install new wooden edging to protect it from damage from farm machinery. St. Anne's Well is now on course to be removed from the Heritage at Risk Register. (Click to read about more medieval wells.)

– Michael Phelps will be swimming in his fifth Olympics next month in Rio, and if he wins one of the three individual races he's entered—the 200-meter butterfly, 200-meter individual medley, and 100-meter butterfly—he'll become the oldest person ever to win an individual gold medal at the Olympics, USA Today reports. Dutch swimmer Inge de Bruijn won the 50-meter freestyle at the 2004 Games in Athens at the age of 31—three days before her birthday. If Phelps wins one of those three races, he'll also tie Mark Spitz's record of seven golds in a single Games. Bleacher Report looks back at Phelps' four previous Olympic appearances, including his first in Sydney at the age of 15.

– A 27-year-old man who allegedly set off a pipe bomb strapped to his body in a crowded New York City subway tunnel Monday has been identified as Akayed Ullah, a Bangladeshi immigrant who came to the US in 2011, the New York Times reports. According to the Washington Post, Ullah reportedly told investigators he was inspired by ISIS propaganda. Ullah suffered burns and cuts to his hands and abdomen in the attack, which did not cause any major injuries to commuters. Three people suffered minor injuries. Ullah reportedly entered the US on a visa that allows relatives of US citizens to come to the US for up to five years. He reportedly told investigators he came to the US to fight for ISIS. The FBI is investigating the attack, and federal charges are expected soon.

– Verizon's new "Share Everything" data plan is here, and it's going to change the way we use our smartphones and tablets. Under the plan, which goes into effect June 28, each device on a family plan will draw from the same data pool, meaning each member of the family will pay the same price for the same amount of data, CNET reports. The move is designed to make it easier for families to share devices, but it's also designed to increase revenue for Verizon. "Individual consumers, on average, use about 2.2GB of data a month on their smartphones. Under many contracts, such as AT&T’s 3GB for $30, they are paying for data they do not use. In the new Verizon system, those users would be punished for going over their 2GB allowance," writes Darren Murph at CNET. "In the old family plan, a company like Verizon would measure average revenue per user (ARPU). In the shared data plan scenario, the measurement structure changes. The family, instead of being measured as a group of individuals, becomes a unit. When taken as a unit, an individual’s excess data use gets rolled into a lump sum without damaging (or theoretically, enhancing) Verizon’s ARPU."

House Bill 1456 would make it a misdemeanor for a physician to perform an abortion based on gender or genetic abnormalities, and House Bill 1456 would make it a felony for a physician who willingly performs an abortion after the detection of a heartbeat. The bills are headed to the governor's desk, and if Gov. Jack Dalrymple signs them, they would make North Dakota the first state to ban abortions after a heartbeat is detected, as early as six weeks after conception. Arkansas already has a ban on abortions after 12 weeks, and the North Dakota bill would make it even tougher. "The time has come to choose life," said Sen. Spencer Berry, who spoke briefly in favor of the bill. The debate included emotional appeals and personal stories from senators, as well as a brief delay during floor votes on two divided portions of the bill when a Democratic member of the Senate left the chamber. "We started a story on her," Graydon Carter says. "We have a very good writer and it'll run." Paltrow had reportedly warned her pals not to talk to Vanity Fair about her, and the editor-in-chief says she "sort of forced my hand" by going public with her concerns. – US workers have been largely insulated from a global slowdown. Job growth remains steady and wages are finally picking up— trends that will be put to the test in Friday's employment report for February, the AP reports. Economists have forecast that employers added a solid 195,000 jobs last month, up from the 151,000 added in January, according to data firm FactSet. And the unemployment rate is expected to remain at a low 4.9%. Hiring by construction companies, retailers, and health care providers have offset layoffs at manufacturers and fossil fuel companies—two sectors squeezed by the pressures of uncertainty in China, sluggishness in Europe, declining oil prices, and a stronger dollar. Consumers have provided the foundation for much of the job market's improvement in what's become something of a self-sustaining cycle. The 2.7 million workers hired in the past 12 months have bolstered spending on autos, housing, and meals out. As unemployment has dropped, more companies have begun to raise pay to attract workers, thereby fueling more hiring as people's ability to spend, invest, and save has increased. – NBC has fired the person who posted footage from a 1994 Today show in which Bryant Gumbel and Katie Couric try to figure out the Internet. The clip, which can be seen here, made the rounds on the Internet last week, and was even featured on the Today show itself. "The individual in question violated the company's standards of conduct by repeatedly copying and distributing a variety of materials without permission," NBC said in a statement. PaidContent points out that the clip is funny and interesting, and reminds us of what Gumbel and Couric used to look like. But there are lots and lots of companies that fire people for distributing things on the Internet that aren't supposed to be distributed on the Internet, writes Andrew Wallenstein.

– Mitt Romney's campaign is pretty happy with the decision by Nevada to move its caucuses up a week, but New Hampshire's secretary of state is threatening to move the state's primary up as well, the New York Times reports. New Hampshire law requires the state's primary to be held before any other, but not necessarily a caucus, and there's a week between the primary and the next nomination contest. Secretary of State Bill Gardner says he's considering moving the primary to Dec. 6 or Dec. 13. That would leave New Hampshire as "something of an orphan" on the calendar, and leave a four-week gap between the Iowa caucuses on Jan. 3 and the New Hampshire primary on Dec. 6, which would be too close to the Christmas holiday. "The news media, annoyed that the earlier date would require them to revisit their own plans for the campaign, might be happy to play along," writes Chris Cillizza in the Washington Post. "Fortunately for Mr. Romney, there is a relatively elegant solution to this problem."

– A sterilization drive in central India ended in tragedy last week when 10 women died and another 69 were hospitalized after the surgeon used infected instruments to sterilize 83 women in just six hours, reports the AP. The state's chief minister calls the incident "a case of negligence" and says the surgeon broke guidelines that limit surgeons to performing no more than 30 sterilizations a day. The director of the Reproductive Rights Initiative at Human Rights Law Network in New Delhi calls it "an exceptional case which unfortunately happens once every four or five years." India has the world's third-highest female sterilization rate after the Dominican Republic and Puerto Rico. "It's so commonplace in India for women to suffer these surgeries" under poor conditions, she says. Four women were still in critical condition after the Nov. 8 surgeries, according to Amar Singh Thakur, chief health officer for Bilaspur district. "The deaths were due to infection causing septic shock," Thakur says. "We are investigating but it is too early to say that it was due sterilization." Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Chhattisgarh's leader to ensure a "thorough investigation and action" on the "unfortunate tragedy," his office tweeted.

– The Episcopal Church today joined the Presbyterian Church (USA) and the United Church of Christ in performing same-sex marriage ceremonies. The church's House of Deputies, the voting body of clergy and lay participants at its General Convention, voted 184-23 to approve a new liturgy that will allow parishes to offer "trial" ceremonies for same-sex marriages where they are legal, the AP reports. The church also voted 173 to 27 to approve changes to its canon that will redefine marriage as being between two people instead of a man and a woman. The Episcopal Church voted in 1976 that gays and lesbians were "a full and equal claim with all other persons upon the love, acceptance, and pastoral concern and care of the (c)hurch." But the Rev. José Luis Mendoza from Honduras opposed the move, saying it would cause schism in the church. "This resolution goes against the biblical principles of our church," he said. "Don't be seduced by the fashion of society." The Episcopal Church voted just days after the US Supreme Court legalized gay marriage nationwide.

– The "Occupy" protests sweeping Spain have turned into a global phenomenon, with tens of thousands taking to the streets in dozens of cities across the country, reports the Guardian. Protesters—many of whom have camped out in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square—say they're fed up with austerity measures and political corruption. "We want real democracy. Not just freedom bankers. You're not from the Spanish press, are you? We don't speak to them," one protester tells the Guardian. "We want change as a whole. Things just can't carry on as they are," says another. "I was sacked when the Madrid regional government closed down a women's center last year when it imposed cuts," says another protester. "The unions didn't even bother to turn up." The protests are a major challenge to Spain's Socialist government, which has slashed public spending and hiked taxes in the face of a recession that has left the country with a 21% unemployment rate, the highest in Europe. "This is the first time in history that the world has seen such a large number of people at the same time taking to the streets," says the president of the International Monetary Fund.

– The man accused of murdering a Tennessee woman and her teenage daughter and kidnapping her two younger daughters has been added to the FBI's Ten Most Wanted fugitives list. "We will hunt down Adam Mayes and rescue those two little girls," said an FBI agent at a press conference. Adam Mayes, 35, and his wife Teresa, 31, have been charged with first-degree murder and especially aggravated kidnapping in the deaths of Jo Ann Bain and her 14-year-old daughter, Adrienne. Teresa Mayes told police she witnessed Adam kill JoAnn Bain in the garage of the Bain home in Hardeman County, Tenn., and then kill Adrienne in the home itself, according to court documents obtained by the AP. Adam and Teresa Mayes then took the bodies and items from the Bain home to their home in Mississippi, where they buried them, the documents state. The bodies of Jo Ann and her daughter were found buried in the backyard of the Mayes' home this week. Adam and Teresa Mayes have also been charged with unlawful flight to avoid prosecution, a federal crime which gave the FBI jurisdiction in the case. The FBI is offering a $71,000 reward for information leading to Adam Mayes' whereabouts and arrest.

Panama disease, for instance, wiped out 90% of bananas in the Central American country in the 1870s and 1880s, the Washington Post reports. Now, a new study published in the journal PLoS Pathog finds that banana varieties developed over the years are genetically identical to one another—and that's not a good thing. The study's lead author, a professor of plant pathology at Wageningen University in the Netherlands, tells the Post that banana varieties developed over the years "have a lot in common with each other," but "when you have a lot in common with a disease, you have a lot in common with that disease." That's why it's so alarming that researchers are working to develop banana varieties that are resistant to Panama disease, the Post reports. According to the study, the only way to stop the disease from spreading is to develop new banana varieties that are resistant to it. Researchers are already working on that, but it could take years to develop new banana varieties that are resistant to the fungus that causes Panama disease, Phys.org reports. – For the fourth year in a row, the 1994 Honda Accord is the most stolen car in the US, according to the National Insurance Crime Bureau's annual "Hot Wheels" report. The popularity of the Accord—and its lack of security features—is one of the main reasons it's so often stolen, the Christian Science Monitor reports. In 1997, Honda began equipping its vehicles with immobilizer systems, preventing them from running unless the driver had the key. In second place was the 1998 Honda Civic, followed by the 2006 Ford F-150, the first full-size pickup to make the list since the NICB began tracking thefts in 2000. Two other full-size pickups, the 1999 Chevrolet pickup and the 2004 Dodge pickup, came in at spots number seven and eight, respectively. The most stolen car of 2011 was the 1991 Toyota Camry, followed by the 1994 Acura Integra and the 1994 Nissan Sentra. The Dodge Caravan was the fifth most stolen vehicle.

– The body of a headless sphinx unearthed from the desert set of Cecil B. DeMille's The Ten Commandments will be unveiled Friday at a gala in California, the San Luis Obispo Tribune reports. The 1923 silent film was shot in Guadalupe's Guadalupe-Nipomo Dunes, and DeMille left the set there after filming ended. It's not clear what he did with it, but the center that now houses it has a number of photos from the film and a $120,000 excavation project to thank, the Los Angeles Times reports. The sphinx's unveiling is at the Guadalupe-Nipomo Dunes Center, which is also hosting a new exhibit that includes other artifacts from the film. The sphinx is 1012-foot long and was custom-made for the movie.

Police in Evansville say they found the video on the phone of Michael Barnes, who was arrested Thursday after agreeing to sell a handgun to an undercover officer. In the video, the baby is seen putting the muzzle of the gun in her mouth. "At no point does Barnes try to stop the child from playing with the gun," police say. The child's mother, 22-year-old Toni Wilson, was also present in the video and was charged with child neglect, criminal recklessness with a deadly weapon, and allowing a child to possess a firearm, police say. The couple's 1-month-old twins were removed from the home and placed in emergency care, NBC News reports. Barnes, who was wanted for armed robbery, was charged with resisting law enforcement with a weapon, carrying a handgun without a permit, and carrying a handgun without a permit within 500 feet of a school after his arrest.

– When it comes to the weight of all life on Earth, humans are about one-thousandth of the weight of all animals, according to a first-of-its-kind global census of the footprint of life. Humans only add up to about one-thousandth of the life on Earth, measured by the dry weight of the carbon that makes up the structure of all living things, also known as biomass. The planet's real plants outweigh all other kingdom of life by about 80%. Plants make up 450 gigatons of carbon, followed by bacteria at 70 GT C and fungi at 12 GT C, scientists report in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Animals comprise a mere 2 GT C, of which half are arthropods—including insects, spiders, and crustaceans. And although humans weigh in at just 0.06 GT C—on par with krill and termites—our impact on biomass has been huge, scientists say. Humans have also had an impact on plant biomass, which has been cut half in the past 10,000 years. To figure out the biomass of each creature, quantitative biologists spent three years combing the scientific literature. – A 42-year-old South African man lost both legs to a great white shark today after ignoring warnings to stay out of the water at a Cape Town beach, the Telegraph reports. Michael Cohen, a British citizen born in Canada, was swimming about 50 yards from shore at Fish Hoek beach when the shark attacked. "It repeatedly bit at both of his legs and caused serious wounds on both the right and left side," a spokesman for the National Sea Rescue Institute tells the Telegraph. "When medical teams arrived, the found the swimmer with his right leg bit off above the knee and the left leg bit off below the knee," he says. "The man was conscious when paramedics attended to him on the beach, but was sedated on-scene by paramedics in their efforts to stabilize the patient." A shark warning flag was raised and a siren sounded, but it didn't go off because there was a power cut in the area. Cohen is in critical condition in the hospital.

– Today is National Equal Pay Day, and President Obama is marking it with two executive actions that he says will close the wage gap between men and women. One will make federal contractors disclose how they pay their employees, and the other will forbid retaliating against workers who discuss their salaries with one another, the Washington Post reports. "Unfortunately, pay inequity is a real and persistent problem that continues to shortchange women, their families, and our economy as a whole," Valerie Jarrett, the White House's senior adviser on women's issues, said yesterday. "What we do know is there are more things we can do to close that gap." The executive actions are part of a broader effort by the White House to get more female voters to turn out for the midterm elections, the Post notes. The executive actions don't apply to private sector employers, the New York Times reports, but the legislation they're based on—the Paycheck Fairness Act—has already failed to pass Congress twice. "What we really need is for Congress to pass the Fair Paycheck Act, which would get at all workers," an employment advocate tells Al Jazeera.

The White House says China has cut tariffs on $200 billion in goods and services, which Trump blames for rising trade tensions, the Wall Street Journal reports. Trump says the move is a response to China's "theft of our intellectual property" and a move that shows the Trump administration is "unwavering in our commitment to free trade." The White House says Trump has been briefed on the situation, though it's not clear whether he has been briefed on the specifics of the trade fight. "We're trying to do the best we can with what we have," Trump said in a recent interview with Fox News. "We're trying to get the best deal for the American people." (China has threatened to retaliate against the US if it slaps tariffs on Chinese goods.)

McCartney filed a lawsuit in New York against the music giant on Tuesday, Reuters reports. He says he signed a contract with Sony/ATV in 1962 that gave him ownership of songs co-written by him and John Lennon. He says he transferred the rights to those songs to various music publishers between 1962 and 1971 and is entitled to them back under the 1976 Copyright Act. McCartney says Sony/ATV has been refusing to confirm or deny his termination rights, and he wants a declaratory judgment that he will soon get his rights back. The lawsuit states McCartney has been serving termination notices for nearly a decade and expects to get his rights back by Oct. 5. Sony chairman Martin Bandier has been conversing directly on this issue, and the defendant has retained attorney Donald Zakarin for its legal defense.

The man, who had a gun and threatened to commit suicide, died "apparently by his own hand" after a SWAT team entered a Verizon Wireless store in La Crescenta last night, police say. The incident began around 4pm yesterday, when the man walked into the Rite Aid pharmacy and demanded a prescription, NBC Los Angeles reports. When a worker gave him the pills he wanted, the man ran from the store. Nobody was injured in the incident, and the shopping center, which also houses a Ralphs, Rite Aid, US Bank, and Starbucks, was evacuated as a precaution.

– Janet Yellen's first press conference as Fed chief didn't go well for her. When she was asked what the Fed meant by "a considerable time" after its bond purchases end, she said, "This is the kind of term it's hard to define," reports MarketWatch. "But, you know, probably means something on the order of around six months, that type of thing." The markets quickly sold off, and the Wall Street Journal notes that Yellen's phrasing "sent equity markets into something of a tailspin." It's a "gaffe," writes Michael Wallace at Action Economics, and Yellen should have known that. "The Fed has always loosely defined 'considerable period' as about half a year," he writes. "It's supposed to be a little vague. She probably didn't intend to give any hints about timing beyond what the 'dot plot' said. Now that she's leading the Fed, the markets will react to what she said, not what she means." It's up to Yellen and her colleagues to walk this back, if they don't like what the market heard.
